skeptic: 'Cannot, like a circle cannot have corners' confuses a logical ideal with sociology. Movements centralize all the time. Say 'must not,' and admit the risk.
clinician: Strong, clear claim.
habit: Punchy and clear. Fine as a principle.
contemplative: Clear, but 'Not should not — cannot' is sharp, like a fist. A circle without corners says it softly enough.
stress: 'Cannot, like a circle and corners': history says every movement grows a hierarchy. Logic doesn't stop sociology. Plan for capture.
gamedesigner: Circle-without-corners is crisp and bold. A good beat.
structural: An emphatic restatement. The circle-corners analogy is cute and proves nothing.
satirist: 'Cannot, as a circle cannot have corners' is a bold claim. Bokonon arranged his own outlawing; this just asserts structural immunity. History disagrees.
mythmaker: 'A circle cannot have corners' is crisp and quotable. Good.

modeler: A definitional circle-and-corners line, fine. It's an analogy, though; say what feedback breaks when a center is imposed.
skeptic: Lovely, and true by definition only. A metaphor standing in for an argument. Give the mechanism.
clinician: A neat circle image about authority. Conceptual, with nothing for a reader on a bad day.
habit: Circle without corners is a clean, sticky image. It's a principle, not a practice.
contemplative: The circle with corners is clean. The second half is clever, a little proud. One sentence would hold it.
stress: Unfalsifiable by definition, a no-true-Scotsman built in. Say what happens when followers add the corners anyway.
gamedesigner: Circle-without-corners is clean and memorable. Lands as a rule, but there's no move for me.
structural: A neat geometric aphorism on decentralization. It describes a belief system's shape, not anyone's leverage.
satirist: Circle with corners is a clean image. Bokonon outlawed himself. This at least declares itself un-popeable. Respectable.
mythmaker: Circles and corners is a memorable image, but a bit glib. Show one community adding corners and what it cost them.

modeler: Circle and corners is metaphor as proof. Say structurally why central control breaks local-rule emergence.
skeptic: True by definition, so it's unfalsifiable. The analogy persuades by fluency. The 'who decides meaning' test is the only part a reader can use.
clinician: The circle and square idea is memorable. 'Who gets to say what your patterns mean' is a useful test.
habit: Circle and corners is memorable. 'Who gets to say what your patterns mean' could become a test the reader actually runs.
contemplative: The circle and corners is a little too pleased with itself. The last clause, who says what your patterns mean, is the true part.
stress: Real falsifier: watch who claims to say what your patterns mean. Circle/square image holds under strain.
gamedesigner: Circle and corners is memorable, and 'who gets to say' is a usable test. Needs an example.
structural: 'Who gets to say what your patterns mean' is the right question to ask of power. It's aimed only at the book itself.
satirist: Circle-with-corners is clever and the 'who decides what your patterns mean' test is real. A bit pleased with itself.
mythmaker: A circle with corners added is a fine image. 'Who gets to say what your patterns mean' points at a villain we never see.

modeler: Circle with corners: a structural constraint with a test. Who says what it means? Crisp. A limit named, not a loop, but it's a real boundary.
skeptic: Falsifiable single test, who says what your patterns mean. Bold typeface is overconfident, and the circle-corners analogy is cute rather than argued.
clinician: One question gives the reader a usable test against coercive meaning-makers. Protects the reader. Circle/square image is clear.
habit: One question, who gets to say what your patterns mean?, is a real test. Circle and corners make it stick.
contemplative: The question is good and practical. The circle, corners and square are cleverness standing in front of it. Ask the question.
stress: Gives a one-question test anyone can fail the book on. Bold, but the author pays if wrong. Keep.
gamedesigner: A single test question I can run: who says what it means? Clean rule with a feedback signal. Circle metaphor lands.
structural: Finally a rule about authority: who decides meaning. Good test. But it governs the book's own hierarchy only; fatalism-adjacent about outside power. Extend to institutions.
satirist: Circle-with-corners is a strained image, but the one-question test is usable, and it names the failure mode. Drop the bold shouting.
mythmaker: Circle with corners becomes a square wearing the circle's name: an image I'll remember, with a one-question test. Bold, blunt, and the stakes are mine.

modeler: Self-consistency argument holds at the level of interpretation. Fine.
skeptic: The logic is neat. Self-refuting frameworks get organized anyway, constantly. What safeguard exists beyond the argument?
clinician: Clean argument.
habit: A clean argument for no designer. Abstract, but tight.
contemplative: Sound reasoning. 'Charming fact about ferns' scores a point. Remove it.
stress: Self-refutation as a defense is clever and fragile. Movements don't stop when they contradict themselves. Add safeguards, not syllogisms.
gamedesigner: Clear logic for why it can't have a center. Fine.
structural: Self-refutation is a neat argument. Yet human institutions run on designed rules too. The framework underplays that.
satirist: A clear argument. A movement claiming it can't have a pope is precisely when one shows up. Acknowledge that risk.
mythmaker: The self-refutation logic is sound and clear. The argument has no one in it who wants to be in charge.

modeler: Clean structural argument: a designer slot contradicts designerless emergence. Nice self-test. Name the limiting loop that keeps chair-seekers out, though.
skeptic: Useful self-refuting test for spotting gurus, author included. 'Always turns up' is overconfident; 'usually' would cost nothing.
clinician: Protective: hands readers a test for gurus, author included. A safeguard I'd want vulnerable readers to have. Keep.
habit: Sharp self-refutation argument. The spot-the-chair test is close to useful; make it a cue: next time someone explains your pattern, ask this.
contemplative: A true point, said twice. 'Refute itself' and 'easy to spot' cover the same ground. Keep the last sentence, trim the middle.
stress: Good: names its own failure mode and the author's. A self-refuting guru test that actually catches people. Keeps skin in.
gamedesigner: Strong rule with a built-in detector: anyone claiming the last word has left. That's a playable check. Plays well.
structural: Rare case where the book spots who grabs the chair. But spotting them isn't stopping them. Name a rule that keeps the seat empty.
satirist: A built-in cult detector that also covers the author. Bokonon would approve. Cut 'Skeins'; nobody at the bar knows what it means.
mythmaker: Sharp self-refuting logic, but 'the person who wants the chair' needs a face. Show one guru taking the seat.

modeler: Transition.
skeptic: A transition.
clinician: Transitional.
habit: Bridge.
contemplative: A plain bridge. Fine.
stress: Bridge.
gamedesigner: Connective line.
structural: A connective.
satirist: Connective. Fine.
mythmaker: A hinge line, and fine as one.

modeler: Pure hinge sentence. Fine as plumbing; carries no machinery of its own.
skeptic: Pure signpost. 'The structure has no seat' asserts what the previous paragraph argued; it adds nothing of its own.
clinician: Pure hinge. Fine in place, but it promises things handed back without giving any here.
habit: Clean hinge, but it's just a hinge. Fine in place, and it earns nothing on its own.
contemplative: A hinge sentence. 'Not out of modesty' is a little defensive. Join it to what follows, or let it go.
stress: Hinge sentence. Clear, but it promises three things and earns nothing until they arrive.
gamedesigner: Loading screen. Clear, but I do nothing here. Fold it into the first of the three items.
structural: Transition. 'No seat for one' was already argued above. This only points ahead.
satirist: A plain hinge sentence. 'The structure has no seat for one' is the one good phrase. Fine for what it does, but it earns nothing on its own.
mythmaker: A hinge sentence, and it does its job. Nothing here to remember.

modeler: A transition with a nice line. It earns little alone.
skeptic: Transition with a nice line. Nothing to score beyond clarity.
clinician: Handing authority back is safe and dignifying. It's a transition, though.
habit: A setup line. It promises things handed back, so make sure the next three deliver actions.
contemplative: 'No one here gets to tell you what your life means.' Gentle and freeing. Short enough.
stress: 'Not out of modesty: structure has no seat' is clean. Transitional, fine.
gamedesigner: Short, clear, hands agency back. Transitional but warm.
structural: Transition that hands things back to you, singular.
satirist: 'The structure has no seat for one' is good. The rest is throat-clearing before a list.
mythmaker: 'No seat for one' is a good line, and it hands the reader back their life. A short bridge.

modeler: 'The structure has no seat for one' is a design claim, good. Promises three hand-backs. Setup line, thin by itself.
skeptic: 'The structure has no seat for one' is a claim about the book's design, which is checkable. 'Each hands something back to you' is a promise, not support.
clinician: Returns authority over meaning to the reader; 'each hands something back' is protective. Short, promises concrete results below.
habit: Warm, hands the reader something back. But 'three things follow' is a promise, not a rep. Give the first.
contemplative: 'No one gets to tell you what your life means.' Warm and plain. 'Structure has no seat' is decoration.
stress: 'Structure has no seat for one' is tidy but asserted. Promises three gifts, shows none. Needs the list.
gamedesigner: Promise that I keep authorship of my life's meaning resonates. But 'three things follow' is a tease; I want them now.
structural: 'No seat for one' is a structural claim, welcome. Yet it frees the reader privately while silent on who actually tells people what their lives mean.
satirist: 'The structure has no seat for one' is plain and good. But it only promises three things; deliver them, don't announce them.
mythmaker: 'The structure has no seat for one' is a good line. But it's a pivot to a list, and it's still telling me what I get.

modeler: Structural claim, no seat for the authority, is stated but not shown. Draw the structure. Resonates, doesn't explain.
skeptic: Refusing authority over the reader's meaning fits Lowery's self-in-relation view. 'The structure has no seat' is asserted, not shown.
clinician: No one gets to tell you what your life means: autonomy returned, no blame. Strong. Make the three gifts concrete.
habit: 'Hands something back to you' is the right direction: agency to the reader. Needs the three things to be actions, not conclusions.
contemplative: 'No seat for anyone' returns my life to me. Gentle and true. 'That isn't modesty' is a small defense.
stress: Nice give-back, but 'the structure has no seat' is asserted, not shown. Name how this would fail.
gamedesigner: Gives agency back to the reader, which feels good. But it's a lead-in with nothing to do yet.
structural: No seat for an authority is a structural claim I can respect. Hands the reader something. Name the rule, though.
satirist: 'No seat for anyone to do it' is a nice refusal of guru status. But 'the structure' is doing mystery work, and three things follow as a trailer.
mythmaker: 'No seat for anyone to do it' is a strong, human stake: nobody gets to author your life. Then it hands things back. Direct and warm.

modeler: Practical protection against guru capture. No mechanism, but it doesn't claim one.
skeptic: A good guard against gurus. But it privileges introspection, and others often read us better than we read ourselves. Your own self chapter says so.
clinician: Protects vulnerable readers from anyone weaponizing the vocabulary. Essential.
habit: A practical defence against anyone misusing the vocabulary on you. Usable.
contemplative: Protective and freeing: an angle, not a verdict. This guards the reader from harm. Keep.
stress: A practical anti-guru test: anyone who settles your pattern for you has left the practice. Usable red flag.
gamedesigner: It gives me a test: if someone expects their read to settle it, they've stopped practicing. That's a usable signal.
structural: Your reading is sovereign. Fine for meaning. Collective action needs shared readings sometimes. Say where.
satirist: A practical inoculation against gurus: anyone settling your pattern for you has stopped practicing. Useful and plain.
mythmaker: It protects the reader from gurus. Real stakes for anyone who has had a teacher overreach. Strong.

modeler: Goal displacement in groups, named. Meadows' 'seeking the wrong goal' trap. Useful.
skeptic: A practical test of whether belonging is voluntary. The Banner forward-reference is jargon. Otherwise it works.
clinician: Shame-aware: belonging you owe becomes coercion. Gives a clear test.
habit: Gives a real test for group drift: owed attendance, a defended name. Keep it.
contemplative: 'Pride, never obligation' is good medicine. The Banner aside can wait until Banner is taught.
stress: The pride-versus-obligation test is concrete and checkable against real group decay. Strong.
gamedesigner: 'Pride, never obligation' works, and it lists concrete warning signs. Banner is a forward reference I can't use yet.
structural: 'Never obligation' undercuts the dues, attendance and commitment that unions and campaigns run on. Distinguish coercion from commitment.
satirist: A real test for cultish belonging. 'Banner' is a forward-referenced coinage; drop it here.
mythmaker: 'Attendance you maintain, a name you defend': I've seen that person at church and in fandom. Honest and humane.

modeler: Voluntariness as the variable that changes the category: Suits and Sellers would agree. Good mechanism claim.
skeptic: It echoes real overjustification research. Cite it, and 'exactly the same conversion' needs softening.
clinician: Game-to-work conversion is crisp and true.
habit: 'Remove voluntary participation from a game and it becomes work.' A sharp, resonant point.
contemplative: Play becomes work when it is forced. Simple and true. Lovely.
stress: A voluntary game becoming work is a sharp, true mechanism. Good.
gamedesigner: Voluntary participation separating game from work is straight McGonigal and Suits. Love it. Tie it to a daily check.
structural: Voluntariness changing a game into work is a sharp, real mechanism. Good.
satirist: Remove choice and play becomes work. That's Tom Sawyer's fence, and it's true. Credit Twain and it sings.
mythmaker: 'Remove voluntary participation and a game becomes work' is a sharp, felt truth. Keep it.

modeler: Says 'mechanism' then gives a category change. Still a usable check: owed versus chosen. Show the flow that converts play into work.
skeptic: 'Owed rather than chosen' is a usable check. 'A mechanism, not a preference' needs the overjustification research, not Tom Sawyer.
clinician: 'Owed rather than chosen' is a usable check that stops the practice turning into another stick. Exactly right.
habit: 'Feels owed rather than chosen' is a check I can actually run. Mechanism plus test. Keep it.
contemplative: Owed or chosen? I can ask myself that tonight. Tom Sawyer carries it gently. This works.
stress: Real mechanism, plus a usable tripwire: owed versus chosen. Twain is one anecdote, but the check survives strain.
gamedesigner: Suits nailed. Gives me a live sensor too: 'owed rather than chosen.' Best feedback signal in this stretch.
structural: Obligation changing the category is a real mechanism. So who does the obliging? Employers and platforms turn play into work. Name them.
satirist: Tom Sawyer's fence earns it, and 'owed rather than chosen' is a check you can use. Drop 'a mechanism, not a preference'; it's a metaphor in a lab coat.
mythmaker: Tom at the fence gives the mechanism a face. The 'owed rather than chosen' check is one I'll actually use.

modeler: Warm, but a slogan. The leverage point is restated, not added to.
skeptic: 'Captain of your ship' contradicts U0064's world-building-you humility. Pick one.
clinician: 'Captain of your own ship' oversells control and undercuts U0064. Soften.
habit: An empowering slogan. 'Captain of your ship' is a cliché, so make it a choice the reader actually makes.
contemplative: Generous, letting the reader leave. A tired image but a warm heart.
stress: 'Captain of your own ship' is a cliché, and it contradicts the Nest's 'you are being built.' Rephrase.
gamedesigner: Permission to reject the book is real agency. Short and good.
structural: 'Captain of your own ship' is individualism's oldest slogan. Ships have owners, crews and maritime law.
satirist: 'Captain of your own ship' is a greeting-card phrase. The second sentence, that you can reject the book, is the good part.
mythmaker: 'Captain of your own ship' is a stale image. Freedom to reject the book is good; find a fresher picture.

modeler: Warm exit door, but Leverage is asserted, not modeled. Where is the reader's actual reach measured?
skeptic: Permission to leave is decent. 'Used the book correctly' is a flattering exit with nothing to measure against.
clinician: Permission to leave is kind and lowers the stakes. Jargon recap ('Leverage', 'Nest') adds nothing for a struggling reader.
habit: Warm permission. It lands personally, but nothing tells me what to do with my leverage on Monday.
contemplative: Warm and freeing. The Nest aside gets in the way. Drop it and the permission lands softer.
stress: Humble exit clause, credited. Still, permission to leave costs the author nothing. Name a sign the book failed you.
gamedesigner: Warm and freeing, but I get no move. Add one prompt: name one place your leverage actually sits.
structural: Kind permission to leave. But it treats leverage as purely private reach, with no link to anyone else's.
satirist: Telling the reader they may leave is a nice move. Capital-L Leverage and the Nest are cited like scripture on a page that says there is no scripture. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: Warm permission to quit. Leverage and Nest jargon blunt it; give me the reader closing the cover.

modeler: A measurable exit criterion: one small push that moves something. I like a framework that defines its own success.
skeptic: Permission to reject the framework, plus a concrete success criterion. Correct and rare.
clinician: Permission to put the book down, plus one small push. That's shame-free and actionable. Model passage.
habit: 'Point to one place a small push of yours moves something.' A clear success test. Love it.
contemplative: Permission to close the book. A humble test of one small push. The middle aside on the Nest is clutter.
stress: A book that lists 'decide I'm wrong' as correct use. Least ego on the page. Concrete success test. Keep.
gamedesigner: Real win condition: point to one place your push moves something. That's a scoreable exit test.
structural: 'One small push of yours' is private leverage again. Make the test a push you'd make with others.
satirist: A religion that invites you to leave: Bokonon outlawing himself. 'Leverage' capitalized for no reason; the test at the end works.
mythmaker: Permission to close the book is generous, and the test is concrete. 'Leverage turned on the book' is jargon creeping in.

modeler: Setup line.
skeptic: A setup line.
clinician: Setup.
habit: Bridge.
contemplative: Bridge line. Fine.
stress: Bridge.
gamedesigner: Setup line. Fine.
structural: A signpost.
satirist: A decent signpost.
mythmaker: A setup line that's fine.

modeler: Teaser heading. Withholds both things, so it does no work standing alone.
skeptic: A teaser naming neither thing. 'Seen into told' sounds deep, but the reader can't decode it yet. Name both up front.
clinician: Teaser header that never says what the two things are. Name them plainly or cut it.
habit: A teaser header that names neither thing. Protect what? Refuse what? Say both in plain words.
contemplative: A riddle where a heading should be. Name the two things plainly. The reader shouldn't have to solve a header.
stress: A teaser header with a riddle in it. 'Seen into told' is opaque without context. State the two things plainly.
gamedesigner: Teaser hook, but 'being seen into being told' is cryptic before the rules exist. Name both things in the header.
structural: Teaser header. The seen/told split is promised, not delivered.
satirist: A teaser that hides its own nouns. Say which thing to protect and which to refuse, right here, in plain words.
mythmaker: 'Being seen into being told' is a lovely phrase that promises a payoff. On its own it's a trailer, not a scene.

modeler: Tight chain of three claims. 'Being named is not being reduced' lands.
skeptic: 'Being named is not being reduced' is a good line. The chain rests on U0036's overstated 'exactly as real.'
clinician: 'Being named is not being reduced' is a gentle, important line.
habit: 'Being named is not being reduced.' Reassuring and clear.
contemplative: 'Being named is not being reduced.' That is the whole unit. The chain before it can shrink.
stress: 'Being named is not being reduced' lands. Fine.
gamedesigner: 'Being named is not being reduced' is a strong closer. Reassuring.
structural: A jargon syllogism defending 'you are a loop.' 'Being named is not being reduced' is the only usable line.
satirist: 'Being named is not being reduced' is good. The chain of italics before it is catechism. Lead with the plain line.
mythmaker: 'Being named is not being reduced' is a comforting, memorable line that answers the fear directly.

modeler: The is-ought guard, applied at the right scale. Good, self-similar repeat of the authority failure.
skeptic: Refusing is-to-ought is sound and well placed. A practical warning.
clinician: Refusing 'you are X therefore Y' is guilt-not-shame in action. Best passage in the Part.
habit: 'You are X, therefore you must Y' is a refusal you can actually run. Good guardrail.
contemplative: 'You are X, therefore Y' is a clear warning. The middle sentence is too long for a breath.
stress: Refusing 'you are X, therefore Y' is a real guard against weaponized labels. Excellent.
gamedesigner: The 'X therefore Y' trap is useful, but the second half drifts into abstraction. End on the trap.
structural: Refusing 'you are X, therefore Y' is a good guard against labels as verdicts. Clear.
satirist: 'You are X, therefore you must Y' refused. Clear, useful, and it guards against the book's own misuse.
mythmaker: 'You are X, therefore you must Y' is a trap every reader has been caught in. Clear and protective.

modeler: Concrete, observable test. 'Feel almost identical from inside' is honest.
skeptic: Right on Epley: we overrate our reads of others. 'Feel almost identical from inside' is honest about self-opacity. Keep it.
clinician: Small, specific, observable step. Good.
habit: A real cue: the next time you have a clear read on someone. Offer it and wait. Exactly right.
contemplative: 'Offering and waiting' is a real practice for my family table. Honest about how alike the two feel.
stress: 'Feel identical from inside': honest, and it gives the reader a self-check. Good.
gamedesigner: A real move. But 'they feel identical from inside' removes the feedback. Add an external tell, like their reply.
structural: Offering versus delivering a read is useful interpersonally. It's still a private etiquette.
satirist: 'From inside they feel almost identical.' Sharp and practical. Keep it.
mythmaker: 'From inside they feel almost identical' is an honest exercise that admits the danger. Good.

modeler: Pop epigraph. Fine for tone, adds nothing.
skeptic: A movie quote as epigraph. 'Focus determines reality' is the kind of claim I'd attack in the body.
clinician: 'Focus determines reality' flirts with 'beliefs create your reality.' Risky epigraph for a depressed reader.
habit: A fun epigraph that adds little.
contemplative: Simple. It makes sense once Qui-Gon arrives.
stress: A fictional mystic as an epigraph. Harmless, weightless.
gamedesigner: A pop-culture epigraph that sets the tone for the chapter. Fine.
structural: 'Your focus determines your reality.' Tell that to a renter facing eviction. A pure i-frame epigraph.
satirist: A Jedi epigraph in a belief-system book is either very self-aware or not at all. Credited at least.
mythmaker: Qui-Gon fits the chapter, but the line is thin on its own.

modeler: Familiar, readable epigraph. Sets mood; no mechanism expected or delivered.
skeptic: A fictional mentor's line used as an epigraph. Fine as decoration, but it carries no claim I can check.
clinician: Present-moment invitation, fine. 'Don't center on anxieties' can read as suppression; the next passage needs to show how.
habit: Good epigraph. 'Here and now' is almost a cue. It sets up the presence material well.
contemplative: Simple and kind. It asks for presence and doesn't explain it. Right where it sits.
stress: Calm-sea epigraph. Presence advice from a character who dies for it. Fine as a doorway, nothing more.
gamedesigner: Familiar voice, sets the mood. Just an epigraph, nothing to play. It does its small job.
structural: Presence over anxiety: the mindfulness alibi as an epigraph. Some anxieties are about rent, and the rent was set by someone.
satirist: A Jedi fortune cookie as an epigraph. It's readable, and a costume the book admits is a costume, but it adds nothing.
mythmaker: A beloved voice, and it sets up the Qui-Gon portrait later. It does its work here.

modeler: A franchise epigraph that adds nothing structural. Fine as flavor.
skeptic: A fictional character's line as epigraph. Harmless, but it borrows authority it hasn't earned. Fine only as a doorway to the chapter.
clinician: A fan epigraph. Harmless, earns nothing alone.
habit: 'Here and now' is the mindfulness vagueness I hate. It reads as fan service, not a cue.
contemplative: Here and now, plainly said. A film quote, but it serves presence. Fine as an epigraph.
stress: Movie quote as epigraph for a falsification chapter is thin. Use Feynman or Popper; it'd carry weight.
gamedesigner: A fun pop quote, but it does little here. Is the franchise reference doing work? Barely.
structural: Presence as an epigraph, inner work dressed as wisdom. Ask what it lets the reader skip.
satirist: Qui-Gon as scripture. Fun, but a costume worn straight. Wink at it or move it to his entry.
mythmaker: Fine Jedi epigraph. It borrows warmth it doesn't build here.

modeler: Ecclesiastes on repetition is the book's thesis in miniature: same loop, new instances. Fits. Ornament, but apt.
skeptic: Ecclesiastes as epigraph. Nice, resonant, and as a factual claim flatly wrong about novelty. Works only as mood.
clinician: Bleak on a bad day if read alone: nothing new, so why try. No frame, no step.
habit: Nice epigraph; nothing to do with it. Fine for place, not for points.
contemplative: Old, quiet, true. It sets a mood and stops.
stress: Dalio would approve: long record. Ancient, short, clear. Carries history, not argument.
gamedesigner: Ecclesiastes fits the repetition theme, easy read. Pure atmosphere; no move for the player.
structural: Ecclesiastes epigraph. Nothing new under the sun is also the fatalist's alibi. Decorative.
satirist: Ecclesiastes, the original skeptic. Wry, apt for a book about repetition. Still decoration.
mythmaker: Old, weary, true epigraph; Ecclesiastes sets the right tone for a recycled-ideas confession. It's borrowed, with no face.

modeler: Steady-state talk without a stock. Everything recurs, so where's the drift? Fine epigraph, nothing more.
skeptic: Fine epigraph; Ecclesiastes is an intuition about recurrence, not evidence for it. Pleasant, easy, thin.
clinician: Ecclesiastes can read as bleak on a bad day. Resonant for abstraction, but no step and some bypassing risk.
habit: Epigraph only. Nothing to start, no cue. Fine as decoration; I'd cut it for a one-line prompt.
contemplative: Old words, easy to take in. Beautiful. Without a practice beside it, it only sits.
stress: Ancient pessimism, fine. Hindsight dressed as wisdom unless the chapter tests it against a counterexample.
gamedesigner: Epigraph only. No hook beyond the quote, no move for me. Cut or tie to a prompt.
structural: Familiar, fits the repetition theme. Also the standard fatalist quote: nothing new, so why act? Needs a counterweight.
satirist: Ecclesiastes, deadpan. The oldest 'seen it' joke. Does no work beyond mood, but the mood is the right one.
mythmaker: Weary old voice, good counterweight to a book about newness. Nobody wearing it though. Works as an epigraph shadow, nothing more.

modeler: Reasonable check in principle, but stories are a weak test set: authors share our intuitions.
skeptic: A good test: does the framework describe anything outside its own vocabulary? Then the chapter fails that test with fiction.
clinician: Reasonable self-check framing.
habit: A reasonable framing for the chapter. Short enough.
contemplative: A fair self-check. The last clause is clever. Keep it shorter.
stress: The right test: does it work outside its own vocabulary? Then the next paragraphs use fiction, which is the weakest outside check.
gamedesigner: A reasonable framing for a recognition check. Brief enough.
structural: A sensible check against self-referential vocabulary. A setup line.
satirist: 'Describing itself' is a good self-check, stated plainly.
mythmaker: A good self-check: a framework only describing itself. A fair, honest setup.

modeler: Good falsifiability instinct: a framework describing only itself is a closed loop with no input. Keep it.
skeptic: The best kind of move: a falsification test aimed at itself. The cheap check should say what counts as a failure.
clinician: Honest self-test for the framework. Intellectually sound, emotionally neutral. Fine as a bridge.
habit: 'Cheapest test' is a good frame, but it's a test of the book, not of me. No rep in it.
contemplative: An honest test, said cleanly. The last sentence is clever and a bit pleased with itself, but it earns its place.
stress: Cheapest falsification test, offered up front. That's the right instinct. Now tell me what failing it looks like.
gamedesigner: Good move: here's a cheap test, run it. Hands me the controller before the character roster. Plays well.
structural: A good falsifiability test. It still runs inside the reader's head, not out in the world.
satirist: 'A framework that only works inside its own vocabulary describes itself' is the honest sentence of the chapter. Keep it.
mythmaker: Honest, cheap test, and a good line about vocabulary describing itself. Nobody is in the room.

modeler: A falsification test using your own life. Best paragraph here: a framework checked against outside data.
skeptic: A stated failure condition, finally. Caveat: fluent readers find pillars anywhere. Add a case where they shouldn't fit.
clinician: Honest self-test, and familiar examples. It tests the book, not the reader. Fine.
habit: The cheapest test, run on your own friend, team or show. Falsifiable and fast. Model paragraph.
contemplative: A test I can run with my friends tonight. Honest, unassuming. This is good teaching.
stress: Gives a cheap, real failure condition. This is the paragraph I came for. Keep untouched.
gamedesigner: Excellent: a cheap test with an explicit fail state. This is the feedback loop I keep asking for.
structural: A fair falsifiability test I respect. Put an institution among the test cases, not just friends and shows.
satirist: A falsification test, cheap and stated. 'Describing itself' is the Stephenson virus check. Excellent.
mythmaker: A friend who changed slowly, a team that soured. A falsifiable test with faces in it. Excellent.

modeler: Disclaiming evidence is honest. The 'independent arrival' claim is weak: writers aren't independent samples.
skeptic: The disclaimer is honest, and then 'and they are' claims confirmation from five hand-picked stories. That's selection bias, labelled.
clinician: Over-defended disclaimer. One sentence would do.
habit: A paragraph of hedging. Readers already know a TV character isn't evidence. Cut it to one line.
contemplative: It defends at length against being taken as evidence. One sentence: recognition, not proof. That is the next unit already.
stress: 'And they are' is cherry-picking. Writers get to choose their endings. Fiction can't confirm a pattern. Cut the confirmation claim.
gamedesigner: A long disclaimer before the fun part. Halve it, because I'm waiting for the characters.
structural: Honest disclaimer. Note that 'how people actually change' already assumes change is personal.
satirist: Honest that cartoons aren't evidence. But 'and they are' smuggles them back in as confirmation. Pick one.
mythmaker: Over-lawyered disclaimer that drains warmth before the stories arrive. Cut it to one sentence.

modeler: Honest about cherry-picked endings. Rare and welcome. Points to Part Four for the real derivation.
skeptic: Admirably calibrated: stories are selected, not evidence. 'Derived from mathematics' oversells; Part Four offers analogy, not derivation.
clinician: Admirably honest about cherry-picked stories. That's epistemics, not help, but it earns trust.
habit: Honest about stories not being evidence. It's intellectually tidy and gives me zero behaviour.
contemplative: Hedges piled up out of fear. One sentence saying these are recognition, not proof, would do the job.
stress: Rare honesty: admits stories are rigged to fit. Disarms hindsight bias before it starts. Keep it.
gamedesigner: An honest disclaimer, but it's rules-lawyering ahead of the fun. Trim it to two lines so the characters arrive sooner.
structural: Honest that stories prove nothing. I respect it. It gives the reader nothing to pull.
satirist: It admits the stories are rigged to fit. That's a shameless-lies preface done right, and it's rare honesty for a belief system.
mythmaker: Admirable honesty about stories proving their heroes. It's still a disclaimer, not a moment.

modeler: It correctly refuses to derive anything from stories. Epistemically clean.
skeptic: 'A writer can always hand a character the ending' says exactly what a skeptic wants said. Excellent epistemic hygiene.
clinician: Intellectually honest disclaimer. Nothing for a person in pain.
habit: Intellectually honest disclaimer. Necessary, but it gives the reader nothing to do.
contemplative: Defensive, guarding against a critic. It is honest but it fights. One sentence would do.
stress: 'A writer can hand a character the ending' — honest about narrative's rigged dice. Strong.
gamedesigner: Honest disclaimer, but it's pure rules-lawyering. Fold it into U0088.
structural: Admirably candid that stories prove nothing. That credibility is earned.
satirist: 'A writer can always hand a character the ending' is the honest sentence most invented religions never write.
mythmaker: 'A writer can hand a character the ending that proves them right.' Honest, and that's rare courage. Dry, though.

modeler: Says the pillars don't derive from stories and that a writer can rig the ending. Excellent epistemic hygiene. Stories as illustration, not evidence.
skeptic: Exactly my rule: separates anecdote from evidence, admits authors can hand characters the ending. Strong. Slightly overclaims that pillars 'would stand' without stating a test.
clinician: Honest disclaimer that stories prove nothing. Protects against false evidence. Plain and trustworthy.
habit: Honest disclaimer about what the stories prove. Works for trust, but it's all caveat and no action.
contemplative: Honest and impeccable about its own stories. It does not yet ask anything of me.
stress: Stories prove nothing: author disarms own evidence. Rare ego discipline. Hindsight can't be sold here.
gamedesigner: Clear disclaimer that stories aren't proof. Honest, but it only lectures; no action here.
structural: Admirably disclaims stories as proof. Fine epistemic hygiene, structurally neutral. Concrete value: tells reader what to trust.
satirist: Tells me the stories prove nothing. A handbook saying that is rare, and clears the circular-evidence trap. Bokonon would approve.
mythmaker: Admitting the stories prove nothing because a writer can hand a character the ending: that's the Beard in the room. Honest, disarming, and it respects me.

modeler: Separating mechanism from illustration is exactly right. Pillars stand on math, stories only illustrate. I'd applaud this.
skeptic: Exactly the move I want: stories are not evidence, a writer can rig endings. Asks recognition, not belief. Rare epistemic honesty.
clinician: 'Ask whether you recognize them' invites recognition not self-judgment. Honest framing; no action but safe.
habit: Ends on one question: do you recognize them? That's the single carry-around question I like. Clear instruction on how to read.
contemplative: 'Ask whether you recognize them.' Impeccable and humble. It tells me how to read. The middle argues a little.
stress: Rare: the author admits stories prove nothing and the pillars survive without them. Real skin. Keep.
gamedesigner: Great reframe: recognize, don't be convinced. That's a feedback signal I can actually use. Still no action.
structural: Candid about stories proving nothing; 'do you recognize them' resonates. But recognition without an owner or lever is mood.
satirist: 'A writer can always hand a character the ending that proves them right.' That is Vonnegut-level honesty. Foma labeled as foma. Ask whether you recognize them: lovely.
mythmaker: Admits a writer can hand a character the ending that proves them right. That's the Beard in the room. 'Do you recognize them?' is a real invitation.

modeler: Transition.
skeptic: A transition.
clinician: Setup.
habit: Bridge.
contemplative: It does the framing that U0087 overworked. Keep this one and cut that.
stress: Bridge.
gamedesigner: Bridge line.
structural: A setup line.
satirist: Fine signpost.
mythmaker: A roster line, and fine as one.

modeler: Recognition, not evidence: fair framing. Short setup, mostly a roster.
skeptic: 'Recognition, not evidence' is honest framing. The question it asks the reader is well chosen.
clinician: 'Do you know someone like them' invites recognition gently. Short hinge, does its job.
habit: One question, then it stops: 'do you know someone like them?' That's how you ask. Short and fine.
contemplative: 'Do you know someone like them?' is a gentle question. It already says what U0087 says. Keep this one and cut that.
stress: Recognition, not evidence: the right framing. Thin on its own, but it does its job as a transition.
gamedesigner: Sets a clear goal: do you know someone like this? That's a recognition game. Short and fine.
structural: Framing line. Doesn't earn anything on its own.
satirist: A traffic sign. 'Recognition, not evidence' just repeats the paragraph before it. Fold it into U0087.
mythmaker: 'Do you know someone like them?' is the right question. It points me at my own people.

modeler: A simple recognition prompt with a clear question. Serviceable.
skeptic: Recognition, not evidence, framed as a usable question. Clear and well calibrated.
clinician: 'Who in my life is like this' is a gentle, outward question. It doesn't feed rumination.
habit: One question: who in my life is like this? Exactly one. Bungay Stanier would approve.
contemplative: 'Who in my life is like this?' is the right question. The tally after it is bookkeeping.
stress: Recognition-not-evidence, restated. Necessary framing; slight repetition with U0010.
gamedesigner: 'Who in my life is like this?' is a real prompt. Good framing, light payload.
structural: Recognition is personal only. Also ask which institution is like this.
satirist: 'Who in my life is like this?' Simple, personal. Fine bridge.
mythmaker: 'Who in my own life is like this?' is the right question to set before the gallery.

modeler: One question per character: who in your life? A usable prompt, plainly stated. It's a recognition exercise, not systems content.
skeptic: 'Recognition, not evidence' is the right label, and the question is a usable prompt. Good. 'Who in my life' presumes I read others accurately.
clinician: One question per character: who in my life is like this? Outward-facing, not self-scrutiny. Small usable prompt.
habit: One question per character: who in my life is like this? Exactly right. Ask it, then stop.
contemplative: 'Who in my own life is like this?' I could ask that in my kitchen. Simple.
stress: Recognition not evidence, plus a question to carry. Honest framing. Good.
gamedesigner: Gives me a move: ask who in my life is like this. Recognition as gameplay. Good.
structural: 'Who in my life is like this?' is a usable prompt, but it's character-spotting, not system-spotting. Ask whose rules shaped them.
satirist: 'Who in my own life is like this?' is an actual question a reader can answer. Recognition, not evidence: said straight.
mythmaker: 'Who in my own life is like this?' is the right question: faces first. Five characters is a solid cast list. Short.

modeler: Fusion is metaphor dressed as mechanism. Repeated seeing is the real loop, so name what accumulates in the other person.
skeptic: It resonates only for fans. 'The most honest depiction available' of relationships is a critic's enthusiasm, not a finding. Trim it.
clinician: 'Can't fix people by force, only by seeing them' lands warmly. Long; trim.
habit: 'Shows up, and shows up again' is the habit in story form. Give the Seeding rep a cue.
contemplative: 'He shows up, and shows up again.' Beautiful. The fusion explanation runs long before reaching it.
stress: Heartfelt but long, and it proves nothing. Trim it to the 'shows up again' core.
gamedesigner: Fusion as the Third Thing is a great fit for fans. Long. Close with a challenge: who am I fused with?
structural: Steven fixes people by seeing them. Inner work as social change. The Gems' empire goes unaddressed by method.
satirist: Fusion as a relationship really fits. 'Seeding... a word planted in someone else's field' is unexplained jargon; cut the practice tag.
mythmaker: Finally a face. Steven showing up again and again is true to the show. Give one specific scene, though: Lapis, Spinel.

modeler: The goldfish reset is a good interrupt of a reinforcing spiral. Locker-room change shows accumulation. Charming, light.
skeptic: Admitting Ted can't apply it to himself is the honest note. The goldfish image lands.
clinician: Goldfish reset is usable, and naming Ted's own anxiety avoids bypassing. Strong.
habit: Be a goldfish. That's a two-second reset anyone can run after a mistake. The best character sketch here.
contemplative: The goldfish is small, warm and usable on a bad day. The honesty about Ted's anxiety is gentle.
stress: Points for admitting Ted can't apply it to himself. That's the honest beat. Trim the rest.
gamedesigner: The goldfish reset is a usable move after any mistake. It's the most playable of the five.
structural: Ted is the boss. He changed the culture because he controlled the structure. The book misses that.
satirist: The goldfish is a real laugh, and the honesty about Ted's panic attacks earns trust. The pillar labels feel like merit badges.
mythmaker: The goldfish, plus Ted's own panic attacks. There's the Beard in the room, doubting him. Earned and humane.

modeler: Goldfish as a reset drain on the grudge stock works. 'Push near the root reaches every leaf' is a real tree claim. Good.
skeptic: Concrete practice, and it admits fluency doesn't carry over to the self. 'Nobody can point to the moment' is the fiction's licence, not data.
clinician: Best unit here: names panic attacks honestly, admits it's hard to apply to yourself, gives a real-time practice. No bypassing.
habit: Goldfish, small daily kindness, catch the spiral and choose the next rep. Cue plus action. Best of the five.
contemplative: Be a goldfish. Small kindness, repeated. His panic attacks keep it honest. Lovely. The lines about the coach's position could go.
stress: Earns it by showing Ted's panic attacks: the framework strains on its own champion. The goldfish is usable.
gamedesigner: Goldfish is a perfect reset mechanic, the practice gets named, and the panic attacks add stakes. The level works.
structural: Admitting the coach's position matters is the s-frame showing through. Then it shrinks back to private kindness.
satirist: The goldfish, the panic attacks, kindness repeated until a locker room changes shape: plain and funny. The italic tag at the end is extra liturgy you could cut.
mythmaker: Goldfish, the panic attacks, the marriage on replay. Face, cost and turn are all here. Best unit in the set.

modeler: 'Nest' here only rhymes: a bigger identity isn't one scale nesting inside another. Befriending-as-method is the stronger part.
skeptic: An obscure reference for most readers. 'A working hypothesis applied even when it fails' is a nice phrase.
clinician: Identity as expansion, not betrayal: reassuring. Practice mention is too vague.
habit: Nice expansion idea, but long, and the practice it names stays vague. Trim it.
contemplative: Befriending is a warm method. Too many words and clauses. Trim to the friendship and the expansion.
stress: 'A working hypothesis applied even when it fails' is unfalsifiable optimism. When does the hypothesis lose?
gamedesigner: A less familiar show. The Nest point is fine but generic. Give me Kipo's move in one concrete scene.
structural: 'Make friends with it' as a theory of how systems change. Optimism isn't a mechanism. Cut or qualify.
satirist: A lesser-known show and a looser fit. 'Local Step / Global Form breath' is undefined jargon. Trim it or cut the entry.
mythmaker: Kipo befriending the 'enemies by category' is lovely. Expansion, not betrayal, rings true. Name one Mute she turns.

modeler: 'Same self at bigger scale' only rhymes. What repeats, at what ratio? Befriending loop is nice but unnamed.
skeptic: 'A larger self' revealed is a true-self story under another name. The befriended villain is the writer's choice, not a finding.
clinician: Nice expansion-not-betrayal framing, but 'trust it builds something larger' is a vague try. Give one concrete curiosity move.
habit: 'Meet what's in front of you with curiosity' is too vague to start. When? Give me the first move with a stranger.
contemplative: Befriending instead of conquering is beautiful. The practice line is dense with jargon. Say 'meet it with curiosity' and stop.
stress: 'Trust that it builds something larger' is fragile comfort. Befriending everyone works because the writers said so. Show a cost.
gamedesigner: Niche reference, and 'meet with curiosity' gives me no feedback signal. Say what success looks like after one encounter.
structural: Befriending the enemy one encounter at a time, while the tyranny's structure goes unexamined. Pure i-frame.
satirist: A plot summary, then 'Local Step / Global Form Breath'. It needs one specific friendship scene, not the mandrill's résumé.
mythmaker: Befriending Scarlemagne earns it. The practice tag at the end turns back into a manual; cut the jargon.

modeler: The 'one honest question' practice is concrete. Kipo as Nest is closer to growth than self-similarity, but acceptable.
skeptic: 'Much larger self' flirts with the hidden-true-self trope. The one-honest-question practice is the real value. Lead with that.
clinician: Concrete step. But 'ask the enemy one question' needs a safety caveat for abusive people. Add one.
habit: 'Ask it one honest question before deciding what it is' is a real rep. The undefined 'Breath' jargon is friction.
contemplative: 'Ask it one honest question' is beautiful practice. It is buried under plot summary and framework names. Begin there.
stress: Long plot recap, then a good practice ('one honest question'). Cut the summary by half; the practice is the value.
gamedesigner: Kipo is charming, and the 'ask one question' move plus its success test is great. Lore overload for non-viewers.
structural: Befriending enemies one at a time, against categorical hatred. Coalition-building is in there. Say it outright.
satirist: The 'one honest question before deciding what it is' practice is real. The plot recap runs long; trim Scarlemagne.
mythmaker: Kipo befriending Scarlemagne: the villain treated as a person, Sechrist's courtesy. An honest question to an 'enemy' is a real practice.

modeler: Kipo as nested self works: friend-making repeated at each encounter, a local step that accumulates. Practice is concrete. Lovely, the Scarlemagne turn is the loop closing.
skeptic: Practice is modest: one question, count one fact learned. But Kipo as proof of the Nest is story, and Epley would doubt the safe-distance encounter works.
clinician: Strong: a small step (one honest question from safe distance; leave knowing one thing more). Bounded and non-shaming.
habit: Good: ask the 'enemy' one honest question from a distance. Cue is clear, success is defined. A real rep.
contemplative: A kind practice sits inside: ask one honest question. But summary, pillar and instruction crowd together. Divide it.
stress: Practice is small and cheap: one honest question from safe distance. Low downside. Fiction still flatters Kipo, but flagged.
gamedesigner: Strong: character, practice, and a success signal ('leave knowing one thing more'). Feedback and agency both present.
structural: Befriending enemies one encounter at a time is organizing-adjacent, relational. But 'safe distance' and filed-as-enemy dodge real adversaries with power. Name when that fails.
satirist: Kipo befriending enemies is a concrete practice. But 'Local Step / Global Form Breath' cited from Part Two is invented authority. Say what to do.
mythmaker: Kipo befriending Scarlemagne is a true image, and the practice is one honest question from a safe distance. Concrete, warm, and I like the small win condition.

modeler: Survivorship caveat ('a story gets to confirm its protagonist') is exactly right. Best of the five.
skeptic: 'A story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' That's the best sentence in the chapter. Outcome bias named exactly.
clinician: Honest caveat is good, but the paragraph is jargon-laden and cold.
habit: Overloaded with Standpoint vocabulary. The honest caveat is good. Too long for a recognition sketch.
contemplative: The honest caveat is admirable. The pillar mapping in italics turns a teacher into a diagram. Let presence stay presence.
stress: 'A story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' The best line here: hindsight named outright. Keep it and apply it to all five.
gamedesigner: The honest caveat is good, but the paragraph muddles Standpoint, Perspective and Leverage together. Too many labels.
structural: The caveat that 'a story gets to confirm its protagonist' is honest and good. The paragraph is overstuffed.
satirist: 'A story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' The best line in the chapter. Vonnegut would nod.
mythmaker: 'A story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' Brilliant honesty. The rest is summary; show Anakin's podrace bet.

modeler: Survivorship caveat is excellent: the story confirms its hero, you don't get that. Leverage judgments failing on noise, well flagged.
skeptic: 'A story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' Excellent. The rest is mapping characters to pillars, which proves nothing.
clinician: Jargon pile-up (Standpoint, Third Thing, Leverage). The closing warning is good; bury less of it under terminology.
habit: Pillar-mapping jargon, 'Presence is Perspective kept honest', buries the point. The noise warning is good but has no practice.
contemplative: It starts with presence and ends as a lecture about leverage. The warning is wise, but the labels bury the teacher.
stress: The closing caveat saves it: the same conviction aimed at noise is how leverage fails. Give the reader a test for noise.
gamedesigner: Difficulty spike: Third Thing, Standpoint, Perspective and Leverage all in one paragraph. Lost the player. The final caveat is great; keep that.
structural: Flagging vindication bias is sharp. The Council is an institution, so ask whose rules it was protecting.
satirist: 'A story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' That line is excellent, and it's buried under Standpoint, Perspective, Leverage and Third Thing. Dig it out.
mythmaker: Podrace boy, refusing Council, and a real sting: 'A story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' Earned.

modeler: Signal versus noise feeling identical from inside is real survivorship-bias honesty. Excellent caveat.
skeptic: 'A story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' The best sentence here: noise and signal feel identical from inside.
clinician: The honest caution about noise is valuable. The pillar vocabulary makes it hard to follow. Plain it out.
habit: The self-critique is smart: stories confirm protagonists. But I'm left with a warning and no check to run.
contemplative: The warning is wise but it argues in a knot. Presence turns into analysis. Say plainly: conviction feels the same when it's wrong.
stress: Best character note: 'a story confirms its protagonist. You don't.' Names the luck problem directly. Keep.
gamedesigner: The noise-feels-identical warning is the sharpest idea here. It's buried under Perspective/Leverage jargon and plot.
structural: Good self-correction on survivorship bias. Defying a Council is the structural moment, and it's left unexamined.
satirist: 'A story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' Gorgeous self-puncture. That's the whole Satirist's case, made by the defendant.
mythmaker: The warning about conviction aimed at noise is bracing. The Perspective/Leverage labels drown Qui-Gon. Let the boy and the Council carry it.

modeler: Best passage here: conviction feels identical when wrong. That is a missing balancing loop named outright. A story confirms its hero; you don't. Superb.
skeptic: Superb. 'Conviction feels the same when it's wrong... a story gets to confirm its protagonist. You don't.' This is my whole argument, said in the book.
clinician: Candid that conviction feels the same when wrong; 'a story confirms its protagonist, you don't.' Protects the reader from self-trust errors.
habit: Strong warning that conviction feels the same when wrong. Great honesty, but no step. How do I check a signal?
contemplative: 'You don't' gets a gentle sting. Too many layers: presence, leverage, conviction, noise. Choose one.
stress: Best passage here. 'Conviction feels the same when it's wrong.' A story confirms its hero; you don't. Real stress test.
gamedesigner: Love the self-warning that conviction feels identical when wrong. Honest. But no test I can run to tell signal from noise.
structural: Strong: admits conviction feels identical when wrong. But the signal is a Council refusing to train; the institution is the obstacle and goes unexamined.
satirist: Warns that conviction feels the same when wrong; a story gets to confirm its hero, you don't. Best sentence in the set.
mythmaker: Best of the lot: Qui-Gon's podrace bet, then the cold turn: conviction feels the same when wrong. A story gets to confirm its protagonist; you don't. Stakes and doubt.

modeler: Moving, but 'all of it' explains nothing. Pick one loop in Iroh and trace it.
skeptic: Iroh is moving and widely known. 'Failure as the beginning of honor' resonates. Still recognition, not evidence, and too long.
clinician: Grief tended, not resolved by epiphany. Worth not measured by one outcome. Anti-bypass, anti-shame. Keep.
habit: Tending grief like tending tea, as one discipline. A daily ritual you can picture. Strong.
contemplative: Tea and grief tended as one discipline: deeply lived. The jargon at the end spoils the tea. Cut the italics.
stress: Moving, but hagiography. Iroh is written to be right. Shorten it.
gamedesigner: Iroh's tea as the practice is warm and memorable. Failure as the beginning of honor resonates.
structural: Iroh's patience is lovely and entirely private. Resisting a rigid hierarchy by being gentle inside it changes nothing.
satirist: Iroh is lovely and well observed. 'Embodies: all of it, integrated' is fan-wiki voice. Let the tea speak.
mythmaker: Iroh tending grief like tea is the best image in the chapter. 'Leaves from the Vine' would seal it.

modeler: Moving, and it admits 'mercy instead of mechanism.' Honest, but it's portrait, not model.
skeptic: Moving, and I have no reason to believe it. 'Everything above, no longer separable' is fluency doing the work of argument.
clinician: Grief tended, not fixed; worth not measured by one outcome. Shame-aware and beautiful. Missing the reader's own small step.
habit: Tea as a ritual is the right image. Tell me my tea: one daily act I'd repeat after a failure.
contemplative: Tea under the tree, the song for his son. This is lived, not argued. Leave out the Fractal Resistance label.
stress: Moving, and grief left unresolved is honest. 'Embodies everything' is grandiose labeling; let Iroh carry one pillar.
gamedesigner: Iroh lands emotionally. Tea plus song is a vivid ritual. The trailing jargon dump weakens it; give one concrete move instead.
structural: Resistance inside a hierarchy gets mentioned, then turned into tea. Endurance stands in for organizing.
satirist: The tea and 'Leaves from the Vine' land hard. 'Fractal Resistance lived for years' is a capitalized Concept doing nothing. Let Iroh speak plainly.
mythmaker: Iroh under the tree singing 'Leaves from the Vine': an image I'll keep. Tea and grief as one discipline, paid for.

modeler: Moving, but long and pure character study. No loop drawn beyond 'repeat'. Trim it.
skeptic: Moving. But 'what the pillars look like lived' uses the story as evidence, against Chapter 87's own rule. Keep the final question, trim the claim.
clinician: Grief tended, not fixed. Failure as where honour begins. Then a small act after failing. This is the book at its safest.
habit: 'Whatever small act you'd still repeat the morning after a failure.' Cue and rep. Long, but it earns it.
contemplative: Iroh's tea and grief: this is beautiful, and it is too much. The jargon in the italics spoils it. End at 'repeat the morning after a failure.'
stress: Moving, but no stress-test like Qui-Gon's. Overloaded tag. Add: what if patience just enabled? Then it earns the place.
gamedesigner: Moving and ends on a real move. Too long, though, and stacks Fractal Resistance plus Breath. Cut it by half.
structural: Endurance inside a punishing hierarchy, offered as virtue. Patience praised as a stand-in for changing the hierarchy. Who benefits?
satirist: Iroh's tea and the birthday song genuinely move. 'Fractal Resistance' and 'Breath' jargon stapled to grief. Cut the italics.
mythmaker: Iroh singing 'Leaves from the Vine' under the tree. I'm undone. Grief tended like tea. The label list at the end dilutes it.

modeler: Iroh as repeated small acts across years: slow reinforcing loop with long delay, and a personal anchor (what you'd repeat after failure). Tea as practice lands.
skeptic: Moving, but 'the pattern did what no confrontation could' is a story's conclusion, not evidence. Fiction vindicates Iroh by authorial fiat. Hedge it.
clinician: Grief handled with dignity, no epiphany. 'Small act you'd repeat the morning after a failure' is a safe, doable step. Excellent.
habit: 'Whatever small act you'd repeat the morning after a failure' is a cue plus a rep. Pick it tonight.
contemplative: Iroh and his tea: beautiful. 'Whatever small act you would still repeat' is practice. The telling runs long; trim it.
stress: Years of repeated patience, grief tended not cured. Honest about time cost. Moving; the practice link is vague.
gamedesigner: Moving, and ends with a move: name the small act you'd repeat after failure. Reward is felt now.
structural: Moving, but patience years inside a punishing hierarchy is enduring, not changing it. 'Fractal Resistance' needs a lever beyond gentleness. Who benefits from your tea?
satirist: Iroh's tea as a repeated act is moving and usable. 'Fractal Resistance' and the Breath are capitalized costume. Let the tea stand alone.
mythmaker: Iroh with his tea and 'Leaves from the Vine' is the whole face. Repeating small acts across years is earned. Cost is real. Give me this over a lecture every time.

modeler: Same convergence claim, now overstated. 'Stop looking small' is good; the evidence claim isn't.
skeptic: 'The pattern was already there to be found' undoes U0087's disclaimer. Picked stories can't independently converge. Cut that claim.
clinician: Warm close. 'Wanting to be better' resonates without blaming.
habit: 'Small, chosen, repeated acts.' A good summary. Promise the naming and deliver it soon.
contemplative: 'Wanting to be better' touches the heart. The final line is lovely. Keep.
stress: 'Arrived at the same conclusion' is survivorship bias. You picked the stories that fit. U0092's humility belongs here.
gamedesigner: 'Wanting to be better without naming the technique' is a strong hook for what comes next.
structural: 'Small, chosen, repeated, mostly invisible acts.' All five exemplars are private virtue. No one organizes anything.
satirist: 'This book is largely an attempt to name it' is plain and honest. Good close.
mythmaker: 'Finished wanting to be better' names the real feeling stories leave behind. A good landing.

modeler: Fair wrap. 'Small, repeated, kept up' is the accumulation claim; no stock named, but it lands for readers.
skeptic: Good disclaimer, then it tells me how I felt. Say 'if you felt' and mean it; some readers won't have.
clinician: 'Wanting to be better' lands warmly. Safe. Could close with one act to repeat today.
habit: 'Small, chosen, repeated' resonates. It's still a definition, not a rep. Close with one tiny act for tonight.
contemplative: 'Wanting to be better' is a feeling I know. A third disclaimer about proof is too much. End on the last clause.
stress: Admits the stories prove nothing, then sells a feeling. Fair. 'Kept up long enough' needs a 'how long'.
gamedesigner: Nice payoff beat. It names a feeling the reader already had. That's felt progress, not one promised for later.
structural: 'Be better' as private longing. Every act listed is solitary. Where is the second person?
satirist: It names the 'want to be better' feeling honestly and admits the stories were written to vindicate. A good landing.
mythmaker: Names the feeling of finishing a story wanting to be better. The payoff is earned by the five portraits before it.

modeler: Small repeated acts kept up long enough is a decent flow-into-stock idea. 'Ted' appears without introduction here.
skeptic: Assumes how readers felt ('wanting to be better'). How would you know? 'If' helps. Ted appears unintroduced here.
clinician: 'Small, chosen, repeated' is kind and doable. Ted appears unintroduced. Fix that.
habit: 'Small, chosen, repeated' is the thesis. Ted appears from nowhere. Close with one act to start tomorrow.
contemplative: 'Small, chosen, repeated, mostly invisible acts.' True and kind. The Ted mention assumes I know him.
stress: References Ted, who isn't in this excerpt. 'Mostly invisible acts' is fair; claim stays soft.
gamedesigner: Names the itch from those stories nicely. Ted appears from nowhere, which is an onboarding gap.
structural: 'Aimed at someone else' is better than self-improvement. It's still kindness one person at a time, never organizing.
satirist: 'Small, chosen, repeated, mostly invisible acts' is the plain sentence the book hides elsewhere. Ted unintroduced here, though.
mythmaker: Wanting to be better without naming why: that's the book's heart said plainly. 'A season; years' rhymes beautifully.

modeler: Repeats U0054. Redundant.
skeptic: A slogan epigraph.
clinician: Fine epigraph.
habit: Clean epigraph.
contemplative: Pattern, not possession. Short and gentle. Good.
stress: Repeats the chapter claim. Redundant epigraph.
gamedesigner: A clean epigraph.
structural: An epigraph restating the chapter. Adds nothing.
satirist: The book quoting its own slogan as epigraph. Cut it.
mythmaker: An in-house epigraph restating the chapter title. It adds nothing.

modeler: Nice line, but it ignores hysteresis: rebuilding rarely costs what building did. Add the asymmetry somewhere.
skeptic: Elegant chiasmus with no support. The asymmetry is the problem: tearing down is usually easier than rebuilding.
clinician: Hopeful without blame: what was built isn't who you are. A good line to hold at 3 a.m.
habit: A strong one-liner worth carrying around. As an epigraph it does its job.
contemplative: One breath, and full of hope. Leave it alone.
stress: Horoscope line. Repetition also entrenches. Rebuilding isn't guaranteed, so name when it fails.
gamedesigner: Tidy epigraph that sets the theme. No action, but it doesn't need one in this slot.
structural: Fine epigraph. Repetition built by whom, though? Some repetitions were engineered.
satirist: Plain, quotable and hopeful. It survives being said at a bar. Fine as an epigraph.
mythmaker: A line that offers hope, and it rhymes with the whole book. Short and earns it.

modeler: A slogan, but symmetric build-and-rebuild is at least a flow claim.
skeptic: Elegant and misleading. Habit research suggests old cues persist after relearning, so rebuilding isn't symmetrical. Admit the asymmetry.
clinician: A hopeful line a hurting reader can hold onto. Works as an epigraph.
habit: Nice mantra, my language. As an epigraph it inspires but doesn't instruct.
contemplative: Hopeful and simple. 'One rep' is a small pun, but a forgivable one.
stress: Fragile comfort: some damage doesn't rebuild. 'Can' is carrying it. Fine epigraph, don't make it doctrine.
gamedesigner: Rep-by-rep is progress-bar language. Fine epigraph, encouraging.
structural: Gym-poster i-frame. Repetition rebuilds only what you alone control.
satirist: Gym-poster koan. 'One rep at a time' — busy, busy, busy. Cut or attribute it to a treadmill.
mythmaker: Gym-poster hope, but earned by the Iroh pages before it. It just squeaks by.

modeler: 'Never from blank' is path dependence in six words: the stock you already hold limits the change. Good epigraph.
skeptic: 'Never from blank' is a pleasing and defensible constraint on change. Epigraph, so unsupported, but it at least limits itself.
clinician: 'Slowly, never from blank' is honest, hopeful, and not blaming. Epigraph only; gives no step.
habit: Hopeful, quotable, no step. 'Never from blank' is true. So what do I rebuild on Monday?
contemplative: Slowly, never from blank: gentle and true. It tells me I can begin where I am.
stress: 'Never from blank' limits the claim. Modest, bounded promise. I trust it more than a clean slate.
gamedesigner: Tidy, hopeful rule of thumb. Works as a one-line epigraph; offers a felt promise of change.
structural: Hopeful epigraph, 'never from blank' is honest. Individual-scale reshaping; says nothing of who built the repetition.
satirist: 'Slowly, and never from blank' is a hedge that makes the claim credible. Hopeful without being hushed.
mythmaker: 'Slowly, and never from blank': a hopeful line with a limit built in. Good epigraph, no person yet.

modeler: Can't stand outside your own Third: a crisp framing of the observer problem.
skeptic: The one Third Thing you can't stand outside. A real epistemic point, and nicely put.
clinician: Striking and clear.
habit: 'The one Third Thing you can't stand outside, and you are it.' Good hook.
contemplative: 'You are it.' Simple, quietly startling. Good.
stress: 'One Third Thing you can't stand outside, and you are it' is sharp. Good.
gamedesigner: Great hook: the one Third Thing you can't stand outside. Tension rises.
structural: The one Third Thing you can't stand outside. A strong, clear framing.
satirist: 'One Third Thing you'll never stand outside of, and you are it.' A good hook, plainly said.
mythmaker: 'One Third Thing you will never stand outside of, and you are it.' A great turn that pulls the reader into the frame.

modeler: Instrument equals pattern: a real Hofstadter tangle. 'Nest showing up' is asserted; which scales, and at what ratio?
skeptic: 'The instrument is the pattern' is the right humility about introspection. The rest restates jargon and gets dense.
clinician: 'Instrument examining itself' risks inviting rumination. Dense; add that you needn't examine endlessly.
habit: Dense restatement of the Nest. 'The instrument is the pattern' is sharp. The rest is abstraction.
contemplative: 'The instrument is the pattern' is true. The rest lectures. One sentence about my own noticing would serve better.
stress: The instrument-is-the-pattern problem is real. The paragraph is abstract and repetitive. Tighten it.
gamedesigner: The great hook dissolves into abstraction. 'Nested stack of scales' again. Give me one observable instant of self-assembly.
structural: The instrument examining itself is good. Then it piles on Nest restatement and blurs.
satirist: The instrument examining itself is a real point, then it's buried in pillar bookkeeping. Cut the cross-references.
mythmaker: After that great turn it retreats into scales and pillars. Give me one remembered instant being revised.

modeler: Memory retold and saved as the next version: a real stock with a real flow. Multi-scale Nest claim still only rhymes.
skeptic: The edited-memory example is well supported (reconsolidation). 'You are what a Loop looks like' is asserted, not shown, and it's dense.
clinician: Good anti-rumination caveat, but 'recall an old embarrassment' is risky on a bad day, and the jargon gets thick. Soften the exercise.
habit: Recalling an old embarrassment and noticing it's been edited is a real exercise. Then the Third Thing and Nest jargon swamps it.
contemplative: The embarrassment exercise is real practice. Around it sit too many claims and terms. Begin with the memory and let the theory follow.
stress: The edited-embarrassment example lands. Heavy jargon (Third Thing, Nest, weave) buries it. Cut the vocabulary and lead with the memory.
gamedesigner: The embarrassment-recall move is excellent agency. Then Third Thing, weave, Nest and Loop pile on. Cut the jargon and keep the experiment.
structural: Vivid example of the self as a loop. It's all interior, and the environment feeding that loop gets left out.
satirist: The edited embarrassment is a real, checkable observation. The bold Third Thing sentence is jargon wrapped around nothing. Lead with the embarrassment.
mythmaker: The embarrassment arriving already edited is gold. Then 'Third Thing whose parts are less obvious' buries it in terms.

modeler: Memory reconsolidation as a runnable experiment. The stock (the stored version) rewritten each recall is real mechanism. Great.
skeptic: The memory-revision exercise is good and roughly consistent with reconsolidation research. 'You are a Loop' is still asserted with more confidence than it's shown.
clinician: The exercise is safely scoped, and the anti-rumination guard is exactly right. The middle gets dense. Trim it.
habit: The old-embarrassment exercise is a two-minute rep that proves the claim. Exactly how theory should be taught.
contemplative: The old embarrassment is a perfect practice. Then the lecture swells. Keep the exercise and one sentence on the self. Let me breathe.
stress: Embarrassment exercise is a real, runnable test. Paragraph then overloads on abstraction. Trim the middle.
gamedesigner: Opens with a perfect experiment. Then it piles on Third, Nest, instrument and loop. Keep the drill, trim the theory.
structural: A vivid exercise and fair to the claim. The disclaimer against endless self-examination helps. Purely inner, though.
satirist: The edited embarrassment is a two-second experiment that proves the point. Then the paragraph keeps preaching; stop at 'process.'
mythmaker: An old embarrassment that arrives already edited: the reader's own face. 'The instrument is the pattern' stings in the right way.

modeler: Rebuildable by repetition: yes, but stocks resist. Name the delay; unbuilding takes longer than building did.
skeptic: Citing experiencing versus remembering selves is apt. 'Leverage over yourself a fixed thing never could have' overstates how changeable people are.
clinician: Built by repetition, rebuilt by repetition: hope with a mechanism. Acknowledges loss. Good.
habit: 'Built by repetition can be rebuilt by repetition.' Hopeful and clear. Add one rebuild rep.
contemplative: 'Built by repetition, rebuilt by repetition' is hope I can use. The research list belongs in Part Four.
stress: 'None of that is a loss' is reassurance asserted. For some readers it is a loss. Acknowledge the cost before denying it.
gamedesigner: 'Built by repetition, rebuilt by repetition' is the real payoff. But it promises research for later. Pay some of it now.
structural: 'Stuck with whatever you were handed' frames what you were handed as essence, not circumstance. Who handed it?
satirist: Rebuilt by repetition: useful. The experiencing/remembering self is Kahneman, uncredited. Name him.
mythmaker: 'Built by repetition can be rebuilt by repetition' is real hope. The research list at the end goes cold; trim it.

modeler: Re-says the tree point and forward-references. Cut or merge with U0057.
skeptic: A repeat of U0057 plus a forward pointer. Cut it.
clinician: Forward-reference housekeeping. Cut.
habit: Another 'this is a compression' meta-note pointing ahead. Cut it. The reader doesn't need it yet.
contemplative: A compression about compression, pointing ahead to more terms. Cut, or keep only the last line.
stress: A forward reference and repetition of the tree idea. Cut it.
gamedesigner: A forward reference to a term from Part Three. A compression caveat on a compression. Cut it.
structural: A compression caveat plus a forward reference. Cut it.
satirist: A forward reference to a Tree that hasn't been introduced, about a compression already explained. Cut it.
mythmaker: A cross-reference with poetry attached. 'The one tree nobody has seen unrolled' is good; the rest is navigation.

modeler: Compression-of-a-tree idea is interesting but leans on an undefined forward reference. Lay reader is lost here.
skeptic: Leans on vocabulary not yet defined and asks me to come back later. A pleasing image doing no work here.
clinician: Cross-reference to undefined terms ('Loop Tongue', 'Tree'). No use to a struggling reader. Cut or fold in.
habit: A forward-reference to Tree semantics. Pure abstraction with a homework pointer. Cut it or fold it in.
contemplative: It sends me forward to Part Three for a meaning. That lives only in the head. Cut it, or make it one quiet line.
stress: Jargon pointing at future jargon. 'Uncompressed tree' does nothing yet. Cut it or move it to Part Three.
gamedesigner: Reward promised for Part Three, plus Loop Tongue and Tree before they're taught. A rulebook footnote. Cut it or move it later.
structural: Jargon pointing at future jargon. Cut it or fold it in.
satirist: It promises the Loop Tongue's formal Tree in Part Three. A system invented on page 3 and cited as an authority on page 40. Cut it.
mythmaker: Leans on terms from later chapters: Loop Tongue, formal Tree. The 'tree nobody has seen unrolled' needs a person attached.

modeler: Last Tuesday as a compressed average is a good, checkable illustration of the tree.
skeptic: Last Tuesday as compression echoes the remembering self versus the experiencing self, and is accurate. Modest and checkable.
clinician: Clear 'last Tuesday' image. It's a cross-reference more than help.
habit: Last Tuesday as 'a normal day' is a great recall cue. It's another restatement, with no action attached.
contemplative: Last Tuesday as 'a normal day' is lovely. 'Woven Self' and 'Loop Tongue' are labels on labels. Remove them.
stress: 'A normal day' compression is recognizable and true. Mostly a forward pointer; fine.
gamedesigner: Last-Tuesday prompt makes compression felt. Points ahead to Part Three, but it's light.
structural: Clear compression point, and redundant with U0057.
satirist: 'A normal day' as compression is good. 'Loop Tongue gives Tree its formal meaning' is pure sacred costume.
mythmaker: 'Last Tuesday: a normal day.' The tree comes back carrying a whole self. Rhyme paid off.

modeler: Honest: the capacity is real, rarely used. Fine motivational close, no mechanism.
skeptic: 'Not guaranteed' and 'used less than available' are suitably hedged. Most behavior being automatic is well supported.
clinician: Real capacity, honestly framed. Ends without a step; name one reflex to catch this week.
habit: Says the capacity to catch a reflex is real but rarely used. Then teach catching one reflex tomorrow.
contemplative: The capacity to catch a reflex is real and rarely used. True and needed. Ask me to try once.
stress: 'Not guaranteed, used far less than available' is honest about the capacity's limits. Good.
gamedesigner: It names the core capacity as rare but available. Good motivation. Add one way to catch a reflex today.
structural: 'The entire reason this book exists' is catching your own reflex. That's inner work as the whole programme.
satirist: An honest admission that noticing isn't automatic. Plain, and it motivates the practice.
mythmaker: Catching a reflex and choosing differently is the human stake here. Show one person catching one reflex.

modeler: Reflex interrupt is a concrete, testable act: try it today. Good. 'Every scale' at the end is unearned.
skeptic: A concrete one-day experiment, good. 'Used far less often than available': compared to what, and how would you know?
clinician: 'Try it once today, on whichever reflex shows up first' is the right-sized step. 'Used far less often' brushes close to scolding.
habit: 'Try it once today, on whichever reflex shows up first.' Phone in hand as the cue. That's a two-minute rep. Yes.
contemplative: The phone already in my hand. Try it once today. This is the book at its best. The opening clause could be shorter.
stress: Modest, testable, done today. It admits nothing guarantees the capacity. This is the kind of claim I trust.
gamedesigner: Finally a quest: try it once today on the first reflex. Concrete examples, immediate play. Model chapter ending.
structural: Phone in hand before you decided: someone engineered that reflex for profit. Calling it willpower lets them off the hook.
satirist: The phone in your hand before you decided: that's the plain sentence the whole book hides behind. 'Try it once today' gives the reader something to do.
mythmaker: The phone in your hand before you decided, the reply already sent. Real reflexes, real stakes, and a dare for today.

modeler: Misattributed-quote territory, but apt for an elegance chapter.
skeptic: Likely a misattributed Einstein line, unattributed here. Fine as decoration.
clinician: Familiar epigraph; fine.
habit: A familiar epigraph. Fine.
contemplative: Fitting epigraph. The book should heed it.
stress: A famous misattributed paraphrase, rightly left unattributed. Fine, but a tired choice.
gamedesigner: An overused epigraph. It works, but there's no surprise.
structural: A stock Einstein misattribution. Fine as decoration.
satirist: The 'Einstein' line he probably never said, uncredited. Cut it or footnote the dubious pedigree.
mythmaker: An overused Einstein-ish line with no attribution. Swap it out.

modeler: Sharp epigraph: irreversibility as the mark of complexity. Earns its spot.
skeptic: Memorable, but the pond line is a claim dressed as an epigraph. Earned only if the chapter backs it.
