clinician: Memorable epigraph, sets up the chapter. Earns its place lightly.
habit: A memorable epigraph that sets up the pile and pond split. It's fine where it sits.
contemplative: A good image. It works as an epigraph and needs nothing added.
stress: Sharp epigraph: irreversibility in one line. A real distinction, cheaply stated.
gamedesigner: Sharp, memorable epigraph that sets up the next chapter's contrast well. Hook only.
structural: Neat epigraph. Does nothing structural.
satirist: Cryptic but witty, and the next pages pay it off. A good epigraph.
mythmaker: Memorable image that sets up the pond. It's clever more than felt.

modeler: Car versus pond is the classic complicated/complex distinction, well compressed.
skeptic: Cryptic and unattributed until explained. Intriguing, but the reader can't decode it yet.
clinician: Cryptic until the chapter explains it. That's fine as a hook, not as help.
habit: Punchy, memorable epigraph. It sets up the car/pond contrast.
contemplative: A riddle performing for me. I paused, but not to breathe. Unclear until later pages explain it.
stress: Memorable and correct about irreversibility. That's a stakes claim. Good epigraph.
gamedesigner: Great teaser epigraph; I want to know why. Good hook.
structural: Neat aphorism for complexity. It works as a door.
satirist: Nice line, unattributed. Pays off in U0103-4, so it earns its spot.
mythmaker: Car versus pond is a sticky image. It's a riddle for now. Its payoff comes in the next units.

modeler: Reductionist versus emergent in two sentences. Pond loses its loops when you disassemble it. This is the exact Meadows point.
skeptic: Crisp. Reductionism versus emergence in two sentences. Epigraph is fluent, and fluency is not proof, but it sets up a genuine contrast.
clinician: Crisp epigraph. Nothing for the reader to do; sets up the contrast to follow.
habit: Crisp. A pond isn't a car. Nothing to do yet; the next paragraphs have to cash it.
contemplative: Short and clear. It states a view; I feel the pond, not yet the practice.
stress: Clean contrast between complicated and complex. Good epigraph; testable against the next two.
gamedesigner: Crisp contrast, easy to remember. Epigraph only; sets the trap for the next two paragraphs.
structural: Memorable line on emergent wholes. Systems-as-metaphor; no mechanism, owner or lever. Keep as epigraph.
satirist: Car versus pond is a clean, bar-ready line. Sets up the next paragraphs; asks nothing of me.
mythmaker: Car versus pond: a crisp, memorable contrast, and the lost pond has a tiny elegy in it. Epigraph that sets up the chapter.

modeler: Meadows' complicated-versus-complex point, compact. Sharp. Cut-apart loses the loops, yes.
skeptic: Memorable and unsupported. Reductionism versus holism in one aphorism; elegant, but 'compared to what?' has no answer here.
clinician: Tidy line on systems. Lands as insight with no step; the family reference could sting if not handled gently.
habit: Sticky line, easy. But it states a conclusion with no behaviour attached. Where's the Monday action?
contemplative: Clear contrast in two short sentences. I can feel it. It is a thought, not yet a practice.
stress: Memorable and true of living systems. Break it: some ponds survive dissection. Still, a clean line.
gamedesigner: Punchy line, but receive-only. Fine as a title card, no more.
structural: Good figure/ground shot: dismantling kills the pond. Sound ecology, but I'd ask what a pond's regulator looks like.
satirist: Clean, aphoristic, true enough at a bar. Pond versus car is the right contrast. It's a slogan though; the reader does nothing with it.
mythmaker: Pond or family taken apart, and you've lost it — grief in one line. No person, but the loss is real. Epigraph does its job.

modeler: Framing a diagnostic: good instinct, thin content.
skeptic: A transition, but framing it as a diagnostic is good.
clinician: Promises a diagnostic. Good framing.
habit: Promises the first thing to do. Finally.
contemplative: A plain signpost. Fine.
stress: Framing. Fine.
gamedesigner: Finally a stated goal: a diagnostic in two questions. Clear quest log. Excellent.
structural: A setup line.
satirist: Fine setup.
mythmaker: Procedural framing. Fine as a hinge.

modeler: Signpost. Promises a diagnostic without giving any of it here.
skeptic: Clear roadmap, nothing more. The two examples are well chosen.
clinician: Clear roadmap with a diagnose-first order. Gillihan would approve: structure before fixing.
habit: It promises a two-question diagnostic for the habit that won't stick. A good, concrete setup.
contemplative: Signposting about chapters. It says what is coming instead of giving it. Shorten it to one line.
stress: Signpost. A diagnostic before fixing is good discipline, but the paragraph only announces it.
gamedesigner: Clear quest log: two questions, real problems named. Onboarding done right, though it's only a signpost.
structural: Signpost. 'The team fight' is promising if it ever gets to team rules.
satirist: A roadmap. The habit and the recurring fight are good bait, but this is scaffolding the reader doesn't need.
mythmaker: The 'same fight' team grounds it. Otherwise it's a road sign.

modeler: Asks the reader to carry a real problem through. Good practice design.
skeptic: Asks the reader to carry a real problem through. A good practical frame.
clinician: 'Pick one of yours now' is a concrete, contained first step. Good.
habit: 'Pick one of yours now and carry it through both.' An assigned rep before the theory. Perfect.
contemplative: 'Pick one of yours now and carry it through.' An invitation to practice. Clear and kind.
stress: Asks the reader to carry their own problem through. Skin for the reader. Works.
gamedesigner: Finally: pick your problem now and carry it through. Controller in hand. Excellent.
structural: Diagnose before fixing, for teams too. Useful. Ask 'whose rules' as a diagnostic question.
satirist: 'Pick one of yours now' turns reading into doing. Stephenson test passed.
mythmaker: 'Pick one of yours now and carry it through.' It puts the reader on stage. Good.

modeler: Clean contrast setup. Works.
skeptic: A clear setup. It needs U0105 to pay off.
clinician: Clear contrast setup.
habit: A clear, concrete image.
contemplative: Clear, quiet image. Good setup.
stress: A clean setup example.
gamedesigner: A clean setup for the contrast. It works as a half beat.
structural: Clean assembly-line example. Pairs well with the pond.
satirist: A plain, concrete contrast case. Good.
mythmaker: The assembly line is a clear image. Setup for the pond.

modeler: Clear decomposable-system baseline. Setup only.
skeptic: Clean setup. Real assembly lines do surprise their builders; 'nothing will surprise' overstates it for the sake of contrast.
clinician: Clear setup image, nothing more. Fine as a half of a pair.
habit: A clear illustration with no stakes for me. Fine as a setup, and it earns nothing alone.
contemplative: Clear, but it only sets something up. Fold it into the pond as one contrast.
stress: A clean setup for a contrast. On its own it's just a car plant.
gamedesigner: Setup beat, easy to read. On its own it gives me nothing to predict. Merge it with the pond line.
structural: Clear setup.
satirist: A clear setup with no payoff on its own. That's fine as the straight man for the pond.
mythmaker: Clean setup, but it's a straw man with no worker in the factory. Let a mechanic speak.

modeler: A clear setup, half of a contrast. Works only paired with the pond.
skeptic: Clear setup. Does its job as a contrast case, nothing more.
clinician: Clear setup. Nothing personal yet.
habit: Clear setup but inert alone. Fine as half of a pair.
contemplative: Plain setup, fair enough. On its own it gives me nothing yet. Fine as a half-step.
stress: Clean contrast setup. Predictability is the right test variable.
gamedesigner: Clear setup for the contrast, but it's only half a beat on its own. Fine in sequence.
structural: Setup. Clear, earns little alone.
satirist: Setup only. Clear, but the mechanic's 'like today's' is the only spark; it needs the pond to matter.
mythmaker: The mechanic on the line is a face, briefly. It's setup and does that honestly.

modeler: Assembly line is linear and decomposable: fix the station. A fair foil. Clear contrast case; not a flaw, just groundwork.
skeptic: Clear contrast, but 'tomorrow's car will be like today's' is an easy claim with no comparison class; real lines break and surprise constantly.
clinician: Clear mechanic analogy; fix-the-station is simple. No emotional or practical hook yet.
habit: Clear contrast, easy to follow. Pure setup though. Fine as a foil.
contemplative: Simple, and the image is easy. It is setup only. Nothing to live yet.
stress: Clear and fair. Assembly line is predictable. Setup only; carries no weight until the pond.
gamedesigner: Clear setup, predictable car. But I'm passively receiving; better to ask me to predict first.
structural: Good contrast: fixable stations versus unpredictable wholes. Notably, an assembly line has an owner and a manager; that's the structure missing from the pond.
satirist: Assembly line, mechanic, dishwasher: plain and funny enough. A setup for the pond, needs the pond.
mythmaker: The mechanic on the line gives me a face, and her calm answer 'like today's' is a nice beat. Dishwasher is plain. A bit dry otherwise.

modeler: Good foil: a linear system with no feedback, so parts explain the whole. Sets up the loop contrast cleanly.
skeptic: Clear contrast case: a decomposable system. The claim 'study every station and you understand the whole' is a fair strawman.
clinician: Clear contrast case. Fine as scaffold; nothing here a struggling person can pick up and use.
habit: Clean analogy, easy to picture. But it is abstraction with no action; set up for contrast only.
contemplative: A plain picture, easy to read. It sets up what comes next. Keep it short, as it is.
stress: Good foil: complicated versus complex. Clear contrast, no strain applied yet.
gamedesigner: Clear contrast setup, but I'm only reading. Let me predict what breaks in a pond before telling me.
structural: Clear contrast of complicated versus complex. Oddly, the assembly line has a plant owner and a rulebook, which this ignores.
satirist: The assembly-line mechanic is concrete and funny-dry; 'fix it like a dishwasher'. Good foil. Needs one real number on station counts to be Bryson.
mythmaker: The mechanic is a nice face, but she's a straw figure for the view being argued against. Give her something she knows that the line misses.

modeler: Good punchline beat. Size isn't the variable.
skeptic: A good contrast in one line.
clinician: Nice one-line pivot.
habit: A one-line contrast. It works.
contemplative: One sentence, a whole teaching. Beautiful contrast.
stress: A good contrast. Short and true.
gamedesigner: A pond in one line. A great contrast punch.
structural: One line, effective contrast.
satirist: A one-line pond. Lovely economy.
mythmaker: A one-line punch about the pond. Good contrast.

modeler: Fewer parts, less predictable: a good contrast. Needs the next paragraph to say why (feedback).
skeptic: The contrast lands. 'Nobody can tell you' is overstated; ecologists forecast ponds with modest skill.
clinician: Clean contrast that makes 'no one can predict it' feel ordinary, not like failure.
habit: Nice contrast in one sentence. Abstract hook, no action, which is acceptable here.
contemplative: Simple and true. Even the one who dug it can't say. Good.
stress: Fewer parts, less predictable: a good inversion. It's stated as fact, but it holds.
gamedesigner: Good turn: fewer parts, less predictable. A small surprise that earns its place. Ask me to guess why first.
structural: Clear contrast. Nothing to act on.
satirist: Fewer parts, less predictable. A sharp, plain contrast in one sentence.
mythmaker: The person who dug it and can't predict it is nearly a face. Give us their bafflement.

modeler: Frogs nobody brought is perfect emergence from coupled parts. Lovely.
skeptic: The shrug is a nice admission of unpredictability. Sets up the distinction cleanly.
clinician: Nice contrast, plainly told. It's only setup.
habit: The frogs nobody brought are delightful. One question, well placed.
contemplative: Frogs nobody brought. Gentle and vivid. The question at the end invites me in.
stress: Frogs nobody brought: vivid unpredictability. Good half of the pair.
gamedesigner: Frogs nobody brought, ha. Ending on 'Why?' makes me predict. Good tension.
structural: Good contrast setup. Nothing to score beyond clarity.
satirist: 'Frogs nobody brought' is a genuinely funny, true image of emergence. Keep.
mythmaker: The pond digger's shrug and 'frogs nobody brought.' A delightful image. Lovely contrast.

modeler: Fewer parts, less predictability, because loops couple. Frogs nobody brought: nice. The pond shrug is the whole argument. Fine napkin sketch.
skeptic: Nicely turns the shrug onto the reader's own forecasting, which is where overconfidence lives. 'Why does the pond shrug' is a fair question.
clinician: 'You've given that shrug about your own next year' normalizes uncertainty without shame. Question stays open; no step.
habit: 'You've given that shrug about your own next year.' That lands. Ends on a good single question.
contemplative: The shrug is mine, too. A good question, left open. Plain words.
stress: The shrug lands, you've given it about your own year. Honest uncertainty over false forecast.
gamedesigner: Good: pond shrug, then 'you've given that shrug about your own year'. Hook with a rising question.
structural: The shrug about your own next year resonates. But a pond has no landlord; people's years do. Don't let ecology excuse the owner.
satirist: 'You've given that shrug about your own next year' puts me in the pond. Frogs nobody brought: earned wonder.
mythmaker: The gardener's shrug and 'frogs nobody brought' are lovely. 'You've given that shrug about your own next year' lands in the gut. Good turn.

modeler: Now we're talking: the algae-insect-fish-waste loop, output as input. The feedback test is the right test. Keep.
skeptic: A usable heuristic. Imperfect, since thermostats feed back without emergence, but clear and actionable.
clinician: Feedback distinction clearly made.
habit: Explains feedback plainly with the pond. Good setup.
contemplative: 'A thing that dies when you take it apart.' Clear, useful diagnostic. Keep.
stress: Feedback as the dividing line is a checkable diagnostic. Real tool.
gamedesigner: 'Output becomes input' gives me a concrete test. Clear rule.
structural: Feedback as the dividing line, crisply shown. Good mechanism writing.
satirist: 'A thing you can take apart versus a thing that dies when you do.' Great line, earned by algae and fish.
mythmaker: 'A thing that dies when you take it apart' carries stakes. A lovely food-web loop.

modeler: Solid definition. 'Two parts is enough' needs a loop between them, not just two parts. Say so.
skeptic: 'Two parts is enough' to produce a Third Thing is asserted. Two parts with feedback can be merely a thermostat.
clinician: Clear definitions.
habit: The definitions are crisp. 'Alive' is slightly loose, but fine.
contemplative: Clear distinction. 'Alive in the specific sense' is slightly coy. Say what alive means.
stress: 'Two parts is enough' is generous. A thermostat loops without being alive. Tighten the definition.
gamedesigner: Clear definitions. 'Two parts is enough' is a nice surprise.
structural: Clear definitions. 'Two parts is enough' is a nice sting.
satirist: A clean distinction. 'Alive in the specific sense this book means' gets mystical; keep it mechanical.
mythmaker: Clean definitions. 'Two parts is enough' quietly invites the Dyad.

modeler: Feedback as the dividing line between complicated and complex: exactly right, Meadows would nod. Two-part minimum is crisp.
skeptic: The definition hinges on the double negative 'nothing nobody put there'. Say plainly: feedback between parts produces behaviour no part has.
clinician: 'Third Thing' jargon blurs a distinction that could be said in plain words. Simplify.
habit: A useful distinction, but 'Third Thing' sneaks in jargon. Give the definition, then go straight to the test.
contemplative: Jargon is defining jargon. Two people feeding back into each other is the whole lesson. Lead with that.
stress: Workable definition of complicated versus complex. 'Two people are enough' is a bold minimum. Keep it.
gamedesigner: A crisp definition, and 'two people are enough' makes it playable. 'Third Thing' still assumes I remember the term.
structural: A clean distinction, a mechanism rather than a mood. Good.
satirist: A useful distinction. 'Third Thing' sneaks in again; 'a pattern nobody put there' already did that job.
mythmaker: Definitions with no blood in them, and 'Third Thing' jargon on top. The two people deserve names.

modeler: A crisp definition: feedback makes complexity, size doesn't. Two parts suffice. The couple example makes it usable.
skeptic: The complicated/complex distinction is well drawn. The couple's argument is recognisable. Whether 'belongs to neither' changes anything still needs showing.
clinician: 'The argument belongs to neither of them' takes the blame off a couple instantly. Clinically useful.
habit: The couple's argument belonging to neither is a great reframe. Tell me what to do differently in the next one.
contemplative: The couple's argument that belongs to neither of them. Compassionate understanding. The definitions before it are a bit dense.
stress: Standard, defensible distinction; the two-person argument example makes it usable. Keep.
gamedesigner: Clean definitions, and the couple's argument makes it personal. Gives me a diagnostic I can run.
structural: Clean distinction, and the couple example is sharp. Extend it to a market or agency, where feedback has owners.
satirist: Complicated vs complex, cleanly done, and the couple's argument belonging to neither is the right example.
mythmaker: 'The argument belongs to neither of them.' The distinction gets a couple and a cost. Very strong.

modeler: Actionable binary test. Good.
skeptic: A concrete triage step with an honest exit. Works. (A was meant 0; see note: practical, not big-picture.)
clinician: A real test with a stop condition. Good.
habit: One good question: does anything feed back? Clear instructions either way. This is the model.
contemplative: A question I can ask today. 'Stop reading this chapter' is honest and kind.
stress: A usable triage step, and it gives permission to stop reading. Respectful.
gamedesigner: A branching decision with an exit. A playable test with a clear outcome. Best mechanic in Part One.
structural: An actionable diagnostic anyone can run, on a policy as easily as a pond. Good.
satirist: 'You are looking at a pile.' A plain test with a usable action. And it tells you when to stop reading. Bless it.
mythmaker: A usable diagnostic with a nice 'stop reading this chapter' honesty.

modeler: A one-question triage you can actually run. Pile versus pond. Love that it tells you to stop reading.
skeptic: A usable triage question. Feedback is a matter of degree, not yes or no; admit that the faucet sometimes has a teenager in it.
clinician: One question, a clear fork, and permission to stop reading. A usable decision rule.
habit: One question, 'does anything feed back?', plus a clear branch. Exactly the one-question test. Great.
contemplative: One question I can bring to the faucet or to my child. Plain and usable. Good.
stress: A binary test with an exit ('stop reading this chapter'). The book takes a risk it could lose. Excellent.
gamedesigner: Controller in my hands: point, ask one question, branch. Even an exit path. Textbook tutorial.
structural: A usable diagnostic with an exit clause. Rare and welcome.
satirist: A faucet and a teenager, one question, and permission to stop reading. Useful, and it's funny.
mythmaker: Faucet versus teenager is perfect. Useful, funny, and the reader is holding the problem.

modeler: True and relatable, but a one-liner that needs U0109 to mean anything.
skeptic: Plausible and recognizable. 'A great deal' compared to what? Unmeasured.
clinician: Validating: the frustration is a mismatch of tools, not a defect in you.
habit: Short and true. It resonates.
contemplative: Short, true, recognizable. Good.
stress: True and short.
gamedesigner: A short, resonant beat. Works.
structural: True and relatable. Short. It works.
satirist: True and quick.
mythmaker: True and relatable, but it needs one example of someone wrenching on a pond.

modeler: Patching a part of a loop and the loop regenerates it: exactly the failure mode. Recognizable.
skeptic: Recognizable and practical. 'A great deal' is an unquantified frequency claim, though a plausible one.
clinician: Relieves self-blame: the argument returns because of method, not you. Add what to try instead.
habit: 'Same argument back by Friday' is painfully recognisable and diagnoses the wrong tool. Keep it.
contemplative: 'The same argument back by Friday.' I have lived that. One sentence that does its whole job.
stress: 'Back by Friday' is a failure everyone has paid for. Specific, recognizable, true.
gamedesigner: Friday's repeat argument is instantly recognizable. Shows the failure state clearly. Great beat.
structural: Recognizable frustration. The fix is still a couple talking it over, never the conditions pressing on them.
satirist: 'Back by Friday' is the laugh of recognition. A concrete diagnosis, no costume.
mythmaker: The argument back by Friday: everyone has lived it. Stakes in one sentence.

modeler: A stock of rules with inflow and no outflow. That's a real bathtub, and it explains institutional weight. Excellent.
skeptic: Sharp and partly true. 'A fairly reliable count' overclaims, because some complication is necessary. Hedge it and it keeps.
clinician: Sharp systems insight. Institutional, not personal.
habit: 'Residue of failed leverage' is a strong frame for institutions. Give the reader a personal version.
contemplative: Rules on rules, never removed. Wise and clear. 'Heavy institutions' lands.
stress: A risky, specific claim about institutions: you can check it and it could be wrong. Note Chesterton's fence. Strong.
gamedesigner: 'Residue of failed leverage' is a great insight. It explains heavy institutions.
structural: Institutional and sharp. But many added rules aren't failed fixes. They're loopholes someone won. Ask who profits.
satirist: 'Complication is the residue of failed leverage.' Old institutions are heavy. Witty, true, and you can check it. Keep.
mythmaker: 'Complication is the residue of failed leverage' is a sharp, memorable claim. The exception-to-the-exception is vivid.

modeler: Useful reframe of 'it's complicated.' Practical.
skeptic: A useful self-audit prompt. 'More often' needs a basis, but the habit is good.
clinician: Nice self-check without blame.
habit: Has a cue: when you hear 'it's complicated', including from yourself. Good.
contemplative: 'Including from yourself' is gentle self-examination. Useful.
stress: Practical suspicion of 'it's complicated.' Good.
gamedesigner: It turns 'it's complicated' into a trigger I can catch in conversation. A good feedback cue.
structural: A useful suspicion of 'it's complicated.' Add: sometimes it's complicated because someone benefits from you giving up.
satirist: A gentle jab at 'it's complicated.' Useful and funny.
mythmaker: Re-reading 'it's complicated', including in your own mouth. Personal and useful.

modeler: A ratio is a real definition. The chaos game reference is apt. The tax code contrast lands.
skeptic: Elegance as a ratio is a clean, memorable idea. The tax-code contrast lands.
clinician: Clean ratio definition.
habit: Elegance as a ratio. Clear concept.
contemplative: Elegance as a ratio is a good idea. The tax code jab is a small point scored.
stress: Elegance as a ratio is crisp. Tax code versus chaos game makes it vivid.
gamedesigner: Elegance as a ratio is a designer's definition. Clean.
structural: Elegance as a ratio is great. Tax complexity is not 'accidental.' Prep-software firms lobbied against simple filing.
satirist: Elegance as a ratio, with the chaos game against the tax code. A crisp definition that actually works.
mythmaker: A good ratio definition. The callback to the triangle is rhyme working. The tax-code jab is easy.

modeler: Elegance as an output-per-rule ratio is a real, checkable definition. Chaos game versus tax code is a great pairing.
skeptic: A ratio is a checkable framing, good. 'Mostly what people would never ask for' is editorial; the tax code's complication is partly by request.
clinician: Interesting definition. Nothing here for a person in pain. The tax-code example helps.
habit: 'A ratio: output per rule' is a crisp idea. The tax-code joke helps. But where's my rule audit?
contemplative: 'Three points, one rule, a die' assumes I already know the chaos game. The tax-code joke is mostly for show.
stress: The ratio framing is crisp, and the tax code jab is earned. Fine, but gives the reader no way to measure it.
gamedesigner: A ratio is a usable score idea. The tax-code contrast lands. Give me something to rate myself on.
structural: The tax-code jab lands, but who lobbies to keep filing complicated? The preparer industry profits. Say so.
satirist: The ratio idea plus the tax-code jab works. Name the chaos game and the Sierpinski triangle so the Bryson test is fully paid.
mythmaker: The tax-weekend dread lands, but 'three points, one rule and a rolled die' is a riddle without setup.

modeler: A real ratio, output per rule, anchored by Sierpinski. The tax-code contrast is sharp. A measurable design criterion.
skeptic: Defining it as a ratio is clever, but 'how much comes out' has no measure. The tax-code jab is fluent rhetoric, not analysis.
clinician: The tax-code joke helps it land. It's design theory with no human use yet.
habit: A tidy ratio and a good tax joke. Turn it on me: count the rules in my morning routine.
contemplative: A clear ratio and a good contrast. The tax-weekend joke is a small ego flourish. It lives in the head, not the kitchen.
stress: Ratio definition is crisp. Tax code jab is cheap but true. Unmeasured ratio though; say how you'd compare two systems.
gamedesigner: Ratio framing is a designer's dream, and tax code versus triangle game lands. Gives me a test for my own rules.
structural: Naming the tax code and the preparer industry is welcome. Finish the thought: who lobbies to keep filing hard?
satirist: Ratio, not minimalism, plus the tax code's dreaded weekend: wit and a measurable idea. Bryson would approve.
mythmaker: The dice triangle comes back, and the tax code's 'dreaded weekend every spring' gets a groan of recognition. Good contrast.

modeler: Elegance as ratio out over in is a testable metric. Triangle versus tax code gives both ends. Counting rules is a bit loose, but it's honest.
skeptic: Gives a comparison ratio and a counterexample (tax code), but 'count the rules' is undefined and the ratio unmeasurable. Nice, not rigorous.
clinician: Elegance as ratio is clear, tax-code contrast lands. Gives a comparison tool. Not personal, but harmless and useful.
habit: Count rules in, look at what comes out. A usable test. Tax-code weekend lands. Apply it to my routine.
contemplative: 'Maximum complexity from minimum complication' is a slogan, and a ratio is for the head. Show the triangle, drop the tax code.
stress: Gives a ratio you can actually count, tax code as counterexample. Measurable-ish. Rule counts are slippery, but it's a start.
gamedesigner: Gives me a ratio I can use to compare systems: count rules, look at output. Triangle versus tax code is a fun contrast.
structural: The tax code example is the first real structural jab: complication producing industries nobody asked for. Name who lobbied for it and the lever.
satirist: Elegance as a ratio, tax-code weekend as foil: plain and funny. 'Count the rules' is vague, but the triangle game is a real number.
mythmaker: Tax code as the dreaded weekend every spring is a human wince. But a ratio, a ceiling and corners: ideas doing a person's job. Needs a filer.

modeler: Concrete application to personal systems. Good.
skeptic: Practical, and it applies to my own routines. It works.
clinician: Concrete question about your own routines. Usable.
habit: Four habits or one practice is a real audit question for my routine. Good.
contemplative: A difficult relative, a routine: this lives in my kitchen. Practical and kind.
stress: Directly applicable to routines. Good.
gamedesigner: Applied straight to my routine. 'More parts than the job requires' is an auditable question.
structural: Personal routines only. The same test applied to a benefits application would be a real lever.
satirist: 'A way of handling a difficult relative' — the funniest system in the list. Practical.
mythmaker: 'A way of handling a difficult relative' smuggles a face in. Practical and personal.

modeler: Go is the right exhibit. Local rules stated exactly.
skeptic: Go's rule count is accurate and the history is hedged. A good example.
clinician: Good example.
habit: Go's five rules are a clean example.
contemplative: Five rules of Go, plainly listed. Clear.
stress: Go is a real, long-tested case. Rules held for millennia: history test passed.
gamedesigner: Go's five rules, stated. The designer in me cheers.
structural: Go's five rules is a superb example. Concrete and checkable.
satirist: Go's rules listed, with a date. Bryson would approve: a countable fact behind the awe.
mythmaker: Go's five rules make a great set piece. Two and a half millennia gives it weight.

modeler: Rules actually listed: you can count them. That's how you earn 'minimal complication.'
skeptic: Accurate and clear, with properly hedged dates. It sets up the next paragraph rather than earning its own place.
clinician: Clear and tidy. Purely conceptual.
habit: Five rules, lifetimes of play. It's a vivid, clear example, though nothing I'd act on.
contemplative: Five rules, lifetimes of study. Clear, but it stays a fact about a game, not about me.
stress: Go has survived 2,500 years of strain: a real historical test case, not an anecdote.
gamedesigner: Five rules in a minute: elegance demonstrated, not claimed. A designer's dream example.
structural: Lucid on Go. Doesn't connect to anything a reader governs.
satirist: Five rules, listed, and 2,500 years. Real numbers, real wonder.
mythmaker: Five rules and lifetimes of failure is a lovely contrast. Show me one player's lifetime.

modeler: Five local rules, millennia of depth. Exactly the bottom-up start I want. Last line gestures at your rulebook but doesn't earn it.
skeptic: Accurate, checkable rules; a real case of small rules, deep game. The closing rulebook jab is just there for rhythm. Cut it or earn it.
clinician: Lovely, clear rules list. The closing jab at 'your rulebook' lands as a nudge; what would trimming one rule look like today?
habit: Five rules, lifetime depth: lovely. The last line nods at action but gives no rep. Make it one: cut a rule from your routine this week.
contemplative: Plain and lovely. Five rules, a child, an old man. The last line pokes the reader; let the stone speak instead.
stress: Go's rule count is checkable and the age claim is hedged. Good. The closing jab about your own rulebook is a nudge, not a tool.
gamedesigner: Great hook: five rules, a whole game. The rulebook jab puts a controller in my hands. Solid level one.
structural: Five rules, endless game: clean. But who wrote your rulebook's extra pages? The closing jab blames the reader, not the bosses.
satirist: Go's five rules, plainly listed. Bryson-grade fact. The rulebook jab at the end lands. Keep.
mythmaker: A child at a Sunday table, losing at eighty: that's a face and a lifetime. The closing jab about your own rulebook lands.

modeler: Go in five rules: the minimal local rule case. 'Count the rules in your routine' turns it into a tool. Rules list is slightly loose.
skeptic: Go rules and the 'two and a half millennia' claim are hedged ('roughly', 'something like'). Checkable, vivid, and 'count your own routine' invites self-audit.
clinician: Go's five rules are vivid; 'count the rules in your own routine' is a small step. Careful not to become a self-audit.
habit: 'Now count the rules in your own routine.' That's the rep. Do it tomorrow morning; say when.
contemplative: Go in five rules: clear. 'Now count the rules in your own routine' is a nice turn, but too thin to practice.
stress: Go's 2,500-year record is real history. 'Count the rules in your routine' puts it on the reader.
gamedesigner: Go is the perfect game example, rules fit in a paragraph. Ends on 'count your routine's rules'. Good agency beat.
structural: Go rules are clear and the 'count your routine's rules' prompt is nice. Still a game with no rule-makers in conflict.
satirist: Go, five rules, 2,500 years: Bryson's trick. 'Now count the rules in your own routine' is a good turn to the reader.
mythmaker: A child learns it Sunday and is losing to it at eighty: a whole life in one clause. The closing 'count the rules in your routine' turns it on me.

modeler: The eye as a consequence of a consequence: textbook emergence, built bottom-up. Love it.
skeptic: The missing eye rule is a genuinely illuminating, accurate example of emergence. The best evidence-shaped passage here.
clinician: Lost on non-Go players. Shorter.
habit: Fascinating, but only if you play Go. Non-players will lose the eye logic.
contemplative: A real wonder, but Go vocabulary loses the lay reader. One plain sentence about the eye would carry it.
stress: The eye-rule point is precise and checkable. An excellent example of emergence.
gamedesigner: Brilliant for Go players. Non-players lose 'liberties' and the two eyes. Add a one-line picture of an eye.
structural: 'There is no eye rule' is the clearest emergence illustration in the chunk. Keep it.
satirist: 'There is no eye rule.' Real wonder from a real fact. The best emergence example in the chunk.
mythmaker: 'There is no eye rule' is a genuinely thrilling reveal. The best abstract beat in Part One.

modeler: Best passage here: eye derived step by step from the capture rule. A local rule building a global form, shown, not asserted.
skeptic: Genuinely strong emergence example, and correct. Non-players will stumble on the suicide-rule clause; a diagram would fix it.
clinician: Go capture mechanics lose non-players. Point is good; the walk-through is too technical.
habit: The eye mechanics lose non-players halfway through. Keep the punchline, no eye rule, and trim the capture walkthrough.
contemplative: An admirer's Go lesson. Too much mechanism for anyone who doesn't play. One sentence would carry the point.
stress: Rigorous: eye logic is derived, not asserted. The best emergence evidence in the book. Dense but earned.
gamedesigner: Brilliant point, but the capture-exception sentence will lose a non-player. A tiny diagram would make it teach itself.
structural: Emergence from the capture rule is elegant. The explanation is dense for lay readers.
satirist: The eye as a consequence of a consequence: earned wonder with the working shown. It's dense, but it plays fair.
mythmaker: The eye insight is wonderful, but the capture mechanics read like a rulebook. A diagram or a beginner's first lost group would help.

modeler: Two eyes as a consequence of a consequence: real emergence, mechanism shown step by step. Best passage in the batch.
skeptic: Eye explanation is correct and plainly told. 'Consequence of a consequence' is earned here, which is rare. Real emergence, no overclaiming.
clinician: Elegant emergence point, but the eye mechanics lose a lay reader. No person in it; fine as theory, not as help.
habit: Eye mechanics get dense fast, two holes, one breath. Fascinating, but nothing to do Monday and tough sledding for a non-player.
contemplative: The breath image carries the eye well. 'Consequence of a consequence' is clever. End on the vanished group instead.
stress: Two eyes as a consequence of a consequence is real and testable. Stays inside the game, so the reader risks nothing.
gamedesigner: Eye explanation plays well: one hole dies, two live. All spectacle for me though; give me a move to try.
structural: Eye explanation lands for a lay reader. Emergence shown with a real mechanism. Still no human lever anywhere.
satirist: The eye explained by mechanism, not mysticism. 'A consequence of a consequence' earns its wonder honestly.
mythmaker: The big group vanishing in front of a beginner is a real scene. Put that watching beginner on the reader and it'd hit home.

modeler: Eyes appear nowhere in the rules: a global form as consequence of a consequence. Precise, mechanistic and correct. One eye versus two is lovely.
skeptic: Eye consequences are accurate and precisely stated. 'A consequence of a consequence' illuminates emergence without overreaching. Good evidence, if from games only.
clinician: Fascinating but Go-heavy; eye mechanics demand attention the reader may lack. Insight without step. Trim.
habit: Insightful for Go players, heavy for everyone else. Eyes, breaths, groups. Cut to one idea: rules never mention the thing.
contemplative: This is a lecture on Go. 'A consequence of a consequence' is cleverness. Fewer eyes, fewer words.
stress: Eyes as consequence of a consequence is precise and checkable. Dense in places; a beginner loses a group, learns.
gamedesigner: Insight is great but eye mechanics need a board in my hands. Lost the non-Go player; add a diagram or drop the detail.
structural: Eye as consequence of a consequence is elegant. Pure beauty of emergence; zero about power. Who writes real-world rules is the question.
satirist: The eye appearing nowhere in the rules is a genuine fact, well explained. 'Consequence of a consequence' is the plain sentence. Earned wonder.
mythmaker: The one-eyed group vanishing is a real loss every beginner feels. 'No eye rule' is a great reveal. Gets technical in the middle, though.

modeler: Real emergence from local rules: eyes aren't in the rules, they're consequences of consequences. Napkin-ready. Loved it.
skeptic: Go example is vivid and checkable: no eye rule exists. Good lay explanation. 'Consequence of a consequence' is neat, still true.
clinician: Eye-as-consequence is a genuinely clear explanation. Wonderful abstraction, zero usable step.
habit: Interesting Go detail, but dense and eye-rule detour. Nothing I can do before breakfast. Trim and add a noticing task.
contemplative: Too much. Rules, eyes, breaths, consequences of consequences. I cannot take it in one exhale. Choose one image and stay.
stress: Go eyes as consequence-of-consequence is checkable and vivid. Concrete in the game, abstract for the reader's life.
gamedesigner: Go eye explanation is great level design talk: rules say nothing about the thing. Clear and surprising. No move for me.
structural: Go makes rule-versus-outcome vivid, and 'consequence of a consequence' is a mechanism. Still a game; no owner, no lever.
satirist: Go's rules never mention an eye; 'two eyes live' as a consequence of a consequence. Real, checkable, wonderful. Best paragraph so far. Concrete knowledge, little to do.
mythmaker: The eye as a hole in your own stones — and everyone's watched a big group vanish. Stakes, a loss, a turn. 'Consequence of a consequence' lands.

modeler: Sharp contrast: properties live in arrangements, not pieces. Sellers would nod.
skeptic: A fair contrast, though Go's rules shape strategy more than this admits. Mostly sound.
clinician: Chess comparison is a detour. Cut.
habit: Chess versus Go is a third pass on one point. Cut it.
contemplative: The comparison to chess adds length, not light. Cut it, or reduce it to one line.
stress: A fair comparison. Clear.
gamedesigner: A sharp contrast, but it slips into Global Form jargon. Say 'patterns the rules never named'.
structural: The chess contrast sharpens the point. Good.
satirist: The chess contrast sharpens it. A stone has no properties; only arrangements do. Good.
mythmaker: The chess comparison gets inside-baseball. Fine for players, opaque for others. Trim it.

modeler: Identical, worthless units whose properties live only in arrangements. Good contrast with chess's built-in powers.
skeptic: Good contrast. Overstated: chess mastery is also mostly pattern knowledge the rules never mention.
clinician: Ends in capitalized jargon. Letters analogy helps; 'Global Forms/Local Rule' undoes it.
habit: The Chess vs Go contrast closes on Global Forms and Local Rule jargon. It's abstract and slightly dense.
contemplative: The letters image is good. The chess contrast and the capitalized terms crowd it. Keep only the letters.
stress: The chess contrast sharpens it. The letter analogy works. Short and correct.
gamedesigner: The letters analogy makes the chess/Go contrast click. Clean, short, and it earns the jargon at the end.
structural: Good contrast. Still only about games.
satirist: The letters analogy is good. Capitalized Global Forms and Local Rule show up like ushers nobody hired.
mythmaker: The letters analogy works. It's still pieces and patterns, with nobody at the board.

modeler: The letters analogy works. Properties exist only in arrangements, and that's a structural claim, not a mood.
skeptic: Letters analogy works. 'Only arrangements have properties' overstates it, since a stone's liberties are local. Say 'mostly'.
clinician: Letters-on-a-page analogy makes it easy. Pure concept, no reader stake, no step. Acceptable in an explanatory chapter.
habit: The letters-on-this-page analogy lands. Still pure concept. What arrangement of my day has a property no single habit has?
contemplative: The letters on this page: beautiful, I feel it as I read. The capitalized terms at the end cool it. Trust the letters.
stress: The letter analogy lands. Then the book's jargon gets slapped onto Go after the fact. Leave it as a claim about arrangements and stop there.
gamedesigner: Letters-on-the-page analogy lands mid-read. The Global Form/Local Rule tag at the end is a rulebook line, not a move.
structural: Letters-to-sentences analogy works. Pure abstraction; nothing a group could pull.
satirist: Letters-and-sentences analogy works. Then 'Global Forms that no Local Rule anticipated': capitals arrive in costume. Busy, busy, busy. Cut that last line.
mythmaker: The letters-on-this-page turn is clever. Then 'Global Forms' slams the door. Nobody here is holding anything.

modeler: Chess versus Go on stone identity; letters in sentences. Defines Global Forms no Local Rule anticipated. Clean, but 'almost only arrangements' is fussy.
skeptic: Chess versus Go and the letters analogy are clear. 'Almost only arrangements' is hedged. Leaps a bit from game to a general vocabulary of mastery.
clinician: Letters-and-sentences image is lovely and clear. Pure concept; no action for a struggling reader.
habit: Letters on a page is a good metaphor. No action. A one-liner of what I'd look for would help.
contemplative: The letters image is good. 'Almost only arrangements' and the closing term stiffen it. Say it simply.
stress: Chess versus Go and letters in sentences: tight, memorable. Names the book's term earned by example.
gamedesigner: Letters versus stones lands. Nice payoff naming Global Forms. But I'm still spectating; no prediction or task.
structural: 'Rules never mentioned' patterns: but real rules were mentioned by someone, with interests. Alphabet analogy is lovely and evasive.
satirist: Chess versus Go, letters versus sentences. Good. Then 'Global Forms that no Local Rule anticipated' puts the costume back on. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: Letters on the page mean nothing alone, yet you read sentences: a good image that lives in the reader's own eyes. Knight versus stone is clear. Few stakes.

modeler: Chess versus Go and the letters analogy make the global-from-local point cleanly. Name the Local Rule once, explicitly.
skeptic: Chess versus Go contrast is clear and the letters analogy helps. Coins a name for emergence without showing why the name earns its keep.
clinician: Letters-to-sentences analogy is clean and names the book's term. Concept only; no application yet.
habit: Letters-and-sentences comparison lands well. Still a concept with no rep; name something I can spot today.
contemplative: The letters on the page image is lovely and close. The chess comparison and the term arrive too fast.
stress: Chess versus Go sets up emergence cleanly. Letters-and-sentences helps. Still a framing, not a test.
gamedesigner: Chess vs Go plus the letters analogy plays well. Names a term without a trial. Lecture, but a good one.
structural: Chess versus Go and letters-to-sentences land well. Emergent form named. Don't let emergence hide who set the rules.
satirist: Chess versus Go and the letters-on-a-page comparison are good. Then the capitalized Global Forms and Local Rule arrive, a Concept doing the work of a name.
mythmaker: Letters on this page meaning nothing alone, yet you're reading: a good rhyme with the Go image. Still no human; the knight versus stone is neat.

modeler: The rule set evolved by play-testing patches: that's design by iteration. The ruleset as Global Form is a nice second-order point.
skeptic: 'As far as anyone can tell' is the right hedge. The rules accumulating is historically defensible.
clinician: Interesting, clear.
habit: 'The elegance emerged too.' A nice close to the Go section.
contemplative: 'The elegance emerged too.' That is quietly beautiful. The middle list can shorten.
stress: Rules refined through centuries of play: a real historical record. Good.
gamedesigner: A rule set that emerged by play is a great second beat. Satisfying payoff.
structural: Rules as an accumulated Global Form. Strong. Constitutions amended by use would make the civic parallel.
satirist: 'The elegance emerged too.' Ko and komi as historical patches. Concrete and delightful.
mythmaker: 'The elegance emerged too' is a satisfying closer to the Go arc.

modeler: Rule set evolving by patches through play: Sellers' test-and-tweak, at civilizational scale. Self-similarity that actually holds.
skeptic: 'As far as anyone can tell' is the right hedge. 'The elegance emerged too' slides from history to slogan.
clinician: Family traditions example makes emergence relatable. Conceptual only.
habit: Rules that accumulated with no author. The family-traditions line makes it relatable. Still no rep.
contemplative: A family's traditions reach me, but they come last. Put them first and shorten the rules list.
stress: Hedged properly ('as far as anyone can tell'). Accumulated rules as emergent form: a strong historical claim.
gamedesigner: Satisfying twist: the rulebook itself emerged. Family traditions make it relatable. Good payoff.
structural: 'No author anywhere' is false for most rules that govern lives. Customs, yes. Codes get lobbied for. Distinguish the two.
satirist: Go accumulated patches, with no author. That's history doing the argument's work. Good.
mythmaker: 'The elegance emerged too' is a fine turn. The family traditions hint is a face; use it.

modeler: Rules patched by play over centuries: a slow balancing loop with a long delay. The holiday-traditions line makes it personal.
skeptic: 'As far as anyone can tell' is honest calibration. The leap to 'your routines probably came about the same way' is asserted, not shown.
clinician: Holiday traditions and 'your best routines' bring it home without blame. Still no step, but warmly framed.
habit: Holiday traditions and 'your own best routines' bring it home. No action, but I recognise my mornings in it.
contemplative: Holiday traditions make this warm and true. The last two sentences repeat the point; one would do.
stress: The historical hedge is honest. 'Your best routines came about the same way' is asserted with no test. Say how a reader could tell.
gamedesigner: Holiday traditions and 'your best routines' bring it home. The rules-as-patches payoff closes the Go arc nicely.
structural: Authorless rules is a convenient myth. Tax codes have authors and lobbyists. Add one line contrasting Go with rules that do.
satirist: Undesigned Go plus holiday traditions: plain and true. 'The elegance emerged too' is a mild flourish, but you've earned it.
mythmaker: Holiday traditions nobody wrote: that's warm and true. 'Your best routines' brings it home. Good rhyme with the elegance line.

modeler: n(n-1)/2, stated plainly. Real arithmetic, not metaphor. 'One property, two outcomes' is well put.
skeptic: The pairwise arithmetic is correct and checkable: 1,225 pairs. A real, usable insight.
clinician: Pairs arithmetic is clear and sets up a later payoff.
habit: Rules multiply as pairs. Concrete arithmetic that explains real overload.
contemplative: Pairs, not counts: clear arithmetic. The last sentence overreaches. End at 'unmanageable'.
stress: Pairwise arithmetic is concrete and cuts both ways. A strong, testable claim.
gamedesigner: The pairwise arithmetic is concrete and checkable. It sets up the commitments payoff later.
structural: Rules multiply pairwise. This is the regulatory-burden argument. Apply it to a real rulebook and it becomes a lever.
satirist: Fifty rules, 1,225 pairs. Actual arithmetic, correctly done. Generative and unmanageable as one property. Keep.
mythmaker: The arithmetic of pairs is clear and pays off later with commitments. Good setup.

modeler: Healthy limit on the framework's reach. Good.
skeptic: The taxes line is funny and it limits the framework's reach. I trust a book that tells me where it doesn't apply.
clinician: Permission to just do the boring task. Anti-avoidance without shame. Good.
habit: 'Filing your taxes. Do it.' A refreshing permission to just act.
contemplative: 'Do it, and spend the search elsewhere.' Humble and practical. I smiled.
stress: 'Do your taxes': the framework admitting its own limits. Love it.
gamedesigner: 'Just do your taxes' is honest, funny and useful. It prevents over-application.
structural: 'Filing taxes, just do it' accepts designed friction as fate. Return-free filing is a lever a group can pull.
satirist: 'Filing your taxes is not secretly a beautiful system.' The book laughing at its own temptation. More, please.
mythmaker: 'Filing your taxes is not secretly beautiful. Do it.' Funny, human, and it forgives the reader.

modeler: Produced by isn't traceable from. Right. 'Feel it before you explain it' is practical.
skeptic: 'You'll feel its state before you can explain it' licenses intuition in exactly the noisy domain where intuition misleads. Caution needed.
clinician: Stops the hunt for the one cause; anti-rumination. 'Work with the pattern' needs a concrete example.
habit: 'You'll feel its state before you can explain it' stops over-analysis. Useful.
contemplative: 'You'll feel its state before you can explain it.' This honors lived knowing over analysis. Beautiful.
stress: 'The fix isn't better analysis' risks licensing gut feel. Say when data does help.
gamedesigner: The marriage-mood example lands. 'Feel its state before you explain it' is a usable stance.
structural: 'Produced by' versus 'traceable from' is a good distinction. The marriage-mood example is clear.
satirist: 'No spreadsheet of their individual states outputs it' is plain. 'Feel its state before you can explain it' is honest.
mythmaker: 'No spreadsheet outputs a marriage's mood on a given evening.' A face and stakes. Lovely.

modeler: Sensitive dependence plus open boundaries, correct. Lose the forecast, keep the leverage: good. Dense phrasing.
skeptic: Sensitivity to initial conditions is real. 'Costs forecast, not leverage' is asserted. Leverage needs some forecasting too.
clinician: Chaos theory compressed too hard. Defer to Part Four.
habit: A chaos-theory paragraph that defers to Part Four. 'Rules over outcomes' is the payload. Keep just that.
contemplative: Dense and deferred. 'It costs the forecast, not the leverage' is the gem. Keep only that.
stress: Lose the forecast, keep the leverage: sound Taleb logic. Dense phrasing. Simplify it.
gamedesigner: Chaos plus incompleteness, compressed and deferred to Part Four. Too heavy for here. Shrink it to the forecast-vs-leverage line.
structural: Forecast lost, leverage kept: an important claim. Too compressed to follow here. Expand it or defer it.
satirist: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions, unnamed and compressed into one sentence. Say 'chaos,' name Lorenz, slow down.
mythmaker: Chaos and open systems compressed into a lecture. The forecast-versus-leverage line is the keeper; illustrate it.

modeler: Forecast lost, leverage kept: correct reading of sensitive dependence. Garden watering is the right napkin.
skeptic: Forecast versus leverage is the right distinction, and the garden makes it plain. It defers the maths honestly.
clinician: 'You can't forecast August but you can still water it' eases outcome anxiety. A good reframe, one step short of a step.
habit: 'You can't say what a garden will look like in August, but you can still water it.' Lovely. Name my watering.
contemplative: 'You can still water it' is the heart. Chaos and the Nest come before it as noise. Let the garden lead.
stress: Gives up the forecast, keeps the leverage. Garden watering is the right antifragile stance. Holds up.
gamedesigner: 'Can't forecast, can still water' is a clear operating rule. Promising Part Four is fine here, since the payoff already lands.
structural: 'Push on rules, not outcomes' is my creed. Now tell me whose rules and who holds the pen.
satirist: 'You can't say what August looks like, but you can water it.' That's plain speech carrying chaos theory.
mythmaker: 'You can't say what August looks like, but you can still water it.' Good image buried mid-paragraph; lead with it.

modeler: Preferential attachment gives skew: a real mechanism behind Pareto. Good derivation from the loop itself.
skeptic: Preferential attachment behind skew is properly called 'one mechanism.' Good calibration.
clinician: Pareto rehash, wordy. Little for the reader.
habit: A Pareto aside in abstract terms. It doesn't tell me what to do differently.
contemplative: The idea of skew is fine. It is wordy, hedged, and abstract. Halve it and give one human example.
stress: Fat tails from reinforcing feedback is correct and well hedged. Good.
gamedesigner: 'Expect skew' is a useful prediction, but it's one more bolt-on to a long chapter. The curve sags.
structural: 'A skewed result isn't evidence something's broken' launders inequality as physics. Say the rules can be changed.
satirist: Pareto in a trench coat. Name the 80/20 rule and preferential attachment; the hedge 'one well-studied mechanism' is good.
mythmaker: Pareto in systems-speak. 'Fuller stock filling faster' is jargon. Who is on the losing end of the concentration?

modeler: Matthew effect named as the mechanism behind skew. Real reinforcing loop, with the balancing side promised next. Good.
skeptic: Properly hedged as 'one mechanism'. It points to a next paragraph that isn't in this unit; fix the dangling reference.
clinician: 'Skewed isn't broken or destiny' is protective, but the dangling 'next paragraph' reference confuses.
habit: A clear 80/20 explanation. Tell me what to do when I see skew: look for the reinforcing loop?
contemplative: A fair caution. 'As the next paragraph shows' points at nothing here. It is longer than its point.
stress: A real prediction about skewed outcomes, with a caveat against fatalism. The dangling 'next paragraph' reference needs fixing.
gamedesigner: Reframes skew as expected rather than a sign something's broken. That's a useful prediction. The examples are clear.
structural: Cumulative advantage is a real structure. Recommendation engines have owners. Name the lever: regulation, design choices.
satirist: Readers and recommendations make 80/20 mechanical, not mystical. Calling it 'well-studied' needs one name or one study.
mythmaker: The child who reads more is a face, so keep her. 'As the next paragraph shows' dangles.

modeler: Finally, the balancing side for success-to-the-successful, with draft picks as the example. Meadows' own trap and fix. Keep.
skeptic: A concrete intervention with real examples. Draft picks and rotating chairs make it usable.
clinician: Concrete intervention with familiar examples.
habit: A periodic scheduled reset, like rotating who runs the meeting. A real intervention, with a cadence.
contemplative: Rotating who runs the meeting is small, practical and fair. Good.
stress: Periodic resets with draft picks as the example: concrete, historical, actionable. Strong.
gamedesigner: Draft picks and rotating chairs are concrete reset mechanics. Game designers do exactly this.
structural: Finally a lever: scheduled resets from outside the loop. Draft picks, rotation. Extend to antitrust and estate taxes.
satirist: Draft picks and rotating meeting chairs: concrete fixes for rich-get-richer. Plain and useful.
mythmaker: Draft picks and rotating who runs the meeting are concrete fixes. Nice.

modeler: 'There isn't one' overclaims: loops can contain broken parts. Say 'the loop may be the problem, not a part.'
skeptic: 'There isn't one' broken piece is overconfident. Loops can contain broken parts. Say 'probably not only one.'
clinician: 'Stop looking for the broken piece' relieves self-blame. Add what to do instead.
habit: A doable exercise. Add the cue: tonight, about the thing that annoyed you today.
contemplative: 'There isn't one' releases blame. That is kind and usable. Keep.
stress: 'There isn't one' is too absolute. Loops can have broken parts too. Say 'probably not one.'
gamedesigner: A real move, but 'there isn't one' overclaims. Give me what to look for instead of the broken piece.
structural: 'No broken piece.' True, but there's often a broken rule with an author. Point the reader there.
satirist: Doable. But 'there isn't one' overclaims; loops can contain broken parts too. Soften it to 'probably.'
mythmaker: 'There isn't a broken piece' is a bold, freeing exercise.

modeler: Familiar quote, loosely tied to acceleration. Inert.
skeptic: A borrowed epigraph that doesn't connect to derivatives. Swap it or cut it.
clinician: Familiar quote, loosely connected.
habit: A borrowed poster quote that's only loosely linked to acceleration.
contemplative: Familiar but warm. Unattributed. Its fit with acceleration is loose.
stress: A well-worn line. It fits loosely.
gamedesigner: A familiar epigraph, loosely connected.
structural: A cliché epigraph, loosely tied to the chapter.
satirist: A John Shedd poster quote, uncredited and only loosely related. Credit it or cut it.
mythmaker: A familiar ship epigraph, loosely tied to derivatives. Pick something about motion felt.

modeler: Epigraph with no anchor to motion-as-derivative until you read on. Thin.
skeptic: Flagged as 'attributed', which is credit due. As an epigraph it just decorates.
clinician: Epigraph with little link to what follows. Weak in place.
habit: A familiar quote that does minimal work here. It's harmless as a chapter mark.
contemplative: Short, but it doesn't connect to anything in the chapter yet. Clever more than it serves.
stress: Attribution properly hedged. Pure ornament, but harmless.
gamedesigner: A stock quote with only a loose link to acceleration. Swap in something that sets up the chapter's hook.
structural: Galileo stood against an institution. That subtext is wasted here.
satirist: 'Attributed' is honest. Otherwise it's decor; its link to acceleration is left implied.
mythmaker: A defiant man under pressure, good stakes. The tie to acceleration is loose.

modeler: Fitting setup for imperceptible motion, but on its own it's decoration. Fine as an epigraph.
skeptic: 'Attributed' is properly hedged and it fits the next chapter's point. A good epigraph that doesn't claim more than it can.
clinician: Apt epigraph for invisible motion. Does its small job; nothing to use.
habit: Fine epigraph, sets up felt-versus-real motion. Does its small job, nothing more.
contemplative: A quiet epigraph that fits the chapter. It asks nothing of me, but that is fine here.
stress: An apocryphal quote doing a mood job. It sets up the plane passage, barely. It risks nothing.
gamedesigner: Neat setup for the felt-acceleration chapter. It works as an epigraph and earns its slot without asking for more.
structural: Decorative epigraph. Galileo's actual fight was with an institution, and the book ignores that.
satirist: An attributed, probably apocryphal epigraph, and you do flag the hedge. It's ornament doing no work; the plane does this job better.
mythmaker: A fine epigraph, and it sets up the plane nicely. On its own it's a borrowed face, not ours.

modeler: Galileo epigraph: the felt-still-but-moving theme fits the position/velocity chapter. Apt, but the attribution is shaky and it's decoration.
skeptic: 'Attributed to' is honest, since the quote is probably apocryphal. A fine epigraph. 'Feels perfectly still' nicely names the gap between sense and fact.
clinician: Hopeful for anyone feeling stuck: things move though they feel still. Good epigraph. Attribution hedge is honest.
habit: Fun epigraph, perfect for the idea. Doesn't do anything yet.
contemplative: Quiet and true. It asks me to trust what I cannot feel.
stress: 'Attributed' is honest; the line is likely apocryphal. Tiny, apt, but decoration only.
gamedesigner: Fun, defiant epigraph; clean hook for something unseen yet real. No move.
structural: Galileo epigraph. Defiant, decorative. Doesn't name rules or levers.
satirist: 'Attributed to' is the honest hedge: Galileo probably never said it. Fine epigraph; no work done.
mythmaker: Galileo muttering under his breath, defiant: the human cost sits behind the line. A good doorway. Attribution hedge is honest.

modeler: Evocative for stuck lives, but stuck is a balancing loop, and the line doesn't say what holds it. Pretty, not mechanism.
skeptic: Attribution is flagged as 'attributed', honest. The stuck-life comparison asks a feeling of the reader without support. Mild resonance.
clinician: 'Much as a stuck life does' names stuckness gently and offers hope without blaming. Needs a step to follow.
habit: Stuck-life tie-in is personal and sticky. But a quote isn't a practice. What do I do while it moves?
contemplative: A stuck life, felt as still ground. This touches me. The gloss after the dash is explaining the poem.
stress: Attribution is shaky (apocryphal) and it is flagged only softly. Stuck-life tie is warm, not tested.
gamedesigner: Short and resonant for a stuck player. No next action, though.
structural: Stuck-life analogy resonates and is quick. But stuck for whom, and why? Some stillness is designed.
satirist: Galileo's 'and yet it moves' applied to a stuck life: wry, short, relatable. The attribution caveat is the kind of honesty I like.
mythmaker: Galileo muttering at a still Earth, mapped onto a stuck life. Defiance with a person inside it. Small and it works.

modeler: Good gating: no feedback, no compounding. Brief.
skeptic: Gating the question on the prior answer is good structure. A transition.
clinician: Gating line; fine.
habit: Gating logic, clear and brief.
contemplative: Honest gating. Fine. It could be shorter.
stress: Sensible gating. Fine.
gamedesigner: A gated branch from the last test. Good flowchart onboarding.
structural: A gating instruction. Fine.
satirist: A clear gate. Fine.
mythmaker: A conditional gate. Procedural.

modeler: Correct gate: no feedback, no compounding. Bricks versus savings is clean, but it's a doorway.

clinician: Clear gating sentence. Functional only.
habit: Gatekeeping transition. It's clear and functional and earns nothing on its own.
contemplative: Gate-keeping instructions. The bricks and the savings account are clear. The rest is book plumbing.
stress: A gate condition. Useful structure, little content.
gamedesigner: A gating rule, which is good level design, but it's dry. A beat I just pass through.
structural: Gate sentence. Fine.
satirist: Bricks don't accelerate, savings do. It's a serviceable gate.
mythmaker: Bricks versus savings is clear and functional. A gate, not a scene.

modeler: Right gate: no feedback means no compounding. But this is a router, and the bricks-versus-habit contrast needs a stock named.
skeptic: 'Tell you everything' is overconfident, and the passage leans on an unseen prior chapter. Compared to what? Spell out the condition here.
clinician: Gate references the prior chapter abstractly; 'feedback' and 'compounds' unexplained here. Reader arriving cold is lost.
habit: Bricks versus habits is clear. But 'only ask this if last chapter said yes' is gating, not a cue. Tell me what to check.
contemplative: The opening condition confuses me before I arrive. Bricks against friendship is good. Start there.
stress: A useful gate: no feedback means no compounding. The bricks line is clear. It's routing, not insight.
gamedesigner: Lost the player: 'ask this one if the last chapter came back yes' points at a check I can't see. Restate the gate.
structural: 'If the last chapter came back yes' is opaque out of context. A throat-clearing gate. State the test plainly.
satirist: 'Only if the last chapter came back yes' leans on context I don't have. Bricks versus savings is fine. Murky as a doorway.
mythmaker: The opening gatekeeping line confuses. The bricks against the friendship are good. Lead with the friendship that surprised you.

modeler: Bricks versus savings: acceleration needs feedback inside the thing. 'No feedback never compounds' is the right gate. Short, exact, usable.
skeptic: Clear gating condition: ask only if feedback exists. States where the tool does not apply. Calibrated and useful. Bricks versus savings is crisp.
clinician: Gate question ('only if last chapter came back yes') avoids overreach. Bricks versus habits is clear. Scoped, honest.
habit: Gate question: is there feedback in it? Bricks versus habit. Good filter, a single question to carry.
contemplative: Bricks, savings, a friendship: easy to feel. Cut the conditional about the last chapter; it fusses.
stress: Gates itself: only ask if feedback is present. Specific limit, bricks versus savings. Good.
gamedesigner: Bricks versus savings account is a good gate: ask only if feedback is present. A usable test for the player.

modeler: Parable disclaimed as parable, built as stages with outputs becoming inputs. Honest framing. 'Week at the largest scale' is a real scale claim.

modeler: Distinction as first act is Spencer-Brown-ish and evocative. 'Arithmetic was the universe' is mysticism, not mechanism.

modeler: 'Repetition counted itself' is poetry passing as mechanism. Who reads the count? No stock, no loop.

structural: Cosmic abstraction with no use for anyone. Who is this for?

mythmaker: Cosmic abstractions with no face. 'The second time made the first once' is clever but cold.

modeler: 'A second tap makes the first one once' is elegant: counting emerges from repetition. The output-to-input refrain is earned here.

clinician: Mythic prose, tap metaphor helps a little. 'Makes the first one once' is opaque. Liturgy, not help; fine for its place.

structural: The tap image helps, but 'makes the first one once' is a riddle. Mythic register, no use.
satirist: 'In the beginning there was no beginning.' Busy, busy, busy. The tap on the table is nice; the rest is vestments.
mythmaker: The single tap on a silent table, and the second tap making the first one once: that's a myth image. Keep it.

modeler: Two taps and the first becomes one of something: counting from repetition, built up from a local act. Output feeds input. Charming, but pure story.

clinician: Lovely tap-on-a-table image, clear. Pure myth; nothing to use. Fine as parable, not help.
habit: The tap-on-a-table image works. Cosmology with no step. Fine as mythos.
contemplative: Two taps on a silent table. This is beautiful, and almost enough. The italic closer repeats what you have shown.

mythmaker: The two taps on a silent table: first a sound, then one of something. A memorable image, and the refrain returns. No one's there, by design.

modeler: Output becomes input: genuine iteration, the second tap makes the first countable. But 'without cause' is hand-waving. Keep the recursion.

clinician: Lovely, readable origin myth. Pure story; no pain named, no next step, but harmless.

gamedesigner: Taps on a table: lovely, concrete image of counting. But it's pure cutscene. Let me tap.

mythmaker: Two taps on a silent table makes the first count only after the second. Real myth-craft, and the italic line sets up a return. Nobody there, by design.

mythmaker: Dots settling into triangles is wonder you can try yourself. Strong. It's still a cosmos with no one in it, which is fine here.

mythmaker: Pencil, triangle, ten thousand dots: you can do it tonight. 'A picture no single step could show you' is a good turn. Hands-on, no cast needed.

modeler: Noise as resilience: plausible (variation buffers shock). The claim is good; it needs the redundancy mechanism stated.

satirist: Noise as robustness is a real idea, stated cleanly inside the myth.

modeler: Correlated failure versus diversity: a real resilience mechanism, cleanly stated. Strongest of the iterations so far.

mythmaker: Chance as survival is a real turn with real stakes for structures. Still no one to care about.

modeler: The monoculture blight is a genuine mechanism: correlated failure. Diversity as resilience is shown, not asserted. Good.
skeptic: The monoculture blight is a solid historical example. 'Imperfection was never the defect' overreaches. Variation helps in some conditions, not always.
clinician: Reframing imperfection as resilience is shame-reducing, earned through the wheat example, not bypassed. Works.
habit: Wheat field makes diversity-as-resilience obvious. Big-picture only; one line on varying my own routine would land it.
contemplative: The wheat field explains it simply. Turn it to me once: my own imperfections as endurance.
stress: Monoculture blight has history behind it: the Irish famine, Gros Michel bananas. This is antifragility done right. Keep it.
gamedesigner: The wheat blight makes the abstraction stick. It's still narrated at me; tie the variety point to my own habits.
structural: Monoculture blight is a policy story: subsidies, seed patents. It gestures at structure, then retreats into myth.
satirist: Monoculture blight is a real fact (Irish potato famine, name it). It's the one sermon with a farm in it.
mythmaker: The blighted field against the mixed field is a clean image with stakes. A farmer watching it happen would give it a heart.

modeler: Monoculture versus mixed wheat is variance as buffer. Real mechanism, mapped onto your week. Good, if brief: one weak point breaks whole.
skeptic: Monoculture-versus-diversity is real ecology, applied by analogy to a week. 'Your week works like the field' is asserted; say 'may'. Imperfection-as-raw-material is overstated.
clinician: Wheat blight to your week: build in a few ways of getting done. Reframes imperfection without blame. Real, usable advice.
habit: Wheat field to your week: a routine with one weak point breaks whole. Make it a question: where's mine?
contemplative: Wheat field, then my week: clear and true. A few lines too many, but it can be lived.

gamedesigner: Wheat field then 'your week works like the field' is a clean map from parable to action. Great.
structural: Monoculture wheat is a genuinely structural example: shared weak point. Applied to your routine only; apply to supply chains and institutions too.
satirist: Wheat blight is a concrete fact, and 'your week works like the field' is a usable test. Imperfection as survival: earned.
mythmaker: The wheat field and the blight is a stake and a cost. Imperfection saves, and then it lands on your week. Echoes the refrain too.

modeler: Chance per roll vs shape across many rolls: correct, useful, humane. Keep.
skeptic: 'A better shape across many rolls, never a guarantee on any one.' This is base rates versus outcomes, plainly. The best calibration here.
clinician: Good rule, bad roll: losing isn't proof you failed. Strongly anti-self-blame.
habit: 'A good rule buys a better shape, not a guarantee.' This keeps people from quitting after one bad roll.
contemplative: 'You can still lose on the one roll that mattered' is mercy for good people having bad luck. It breaks the myth's voice, though.
stress: 'Chance doesn't retire because the rule was good.' A good rule buys a better shape, never a guarantee. The book's most robust paragraph.
gamedesigner: 'A good rule buys a better shape, not a guarantee' is honest, practical and resonant. Keep.
structural: A good rule buys a better shape, not a guarantee. Honest, and it refuses the just-world gloss. Good.
satirist: 'Chance doesn't retire because the rule was good.' Plain, useful, and it consoles without lying. Best unit in the section.
mythmaker: 'Lose on the one roll that happened to matter.' Finally a person with something at stake. It grants grief its place.

modeler: Reinforcing plus balancing, run simultaneously: exactly the structure I demand. Best mechanism in the myth.

mythmaker: The myth turns into a systems textbook mid-verse. Put reinforcing and balancing into an image, like breath or heartbeat.

contemplative: Your warm body renewing itself: lovely. The two loops arrive too fast. One loop per paragraph.

structural: Build-and-hold loops explained cleanly. Mechanism named, which I respect. But 'life' parable lacks any institution or lever.
satirist: Build only and you consume yourself; hold only and you never last. Body doing both while you read is good. 'Arriving at a rule' is metaphor-as-mechanism.
mythmaker: Build-only consumes itself, hold-only never lasts: a real pair of failures. 'Your body is running both as you read' is a good pull-in. Dense, but earned.

modeler: Self-model is named, but not yet a strange loop: show the self-symbol changing a decision.
skeptic: 'Revisable by repetition' repeats the self chapter's optimism without new support.
clinician: Revisable self, clearly said.
habit: 'Built by repetition, revised by repetition' again. Clear, and repetitive within the chunk.
contemplative: 'Arrived as a habit still being built.' Gentle and hopeful. Good.
stress: Fine myth beat, consistent with earlier claims.
gamedesigner: Revisable by repetition carries the practice into the myth. Good.
structural: Self-revision by repetition again. Interchangeable with Chapter 7.
satirist: A loop representing its own looping: Hofstadter, uncredited, in hushed tones. Clear enough to fans only.
mythmaker: The self arrives with no face and no wonder. This should be the myth's Adam moment. Give it a first look.

modeler: A real strange loop: the self-picture changes the next step. Hofstadter would sign it. It never names what limits the folding.
skeptic: A self that is 'never fixed' at least respects Selfless. It is still myth dressed as mechanism; label it story outright.
clinician: Lovely cosmology, but abstract and dense. 'Never fixed' is quietly hopeful; say it to the reader plainly instead of to the universe.
habit: Lovely cosmology, zero reps. 'That is what I keep doing' is the seed of a habit; hand me the question, not the myth.
contemplative: 'That is me, and that is what I keep doing' is the heart. 'Folded inward one level further' and the italic coda are too much. Let the recognition stand alone.
stress: Cosmic origin-myth for selfhood. Nice fold, but nothing here can be wrong. Story, not claim; fine if labeled as such.
gamedesigner: 'That is me, and that is what I keep doing' lands. The closing italic line is a cryptic cutscene. Cut it or say plainly what's being made.
structural: Cosmic self-reflection loop, elegantly turned. No rule, no owner, no lever; a mood about systems, not a mechanism.
satirist: Genesis in a hushed voice, never labeled foma. 'Folded inward one level further.' Busy, busy, busy. Admit it's a myth, then say 'you notice your habits.'
mythmaker: The 'that is me' moment is a real turn. But nobody has it. Show one creature catching its own reflection, then let the story go cosmic.

modeler: The self-model changes the next step: a true Hofstadter loop, not mere recursion. Catching a habit midway makes it real.
skeptic: The 'never fixed' self is defensible. But the self here makes itself alone. Lowery would ask where the other people are.
clinician: 'Catching yourself halfway through a habit' plus 'never fixed' is kind: the self as unfinished, not broken.
habit: 'Catching yourself halfway through a habit' is the moment I train for. Myth that points at a real rep. Good.
contemplative: Catching yourself halfway through a habit. Yes. Gentle, inward, honest about never being finished.
stress: Catching yourself mid-habit is recognizable. The sweep of evolution is myth. Fine as long as it never claims to be more.
gamedesigner: 'Catching yourself halfway through a habit' is a felt moment every player knows. A strong beat.
structural: Catching yourself mid-habit resonates. Inward by design, and acceptable as an origin beat.
satirist: Catching yourself mid-habit is relatable. 'The only thing left to make: meaning' is the hushed voice again.
mythmaker: Catching yourself halfway through a habit: the myth finally finds the reader. That's an earned turn.

modeler: Meaning supplied, not found: consistent with U0070's worth. Good closing turn, no overclaim.
skeptic: Meaning as supplied rather than found is honest, and it hands the work to the reader. It works as myth.
clinician: 'Universe supplies no meaning' can sink a bad-day reader. Pair it with something warmer than duty.
habit: Hands the meaning-making work to you, and the contrast with the seventh day lands. Resonant close.
contemplative: The work handed to you, not a rest. This is meaningful and warm. The middle could be one breath shorter.
stress: Honest that the universe supplies no meaning, and it hands the work to the reader. Humble and resonant.
gamedesigner: Handing the seventh day to the reader is a strong ending and real agency. Great payoff.
structural: The universe offers no meaning; readers make it. A clear ending. 'Each generation' could have meant institutions too.
satirist: The universe supplies no meaning; you do. The sabbath inversion is genuinely witty. Earned.
mythmaker: Handing the seventh day to the reader instead of resting is a genuinely moving inversion. A good climax.

modeler: Pointer only.
skeptic: A navigation pointer. Nothing to score beyond that.
clinician: Pointer; fine.
habit: Pointer to the appendix. Fine as navigation.
contemplative: A useful pointer. Fine as it is.
stress: A pointer only.
gamedesigner: A cross-reference note. Fine as navigation, and it does nothing else.
structural: A cross-reference. Fine.
satirist: Pointer. Fine.
mythmaker: A cross-reference. Fine, though it earns nothing.

modeler: A signpost and nothing more. It does no work in its place. Cut it, or fold it into the line before.
skeptic: A signpost. Clear, and it claims nothing, which I appreciate.
clinician: Signpost only. Fine as navigation, earns nothing on its own; fold into the preceding paragraph's last line.
habit: Signpost, clear and harmless. Doesn't need to earn more than it does; fine as a pointer.
contemplative: A plain signpost. It does its small job and asks nothing more.
stress: Pointer. Does its job, earns nothing beyond that.
gamedesigner: A signpost. Clear, but it gives me nothing to do here. Fine as a pointer, not a beat.
structural: Pure signpost. Fine as navigation, earns nothing beyond clarity.
