satirist: A signpost. Harmless and clear, and it does nothing more.
mythmaker: A signpost and nothing more. It's fine where it is but has no heart. Keep it short.

modeler: Pointer only. Fine in place, nothing to judge.
skeptic: A navigation pointer. Harmless, but it earns nothing beyond clarity.
clinician: Pointer only. Does its signposting job; earns nothing else.
habit: Signpost. Fine, does nothing else. Tell me when to say it aloud, who with, or drop it.
contemplative: A signpost. It does its small job, and asks nothing.
stress: A pointer to the appendix. Fine for navigation, no substance.
gamedesigner: Pure signpost with no play in it. Fine as a parenthetical, but it earns nothing on its own.
structural: Cross-reference. Fine, does nothing.
satirist: A cross-reference to the chant version. Harmless signage. It does its small job and claims nothing.
mythmaker: A signpost and nothing more. Fine in place, earns nothing.

modeler: A pointer to an appendix. Clear and helpful for sharing aloud; nothing else to score.
skeptic: Pointer to an appendix. Harmless and clear; nothing to score beyond signposting.
clinician: Useful pointer to a short version for sharing aloud. Practical and plain; minimal content.
habit: A pointer. Harmless and short. Doesn't earn more than that.
contemplative: A small pointer. Honest and clear.
stress: Pointer only. No claim, no risk. Keep as navigation, not as content.
gamedesigner: A pointer with no content and no move. Cut or fold into the stage list.
structural: Pointer to an appendix. Clear. Nothing else.
satirist: A parenthetical pointer to Appendix A. Plain and fine; nothing to score beyond that.
mythmaker: A stage direction about an appendix. Useful for groups, nothing to feel.

modeler: Navigation aside. Harmless, does no work worth scoring.
skeptic: A practical pointer for group recitation. Harmless and clear; no claim to test.
clinician: Practical pointer to a short spoken version. Small, specific, and easy to follow.
habit: Tiny pointer, but actionable: here is where to say it aloud. Useful, not exciting.
contemplative: A short, practical pointer for speaking together. Plain. It does exactly one thing.
stress: Pointer to Appendix A. Useful, modest. Nothing wrong, nothing earned beyond navigation.
gamedesigner: A pointer with no stakes. Fine as a footnote, nothing to score.
structural: Cross-reference. Clear, nothing more. A group ritual pointer is the only hint of collective use.
satirist: A stage direction pointing to an appendix. Useful, brief, and slyly admits the thing is ritual. Not much to score, but harmless.
mythmaker: Pointer to a spoken version. Functional and kind, but it's a stage direction. No image, no person, no cost.

modeler: Nice: a belief with a balancing loop that resists pushing. But it's an epigraph, so it does no mechanism work of its own.
skeptic: Apt, familiar, inert. It decorates the chapter rather than arguing anything; fine as an epigraph, earns nothing more.
clinician: Clear epigraph, but it gives nobody anything to do. Pure framing.
habit: Familiar quote, no rep attached. Tie it to the chapter's action or cut it.
contemplative: An old saying, plainly put. It sets the chapter's question well. It asks nothing of me yet.
stress: Old proverb, borrowed weight. Fine as a door, but it asks nothing of the reader and risks nothing.
gamedesigner: Clean epigraph, but it sets no goal for the chapter. Tie it to a move the reader will make.
structural: Familiar couplet about persuasion. Fine as a door, but it sets up belief as private conviction, not something institutions manufacture.
satirist: Borrowed proverb, unattributed. Fine as a door-knocker; credit Butler and it stops looking like the book's own wisdom.
mythmaker: Familiar proverb, sets the problem cleanly. Borrowed though; no face of its own.

modeler: A fine balancing-loop epigraph: opinion resists outside force. It lands only if the next paragraph names that resistance.
skeptic: Apt: persuasion against will fails. Earns its place if the chapter then lives by it.
clinician: Clear epigraph, but it's about persuading others, not helping a struggling reader. Decorative here.
habit: Sharp epigraph, instantly lands. Sets up the honesty argument well; no action, but it isn't trying to give one.
contemplative: A fair warning against forcing belief. It frames the chapter gently, though it stays a quote and never becomes a practice.
stress: Old line, true under strain: persuasion fails. Sets up the honesty section well.
gamedesigner: Tight epigraph that sets up the persuasion theme. It doesn't touch the reader yet. Fine to keep as framing.
structural: Familiar couplet on persuasion; sits there decoratively. Tie it to who does the convincing and why.
satirist: A good line with real teeth, and a fair warning to the book itself. It earns its place.
mythmaker: A sharp old couplet that sets up the chapter. It just needs the next passage to answer it with someone actually being convinced.

modeler: Apt epigraph on belief resisting force. Decoration, though it does foreshadow policy resistance.
skeptic: 'After Butler' honestly hedges a misquoted couplet. It fits a chapter on belief and persuasion. Good attribution discipline.
clinician: Familiar epigraph, clear. Connection to the chapter unproven here; decorative.
habit: Old couplet, clear point about persuasion. Serviceable epigraph, nothing to carry into the morning.
contemplative: An old truth about persuasion, softly placed. It disarms rather than fights. Good.
stress: A sturdy old couplet that sets up the argument. Some use as an epigraph, nothing beyond that.
gamedesigner: A familiar, wry epigraph that primes the persuasion chapter. Light, but it does its job.
structural: Apt epigraph, inert alone.
satirist: A sharp epigraph, correctly hedged with 'after'. Fine, but an ornament by itself; it depends on what follows.
mythmaker: A sharp old couplet that frames persuasion well. Borrowed wit, not our own face.

modeler: Forced assent breeds no change: a reactance loop in one line. Apt for the transparency argument. Epigraph only.
skeptic: Apt epigraph, and attribution 'after Butler' is honest about wording. It points at real persuasion research on reactance. Sets up the seams argument.
clinician: Wry epigraph; pushes against coercion. Good for tone. No step or reader pain addressed.
habit: True and quotable: you can't force belief. Great setup; no step yet.
contemplative: Plain and true; I have been that man. It stands alone.
stress: Known truth about persuasion, sets up the transparency promise. Old, repeated across cases.
gamedesigner: Relatable line, anyone who's argued knows it. Sets the premise; nothing to do yet.
structural: Apt epigraph on coercion and belief. Doesn't touch power structures. Fine as ornament.
satirist: Butler's couplet is a perfect rim shot, and everyone knows the guy convinced against his will. Sets up the seams.
mythmaker: Butler's couplet is the stubborn uncle at every family dinner. Sets up the book's opposite approach well. Funny and true.

modeler: Resonant proverb about forced persuasion. Implies resistance as a balancing loop, but never says so.
skeptic: True and well known: persuasion by force fails. Sets up transparency about seams, which I welcome. Not itself new.
clinician: Easy proverb, but it doesn't help the reader do anything. Sets tone only.
habit: Advice Monster in proverb form, nice. But no action here; it's an epigraph.
contemplative: True, and I have felt it. A gentle warning against forcing. Short enough to breathe with.
stress: Apt: forced belief fails. Sets up the no-persuasion stance, and it undercuts the author's own pull.
gamedesigner: Resonates, but sets up no move. Epigraph does lore work only.
structural: Wry and clear. Persuasion by coercion fails, true, but it says nothing about how groups actually change.
satirist: Butler's old chestnut earns its keep: nobody was ever argued into anything. Honest preface to a book that shows its seams.
mythmaker: Everyone has been the convinced-against-his-will man, or tried to convince him. Funny and true, and it earns the next move.

modeler: Interesting meta-move, discovery against construction. No stock or flow, just a stance. Fine as a setup.
skeptic: Disclosing construction is exactly the calibration I want. Name one belief system that does otherwise, to make the contrast checkable.
clinician: Honest about sources, which I respect. Nothing here for a struggling reader to use.
habit: Nice meta-honesty, zero action. Nothing for me to do Monday.
contemplative: Honest about its sources, and that is good. 'At first glance' and 'weaker kind of truth' could go. One sentence fewer.
stress: Admitting construction is humility with teeth. Good. Name one belief system that hid its origins and how it cost them.
gamedesigner: Nice meta-hook about provenance. The reader just receives it. Ask them to name where one of their own beliefs came from.
structural: Disclosing provenance is a real virtue. Disclosing who benefits is the next step, and the passage skips it.
satirist: Honest about its seams, which is the Bokonon move. Says it in two sentences too many.
mythmaker: Interesting meta-move, but it's the book talking about itself. Who discovered they'd been sold a 'discovery'?

modeler: Good audit move. 'Can you say where you got it?' is a test the reader can actually run.
skeptic: 'Can you say where you got it?' is a real calibration prompt. 'Most belief systems don't' wants a qualifier.
clinician: Good: ends with a small, safe self-question. Gentle enough that nobody gets hurt asking where a belief came from.
habit: 'Can you say where you got it?' One question, one belief, doable today. That's a rep. Keep it.
contemplative: The invitation to name where one of my own beliefs came from is good. Make that the first line, not the last.
stress: Good: provenance as a habit, with a test the reader can run on themselves. Humble and checkable.
gamedesigner: Controller in hand: 'can you say where you got it?' Good move. Ask me to name the belief first so I know I answered.
structural: Provenance as virtue, plus a test the reader can run. Next step: ask who benefits when origins are hidden.
satirist: An honest preface that Bokonon would toast. 'Can you say where you got it?' is a bar-worthy question.
mythmaker: Turning it back on the reader ('can you say where you got it?') works. That's the reader's own face. Good.

modeler: Pure hinge sentence. Fold it into the next paragraph.
skeptic: Pure signpost. Harmless; could merge into the next paragraph.
clinician: Pure transition. Cut it or fold it into the next paragraph.
habit: Pure transition. Fold into the next paragraph.
contemplative: A doorway with no room behind it. Cut it and let the next paragraph begin.
stress: Pure hinge. Cut or fold into the next paragraph.
gamedesigner: A transition beat and nothing more. Fold it into the next paragraph.
structural: Pure transition. It earns nothing on its own.
satirist: Throat-clearing. Cut it, start with the reason.
mythmaker: Pure hinge. Cut or fold into the next paragraph.

modeler: Show the seams so you can pull them. Good stance, but one line with no mechanism. A hinge sentence.
skeptic: A promise to expose seams is welcome, and testable by the reader. Brief and honest. Showing seams doesn't ensure they're pulled, but it helps.
clinician: Shows its seams so the reader can pull on them: trust-building and agency. One line; concrete enough as a stance.
habit: Clean one-liner, 'shows its seams.' Pull on them how? Needs the next line to tell me.
contemplative: Short and honest. 'Pull on them' is a nice invitation, though it is thin alone.
stress: Shows its seams so you can pull. That is the stress-test invitation. Short and good.
gamedesigner: Seams you can pull on: great design stance, but a single line with no demonstration.
structural: Short promise of transparency. Good stance, but unsupported here. 'Pull on the seams' is nice; point to who can.
satirist: 'Shows you its seams, so you can pull on them': plain and a little brave. Bokonon would admire the posture.
mythmaker: 'Shows you its seams so you can pull on them': good, plain defiance, and a clean image. Short, and the setup is in the previous page.

modeler: Showing seams is a good design stance, but the sentence is bare assertion. Show one seam being pulled.
skeptic: Showing seams so readers keep only what holds is the right epistemic posture. Claim is a promise; the proof is elsewhere.
clinician: Showing seams and letting the reader keep what holds respects autonomy. Good; no concrete step.
habit: 'Pull on the seams, keep what holds' is an invitation to test. Short, honest, mine to use. Could name one seam to pull first.
contemplative: 'Shows you its seams' is honest and kind. The 'opposite position' sets up a fight. Say what it does, not who it opposes.
stress: Shows seams on purpose: the right instinct. Short to the point of being a promise. Back it with an example.
gamedesigner: Strong design stance: show your seams, let players pull. Promise without a first pull.
structural: Showing seams is honest and easy to grasp. But the seams shown are the book's, not the world's.
satirist: 'Shows you its seams, so you can pull on them.' That is the Bokonon move, stated plainly. A religion that invites unraveling gets my respect.
mythmaker: Showing the seams is a brave stance, but it's a thesis with no scene. Who pulled a seam and found it held? Show them.

modeler: 'Don't look closely at the foundation' teaches a general habit: that's a real transfer claim. I'd like the habit loop named.
skeptic: Lovely, and I have no reason to believe the slippery slope. The 'old quiet tradition' goes unnamed; cite one novel or cut it.
clinician: Thoughtful about built beliefs, but it's one long sentence chain. Split it, and give the reader the habit it praises.
habit: 'Not looking closely at anything' is a good line buried in a long abstraction. Give me a checking habit.
contemplative: The closing thought is beautiful. Too many dashes get in the way. Keep only the last sentence and the one about novels.
stress: Strong final line. But 'an old, quiet tradition' is uncited hand-waving. Name the novels, or drop the appeal to tradition.
gamedesigner: Strong idea, but it's one long lecture with no controller. Split it, and end on the 'look closely' habit as a move.
structural: Good point that a belief forbidding inspection trains you not to inspect anything. Aim it at the ad industry and power and it bites.
satirist: The 'old quiet tradition found in novels' is Cat's Cradle. Name it. Hiding your one true ancestor is the only dishonest move here.
mythmaker: Strong closing turn about not looking closely. Lovely thought, who's holding it? Name one such novel.

modeler: Bokononism earns its place. 'Judge it by what it makes of people' needs a measure, though. What gets counted, and over what delay?
skeptic: 'Teaching you not to look closely at anything' is lovely and I have no reason to believe it. Soften or support.
clinician: Honest and readable, but it's about the book, not the reader's day. No step, no pain named.
habit: Good argument, Vonnegut detour. 'Look closely, starting here' wants a cue: look closely at what, when?
contemplative: Honest, but long. The Vonnegut detour performs reading. Keep the first two sentences and the last one. Let the rest go.
stress: Bokonon is apt. 'More durable' is asserted, not shown; name a built belief that survived strain.
gamedesigner: Bokononism is a sharp reference. It's still a lecture. 'Look closely, starting here' needs a concrete first look I can make right now.
structural: Strong line on foundations that discourage scrutiny. Still a reading habit, not a lever anyone pulls together.
satirist: It names its own mirror and passes the test. 'Look closely, starting here' is plain and good. Bokonon would like it.
mythmaker: Bokononism is a memorable image, and 'look closely, starting here' pays it off. It treats the opposing view fairly.

modeler: Habits of not-looking spread across domains: a real transfer claim. The Bokonon citation is apt. A strong close.
skeptic: 'Check where this book came from' is the right instinct. 'Not less true in the way that matters' is slippery. Say which way.
clinician: Honest, non-coercive stance I respect; 'check where this book came from' is a step. Long and essayistic for a practitioner.
habit: Long argument for self-aware belief. The close 'check where this book came from' is the only rep; lead with it, cut the rest.
contemplative: Honest, but it argues against an unnamed opponent. The final line is the gift; much before it is defense.
stress: 'Check where this book came from' gives the author skin in the game. The habits-spread argument holds up. Strong.
gamedesigner: A long lecture paragraph that finally ends on a move: check this book. Lead with that challenge and trim the Bokononism.
structural: 'Check where this book came from' is the habit I want trained. Point it at institutions next, not just scripture.
satirist: Names Bokonon outright and invites the check. The closed-eye habit spreading is a genuine Stephenson point. Honest. Keep.
mythmaker: The eye you're told to close gets harder to open: that's a real image with a cost. Bokonon is a fine ally. It runs long, though.

modeler: Closed-eye habit spreading is a real loop: the practice of not looking trains not looking. Bokonon as precedent. Self-checking invitation. Strong.
skeptic: Bokononism comparison is apt and self-implicating, and 'check where this book came from' is what I want. 'Habits spread: the eye you close' is claimed without support.
clinician: Honest about being built; 'check where this came from' is a safe act. Avoids guilt-bypass. A little long, but protective.
habit: 'Check where this book came from before you trust it' is a real instruction. Bokonon is a lovely reference.
contemplative: Honest about being built: Ruiz would nod. Too many examples and claims. Keep the last sentence.
stress: Bokononism as honest precedent; 'check where it came from before you trust it.' Author puts itself under the knife.
gamedesigner: Bokononism comparison and 'check where this came from' invites me to test it. Honest. No concrete check offered here.
structural: Bokonon candor is good: a belief that hides its foundation trains habits. Closest to a spillover test. Invites checking sources, a real act.
satirist: Cites Vonnegut by name and says what it borrows. 'The eye you close in one place gets harder to open' is a real claim. Very good.
mythmaker: Bokononism opening by calling itself lies is a perfect doubter's friend, and 'the eye you're told to close' is a warning with teeth. Earned candor.

modeler: Good: replicators selected for spread, not truth. That's a real selection mechanism. Name the fitness function and it's a model.
skeptic: Memetic point is real and honestly uncomfortable. Strong. Just say 'compete on similar terms'; 'exactly' overstates it.
clinician: Sharp point that ideas spread whether or not they're true. All meta, no help for the reader's own day.
habit: Beliefs spread like code: big-picture itch, no behaviour. What do I check before repeating a claim?
contemplative: The meme idea is clear. 'This book doesn't intend...' is the author standing in front. End on 'same terms'.
stress: Falsehood and truth spread on equal terms: a hard, uncomfortable claim, honestly held. Survives strain. Promise less, show it later.
gamedesigner: Memes-as-code is a good hook. Then 'returning to properly later' promises the payoff for chapter twelve.
structural: The strongest systemic claim here: ideas spread by fitness, not truth. Now name who funds the spreading and what rule could check it.
satirist: Snow Crash with the serial numbers filed off. Good idea; cite Dawkins or Stephenson, then it's knowledge rather than foreshadowing.
mythmaker: 'Catchy falsehood and careful truth compete on the same terms' sticks. Give me one rumor and one person who believed it.

modeler: A real mechanism: things get selected for spreadability, not truth. The rumor and its correction are honest flows. Missing: what slows the spread?
skeptic: Spread by ease, not truth: Kahneman would nod. And it admits the book competes on those same terms. Good.
clinician: 'Everyone has' is exactly the shame-aware move: names a common lapse without making it a character flaw. Works.
habit: 'You have passed on a story... before checking' hits home. Give me the two-minute check before I forward something.
contemplative: 'You have passed on a story because it was good to tell' is true and humbling. Drop the Snow Crash framing and say it plainly.
stress: Rare admission against interest: virality beats truth, including possibly this book. That's skin. Keep.
gamedesigner: Good hook: 'you've passed on a story' implicates me. Missing a second beat, a quick test I can run before I share something.
structural: Virality beats truth: good. Who builds the platforms that reward the catchy? Name the incentive, not just the contagion.
satirist: The Snow Crash point is made honestly, and 'everyone has' lands. Cut 'a sharper idea belongs here too'; the throat-clearing is pompous.
mythmaker: 'You have passed on a story because it was good to tell' convicts me warmly. The rumor outrunning its correction is a picture I'll keep.

modeler: Self-application is tidy, but 'pattern held together on its own' skips what made it hold. What was the balancing check?
skeptic: Neat self-application, though the rhythm does most of the persuading. 'Psychology that's tested' needs a pointer to which tests.
clinician: A tidy statement of method. Writer-facing, not reader-facing.
habit: 'The method, stated once, applied to itself.' Tidy. Still no rep.
contemplative: 'Not a confession. It's the method.' is strong. The last sentence is a mirror trick. Let it go.
stress: Close to admiring its own cleverness. 'Psychology that's tested' needs at least one test named here.
gamedesigner: The self-application lands neatly. It's still a cutscene, though: nothing for the reader to do.
structural: Self-congratulation about method. Elegant, inert, and nobody's rules are named.
satirist: 'Honest about being exactly what it says everything else is.' Busy, busy, busy. 'Yes, we made it up' was enough.
mythmaker: Neat self-reference, but it's a chant, not a scene. Earned by nothing on the page yet.

modeler: The method applied to itself is neat recursion. 'You can check it' needs the check named right here, not just promised.
skeptic: 'Tested psychology' is asserted, not shown. Say which claims are tested and which are story.
clinician: Clear method statement. Self-referential and reader-distant; nothing here someone could use tonight.
habit: Clear restatement of method. Says 'you can check it' but never says how or when. Point to Day 1.
contemplative: 'Not a confession, it's the method' is a little clever. One sentence would do: built this way, so check it this way.
stress: 'Tested psychology' oversells. Self-application is clever but circular; show one place the book failed its own check.
gamedesigner: A nice self-referential turn, but 'check it the way it tells you' points forward with nothing to check yet. Name one check.
structural: Self-referential throat-clearing. Checkable in principle, but it adds nothing the prior passages didn't say.
satirist: 'That is not a confession. It's the method.' A little smug. Saying it can be checked is good. Show one check.
mythmaker: It's clever recursion, but it's the book talking about itself. Lovely thought. Who's holding it? No one here.

modeler: A self-similar test: judge the book by its own rule, at a stated cost of a week. Falsifiable-ish. I like it.
skeptic: It offers a cheap test, which I respect. But one week of self-report is anecdote. Name what a failed week would look like.
clinician: Gives a realistic test: seven days, about a week. Gillihan would approve the timeline. Sentence one is overloaded.
habit: 'Seven days, about a week': that's a concrete test with a cost. Good. Opening sentence is too long; trim.
contemplative: 'Cost about a week' is a humble invitation. The long build-list sentence could be half its length.
stress: A one-week falsification test with a price tag. The most stress-test-friendly line here. Say what a failed week looks like.
gamedesigner: Gives a clear test and its price: seven days, about a week. Good win condition, stated plainly.
structural: Candid about construction. 'Test it by what it builds' is fair, but a week of private practice isn't much of a test.
satirist: 'Built from real mathematics' is a claim; the week-long test is the real offer. Plain and checkable, a little self-congratulatory.
mythmaker: Honest, and 'costs about a week' is a concrete price. Still a book talking about itself rather than a person.

modeler: A falsifiable test: seven days, and if you can't see a loop, the book failed. Cost and criterion named. Rare honesty.
skeptic: Names its own failure condition: finish seven days, still no loop, the book failed. Rare and excellent. Self-selected trial is weak evidence, and no comparison condition.
clinician: Falsifiable: a week of Part Two, and if you can't see a loop, the book failed, not you. Shame-aware and bounded.
habit: A testable promise: seven days, then see a loop run. This is the engineer's dream. Name day one.
contemplative: A week, seven days, and an honest test. Concrete and humble. Cut 'tested psychology' flourish.
stress: Names a failure condition: finish the week, still can't see a loop, book failed. Skin in the game. Exactly right.
gamedesigner: Excellent: a falsifiable test, a week-long cost, a stated failure condition. Real feedback signal.
structural: Falsifiable: seven days, and the book admits failure if you can't see a loop. Rare accountability. But the test is purely private.
satirist: Seven days, one week, and 'the book has failed its own test' is a falsifiable promise. 'Real mathematics, tested psychology' is trailer copy.
mythmaker: 'So: yes.' Disarming. Seven days, a week of cost, and it names its own failure condition. Stakes the book itself. Brave.

modeler: 'Rising tide does its own work' is a mechanism waved through. Which flow couples my help to yours? Show the coupling.
skeptic: 'Trusting a rising tide' is faith posing as an aim. What happens when helping yourself costs others? Address that.
clinician: Good scoping. 'Rising tide' is vague, so name one way helping yourself helps someone nearby.
habit: Helping yourself in ways that help others resonates. Name one tomorrow-sized example.
contemplative: 'Help yourself in ways that help the people around you' is warm and true. The jabs at other genres feel like a fight. Soften them.
stress: 'Rising tide lifts every boat' is calm-sea comfort. Tides also drown people. Either show the mechanism or cut the metaphor.
gamedesigner: It defines the genre by negation. 'Rising tide' is pleasant but untestable, so there's no signal.
structural: A rising tide 'without needing to be managed' is exactly the alibi I prosecute. Tides get engineered: who manages them, and who profits from you trusting them?
satirist: 'A rising tide lifts all boats' is the most self-help sentence in the language. You say you aren't self-help, then you use it. Cut.
mythmaker: Rising tide is a stock image with no boat. Show one person whose help spilled onto a neighbor.

modeler: The snapping example is a real spillover flow: one change drains tension across the house. Concrete, and true at household scale.
skeptic: Tired-snapping example lands. 'Nobody had to manage that. It spread' claims a mechanism with no evidence behind it.
clinician: 'Stop snapping when tired' lands. But it's illustration, not instruction; one line on how would make it usable.
habit: 'Stop snapping when you're tired, and the whole house gets quieter.' That's a habit I can picture tonight. Works.
contemplative: 'Stop snapping when you're tired, and the whole house gets quieter.' This is beautiful. I can live this today.
stress: Snapping-when-tired example is small and real. Modest claim that holds. Good.
gamedesigner: The snapping-when-tired example plays well: concrete, felt, and the house getting quieter is visible feedback. Keep it.
structural: Rejects self-help, good. But 'nobody had to manage that' romanticizes spillover; household calm isn't collective change.
satirist: 'Stop snapping when you're tired, and the whole house gets quieter.' This is the plain sentence the book should hide behind more often.
mythmaker: The house going quiet when you stop snapping is a small scene that earns its keep. The self-help disclaimer before it is filler.

modeler: Header line. It just announces the next point.
skeptic: Header line. Fine as a transition, no content of its own.
clinician: Bold signpost with no content of its own. Merge it into U0173.
habit: Signpost only. Fine as a header, earns nothing alone.
contemplative: A heading that announces plainness instead of being plain. Cut it, and let the next line say it.
stress: Header line. Does its job, earns nothing.
gamedesigner: A header-only beat. Merge it into the next line.
structural: Signpost. It does its job and nothing more.
satirist: A header that says it's going to say something plainly. Just say it.
mythmaker: Header doing a header's job. Fine in place, earns nothing alone.

modeler: A necessary limit, said plainly. It's a boundary, not a mechanism, but it names where the system hands off. Short and humane.
skeptic: Responsible boundary, plainly said. Respects limits of a handbook and of the author's competence. Brief, useful, not intellectually exciting.
clinician: Right call: tells readers the book isn't a substitute for help. Protective. Wants a concrete pointer to what to do next, here or below.
habit: Warm, plain and responsible. Not a rep, but the right thing to say. Brief.
contemplative: Said plainly, and with care. This is impeccable. Nothing to remove.
stress: Humility with real stakes: someone in trouble needs help, not a book. Plain and honest.
gamedesigner: Responsible and plain. Matters to someone struggling; it's a safety rail rather than a game beat.
structural: Refusing to be a substitute for help is exactly right. Heading alone, but it concedes inner work is not remedy. Spell out which help.
satirist: Said plainly and early, and that is the point. A handbook that tells you to get help earns trust. Short.
mythmaker: A bold, plain line that protects the reader. Needs a face and a case for it, but as a headline it shows the author cares.

modeler: Clean, honest scope limit. Every model needs its boundary stated, and this one does it.
skeptic: An honest boundary, stated plainly. Exactly the calibrated modesty most such books lack.
clinician: Exactly right: a way of looking, not treatment. This protects the reader at 3 a.m. Keep.
habit: Clear limit-setting, but U0174 does the real work. Could merge.
contemplative: Plain, humble, needed. 'It is not the same as being helped' is impeccable. Keep it.
stress: Modest and true. The book naming its own limits is the best thing an author with skin can do.
gamedesigner: A clear boundary marker. It tells the player what this game can't do. Good.
structural: Admits it is a way of looking, not help. Honest limits, and a rare thing in this genre.
satirist: Plain, true, needed. 'It is not the same as being helped' is a good, clean line.
mythmaker: Honest, plain, necessary. Clear boundary, no dressing.

modeler: A necessary limit, stated plainly. It reads as a disclaimer, not an idea, which is fine for what it has to do.
skeptic: A plain and necessary limit, stated without hedging. It is the most calibrated line here.
clinician: Exactly right and honest. 'Not the same as being helped' protects vulnerable readers. Add one line pointing to real help.
habit: Necessary, plain, honest disclaimer. Doesn't need scoring higher; it does its job in one breath.
contemplative: Clear, needed, kind. Nothing to remove.
stress: Honest limit stated plainly. Exactly the humility I want. No notes.
gamedesigner: Necessary safety rail, said clearly. Not engaging, but it doesn't need to be.
structural: Honest limit-setting, but just a disclaimer. Pointing to actual care resources would make it do work.
satirist: A necessary, plain disclaimer. 'It is not the same as being helped' is honest. Fine.
mythmaker: It's clear and honest but has no blood in it. Add the person who needed more than a way of looking and the line will land.

modeler: Names the limit of the model. Necessary and clear. The hole image works.
skeptic: Clear scope limit, stated plainly. The hole image is apt. This is how a handbook should know its edges.
clinician: Exactly right. 'It cannot climb down and help you out; that takes a person.' Add one line on how to find that person.
habit: Clear, honest boundary. 'That takes a person' is the right instruction. Keep it plain like this.
contemplative: It shows the hole but cannot climb down: impeccable and kind. This is a sentence as an act.
stress: Humility with a clear boundary: it is not treatment. The hole image works. I'd keep every word.
gamedesigner: Honest scope-setting, and 'the hole you're in' is clear. Needed safety rail, well phrased.
structural: Good: it refuses to pose as treatment and sends the reader to a person. Rare honesty in self-help.
satirist: 'It cannot climb down and help you out' is plain, humble and necessary. Good.
mythmaker: 'It cannot climb down and help you out; that takes a person.' This one I trust. It's earned humility.

modeler: Concrete and correct: a trained person is an adaptive controller with feedback. A book is open-loop. Keep it.
skeptic: Concrete, correctly ordered, says why professionals differ. Keep as is.
clinician: Warm, specific and it says 'go there first.' Add a crisis line or how to find a therapist and it's perfect.
habit: 'Go there first.' A real, concrete instruction. Keep it.
contemplative: Kind and direct. 'Go there first' is a sentence that acts. Keep it as it is.
stress: Clear redirect to real help. 'Go there first' is the right priority. Keep.
gamedesigner: A direct, actionable exit: go here first. It's the clearest instruction in the chapter.
structural: Points to real, accountable help outside the book. It would be stronger if it admitted that access to care is itself structural: cost, waitlists.
satirist: Does its job and gets out. 'Four things no book has ever been' has real wit.
mythmaker: 'Present in the room with you' gives this a body. Real stakes, real direction. Keep.

modeler: Best kind of caution: a mechanism. The practice draws on an energy stock that's empty for exactly the people who need it. Bathtub named.
skeptic: Best passage here: a mechanism for the book's own limits. The bold line is fluent and true.
clinician: 'Fails exactly the people who need it most' is honest and blame-free. Best safety paragraph in the book.
habit: 'A framework that needs energy to run fails exactly the people who need it most.' Strongest honest line here.
contemplative: The bold line is the truest sentence in the chapter. The opening bold line can go. The mechanism already speaks.
stress: Best passage here: names exactly where the framework breaks. That's a stress test the author ran on himself. Keep untouched.
gamedesigner: Great: it names the energy-cost precondition the way a game names its minimum spec. The bold line sticks.
structural: Excellent: a tool that needs energy fails the depleted. That is a structural self-critique. Now apply the same logic to who has slack at all.
satirist: 'A framework that needs energy to run fails exactly the people who need it most.' Best sentence so far, and the book wrote it about itself.
mythmaker: Best line in the chapter: a framework needing energy fails those who need it most. Real cost, honestly faced.

modeler: Naming the loop isn't changing the flow. Honest. Slightly repeats U0174-5, so trim the overlap.
skeptic: Fluency mistaken for competence, applied to itself. Kahneman would nod. Keep.
clinician: Says insight is not relief. That protects readers from blaming themselves when naming the pattern doesn't fix it.
habit: Naming isn't relief. Important and clear. Slightly repeats U0175; trim one.
contemplative: Gentle and honest about limits. The last clause about 'fluency' turns back into argument. Stop at 'Fractalism makes no claim otherwise.'
stress: Understanding is not relief: a falsifiable warning against its own fluency. Rare and valuable.
gamedesigner: Honest, and it keeps the fluency-versus-competence point. It repeats U0175's job, so trim the overlap.
structural: Naming is not relief, and it says so properly. It undercuts the inner-work-as-remedy pattern the book otherwise leans on.
satirist: Naming something isn't curing it. Good. 'Fluency for competence' is a self-aware jab that lands.
mythmaker: Clear and humble, though it repeats the prior two. Trim the overlap; the fluency-for-competence close earns it.

modeler: 'Keep checking it' is the balancing loop on belief. That's the right compression.
skeptic: 'It matters that you believe something': compared to what? A careful agnostic who keeps checking seems to fail this for no reason.
clinician: Memorable and humane. 'Keep checking it' needs a 'how' if it's going to be more than a motto.
habit: Good compression. 'Keep checking it': when? Give a cue, like a monthly review.
contemplative: A sentence I could carry home. Remove 'if the whole chapter had to compress to one'. Just say it.
stress: 'Keep checking it' saves this. But 'doesn't matter what you believe' breaks on any cult. Add the checking criteria.
gamedesigner: A good compression, and 'keep checking' hints at a feedback loop. Say what checking looks like.
structural: Checking your belief honestly is fine as private hygiene. No lever follows from it.
satirist: It works as a slogan you could say in a bar. 'Keep checking it' does the work, and the rest is a shrug.
mythmaker: A memorable compression. Would land harder after a person we watched keep checking.

modeler: Build-plus-accept as reinforcing-plus-balancing is right. But the 'Fifth Iteration' callback leaves new readers out. State the consequence inline.
skeptic: Asserts what belief 'is' underneath, unsupported. Leans on Fifth Iteration jargon. Say the build/accept idea plainly.
clinician: Pairing building with accepting is wise, but leaning on the 'Fifth Iteration' shuts out anyone who hasn't read that far.
habit: Build-versus-accept is abstract and leans on Fifth Iteration jargon. Nothing to do.
contemplative: Building and accepting, together, is lovely. 'Fifth Iteration' shuts the newcomer out. Name the danger in plain words.
stress: Build-and-accept is sound. 'Fifth Iteration' jargon locks the reader out. Explain it in a clause or cut it.
gamedesigner: The Fifth Iteration callback assumes a rule the newcomer may not hold. Build-versus-accept needs an example.
structural: 'Build what should exist' gestures at action, then turns abstract. Which things, built by whom, and with what tools?
satirist: 'The Fifth Iteration has already told you.' A system invented a few pages back now cites itself as scripture. Spell out the actual point.
mythmaker: Build-and-accept is a real idea, smothered by 'Fifth Iteration' callback. Give me someone building and accepting at once.

modeler: Yes: building is the reinforcing loop, accepting is the balancing side. The dementia carer shows both. This is the book's best structural claim.
skeptic: The dementia caregiver grounds it well. 'Underneath any tradition' is a universal claim with no support; say 'often'.
clinician: The dementia caregiver example names real pain before acceptance. No bypassing. Strong. The Fifth Iteration tag-on is jargon.
habit: Caregiver image earns it. Two halves is a good frame; ask me which half I'm skipping this week.
contemplative: The caregiver holds both halves, and I feel it. End there. The Fifth Iteration callback goes back to the head.
stress: Dementia caregiver example carries it. 'Underneath any tradition' is grandiose; plenty of believers would object. Narrow it.
gamedesigner: The dementia caregiver makes both halves felt. The Fifth Iteration callback is fine. I'm still only watching; ask me which half I neglect.
structural: Caregiver example lands. Yet 'accept what can't be moved' never asks who decided it can't, like unfunded eldercare.
satirist: The dementia caregiver earns the two halves. 'As the Fifth Iteration showed' cites the book's own myth as proof. Cut it.
mythmaker: The dementia caregiver is the face this idea needed, with building and accepting both shown in one life. This is the best passage here.

modeler: Two ports onto one pattern only rhymes until you show the shared structure. Equifinality needs evidence, not assertion.
skeptic: Overconfident. Many disagreements are about content, not dressing. 'Most' needs evidence or a softer word.
clinician: 'Ports of entry' is jargon. Interesting about disagreement, and of no use to someone who's hurting.
habit: 'Two ports of entry' is opaque. Fine idea, no rep.
contemplative: A reconciling thought, and I welcome it. 'Ports of entry' is a private word. Say 'two doors'.
stress: Most disagreement isn't real conflict: comforting, and untested against history's wars of religion. Show cases or hedge harder.
gamedesigner: 'Ports of entry' is undefined jargon. Lost the player. Give two concrete traditions and the shared want.
structural: Dissolving conflict into shared want erases conflicts of interest. Who profits from you believing nobody's interests really clash?
satirist: 'Two ports of entry' is jargon carrying the whole argument. Plain version: most religious fights are about vocabulary. Then give one example.
mythmaker: 'Ports of entry' is opaque. Two named neighbors of different faiths would do this in one line.

modeler: Same goal, different flows, so not opposed. Convergence offered as evidence of structure works here. The Sabbath and hike example is tidy.
skeptic: Sabbath versus hike assumes I can read both neighbors' wants. Epley would ask how you'd know. Compared to what?
clinician: Warm, clear example, but it addresses interfaith tension, not anyone's struggle. Pleasant, not helpful.
habit: Sabbath vs phone-free hike is a perfect, graspable example. Abstract payoff, no action; that's fine here.
contemplative: Sabbath and the Sunday hike are lovely. The 'two doors' closing line is ornament. Stop after 'not opposed.'
stress: Sabbath vs hike flattens real theology. Calm-sea reconciliation; ask a devout neighbor. Show where it breaks.
gamedesigner: Sabbath versus hike is a clean, quick picture. 'Two doors' is pleasant but asks nothing of me. Try: name a rival belief and its want.
structural: Sabbath versus hike is charming, and it quietly dissolves real conflict. Shared wants don't settle whose rules govern Sunday labor.
satirist: Sabbath versus phone-free hike: concrete and charming. 'Two different doors' piles one more metaphor on top. Stop at the hike.
mythmaker: Sabbath beside a phone-free hike is a lovely paired image. 'A day the week can't have' will stay with me.

modeler: Same function, different form: convergence as evidence of a real pattern. It only rhymes unless you test the want.
skeptic: Nice example, but it assumes both neighbors' answers would rhyme. Epley would warn we project our wants onto others. Hedge 'often'.
clinician: Sabbath/hike example is gentle and clear. Interpersonal insight, but no step for the reader in an actual conflict.
habit: Sabbath and phone-free hike rhyme nicely. 'Ask each what the day gives them' is almost a rep; make it explicit.
contemplative: The Sabbath and the phone-free hike rhyme. Reconciling, not scoring. This is Thầy's spirit.
stress: Sabbath versus hike is nice, but it cherry-picks a benign pair. It glosses over the disagreements people actually fight over.
gamedesigner: Sabbath and phone-free hike is a lovely pairing I can test on my own neighbors. Plays well.
structural: The Sabbath and the hike rhyme nicely. But both are fighting the same seven-day work week. Name that common opponent.
satirist: Sabbath versus phone-free hike is a lovely plain example. 'Hands that never touched' gets slightly misty, but it's earned.
mythmaker: The Sabbath next to the phone-free hike gives two neighbors with faces. 'Hands that never touched' rhymes beautifully.

modeler: Lifeline-to-holder, snare-to-nest is a real cross-scale test. Buried under jargon: tending, fraying, lifeline, snare in one breath.
skeptic: The test's last clause (for whom?) is valuable, but the jargon stack buries it. Lead with that clause in plain words.
clinician: Tending, fraying, lifeline and snare all at once is a stack of vocabulary. Give one plain question the reader can ask of their own belief.
habit: Tending, lifeline, snare: three jargon terms in one question. Ask one plain question instead.
contemplative: Tending, fraying, lifeline, snare: four terms in one breath. The test is good. Ask it in one plain question.
stress: The 'for whom' test has teeth, but it's buried under Tending, lifeline and snare jargon. Say it plainly.
gamedesigner: Tending, fraying, lifeline and snare all land in one sentence. That's a difficulty spike. Give the test as steps.
structural: Good test: a lifeline to its holder, a snare to everyone else. The coined vocabulary blunts it. Give one example of an institution.
satirist: 'Tending, lifeline or snare, and for whom' turns a sentence into a liturgy. Plain version: ask who a belief helps and who it costs.
mythmaker: Jargon stack: Tending, lifeline, snare, nested. The half-that-won't-object turn is good, buried.

modeler: 'For whom' is the right question: a loop can stabilize one stock while draining another. The company-as-family example proves it.
skeptic: 'For whom' is a real test, and the 'like a family' example shows it biting. Works.
clinician: 'For whom' is a real tool; the company-family example will hit home. The bolded question stacks too much jargon to use.
habit: Four-part stacked question in bold. Cut to one: 'Who is this belief holding down?' The family-company example is the keeper.
contemplative: The 'like a family' company example lands. The bolded question piles four tests into one breath. Ask only 'for whom?'
stress: 'For whom' is the teeth. Company-as-family example bites. Best test in the section.
gamedesigner: A real test question I can apply, and the 'family' company shows the 'for whom' trap well. Bolded question carries a few too many clauses.
structural: Finally: 'and for whom.' The 'like a family' company names who profits. This is the book's best structural test.
satirist: The 'like a family' company is a scalpel. The bolded question is a jargon pileup, 'Tending or Fraying' capitalized. Ask 'who does this help?'
mythmaker: The 'like a family' company bites, and the staff who can't say no have real stakes. The bolded test is jargon soup, so simplify it.

modeler: Policy Resistance is real Meadows, and the rivalrous finite-stock caveat is sharp. 'Two loops, two tongues' undercuts it. Cut the flourish.
skeptic: Admitting finite-resource conflict is a different shape is good calibration. Too many forward references to parse on first read.
clinician: Policy Resistance, figures, false resemblance. Theory with no handhold. It belongs in Part Five.
habit: Forward reference plus caveat plus caveat. Abstraction stacked on abstraction.
contemplative: Too many forward references and qualifications. Keep the last two sentences. Move the rest to Part Five.
stress: Good that it admits zero-sum conflict exists. Too many forward references. Give one concrete finite-resource case.
gamedesigner: It forward-references Part Five and adds the finite-goods caveat. Too many rules, and no move for the reader.
structural: It at least admits that real opposed stakes and scarce resources exist. Then it retreats to 'two tongues'. Distribution conflicts deserve more than a footnote.
satirist: Two cross-references to later Parts and a hedge on the hedge. The bar test kills it. One example of real opposed stakes would rescue it.
mythmaker: Forward references and caveats, no blood. Straw-free, but faceless. Cut to the last two sentences.

modeler: Two real archetypes: policy resistance, and tragedy of the commons over one well. That is proper Meadows. More of this, please.
skeptic: Two shapes is useful. 'Most' disagreement being neither is still unmeasured; the last line is all rhythm.
clinician: The farmers-and-well image is clear, but this is taxonomy of conflict. No reader, no step.
habit: Taxonomy of disagreement with forward references. Two farmers is good; rest is jargon. No step for my next argument.
contemplative: Two farmers and one well is enough. 'Policy Resistance' and 'its own figures' are vocabulary standing in the way. Look again.
stress: Two farmers, one well: finally a case where the frame admits limits. 'Most is neither' still unfalsified.
gamedesigner: Two farmers and a well is clear. Policy Resistance is a forward-referenced term the reader hasn't met. Lecture tone, no move.
structural: Commons problem acknowledged, then waved off as rare. Scarcity and distribution are the main event. Name allocation rules.
satirist: 'Two farmers, one well' is perfect plain speech. 'Two loops describing one shape in two tongues' undoes it. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: Two farmers and one well is the right picture, but it's buried under Policy Resistance and 'instruments.' Let the farmers carry the passage.

modeler: Two named shapes: a finite shared resource and policy resistance. Classifying the structure before arguing is real systems hygiene.
skeptic: The diagnostic split is useful. 'Rarer than it looks' and 'most... is neither' are base-rate claims with no base rate. Hedge or support.
clinician: 'Ask which shape you're in' is a step, but Policy Resistance and 'two tongues' make it hard to apply.
habit: 'Before an argument, ask which shape you're in' is a usable cue. Two shapes, Policy Resistance, two tongues: too much packed in.
contemplative: Two farmers, one well: plain. Then jargon and the 'false resemblance' turn. Too many shapes for one breath.
stress: It concedes that real conflict exists and names two shapes. The diagnosis is usable. 'Most is neither' still wants evidence.
gamedesigner: Two farmers and one well is clear, and 'ask which shape you're in' is a move. The Policy Resistance name-drop is fine.
structural: It finally admits scarcity conflict exists. Then it shrugs 'its own arithmetic'. Point to who allocates the well.
satirist: Two farmers and one well is a good, concrete example. Then 'Policy Resistance' and 'false resemblance' stack up the jargon. Cut a capital.
mythmaker: Two farmers and one well is vivid, then 'Policy Resistance' and 'two tongues' blur it. Keep the farmers and lose the label.

modeler: Two farmers, one well: scarcity stock. Policy resistance: opposing pushes cancel. Real archetypes, plainly stated. Ask which shape you're in: nice diagnostic.
skeptic: Distinguishes scarcity from policy resistance and says 'often', not 'always'. Asking which shape you're in is usable. The well example is clean.
clinician: Two shapes of disagreement and a question to ask first. Well-scoped, concrete, kind. Dry-summer farmers are easy to picture.
habit: 'Before an argument, ask which shape you're in.' A cue and one question. Two farmers, one well is a perfect image.
contemplative: Two farmers, one well: I see it. 'Which shape am I in?' is a question I can ask. 'Two tongues' is lovely.
stress: Two shapes of disagreement, farmers and well. Gives a pre-argument test. Hedged 'often'. Useful.
gamedesigner: Two shapes and 'ask which shape you're in' is a usable diagnostic with a decision. Two farmers is a clear example.
structural: Two farmers, one well: genuine conflict over scarce stuff, resolved by someone deciding. That is politics. Best passage here. Add who decides and how.
satirist: Two farmers, one well, versus two pushing sides. Concrete, and the diagnostic question is usable. 'Two tongues' slips in a little poetry.
mythmaker: Two farmers, one well, a dry summer: stakes and faces. Straw men avoided: 'one shape in two tongues' respects both sides. Short, but good.

modeler: Test and tweak: Sellers would approve. It needs a measurable 'watching what it builds' to be more than a slogan.
skeptic: Test by practice, fine, but self-observed results invite effort justification. Say what result would count against it.
clinician: Good invitation to test rather than trust. 'Watching what it builds' needs a timeframe and a sign to look for.
habit: 'Repeat the practice and watch.' Right instinct. Which practice? Name it.
contemplative: Test it by practice. That is the right invitation. Simple and complete.
stress: Test by practice: the right posture. It would bite harder if it said what result should make you quit.
gamedesigner: Practice-as-test is the right spirit. 'Watching what it builds' needs a concrete signal to watch for.
structural: Test it by practice. Fine, but the practice measured here is entirely personal.
satirist: Fine, but chapter 11 already closed three times. Pick one ending.
mythmaker: Fine sentiment, already said. Redundant with U0177.

modeler: A falsifiable stance. 'If nothing changes, that's an answer' closes the loop. It should say how long to wait first.
skeptic: Falsifiable, so I like it. Add a baseline: changed compared to what, and watched how?
clinician: Concrete step, and 'if nothing changes, that is an answer' removes the self-blame. Good. Short and safe.
habit: Exactly right: do the seven days, watch. 'If nothing changes, that is an answer too.' Honest and actionable.
contemplative: Simple and humble. 'If nothing changes, that is an answer too' is impeccable.
stress: Falsifiable on purpose: 'if nothing changes, that is an answer.' Exactly right. Say what counts as change.
gamedesigner: Great: a clear goal, a test, and a feedback rule, 'if nothing changes, that is an answer.' That's how you onboard.
structural: Empirical invitation is fair. Purely private test, though; nothing here reaches beyond the reader's own week.
satirist: 'If nothing changes, that is an answer too.' Honest and falsifiable. More of this, please.
mythmaker: 'If nothing changes, that is an answer too' is honest and doesn't oversell. It's a plain invitation that has earned its place.

modeler: Navigation note. Harmless, does no conceptual work.
skeptic: Navigation note. 'Exactly right' asserts more than it knows; harmless.
clinician: Friendly navigation. 'Exactly not enough' could sting a reader who's already depleted; soften the phrase.
habit: Warm handoff. 'Come back' needs a cue: after Day 7, reread this.
contemplative: Warm, and it permits rest. 'Come back once it's had time to work on you' is gentle teaching.
stress: Navigation note. Harmless, inert.
gamedesigner: Good save-point messaging that sets expectations for a return visit. It reads like a nice level-end screen.
structural: Navigation note. It does its job.
satirist: Warm and brief, with some charm. Keep.
mythmaker: Warm, direct address. 'Exactly not enough' has a nice sting.

modeler: It honestly admits a delay: reread after seven days. A useful navigation note, and not much else.
skeptic: Sensible pacing advice. 'Once it's had time to work on you' assumes it will work.
clinician: 'That's right for a first pass' gives permission, not judgment. Clear next step. This is how to talk to people.
habit: Clear cue: come back after seven days. Useful pacing instruction, small and earns its place.
contemplative: Warm and permissive. It tells me what to do next without hurry.
stress: Signpost. Harmless, earns little.
gamedesigner: Warm save point with a return trigger. It respects the player. Light, but it earns its line.
structural: Reading instruction. Harmless, earns nothing.
satirist: Reading instructions dressed as a benediction. Clear enough. It could be one line.
mythmaker: Kind stage directions, but there's no image in them. Fine as connective tissue.

modeler: Clear routing instruction. Does its job.
skeptic: Clear reading guidance, but it's just a signpost. 'Read differently' is a promise I can't yet check.
clinician: Clear, permission-giving navigation: do the seven days. Useful direction, no pressure.
habit: Tells me exactly what to do next: the seven days. Good transition, no fluff.
contemplative: Gentle permission to go practice. A little long for a threshold; two sentences would do.
stress: A transition note. Pointing to practice over reading is right, but it has no stakes of its own.
gamedesigner: A good checkpoint: it tells me where play begins. A save-point, functional and clear.
structural: Signpost. Serviceable, no substance.
satirist: A plain signpost, unpretentious. It does its job, and nothing more is asked.
mythmaker: Useful directions. 'Watched a loop of your own run' promises a return. It's navigation, not story.

modeler: Do the seven days, then return: reading changes once you've watched your own loop run. Good feedback-based instruction.
skeptic: Claims pages 'read differently' after practice, a plausible but untested prediction. Honest about first pass. Useful navigation.
clinician: Says reading straight through is 'not yet the point'; sends you to seven days of practice. Releases pressure, offers action.
habit: Do seven days, then come back. Clear next step. Add a start trigger, like tomorrow before email.
contemplative: Gently sends me to do, not to read more. Short and kind.
stress: Claims reading differs after doing: checkable by the reader. Honest nudge to practice.
gamedesigner: Good level-end beat: do the seven days, then return. Promises felt progress and sends me to play.
structural: Clear nudge to do the days then return. Good pacing advice. Nothing about collective work.
satirist: Tells me to go do Part Two and return. Honest instruction. 'Read differently' is a promise I can't check yet.
mythmaker: 'These pages read differently once you've watched a loop of your own run.' A real promise of return. Brief sign-off, with a pull toward Part Two.

modeler: Signpost only.
skeptic: Signpost. Clear, does its job, nothing more.
clinician: Clear signpost and nothing more.
habit: Framing line. Fine, earns nothing on its own.
contemplative: A useful signpost, plain enough. It earns little beyond orientation.
stress: Signpost. Fine.
gamedesigner: A plain signpost and functional. It doesn't need to earn more.
structural: Signpost. It does its job.
satirist: Signposting. Harmless, inert.
mythmaker: Signpost. Functional, inert.

modeler: Map and walking is a stock phrase. It tells me nothing the part's title doesn't. Could merge with U0185.
skeptic: Map and walking. Clear, and it adds nothing.
clinician: Map-versus-walking is clear but empty. One line that could merge with the next.
habit: Map vs walking, fine signpost. Thin; could merge with U0186.
contemplative: Map and walking. Gentle, small, enough.
stress: Map/walking is fine. Pure navigation.
gamedesigner: Map versus walking is a cliché with no payoff. U0185 already does this job. Cut or merge.
structural: Map/walking framing is clear but empty. Signpost only.
satirist: Map versus walking: a cliché doing signage duty. Harmless and forgettable.
mythmaker: Map versus walking is a familiar image that's used once and not developed. It's serviceable.

modeler: Signpost. Says what the part is for, nothing more.
skeptic: A plain statement of purpose. Clear, functional, and it earns nothing more.
clinician: Plain orientation. Fine signpost; nothing more.
habit: Purpose line, fine. Merge with U0185 and U0186; three italic preambles is two too many.
contemplative: Clear framing. It orients without moving me.
stress: A signpost. Clear, and nothing else.
gamedesigner: A generic part header. It could fold into U0185, which actually states the win condition.
structural: Signpost. One line of orientation; nothing to score.
satirist: A clear statement of purpose. It's signage, with no claim to judge.
mythmaker: Framing exposition with no blood in it. It can stay as a map line.

modeler: Part opener: clear job statement, small repeated acts build a life. Fine navigation, nothing else.
skeptic: Clear orientation: this part is for doing. Plain and honest about priority. Nothing to test or doubt here.
clinician: Clear signpost: this is the working part, make something. Orientation without pressure. Short, usable, impersonal.
habit: 'Here you make some.' Right orientation, action-first. Say which first practice to do tomorrow.
contemplative: Here you make some. Short, warm, and it turns me toward action. Last sentence is filler.
stress: Clear orientation: this is the working part. Plain and brief. No claim to attack.
gamedesigner: Clear part goal: here you make some. Tells me this is where the play is. Short and honest.
structural: Orients reader: this part is for making. Plain and honest. 'Small repeated acts build a life' is the i-frame thesis.
satirist: 'Here you make some' sets the bargain. Short, plain, tells me what the part is for.
mythmaker: 'Here you make some' is a call to action with a turn from explanation to doing. Brief and purposeful, no image.

modeler: Clear handoff: explanation to practice. Good orienting line, small and honest.
skeptic: Short orienting note; 'first small thing, today' is actionable and modest. No overreach.
clinician: 'The first small thing, today' is exactly right: small, immediate, no overwhelm. Safe entry point.
habit: 'First small thing, today.' That's my language. Cue is today, step is small. Name the small thing and it's perfect.
contemplative: Warm, simple, and it points to today. 'Starting with the first small thing' is the right invitation.
stress: Clear handoff from theory to action. Starting small today is a testable ask. Keep.
gamedesigner: Good transition: tells me I'm moving from lore to play, and today is first. Felt progress now.
structural: Promises action today and bridges parts cleanly. Still a first small thing; where it leads beyond the self isn't said.
satirist: Clear part-opener: what's here, what to do, 'starting today'. No pomp. Does exactly what it promises.
mythmaker: Short bridge from explanation to doing: 'starting with the first small thing, today.' Clear, warm, speaks to me. No image though.

modeler: A promise, not a point. Fine as a signpost.
skeptic: Promise of twenty practices. A count, not a point.
clinician: Sets expectations. Twenty practices may sound like a lot to someone already overwhelmed.
habit: Twenty practices is a promise, not a rep. Okay as orientation.
contemplative: A clear promise of what I can do. Fine as wayfinding.
stress: A promise of twenty practices. Counting isn't proof; say what they'll do for you.
gamedesigner: It states the win condition up front, about twenty practices at three scales. That's good onboarding.
structural: Promises group practices. I will hold it to whether any of them is a group lever rather than a group mood.
satirist: 'About twenty' practices. Count them. Bryson would.
mythmaker: Concrete promise of what you'll do. Good wayfinding.

modeler: A clear promise with three scales named. 'About twenty' is honest. It still reads as packaging, not insight.
skeptic: Promises the ability to change patterns in groups. That is overconfident; say 'try to' and how you'd tell.
clinician: Clear promise of concrete outcome. 'Change it in a group' may oversell; keep the promise modest and realistic.
habit: Promises twenty concrete practices. Good outcome statement; I'll judge it by the practices.
contemplative: A clear promise. 'About twenty' is honest. It is a list of outcomes, not yet a felt thing.
stress: Concrete promise, checkable. 'Change it' in a group is a big claim for twenty practices.
gamedesigner: A clear win condition stated up front, which is good level design. 'About twenty practices' sounds heavy; maybe promise day one instead.
structural: Promises group-scale change. A promise isn't a lever; we'll see if 'twenty short practices' touch any institution.
satirist: A plain promise with a number in it, about twenty practices. Bryson nods. Now deliver them.
mythmaker: A clear promise. It's a list of deliverables with no person in it.

modeler: Concrete outcomes, named examples. A useful promise.
skeptic: Concrete, recognizable targets: the same argument, the unchosen scroll. 'Able to do' overpromises outcomes. 'Will try' would be honest.
clinician: 'The argument that always goes the same way, the scroll you didn't choose' names real pain, promises concrete tools.
habit: 'The scroll you didn't choose' hooks me. Promise of twenty concrete practices is the right sell.
contemplative: The argument that always goes the same way, the scroll you didn't choose. I know these. Concrete promise.
stress: The argument that goes the same way and the scroll you didn't choose are real targets. A concrete promise you can check.
gamedesigner: Clear goals with recognizable examples, the argument and the scroll. This is how a quest log should read.
structural: 'In a group' is promised; the scroll you didn't choose was chosen by someone. Name the feed's designers.
satirist: 'The scroll you didn't choose' makes a concrete promise with a countable offer. Good.
mythmaker: 'The argument that always goes the same way' and the unchosen scroll are recognizable at once. Good promise.

modeler: Useful routing: it tells the reader exactly where to start.
skeptic: Useful routing for an impatient reader. Earns its line.
clinician: A concrete entry point: start Chapter 1, do seven days. That's the next step I want.
habit: 'Do the seven days.' Exactly what I want. Direct and startable.
contemplative: Kind to the impatient reader. Small and useful.
stress: Useful routing for the impatient reader. Earns its line.
gamedesigner: A skip-to-gameplay button. Exactly what an impatient player wants.
structural: Navigation. Nothing to judge.
satirist: Useful navigation: it tells the impatient reader where to go. Good.
mythmaker: Practical, kind to the impatient reader. Works.

modeler: A short entry instruction that does its job. 'Inside the days you're already having' is a good constraint.
skeptic: A practical entry point. Fine.
clinician: One small thing a day, inside days you already have: realistic, low-burden. Exactly the Gillihan structure I want.
habit: 'One small thing a day, inside the days you're already having.' That's habit stacking. Love it.
contemplative: 'Inside the days you're already having' is the right spirit. Plain and useful.
stress: Clear on-ramp. Low cost, low claim. Fine.
gamedesigner: Fast-path onboarding, clear and short. Does the job.
structural: Low-friction entry, fine. 'Inside the days you already have' accepts the days as given. Who set them?
satirist: Direct and useful, and it gets out of the way. Good.
mythmaker: Useful directions. 'Inside the days you're already having' has a little warmth.

modeler: Low entry cost, stated plainly. Good onboarding.
skeptic: Low-cost entry instructions. Useful and plain.
clinician: Low barrier, realistic: one small thing a day, no time set aside. This is how you meet a struggling reader.
habit: 'One small thing a day, inside the days you're already having.' That's a Two-Minute Rule in spirit. Works.
contemplative: 'Inside the days you're already having.' Warm, small, practiced. Exactly right.
stress: A low-cost entry point with no time set aside. Practical routing, and nothing more.
gamedesigner: A great fast-start path: low barrier, no time set aside. Onboarding done right.
structural: Navigation note. Fine.
satirist: Practical shortcut that respects the reader's time. Fine.
mythmaker: Clear and kind. It's an on-ramp, not a moment.

modeler: Clear entry ramp, useful navigation. No stock or loop here, but as a handbook on-ramp it works. Name the seven-day sequence as a loop later.
skeptic: Clear, claims nothing, and lets the reader skip ahead. Useful signpost, but it gives me nothing to doubt or admire.
clinician: Low-barrier entry, no extra time demanded. Safe on a bad day. Small and doable today.
habit: Good: one small thing a day, no time set aside. I can start tomorrow. Name the first thing and its cue.
contemplative: Plain and kind. It tells me I am already here and gives one small thing to do. Nothing to remove.
stress: Low-cost entry, clear and doable. Claim is modest and testable: seven days, one thing. No grand promise. Fine signpost, nothing deeper.
gamedesigner: Great skip-the-lore door: one small thing a day, no time set aside. Clear onboarding, low barrier. Not abstract, but I'd start playing here.
structural: Navigation blurb. Easy and inviting, but names no rule, no lever, no group. Private seven-day start only; nothing here shows the playing field.
satirist: Plain, useful bypass for the impatient. No costume. Says what to do and how little it costs. Good.
mythmaker: Clear door for the impatient, but no face, no stake. Name who walks in and what they're tired of.

modeler: Claim implies obligation to be actionable: good engineering ethic. Short and does its job.
skeptic: Actionability as an obligation is a decent standard. The claim's own truth goes unexamined, but it's acceptable framing.
clinician: Fine bridge, but it promises action without giving any. Keep it short.
habit: 'Isn't finished until it's actionable.' Good principle. The paragraph itself isn't action.
contemplative: 'This part is the action' is good. The sentence about obligation is the head talking. Trim it.
stress: 'A claim isn't finished until it's actionable' is good discipline. The rest is setup.
gamedesigner: Claim-to-action framing works. It's a little throat-clearing before the controller arrives.
structural: 'Actionable' is promised, but the action is all aimed below the level where the rules get written.
satirist: 'This part is the action.' Recaps Part One without adding anything. Cut to the last line.
mythmaker: Clean bridge from claim to obligation. Still a thesis, not a person.

modeler: Accumulation below attention is the stock idea in miniature, but this restates Part One. Name one stock to make it fresh.
skeptic: Restates the thesis as if Part One proved it. 'Below attention' is plausible; 'the world' is a stretch.
clinician: Mornings, arguments, moods: relatable. Careful: 'built by your acts' can read as 'your mood is your fault' at 3 a.m.
habit: 'Your mornings, your arguments, your moods' makes it personal. 'This part is the action' — good, now deliver.
contemplative: Mornings, arguments, moods: I recognize myself. 'This part is the action' is a good, short turn.
stress: 'The world is built by small acts' is sweeping. Credit for demanding action over assent.
gamedesigner: Mornings, arguments, moods hooks me personally. 'This part is the action' promises play. Make sure it delivers fast.
structural: 'World built by small repeated acts' is the individualist premise BP would love. Add the rules those acts run inside.
satirist: A claim restated plainly, mornings and arguments and all. 'This part is the action' is clean.
mythmaker: 'Your mornings, your arguments, your moods' gives the claim a body. The pivot to action is clean.

modeler: Act, then observe: right order for an experiment. Needs to say what you'd measure.
skeptic: 'Certainty will come from doing' worries me. Doing breeds commitment, not accuracy. Promise information, not certainty.
clinician: 'Practice first, settle opinions after' takes pressure off and is sound behaviorally. Good.
habit: Practice first, opinions after. That's habit-first thinking. Love it.
contemplative: Practice first, certainty after. This is the whole spirit of the book, said gently. Keep it.
stress: Practice first, believe after: also how every cult recruits. Add what should count as the practice failing.
gamedesigner: 'Practice first, opinions after' is a great onboarding philosophy. The jargon list in it is noise to a newcomer.
structural: Practice before belief is sensible pedagogy. There is no structural content.
satirist: 'Practice first, opinions after' is a good, disarming idea. The Third Thing and Genesis name-drops lose newcomers.
mythmaker: Permission to start unsure is generous. Jargon names (Third Thing, Genesis) clutter it.

modeler: Practice before belief, with a built-in failure check. Good loop design: the outcome feeds back into the opinion.
skeptic: Practicing first invites effort justification: people value what they labored over. Name that bias, then the checking question earns trust.
clinician: 'Start here, sure or not' lowers the bar beautifully. Practice before conviction is clinically sound.
habit: Practice before belief, start unsure. That's Clear's identity-through-reps idea. Removes the barrier to starting.
contemplative: Practice first, opinions after. This is right. Trim the list of Part One terms. They agitate before the release.
stress: Practice before belief, with a built-in failure check. Antifragile instinct. Good.
gamedesigner: Removes the gate, practice before belief, with a built-in feedback check. Excellent onboarding philosophy, plainly said.
structural: Practice-first epistemics, stated clearly. Procedural, with no stakes beyond the self.
satirist: Practice before opinion, with a built-in way to fail. That's a teaching, not a virus. Good.
mythmaker: Practice before belief is sensible. It's an argument about method, and nobody is shown hesitating or trying.

modeler: Real claim: single-scale loops calcify or burn out. 'Banner, Chapter 19' jargon blocks it. Name the missing balancing flow at each scale.
skeptic: Each 'tends to' is asserted, not shown. Banner jargon. The three-scale claim needs one example per failure.
clinician: The structure is clear enough, but Banner, Dyad and Skein arrive all at once. The reader gets lost before the practice starts.
habit: Scale theory plus Banner jargon. Map, not a move.
contemplative: Banner, Skein, Dyad, chapter numbers. Too much vocabulary before I have practiced anything. Say self, two people, group.
stress: The scale claim is interesting but asserted, not tested. Banner, Skein and Dyad land on the reader all at once.
gamedesigner: Self, Dyad, Skein, Banner and Chapter 19 all hit before the tutorial. That's the rulebook nobody reads. Defer the names.
structural: Rightly warns that self-only practice calcifies. The Skein scale is promising, but it needs institutions, not just groups of practitioners.
satirist: Self, Dyad, Skein, Banner, Local Rule: five capitalized Concepts in one paragraph. Busy, busy, busy. Say 'you, a pair, a group.'
mythmaker: Three scales argument is sound but jargon-heavy. The burned-out giver deserves a face, not a clause.

modeler: A scale check done properly: each level fails without the others. The journaling and burnout cases are real failure modes at each scale.
skeptic: 'Tends to' is honest hedging. The jargon load (Banner, Skein, Dyad) hurts it, and the core claim is asserted.
clinician: Structure overview buried in coined terms. 'Journaling that changes nothing' stings readers who journal to cope. Soften and de-jargon.
habit: Structure lecture heavy with coined terms (Local Rule, Banner, Skein). The journaling line lands; the rest is a table of contents.
contemplative: 'A year of journaling that changes nothing' stings truly. Banner, Skein and Dyad crowd one breath. Name the scales plainly and stop.
stress: Journaling-that-changes-nothing and burnt-out giver are real failure modes named. Strong.
gamedesigner: Difficulty spike: Local Rule, Banner, Dyad, Skein and Nest in one paragraph. The journaling jab is great. Defer the vocabulary.
structural: Rightly attacks journaling that changes nothing between people. Self, Dyad, Skein is promising. Skein still needs institutions, not just groups.
satirist: The journaling jab is great. Local Rule, Banner, Dyad and Skein on one page is a vocabulary tax. Say 'you, two people, a group.'
mythmaker: The useless journaling year and the giver who burns out are real faces. Banner, Skein and Dyad pile up too fast.

modeler: Each scale fails alone, and the failure modes are named. A nested loop, not a hierarchy. A sound structural claim.
skeptic: 'Tends to' is properly hedged and the journaling example lands. The three-scale claim is still asserted. What evidence says single-scale practice fails?
clinician: The burnout and inward-turning warnings are clinically sound. Banner reference and scale jargon thicken it.
habit: Journaling that never reaches anyone is a sharp example. Rest is structure-talk; I'm told the map, not given a step.
contemplative: The journaling and giving examples are true. Banner, Dyad, Skein pile up names. Teach the scales without coinages.
stress: Each scale's failure is named: inward journaling, burnout, an empty Banner. Specific failure conditions. This survives strain.
gamedesigner: Jargon pileup: Banner, Self, Dyad and Skein in one paragraph, front-loaded rulebook. Teach each scale when I reach it.
structural: It warns explicitly against journaling that never reaches others. That's the spillover test passed. Rare and welcome.
satirist: Self, Dyad, Skein, Banner: four coined nouns in a paragraph. The journaling example is good; the vocabulary tax isn't.
mythmaker: Real stakes here: the inward-turning journal, the giver who burns out. Banner, Dyad and Skein in one breath drown them.

modeler: Good: names failure modes of each single scale (inward spiral, giver burnout, empty Banner) and nests them. Wants a balancing loop named between scales.
skeptic: 'Tends to' is honest hedging, but the one-claim thesis rests on invented illustrations. Compared to what? Name a case where single-scale practice lasted.
clinician: Clear structure, good bigger-picture claim, but it's roadmap, not help. No step a struggling reader can take from this paragraph.
habit: Neat scale argument, but I get no rep out of it. What do I do on Monday? Give one two-minute move per scale.
contemplative: The claim is sound, but Banner, Dyad and Skein arrive before I can breathe. Name one scale, give one picture, let the rest wait.
stress: Names failure modes of each single scale, so the claim can be wrong. Good. 'Tends to' hedges nicely. Banner jargon slightly heavy; reader isn't yet addressed personally.
gamedesigner: Good level-structure map: three scales, each unlocking the next. But Banner, Dyad, Skein arrive at once. Difficulty spike; no move for me to make.
structural: Good: refuses self-only work and names a scale ladder to a group. Still no rules, owners or incentives, but it pushes toward collective action.
satirist: The journaling example is real, but 'Banner' is jargon cited as authority from Chapter 19. Busy, busy, busy. Say 'a group in name only'.
mythmaker: The year of journaling and the burnt-out giver have blood in them. Give each a name and a Tuesday, then the claim lands.

modeler: Each single-scale failure is a loop with no balancing side or no feedback: turns inward, burns out. Scale check done. Nested-loop ending is good.
skeptic: 'Tends to' hedges are welcome; the single-scale failure modes read plausibly but are asserted without evidence. Clear structure and usable.
clinician: Journaling-that-never-leaves-you is real rumination risk, well named. But Self/Dyad/Skein/Banner jargon piles up; simplify.
habit: Self, Dyad, Skein is a useful ladder, but the paragraph is dense and jargon-heavy. Cut the Banner aside; give a first step.
contemplative: Wise idea, buried in a long paragraph. Too many examples, a parenthesis, a coined word. Keep three scales, drop the rest.
stress: 'Tends to' hedges nicely and the failure modes are named: journaling inward, burnout. Dense, and the nested-loop ending is asserted.
gamedesigner: Difficulty spike: Banner, Dyad, Skein, nested loop in one paragraph. Three new terms, rulebook feel. Introduce one per beat.
