structural: Best here: refuses inward-only practice and climbs to a group. Names burnout and Banners. Wants a named lever at Skein scale.
satirist: Journaling that never reaches anyone, giving that burns out the giver: real failure modes. But Banner, Dyad, Skein and Self capitalized in one paragraph is jargon fog.
mythmaker: The journaling year that never reaches anyone, the giver who burns out — real faces in sketch. But it's dense with terms. Name one person per failure.

modeler: Read, begin, raise, lower is an exhaustive operator set on a loop. Hold as active set-point control is exactly right.
skeptic: A clean, usable taxonomy. 'That is everything that can be done' is tidy overreach; say 'the moves this book uses'.
clinician: Four moves plus Hold is a neat map but dense. 'Holding is not doing nothing' is gold; give it room.
habit: Look/Plant/Tend/Thin is a usable kit. Too dense; Hold muddies it. One example per move.
contemplative: Look, plant, tend, thin is beautiful. The three rules and Hold crowd it. Give me the four verbs, then breathe.
stress: Look, plant, tend, thin: compact and usable. 'That is everything' overreaches. Hold is a good honest addition.
gamedesigner: Four verbs is a real controller layout, which I love. Then three rules plus Hold spike it. Teach Hold later.
structural: A clean taxonomy of moves. It is still a loop with no owner: who wrote the loop you are thinning?
satirist: Look, plant, tend, thin is clean and memorable. Then it adds a 'not-a-fifth' move, and that dilutes the tidy four.
mythmaker: Four verbs are a gift; Hold is lovely. Three rules crammed in mid-paragraph bury it. Give each move an image.

modeler: Read, begin, raise, lower really covers the controls on a loop. Hold as dynamic equilibrium is correct. Somewhat dense for first contact.
skeptic: A usable taxonomy. 'Everything that can be done with a loop' is overreach. Dense; Hold muddies the clean four.
clinician: Honoring 'staying with a practice that stopped showing results' as work is kind. But four moves, three rules, plus Hold overloads.
habit: Four moves is a usable toolkit, mid-scroll example helps. Then Hold and three rules pile on. Trim to four verbs.
contemplative: Four moves is beautiful. Three rules plus a non-fifth move is too much. Keep look, plant, tend, thin. Give Hold its own page.
stress: 'That is everything that can be done' is a theory-of-everything tell. Then a fifth that isn't. Trim the closure claim.
gamedesigner: Four moves is a lovely core mechanic. Then three rules plus Hold pile on. Lost the player. Teach the four, earn the rest later.
structural: Clean taxonomy; Hold is a smart addition. The moves have no target beyond loops; no rule-changing, no owner.
satirist: Four moves, three rules, then a fifth that 'is not a fifth.' Bokonon would giggle. Keep look, plant, tend, thin. Cut Hold or make it a move.
mythmaker: Mid-scroll is the only face. Four moves, three rules and a non-fifth is a rules manual. Show me one person doing all four.

modeler: Four flow verbs plus Hold as the balancing move. Mechanically coherent. Slightly dense, but the scroll example rescues it.
skeptic: The scroll/walk example helps, but adding Hold after 'four moves' undercuts the tidy count. The neatness feels fluent rather than true. Simplify.
clinician: Scroll/walk example is gold. Then rules plus Hold pile on. Valuing 'Hold' as work is kind; cut the governance.
habit: Mid-scroll, plant a walk: perfect. Then three rules plus Hold, not a fifth move. Too much grammar; stop after the scroll.
contemplative: Four moves are clear; the scroll-and-walk example lives. Then three rules and a not-fifth move. Stop after the walk.
stress: The scroll example is good. Then three rules, plus Hold as 'not a fifth move', make it heavy. Cut the taxonomy down.
gamedesigner: The four moves plus the scroll example are great controls. Then three rules and a not-quite-fifth move arrive. Hold the Hold for later.
structural: Four moves plus Hold, three rules: an overloaded paragraph. The scroll example helps; the scaffolding drowns it.
satirist: Four moves plus a not-a-fifth move, plus three rules. The scroll-to-walk example saves it. The taxonomy is breeding.
mythmaker: Scroll to walk is a nice mini-arc. Then rules, plus a not-fifth move, pile up. Cut Hold or give it a scene.

modeler: Four moves map to reinforce/weaken a loop; Hold as tend+thin is a nice stock-held-steady idea. Mid-scroll example makes it usable.
skeptic: The scroll-to-walk example makes four moves usable. 'Hold is work, not nothing' is asserted, not shown; I'd want a test.
clinician: Catch the scroll, plant a walk: small, shame-free steps. Hold as real work is kind to a reader whose results have stalled.
habit: Catching yourself mid-scroll, planting a walk: that's a real rep with a cue. Four verbs I can carry. Hold is slightly abstract.
contemplative: The scroll-to-walk example is lovely. Then Hold, a fifth non-move, and nested clauses pile on. Say four moves plainly and stop.
stress: Four moves with a concrete scroll/walk example. Risk: a scheme that sorts everything is unfalsifiable. Hold as 'not nothing' is a good touch.
gamedesigner: Four-verb control scheme, with the scroll-to-walk example showing the combo. Tutorial with a controller in hand. Hold bit adds a fifth button, but it's fair.
structural: Four moves are usable and scale-agnostic. But the example is scroll-thinning as personal willpower; who designed the scroll? Hold-as-work excuses passivity slightly.
satirist: Scroll-to-walk example passes the bar test. Then 'Hold' arrives as a not-fifth move and 'made by what the two of you make' goes hushed. Cut.
mythmaker: Mid-scroll to walk is a real moment. But four moves plus Hold in one paragraph is a glossary, not a story. Let someone do them.

modeler: Instrument before tuning, in one line. Lovely.
skeptic: Rare and welcome: an epigraph that lowers expectations. Calibrated and memorable.
clinician: Lowers the stakes nicely. 'Find out whether you can watch' is an achievable, kind goal.
habit: Honest epigraph that sets the right expectation. Keep.
contemplative: This is beautiful. Humble about what a week can do. It makes watching enough.
stress: Modest epigraph that undersells. I like it. A claim that can be checked in a week.
gamedesigner: Excellent hook. It reframes the week's goal as watching, an achievable win condition.
structural: A good modest epigraph. It caps the promise honestly.
satirist: Good epigraph: dry, modest, and it promises something you can actually test.
mythmaker: Terrific epigraph. Low promise, sharp stakes. Sets the week's question perfectly.

modeler: Correct, but a near-duplicate of Part One's caution. One sentence and a pointer would do.
skeptic: A necessary repeat for readers arriving here directly. Brief enough.
clinician: Repeats the care disclaimer exactly where people enter. Correct placement.
habit: Safety note placed where readers arrive. Concrete and necessary.
contemplative: The care caution, repeated for those who skipped ahead. It is caring, and in the right place.
stress: A needed repeat for readers who skipped ahead. Keep it short like this.
gamedesigner: A needed safety gate for direct entrants. It's brief and actionable.
structural: A necessary care disclaimer repeated at the point of entry. Responsible.
satirist: A responsible repeat for readers who skipped ahead. Could be one sentence.
mythmaker: Necessary repeat for practice-path arrivals. Fine.

modeler: A responsible limit, placed where newcomers arrive. It does its job and claims nothing more.
skeptic: A correct, plain referral. Keep it.
clinician: Essential and well placed: names who to call, regardless of usefulness. Keep exactly as is.
habit: Clear, actionable safety pointer: seek a trained person. Does exactly what it should.
contemplative: Kind and necessary. Said with care, without fear-piling.
stress: Repeated disclaimer, but placed where the risky reader arrives. Correct call.
gamedesigner: Safety rail placed right before play begins. Clear and necessary.
structural: Points to real trained help rather than offering practice as cure. Concrete and responsible.
satirist: Repeated at the right door, plainly. A responsible disclaimer that doesn't preen.
mythmaker: A necessary, caring boundary, stated clearly. No notes.

modeler: A necessary safety rail, plainly put.
skeptic: A necessary, well-placed disclaimer for readers who skipped ahead. Direct and humane.
clinician: Right placement, right message, warm. Name a concrete route: a crisis line or GP. Otherwise strong.
habit: Necessary safety note, clear and direct. Does its job. Repeats U0173, so keep only one in full.
contemplative: Caring and plain. Seek a person. Nothing to remove.
stress: A necessary safety line, plainly said. Humble and correct.
gamedesigner: A necessary safety note, short and humane. It earns its place for fast-path arrivals.
structural: A clear referral to trained help. Responsible and plain.
satirist: A necessary, plain disclaimer. Says what it is.
mythmaker: 'Or someone you love is' gives the warning a face. Necessary and sincere.

modeler: Small perturbations, not shocks. Consistent with the model, and practical.
skeptic: Sound advice about scoping change. Plain.
clinician: Prevents the all-at-once overhaul that sets people up for failure and self-blame. Good.
habit: Don't adopt everything at once. That's Clear's whole point. Good.
contemplative: Gentle restraint. 'Do not try to adopt everything' is exactly what an eager reader needs.
stress: Don't adopt everything at once. Small bets beat big ones. Sound.
gamedesigner: Good scope control. It stops the player from trying every mechanic at once.
structural: Small steps. Standard self-help advice, harmless here.
satirist: Fine, but obvious. Merge it into the next line.
mythmaker: Clear guardrail. Plain and useful.

modeler: Clear structure: each day builds on the last. Self-contained page, good.
skeptic: Self-contained instructions. Good design.
clinician: Clear structure with a realistic dose. This is what a good onboarding looks like.
habit: One small thing per day, all on this page. Exactly the right design.
contemplative: Simple and reassuring. One small thing per day. Good.
stress: Clear structure, self-contained. Practical.
gamedesigner: A clear structure: one thing a day, self-contained. That's the tutorial promise, stated.
structural: Logistics. Nothing to judge.
satirist: A promise of self-containment. Workmanlike.
mythmaker: Good structural promise. Self-contained page is a real kindness.

modeler: A clean setup with dependencies stated. 'Each resting on the one before' is honest sequencing.
skeptic: Clear logistics. No claims to check.
clinician: Clear, realistic structure, no prerequisites. Functional transition, not much more.
habit: Seven days, one thing each, no prerequisites. Removes friction. Short and right.
contemplative: Reassuring and plain. It does one thing.
stress: Clean, self-contained. Low claim, does its job.
gamedesigner: Reassuring, but it's a menu screen. Fold it into the Day 1 header.
structural: Logistics. Clear, nothing more.
satirist: A transition sentence. Clear, and it adds nothing.
mythmaker: Plain setup and reassuring. Nothing to remember, and that's fine here.

modeler: Practical framing: zero setup, built on existing routines. Fine.
skeptic: Practical framing that lowers the cost of starting. Clear. No claims to doubt.
clinician: Reassuring structure, fits real days, nothing to fetch. Gillihan-style roadmap. Good.
habit: 'Everything you need is on this page.' Love it. Habit stacking on the walk you already take. Classic good design.
contemplative: Reassuring: everything on this page. The dashes stack examples; one would breathe easier.
stress: Low friction, self-contained. A logistics claim that holds. Not interesting, just useful.
gamedesigner: Promises a self-contained level, which is good onboarding. It's still a promise, not a move.
structural: Logistics. Readable; promises nothing beyond private routine.
satirist: Plain setup with no prerequisites. Does its job.
mythmaker: Reassuring logistics. Clear, and nothing memorable.

modeler: Practical recap, plainly said. 'Each resting on the one before' is the only structure. No mechanism, just a runway.
skeptic: Plain summary of the structure, with 'days you're already having' keeping demands low. No evidence offered that seven days does anything.
clinician: Reassuring and plain: use days you already have. Connective tissue, though; it earns little beyond lowering the barrier.
habit: Fitting practice into the walk you were taking is a proper cue. Recap only, though; no new rep here.
contemplative: Short, warm, doable in days I already have. The walk and the conversation are real. Nearly impeccable.
stress: Plain, low-stakes recap. Promises little, so little to break. Useful reassurance but nothing tested against strain.
gamedesigner: Clear scope: seven days, tiny moves, fits your existing day. Sets expectations and lowers the barrier. Rules are light, little new content, but it's a good start prompt.
structural: Logistics recap. Fitting practice into days you already have is private and cheap; no lever, no structure named.
satirist: Walk you were taking, conversation you were having anyway. Plain recap, tells the reader what to do. Passes.
mythmaker: Tidy recap, nobody inside it. Fine as signage; I'd trade it for one person finishing day seven.

modeler: Bounded, stacked, fits into existing days. Good for adoption. No mechanism needed here.
skeptic: Fits practice into existing days, realistic. 'Everything you need is on this page' is a confident promise; 'by day seven you will have done all' is safe.
clinician: Seven days, one small thing, fitted into days already happening. Realistic, Gillihan-like. Strong.
habit: Seven days, one small thing, fitted into existing walks and talks. Habit stacking done right. Exactly the cue I want.
contemplative: Seven days, small things, inside the life I already have. This I could do. 'Everything you need is on this page' is reassuring.
stress: Fits the week into existing days, so cheap to try. 'Everything you need is on this page' is an overclaim.
gamedesigner: A seven-day quest with scaffolded days and a promised finish. Tutorial structure done right.
structural: Concrete, fits into existing days, clear. Private week of tiny acts; fine start, but who joins on day eight?
satirist: Seven days, fitted into the walk you were taking anyway. 'Everything you need is on this page' is a promise worth making. Plain and doable.
mythmaker: The walk you were taking, the conversation you were going to have anyway: lives fitted into lives. Promise is concrete and kind.

modeler: Sets a falsifiable goal: can you observe the loop? Building measurement capacity first is the right call.
skeptic: Says what success looks like, so failure is detectable. Exactly right. 'Nothing can give it faster' is unproven; soften it.
clinician: Honest success criterion that won't turn into a failure verdict. Exactly Gillihan's realistic timing.
habit: States the success test for the week. Rare and excellent.
contemplative: It names honestly what the week is for. 'Selling something' has a little bite. Otherwise clear.
stress: States its success criterion and refuses to oversell. Exactly how a claim should take risk.
gamedesigner: Best beat yet: an explicit success criterion, so I can tell whether the week worked. More of this.
structural: An honest goal: learning to see, not changing a habit. It refuses the overpromise. Good.
satirist: 'Any book promising otherwise is selling something.' Honest, plain, and a success test you can check. Exactly right.
mythmaker: Honest stakes: you're testing whether you can watch. Refuses to oversell. Strong.

modeler: Observe without intervening, three catches. A concrete sampling protocol. Good.
skeptic: Concrete, low-stakes, countable (three catches). 'Tends to produce guilt' is asserted; drop it or source it.
clinician: Low-stakes and capped at three catches, with 'don't judge' and the warning about guilt. Safe observation, not rumination.
habit: 'Catch it three times.' Countable, startable, low-stakes. Model unit.
contemplative: Notice, change nothing. I can do this in my kitchen today. This is pure practice.
stress: Concrete, low-stakes, measurable: three catches. Good first rep.
gamedesigner: Perfect level one: a tiny goal, one rule and a countable target of three catches. It plays.
structural: Noticing a habit is fine. Picking 'what you reach for when bored' and never asking who designed what's within reach is the omission.
satirist: Concrete, small and doable. 'Three times' gives it a number. Good.
mythmaker: 'What you say when someone asks how you're doing' is a face. Concrete, doable, kind.

modeler: Trees are only statistically self-similar, and only for a few levels. Tell readers to count splits and check the ratio holds.
skeptic: Pleasant exercise. What problem it solves stays unclear until the next unit, and there it stays unproven.
clinician: Simple grounding, three minutes. Safe on a bad day and outward-facing.
habit: Three minutes, any branching thing. Startable. Add a cue: on your commute.
contemplative: Lovely. Three unhurried minutes with a leaf. It calms the mind.
stress: Pleasant, but nothing shows it changes behaviour. Calm-weather exercise.
gamedesigner: A concrete, short and sensory task. It needs a 'you'll know it worked when' line.
structural: A nice perceptual exercise. It has no bearing on any rule anyone could change.
satirist: Finally a leaf. It still needs a ratio, or the word 'self-similar' with a fern, to earn the wonder.
mythmaker: Simple, sensory instruction. The tree image will return, good.

modeler: 'Until the likeness gives out' is Linton-honest: real fractals have finite range. A rare correct use of self-similarity.
skeptic: Concrete, bounded instructions. 'Until the likeness gives out' is nicely honest.
clinician: Outward-facing, three minutes, specific. Great grounding exercise for an anxious mind; nothing to ruminate on.
habit: Concrete, timed, three minutes, on your way somewhere. Cue is loose but it's startable tomorrow. Good rep.
contemplative: I can do this at my window. 'Until the likeness gives out' is lovely. Keep every word.
stress: Simple instruction, 'until the likeness gives out' admits limits. Good. Payoff unproven.
gamedesigner: Controller in hand. Clear task, a clear stop ('until the likeness gives out') and a time box. That's a well-built tutorial.
structural: Tree-gazing exercise. Pleasant attention training; zero purchase on any structure.
satirist: Finally a fern. Now Bryson it: say how many times a branch repeats before 'the likeness gives out.' Give one number.
mythmaker: Following a branch until the likeness gives out is a vivid image I can do. It should come back later, and it does.

modeler: 'Until the likeness gives out' is honest: real fractals are finite-depth. Counting the splits makes it measurable. Love it.
skeptic: 'Only a handful' honestly admits where self-similarity gives out. A concrete, checkable exercise. Good calibration.
clinician: Clear, outward-facing, time-bounded exercise. Safe on a bad day because attention goes out, not in.
habit: Specific, timed, cued to your route: three unhurried minutes. A real rep. Problem it solves stays implicit, but it's startable.
contemplative: Three unhurried minutes with a branch. This I can do at my window today. Beautiful practice.
stress: Clear instructions, and 'until the likeness gives out' is honest about limits. The payoff is still unproven.
gamedesigner: Clear task, time box and stop condition (the likeness gives out). Counting splits is a nice feedback signal.
structural: Tree-tracing as inner calm. Pleasant, private, zero spillover. This is the alibi risk in miniature.
satirist: A real fern and real counting that admits 'only a handful.' That's honest wonder with a stopping rule. Keep.
mythmaker: 'You've walked past this every day; today you follow it.' A real act, an image, and a turn. This is the book at its best.

modeler: 'Same perceptual shift turned inward' is asserted transfer. Plausible, unproven. Hedge it or cite it.
skeptic: Transfer from tree branches to habit loops is assumed. Training transfer is notoriously narrow. Hedge it as a hope.
clinician: The rationale is clear. Abstract justification, fine as support.
habit: Explains why the oddest day matters. Short enough to earn its place.
contemplative: A fair reason, but Day 2 needed no defense. Keep the first sentence and drop the rest.
stress: The perception-transfer claim is plausible but untested. Hedge it, or cite something on attention training.
gamedesigner: A good why-this-level-exists note. It explains the skill transfer without padding.
structural: Pattern over event is a valid principle, but it stays perceptual and private.
satirist: It claims a perceptual shift from three minutes with a tree and gives no evidence. A metaphor wearing a lab coat.
mythmaker: Justifies the tree well. A touch lecture-y, but short.

modeler: Event versus pattern: the bad night against a month of them. That is Meadows's iceberg in one sentence.
skeptic: 'Is meant to' admits the transfer from trees to habits is unproven. Good. The bad-night line resonates.
clinician: 'One bad night rather than a month of them' reframes person into pattern. Good shame-aware move.
habit: 'The one bad night, rather than the shape of a month of them' — that lands. Justifies the rep well.
contemplative: 'The one bad night, rather than the shape of a month' is true and gentle. It works.
stress: 'Meant to let you' is honestly hedged. Bad-night vs month-of-them lands. Transfer from trees to habits unshown.
gamedesigner: Explains why the easy level matters. 'One bad night versus a month of them' makes it felt. Strong.
structural: Pattern over event, the 'month of bad nights,' is the i-frame-to-s-frame move. Extend it: what produces the month?
satirist: 'The one bad night, rather than the shape of a month of them.' That's the plain sentence, and it lands.
mythmaker: 'The one bad night, rather than the shape of a month of them' is a cost I recognize. That line is the hook.

modeler: Cue, craving, response, reward gives a named causal chain to observe live. Concrete.
skeptic: A borrowed habit model, applied concretely. Fine. Note the four-beat model is a heuristic, not established science.
clinician: A concrete labeling task. The four beats are easy to hold.
habit: Four beats named live. Concrete and builds on Day 1. Great.
contemplative: The four beats, named simply while they happen. Practicable.
stress: The habit-loop beats, borrowed but workable. Credit the source; it costs nothing and buys trust.
gamedesigner: It builds on Day 1 and adds one new rule. That's textbook difficulty ramping.
structural: The habit loop applied to the self. The cue and the reward are often engineered by someone. Say so.
satirist: Cue-craving-response-reward is Duhigg and Clear, uncredited. Usable, but give the source.
mythmaker: Clear, builds on Day 1. The plain gloss of the four beats is good.

modeler: 'Most people never once' is an unmeasured flourish. The precondition point already landed.
skeptic: 'Most people have never once done this deliberately': how would you know? Cut the claim and keep the reassurance.
clinician: Reassurance, but 'most people have never once done' adds a faint competitive edge. Unnecessary.
habit: Encouraging rationale. Could be a single sentence on U0199.
contemplative: Encouraging, but 'most people have never once done' is an assumption. Remove it.
stress: 'Most people have never once done this deliberately' is unsupported. Cut the boast; the practice stands alone.
gamedesigner: Reinforces the felt win, 'proving to yourself'. Short and motivating.
structural: Watching in real time is a precondition. Fine, and limited.
satirist: 'Most people have never once done this deliberately.' Says who? Short and fine otherwise.
mythmaker: Encouraging, brief. 'Most people never once did this' gives a small thrill.

modeler: The rearview line is apt: feedback seen only after the delay can't steer. Brief, and it does its job.
skeptic: Rearview mirror is fluent. 'The actual precondition' is stated far more firmly than anyone knows.
clinician: 'Not stopping it' is good Harris: watch, don't control. But the step lives elsewhere; this is reassurance only.
habit: Rearview mirror line is nice but it's reassurance, not a step. Fine as a short bridge.
contemplative: The rearview mirror line is fine but restates the paragraph. One sentence would do.
stress: Rearview mirror line is fine. Restates; tighten or merge.
gamedesigner: Reframes success as watching, not stopping, which is good feedback calibration. The rearview mirror is apt.
structural: Rearview mirror line is fine filler. Restates the previous day.
satirist: The rearview mirror is a tired image, but it's honest and short. Fine.
mythmaker: The rearview mirror is a stock image but it works. Short and earned.

modeler: Watching during the run beats the postmortem. The rearview line is good, but it's a slogan with no mechanism.
skeptic: The empty bag, the hour gone: recognizable. The rearview line is pure rhythm. Is there evidence that watching mid-loop helps?
clinician: 'You are still not stopping it' is permission, not failure. The empty bag lands. Kind and clear.
habit: Empty bag, hour gone: I know that. Rearview mirror line lands. Short reassurance, not an action, but it fits.
contemplative: The empty bag, the hour gone. Kind and recognizable. The rearview line is one image too many.
stress: 'The empty bag, the hour gone' is recognizable. The rearview line is a cliché. Fine as a pivot.
gamedesigner: 'The empty bag, the hour gone' is vivid, and the rearview mirror line sticks. Reassures the player mid-level.
structural: Empty bag, hour gone: it lands. The rearview line is crisp.
satirist: 'The empty bag, the hour gone' stings truly. The rearview line is a cliche, but a useful one.
mythmaker: The empty bag and the hour gone are faces of regret. The rearview mirror is a bit stock. Still lands.

modeler: Real insight: observing a loop while running versus meeting its outcome after. Steering needs feedback during, not afterward. Delay-aware and lovely.
skeptic: Modest and correct: observing a loop beats post-mortem. 'Nothing left to steer' is neat rhythm, though; how would you know it works?
clinician: Good: watching, not stopping, removes failure pressure. 'Nothing left to steer' lands cold; 'the hour gone' could sting. Soften.
habit: Empty bag, hour gone: I recognise that. But watch it how, and when? Add the trigger and a one-line action.
contemplative: Gentle and true. Watching instead of fixing is a practice I can do tonight. The empty bag lands without argument.
stress: Honest about limits: you're not stopping the loop, just watching it. Modest claim that survives. 'Nothing left to steer' sharpens the stake.
gamedesigner: Reframes the goal: watch the loop mid-run, not post-mortem. Clear win condition and a vivid failure state. Good feedback signal: did I catch it while running?
structural: Watching the loop beats willpower claims, honest enough. But empty bag, hour gone: whose feed, whose design? Observation without an owner.
satirist: 'Afterward, there is nothing left to steer' is a plain sentence doing real work. Empty bag, hour gone: relatable. No fix offered though.
mythmaker: The empty bag, the hour gone: that's a face. 'Nothing left to steer' earns its sting. Keep.

modeler: A specific intervention with a specific trigger. Testable.
skeptic: Clear, doable, the right size. Keep.
clinician: Specific and brief, and it names worry spirals. Useful in the moment.
habit: Cue (feel swept in), action (ten breaths). Textbook habit design.
contemplative: Ten breaths with two short phrases. A real practice I can carry. Keep.
stress: A specific interrupt with a count. Testable tonight. Good.
gamedesigner: A clear trigger, a clear action and a count of ten breaths. A playable move.
structural: Prescribing ten breaths for the doom-scroll is the BP footprint move. The feed is designed; name the design and the regulators.
satirist: Concrete instruction. The mantra is a bit hushed-voice, but ten breaths is a real thing you can do.
mythmaker: Doom-scroll, flash of irritation: we've all been there. Concrete and usable.

modeler: Attention as a contested resource the loop draws on: a real mechanism, plainly told. Good.
skeptic: Attention competition is plausible, but 'mechanical' oversells a hypothesis. Say 'probably works because'.
clinician: Plain mechanism. Warn that if the breath is used to make the feeling go away, it becomes a control strategy.
habit: Mechanical reason plus 'a small one is a better teacher.' Explains without preaching.
contemplative: A plain mechanism, kindly told. 'A small one is a better teacher' is wise.
stress: Mechanical, not mystical, and plausible. 'A small one is a better teacher' is wise. Keep.
gamedesigner: The mechanical reason earns trust. 'A small one is a better teacher' is good design.
structural: The attention-competition mechanism is plausible. But the spiral 'feeds on your attention' because someone is monetizing it.
satirist: 'Mechanical, not mystical.' Good instinct. Name the mechanism's source (attentional capacity research) and it passes Bryson.
mythmaker: Mechanical reason given plainly. 'A small one is a better teacher' is nice.

modeler: An actual mechanism: attention is a finite stock, and you compete for it. 'A small one is a better teacher' is nice dosing.
skeptic: 'Attention is limited' is real psychology. 'Compete for the machinery' is loose, but the advice to start small is sound.
clinician: Starting small ('a twitch in a queue') is right. Watch the 'compete with the loop' framing; it drifts toward control strategy.
habit: 'A twitch of irritation in a queue will do.' Named cue, mechanism, small rep. This is my standard.
contemplative: 'A twitch of irritation in a queue will do. A small one is a better teacher.' That is real teaching.
stress: Mechanical not mystical, small irritation as teacher. Claim specific enough to fail. Good.
gamedesigner: Mechanical reason plus 'a small one is a better teacher.' That's tuning difficulty for the player. Love it.
structural: Mechanical account of attention, good. Silent on the industries engineered to capture that same limited attention.
satirist: 'Mechanical rather than mystical,' plus irritation in a queue. Good. Name the attention research and it passes Bryson too.
mythmaker: The twitch of irritation in a queue is a real moment. 'A small one is a better teacher' is warm.

modeler: Diagnostic before fix. Right engineering order.
skeptic: Specific prompt with a time threshold. Good.
clinician: Bounded diagnostic of one stuck thing. A good prompt.
habit: Pick one thing stuck a month. Clear scope, clear task.
contemplative: A real stuck thing, an honest question. Good.
stress: One-month threshold, a forced choice. A concrete diagnostic.
gamedesigner: A concrete pick-one task with a time threshold. It hands me the controller.
structural: A useful setup for diagnosing what's missing. Personal, but honest.
satirist: A practical prompt. 'More than a month' is a nice specific threshold.
mythmaker: Everyone has a month-stuck thing. Immediate hook.

modeler: Three orthogonal failure modes. A clean diagnostic taxonomy.
skeptic: A compact three-way diagnosis. Useful whether or not it's exhaustive.
clinician: Three plain categories that point at the problem rather than the person. Shame-safe.
habit: Three tight definitions. Easy to run in two minutes.
contemplative: Three words a child could hold. Clear and usable.
stress: Tight triage. Each leg is clear enough to be wrong about, which is the point.
gamedesigner: Three crisp options, so a real choice. Agency delivered.
structural: A clean three-way split. Capacity should name time and money explicitly; structural scarcity hides inside 'what it takes'.
satirist: Three words, plain definitions, and you can use it. Good.
mythmaker: Three clean words. 'It isn't yours to want' cuts deep.

modeler: A cheap, sharp test that separates want from obligation. 'It's owed' lands.
skeptic: The starting-versus-finished test is clever, untested and memorable. Add 'usually'. Dread of starting can coexist with genuine want.
clinician: The starting-versus-finishing test is crisp and usable. Note that depression can make everything feel owed.
habit: 'Starting or having finished?' One question to carry all day. Best in the chunk.
contemplative: 'It isn't wanted. It's owed.' A test I can use tonight. Beautiful and precise.
stress: Starting versus finishing is a sharp, cheap, falsifiable test. 'It's owed' lands hard. Keep.
gamedesigner: The starting-versus-finished test is a real feedback signal. 'It's owed' hits hard.
structural: Owed versus wanted is a sharp diagnostic that actually solves misdirected effort. It also has a social edge: who loaded the obligation on you?
satirist: 'It isn't wanted. It's owed.' The best line in the chunk. You could say it to anyone at a bar and they'd wince.
mythmaker: 'It isn't wanted. It's owed.' An image I'll carry tomorrow, and the book brings it back. Keep.

modeler: Transition with a dramatic claim it doesn't yet earn. Merge into U0207.
skeptic: Transition. 'The day the week turns on' is asserted drama.
clinician: Transition. Fine, but it could merge into U0207.
habit: Hype line. Cut 'the week turns on'; go straight to U0207.
contemplative: A small turning point. Fine, though 'the day the week turns on' is a touch dramatic.
stress: Setup line. Fine.
gamedesigner: A setup beat with a good sense of stakes rising. Fine as a header.
structural: A transition into the social. Promising.
satirist: Announces importance instead of showing it. Cut the second sentence.
mythmaker: Signals the turn, does no work itself.

modeler: A header that moves the practice to a new scale. Functional, nothing more.
skeptic: A header. Nothing yet to test.
clinician: Header and bridge. 'Hold your read' is undefined here; one plain gloss would make it usable.
habit: Header and transition only. Clear, earns nothing more; the content below must carry it.
contemplative: A clean step outward from the head into the room. Simple.
stress: Header and transition. Neutral.
gamedesigner: Clean escalation beat: inner game to the real world. Good rising curve.
structural: Transition into dyad. Header-level; earns only clarity.
satirist: A header and one bridge line. Clear, inert.
mythmaker: A good turn: the practice finally goes into the room with another person. The stakes rise, as they should.

modeler: A clear setup, a concrete situation, and the snap read named. Works.
skeptic: Holding your read targets exactly the mind-reading overconfidence Epley documents. The best-grounded practice here.
clinician: Recognizable moment, well framed. Setup only; the step must follow immediately or this is just a diagnosis.
habit: Names the exact moment: your read leaves your mouth before they finish. That's a cue. Need the rep right after.
contemplative: Your read leaving your mouth before they finish. I have done this. Honest setup.
stress: Your read leaving your mouth before they finish is a real, costly habit. Good setup.
gamedesigner: A good setup with a familiar stakes moment, but no move yet. That's fine if the instruction follows immediately.
structural: Moving into a room with another person is the right direction. The read-before-they-finish is recognizable.
satirist: Defining 'read' as the guess that leaves your mouth early is plain and familiar. A decent setup.
mythmaker: A read leaving your mouth before they finish: that's a real scene with a cost. Good stakes for Day 6.

modeler: Good concrete: the read leaves your mouth before they finish. Names the fast-reaction loop; setup only, so the mechanism is thin.
skeptic: Good that 'read' is named as a guess about another mind. It says it 'usually' leaves your mouth, though, which is an unsupported claim about me.
clinician: Names a real moment, interrupting, without blame. One concrete conversation, one small act. Usable today.
habit: Strong cue: your read leaves your mouth before they finish. One conversation, one behaviour. Say what to do instead.
contemplative: One conversation, one restraint, and I can feel the read leaving my mouth. Simple and doable at my own table.
stress: Specific failure named: the read leaves your mouth early. Testable on the next conversation. Concrete and personal; not a big-picture idea.
gamedesigner: Nice level-up beat: from solo practice into a live room, with a concrete trap, your read leaving your mouth first. Clear challenge, relatable. Wants a success check.
structural: Moves practice into a room with another person, which helps. Still a private interaction skill; no spillover to group action named.
satirist: Defines 'read' in plain words and names the exact failure: guess leaves mouth before they finish. Bar-table proof.
mythmaker: Your read leaving your mouth before they finish talking: I've done that. Real cost implied. Show the other person's flinch.

modeler: Concrete protocol: withhold your read, ask twice, tolerate the pause. Doable today.
skeptic: Withholding your read corrects the 'lesser minds' bias in practice. Epley would approve. Keep.
clinician: Concrete relational skill with a clear count. Good.
habit: 'What else?' twice, sit through the pause. Pure Bungay Stanier. Perfect rep.
contemplative: Hold your read, ask 'what else' twice, sit in the pause. This is deep listening. Keep it.
stress: Concrete, uncomfortable and checkable. Sitting through the pause is a real cost. Good.
gamedesigner: Specific and countable: ask 'what else?' twice and survive the pause. Great social level.

modeler: Gentle and iterative. Fine as a prompt, no content to test.

modeler: Repeat-and-refine is a real local rule, but it's a one-line comfort. No stock, no limit. Kind, not machinery.

clinician: Permission to repeat yesterday's small thing. Warm, no shame, tiny step. Exactly right for a bad day.

stress: Gentle comfort. Lovely in a calm sea; no storm. What if yesterday's thing failed? Nothing to break, nothing to test.
gamedesigner: Warm save-point line: repeat yesterday, a bit better. Easy and kind, but it's flavor text. No feedback signal, no move to make.
structural: Gentle epigraph about repeating yesterday. Soothing, and exactly the inner-work comfort that excuses nothing being asked of the world.
satirist: Do yesterday's thing again, slightly better. Small, doable, no sacred costume. Would survive a skeptic at a bar.
mythmaker: Warm Lasso pep talk, but no Beard in the room to doubt it. Gentle, not yet earned.

modeler: Permission to repeat small is real behavioral advice. 'A little better or the same' is a gentle gain and floor.

clinician: 'The same if it doesn't' is permission for a bad day. Best line here; protects against all-or-nothing shame.
habit: Do yesterday's small thing again. That's the Two-Minute Rule in a sentence. Keep it, put it where people slump.
contemplative: Permission to repeat gently. Calming, doable, true. This is how to teach.
stress: Antifragile advice: works on the bad day too, 'the same if it doesn't.' Strong. Keep.
gamedesigner: Forgiving difficulty setting: repeat is allowed. Lowers the quit risk. Good.
structural: Gentle, resonant, and the kind of line that soothes. Repeat yesterday's thing: does that ever touch the rules?
satirist: 'Do yesterday's small thing again, the same if it doesn't.' Kind, plain, usable, and survives a bar. Not wonder, just sense.
mythmaker: 'The same if it doesn't' is mercy with a cost admitted. Gentle, lived-in, and I'd quote it. Stakes are quiet but real.

modeler: The 'explainable, not vaguely spiritual' promise is good. Now each section must keep it.

mythmaker: Throat-clearing. Fine but inert.

contemplative: Ten breaths, a question in passing: humble. 'Check whether it works on you' is respectful.

satirist: 'Check whether it works on you instead of taking it on faith' is the right posture. Good.

modeler: Inventory of gap-fitted practices, with a promise to explain what each does so I can test it. Good, but the mechanism is deferred.

contemplative: Ten breaths, a few minutes outside: these I could do in my kitchen. Test it on yourself, not on faith. Good.

structural: Breaths, outdoors, pauses: individual coping for conditions likely designed upstream. Testable-not-faith is a virtue; no rule, no lever.
satirist: Four named gaps, and 'test it on yourself instead of taking it on faith' is exactly the Bokonon honesty. Welcome.
mythmaker: Useful index of gaps, zero people. 'Test it on yourself' is a good dare; put someone mid-spiral to take it.

modeler: Clear trigger condition. Fine.

modeler: Duplicate of Day 4 but standalone-usable. Fine.

contemplative: Follow a branch until it splits. I can do it on the walk. 'Rest on the repetition' is a little clever.

contemplative: The shadow, the gust, the wall are good. Naming it 'a Tree' in Part Three adds a term I don't need here.
stress: Rule meeting conditions is a good image. 'Gets easier to see in a habit' asserted, not evidenced.
gamedesigner: A solid explanation, but it dilutes U0220's punch, and the Part Three 'Tree' term is a promise for chapter twelve. Trim.
structural: Tree as unrolled loop is a good teaching image. Conditions are weather, never policy; that's the gap.
satirist: The tree as a slow loop works. Then it gets capitalized into a Tree term for Part Three. A metaphor drafted into jargon.
mythmaker: The shadow, the gust and the wall give the tree a biography. The jargon tag at the end flattens it.

modeler: One rule plus varying conditions gives varied branches: essentially an L-system with noise. A real mechanism, well mapped to habits.
skeptic: The 'safe rehearsal' rationale is plausible. 'Your habits grow the same way' is analogy presented as identity. Mark it as a metaphor.
clinician: 'Nothing of yours at stake, a safe place to rehearse' is exactly right before turning attention inward. Thoughtful.
habit: 'One rule meeting each day's weather' is gorgeous. Safe rehearsal ground makes sense. Explains why, which helps keep the rep.
contemplative: One rule meeting each day's weather. A safe place to rehearse seeing. The last naming sentence can go.
stress: Rehearsing on low stakes before high stakes is a sound principle. The tree-as-habit analogy is asserted, not shown.
gamedesigner: 'A safe place to rehearse' is great design logic, a tutorial zone with no stakes. The Tree term arrives earned.
structural: One rule meeting new conditions is a clear mechanism. 'Rehearse before turning it on yourself' stays i-frame.
satirist: The tree as rehearsal space with nothing at stake is a good rationale. The metaphor stays a metaphor. Mostly earned.
mythmaker: One rule meeting each day's weather. The tree comes back with new weight, a safe rehearsal. Lovely.

modeler: Directed attention as a depletable stock, restored by nature: an actual bathtub. Good, short.
skeptic: 'There is evidence' is correctly hedged; attention restoration findings are mixed. Exactly the right confidence. Keep.
clinician: Evidence-aware and compassionate: 'pays most on the day hardest to start.' Good.
habit: 'Pays most on the day it's hardest to start.' A reason that fights skipping. Good.
contemplative: Kind and practical. 'Pays most on exactly the day it is hardest to start' is true. Keep.
stress: Attention restoration, appropriately hedged as 'there is evidence'. Name the research and it's solid.
gamedesigner: 'Pays most on the day it's hardest to start' is a great retention hook.
structural: Attention restoration through nature is real. So is unequal park access, a policy lever left unnamed.
satirist: 'There is evidence.' Whose? Name Kaplan's Attention Restoration Theory and this becomes knowledge. Good last line.
mythmaker: 'Pays most on the day hardest to start.' Practical and kind.

modeler: Label line.
skeptic: Usage cue. Fine.
clinician: A clear cue.
habit: Cue named. Good spec line.
contemplative: Clear cue for use. Fine.
stress: Trigger line. Fine.
gamedesigner: A clear trigger. Fine.
structural: A trigger cue. Fine.
satirist: Label line. Inert.
mythmaker: Clear cue.

modeler: A precise trigger: the hand already reaching. That is the exact moment a balancing intervention can fire.
skeptic: The cue is vivid and recognizable.
clinician: Hand already reaching for the phone: precise, recognizable cue. Exactly when to use it.
habit: 'Hand already reaching for the phone' — a precise, physical cue. Perfect trigger.
contemplative: 'Hand already reaching for the phone' is exactly the moment. Good cue.
stress: Specific, recognizable trigger. Works.
gamedesigner: A vivid trigger: 'hand already reaching.' The player recognizes the moment instantly.
structural: Phone, snack, sharp reply: all products of design, framed as personal reaches. Who profits from the reach?
satirist: 'Hand already reaching for the phone, the snack, the sharp reply.' A precise, recognizable cue.
mythmaker: The hand already reaching for the phone is caught mid-gesture. That's the face.

modeler: 'Only place a loop can be changed from' overclaims; environment design changes cues too. Otherwise solid.
skeptic: 'The only place a loop can be changed from' overclaims. Environment design changes loops without awareness. Soften.
clinician: 'You don't have to stop it' is defusion done right.
habit: Pause and name four beats. Simple, startable, no stopping required.
contemplative: Name it, don't fight it. Simple mindfulness. Keep.
stress: Usable, but 'the only place a loop can be changed from' overclaims. Environment design changes loops too.
gamedesigner: A simple move with low pressure: you don't have to stop it. Good onboarding.
structural: Awareness as 'the only place a loop can be changed from' is false. Loops also change when someone changes the cues.
satirist: Practical. 'The only place a loop can be changed from' overclaims; cut 'only.'
mythmaker: Plain instruction, third telling. Fine.

modeler: Finds the leverage point: the interpretive link between cue and craving. Meadows would nod.
skeptic: Locating the leverage in appraisal is a good, testable idea. Present it as a hypothesis with appraisal research behind it.
clinician: A useful map of which beat you can reach. It needs one example of reassigning the meaning of a cue.
habit: Craving as the interpretive beat is sharp. Turn it into a rep: ask 'what does this cue mean?'
contemplative: A real insight: meaning sits between cue and craving. Its bold opener could be one plain sentence.
stress: Locating the one interpretive beat is a precise, testable insight. That's real leverage.
gamedesigner: Shows where the player can actually act within a loop. A useful map of the hit-box.
structural: 'A cue arrives whether you like it or not.' So who placed it? Moving the cue is the s-frame lever, and it's ignored.
satirist: A real insight: the cue's meaning is the one beat you can reach. That's Epictetus. Credit him and it gains weight.
mythmaker: Meaning at cue-craving is a genuine insight. Needs one person reading a buzzing phone differently.

modeler: Defines the success state as cue in, no flow out. Concrete and rarely said.
skeptic: A concrete success criterion, usefully undramatic. Good.
clinician: A concrete picture of success, undramatic and humane. Excellent.
habit: Paints what success looks like. Readers rarely get this. Keep.
contemplative: A cue arrives and nothing follows. This is peace, described without drama. Beautiful.
stress: It defines success concretely, and it's undramatic. That's honest. Keep.
gamedesigner: It finally tells me what success looks like. A rare, explicit feedback signal. Excellent.
structural: A quiet success condition. Personally resonant, and private all the way down.
satirist: A success state described with no drama, and that's why it's convincing. Good, honest writing.
mythmaker: Success as 'nothing follows' is quiet and true. Lovely, no drama, exactly right.

modeler: 'Tax paid in attention' is a nice flow framing. Dual-process is a simplification, but it's serviceable here.
skeptic: Kahneman's System 2 is lazy. Naming may engage it briefly, or not at all. 'Forces' is too strong.
clinician: Fine mechanism, but standard fast/slow-system material. Support, not substance.
habit: Fine dual-system gloss. Mechanism, not a move.
contemplative: A clear explanation, but more head than heart. It could be one sentence.
stress: A dual-process gloss, borrowed and simplified. Fine, but credit Kahneman and note the replication caveats.
gamedesigner: Dual-system explainer, decent. 'A small tax on autopilot' is a nice image.
structural: System 1 and System 2 boilerplate. Accurate, and it adds nothing to the playing field.
satirist: Kahneman's System 1/2 without the name. 'A small tax' is a nice phrase. Cite him.
mythmaker: Fast/slow system mechanics, no face. Attention-as-tax is a decent image.

modeler: 'Tax on autopilot' is a decent flow image. Leaning on System 1 and 2 as machinery overstates a descriptive model.
skeptic: It misstates Kahneman: System 1 runs by default and System 2 is lazy. Fix 'whichever the moment demands'.
clinician: Clear mechanism, but it's explanation. 'Tax on autopilot' is nice; no new action for the reader.
habit: Kahneman mechanism, clear. 'That second is where a choice becomes possible' — nice, but explanatory, not a step.
contemplative: Citing Kahneman and the 'tax on autopilot' explains, but it doesn't help me do it. Keep only: 'That second is where a choice becomes possible.'
stress: Kahneman framing is fair and hedged ('if only for a second'). Modest mechanism. Good.
gamedesigner: Kahneman, used well and briefly. 'Tax on autopilot' is a memorable rule. Clear why the move works.
structural: Kahneman nudge-to-self. Easy to study, scales to nobody. Fine as a tool, not as the answer.
satirist: Names Kahneman and passes the Bryson test. 'A small tax on autopilot' is witty and true enough. Good.
mythmaker: A clean explanation of Kahneman, and 'a small tax on autopilot' is good. It's still a lecture, not a scene.

modeler: Names the mechanism, with a source, and locates the choice point in the latency. That's how you justify a practice.
skeptic: Kahneman called the two systems useful fictions. 'Naming brings in System 2' is a proposed mechanism, not a finding. Say 'may'.
clinician: Kahneman made plain; the phone-buzz gap gives a concrete moment of choice. Works, without demanding constant vigilance.
habit: 'Between the phone's buzz and your hand reaching': that's the cue. Mechanism plus moment. This is how to explain a practice.
contemplative: The second between buzz and hand: true. 'Tax paid in a currency' is clever ornament; let the second stand alone.
stress: Kahneman's two systems, invoked cleanly. The 'second between the buzz and the hand' is concrete. The mechanism is plausible but untested here.
gamedesigner: The mechanism is explained, and the gap between buzz and reach is a moment I can actually catch. Strong.
structural: Solid mechanism. But the phone's buzz was tuned by people paid to win that second. Name them.
satirist: Names Kahneman, gives the mechanism, and the phone-buzz moment is the payoff. 'Here's how we know.' Keep.
mythmaker: The second between the buzz and your hand is a face and a stakes moment. Kahneman, made human.

modeler: Label line.
skeptic: Usage cue. Fine.
clinician: Label line only.
habit: 'Standing practice' with no cue. U0229 fixes it.
contemplative: Simple framing for a speech practice. Good.
stress: Framing line.
gamedesigner: A header blurb. Fine.
structural: A label. Fine.
satirist: Label line.
mythmaker: Use note. Fine.

modeler: Sets up the practice clearly. Inner speech and outer speech are two flows into one stock. Fine.
skeptic: A framing line. Clear, and it does nothing yet.
clinician: Monitoring 'words in your head' risks rumination. Specify a brief, bounded check, not a standing watch.
habit: 'Standing practice' with no cue or time. Say when: first sentence you say to yourself in the morning?
contemplative: A header that signals the practice. It earns little alone.
stress: Framing line only. Neutral.
gamedesigner: A vague cue: 'standing practice' gives no trigger moment. Name when to use it, like the others do.
structural: Framing line for affirmations. Nothing to grip.
satirist: A label for a practice, clear and empty on its own.
mythmaker: A one-line frame. Fine, but there's no image or stakes yet.

modeler: Clear usage spec. Fine.
skeptic: Two specific moments, one of them self-harshness, which many will recognize. Clear and usable.
clinician: Naming self-harshness as a use case is good. Make sure the practice that follows is self-compassion, not self-correction.
habit: Two named moments: before a hard conversation, when harsh with yourself. Cues done right. Good setup.
contemplative: When you are harsh with yourself: Ruiz would nod. Two clear moments to practice.
stress: A clear use case at two moments. Pure framing.
gamedesigner: Two clear trigger moments for the practice. Good controls.
structural: A setup line for a practice. Nothing to grip.
satirist: Two clear trigger moments. Serviceable stage direction.
mythmaker: 'Harsh with yourself' names a real wound. A clear setup for the practice.

modeler: Judge a thought by its growth trajectory, not its truth value. A usable reframe.
skeptic: Usable question, but 'not true or false' worries me. A harsh true thought still deserves checking. Ask both questions.
clinician: Asking whether a thought helps rather than whether it's true is pure Harris. Good for harsh self-talk.
habit: Cue (before hard talk, harsh thought) plus one question. Works.
contemplative: A seed of fear, or a seed of care? This is right speech, gently asked. Keep it.
stress: 'Not true or false' dodges the truth. Some fear-seeds are accurate warnings. Add: check it first, then ask what it grows.
gamedesigner: One clear diagnostic question with a trigger. Playable.
structural: Fear versus care in self-talk. Inner framing only.
satirist: 'Fear or care' is a usable two-way sort. 'Seeds aren't judged that way' is a bit cute, but it holds.
mythmaker: Fear or care seed: simple, usable before a hard talk. Good.

modeler: Liturgy. Warm, no mechanism. Fine in place.
skeptic: Affirmations have weak evidence, and can backfire for low self-esteem. Optional at best.
clinician: Usable scripts, but after a bad day 'what I did today becomes tomorrow' reads like a threat. Add a forgiving version.
habit: Morning and evening anchors. Ready-made bookends. Good.
contemplative: Two small verses for morning and evening. Warm, and easy to memorize. Keep.
stress: Affirmations. Calm-sea decoration. Nothing here survives a bad morning.
gamedesigner: Affirmations with no feedback loop. They're mood text, not moves. Pair each with a check.
structural: Affirmation scripts. This is exactly the inner-work genre this book claimed not to be.
satirist: 'I tend the field of my mind.' Hushed-voice foma. Admit it's a liturgy, or cut it. Bokonon would have rhymed it and winked.
mythmaker: Prayers a little greeting-card. Usable, unearned.

modeler: 'Easier tomorrow' states reinforcement honestly, and the evening line adds the exit. Good liturgy, not much mechanism.
skeptic: Affirmations. 'Easier tomorrow' is the plausible part; the rest is incantation.
clinician: The evening line forgives without demanding. Morning line edges toward pressure, but 'if saying it helps' keeps it optional.
habit: Morning and day's-end bookends: real cues, short lines. The second line is a tidy review habit.
contemplative: Two lines to say at morning and at night. This is how a teaching becomes lived. Beautiful.
stress: Affirmations: fragile comfort in a bad week. Second line's escape hatch saves it a little.
gamedesigner: Pleasant recitations, but no feedback signal. Add an evening check, something like 'what did I repeat today?'
structural: Affirmations. Exactly the inner-work-as-remedy register I distrust; earns only readability.
satirist: 'I tend the field of my mind today.' Hushed-voice foma. Either wink at it or make the line something you'd actually say.
mythmaker: The field-of-the-mind lines are sayable and kind. The planting image has come back across chapters, and that earns them.

modeler: Self-aware about earnestness, which helps. A liturgy, not a mechanism; fine in its place.
skeptic: The self-aware 'earnest' aside is disarming. 'It will be easier tomorrow' is an unconditional promise. Make it 'can be'.
clinician: Optional, earnest, gentle. 'Tomorrow I can plant something else' offers a way forward, not a verdict. Good.
habit: Morning and evening lines, cued by time of day, honestly framed. I'd actually say the evening one. Works.
contemplative: Simple lines to say aloud. The evening one is gentle and forgiving. Good prayer.
stress: It admits the earnestness, which is honest. The affirmations are still fragile comfort. 'It will be easier tomorrow' is a promise nobody backs.
gamedesigner: Charming self-awareness about sounding earnest. There's no feedback signal, though: what tells me it worked?
structural: Self-talk liturgy. The self-aware hedge is charming; it is still inner work only.
satirist: Its self-awareness ('sounding a little earnest to an empty room') rescues it. But 'field of my mind' is still vestments.
mythmaker: The self-aware 'empty room' wink earns the earnestness. The lines are gentle, if a bit greeting-card.

modeler: Ritual lines have a feedback gesture: review what repeated, replant. Warm and self-aware, but no stock or delay. Charming, not mechanism.
skeptic: Self-aware about sounding earnest and 'can be easier' hedges. A ritual, not evidence; fine as one, and honest about it.
clinician: Acknowledges self-consciousness, then offers non-punishing lines. 'Tomorrow I can plant something else' is shame-safe. Keep.
habit: Morning and evening lines are fixed cues, tiny and speakable. The evening question is a good single question.
contemplative: Two short lines I could say aloud. The admission of sounding earnest is honest. Trim 'It can be easier tomorrow' to stay impeccable.
stress: Self-aware about sounding earnest, which I respect. But incantation, not test. 'It can be easier tomorrow' is soft comfort that never faces a bad day.
gamedesigner: Morning and evening lines are a decent checkpoint ritual, and the self-aware hedge is charming. But no feedback signal; it's a spell, not a move.
structural: Personal affirmations. 'Tend the field of my mind' is the inner-work alibi in miniature; nothing reaches anyone else.
satirist: 'Sounding a little earnest to an empty room' shows the author knows the costume is a costume. Bokonon would nod. Mostly liturgy though.
mythmaker: 'Sounding earnest to an empty room' is honest and human. The lines themselves are soft; give them a bad morning to push against.

modeler: The evening question is a real sensing step: what did I repeat. That closes a small loop. Nice.
skeptic: Self-aware about sounding earnest; optional. Rituals plausibly help habits, though no evidence offered. Usable and low-risk.
clinician: Nonjudgmental evening line: tomorrow I can plant something else. Warns about sounding earnest, kind. 'Worth becoming' risks evaluation.
habit: Morning line and end-of-day question are anchored to when. Evening question 'what did I repeat?' is the one worth carrying.
contemplative: Two short lines to say aloud: breath-sized. The aside about sounding earnest is kind. Good practice.
stress: Self-aware about sounding earnest, and the evening line allows failure. Optional, low risk. Fine.
gamedesigner: Morning and evening check-ins form a feedback loop. Self-aware about the earnestness. Nice.
structural: Clear, but a morning mantra for the mind-field is inner work as a ritual. Who profits from my doing it alone?
satirist: 'Sounding a little earnest to an empty room': the author knows the costume is a costume. Short lines, usable. Bokonon would sign it.
mythmaker: 'A little earnest to an empty room' — he knows the reader's embarrassment. That's the Beard doubting. The lines themselves are sweet and usable.

modeler: Fluid pooling at the extremities is a physiology metaphor posing as mechanism. What's the stock of 'residue'? Cut it or model it.
skeptic: The fluid-pooling analogy is confusing and physiologically loose. 'Residue' is undefined. Cut.
clinician: The fluid-pooling metaphor is odd and lands nowhere. Cut it or replace it with a plain reason.
habit: Body-fluid metaphor is odd and weak. Cut, or say 'end-of-day reset'.
contemplative: The fluid-at-extremities image confuses more than it calms. Cut it, or simply say: evenings gather what the day left.
stress: A fluid-pooling analogy for mental residue is loose physiology doing rhetorical work. Cut it, or give a real reason for evening review.
gamedesigner: Lost the player. The fluid-pooling metaphor confuses and justifies nothing. Cut it.
structural: An odd bodily analogy that explains nothing. Cut it.
satirist: Fluid pooling at the extremities as a reason for evening reflection? The analogy is strange and proves nothing. Cut.
mythmaker: Fluid pooling in extremities is odd and dropped instantly. Cut or give the residue a face.

modeler: A reinforcing loop with no goal-check, named honestly. Seeding supplies the missing selector. Good.
skeptic: Repetition breeds ease, ease breeds belief. That's real, and it's the illusory truth effect. Name it and it's airtight.
clinician: Clear and true. 'Choosing what you're willing to make effortless' resonates.
habit: 'Choosing what you're willing to make effortless.' Great framing line.
contemplative: Choosing what you make effortless. Clear and true, and it serves me.
stress: Repetition doesn't care about value: true, sobering, actionable. Short and strong.
gamedesigner: 'Choosing what you're willing to make effortless' is a sharp reframe. Good.
structural: Repetition makes thoughts effortless. True. Now apply it to repeated advertising and who pays for that repetition.
satirist: 'Choosing what you're willing to make effortless.' A crisp payoff line. The neuroscience is hand-waved but harmless.
mythmaker: 'Choosing what you're willing to make effortless.' Memorable line. Keep.

modeler: Inflow is always on; the practice only adds observation. Correct systems reading.
skeptic: Good reframe: you're always planting. Plausible, and it lowers the stakes of starting.
clinician: 'Planting either way' risks becoming 'everything I think is my fault.' Add that seeing it is a gift, not an indictment.
habit: You're planting either way. Useful reframe, but no action in it.
contemplative: 'You are planting either way.' This is beautiful. Drop the bold opener about misreading.
stress: 'You're planting either way' removes the opt-out. A good reframe.
gamedesigner: 'You're planting either way' raises the stakes nicely. Strong second beat.
structural: 'You are planting either way' is a fair reframe, but it pins all the planting on you. Feeds and employers plant too.
satirist: 'You are planting either way.' A good turn, plainly put.
mythmaker: You're planting either way: a real turn. Stakes without melodrama.

modeler: A short feedback loop to sustain motivation through a long delay. Exactly how you manage delay. Lovely.
skeptic: Builds in a feedback loop, which intuition needs before it can be trusted. Good.
clinician: A small, concrete check, explicitly 'not to judge the crop.' Shame-aware feedback.
habit: 'Before the day ends, check one thing.' Cue plus rep plus a fast return. Excellent.
contemplative: Go back and look, not to judge. A gentle evening practice. Keep.
stress: A fast feedback loop to sustain slow work. Practical, and honest that most plantings show nothing.
gamedesigner: A built-in fast-return feedback loop. This is exactly how you keep a player through slow progress.
structural: A fast feedback check for agency. A personally useful loop.
satirist: A practical check-back step. 'Confirm the ground answers at all' is nicely modest.
mythmaker: Go back and look: practical, keeps hope fed. Good garden image held.

modeler: Names the measurement bias in its own feedback channel. A model that audits its sensor. Good.
skeptic: Flags confirmation bias in its own practice. Exactly right; the fix is ordinary and honest.
clinician: A sound confirmation-bias caution, but the correction is generic. How do you look for what actually happened?
habit: Confirmation-bias caveat. Needs a concrete check, like writing what you expected beforehand.
contemplative: An honest caution. The Part Five reference can go. Look at what happened, not at what you hoped for.
stress: It names its own confirmation-bias failure mode. Exactly the stress test I want. Keep.
gamedesigner: A good warning about biased feedback. The Part Five reference is unnecessary.
structural: A confirmation-bias caveat. Correct and brief.
satirist: Confirmation bias, honestly flagged. The Part Five cross-reference is unnecessary; just say the bias's name.
mythmaker: Sensible caution against confirmation. Dry; fine.

modeler: Excellent: it names the runaway confirmation loop and installs a balancing check by stating predictions before you look.
skeptic: Predict before you check: a genuine debiasing move. Best passage in the set.
clinician: Say what you hope, then look, including what didn't happen: a real debiasing step, plainly said.
habit: Concrete fix: say what you hope to see before you check. That's a usable, specific correction.
contemplative: The correction is good: say what you hope, then look. 'Part Five's figures' is an assumption the reader remembers them.
stress: Pre-register your hope, then look. Real anti-bias discipline. Exactly what I want.
gamedesigner: Excellent: it builds a feedback correction against confirmation bias. 'Say what you hope first' is a playable rule.
structural: Pre-registering what you hope to see is a real, usable correction. Concrete method, honestly stated.
satirist: Names confirmation bias and gives a usable correction: predict, then look. Exactly the honesty I want.
mythmaker: An honest look at its own failure mode, with a practical correction. Dry, but it lands.

modeler: The reinforcing confirmation loop gets an explicit balancing check: pre-register, then count the misses. Exactly right.
skeptic: Predict first, then count the misses. That is real debiasing. The best paragraph here by my lights.
clinician: Correction is concrete. But 'count the times you snapped anyway' could become a self-scolding tally; add 'without judging.'
habit: Say what you hope first, then count the snaps. Concrete debiasing step. Opening sentence drags; start at 'Go looking'.
contemplative: Say what you hope first, then count the snaps anyway. Honest, impeccable, livable.
stress: Write the prediction down, then count the misses. This is the falsification step. The best paragraph in the batch.
gamedesigner: Best feedback design in the batch: say your prediction first, then count the snaps. Exactly right.
structural: A pre-registered hope plus counting the misses: an actual debiasing tool. Good.
satirist: Confirmation bias named, plus a counting fix. 'Count the times you snapped anyway' is wonderfully deflating. Keep.
mythmaker: 'Then count the times you snapped anyway': that's honest, and it bites. The doubter is in the room. Good.

modeler: Mapping table in prose. Tidy, but 'breath is thinning' contradicts its earlier framing as attention-loading. Reconcile it.
skeptic: A tidy mapping that feels true because it's tidy. It also recasts the breath as thinning, at odds with earlier framing.
clinician: Neat synthesis that serves the system more than the reader. Fine to keep short.
habit: Mapping practices to moves is bookkeeping. Readers don't need it to act.
contemplative: Mapping breath to 'thinning' feels forced. Let the practices be practices. Cut it, or keep only 'Look, plant, tend, thin.'
stress: Retrofitting four practices onto four moves is tidy, but it's after-the-fact neatness. 'That is the whole of it' is grandiose.
gamedesigner: The mapping onto four moves feels forced. Breath equals thinning isn't intuitive. Show it with an example or drop it.
structural: Bookkeeping that maps practices onto moves. Internal tidiness, no payoff for the reader.
satirist: Bookkeeping that maps practices onto moves. The reader didn't need the filing system. Cut.
mythmaker: Useful map, but bookkeeping. Okay in place.

modeler: Mapping practices onto flows is structural. 'A spiral without attention starves' names the drain. The tidy fourfold mapping feels slightly forced.
skeptic: Tidy mapping. 'A spiral without attention starves' is fluency standing in for evidence.
clinician: Synthesis for the architect, not the struggling reader. 'A spiral without attention starves' sets up a control fantasy.
habit: Mapping practices to moves is bookkeeping. Thinning-as-breath gets tangled. Readers want the reps, not the taxonomy.
contemplative: Mapping each practice onto a move is the author admiring the system. Breath as 'thinning' feels forced. Let the practices speak.
stress: Forcing four practices into four moves smells retrofitted. 'Everything else is those four' is closure hubris.
gamedesigner: Ties the system together, but the breath-as-thinning mapping feels forced. This is a recap the player didn't need.
structural: Maps practices onto moves. Bookkeeping; 'a spiral without attention starves' ignores who keeps feeding it.
satirist: Forcing four practices onto four moves reads like a filing system admiring itself. 'Breath is thinning' is a stretch. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: A tidy synthesis, but bookkeeping, and there's no one in the room. Cut it to the last two sentences.

modeler: The mapping holds except breath-as-thinning, which is a stretch. Say what flow the breath actually drains.
skeptic: Too tidy. Breath as 'thinning' is forced to complete the set. When a mapping fits this perfectly, suspect the fit.
clinician: Tidy synthesis; reclaiming attention from a spiral is a nice line. Mostly structural, little to do.
habit: Tidy mapping of practices to moves. Useful synthesis, but it's taxonomy, not a rep. Keep short.
contemplative: Mapping practices to moves lives in the head. 'The breath is thinning' needs too much context. Shorten to one line.
stress: Neat, maybe too neat. Calling the breath 'thinning' looks retrofitted. A tidy mapping is a warning sign, not proof.
gamedesigner: A tidy mapping that turns the list into a system. It's recap, though; give me a quick self-check.
structural: Taxonomy tidying. 'Done with someone else in the room' gestures outward, but no lever.
satirist: Mapping four practices onto four moves is the system admiring its own symmetry. The breath as 'thinning' is a stretch.
mythmaker: A tidy mapping, but it's ledger work. Nobody does any of the four moves here.

modeler: Maps practices onto moves; breath thins a spiral by starving its attention inflow. That's a stock-and-flow claim. Ends on a useful daily question.
skeptic: Tidy mapping of practices onto moves. Tidy is my warning sign: coherence isn't evidence the breath really 'starves' a spiral. Say how you'd know.
clinician: Neat unification, and the breath as starving a spiral is useful. Closing question is mild. More mechanism than comfort.
habit: Ends on one question, good. But the four-to-four mapping is dense. Trim to which practice, when, how long.
contemplative: Mapping practices onto moves is tidy but made for the head. Too many correspondences. The closing question is the only part I can live.
stress: Maps practices to moves, ends with a checkable question. Risk: everything fits four moves, so nothing could count against it. Still useful.
gamedesigner: Great reveal: the four practices map to four moves, so the game has one rule set. Ends on a question I can answer today. That's feedback.
structural: Tidy synthesis with a bigger-picture payoff. But the breath 'thins' a spiral that was likely engineered; blame stays on the individual.
satirist: Tidy mapping, but four practices times four moves is a codebook for a reader who hasn't memorized either. Breath-as-thinning is nice though.
mythmaker: The mapping is neat, but it's all nouns talking to nouns. Final question is the only human thing. Lead with it.

modeler: Epigraph. Fine.
skeptic: Slogan. It sits uneasily with Lowery: there may be no 'own loop' apart from others.
clinician: Motto. 'Close your own loop first' could read as self-sufficiency pressure.
habit: Short, clear motto.
contemplative: Short and inviting. It works as a threshold.
stress: Motto. Fine.
gamedesigner: A clean section motto. Fine.
structural: 'Close your own loop first' is the i-frame made doctrine. Figure and ground, not first and later.
satirist: A motto with no purchase. Fine as a header.
mythmaker: Short motto. Fine.

modeler: A decent epigraph for the self scale. It implies propagation without showing it, but U0238 does.
skeptic: A memorable epigraph. It assumes the carryover it asserts.
clinician: 'Close your loop' is jargon on a bad day. Vague directive; what does closing look like?
habit: Short epigraph, personal pull. Doesn't give a step, doesn't need to.
contemplative: Gentle and true. It invites without commanding.
stress: Fine epigraph, slightly self-help. Earns its spot.
gamedesigner: A short, sticky epigraph. Earns its place.
structural: 'Close your own loop first' sequences self before collective. That ordering is the alibi.
satirist: A plain epigraph with a real point: the loop you carry into every room. It earns its line.
mythmaker: 'The one you carry into every room' is a memorable image for an epigraph.

modeler: Neat epigraph. 'It comes with you' is the actual reason, and it's stated.
skeptic: A sensible reframe that avoids selfishness. As an epigraph, it does its small job.
clinician: Kind justification for self-work, not selfishness. Epigraph does its job.
habit: Oxygen-mask logic, warmly put. Fine epigraph; nothing to start, but it motivates the chapter.
contemplative: It comes with you into every room. Warm and true; not selfish. Keep.
stress: A decent aphorism, and 'not because you come first' heads off ego. It stakes little.
gamedesigner: A short, sticky reframe of self-first that dodges selfishness well.
structural: Fair framing: self first, as a carrier, not a priority. Spillover implied, not shown.
satirist: Oxygen-mask logic, said plainly. It earns its spot.
mythmaker: 'It comes with you into every room' is a quietly good epigraph. Warm.

modeler: Aphorism. Pretty line, but where's the stock? 'Walks into every room' hints at carryover, no mechanism offered.
skeptic: 'It walks into every room with you' is asserted as fact about everyone. Pleasant, rhythmic, untested.
clinician: Cryptic. 'Close your own loop first' risks sounding like self-focus advice. No action named; epigraph needs a step.
habit: Pretty, but close your loop how? No cue, no step. Give me the two-minute version.
contemplative: Beautiful and not too much. It says why to start with myself without pride. I could carry this into any room.
stress: Neat line, unproven. Does your own loop actually walk into every room? Assertion without a case. Aphorism, not evidence.
gamedesigner: Neat epigraph with a real insight: your unclosed loop enters every room. Clear but no action, no signal. Fine as a chapter pip.
structural: Close your own loop first: at least admits it walks into every room. Still self-first sequencing; spillover claimed, not shown.
satirist: Reads clean, but 'closes your own loop' is mantra-speak. Which loop? Give the room it walks into.
mythmaker: Nice turn on 'not because you come first.' Short, kind, true. Needs the room it walks into.

modeler: Nice line about carrying the loop into rooms, but it asserts. What does closing it do to the next loop?
skeptic: Reasoned in plain language, but 'walks into every room with you' is a lovely claim with no support. Mildly useful framing.
clinician: Reframes self-focus as service to others, avoiding selfishness guilt. Nice; 'close your loop' is still vague.
habit: Kitchen, meeting, call home: concrete rooms, and it's about me. But it's a rationale, not a rep.
contemplative: The kitchen, the meeting, the call home. It is lived and plain. The dash and 'not because' qualify slightly.
stress: Pretty, and the 'because it walks into every room' reason is thin. Show one room where it fails.
gamedesigner: Warm and memorable, but a motto, not a move.
structural: Claims spillover into kitchen, meeting, call home. That's my test three, but asserted, not shown. Show it reaching a group.
satirist: 'Walks into every room with you: the kitchen, the meeting, the call home.' Plain and concrete, and it tells me why to start here.
mythmaker: Kitchen, meeting, call home: the loop walks in with you. Specific rooms, a real cost to skipping. Short and it lands.

modeler: Rules propagate up a scale: real claim. Nest, Dyad and Skein jargon all at once. Give one example of the travel.
skeptic: 'Rarely stays contained' is asserted. Nest, Dyad and Skein jargon stack up. One example would help.
clinician: The jargon (Nest, Dyad, Skein) outruns the point. Say it plainly.
habit: Nest/Dyad/Skein jargon justifying the order. No action.
contemplative: Nest, Dyad, Skein in one breath. Say it plainly: what you do alone travels into those you love.
stress: 'Travels into a Dyad or Skein' is jargon stacked on an assertion. One real example would carry it.
gamedesigner: Nest, Dyad and Skein are stacked again. Say 'it spreads into your relationships'.
structural: It at least says a rule travels outward. Justifying self-first is weaker than doing both together.
satirist: Local Rule, Nest, Dyad, Skein in one sentence. A cathedral of jargon around 'your habits affect others.'
mythmaker: Nest, Dyad, Skein jargon in one breath. Faceless. Show a dishonest rule leaking into a marriage.

modeler: A real scale-propagation chain: fudging at self, then the dyad stops asking, then the skein learns it. Holds across levels.
skeptic: The money-fudging slide is an anecdote treated as mechanism. 'Soon' and 'learns' want a 'can'.
clinician: Fudging-money example rings true and targets actions, not identity. 'Not because you come first' guards against selfishness. Good.
habit: Money-fudging example stings in a good way. Jargon wall (Local Rule, Nest, Dyad, Skein) blunts it.
contemplative: The fudging-money example is painfully real. Nest, Dyad and Skein in three lines make me stop and decode. Use plain words.
stress: Fudged money spreading to partner then family: concrete, plausible, has skin. Strong.
gamedesigner: Fudging money numbers spreading outward is vivid and personal. Nest, Dyad and Skein in a row creep the jargon up again.
structural: Money-fudging spreading from self to partner to group is a real spillover account. It runs one direction only: outward, never upward.
satirist: Fudging money to yourself and then to your partner is a gut-punch example. Nest, Dyad and Skein crowd it. Let the example carry it.
mythmaker: Fudging money to yourself, then to your partner, then a Dyad that stops asking: cost and spread in one chain. Excellent.

modeler: Epigraph, inert.
skeptic: Generic epigraph. Nothing to test.
clinician: Epigraph, light.
habit: Generic epigraph. Doesn't add.
contemplative: A thin motto. It borrows game language without warmth. Try a gentler question about what you return to.
stress: Generic epigraph. It doesn't fit the chapter's 'installed rules' honesty.
gamedesigner: A designer's epigraph that frames choice as play. Works.
structural: 'Choose the game'. My line is 'change the game'. Choosing among rigged games is consumer agency, not reform.
satirist: Fortune-cookie epigraph. Does nothing.
mythmaker: Generic slogan epigraph. Weak.
