contemplative: Beginner's Spanish is honest and clear. It protects me from false cheer. Good.
stress: Good. It names its own failure mode, denial, and draws a clear line between fact and story. Survives strain.
gamedesigner: The Spanish example gives me a clean fact-or-story sorting test I can run myself. Clear rule.
structural: Honest about real limits, which I respect. The Spanish example is fine but low stakes.
satirist: Beginner's Spanish is the right example: fact versus story, said plainly. 'Defusion' slips in undefined, so gloss it or cut it.
mythmaker: Beginner's Spanish keeps fact and story apart, and it's fair to the opposing view. Clean, humane, useful.

modeler: Forward-deterministic, backward-ambiguous via stretch and fold: real chaos math, aptly used. Dense. One example would unlock it.
skeptic: Hindsight and the narrative fallacy, well put. 'A clean story is easier to hold' is exactly right.
clinician: Strong idea, but the forward/backward process talk is abstract. Let U0275 carry it.
habit: Forward/backward determinism is clever, but heavy. Let U0275 carry it.
contemplative: The forward-and-backward idea is good, and too technical. The 'Try this' that follows does it better.
stress: Backward ambiguity versus forward determinism: interesting, and it loosens a story's grip. Some histories really are single-cause; say so.
gamedesigner: The forward/backward determinism point is abstract. The Try This that follows does the work better.
structural: Multiple honest histories is a good point, made dense by the dynamics language.
satirist: Forward determinism, backward ambiguity. A real, interesting idea. Tighten the folding-and-stretching aside.
mythmaker: Backward-ambiguity idea is real, but abstract math. The exercise next does it better.

modeler: Real dynamics: a map that folds and stretches is many-to-one going backward. The dropped-class triple makes it usable. The best mechanism in this batch.
skeptic: Strong take on hindsight and the single-cause story. The 'folds and stretches' line is fog. Cut it and the dropped-class example carries the point.
clinician: The dropped-class example frees the reader from self-blame. The 'folds and stretches' math clause loses the struggling reader. Cut it.
habit: The dropped-class example is great. 'Folds and stretches the path' loses me. Turn it into a drill: write three true tellings.
contemplative: The three reasons for dropping the class land. Rules that fold and stretch the path are lecture. Keep the example and drop the mechanism.
stress: A hindsight-bias antidote with a concrete three-cause example. Cut the murky "folds and stretches" line.
gamedesigner: Dropped-class example gives me three tellings to try. 'Folds and stretches' line is fog; trim it.
structural: "Work doubled your hours" finally lets circumstance compete with character. Multiple honest histories is a real check on self-blame.
satirist: The dropped-class example is excellent. 'The rule folds and stretches the path' is dynamical-systems cosplay. Cut it and the paragraph still stands.
mythmaker: Dropping the class, with three true reasons, is a real person. The sentence about folding and stretching the path is lecture fog. Cut it and keep the class.

modeler: Write three true histories. Concrete, cheap, effective.
skeptic: A good exercise against single-cause stories. Concrete. Keep.
clinician: A concrete writing exercise with a gentle aim: feel it stop being the only story. Good.
habit: Write two other true histories. Concrete, startable, powerful.
contemplative: Write two other true tellings. Feel the story loosen. Excellent practice.
stress: 'Not nicer, just other true ones': a disciplined exercise. Good.
gamedesigner: A great exercise with a felt payoff: 'feel the story stop being the only one.'
structural: Writing alternative histories is a usable exercise. Private.

gamedesigner: Recognizable catastrophizing shape. A good setup.

modeler: The 3 a.m. chain is recognizable, but this is setup only. Show where each link's probability multiplies down, or merge it with the payoff.

stress: The 3 a.m. chain is recognizable. It's only setup, so the payoff has to follow quickly.

modeler: You promise arithmetic and don't show it here. Multiply the link probabilities on the page, say 0.5^3, and this becomes a tool.

habit: The 3 a.m. cue lands, and everyone knows that chain. It promises arithmetic but doesn't hand me the calculation here.
contemplative: The 3 a.m. chain is familiar. It names my fear but leaves me in it. Give me the next breath here.
stress: The 3 a.m. chain is real and recognizable. The arithmetic is promised but not shown in this unit, so the claim hangs on a debt.
gamedesigner: Strong hook: I know that 3 a.m. chain. It promises arithmetic, so the next beat needs to pay it off fast.
structural: The cascade from deadline to client to apartment is real precarity, and it gets passed off as a thinking error. Who made one missed deadline cost you your home?
satirist: The 3 a.m. chain is recognizable. It promises arithmetic and delivers none here, which fails Bryson. Put the multiplied probabilities in this paragraph.
mythmaker: The 3 a.m. chain of deadline, client, job, apartment is true dread. A strong setup that needs the arithmetic payoff right after it.

modeler: Conditional probabilities multiply: real math defeating a felt certainty. Exactly the build-from-arithmetic I want.

clinician: The probabilities-multiply point is clear. Drop the Part Four civilizations reference here.

contemplative: Probabilities multiply. A clear, kind correction. The Part Four reference is a detour.

gamedesigner: Probabilities multiply: clear, true and freeing.
structural: Probabilities multiply. A real mechanism, well applied to personal doom chains.
satirist: Probabilities multiply. Bryson-grade, but show the numbers: five steps at 80 percent gives about 33 percent. Then it's devastating.
mythmaker: Multiplying probabilities is useful. Drake-equation callback heavy; show one person's actual chain.

modeler: Count the links. An operational instruction. Good.
skeptic: 'Count the links' is concrete and testable. Good.
clinician: A specific decatastrophizing step. Cap it at one pass so anxious readers don't relitigate every link.
habit: 'Count the links.' A rep I can run at 3am. Great.
contemplative: Count the links. Don't argue the ending. A practice for 3 a.m. Keep.
stress: 'Make it show its work.' Specific, not reassuring. Exactly right.
gamedesigner: Count the links: a concrete move. 'Make it show its work' is great.
structural: 'Count the links' is a concrete, usable move against catastrophizing.
satirist: 'Make the story show its work.' Plain, practical, witty.
mythmaker: 'Rarely survives being made to show its work.' Practical and memorable.

modeler: A reputation becomes a second stock that's defended separately. Good. The 'Braid, two scales down' jargon obscures it.
skeptic: Strength hardening into a reputation to defend: perceptive, with a usable test. Braid jargon blocks the lay reader.
clinician: Real insight about defending a reputation. The 'Braid, two scales down' jargon obscures it.
habit: Defending the name is a strong insight. Drop 'Braid'; add a cue: when praised.
contemplative: Real insight: the reputation needs defending, not the trait. 'Braid' and 'two scales down' get in the way.
stress: Defending a reputation versus practising a trait is pure Ego Is the Enemy. Strong. Drop the Braid jargon.
gamedesigner: The reputation trap is a sharp self-test. Drop the 'Braid, two scales down' jargon.
structural: Strength turned into reputation to defend. Sharp and personal.
satirist: The reputation-defense test is good. 'Chapter 19 calls a Braid, two scales down' strangles it. Cut the jargon.
mythmaker: 'The reliable one' snapping on a bad day: real face. Braid jargon trips it.

modeler: Convergent discovery as evidence is a fair argument. Otherwise this recaps the chapter.
skeptic: Convergence across traditions shows shared human minds, not validity. Cite trial evidence for trainability instead.
clinician: Trainable, not innate, is hopeful. 'Haven't yet practiced watching' risks implying blame for involuntary feelings.
habit: 'Trainable' is good news, but there's no new rep. Fine closer, could trim.
contemplative: Watching is trainable. Encouraging. The last sentence about traditions is a nice humility. Could be shorter.
stress: Cross-tradition convergence is the right kind of evidence: repeated, independent cases. Name two traditions.
gamedesigner: Says the observing self is trainable, which is fine. Closing exposition with no new move.
structural: The appeal to convergent traditions is a weak argument. Trainability is fine. Purely inward.
satirist: 'Contemplative traditions arrived at similar practices.' Name two (vipassana, the Stoics), or this is an unearned flourish.
mythmaker: Convergent traditions point is nice; otherwise recap. Fine.

modeler: 'Trainable' asserted, no training schedule. Convergent traditions is decent evidence. Give the dose and the delay before it shows.
skeptic: Convergent traditions are weak evidence; shared intuitions converge too. 'Isn't a failing' tells me how to feel.
clinician: 'Not a failing, just untrained' is shame-aware and hopeful. The tradition argument is fine, but there's no concrete next step.
habit: 'Trainable' with no training plan. How many reps, and when? Cut the tradition roll-call and add one daily drill.
contemplative: Trainable, not lacking: that is gentle and true. The traditions sentence argues for credibility. It doesn't help me practice.
stress: Convergence across traditions is a proper history argument. "Trainable" is asserted without evidence. Cite something.
gamedesigner: 'Trainable' is encouraging, but no drill or progress marker. Tradition convergence is lore, not gameplay.
structural: "Not a failing, just untrained" is kind. Traditions converging is weak evidence. It's inner work all the way down.
satirist: 'Trainable, not innate' is useful. The convergent-traditions claim needs one named practice from each tradition to pass Bryson.
mythmaker: The point that separate traditions converged is decent, but it's a closing lecture. No Iroh in the room. Give one meditator, one Stoic, one moment.

modeler: One noted thought equals one rep: trainable, countable, good. The convergence-across-traditions argument is weaker than you think. Minds converge on errors too.
skeptic: Convergence across traditions is weak evidence, and U0424 admits minds converge on comforting beliefs. 'One repetition' says trainable but shows no training effect.
clinician: 'Not a failing; it just hasn't been trained yet' is shame-aware. 'I'm having the thought that' is a usable rep. The traditions tangent is padding.
habit: 'I'm having the thought that…' counts as one rep. That's my favourite line. Cut the history tail, it slows the ending.
contemplative: "I'm having the thought that" is a real practice. Then it turns into a lecture on traditions. End at the repetition.
stress: Convergence across traditions is the right kind of evidence: repeated cases, not one guru. Trainable, one rep at a time. Holds up.
gamedesigner: Counting each 'I'm having the thought' as a rep is a real feedback signal. The traditions tail drags, so trim it.
structural: Citing convergent traditions is a decent argument. Still mind-training as the whole remedy, with no spillover to anyone else.
satirist: 'I'm having the thought that' is a usable rep. The Buddhist-Stoic convergence is a fair argument, though 'little or no contact' needs hedging.
mythmaker: 'I'm having the thought that' is a usable rep. Then it drifts into a lecture on traditions. Who's holding the muscle? Cut the second half.

modeler: Overused quote. It earns nothing new here.
skeptic: Cliché, and the attribution is shaky. It also cuts against the compost framing. Replace it.
clinician: Grind-culture epigraph that sits badly with a book about sustainability. Swap it.
habit: Overused quote. Pick something fresher or cut it.
contemplative: A worn quote, and it praises grinding. Compost asks for patience, not sweat. Choose another.
stress: A shaky attribution and a worn cliche. A stress-tester winces. Find a fresher, verified line.
gamedesigner: A worn quote and slightly off-theme. Pick something about iteration or failure.
structural: The Edison perspiration cliche is the willpower myth in a quote. A poor pick for a book wary of grind.
satirist: Edison, credited at last. Shame it's the most worn quote alive, and possibly not even his.
mythmaker: Worn Edison quote. Find a fresher one.

modeler: Apt epigraph for compost, but it only rhymes. It earns its place only if the chapter actually delivers the mechanism.
skeptic: A borrowed epigraph doing mood work. It proves nothing and needs to prove nothing.
clinician: A fitting epigraph, but it's ornament. It does little for someone who is hurting.
habit: A fine epigraph that frames compost. It does its framing job, nothing more.
contemplative: Whitman says the whole chapter in one line. It is quiet and well placed.
stress: Apt epigraph, and it earns its place by setting up compost. It does nothing else.
gamedesigner: Fine title card for a compost chapter. Sets theme; asks nothing of me.
structural: A pleasant epigraph. It sets up compost and does no other work.
satirist: A good Whitman line that suits the compost chapter. It's an epigraph, so it decorates and does no more.
mythmaker: Whitman sets up the compost image well. It only pays off because the chapter comes back to it, and it does.

modeler: Pretty line, and compost is a real stock-and-flow. But the epigraph only gestures. It works only if the chapter cashes it.
skeptic: A lovely line, and it sets up the compost frame efficiently. Nothing to evaluate beyond that.
clinician: A lovely compost image. It's an epigraph doing tone work and not much else.
habit: Lovely line, and it sets up compost. No action, but it's fine as an epigraph.
contemplative: Lovely, but archaic and oblique without the chapter around it. A reader may stumble on "corruptions."
stress: An archaic epigraph doing decorative work. The compost idea comes later anyway. Ornament, not load-bearing.
gamedesigner: Fine epigraph, but it's flavor only. The compost image earns its keep later, not here.
structural: Fitting compost epigraph. It sets a mood and asks nothing of anyone.
satirist: Whitman on compost, well chosen. It sets up the chapter's metaphor honestly.
mythmaker: Whitman sets up compost well, and the image does come back later. It's someone else's line doing the work, but it's allowed.

modeler: Whitman epigraph on rot becoming growth. Decomposition does feed the next cycle, a real flow, but a quote only gestures.
skeptic: Poetry, not evidence, and labelled as a gloss on rot becoming growth. Harmless; contributes mood, not argument.
clinician: Lovely epigraph, but nothing to do with it. Rot becoming growth can bypass the rot if not acknowledged first.
habit: Whitman is lovely but gives me nothing to do. Epigraph earns only the abstract itch.
contemplative: Whitman's line makes rot into soil, simply. It is beautiful, and it asks nothing of me. A fine door, not a room.
stress: Whitman on rot into growth. Pretty, borrowed. Survivorship: plenty of rot just rots. Ornament, no stake.
gamedesigner: Pretty Whitman epigraph about rot becoming growth. Sets the tone, but no goal, no move, no feedback. Pure decoration for me.
structural: Whitman on compost. Lovely, decorative, zero policy content. Rot becoming growth is also a fine excuse for leaving rot in place.
satirist: Whitman on rot becoming growth is lovely and earned wonder. But it's decoration; nothing here makes the reader do anything.
mythmaker: Whitman on compost is a real image of rot becoming growth. Keep it, but the book must come back to the compost.

modeler: Compost is a great loop image: decay feeds growth. Whitman does the work, but the passage doesn't say why.
skeptic: Whitman compost epigraph is apt and pretty. Poetry is not evidence; fine as mood-setting.
clinician: Compost image reframes the painful as raw material, but risks bypassing if pain isn't named first.
habit: Compost image is nice, but epigraph only. Nothing to start tomorrow.
contemplative: Whitman's compost is beautiful and warm. The gloss on the heap is more words than it needs.
stress: Whitman is lovely on compost. Decoration; the chapter has to do the work.
gamedesigner: Pretty epigraph, no onboarding value. The compost link needs the chapter to carry it.
structural: Compost image is apt and easy. Pretty, sure, but soil is also something someone owns.
satirist: Whitman on compost is well chosen, earthy and a little gross. Fits a chapter on rotten self-stories. Epigraph earns its slot.
mythmaker: Whitman's compost is a great image and it returns the chapter's work to the heap. Nobody standing in it yet, but the smell is there.

modeler: Setup, recognizable. Fine.
skeptic: Relatable framing of creative mess. Setup only.
clinician: Treats the mess as material. Normalizing.
habit: Names the real pain point of creative work. Setup only.
contemplative: Mess as material is a kind framing. Fine.
stress: Intro. Fine.
gamedesigner: Names the moment players quit. A relatable setup.
structural: A setup. Fine.
satirist: Framing paragraph. Fine, forgettable.
mythmaker: Wading into a mess: recognizable. Okay setup.

modeler: A relatable intro, and the third draft worse than the second is real. No structure yet. Fine as a doorway.
skeptic: The third draft worse than the second is recognizable. The rest is framing with nothing to test.
clinician: The 'third draft worse than the second' moment rings true. Treating the mess as material is good framing. As an intro it offers no step yet.
habit: 'The third draft that's worse than the second' hits home. As an intro it's fine, but there's no action yet.
contemplative: The worse third draft is recognizable. It is a clear opening, and nothing is in excess.
stress: Honest about where people abandon the work. Framing only, with no claim to test.
gamedesigner: Third draft worse than second: names the exact quit point. Good hook. Promise is set up clearly.
structural: Honest about where practice gets abandoned. It frames the mess as material. As a chapter opener it is adequate and makes no claim.
satirist: 'The third draft that's worse than the second': every writer winces, which is the point. It's a serviceable setup.
mythmaker: 'The third draft that's worse than the second' is a gut-punch of recognition. Mess as material is a good promise to make.

modeler: The abandonment moments ring true. 'Mess as material' is still just framing. Say what accumulates across failed drafts.
skeptic: The abandoned file at night rings true. 'Abandoned fastest' is a base-rate claim with no base rate behind it. Soften it or cite something.
clinician: The closed file you don't reopen is real pain, accurately named. Reframing the mess as material is gentle. The step comes later.
habit: 'The evening you close the file and don't open it again' is real. It's framing, though, not a step.
contemplative: The closed file I never reopen: yes, I know it. The middle sentence lectures. Trust the images.
stress: The abandonment scenes are honest and specific. 'Mess as material' is still only a promise. Show the storm next.
gamedesigner: The 'third draft worse than second' line is exactly where players rage-quit. It names the fail state, which makes a good hook.
structural: Relatable abandonment scene. It never asks why creative work gets no time or pay, so the mess stays purely personal.
satirist: 'The third draft that's worse than the second' is true and stings. 'Tending your Local Rule' is jargon on a shrine. Say 'your habit.'
mythmaker: 'The evening you close the file and don't open it again' hurts in the right way. It promises a fix but doesn't hand one over yet.

modeler: Dropping creative work at the worst-draft stage, mess as material for the next attempt. Names where the loop breaks. Wants the delay named.
skeptic: Names real failure points (worse third draft, closed file) rather than promising smooth progress. 'Mess as material' is reframing, untested.
clinician: Names the worse third draft and quit evening accurately. Treating mess as material is kind. Next step could be sharper.
habit: Third draft worse, file closed: I've lived that. But mess as material is a reframe, not a rep. Add the next move.
contemplative: It names the third draft and the closed file honestly. Treating mess as material is a warm turn. Slightly long, still clear.
stress: Names real failure points: worse third draft, abandoned file. Mess as material is antifragile thinking. Specific, honest about where people quit.
gamedesigner: Names the exact quit point: third draft worse than second. Real playtester insight. Treating the mess as material is a good reframe; wants a concrete move.
structural: Honest about why creative work gets dropped. But no word on who funds time or space to make things; mess is treated as personal.
satirist: Third draft worse than the second: true and specific. Rare honest note about where practice dies. Mess as material, not clutter.
mythmaker: Third draft worse than the second, the closed file: lived and true. Mess as material is a good turn. Give it one maker.

modeler: Compost asserted before its mechanism. U0289 does the real work; move it up and shorten this.
skeptic: 'Nothing stays wasted' is comforting overreach. Some failures teach nothing. Keep the narrower claim and drop the absolute.
clinician: The compost reframe helps, but 'rot resentfully in a corner' shames the reader who's struggling. Cut that line.
habit: Compost framing resonates. Give a rep: keep a scraps file, reread it weekly.
contemplative: 'Failure is compost' is lovely. The paragraph says it four times. Keep the first and last sentences.
stress: 'Nothing stays wasted' is unfalsifiable comfort. Some failures are just losses. Admit it and the compost claim gets stronger.
gamedesigner: The compost reframe resonates. Give a move: list what last failure left usable.
structural: Failure as compost is a familiar consolation, decently argued. Personal only.
satirist: Compost is a good plain metaphor. 'What Chapter 12 calls the Fold' adds a Concept that does no work. Cut it.
mythmaker: Compost is a strong image; 'rot resentfully in a corner' bites. Fold jargon unneeded.

modeler: Scaffolding is normal: a practical relief. The Skein analogy rhymes rather than holds.
skeptic: Creation as social is accurate, and removes a real trap. Lowery-compatible. Keep.
clinician: Needing help isn't incapacity. A shame-dissolving point. Add one ask: name one person to show a draft to.
habit: Needing help isn't weakness. True. Add: name one person to show a draft to this week.
contemplative: Needing help is not weakness. Warm and true. The Skein comparison can go.
stress: Scaffolding isn't a crutch: removes a real trap. Well-supported by how work actually gets made.
gamedesigner: Kills the solo-genius trap with concrete helper roles. Useful.
structural: Creation is social scaffolding. Right, and it punctures the lone-genius myth. It could name the institutions: grants, editors, studios.
satirist: A true and comforting point. Dropping in Skein again is decoration. Name one real editor and author pair.
mythmaker: Editor, trusted listener, readers: faces. Removes real shame about needing help.

modeler: Externalize working memory, generate volume first. Solid, concrete advice.
skeptic: Externalizing is sound cognitive advice. 'Volume is where useful ideas hide' is mixed in the brainstorming literature. Hedge it.
clinician: Practical: write more than you need, in view. Good.
habit: Write more options than you need, in view, before judging. Practical.
contemplative: Practical and clear: write more than you need before judging. A little long.
stress: Externalise, then generate volume before judging. Practical, proven. Slightly long.
gamedesigner: A practical generate-before-judge rule. Clear.
structural: Externalize ideas and generate volume. Practical and correct, with no systemic stakes.
satirist: Externalize and generate volume. Solid, practical advice. Long, but it pays.
mythmaker: Useful whiteboard advice, generic. Fine.

modeler: Working memory is a tiny, leaky buffer, so an external stock fixes it. Concrete instruction: generate in view, judge later. Solid.
skeptic: Grounded in working-memory limits and actionable. 'Volume hides the useful ones' needs a 'sometimes'.
clinician: Concrete and low-risk: write more than you need, in view, before judging. Takes the strain off working memory.
habit: Write more options than you need, in view, before judging any of them. That's a real practice. Add a number: ten.
contemplative: Write more than you need, in view, before judging: I can do this tonight. The memory taxonomy could shrink.
stress: Practical and modest: write more than you need, then judge. It holds up.
gamedesigner: Concrete move with a rule: write more than you need, judge later. Feedback is visible volume. Plays.
structural: Practical and well-grounded: externalize, generate volume, judge late. A useful technique, even if it's a personal one.
satirist: Shower idea gone by breakfast, a wall instead of a skull, write more than you need. It's plain, useful advice with no robe on.
mythmaker: The shower idea gone by breakfast is the face here. It's practical, it's vivid, and I could act on it tonight.

modeler: Three observations to see a second derivative. Real instrumentation logic. My favorite paragraph here.
skeptic: Memory can't show acceleration; three observations can. A rare, precise, checkable claim. Keep.
clinician: 'Three observations to see acceleration' is a clever, concrete case for keeping a record.
habit: Three spaced observations to see acceleration. A smart reason to log.
contemplative: Three observations to see speed. Useful. 'Only order of change you can act on' is opaque. Simplify.
stress: You need three observations to see acceleration. A precise, falsifiable argument for records. Excellent.
gamedesigner: Three observations to see acceleration is a real instrumentation rule. A designer's dream.
structural: Three observations to see acceleration. Good instrument logic, and it scales to any group measuring progress.
satirist: 'You cannot see acceleration from memory; you need three points.' An actual mathematical fact turned into practice. Bryson approves.
mythmaker: 'You cannot see acceleration from memory.' Sharp, original, useful.

modeler: Repeats Chapter 4 at lower resolution. No new mechanism. Cut or merge.
skeptic: Vague, and recycles Chapter 4. 'Kills the material' is unsupported. Cut or give an example.
clinician: Re-applies Chapter 4 abstractly. Give a creative example.
habit: 'Name the chaos' rehashes Chapter 4 without a step. Cut or compress.
contemplative: It repeats Chapter 4 at length. Say it in one line: let strange ideas stay strange a while.
stress: Vague. 'Hold it playfully' doesn't survive a deadline. Give one concrete move.
gamedesigner: Recycles Chapter 4 without a new move. A lecture; cut or compress it.
structural: It recycles the Chapter 4 move for creative chaos. Redundant and vague.
satirist: It re-runs Chapter 4 on creative chaos. The point is thin and well padded.
mythmaker: Abstract 'chaotic material' with no maker. Show one strange idea someone nearly killed.

modeler: Reusing the defusion move on creative verdicts is practical. 'A page or a day' gives a delay. It's good that the delay is explicit.
skeptic: A concrete defusion step applied to creative work. The final either/or is too neat. Some suppression is just good editing.
clinician: Reuses the defusion phrase on the inner critic and gives a timeframe: a page or a day. Playful, not fearful. Good.
habit: 'Let it stay strange for a page or a day' is a concrete dose with a timeframe. Good.
contemplative: Let the idea stay strange for a day. That is gentle and practical. The last two sentences could become one.
stress: A usable move. "A page or a day" gives it a bound. Good.
gamedesigner: Reuses Chapter 4's move in new terrain. That's good level design: known mechanic, new context, a day's timer.
structural: Keeping a strange idea alive for a day is usable advice. It recycles Chapter 4 competently.
satirist: Practical: keep the strange idea for a page or a day. The defusion callback earns its place here rather than just name-dropping.
mythmaker: The absurd plot turn and the urge to kill it before it embarrasses you. Real, and it has stakes. Reusing the Chapter 4 move rhymes nicely.

modeler: The forest nutrient cycle is the mechanism, not consolation. Good turn.
skeptic: Forest nutrient cycling is real. The analogy to personal failure is still only an analogy, presented as mechanism.
clinician: The forest image makes failure fertile rather than consoling. Lands.
habit: Forest image works. Still consolation, not a move.
contemplative: The forest floor feeds the next growth. Beautiful, and plain. Drop the bold apology at the start.
stress: The forest-nutrient mechanism is better than consolation. Fair point, though it's still a metaphor.
gamedesigner: The forest mechanism is vivid. Nice upgrade from consolation.
structural: The forest-fertility image is vivid. It's consolation dressed as mechanism.
satirist: The forest floor as nutrient supply. Finally a real fact under a metaphor. Give one number (a nurse log, decades of rot) and it sings.
mythmaker: Forest floor brings compost back with weight. Good rhyme.

modeler: The nurse log is real ecology, but it claims 'mechanism' without saying what decomposes in a draft. Name the nutrient: reusable parts, learned failure modes.
skeptic: Calls a metaphor a mechanism, which is exactly what I pounce on. A draft is not a nurse log. Show the transfer or soften the claim.
clinician: The nurse log is a lovely image and avoids empty consolation. It still needs one thing to do with the abandoned draft.
habit: The nurse log is a lovely image. So what do I do with the abandoned draft tomorrow? Reread it for one salvageable line?
contemplative: The nurse log is a true and beautiful image. The final two sentences insist, so trust the log instead.
stress: Lovely log. "Mechanism, not consolation" overclaims, because a draft is not wood. Show the mechanism working.
gamedesigner: Nurse log is a vivid image. Reframe only though; give me a compost action for the abandoned draft.
structural: The nurse log is a vivid, accurate image. "Mechanism, not consolation" is claimed but never shown for the draft itself.
satirist: Nurse log: a real term, a real forest, decades of rot. Bryson would nod. The 'mechanism, not consolation' header is a touch grand.
mythmaker: The nurse log is the image I'll remember tomorrow. 'Your abandoned draft is that log' turns it toward me. This is myth done right.

modeler: Compost is a stock that raises the growth rate: yes. Now name the drain. Does unattended compost leach away?
skeptic: 'The fifth attempt is easier': how would you know? Repeated failure can also deplete. Name the conditions under which it accumulates.
clinician: 'Not because you became a better person' locates progress in the ground, not your worth. Shame-safe.
habit: 'Ground that four previous attempts fed.' Encouraging and clear.
contemplative: The fifth attempt is easier because the ground was fed, not because you're better. Gentle and true.
stress: Compost as a stock is a sharp reframe. Does the fifth attempt reliably get easier? Show a case.
gamedesigner: 'The fifth attempt is easier because the ground is fed' is felt progress. Good.
structural: Compost as a stock, 'not because you became a better person'. A good anti-moralizing move.
satirist: 'Not because you've become a better person.' A dry, honest punchline. 'Compost is a stock' earns its systems term.
mythmaker: Fifth attempt fed by four: earned and warm.

modeler: Closes the material cycle. Still no limit named. What saturates? A soil can't absorb infinite failure.
skeptic: A tidy cycle that can't fail, which is exactly my worry. An unfalsifiable loop. Say what would count as soil not improving.
clinician: 'No part requires anything to have worked.' Deeply kind to readers who feel they're failing.
habit: Repeats the cycle again. Third time this chapter.
contemplative: 'No part of it requires anything to have worked.' This is peace. Keep.
stress: 'No part requires anything to have worked': a system that can't fail is a horoscope. Name the condition where the soil doesn't improve.
gamedesigner: A cycle summary that repeats U0289. Trim it.
structural: 'What others planted and what fell before you arrived' acknowledges inherited ground. It needs to say who owns the soil.
satirist: A cycle summary. 'No part requires anything to have worked' is good; the rest restates.
mythmaker: Nice cycle, a bit summary. 'Nothing required to have worked' is generous.

modeler: Finally the condition: compost must break down, and unexamined failure feeds nothing. That's the missing flow, named. Good loop closure.
skeptic: Credit for stating when it fails: an unexamined draft feeds nothing. That condition is what makes the metaphor honest.
clinician: 'Look at why it failed' needs a limit or it becomes a post-mortem spiral. Name one question to ask the failure, then stop.
habit: 'Buried unread feeds nothing' hints at a rep. Make it explicit: after each failure, write one line on why.
contemplative: Compost must break down. That is honest and useful. The inheritance clause crowds the breath, so trim it.
stress: Names its own failure mode: buried drafts and repeats without review. That is the storm test passed.
gamedesigner: Finally a feedback signal: is the ground getting richer? Buried-unread failure state is sharp. Good.
structural: The nod to what others planted is the first glimpse of other people. Then it goes straight back to one gardener.
satirist: The caveat saves it: a draft buried unread feeds nothing. A metaphor that admits its own failure condition is rare and welcome.
mythmaker: The cycle-closing is earned, but it's told rather than lived. 'The compost sitting in a corner' is good. Hand it to someone.

modeler: Recap of the chapter. Trim it.
skeptic: Summary of claims already made. Trim.
clinician: A decent close, 'neither sacred nor shameful.' Slightly repetitive.
habit: Recap paragraph. Cut; the chapter already said it.
contemplative: A summary of what I just read. Cut it. Let the forest close the chapter.
stress: A summary restating the chapter. Cut it.
gamedesigner: A third wrap-up in a row. Flat interest curve. Cut it.
structural: A summary restating the chapter. Cut it.
satirist: A closing recap of the recap. Cut.
mythmaker: Recap of the chapter. Cut.

modeler: A summary restating the last paragraph. 'Cumulative' is the right word, but it needs no paragraph of its own.
skeptic: 'Usually already sitting in the wreckage': how would you know? Consoling, and it feels true without support.
clinician: 'Sacred or shameful' names the trap exactly. A warm close, though it summarizes rather than adds.
habit: Cumulative, not easy: a nice close. It's a summary with no step, but it's short enough to keep.
contemplative: Sacred or shameful: a good pair. It is warm and whole, and it ends where it should.
stress: Warm wrap-up, but it only restates. "Usually already sitting" has no evidence behind it.
gamedesigner: Recap beat. Warm, but repeats prior paragraph. Could end on 'go dig in the last draft' instead.
structural: A tidy close that repeats the compost point. Cut it or fold it in.
satirist: 'Sacred or shameful': a tidy closing sentence that adds nothing new. Keep it short, as it is.
mythmaker: 'Sacred or shameful' is a tidy, warm button. It pays off the compost setup without getting sappy.

modeler: 'Cumulative' is the key word: attempts are a stock you draw from. Concrete instruction: return to the last wreck first. Good.
skeptic: Concrete and usable: go back to the last attempt before starting fresh. 'Cumulative, not easy' is honestly limited. Good.
clinician: Clear step: reopen the last attempt before starting fresh. 'Neither sacred nor shameful' disarms self-blame nicely.
habit: Real cue: when you stall, open your last attempt first. That's a rep I can do tomorrow.
contemplative: Go back to the last attempt. Compost, not sacred or shameful. I can do this tonight.
stress: 'Not easy, cumulative' is a modest claim that survives contact. Go back to the wreckage first: a concrete move.
gamedesigner: A concrete move: go back to the last attempt before starting fresh. Tidy payoff.
structural: Concrete and usable: go back to the last attempt. Private, but harmless. It doesn't steal attention from any collective fight.
satirist: 'Not easy, cumulative' is plain and useful. 'Go back to the wreckage before starting fresh' is an actual instruction. Good.
mythmaker: Compost comes back with weight: 'sacred or shameful' against compost. The image rhymes and the instruction is clear. Keep it.

modeler: Motto epigraph. Inert.
skeptic: Slogan epigraph. Nothing to test.
clinician: Motto epigraph.
habit: Motto epigraph, adds nothing.
contemplative: Four words, an echo of the book's thesis. It passes the breath test. Thin, though.
stress: Slogan epigraph.
gamedesigner: A motto epigraph. Fine but inert.
structural: A motto. Inert.
satirist: 'Step repeats, form emerges.' A slogan from the gift shop. Cut.
mythmaker: Slogan epigraph. Fine, thin.

modeler: A serviceable epigraph that sets up the chapter. Nothing to model.
skeptic: Aphorism with no content to check. Harmless as an epigraph.
clinician: Clear epigraph, but it's thin and doesn't hold or help anyone.
habit: Clear epigraph, but 'learn which way' how? It points at a practice it never names.
contemplative: Simple and lived. It invites noticing before pushing. That is enough.
stress: A fortune-cookie epigraph that says nothing the chapter doesn't. Cut it or sharpen it.
gamedesigner: Epigraph is clear but inert. 'Swings' is vague until the chapter defines it.
structural: The epigraph is clear but inert.
satirist: Fortune-cookie epigraph attributed to nobody. If the book wrote it, own the foma or cut it.
mythmaker: A fortune-cookie epigraph. Swing and push mean nothing until the chapter fills them in. It doesn't earn its weight on its own.

modeler: Reinforcing versus balancing in one line, nicely compressed. As an epigraph it primes the chapter. I'll take it.
skeptic: Clear but slight. 'Learn yours' says nothing about how you'd learn it. That's the paragraph's job, so the epigraph adds little.
clinician: Terse and a little cryptic out of context. 'Learn yours' points somewhere, but the line doesn't land on its own.
habit: 'Learn yours before you push' points at an action, but the line gives me no way to learn it.
contemplative: Readable, but "swing back" tells me nothing yet. It is a summary pretending to be a saying.
stress: Clear enough, but it's a fortune-cookie line. Nothing at stake and nothing to break.
gamedesigner: Sets the goal of learning your shape first. It's a serviceable epigraph but it gives me nothing to do yet.
structural: Snowball and swing-back framing. It restates the chapter without earning a line of its own.
satirist: A homemade epigraph that needs the chapter to decode it. Fortune-cookie foma. Cut it, or quote Meadows instead.
mythmaker: Cryptic before it's evocative: 'swing back' gives me no picture. Pick one image, a snowball or a pendulum, and commit to it.

modeler: Snowball is reinforcing, thermostat is balancing. Compact and right. Quote-sized, so no worked case, but it sets up the distinction.
skeptic: 'Learn which is yours' implies self-knowledge is easy to get. Lovely line; how would I tell my own shape?
clinician: Know your day's shape before pushing: a usable idea in a short line. Metaphors are clear.
habit: Snowball or thermostat, learn which before you push. Fine image, but learn how? Name the observation to make.
contemplative: Two images, one instruction: know your shape before you push. Practical and easy. Snowball and thermostat do the work.
stress: Cute, and it says learn your shape before pushing. But snowball or thermostat can't be wrong; both outcomes confirm it.
gamedesigner: Snowball versus thermostat: know your difficulty curve before you push. Gives a self-test hook and a memorable image. Agency is small but clear.
structural: Snowball versus thermostat days: neat. Know your own shape, yes, but school and work rules set the shape. Epigraph leaves that out.
satirist: Snowball versus thermostat is a clean picture. 'Learn which is yours before you push' is half-actionable. Fair epigraph.
mythmaker: Snowball versus thermostat is a picture I'd remember tomorrow. As an epigraph it's clever; the chapter must earn it.

modeler: Reinforcing versus balancing in two images, with the delay hint: learn which before you push. Exactly my brief.
skeptic: Distinguishes reinforcing from balancing days, a testable, useful idea. 'Learn which is yours' is an exercise, not an assertion. Good.
clinician: Snowball versus thermostat is a usable sorting question before acting. Clear and non-blaming.
habit: Snowball or thermostat: learn which before you push. Actionable diagnostic, one question to carry. Cue could be sharper.
contemplative: Snowball or thermostat: two pictures a child holds. Know your day before you push. Practical and kind.
stress: Two named response types and a 'learn which before you push.' Testable by observation. Strong.
gamedesigner: Snowball vs thermostat gives me two modes and a test: learn which is yours. Real diagnostic. Needs a way to check.
structural: Reinforcing versus balancing loops, plainly put, with a practical test. A real mechanism. Add who sets the thermostat.
satirist: Snowball versus thermostat: two plain pictures, and 'learn which is yours before you push' is a real instruction. Slight aphorism gloss, but it works.
mythmaker: Snowball or thermostat: two vivid images, and 'learn which is yours before you push' is a real stake. Wants a person who guessed wrong.

modeler: Reinforcing against balancing, defined correctly. Good.
skeptic: Clear definitions from systems thinking. Fine.
clinician: Clear distinction between loop types, as setup.
habit: Clear definitions of the two loop types. Fine.
contemplative: A clear distinction, simply stated. It prepares, it doesn't yet serve.
stress: A clean systems distinction. Standard and useful.
gamedesigner: Clean definitions of the two loop types. Good tutorial text.
structural: The reinforcing/balancing distinction is introduced clearly. Standard.
satirist: A clean definition of reinforcing and balancing loops. Credit Meadows, and the reader can go further.
mythmaker: Clear definitions, textbook voice.

modeler: The Meadows vocabulary is introduced correctly. But an evening wind-down isn't a balancing loop until you name the goal and the gap it corrects.
skeptic: Clean definitions with honest attribution to systems thinkers. 'You already know both from the inside' assumes too much.
clinician: Clean vocabulary for the two loop types. It's conceptual, with nothing yet for a hard day.
habit: Clean definitions. 'Learn to feel it in your day' needs a cue: check your energy at 10 a.m. and 8 p.m.
contemplative: Two names, plainly given. 'You already know both from the inside' is the best line. Lead with it.
stress: Clean definitions with credit to the field. Textbook so far, no stakes yet.
gamedesigner: Two terms, one each, with felt examples. Clean onboarding. Needs a 'which are you?' prompt here.
structural: Correct definitions of reinforcing and balancing loops. A loop with no rule and no owner yet is systems as mood.
satirist: It credits systems thinkers rather than inventing the terms, which is honest. Name Forrester or Meadows and it passes Bryson.
mythmaker: A clean taxonomy, and the snowball morning helps. It's still a textbook, though. Who's in the morning?

modeler: Correct names, correct credit to Forrester and Meadows. But the 'set point' for rest is asserted, not shown. What's the goal, what's the error signal?
skeptic: Clean introduction with credited sources. An evening tugging toward rest is a loose example of a set point, since fatigue isn't a thermostat. Tighten it.
clinician: The everyday framing of the two loop types works. Asking which one your day feels like is a gentle prompt but not yet a step.
habit: It ends on one good question about your own day. Make it a prompt to answer tonight in one word.
contemplative: Asking which one my day feels like is good teaching. The names of systems thinkers could go.
stress: Credits Forrester and Meadows instead of claiming the idea: good humility. Clean explanation, but no action yet.
gamedesigner: It teaches from felt experience and ends on a question I answer myself. That's good onboarding.
structural: It names Forrester and Meadows, then shrinks systems thinking down to your mood. It should say how the bigger application works.
satirist: It credits Forrester and Meadows and anchors the terms in your own day. Bryson approves. Clean.
mythmaker: Snowballing mornings and evenings that tug you toward rest put the reader inside the loop. Drop the name-check of thinkers; it's dead weight.

modeler: Good-morning compounding with no limit: what stops it? Name sleep debt or saturation as the balancing side.
skeptic: Relatable. Rightly notes reinforcing loops aren't virtuous. Morning momentum is asserted, not shown.
clinician: The good-morning person risks being the virtuous model. 'Not inherently virtuous' helps; keep it.
habit: Relatable morning person. Add: track your energy at 9, 1 and 6 for a week.
contemplative: A good morning feeding a good day. I can check this against my life. Good.
stress: Relatable, and it rightly flags that bad momentum compounds too.
gamedesigner: The two-people setup invites me to pick which I am. Good, implicit agency.
structural: Good mornings compound, for people who control their mornings. Shift workers, commutes and childcare are invisible here.
satirist: A relatable example, honestly caveated that reinforcement isn't virtue. Works.
mythmaker: Two people, same day: finally a face. Recognizable morning person.

modeler: A reinforcing loop that runs both directions and has named limits. This is exactly the bathtub with a drain. Good.
skeptic: Good: the reinforcing loop comes with its downside and its stopping conditions. That is calibration done properly.
clinician: Honest that snowballs go both ways and that ordinary life interrupts them. Neither mode is moralized. Good.
habit: Relatable morning snowball, and the honest caveats help. Still no rep: which morning domino do I tip first?
contemplative: Two people in one day is real. The caveats pile up at the end. Keep one.
stress: Names the snowball's dark side and when it stops. Exactly the honesty I want.
gamedesigner: I can check my own mornings against this. Snowball-both-ways caveat is good. Slightly long.
structural: It concedes that shifts and sick kids stop the snowball, then treats them as weather. Who sets the shift?
satirist: 'Isn't virtuous by default' and 'a sick kid will stop it' keep the example honest. Good, checkable.
mythmaker: Two people, a sick kid, a shift change. Now there are faces and real interruptions. Give them names and I'd follow them for a whole chapter.

modeler: Chronotype isn't loop polarity. Both people run both loops. The thermostat line is right; the person typing is wrong.
skeptic: A late chronotype isn't obviously a balancing loop. The mapping is forced. Ground it in chronotype research or loosen the claim.
clinician: 'Neither shape is a character flaw.' Good normalizing.
habit: Night-owl contrast lands. 'Neither is a flaw' is kind.
contemplative: 'Neither shape is a character flaw.' Kind and freeing. Keep.
stress: It conflates chronotype with a balancing loop. An evening wind-down isn't a thermostat. Tighten the analogy.
gamedesigner: The thermostat image is clear. 'Neither is a flaw' is reassuring.
structural: 'Neither shape is a character flaw.' Good. It ignores that school and work schedules punish one shape.
satirist: The thermostat is a good image. 'Neither shape is a character flaw' is kind.
mythmaker: Night person gets fair treatment, thermostat clear. 'Neither is a flaw' kind.

modeler: A chronotype isn't a balancing loop. Thermostat needs a set point and a sensed gap. Name the stock, sleep pressure, or drop the mapping.
skeptic: The chronotype point is plausible and kind. The thermostat analogy is doing the arguing. Cite or hedge.
clinician: 'Neither shape is a character flaw' will relieve every night owl who's been shamed by schedules. Shame-aware, though there's no step.
habit: Validating for night owls. 'Active wind-down' is the hidden action, so name one wind-down move.
contemplative: Neither shape is a character flaw. That sentence heals. The thermostat simile adds a second image where one is enough.
stress: Kind to night people. The thermostat analogy is loose. What would they actually do differently?
gamedesigner: Thermostat image works, no-flaw line kind. Still cutscene; ask me to pick my shape.
structural: "Schedules built for the first one" names a structure and drops it. Flextime is a lever. Mention it.
satirist: The thermostat earns the comparison, and the night owls get absolved. Kind and plain, but thin on any action.
mythmaker: 'Neither shape is a character flaw' will matter to every night owl reading. The thermostat is a fine but flat image.

modeler: Sloppy. Both days end in sleep, so both have balancing loops. Energy curves aren't loop types. The kindness lands; the systems claim doesn't.
skeptic: Reassuring, and chronotype research partly backs it, but none is named. 'Different, not worse' is asserted. Cite the evidence or hedge.
clinician: 'Called lazy… a different loop, not a worse one' is exactly the shame repair I want. The thermostat metaphor is clear.
habit: 'Different loop, not worse' will matter to night owls. The wind-down list hints at a step, so make it a step.
contemplative: "Different loop, not a worse one" will heal someone. The thermostat clause is too long. One image is enough.
stress: 'Different loop, not worse' answers a real charge of laziness. The thermostat image is clear. It could flatter real problems, so add a check.
gamedesigner: Reframing 'lazy' as a different loop really lands. The wind-down examples make it playable.
structural: It finally names a rule: schedules built for one chronotype. Then it stops. Who sets school start times, and how do you lobby them?
satirist: The thermostat line and the 'called lazy' reassurance land. 'The other person' has no antecedent here, so name who it is.
mythmaker: 'If you've been called lazy for running the second' turns this into a kindness. The thermostat muddles it; keep one image.

modeler: Energy builds, peaks, gets wound down: a thermostat closing differently. 'Both are loops, they close differently' is exactly structure over character.
skeptic: Kind and useful if you've been called lazy. But two shapes is a clean story over messy variation; cite chronotype research or hedge.
clinician: 'Called lazy, you were running a different loop, not a worse one.' Direct shame relief with a concrete wind-down. Excellent.
habit: Winding down on purpose: a walk, a dim room, an hour off screens. Concrete, no blame. Wins.
contemplative: Compassionate: not lazy, a different loop. A walk, a dim room, an hour off screens. I could do that tonight.
stress: Real consequence: people called lazy who run a different loop. Concrete relief grounded in schedules. Slightly comforting, but it names who pays.
gamedesigner: Two day-shapes that close differently; reframes 'lazy' as a different loop. Relatable and relieving. Wind-down examples are playable. Wants a detect-your-shape check.
structural: Best here: schedules built for one shape, people called lazy for the other. That is whose rules. Missing lever: push for flexible hours together.
satirist: Dismantles 'lazy' with a plain claim: different loop, not worse. Winding down on purpose is concrete. Best sentence: both close differently.
mythmaker: 'Called lazy for running a different loop, not a worse one' is a wound being dressed. Vindication with a face. Keep.

modeler: Tides are forced oscillation, not feedback. A pretty image passed off as structure. Use homeostasis instead.
skeptic: 'Everything that survives has tides' is fluent and unsupported. At least it admits it needs a reason.
clinician: A pretty tide image, but it defers its point. Bridge material.
habit: Tide meditation, then promises an argument. Throat-clearing.
contemplative: The tide image is lovely. The meta-sentences about 'first, the reason' agitate. Let the tide speak.
stress: The tide image is pretty and the book admits it's an assertion. At least that's honest.
gamedesigner: The tide image is nice, but it announces a payoff and delays it. Tighten.
structural: The tide metaphor wanders before the argument arrives. Trim it.
satirist: It admits the claim 'sounds wise.' Credit for self-awareness. 'The tide is how the ocean stays the ocean' is still hushed-voice.
mythmaker: Tide is a fine image. 'First, though' stalls momentum.

modeler: The tide is pretty, but it's gravity, not feedback. Metaphor as mechanism. Cut it or replace it with a real homeostat.
skeptic: 'The tide is how the ocean stays the ocean.' Fluent, pretty, and empty.
clinician: The tide image is pleasant, but it's a transition, with nothing personal or practical in it.
habit: Tide metaphor, then a transition. Pretty, but there's nothing for me to do here.
contemplative: The tide is lovely. 'Here is why a life needs the same' promises a lecture. Let the tide stand alone.
stress: A pretty tide image and a bridge. No claim, so nothing to break.
gamedesigner: Pretty tide image, then a teaser. Transitional; no move.
structural: Tide imagery that is pretty but decorative. It sets up entropy and proves nothing.
satirist: 'The tide is how the ocean stays the ocean.' That's said in a hushed voice. It's foma bridging to the real argument, and it could shrink to a clause.
mythmaker: The tide is a strong mythic image, but it's dropped after two lines. Bring it back when the chapter lands on homeostasis.

modeler: A tide isn't a feedback loop. It's forced by the moon. Wrong image for coupled reinforcing and balancing loops. Swap in predator-prey.
skeptic: The tide metaphor does the persuading. 'How anything stays itself' is fluent but unsupported, and it's only rescued by the physics that follows.
clinician: A soothing tide image, and 'not a sign something is broken' is kind. It's a transition into the physics with no use of its own.
habit: The tide metaphor is pleasant but nothing in it can be done. Transition fluff. Cut it or fold it into the next unit.
contemplative: The tide is beautiful and calming. "Here is the physics" breaks the spell. Let the tide end it.
stress: The tide is pretty, a calm-sea image. 'Not a sign something is broken' is comfort that could hide a real break. Name when it is broken.
gamedesigner: The tide is a pretty image but I'm watching a cutscene. 'Here is the physics' cues more lecture.
structural: Tide metaphor as mood. Pleasant, but it's a bridge, not a mechanism.
satirist: The tide isn't a feedback loop; the moon does it. 'How anything stays itself' is hushed-voice wonder. Cut it and go straight to the physics.
mythmaker: The tide is lovely but gets used once and handed off to physics. Make the tide come back when the physics lands.

modeler: Pull and return, neither winning, and it flags the tide as picture only. Honest about metaphor, and the moon versus self-driven distinction is sharp.
skeptic: 'Though only as a picture' and the moon contrast show the author checking the analogy. 'What staying yourself looks like' sneaks in a self I'd question.
clinician: Swing is not a sign something is broken: reassuring. Tide image works. Gives no action, only comfort.
habit: Tide picture is clear and kind. But it's a picture, not a practice. What do I do when I swing back?
contemplative: A tide, 'only as a picture', then the moon, then drive their own. Three images in one breath. Choose the tide and stay.
stress: 'Only as a picture' flags the metaphor's limit; honest. But 'swing is what staying yourself looks like' risks explaining away any struggle.
gamedesigner: Tide picture is clear, and swing-as-health reframes rest as normal. But it's a cutscene paragraph: nothing to try. Ends on a teaser.
structural: Tide metaphor with a caveat admitted. Pleasant systems mood: pull and return, no rule, no owner, no lever. Mood, not mechanism.
satirist: 'Picture a tide, though only as a picture' is the Bokonon move done right. Metaphor labeled as metaphor. Moon drives tide, you drive yourself.
mythmaker: The tide image is clear, then undercut by 'only as a picture.' Honest, but the swing needs someone caught in it.

modeler: Entropy as state-counting, plainly put. Real physics, well compressed.
skeptic: A fair lay statement of entropy. Correct, interesting, and applied in the next unit.
clinician: Clear entropy intuition. Abstract support.
habit: Entropy explained plainly. Interesting, no action.
contemplative: A clear account of order's cost, abstract. It lives in the head.
stress: A statistical-entropy intuition, accurately stated. Solid.
gamedesigner: An accessible entropy explanation. Pure exposition, no move.
structural: Order costs upkeep. A real systems point, clearly stated.
satirist: Entropy in plain words, without the word. Say 'entropy' and name Boltzmann. Readers like being trusted.
mythmaker: Entropy lecture. 'Paying to stay in a small corner' good; needs a person keeping a room tidy.

modeler: Boltzmann counting is done right: tidy room versus millions of messes. A real big-picture itch, and lay-legible.
skeptic: Accurate lay entropy with proper attribution. Getting from rooms to relationships is the leap; the next passage partly pays for it.
clinician: Entropy is explained well with the room example. It's abstract physics and gives a struggling reader nothing to use.
habit: Tidy room versus messy room is clear. It's a physics lesson with zero behavior attached.
contemplative: The tidy room does the work. Boltzmann is ornament. Paying to stay in a small corner is the true line.
stress: Solid, correctly attributed physics, and the room example lands. Abstract until the next paragraph.
gamedesigner: Messy-room count is a clear entropy primer. Pure lecture; I'm watching, not playing.
structural: Entropy explained clearly with the room. It's abstract scaffolding that doesn't touch anything yet.
satirist: Boltzmann named, the counting explained, the tidy room against millions of messy ones. Wonder turned into knowledge.
mythmaker: The tidy room against millions of messy ones is clear. The physics is cold, and 'this relationship' needs one actual relationship.

modeler: Real mechanism: drift toward disorder is a constant drain, so maintenance is a required inflow. The lost-friend example makes it personal. Lovely.
skeptic: Roughly correct entropy, explained well. Carrying it over to friendships is a metaphor, not physics. Say so once.
clinician: The tidy-room entropy explanation is clear. The physics lesson is abstract, and the reader gets nothing to do with it today.
habit: Tidy room versus messy room is clear. It's a physics lecture with no rep, though: what do I pay daily?
contemplative: The tidy room is clear. Boltzmann and the dashes are decoration. The friend you'd lose touch with matters most. Lead with that.
stress: The entropy explanation is accurate and credited. Maintenance costs continuously, and the friend example makes it sting. Solid.
gamedesigner: The tidy-room count is clear. It's still pure exposition, so ask me to name one arrangement I'm paying for.
structural: Clear entropy explanation. 'Paying to stay ordered' could cover institutions too. Say who pays for upkeep at scale.
satirist: Tidy room, Boltzmann, and the friend you'd lose touch with. That's earned wonder with a name attached. Keep it.
mythmaker: 'The friend you'd lose touch with if neither of you called' smuggles a heart into entropy. That's the move. Lead with it.

modeler: Entropy as counting arrangements, with the honest line that it's physics for rooms and a picture for friendships. Continuous payment to hold a corner. Great.
skeptic: Model calibration: physics for rooms, picture for friendships, said out loud. The drift claim for friendships remains anecdote, but flagged.
clinician: Friendship drift as physics removes blame nicely, and the honest picture-versus-physics caveat helps. Closing question is a gentle step.
habit: Friend drifting makes entropy click, and one closing question. Stays abstract; name a two-minute call.
contemplative: The friend who drifts is true; then Boltzmann and counting arrangements intellectualize it. The last question is the real teaching. Keep that.
stress: Flags physics versus picture explicitly. Entropy bill is a real constraint and the closing question forces a choice. Strong, honest about its borrowing.
gamedesigner: Friend-drift hook, honest about physics versus picture, then a question I can answer: what am I paying for? Entropy gets taught without a spike.
structural: Entropy as friendship drift, honestly hedged as picture. Physics of upkeep, individual bill. Never asks who has time to pay it.
satirist: Boltzmann named, tidy room versus messy room, then 'physics for rooms, a picture for friendships.' Bryson would approve. Closing question is a good jab.
mythmaker: The drifting friend does the work, and the closing question stings. Entropy is the lecture on top. Open there, trim the physics.

modeler: The open-system caveat is exactly right. 'Order is not free' is the honest form.
skeptic: Corrects the common abuse of entropy, the isolated-system caveat. Exactly the calibration I reward.
clinician: An important caveat, but physics-heavy. Nothing for the reader to do.
habit: 'Nothing stopped being paid for stays.' Good line. Name one thing to pay for daily.
contemplative: An honest caveat. The bold line is good: order is not free. The physics before it could shrink.
stress: It corrects the usual entropy abuse. 'Order is not free' is modest and durable. I praise this.
gamedesigner: The isolated-system caveat is honest but technical. 'Order isn't free' is the keeper.
structural: 'Order is not free.' The open-system caveat is precise. Apply it to institutions that stop being funded.
satirist: The isolated-system caveat is honest physics most self-help botches. 'Order is not free' is the plain sentence. Good.
mythmaker: 'Order is not free' lands; marriage as open system nice. Mostly physics caveat.

modeler: The isolated-system caveat is exactly right. 'Order is not free' plus concrete unpaid examples is honest and usable.
skeptic: Admirable self-correction: names how the idea gets abused and narrows the claim. This is the chapter at its most honest.
clinician: 'The friendship nobody calls' lands. It corrects the 'everything decays' fatalism well, but no step: call someone this week.
habit: 'Order is not free' plus the friendship nobody calls stings in a good way. Add: name one thing you've stopped paying for.
contemplative: The friendship nobody calls: I feel that. The isolated-system defense argues with physicists who aren't in the room. Shorten it.
stress: It corrects the usual entropy abuse and narrows to a claim that holds. Admirable restraint.
gamedesigner: Good correction, the uncalled friendship stings. Turn it into: name one unpaid-for order this week.
structural: "The institution whose funding quietly stops" is the one structural line. Who stopped paying? Follow that thread.
satirist: It catches its own metaphor before it becomes a mechanism: isolated systems only. 'Order is not free' is the plain sentence, and it's here.
mythmaker: 'The friendship nobody calls, the garden nobody weeds' is where the blood finally shows up. That line carries the paragraph.

modeler: Balance as active oscillation is good: sway, temperature. The rock 'running loops' is a stretch, since thermal motion isn't feedback.
skeptic: Postural sway and thermoregulation are accurate. 'Balance is evidence of work' is well earned. Long; trim the rock.
clinician: 'Balance is evidence of work' is lovely, but the paragraph sprawls. Trim the rock example.
habit: Rock thermal cycles, sway, tides. Pile of examples, no step.
contemplative: 'Standing upright is falling and catching' is beautiful. The rock and resolution lines are too much. Halve it.

gamedesigner: 'Stillness is the average' is great. The paragraph is too long; split off the rock example.
structural: Balance as active work is a good abstraction. Its personal application stays vague.
satirist: Postural sway and the thermal band are real facts. 'Stillness is the average, never the state' is earned wonder.

modeler: Postural sway and thermoregulation are genuine balancing loops with bands. Good. Add the delay that sets the wobble's period.

clinician: 'A steady week kept getting corrected' reframes wobbling as normal, which is quietly reassuring. Still nothing to do.
habit: Sway and temperature examples work. Too long, and it ends in abstraction. Where's the weekly correction ritual?
contemplative: Standing is falling and catching. That is beautiful. Then come four more examples and a homeostasis summary. Stop after the sway.
stress: "Can't see the work means you're not looking closely" is unfalsifiable. Drop that line and keep the physiology.
gamedesigner: Standing as falling-and-catching is great. Paragraph runs long; payoff line buried at the end.
structural: Sway and homeostasis are accurate. It runs long and is all physiology, with no social analogue such as institutions needing upkeep.
satirist: Postural sway and the temperature band are real facts. The last sentence oversells 'homeostasis from inside a life'. Trim the coda.
mythmaker: 'Standing upright is uninterrupted falling and catching' is a gorgeous image. It runs long, so trim the last two sentences and let the body speak.

modeler: Postural sway and thermoregulation: real balancing loops with real bands. 'Balance is evidence of work' is exactly right. Strong.
skeptic: Postural sway and thermoregulation are real and well used. 'Homeostasis from inside a life' reaches past the evidence, but gently.
clinician: 'A steady week kept getting corrected' gently normalizes wobble. Add one concrete correction move to earn C.
habit: 'Balance is evidence of work' is a good reframe. The payoff is still abstract. Name one correction to make this week.
contemplative: Standing as falling and catching is true and lived. "Homeostasis from inside a life" is too much. Stop at the steady week.
stress: Standing as continuous falling, temperature in a band: real physiology. Balance as evidence of work survives strain. Keep.
gamedesigner: 'Standing upright is falling and catching' is a great felt metaphor. There's no move to make, though, only a payoff claim.
structural: 'Balance is evidence of work' is a good line. It's all body and week, though. No correction mechanism outside the self.
satirist: Postural sway and the temperature band are real facts doing real work. 'Balance is evidence of work' is a line you could say at a bar.
mythmaker: 'Standing upright is uninterrupted falling and catching' is the image I'll keep. No person is standing in it, though. Give me someone.

modeler: The hornet is a curiosity, and correlation isn't loop structure. It doesn't earn its slot. Cut it.
skeptic: One hornet species, 'appears' and 'correlated': all honest hedges. Then 'the rhythm follows the supply' generalizes recklessly. Cut that line.
clinician: A hornet curiosity that does no work for the reader. Cut.
habit: Oriental hornet detour. Cut it; it does nothing for my morning.
contemplative: The hornet is a curiosity, not a teaching. It breaks the flow. Cut it.
stress: The hornet is a single exotic anecdote proving nothing about you. Cut it, or tie it to human circadian evidence.
gamedesigner: The hornet detour adds nothing playable. Cut it.
structural: The hornet fact is a curiosity and does little work. Cut it.
satirist: The Oriental hornet: an actual animal and an actual finding. Bryson test passed. Cite Plotkin 2010. It feels bolted on, though.
mythmaker: Solar hornet is trivia dropped from nowhere. Cut, or make it someone's energy-following day.

modeler: Curious hornet, but supply-tracking is a tangent here. It gives no method for measuring when your own energy arrives. Cut it or make it a log exercise.
skeptic: Hedged hornet trivia, then a jump to your energy. A vivid anecdote standing in for the human base rate.
clinician: A charming hornet fact. The closing question gestures at self-tracking but gives no method.
habit: Ends on one good question: when does your energy actually arrive? Add a tracking rep: log it three days.
contemplative: A curious hornet, then a good question. The insect is decoration. Ask the question directly.
stress: A hedged hornet fact holding up a thin metaphor. Ornament. Cut it or replace it with a usable energy audit.
gamedesigner: Hornet is a fun oddity; closing question gives me a move. Weak link to the reader's actual day.
structural: A hornet curiosity. It's ornamental, and the closing question could stand without it.
satirist: A delightful hornet, and 'appears to' is properly hedged. A citation would help, and the leap to your energy is decorative.
mythmaker: A hornet trivia aside with no stakes. The closing question deserves a person's tired afternoon, not an insect's cuticle.

modeler: The energy log is a good instrument-before-tuning move. The hornet is decoration with an 'appears to' hedge. Cut it or tie it in tighter.
skeptic: I like the instruction not to answer from memory. 'Three observations will tell you more' oversells a sample of three. Say a week.
clinician: A good small step: one-word energy readings for a few days. Data replaces the self-story. The hornet opener is a distracting detour.
habit: Yes. One-word energy reading at fixed times for a few days. Concrete, cued, two minutes. Drop the hornet.
contemplative: Jotting one word a few times a day is a real practice. The hornet is a detour. Begin with the question.
stress: The hornet is a curiosity. The energy log is a real experiment that can prove your story wrong. That's the right instinct.
gamedesigner: A one-word energy log is a real feedback loop. The hornet opener is a detour, so lead with the log.
structural: Logging energy is a real, cheap experiment. The hornet opener is clumsy. The 3 p.m. slump might be your shift, not you.
satirist: The hornet is a fun aside, and the one-word energy log is an actual task. Debunking the morning-person story is useful. Works.
mythmaker: The energy log is practical and the 3 p.m. slump is real. The hornet comes from nowhere and drops off; set it up or cut it.

modeler: Diagnose before prescribing: right. But it rests on U0295's mislabeling. Reframe as finding where your limits bind.
skeptic: Observe before changing: good. A two-type typology is unvalidated; allow mixed or shifting shapes.
clinician: 'Nothing to do with discipline.' Read your cycle first. Practical and shame-free.
habit: 'Read your cycle first.' Practical. Give the method: log energy for three days.
contemplative: Notice your shape before changing it. Gentle, practical, and it removes blame. Keep.
stress: Diagnose before prescribing. Practical, and it spares readers false failure. Keep.
gamedesigner: The practical use is clear, but it lacks a test for which shape you run. Add a three-day log.
structural: 'Nothing to do with discipline.' Good. But redesigning schedules collectively, through flex time, never comes up.
satirist: The practical takeaway, clear: don't force morning-stack advice on an evening person. Useful.
mythmaker: Fighting the wrong kind of loop: practical and forgiving.

modeler: Requirements before motion. A good engineer's epigraph.
skeptic: A useful reframing question. Earns its place.
clinician: Swaps 'why aren't I moving' for 'what would moving require.' Anti-rumination in one line.
habit: Good one-question epigraph. Carryable.
contemplative: A quiet, kind question. It turns me from blame to curiosity.
stress: Decent epigraph, and it fits the chapter.
gamedesigner: A good reframing epigraph. It sets the diagnostic goal.
structural: A fair epigraph. It opens the right question.
satirist: A decent epigraph: it poses a real question rather than a mood.
mythmaker: Decent epigraph, a bit flat.

modeler: The epigraph frames the right question. It does nothing beyond that.
skeptic: A useful reframe in miniature. Fine as an epigraph.
clinician: A good shame-reducing pivot from 'why' to 'what'. As an epigraph it orients well.
habit: A good reframe as epigraph, and it's one question. It works in place.
contemplative: Plain and kind. It turns blame into inquiry.
stress: A decent reframe as an epigraph. It earns attention but solves nothing on its own.
gamedesigner: Punchy reframe card. Sets the question well; nothing to do yet.
structural: A good reframe of the question, from moral judgment to engineering. As an epigraph it works.
satirist: An epigraph that's actually a usable instruction. It's rare for one of these to earn its line.
mythmaker: A coaching-poster epigraph. A Lasso line needs a Beard in the room to doubt it. It reads fine and moves no one.

modeler: Reframes blame into requirements, which is decent. No mechanism yet, but as a chapter door it does its job.
skeptic: A useful reframe that moves attention from the person to the situation. As an epigraph it lands, though it argues nothing.
clinician: It moves the question from what's wrong with you to what moving would take, which is a textbook guilt-not-shame shift. A strong epigraph.
habit: One good question, the kind Bungay Stanier would approve. It survives the day. Fine as an epigraph.
contemplative: Gentle and direct. It turns blame into movement. Good as it is.
stress: Reframing away from a verdict on yourself is useful, but as a slogan it's thin. Fine as an epigraph, no more.
gamedesigner: A punchy reframe that works as an epigraph. It points at a move without teaching it.
structural: 'Stop asking what's wrong with you' is the right refusal of self-blame. 'What moving would take' could include other people.
satirist: Plain and kind. It does its job as an epigraph, nothing more.
mythmaker: A good turn from blame to motion. It speaks straight to the reader and earns its place as a chapter epigraph.

modeler: Reframes diagnosis toward what moving would take, i.e. resistance. Nice, but it's an epigraph without a stock or a force.
skeptic: Swaps blame for a practical question, which I like. 'Stop asking' orders me about, and assumes nothing is wrong with me.
clinician: Replaces self-blame with an actionable question. Exactly what I want at 3 a.m. Short and kind.
habit: Swaps a judging question for a useful one. One question I can carry all day. Keep it.
contemplative: Kind and small. It moves me from blame to a question I can answer. Fits on a single exhale.
stress: Good reframe from blame to cost. Short and useful, but just an epigraph; asserts, shows no test.
gamedesigner: Good reframe from verdict to move. Flips blame into a testable action. Short, punchy, but only a slogan; payoff comes elsewhere.
structural: Stop asking what's wrong with you is anti-blame, which I like. But ask what moving would take could be structural; it does not say.
satirist: Swaps blame for logistics in nine words. Plain, kind, slightly useful. Passes the bar test.
mythmaker: Reframing shame as a question of motion is kind and sharp. A line on a poster; needs a person it was said to.

modeler: Signpost.
skeptic: Transition linking back to Day 5. Fine.
clinician: Transition.
habit: Bridge back to Day 5. Functional.

gamedesigner: Callback to Day 5. Fine connective tissue.

satirist: A signpost back to Day 5. Fine.
mythmaker: Callback to Day 5. Functional.

clinician: Navigation recap. Clear, but nothing in it to hold or use.

contemplative: It only points back and points forward. A signpost needs half these words.

structural: Recap and signpost. It's connective tissue only.
satirist: Signposting with onboarding homework callbacks. Necessary plumbing and no more.
mythmaker: Pure navigation recap. Fine as signage, but there's no heart. Open on someone stalled instead.

modeler: Familiar stall, clean promise. Hinge text only. Fine in place, earns little on its own.
