gamedesigner: Exit-built-in test is clean. Nicely balances the previous warning.
structural: Plant-many-expect-to-thin is a fine coda. Doesn't add much.
satirist: Plant many expecting to thin: good distinction. 'Lifeline and snare' is house jargon again.
mythmaker: The tree dropping thousands of seeds keeps the image alive. The exit-built-in test is clear.

modeler: Overproduce and thin by design: budgeted losses as a balancing side. 'Exit built in' is a real design criterion.
clinician: 'Planting ten while planning to keep three' is a concrete way to plan for losses. Practical and kind.
habit: Planting ten and planning to keep three is an actual planning rule. Usable.
contemplative: Plant ten, plan to keep three. Clear and usable. Warm it with one human example.
stress: Budgeted losses versus hope. That's optionality done right. The 'exit built in' test is concrete. Keep.
gamedesigner: Plant ten, keep three, with a clear diagnostic question. A budgeted-loss rule I can apply this week.
structural: Budget your losses, build in an exit. Practical portfolio advice, structurally inert.
satirist: Ten planted, three kept: budgeted loss is a usable rule. 'Lifeline from snare' is fine.
mythmaker: The seeds rhyme with the tree, which I like. Planting ten to keep three is practical. It still needs a face.
skeptic: 'Budget the losses up front' is a usable test. The seed ratio is decoration posing as a natural law.

modeler: The karma line misdefines karma, then the chapter corrects it. Choose a better epigraph.
skeptic: Odd definition of karma, but readable.
clinician: Epigraph contradicts the chapter's no-ledger stance. Replace.
habit: Odd epigraph; the chapter rejects the karma it quotes. Fine but flat.
contemplative: Simple, warm. It invites kindness.
stress: The epigraph contradicts the chapter's no-ledger karma. Replace it.
gamedesigner: Epigraph contradicts the chapter's no-ledger point. Swap for something about loops closing.
structural: A greeting-card epigraph that the chapter then contradicts. Replace it.
satirist: Karma isn't 'putting others first.' The epigraph is wrong about the word it defines. Cut.
mythmaker: The epigraph contradicts the chapter, which rejects karma as altruism. Replace it.

modeler: Tight epigraph that states the thesis: loop, no ledger. Works.
clinician: A neat epigraph that frames the chapter. It's not addressed to anyone's pain.
habit: A clean epigraph. It works in its place.
contemplative: Neat, a little clever. It reads as a thesis, not a breath.
stress: Tight epigraph that does its framing job.
gamedesigner: A tidy thesis epigraph that sets the chapter's promise.
structural: A clever epigraph that depends on vocabulary not yet earned.
satirist: Witty enough to pass the bar test. Barely.
mythmaker: A clever epigraph, but cool. It works only if the loop later closes on someone we care about.
skeptic: A tidy thesis line. Being tidy is exactly why I check what follows.

modeler: Return without a bookkeeper: a nice compression of mechanism without an agent. It does its epigraph job.
skeptic: 'What goes out comes home' is exactly the feels-true claim I distrust. The next units half-earn it.
clinician: A crisp epigraph that frames the chapter's claim well.
habit: A tight thesis line. Fine as an epigraph.
contemplative: Clear, but it states the doctrine without touching me. Fine as a signpost.
stress: A tight thesis line. As a slogan it could sit on a mug. The following passages have to cash it.
gamedesigner: A crisp thesis line. As an epigraph it states the rule and stops.
structural: A neat compression of the chapter, but nothing for the reader to do.
satirist: Compact and clear about its departure from karma. A workable epigraph.
mythmaker: A clean thesis line. No image, though, and 'comes home' could carry a picture.

modeler: Boomerang needs no bookkeeper: return with no ledger. Clever, but the epigraph asserts return without a mechanism.
skeptic: Boomerang metaphor is catchy, and 'no bookkeeper' removes the unfalsifiable bit. Still fluent; say what comes back, how often.
clinician: Clever, drops the ledger, which spares guilt. No action, and boomerang can still imply what you throw returns.
habit: Boomerang line is catchy, but nothing to do. Epigraph earns abstract and ease only.
contemplative: A boomerang needs no bookkeeper: a warm image that drops the ledger. Pretty, though a little pleased with itself.
stress: Boomerang needs no bookkeeper: cute, and it smuggles in the claim that it comes home. Nothing to check. Slogan.
gamedesigner: Boomerang with no bookkeeper is a neat, memorable image, but it's an epigraph. I can't act on it or tell whether I got it.
structural: Boomerang karma epigraph. Comforting just-world gloss; who profits from believing it all comes back? Cheerful, no mechanism.
satirist: Boomerang is cute and 'no bookkeeper' is a good phrase. But it's a slogan; the next paragraphs must pay it off.
mythmaker: Boomerang needs no bookkeeper is a pretty, usable image. Lovely thought; who threw it?

modeler: Return flow with no ledger: nice contrast to a stock that keeps score. Compressed. Needs a delay or a transform named.
skeptic: Tidy slogan; 'what you throw comes home changed' states a mechanism without evidence. Fluent, and I notice the ease.
clinician: 'Nobody keeps score' is a relief for the shame-prone. Nice; no step.
habit: Neat line, easy. No behaviour attached. Epigraph that restates rather than directs.
contemplative: 'Without the ledger' is a gentle phrase. Nobody keeps score: this calms me. It is a statement, not a practice.
stress: 'Nobody keeps score' is the claim doing all the lifting. Reassurance with no ledger and no penalty. Fragile.
gamedesigner: Compact thesis line but no move. Title card.
structural: Compact, quotable. 'Nobody keeps score' is rich: someone always does, and it's usually the one with the ledger.
satirist: 'Karma without the ledger' is a neat pitch, but 'nobody keeps score' is a hushed-voice claim with no mechanism. Foma, unlabeled.
mythmaker: 'Nobody keeps score' is a nice turn on karma, but the line is abstract. What comes home, to whom, changed how? Show one boomerang.

modeler: Clear statement: no ledger-keeper, an indifferent universe. Sets constraints honestly.
skeptic: A clear setup that declines the cosmic ledger. Respectable.
clinician: Clear framing of indifferent universe. Abstract.
habit: Positions the idea against tradition. Context, no action.
contemplative: Clear framing. A little defensive about tradition, but plain.
stress: Declares the universe indifferent and refuses the ledger. Good discipline.
gamedesigner: Clear setup of what this isn't. Lecture, but short.
structural: Clear positioning against cosmic ledgers. Abstract framing, readable.
satirist: Clear positioning against cosmic ledgers. Fine.
mythmaker: Clear contrast with the cosmic ledger. It's a lecture, but a short one.

modeler: Clean scope cut: no external accountant. Mostly framing, no mechanism yet.
clinician: 'Nothing waiting to even your score' frees readers from punishment, but it may read as bleak. Add a warm line.
habit: Theology setup with no action. Fine as framing, and it could be shorter.
contemplative: Clear, but it argues with traditions instead of blending. Soften the 'can't borrow' tone.
stress: It refuses the cosmic ledger, which is consistent and modest. Nobody's score gets evened. Good.
gamedesigner: Theory exposition with a callback to Genesis. Clear but idle, I'm only receiving.
structural: Refusing a cosmic ledger is good: no one balances the books for you. So who should? Unasked.
satirist: Indifferent universe, said plainly. Citing its own 'Genesis story' is the costume showing; Bokonon would wink.
mythmaker: A clear stance against the cosmic ledger, delivered as a lecture. Who wanted the score evened, and lost?
skeptic: Clear about where it stands and what it won't borrow. Indifference is asserted, but openly, as the book's own premise.

modeler: Removes the external controller and keeps consistency with Genesis. The 'mercy' reversal lands personally. Clean.
skeptic: A coherent position, consistently held. The mercy reading is a nice touch. It doesn't depend on unsupported metaphysics. Good.
clinician: 'Nothing out there is keeping yours either' is genuine mercy for a guilt-laden reader. It's careful not to promise justice.
habit: The mercy at the end is good. The Genesis and noticing-self jargon is heavy. No action.
contemplative: "Nothing out there is keeping yours either" is a real mercy. The Genesis cross-reference could go.
stress: Refuses the comforting cosmic ledger. The mercy turn is honest. It costs the reader the revenge fantasy, which is the point.
gamedesigner: The mercy twist on 'nobody keeps your tab either' is a great second beat. It's still a lecture.
structural: Dropping the cosmic ledger is honest. But if no one keeps score, justice is a human institution to build. Say that.
satirist: 'Nothing out there is keeping yours either' is a real mercy. 'Genesis story committed it' is scripture again, so just say the universe doesn't judge.
mythmaker: The turn from 'nothing keeps their tab' to 'nothing keeps yours' is a real reversal with heart. Excellent.

modeler: Convergent recurrence as evidence is reasonable. It's still an inference about pressure, not a mechanism.
skeptic: Independent recurrence shows a shared intuition, not a real mechanism. Minds converge on just-world beliefs too. Fix this inference.
clinician: Cross-cultural point, readable. Not usable.
habit: Recurrence across cultures. Nice point, nothing to do with it.
contemplative: Respectful toward other traditions. Good tone. Could be shorter.
stress: An intuition recurring across cultures isn't evidence of the mechanism. That's history misused. Weaken the claim.
gamedesigner: Independent recurrence as evidence: interesting. No move; acceptable context.
structural: Convergent recurrence as evidence is a reasonable move. Abstract, harmless.
satirist: 'Shows up independently in cultures' with no culture named. Give three, with dates. Bryson would.
mythmaker: A respectful nod to traditions, with no straw man. Good courtesy.

modeler: Fair epistemics: convergence is suggestive, not proof. Sets up the mechanism honestly.
clinician: Fair-minded context. Intellectual, not personal.
habit: Interesting cross-cultural context. It's still a lecture. Trim it.
contemplative: Respectful, plain. Hosea's whirlwind is well chosen. It stays in the head.
stress: 'Recurrence is not proof' is exactly the hedge I want. It checks against history and admits the bias.
gamedesigner: Interesting convergence point and fair about its limits. Still a lecture, with no prediction asked of me.
structural: Careful about convergence not being proof. Intellectually honest scaffolding.
satirist: Hosea plus 'convergence isn't proof': a believer who checks himself. Bryson-grade honesty.
mythmaker: Hosea's whirlwind is a great image, and the opposing view gets fair courtesy. Still nobody holding it.
skeptic: 'Recurrence is not proof; minds converge on comforting beliefs.' That's the hedge I wanted. Well done.

modeler: Convergence as a weak signal, with comforting-belief bias admitted. Honest epistemics. Name the pressure soon: reciprocity in repeated games.
skeptic: It says outright that recurrence is not proof, and that's calibrated. 'Real pressure underneath' is still a guess. Name what it might be.
clinician: A fair survey of traditions, and it rightly flags that comforting beliefs converge. Context, not help.
habit: A cross-cultural survey. Interesting, zero action. Trim it to two sentences.
contemplative: Careful and fair, but it is scholarship, not practice. Half the length would serve.
stress: It flags that convergence could just be comforting belief. That's rare honesty. It treats history as evidence, not proof.
gamedesigner: Cross-cultural survey is cutscene material, and it follows U0423's point instead of setting it up. Compress it.
structural: Careful about convergence not being proof. Intellectually honest, but no lever.
satirist: Hosea named, and it admits that convergence isn't proof. That's honest. Good.
mythmaker: Fair to the traditions and honest about comforting beliefs. Hosea's whirlwind is the only image; the rest is survey.

modeler: Convergence across traditions might hint at real pressure, and it admits convergence also happens on comforting beliefs. Honest, but not yet a mechanism.
skeptic: 'Minds also converge on comforting beliefs' is the best sentence in the set: it turns its own evidence against itself. Lovely, and sourced.
clinician: Sensible convergent-belief hedge. Interesting, but reader gets no step and 'sow the wind' could feed dread.
habit: Cross-cultural karma tour is interesting, but where do I act? Three paragraphs on belief, none on behaviour.
contemplative: Karma, Hosea, converging minds, comforting beliefs, then pressure promised later. Four hedges before the point. Say what comes back and stop.
stress: Concedes minds also converge on comforting beliefs, so convergence isn't proof. Cross-cultural history, honestly weighed. Good. Little to do with it.
gamedesigner: Cross-culture karma survey is a good hook, and the honesty about convergence is nice. But it's history lecture: nothing to predict or try.
structural: Honestly hedges the convergence argument and declines the ledger. Intellectually careful, but a comparative-religion aside with no action implied.
satirist: Sanskrit, Hosea, 'what goes around.' Admits minds converge on comforting beliefs. Good foma labeling. Hosea is the only checkable fact.
mythmaker: Hosea, karma, 'what goes around': fair treatment of the view it argues against. Honest about convergence. Still all survey, no one.

modeler: Candid on convergence not being proof. Declining the ledger is a clean design choice. Hearing 'real pressure' needs a name.
skeptic: Notes that convergence may reflect comforting belief, not truth; exactly calibration. Pleasantly honest. 'Hints at real pressure' still stretches.
clinician: Declining the ledger protects readers from reading pain as punishment. Honest about convergence not being proof. Good.
habit: Interesting cross-cultural pattern with honest hedging. But it's survey, not practice. What do I do with this pressure?
contemplative: Interesting, and honestly hedged. But it lists traditions and an aside on proof. Keep 'what goes around' and the declined ledger.
stress: Concedes that convergence may be wishful thinking. That is Dalio-grade history use plus humility. Good.
gamedesigner: Cross-cultural convergence is interesting lore. Lecture, though. No reader action.
structural: Honest caveat about convergent comfort beliefs. Good restraint. Karma-adjacent ideas also excuse inequality; address that.
satirist: Hosea, karma, and the frank 'minds also converge on comforting beliefs'. That sentence is the whole Bokonon test passed. Nicely skeptical.
mythmaker: Hosea's whirlwind, 'what goes around' — everyone's said it. Honest about comforting convergence, which earns trust. Respectful to the idea it declines.

modeler: Transition line. Cut it.

gamedesigner: Bridge line. Cut or merge.

clinician: A one-line thesis bridge. Clear, but it doesn't earn more than a bridge.
habit: A summary line. Clear but inert. Fold it into the neighbouring unit.
contemplative: A clean thesis line. It does its one job.

satirist: A plain thesis, plainly said. It's a bridge, nothing more.

modeler: No score-keeper, yet treatment returns through shared groups. Mechanism is the group, a path for the loop to close. Needs delay and loss stated.
skeptic: 'Tends to find its way back' with no data. Group-mediated return is plausible; show a study or admit it's a hypothesis.
clinician: No one keeping score is a relief. But 'finds its way back to you' could reassure or frighten a guilt-prone reader.
habit: Clear thesis, no instruction. How you treat people comes back: so what is one treatment to change tomorrow?
contemplative: No one is keeping score, and the way I treat people tends to return. Plain and kind. The qualifiers are honest.
stress: 'Tends to' is hedged but the claim is vague: through which groups, how often? Survivorship risk. Needs a case where it fails.
gamedesigner: Compact thesis: no scorekeeper, but treatment still returns via shared groups. Clear rule. Promise needs a test or example to be felt.

satirist: 'No one is keeping score' but treatment still returns, through shared groups: plain claim that is arguable. Needs a bar-table example.

habit: Habits ripple out and come home. Clear and personal. 'Loops close' is good.
contemplative: Habits to relationship to culture and back. 'Loops close.' Clear and true.

satirist: Plain chain from habit to culture and back. 'Loops close' is overclaimed; some loops leak forever.
mythmaker: 'Who stays and who drifts' and 'loops close' make a strong core. A single named friend group would seal it.

gamedesigner: Freezing water is a great threshold image and the straining signal is real feedback. Skein, Banner and Dyad stacked together lose the newcomer.

mythmaker: Water freezing all at once is lovely, and 'not a verdict on you' is kind. But the Skein/Banner jargon buries the comfort. Lead with the freeze.

modeler: Completeness and health as separate axes. Correct and brief.

gamedesigner: Clear co-op metaphor: three legs, two sitters, one fails and both fall. Memorable, sets up the check, but it's a caption.

satirist: Three legs, two people on one stool: the metaphor sags under its own load. Funny by accident. Pick stool or people.
mythmaker: Stool with two people on three legs is a bit muddled but memorable. Lose a leg and you both go down: stakes.

modeler: Stool is a structure metaphor, not a mechanism. Trust is a stock that builds slowly and drains fast; say that.
skeptic: Stool metaphor is clear and sticky. Three legs is a construction, not a finding; I'd ask for the basis.
clinician: Stool is easy and sturdy. 'Both go down' may scare an anxious reader; no repair step.
habit: Three-legged stool is easy and sticky. But no step. Which leg do I check tomorrow?
contemplative: A stool with three legs and both of us sitting on it. Clear, shared, and I feel it.
stress: Stool is a clear image and the lose-one-both-fall stakes are real. Is it three legs by evidence or by taste?
gamedesigner: Easy image, no move. Fine as a header.
structural: Stool is an easy, memorable picture of mutual dependence. Pure dyad logic; no reference to anything outside the two.
satirist: Three-legged stool is a plain, load-bearing image: lose one and you both go down. Easy, memorable, and sayable at a bar.
mythmaker: A stool with three legs and both of you on it: lose one and you both go down. Shared fate in one image.

modeler: 'Borrowed and adapted' from whom? Cite it.
skeptic: 'Borrowed and adapted' from whom? Cite Frei and Morriss' trust triangle.
clinician: Setup. Fine.
habit: Setup line. Fine.
contemplative: Simple setup. Fine.
stress: 'Borrowed and adapted' from whom? Credit the source.
gamedesigner: Promise of a diagnostic. Good setup.
structural: 'Borrowed and adapted' from whom? Credit the source.
satirist: 'Borrowed and adapted' from Frances Frei's trust triangle. Name her. Hiding the source looks worse than borrowing.
mythmaker: 'Borrowed and adapted' from whom? A setup with no blood in it.

modeler: A plain bridge. It works in place but does nothing for me by itself.
skeptic: Honest about adapting a leadership model. Still only a transition. Say whether the adaptation has been tested at all.
clinician: Clear setup and nothing more. Fine as a bridge, but it can't earn points on its own.
habit: Just a lead-in. It promises a check but doesn't give one. Could go straight to the three legs.
contemplative: A doorway, nothing more. Fine as it is; drop 'built for leaders, adapted here' to lighten it.
stress: A plain setup with honest credit to Frei and Morriss. It does its job and earns nothing more.
gamedesigner: Loading screen. Only sets up the triangle. Could fold into the first leg.
structural: A leadership framework shrunk to couples. Fine as a hinge but it carries no content of its own.
satirist: Credits Frei and Morriss, so a real name at last. Bryson approves. Still just a turnstile into the list below.
mythmaker: Pure scaffolding. It passes us to the list and does nothing else. Fine as a hinge, not a beat.

modeler: Credits the source and flags that it's untested at this scale. Good honesty. A useful checklist setup.
skeptic: Credits the source and admits it's untested at two-person scale. I'd like more of this candor.
clinician: Honest about being untested, good. It's a diagnostic setup, and 'wobbling' could invite scanning a partner for faults.
habit: A quick diagnostic promise with honest sourcing. Good. Tell me when to run it.
contemplative: The credits and the hedge come before the gift. Thank the source in a note and simply offer the check.
stress: 'Untested at that scale' is the kind of humility I want. It credits the source and admits the stretch.
gamedesigner: Promises a diagnostic. Being upfront that it's untested is good. Now hand me the checks quickly.
structural: Credits its source and admits the adaptation is untested. A usable diagnostic, though it stays strictly inside the couple.
satirist: Credits Frei and Morriss and admits 'untested at that scale.' That's the Bryson move. Respect.
mythmaker: Honest about being untested at this scale, which I respect. Still citation scaffolding with no couple in the room.

modeler: Adapted from a named framework and flagged untested at two-person scale. That's the honesty I want. Practical diagnostic to find the wobbling leg.
skeptic: Credits Frei and Morriss and says it's untested at two-person scale. Exactly right. A self-diagnostic with disclosed limits.
clinician: A quick check naming which leg wobbles, with honest 'untested at this scale'. Diagnostic, not accusatory. Useful.
habit: Quick check naming which leg wobbles: honest about being untested. Diagnostic you can run today. Good.
contemplative: A quick check I could do with my partner, and honest that it is untested at this scale. Impeccable about its limits.
stress: Credits Frei and Morriss and says 'untested at two-person scale.' Rare honesty. Diagnostic check lets reader find the wobbling leg.
gamedesigner: A self-diagnostic with honest provenance and an 'untested at two-person scale' flag. This is feedback: tells me which leg wobbles. Great set-up.
structural: Honest about borrowing Frei and Morriss and untested at this scale. Practical diagnostic for a couple; purely interpersonal, no structure.
satirist: Credits Frei and Morriss, and says 'untested at two-person scale.' That is exactly the honesty I came for. A quick check beats a lecture.
mythmaker: A check you take together, with honest caveat 'untested at two-person scale.' Practical. Show one pair scoring it.

modeler: Performance gap as hidden strain is a decent idea. It's stated, not modeled.
skeptic: 'Being yourself' assumes a true self beneath the performance. Lowery would object. Reframe it as consistency, not essence.
clinician: Performed self is Brown territory; resonant. No step.
habit: Performed self question hits. Leg definitions are fine as reference.
contemplative: The performed self. A real question to ask myself.
stress: Clear, but untested. Say what collapse looks like.
gamedesigner: Clear leg with a recognizable failure. Add a self-check question.
structural: Clear, personal. Fine.
satirist: Clear. Fine.
mythmaker: The gap between performance and person is personal. It needs a scene.

modeler: There's a stock here: the gap between performance and life fills quietly, then collapses after a delay. The check is usable.
skeptic: The 'what do you hide' check works. 'Same person when they're out of the room' assumes one true self; Lowery would object.
clinician: 'What do you routinely hide?' is a small, answerable check. It's about behaviour, not character, so it's shame-safe.
habit: 'What do you routinely hide around them?' is a real two-minute check. Good rep.
contemplative: 'What do you hide around them?' I can ask that tonight. Good.
stress: The 'what do you hide' check is concrete and uncomfortable, and it names the failure mode. Good.
gamedesigner: Controller in hand: 'what do you hide around them?' is a real self-check. Plays well.
structural: The 'what do you hide' check is usable and stings. Strictly interpersonal, so I've no structural quarrel here.
satirist: 'What do you routinely hide around them?' is a question you can actually answer at a bar. Works.
mythmaker: 'What do you tone down around them?' lands right in the gut. The years-long performance collapsing gives it real stakes.

modeler: Empathy versus sympathy is clear. Short and fair.
skeptic: Rightly distinguishes empathy from projection, and 'harder than it sounds' is accurate. Epley would add: ask them.
clinician: Empathy vs sympathy distinction, clear.
habit: Empathy vs sympathy, briefly put. Good.
contemplative: Empathy versus sympathy, briefly. Good.
stress: Empathy versus sympathy is a real, checkable distinction.
gamedesigner: Empathy vs sympathy distinction is useful and clear.
structural: Empathy vs sympathy, briefly. Clear.
satirist: Empathy versus sympathy, briefly and well.
mythmaker: Sympathy faking empathy is a sharp distinction. Good.

modeler: The empathy vs sympathy split is clean. Saying your read out loud closes the feedback loop. Practical.
skeptic: Excellent. Saying your read aloud and asking is Epley's perspective-getting over perspective-taking. Calibrated, and the reader can act on it.
clinician: Best kind of step: say your read out loud and ask. Concrete, kind, and it can be done tonight.
habit: Says your read out loud and asks if it's right. Concrete, testable, and you can do it at dinner tonight. Love it.
contemplative: Say your read aloud and ask. This is deep listening, plainly given. Keep it.
stress: The best check here: say your read out loud and let them correct it. The claim is exposed to being wrong on purpose.
gamedesigner: Best feedback loop in the section: say your read aloud and ask if you got it right. Instant signal.
structural: Saying your read aloud is a real, testable move. It's clean and personal.
satirist: Sympathy versus empathy, plus a check you can run: say it out loud and ask. Plain, useful, done.
mythmaker: Saying your read out loud is a real move. Empathy versus sympathy is clear. It still needs a scene where someone gets it wrong.

modeler: 'Logic' is vague here. 'Coherent throughline' means what, measurably?
skeptic: Vague. What's a 'throughline' in a relationship? It needs an example.
clinician: 'Logic' leg is vague; what does it look like in practice?
habit: 'Logic' leg is vague. What does a coherent throughline look like on a Tuesday?
contemplative: 'Logic' is a cold word for a relationship. 'Fairness' or 'honest structure' might be warmer.
stress: 'Logic' is the vaguest leg. Define it operationally or rename it.
gamedesigner: 'Logic' is the vaguest leg; no example. Give one.
structural: 'Logic' as a relationship leg is vague. What counts as a throughline? Needs an example.
satirist: Frei's 'logic' means your reasoning is sound, not 'relationship throughline.' The adaptation muddied it.
mythmaker: The weakest leg, defined vaguely. What does 'logic' look like over breakfast?

modeler: Consistency across Tuesday and anniversary is a fair test. Mood-driven rule changes are noise in the controller. Clear.
skeptic: The Tuesday-versus-anniversary standard is checkable. The rest leans on 'make sense,' which every couple believes of themselves.
clinician: Resonant question, no step. Add one: name one agreement you both keep and one you don't.
habit: Stacked questions and no check, unlike its siblings. Give one test: name one agreement and ask whether it held last week.
contemplative: One long question, out of breath. Split it. Tuesday versus anniversary is the heart; keep that.
stress: Tuesday versus anniversary is a usable test. It ends as a rhetorical question, though; give one concrete self-check, like the other two legs have.
gamedesigner: Rhetorical questions with no clear check. Give me a move, like naming one rule you both kept this week.
structural: Asks a question but gives no check. Add one, the way the other two legs have one.
satirist: Tuesday versus anniversary is a nice touch. 'Mood and momentum' is fine. The question rambles; cut it to one sentence.
mythmaker: Tuesday versus anniversary is a nice image, and so is 'today's temper.' Still, nobody's at the table. Give me the broken promise.

modeler: Testable: one agreement, did it hold last week. 'Mood and momentum' names the drift. A concrete check.
skeptic: A checkable test: name one agreement, did it hold last week? Behavior over self-report, which is exactly right.
clinician: A specific check: one agreement, last week. A small enough step. 'Mood and momentum' names the problem without shaming.
habit: 'Name one agreement, ask whether it held last week.' That's a rep I can do tonight. Keep it.
contemplative: 'Name one agreement, ask whether it held last week' is a kitchen-table practice. 'Mood and momentum' says it plainly. Good.
stress: 'Did it hold last week?' is a real test with a real failure condition. Mood against rule is sharp.
gamedesigner: This is the model unit: a named agreement and 'did it hold last week?' Clear move, clear signal.
structural: A real check: name the agreement and ask whether it held last week. That's a rule you can audit. Good.
satirist: 'Did it hold last week?' is a test you can actually run. 'Mood and momentum' is the plain sentence. Works.
mythmaker: Ordinary Tuesday against anniversary, an agreement that held last week: a test you can actually run. Good. Can 'mood and momentum' get a face?

modeler: Using the rating gap as a sensor is clever: the disagreement is the signal. A good, cheap measurement loop.
skeptic: Comparing independent ratings to find disagreement is a smart, checkable practice. Good.
clinician: Monthly independent rating, gap as conversation starter. Concrete, good.
habit: Monthly, 1 to 5, compare gaps. Cue, rep, payoff. Model practice.
contemplative: Rate, compare, find where you disagree. A practice for two at the table. Good.
stress: Independent ratings, then look at the gap: a cheap, falsifiable practice. Good.
gamedesigner: Monthly independent ratings, compare gaps — a genuine feedback loop. Excellent.
structural: A concrete monthly practice whose value is the disagreement gap. Usable.
satirist: The rating-gap exercise is genuinely useful. Disagreement is the data. Good.
mythmaker: Rating the legs separately and comparing gaps is concrete and humane.

modeler: A worked case with the diagnosis and the fix. This is how the whole book should teach.
skeptic: A useful worked case, though invented. 'Ten minutes' is a story outcome, not evidence. Label it illustrative.
clinician: Worked case with a specific fix: describe their fear back. Best in chapter.
habit: Worked case with a ten-minute payoff. Describe the other's fear back. Superb.
contemplative: Describe the other's fear back until it is right. Deep listening, shown. Keep.
stress: Concrete, but 'ten minutes' is a too-neat ending. Admit it might take longer.
gamedesigner: Worked example! Shows the move and the payoff. More of these everywhere.
structural: A good worked case. But career-priority fights are also about childcare costs and job markets. Mention that the stakes are externally set.
satirist: Best unit in the chapter: a real fight, diagnosed, fixed in ten minutes. More of these, fewer definitions.
mythmaker: Finally a face and a fight. Describing the other's fear back is the Zuko scene. Name them.

modeler: Interpersonal circumplex: warmth corresponds, control complements. A real, documented mechanism. Excellent.
skeptic: Interpersonal complementarity is real research, reasonably summarized. Name the source and it's strong.
clinician: 'Isn't always failing at empathy' de-shames friction. Clear explanation.
habit: Warmth matches, control complements. Explains real fights. Action comes later; fine.
contemplative: Warmth meets warmth; control meets its opposite. Useful, but long. Two sentences could hold it.
stress: The interpersonal circumplex: long-studied evidence, used precisely. The kind of claim I trust.
gamedesigner: Warmth matches, control complements — a learnable rule that explains real friction. Great.
structural: The interpersonal circumplex, explained cleanly. It replaces personality blame with mechanism. That's my kind of move, at small scale.
satirist: The interpersonal circumplex, explained well. Name Leary or Kiesler and you have the 'here's how we know.'
mythmaker: Warmth matches, control complements. It explains real fights without blaming personality.

modeler: Fitted opposite rules is a good structural point. The Part Five tables reference obscures it.
skeptic: Corrects the book's own tables, which is honest. Inaccessible without Part Five; simplify.
clinician: Part Five table jargon. Lay reader lost.
habit: Corrects Part Five tables. Book-internal housekeeping. Readers won't act on it.
contemplative: Talks to the book's own tables. The reader in pain needs less apparatus here.
stress: Corrects the book's own tables, which is honest. Inside-baseball phrasing; make it reader-facing.
gamedesigner: Corrects Part Five tables I haven't seen. Forward-reference clutter; state 'fitted opposite rules' plainly.
structural: An important point about fitted asymmetry, but it's framed as a correction to Part Five tables the reader hasn't seen.
satirist: Arguing with the book's own Part Five tables. Readers haven't seen them. The point belongs after them.
mythmaker: The fitted-opposite idea matters, but it's framed as a correction to Part Five tables. Show the couple.

modeler: Real structure: complementary rules locked together, neither able to move alone. That's what keeps the pattern stable. Best mechanism in this batch.
skeptic: Fitted opposite rules is a sharp idea. 'Precisely because' claims a mechanism the anecdote can't show; soften it to 'often.'
clinician: Good insight: neither half is the broken one. The Part Five tables reference hurts clarity, and there's no move for the stuck reader.
habit: Good insight, but the Part Five/Dyad-Kin aside gets in the way. What do I do when I spot that I'm the half that always decides?
contemplative: The couple is true. 'Part Five tables, Dyad-Kin' clouds it. Start with the couple; let the jargon go.
stress: Fitted opposite rules is a real insight, and the book corrects its own tables. That's humility. It needs a step for what to do about it.
gamedesigner: Strong insight, but 'that axis' and the Part Five tables lean on rules I don't hold yet. Onboard first.
structural: Fitted opposite rules is an actual mechanism: neither half can move alone. Now say how a pair breaks the lock.
satirist: The decider-and-follower couple is the plain sentence. 'That axis' and 'Part Five tables' bury it. Busy, busy, busy. Lead with the couple.
mythmaker: The decider and the go-along partner is a recognizable couple and a sharp reveal. 'That axis' and the Part Five table refs are clutter.

modeler: Fitted opposite rules: complementary coupling where neither half can move alone. Real mechanism. The Part Five table aside clutters it.
skeptic: Useful reframe. But 'neither can change unless the other does' contradicts moving first. Part Five/Dyad-Kin references lose lay readers.
clinician: 'Neither of them is the broken one' is the line a stuck couple needs. The Part Five table meta-talk buries it, so cut that.
habit: Fitted opposites is a real insight. The Part Five table caveat is housekeeping that clogs it; cut that sentence.
contemplative: 'Neither of them is the broken one' heals. The defence of the Part Five tables argues with a critic who isn't here. Remove it.
stress: Fitted opposites is a strong idea, and it takes the blame off one person. The meta talk about the Part Five tables muddies it, so trim.
gamedesigner: 'Neither is the broken one' is a strong reframe. The Part Five tables aside is designer commentary, so cut it.
structural: Excellent: the pattern is the system, so nobody is the broken half. The cross-references to Part Five tables and Dyad-Kin bury it.
satirist: Strong idea, neither is the broken one. Then 'Part Five tables draw a Dyad-Kin' buries it in house jargon. Cut that sentence.
mythmaker: Strong human setup: neither one is the broken one. Then Part Five tables and Dyad-Kin drown it. Keep the couple, cut the cross-references.

modeler: Reciprocal versus equitable, and who feeds versus who absorbs. A sharp distinction.
skeptic: 'Reciprocal is not equitable' is a sharp, useful distinction.
clinician: Reciprocal is not equitable: key insight for anyone absorbing harm.
habit: 'Who is feeding this, who is absorbing it?' One good question. Keep.
contemplative: Reciprocal is not equitable. Honest and kind to the one absorbing.
stress: 'Reciprocal is not equitable.' Feeder versus absorber is a sharp, usable question.
gamedesigner: Feeding vs absorbing is a clear second question. Reciprocal is not equitable — strong.
structural: 'Reciprocal and not equitable.' Who feeds, who absorbs. Power named inside the dyad. Strong.
satirist: 'Reciprocal and not remotely equitable.' Sharp, honest distinction.
mythmaker: 'Reciprocal and not remotely equitable' is a vital question, clearly put.

modeler: It gives the absorber permission to name harm. Important and practical.
skeptic: Good guard against sincere self-blame. Responsible.
clinician: 'Not your loop to change'; name it. Vital safety for the over-responsible.
habit: Not your loop to change. Clear permission, protects sincere readers.
contemplative: Not your loop to change. Permission that heals. Trim the cross-reference.
stress: Gives the absorbing party a seat outside self-blame. Important.
gamedesigner: Releases the absorbing party from self-blame. Important, clear.
structural: It refuses to make the absorbing partner hunt for their fault. Right. It admits the framework's default misleads sincere readers. Rare honesty.
satirist: Needed and plain: absorbing isn't feeding. Good protection against self-blame.
mythmaker: It protects the absorber from sincere self-blame. Real care.

modeler: The ladder walked rung by rung on one money fight. Concrete and very usable.
skeptic: A worked ladder example, concrete. The inherited paradigm is speculative but marked 'might be'. Fine.
clinician: Ladder walked through money fights: makes the abstraction usable.
habit: Ladder walked through a money fight. 'No money talk after 9pm.' Concrete and memorable.
contemplative: Good to see the ladder in a home. Too many rungs in one breath; pick three.
stress: Walking the ladder on money fights makes it concrete. Works.
gamedesigner: Ladder replayed on money fights. Great level reuse; teaches by example.
structural: A shared budget as information flow is a real lever. Money fights also come from wages and debt. That paradigm wasn't only inherited.
satirist: The ladder with a money example finally makes the ladder concrete. Should have been in Chapter 9.
mythmaker: Money fights walked up the ladder: the best application of the ladder yet. The inherited paradigm lands.

modeler: Diagnose the axis, then a specific move per axis. Clean.
skeptic: A clear, actionable diagnostic before fixing. Good.
clinician: Concrete, small. Add caveat: don't yield in an abusive dynamic.
habit: Name the axis, then go first or yield once. Tomorrow-ready.
contemplative: Go first with the tone you want; yield once on purpose. Aikido at the table. Keep.
stress: Diagnose the axis, then act once on purpose. Testable this week.
gamedesigner: Classify, then specific move per axis. Perfect tutorial step.
structural: A concrete, axis-specific move. Usable tonight.
satirist: Warmth goes first; control yields once. Actionable.
mythmaker: 'Yield once, on purpose' is small, brave and doable.

U0478.chapter: 15. Do I Understand You Well Enough?

modeler: Pseudo-anatomy aphorism. Weak.
skeptic: Folk physiology as an epigraph. Pretty and false; acceptable only as an epigraph.
clinician: Pleasant epigraph.
habit: Pleasant epigraph, a bit greeting-card.
contemplative: Simple and warm. It points toward listening.
stress: Pseudo-anatomy as epigraph. Replace it.
gamedesigner: Pleasant aphorism, no function. Fine.
structural: A fortune-cookie epigraph.
satirist: Ears connect to the heart? Anatomy disagrees. Pretty foma; label it or swap it.
mythmaker: A greeting-card epigraph. It says nothing the chapter needs.

modeler: Pleasant aphorism, no machinery. It's filler unless the chapter cashes it out.
skeptic: Lovely, and I have no reason to believe it. Seeing also tells you meaning, and often wrongly.
clinician: Nice distinction, but it's a performance line. It earns its place only if the chapter delivers the listening step.
habit: Nice line. A bridge, not a practice. Keep it short.
contemplative: Gentle and clear. It breathes. Keep.
stress: A fortune-cookie line. Nothing here can be wrong. Cut it or tie it to a claim.
gamedesigner: Crisp epigraph with a nice split, but there's no move attached.
structural: A pleasant aphorism that doesn't earn its slot. Cut it, or tie it to the chapter's mechanism.
satirist: A tidy epigraph that would look nice embroidered and says little. Foma. Keep it only if you label it foma.
mythmaker: A good rhyming line that points to something bigger. It's still faceless, and it carries the chapter's theme without a person.

modeler: Clean split between observable behavior and hidden state. Works as an epigraph.
skeptic: Epley would approve. Behavior is visible, intent isn't, so ask. A short line that's actually supported.
clinician: Short and usable: ask, don't assume. It interrupts mind-reading, which feeds rumination.
habit: Short, true, and it implies the action (ask). Works as an epigraph.
contemplative: It is simple, true and usable today. It asks me to ask instead of assume. Ruiz would nod.
stress: Short, true, and it can be used. A good epigraph.
gamedesigner: Crisp rule I can test the next time I misread someone. Strong epigraph.
structural: A neat line on behaviour versus intent. Personal and clear, with no machinery behind it.
satirist: Plain, true, quotable without a candle lit. Earns its place as an epigraph.
mythmaker: Simple and true. It works as a door into the chapter, not as a revelation.

modeler: Behavior is observable, intent is hidden: ask. Fixes attribution error with a cheap sensor. Aphorism with a mechanism.
skeptic: Respects that other minds are opaque: behavior is visible, intent must be asked. Epley would agree. Short, true, usable.
clinician: Ask what they meant: one specific act that defuses hurt. Short, humane, usable tonight.
habit: See the act, ask the meaning. That's one good question I can use at dinner tonight.
contemplative: See what they did; ask what they meant. Ruiz would smile. This is a practice I could use today.
stress: Act versus intent: a sound distinction that prevents misjudging people. True, usable, short. Slightly obvious.
gamedesigner: Crisp rule: behavior is visible, intent is not, so ask. A usable move in a sentence. Needs example, but easy to apply today.
structural: Ask what they meant: good communication hygiene. Interpersonal only. Misreadings often follow power differences; unmentioned.
satirist: Act versus intent in two short sentences. Immediately usable in an argument. Plain and right.
mythmaker: Do versus meant: a conflict in six words. Real fix for blame. Sits waiting for its Zuko.

U0479.chapter: 15. Do I Understand You Well Enough?

modeler: A single repeatable check-in question. Simple and usable.
skeptic: Asking rather than assuming is the Epley fix: perspective-getting beats perspective-taking. Excellent.
clinician: One question, out loud: simple and usable.
habit: One question, with a cue: before support or advice. Exactly the Coaching Habit move.
contemplative: The question is Thay's own medicine. Nothing to remove.
stress: One question, said aloud. A modest, durable tool.
gamedesigner: One question, out loud, before acting. Easy controller.
structural: A simple, usable question. Fine.
satirist: Thich Nhat Hanh's question, uncredited. Credit him; the question survives any bar.
mythmaker: The question is the hero of the chapter. Simple and portable.

U0480.chapter: 15. Do I Understand You Well Enough?

modeler: Unchecked misperception as the error source. Good, if a little repetitive.
skeptic: Right direction. 'Very often' and 'enormous amount' need a base rate or a hedge.
clinician: Misperception as source of suffering; small repeatable act. Good.
habit: Love as checking perception. Nice reframe; repeats the question's value.
contemplative: Misperception is the root of suffering. True. Last sentence is long; let it rest earlier.
stress: Sound, but 'enormous amount of damage' is unmeasured. Trim the claim.

structural: Checking perception. Sensible and personal. No structural angle, none needed.
satirist: Unchecked misperception as the source of suffering. Plain and useful.
mythmaker: Love as checking perception, and suffering from unchecked misreads. True, but show one misread.

U0481.chapter: 15. Do I Understand You Well Enough?

modeler: Listening to understand dampens your own anger. A plausible balancing effect, stated plainly.

clinician: Listening protects you from your own anger: practical and kind.
habit: Listening protects you from anger. True, but 'listen to understand' needs a concrete form.
contemplative: Listening to relieve suffering protects you from anger. Deep and plain. Keep.
stress: A testable side-effect: understanding dampens anger. Good.
gamedesigner: Listening protects you from your own anger — a felt payoff right now.
structural: Thich Nhat Hanh uncredited. Calming yourself via listening. Fine inner work, scoped correctly to the dyad.
satirist: Listening dissolves your own anger. Believable, practical. Again Hanh's deep listening.
mythmaker: Listening protects you from your own anger, a real gift. Iroh energy.

U0482.chapter: 15. Do I Understand You Well Enough?

modeler: Presence as an offering is nice. 'Tends to be returned' is a reinforcing loop asserted, not shown.
skeptic: 'Presence offered tends to be returned' is plausible but unsupported. Pleasant framing, little to act on.
clinician: Presence as offering: lovely reframe; light on how.
habit: Presence as offering. Abstract; next chapter does this better.
contemplative: Presence as a gift. Lovely. The Local Rule tag at the end is unneeded.
stress: A nice reframe, but 'tends to be returned' is soft comfort. Say when it isn't.
gamedesigner: 'Be present' with no signal for whether I'm doing it. Add an observable cue.
structural: Presence as an offering. Pleasant, familiar.
satirist: Presence as offering. Pleasant; the reciprocity claim is asserted.
mythmaker: Presence as an offering is warm. Chapter 16 repeats it; consolidate.

modeler: Observable checks (phone face-down, say it back) and an honest return delay. The loop is only gestured at, but it's usable.
skeptic: Observable markers (phone down, could repeat what they said) turn a mood into a behaviour. 'Not always at once' is welcome hedging.
clinician: Phone face-down, eyes up, say back what they said: a step anyone can take. Smart to admit it doesn't always come back.
habit: Phone face-down, eyes up, could say it back. That's an observable behaviour I can do tomorrow. Best presence passage here.
contemplative: Phone face-down, eyes on them. This is lived. End before 'Local Rule seeded into a Dyad'.
stress: Observable tells: phone face-down, you can repeat what they said. 'Not always at once' is honest hedging. It holds up.
gamedesigner: Finally a visible win state: phone face-down, eyes up, you can repeat what they said. Drop the Local Rule jargon.
structural: Concrete tells, phone face-down. Ask who designed that phone to split your attention, and the passage gains teeth.
satirist: Phone face-down, eyes up, could repeat it back: that's a usable test. 'Local Rule seeded into a Dyad' is a costume on the closing line.
mythmaker: Phone face-down and eyes on them: finally a gesture I can see. Concrete and warm. The Local Rule tail is jargon.

U0483.chapter: 15. Do I Understand You Well Enough?

modeler: A pause rule with a defined output (ask one more question). Good.
skeptic: A concrete pause-and-ask habit. 'The entire practice compressed' is overblown, but the habit is good.
clinician: Pause, check your story, say 'not yet.' Exactly the next step.
habit: Pause, ask, say 'not yet,' ask one more question. Cue and rep. Keep.
contemplative: Pause, ask one more question. My own story versus them. A whole practice. Keep.
stress: A good habit. 'Close to the entire practice' is grandiose; cut that clause.
gamedesigner: Pause, ask, say 'not yet'. Concrete, repeatable. Good.
structural: A concrete pause-and-ask habit. Overclaims ('the entire practice') but is usable.
satirist: 'Responding to my own story about them.' Good, compact practice.
mythmaker: 'Responding to my own story about them' is a sharp, usable pause.

modeler: Apt epigraph that sets up the channel idea.
skeptic: A good epigraph that previews the chapter's claim.
clinician: Epigraph that earns its place; true and felt.
habit: Good epigraph, earns its spot.
contemplative: Quiet and true. Good epigraph.
stress: A plain epigraph that sets up the chapter.
gamedesigner: Epigraph actually states the chapter's mechanic. Works.
structural: A decent epigraph for the chapter.
satirist: Plain, true epigraph.
mythmaker: A good epigraph that sets up the chapter's real argument.

modeler: True to experience. It's a threshold condition stated as a mood, so it resonates but explains nothing.
skeptic: 'No one' is an absolute. Plenty of people blurt the real thing to strangers who aren't listening. Overconfident epigraph.
clinician: True and gentle. It resonates, but it's an epigraph with no handhold.
habit: Resonant epigraph. It works as a cue, but there's no action in it.
contemplative: True and warm. It earns its small place.
stress: Rings true from experience, but it's still an epigraph doing mood work. It survives only as a doorway.
gamedesigner: It lands personally and stays short. Works fine as a beat.
structural: It resonates but only as an epigraph. Adequate.
satirist: True, and you'd say it at a bar. As an epigraph it doesn't do much, but it isn't pompous.
mythmaker: True, and it stings a little. Readers recognize the friend who never opened up. It earns its place as an epigraph.

modeler: Disclosure gated on perceived listening. That's an implicit loop, and it rings true.
skeptic: 'Most people'? Plausible, uncounted. Make it 'Many people' and it's honest.
clinician: True and warm. As an epigraph it resonates, but the step comes later.
habit: It resonates. As an epigraph it's fine, but it gives me no move.
contemplative: Gentle and recognisable. I feel it in my own home. It is an epigraph and it works as one.
stress: Rings true and is modest. It works where it sits.
gamedesigner: Resonant but obvious. It works as a title card and does nothing more.
structural: True and familiar. It's a sentiment, not a lever.
satirist: Bar-proof. Anyone who's tried to get a teenager to talk knows it. Keep.
mythmaker: Every therapist's office and every kitchen at midnight. It resonates. It earns its place as an epigraph.

modeler: Disclosure depends on perceived listening: a gate that opens on feedback. Trust as a threshold. Very practical, brief.
skeptic: 'Many people' has no base rate, though it feels right. Actionable if you read it as: show listening before probing.
clinician: True and gentle: listening comes before disclosure. Implies the step, being heard-ready. Brown would nod.
habit: True and warm: people hold back until they feel heard. But how do I show I'm listening? Add one move.
contemplative: Listening comes first, and the real thing follows. Gentle, true, easy to live.
stress: Real pattern: people disclose when they sense listening. Plausible and usable. 'Many' hedges well. Observational, no test offered.
gamedesigner: True and usable: people withhold until they sense listening. Gives a design target, signal of listening. Brief, but no how-to.
structural: People hold back until listened to. True and warm. Epigraph alone; says nothing about who gets listened to and why.
satirist: People test whether you are listening first. True, small, useful. 'Many' rather than 'all' keeps it honest.
mythmaker: People won't say the real thing until you're listening. True, and a stake. Needs a speaker.

modeler: Recap setup. Could be trimmed.
skeptic: Recap setup.
clinician: Recap. Inert.
habit: Recap transition. Could be one line.
contemplative: Recap of the movement. The reader just read it. Cut.
stress: Recap transition.
gamedesigner: Recap. Short enough; could merge with U0486.
structural: A recap and setup.
satirist: Recap opener. Shrink to one clause.
mythmaker: Recap. Cut it to one clause.

modeler: A recap transition. Fine in place, inert on its own.
skeptic: Pure transition; it does its job. Nothing to score beyond clarity.
clinician: Pure transition, readable but inert.
habit: A recap built from jargon. Cut it, or fold it into the next line.
contemplative: A recap in parentheses. Bridges can be one breath shorter. Fold into the next line.
stress: A connective recap. Fine as a hinge, inert on its own.
gamedesigner: Recap screen with no play in it. Merge it into the next line.
structural: Pure connective tissue that recaps and adds nothing.
satirist: A recap sentence acting as a hallway. Cut it or fold it into the next line.
mythmaker: A recap list of past practices with no face and no turn. A connective hinge; trim it or fold it into the next line.

modeler: A pure transition. Fine in place, but it earns little.
skeptic: Transition. Functional and harmless.
clinician: A recap list. It's a bridge, nothing more. Fine, but it earns little.
habit: Bridge sentence that recaps the tools. Necessary glue, nothing more.
contemplative: This is bookkeeping, a list of tools so far. The next passage does its work better. Fold the two together.
stress: A plain bridge sentence. It's fine, but merge it into the next one.
gamedesigner: Pure menu recap, nothing to do. Fold it into the next line.
structural: A transition that recaps the tools. Functional and inert.
satirist: Recap-of-the-movement throat-clearing. One clause would do.
mythmaker: A recap of tools, no blood in it. A pure bridge. Fold it into the next line.

modeler: Transitional sentence: the tools assume an open channel. Sound, but it's a hinge only. No claim to score on its own.
skeptic: Transition only. It does flag an assumption the earlier tools make, which is honest, but the sentence carries no content yet.
clinician: Transitional recap. Clear but gives the reader nothing to hold. Fine in place; earns nothing alone.
habit: Transition line recapping tools. Fine plumbing, no value of its own.
contemplative: A bridge sentence summarizing tools already given. Clear but empty of practice. Cut it; let the next line open the door.
stress: Transition sentence flagging an assumption that the channel is open. Honest but carries no idea of its own.
gamedesigner: Recap line of tools, assuming the channel's open. Transitional setup, no move or feedback. Fine connective tissue, nothing to play with.
structural: Bridge sentence recapping tools. Carries no argument of its own; nothing to score for structure or lever.
satirist: Transitional bridge reviewing tools. Clear enough, but it only sets up what comes next.
mythmaker: Connective tissue, no heart. Fine bridge, nothing to remember.

modeler: Transition. Does name the open-channel assumption, but only as setup.
skeptic: Names an assumption of the tools so far, honest. A bridging sentence; clear but little else.
clinician: Transitional recap that adds no new help. Useful signpost only.
habit: Setup sentence leaning on a list I can't see. Nothing to do or feel here. Merge into the next passage.
contemplative: A bridge sentence. Plain, but it lists tools I have not met yet. It is a summary where I wanted a breath.
stress: A bridge sentence. Fine, but it is only transition and carries no weight on its own.
gamedesigner: Recap in parentheses of unnamed tools. A rulebook callback with no controller. Lost the player here.
structural: A recap sentence with no payoff yet. Too abstract on its own; say what tool fails when the channel is shut.
satirist: A transition that assumes I remember three tools by parenthetical. Useful hinge, but it leans on earlier coined vocabulary.
mythmaker: Bridge sentence listing tools. 'Assumes the channel is open' is a good hinge, but nobody's face or image. Connective tissue.

modeler: Fine one-liner bridge.
skeptic: 'Usually it isn't' is a confident frequency claim. Hedge it.
clinician: Short transition. Fine.
habit: Short pivot. Fine.
contemplative: Fine as a bridge if the recap goes.
stress: A one-line hinge. Merge it.
gamedesigner: Nice hook line. Alone it's thin.
structural: A one-line hinge.
satirist: Fine pivot line.
mythmaker: A one-line hinge. Fine.

modeler: A familiar feeling sets up the problem. A lead-in only.
skeptic: Familiar experience, named well. It sets up the problem but doesn't solve anything yet.
clinician: 'Said with care and heard something else' names a real pain without blame. Still only a promise.
habit: Relatable setup ('hears something else'). Fine as a hook. Make sure the chapter delivers the rep it promises.
contemplative: 'The other person hears something else.' I know this feeling. Simple, good.
stress: The 'you know the feeling' hook lands. It promises work it hasn't delivered yet.
gamedesigner: 'You know the feeling' hooks me. Good second beat after the recap.
structural: The 'you know the feeling' hook lands. Otherwise it's a signpost.
satirist: 'Said with care, and they hear something else' lands. Everyone has done it. Fine as a short bridge.
mythmaker: 'You know the feeling' works: right words said carefully and heard wrong. Everyone has lived that. A good hook.

modeler: Familiar pain: right words heard as an attack. Relatable setup, no mechanism yet.
skeptic: 'You know the feeling' presumes, but this one most readers do know. A fair setup.
clinician: 'The other person hears an attack' names a real pain accurately. Good opener, and the step is promised.
habit: 'The other person hears an attack.' Everyone's felt that. Good hook, and it promises action.
contemplative: 'The other person hears an attack.' I know that feeling. It is short and warm. Keep it.
stress: The failure case is named first: careful words heard as an attack. That's how to open a chapter.
gamedesigner: 'You know the feeling' hooks me with a recognition beat. Good chapter start.
structural: Kind words heard as an attack is a familiar experience, and the chapter's purpose is stated cleanly.
satirist: 'The right words, said with care, and the other person hears an attack.' Plain, painful, recognizable. Good.
mythmaker: 'The right words, said with care, and they hear an attack.' Everyone has lived that. Short and earned.

modeler: Right words, with care, received as attack: closed channel. Names a real failure, with the chapter's purpose stated. Relatable and specific.
skeptic: Familiar scene of kind words heard as attack. But 'closed channel' presumes you know why it landed that way.
clinician: Names the painful experience of right words landing as attack without blaming anyone. Promises a first step. Good.
habit: Right words, heard as attack: painfully familiar. Promises a fix, opening the channel. Deliver the step quickly.
contemplative: Right words, with care, heard as attack: I know that closed channel. Names the pain simply, then promises to open it.
stress: Right words, care, still heard as attack: everyone has been there. Names the failure condition of the earlier tools. Good turn.
gamedesigner: Strong problem hook: right words, care, heard as attack. Names a closed channel. Relatable failure state, with a clear chapter goal.
structural: Closed channel versus right words landing as attack is relatable. Interpersonal repair only; ignores power or history causing the closure.
satirist: Right words, with care, heard as an attack. Everyone has lived it. Names a real problem, promises to open it first.
mythmaker: Right words, care, still heard as an attack: everyone has been there. A closed channel is a good image. Show one.

modeler: Callback housekeeping. Cut it, or reduce it to a clause.
skeptic: Navigation through the book's onboarding. Cut it or shrink it to a clause.
clinician: Cross-ref to Day 6; confusing out of context.
habit: Callback to onboarding day 6 the reader may not recall. Restate the rep or cut.
contemplative: Bookkeeping about Day 6. Cut or reduce to one phrase.
stress: Onboarding bookkeeping. Cut.
gamedesigner: Callback to Day 6 rewards prior play — that's felt progress. Love it.
structural: A back-reference to the Day 6 onboarding. Useless to a reader who skipped it.
satirist: Callback to 'Day 6 of the onboarding.' Course-syllabus voice. Cut.
mythmaker: Onboarding cross-reference homework. Recall the moment instead: that silence you sat through.

modeler: Signpost.
skeptic: A setup line.
clinician: Header. Fine.
habit: Signpost.
contemplative: Announces correction before giving it. Cut.
stress: Announcement. Merge.
gamedesigner: Header promising correction. Cut.
structural: A setup line.
satirist: Signpost. Fine.
mythmaker: Signpost. It earns nothing alone.

modeler: A promissory headline. The payoff has to come in the next paragraphs.
skeptic: A teaser that asserts 'wrong' without saying wrong compared to what. The claim is deferred, not earned.
clinician: Bold hook, clear. 'Wrong' is fine here; nobody gets blamed.
habit: A provocative header, but all claim and no handle. Okay as signage.
contemplative: A promise that the next lines must keep. Fine as a heading, no more.
stress: It claims the ordinary picture is wrong 'in a way that matters' without saying how. That's a guru tease. Lead with the claim instead.
gamedesigner: Good hook that sets up a prediction. Let me guess what's wrong before you tell me.
structural: It claims something matters but defers saying why. A header that withholds.
satirist: Announces that something's wrong 'in a way that matters' and makes us wait for it. A drumroll, not a point.
mythmaker: A promising provocation at header length. It sets up a reversal I want to see paid off.

modeler: Two mental models updated at once. That's a real systems framing of conversation. Now show the update rule.
skeptic: Mutual model-building is a sound framing. It stops at the metaphor without saying what follows for practice.
clinician: A nice reframe, but abstract. Give one thing to do differently in the next conversation.
habit: Nice reframe. Abstract, though. What do I do differently in my next conversation?
contemplative: It is a clear reframe and it stays in the head. Give me one breath of practice: notice the picture you are building of them right now.
stress: Mutual modelling is a decent frame. It needs a failure case to earn its spot as the headline.
gamedesigner: Interesting model, but I'm only receiving. Ask me to predict what my partner's picture of me holds.
structural: A sound reframe of conversation as mutual modelling. Abstract, with no move attached yet.
satirist: Decent reframe, plain enough. A bit grand for what it is; the game example does the actual lifting.
mythmaker: The idea is good, the delivery bold and bloodless. Two people, a table, nobody I can see.

modeler: Two models building each other at once, so each is a picture in the other's head. Mutual feedback, not message passing. Sharp reframe.
skeptic: Right in spirit: we model each other and can be wrong. But 'building a picture at the same time' is stated as fact, not cited.
clinician: Interesting reframe: each of us is a picture in the other's head. No step, and abstract for someone mid-conflict.
habit: Picture in their head, picture in yours: sharp reframe. Still reframe only. What do I do differently Monday?
contemplative: I am a picture in their head while they are one in mine. Striking and gentle. Bold type shouts what the thought whispers.
stress: Reframes conversation as two models building at once. Changes what you do. Claim is specific enough to argue with. Clear.
gamedesigner: Reframes conversation as two simultaneous pictures of each other. Good mental model for why messages misfire. Needs a prompt to apply.
structural: Each building a picture of the other: neat reframing that explains misfires. Still dyadic; no rules, institutions or group levers.
satirist: Two pictures building each other at once is a sharp reframe, though no evidence or example. Ends on a bit of a riddle.
mythmaker: You're a picture in their head while they're one in yours: it makes me feel watched. Strong reframe.

modeler: Sellers' point: the game lives in the player's model. Accurate and well drawn.
skeptic: A game living in the player's model is a nice analogy, clearly told.
clinician: Game-as-mental-model analogy is clear; detour from the hurting reader.
habit: Game-in-the-player's-mind analogy. Clear, a detour.
contemplative: The game lives in the player's mind. Clear, but a detour from the person in front of me.
stress: The game-design analogy is clear, though the detour is long.
gamedesigner: Game lives in player's head — straight Koster. Clear and true.
structural: The game-as-mental-model analogy is clear and interesting. A detour, but it earns the next move.
satirist: Game in the player's head: a good, earned analogy. Koster or Swink would back it.
mythmaker: The game happening in the player's mind is a fresh, clear analogy.

modeler: Sellers would nod: the game is a mental model built through feedback loops. Strong setup for the dyad claim.
skeptic: Evocative, but 'never in the software' is an overreach. Players and designers share far more than this allows. The metaphor carries the argument.
clinician: Vivid metaphor, but it's about games, not the reader's pain. It's a detour for anyone who came here hurting.
habit: Pretty game metaphor, three sentences of abstraction. So what do I do on Monday? Tie it to an action.
contemplative: Lovely, and it is too much cleverness. The game detour asks me to think, not to listen.
stress: Clever analogy, but it's one designer's view sold as structure. Some games do live in the software. It's lovely in a calm sea.
gamedesigner: Speaks my language: the game lives in the player's model. A vivid analogy that teaches the rule.
structural: Building the model in the player's head is a sharp abstraction. It's a detour for anyone who doesn't game.
satirist: The game lives in your head, not the software. That's a genuinely good and concrete image. Stephenson would nod.
mythmaker: The loved game living in your head is a real image with a real person inside it. This is the passage's Iroh moment.

modeler: Pure Sellers: the player's model built one feedback loop at a time. A good analogy that's actually structural.
skeptic: Clever for gamers, opaque for others. The link from game design to conversation is asserted, not drawn.
clinician: The game metaphor is a detour for most readers, and the link to listening stays implicit. Tie it back or cut it.
habit: The game metaphor works for gamers and loses everyone else. It also never connects back to conversation. Tie it back or cut it.
contemplative: It is clever, and it leaves out readers who don't play games. Code, designer, feedback loop: a long road to a simple point.
stress: The game analogy is vivid but drifts from conversation. Tie it back in one line or it's a detour.
gamedesigner: Speaks my language: the mental model built one feedback loop at a time. Great hook. Tie it back to conversation quickly.
structural: The game-design analogy works: a designer shapes feedback loops, not minds. That's the first real nod to a rule-maker.
satirist: Best metaphor in the batch, concrete and earned. The designer never touched that part; it works.
mythmaker: A game you loved: an inspired turn, and it puts the reader inside the image. Have later chapters return to it.

modeler: Game-as-model-in-your-head: designer builds it loop by loop, a conversation does it in two heads. Sellers-grade, and the analogy earns its mechanism.
skeptic: Game analogy makes mental models vivid for a gamer. Accuracy of those models is exactly what Epley says to doubt; mention that.
clinician: Game-world metaphor is accessible and fun. Pleasant but doesn't help anyone talk to a person today.
habit: Game-world analogy lands for a builder. But explanation, not instruction. Finish with one thing to try in the next conversation.
contemplative: The game metaphor is warm but long, and the designer detour wanders. The point is two heads building one picture. Say that.
stress: Game analogy lands for this reader and explains the mental model idea well. Analogy only; proves nothing about conversation.
gamedesigner: Game analogy done right: the world lives in your head, built by feedback loops. Conversation builds one in two heads. Speaks my language, easy.
structural: Game-design analogy for mental models is vivid, and designer-shapes-your-head is nearly my theme, but it never asks who designs.
satirist: Game loved as a model in your head, not the code: good and Sean-shaped. Lovely analogy, but no fact about how the head builds it.
mythmaker: The beloved game, built in your head from a thousand tries: that's an actual memory. Image earns its keep and returns.

modeler: Two mutually modeling ends. A clean structural step.
skeptic: Mutual modelling is accurate and well put.
clinician: Both ends modeling: clean point.
habit: Both ends modelling. Good insight, still theory.
contemplative: Both ends are building. Clear and true.
stress: Both ends modelling: a clean step.
gamedesigner: Both ends modelling — clean escalation from the game analogy.
structural: Two coupled models. Clean.
satirist: Both ends modelling each other. Clear and interesting.
mythmaker: 'Both ends are doing it.' The twist lands cleanly.

modeler: Two coupled modelers, each reading while being read. A real structural difference, with the bored-face example as evidence.
skeptic: Mutual modelling is well supported, and the bored-look example grounds it. One of the better-calibrated paragraphs.
clinician: The 'someone looks bored' moment lands. It's insight without a step, though it lays the ground for one.
habit: 'You talk differently when someone looks bored' lands. Next step: notice the moment you adjust.
contemplative: 'You talk differently when someone looks bored.' That one line carries the paragraph. Lead with it.
stress: The bored-listener example grounds it, and two-way modelling is defensible. Still no condition under which it would fail.
gamedesigner: The bored-listener example lets me check this against memory. Good noticing prompt.
structural: Two-ended modeling is well put, and the bored-listener example proves it. Good.
satirist: 'You talk differently the moment someone looks bored.' That's the earned line. Both ends modelling at once, said plainly.
mythmaker: 'You talk differently the moment someone looks bored' is the face I wanted. It builds well on the game image.

modeler: Coupled models make a different system class. Correct. Now show one emergent behavior.
skeptic: A fair point about coupled models. Slightly redundant with the paragraph before.
clinician: Coupled models: interesting, abstract.
habit: Restates the previous paragraph. Cut.
contemplative: Says again what the last paragraph said. Cut.
stress: Coupled models. Merge with U0490.
gamedesigner: Coupled models as different system class. Clear, but adds no move.
structural: A different kind of system. Fair, abstract.
satirist: Fine; slightly repeats 0490.
mythmaker: It repeats the prior point in systems jargon. Cut.

modeler: Emergent tension neither person brought is real. Name what accumulates (irritation? defensiveness?) and it becomes a mechanism.
skeptic: The tension example earns the emergence claim. 'Different kind of system' is asserted more firmly than shown.
clinician: Freeing: tension neither of you brought means neither of you is to blame. Add what to do once you notice it.
habit: Restates the previous paragraph. The tense-argument line is the only grip. Trim hard.
contemplative: Repeats the paragraph before. Keep only the tense argument line; it is the true part.
stress: The tense-argument payoff is good. 'A different kind of system' edges toward a theory of everything; show that the vocabulary predicts something.
gamedesigner: The tense-argument payoff earns it. The middle sentence lectures a bit. Trim 'different kind of system'.
structural: An emergent product neither person brought. That's systems as a mechanism, not a mood, which I'll credit.
satirist: The argument going tense when neither of you walked in tense is a real observation. The 'this book has the vocabulary' brag is noise.
mythmaker: The tense argument neither person walked in with saves it. The 'different kind of system' talk is exposition, but the payoff lands.

modeler: Good pivot line.
skeptic: A transition.
clinician: Header line. Fine.
habit: Signpost line.
contemplative: A heading-sentence. Let it go.
stress: Hinge.
gamedesigner: Virtue to condition: good reframe headline.
structural: A hinge line.
satirist: Signpost. Fine.
mythmaker: Hinge line. Fine.

modeler: The phone line is a decent threshold image, but it's metaphor carrying a claim the previous paragraph hadn't earned.
skeptic: Neat metaphor and no evidence. Is presence binary like a phone line? Probably not, so the image overstates it.
clinician: The phone-line image is clear. It's a reframe without a next move.
habit: The phone-line image is clear. Still a stance, not a rep.
contemplative: The phone line image is clear. 'Virtue becomes condition' performs a little. Let the image do it alone.
stress: The phone-line metaphor is clear, but it's bolded assertion with nothing at stake. Who pays if presence is merely a virtue?
gamedesigner: The phone-line metaphor is clear, but there's no signal for when the line has connected.
structural: The phone-line simile restates the last paragraph. Fold it in.
satirist: The phone-line simile is fine, but it's a bold headline for a line the previous paragraph already said. Merge it.
mythmaker: The phone line image is serviceable, but it's a new metaphor that drops the game instead of returning to it.

modeler: The phone line is metaphor standing in for mechanism. What's the handshake signal? How do you know it picked up?
skeptic: 'Nothing you say counts' overclaims. Plenty lands without full presence. The phone-call image does work the argument hasn't.
clinician: The phone-line metaphor is clear. 'Less a virtue' usefully removes the moral pressure. There's no step.
habit: The phone-call image is clear. Still a stance, not a step. How do I know the line picked up?
contemplative: The phone call is plain enough. Calling presence 'less a virtue' makes it smaller than it is. Presence is both. Look again.
stress: 'Nothing counts until the line picks up' is too absolute. Some things land anyway. Soften it to hold up.
gamedesigner: The phone-line metaphor is clear. What tells me the line has picked up? Name that signal.
structural: The phone-call metaphor is clear but thin, and it states the point a third time.
satirist: 'Less a virtue than a connection' is aphorism hunting. The phone line image is fine; lose the grand setup.
mythmaker: Phone call metaphor is serviceable but flat. Give me a dial tone, the call that rang out the night it mattered.

modeler: Lovely image, but where's the stock? A phone call is a channel, not a mechanism. Say what accumulates when the line connects.
skeptic: Phone-call metaphor is easy and plausible, but 'only lands once the other end picks up' is asserted, not shown. Cite what listeners actually retain.
clinician: Clear phone metaphor, but no step. What does 'picking up' look like for someone drained? Add one small action.
habit: Nice phone-call image, but it's a claim, not a step. What do I do on Monday to make the other end pick up?
contemplative: A phone call is plain and true. Connect first, then speak. Lovely. Drop 'virtue' and it is lighter still.
stress: Clear phone-call image, modest claim. But it's an analogy, not a test; say what failed pickup looks like.
gamedesigner: Phone-call metaphor is a clean mental model, but no move or signal for knowing the other end picked up.
structural: Neat phone metaphor, but purely interpersonal. No rules, no lever. Fix: say what environments (work hours, caseloads) make 'picking up' impossible.
satirist: The phone-call image is plain and passes the bar test. But 'presence' is still a Concept doing metaphor work; give one concrete failure of hanging up.
mythmaker: Phone call is a clean image, but nobody is on the line. Give me one person dialing, waiting, finally heard.

modeler: Gate before the signal: voicemail is a clean mechanism for why good advice fails. Practical. Nice.
skeptic: Phone-call metaphor makes the point crisply and fits Epley on misjudged listening. 'Voicemail' is the memorable test; claim is plausible.
clinician: Connection before virtue relieves the pressure of saying the perfect thing. Voicemail metaphor lets you check the line first.
habit: Phone call with voicemail: I get it instantly, and it implies a cue: check if they've picked up. Add the check.
contemplative: Voicemail is exactly right. Presence before the message. The bold sentence is long, but the image rescues it.
stress: Voicemail image makes a testable point: speaking before the other picks up fails. Practical and falsifiable.
gamedesigner: Phone-call image is instantly playable: check the line is open before you speak. Clear and practical.
structural: Phone-call image is a practical, usable point: nothing lands unanswered. Useful and plain. Doesn't claim to fix institutions.
satirist: Phone call and voicemail: right metaphor, plain, and it changes what I do. 'Connection before a virtue' is a small, witty inversion.
mythmaker: Voicemail for the right words said to someone who hasn't picked up. Everyone has left that message. Funny, painful, memorable.

modeler: A channel precondition explains why accurate readings land as attacks. 'Precision reads as prosecution' is a real mechanism.

habit: Two minutes, a card, one person per line, huddle analogy. Textbook small rep with a clear job. Love it.
contemplative: The huddle idea is good. The closing line is a long breath I cannot take in one exhale. Shorten it.
stress: Huddle analogy and card are practical. Closing line ends in grand 'everything we choose to build'; ego creeping in. Trim it.
gamedesigner: Huddle analogy is good, but it leans on Chapter 10 and ends with a dense closing line. Print-card tip helps.
structural: Ritual opener, practical, printable card. A group routine, yet it turns attention inward. Add what the group then does outward.
satirist: The huddle comparison is honest about the ritual's job: shift attention. Admitting two minutes helps. Closing line is grand though; the card detail is good.
mythmaker: The huddle comparison works and the card is practical. The closing chain is abstract incantation with no one saying it.

modeler: Huddle opener is a real reset of attention, and the closing sentence is a nice chain of one-step-from-previous. Concrete.
skeptic: Huddle analogy for attention reset is plausible but unsupported. Closing line runs long and reads as liturgy, hurting comprehension.
