clinician: Card and two-minute huddle shift attention outward and away from the day's worry. Concrete. Closing line is long.
habit: Printed card, two minutes, huddle metaphor, one person per iteration. Reduces friction beautifully. Closing line is long but fine.
contemplative: The huddle image helps, but the paragraph is stuffed: card, voices, closing line, and a long chant. Give the step, then the line separately.
stress: Huddle analogy shows purpose, and the card prevents memory failure. The closing line is grand: 'everything we choose to build.' Trim it.
gamedesigner: Huddle-before-the-game is a good warm-up mechanic with a clear job. Playable, if a bit ritual-heavy.
structural: Concrete group ritual with a card and a huddle analogy. Practical, collective, easy. But it attends to the pattern, not its rule-makers.
satirist: Huddle-before-a-game is a good comparison. But reciting 'Seven Iterations' aloud is liturgy, and the closing chant slides into hushed-voice territory.
mythmaker: The huddle before a game, one voice per iteration, a printed card so nobody has to remember: a ritual with people in it. The closing line pays off.

modeler: Naming a loop in front of witnesses adds an information flow. Practical. 'Does most of the work' wants evidence.
skeptic: Concrete step. 'This alone tends to do most of the work' is a confident claim of effect size with nothing behind it.
clinician: 'No advice yet, just naming, with witnesses.' That's clinically sound. Add permission to pass if today is too raw.
habit: 'Share one loop, no advice' is great anti-Advice-Monster design. This is the rep.
contemplative: Naming with witnesses, no advice. This is deep listening. Beautiful and doable.
stress: Name it aloud, no advice. Simple, testable, and support groups have run it for decades. Good.
gamedesigner: A clean turn-taking mechanic, and saying it with witnesses is the feedback. Very playable.
structural: A real group procedure. But it shares private habits only. Add a loop the group itself is caught in.
satirist: The real practice. 'No advice yet, just naming, with witnesses' is plain and workable.
mythmaker: 'Naming, out loud, with witnesses.' That's the heart of the gathering, practical and human. Keep it.

modeler: Outside eyes on your leverage point: the classic case for an external observer. Good use of Meadows's ladder.
skeptic: The best move here: it outsources the view of your system because you're badly placed to see it. That's the outside view, correctly applied.
clinician: Unsolicited lever-guessing about someone's pain risks feeling judged. Make it opt-in, and drop the ladder jargon.
habit: Clear second round, and the 'free to ignore' release is smart.
contemplative: Clear. 'Level of leverage' asks the group to learn a ladder first; offer a plainer question.
stress: Outside eyes on your lever. Sound. 'You're free to ignore it' keeps ego in check.
gamedesigner: Good mechanic, but 'which level of leverage' assumes the ladder is fresh in memory. Inline a mini-menu.
structural: Outside eyes find levers you can't see. Good. It edges toward the s-frame without saying so.
satirist: Outside eyes is useful advice. 'Which level of leverage' assumes the reader memorized a ladder. Say 'what to change.'
mythmaker: Others see your system better than you do. That's useful. A tiny example of someone's guess landing would sell it.

modeler: Meadows' leverage points used properly (information, rules, goals), with an outside observer. The snack question is perfect.
skeptic: Outsiders often do see our systems better. Well supported, and the snack example is perfect. Keep it.
clinician: The snacking question is perfect. 'Take it or leave it' protects against shame. Add 'ask first' before offering.
habit: 'Do you only snack on the days you skip lunch?' The best question in the batch. Keep it exactly.
contemplative: The snacking friend makes it live. Let others see for us. Good, humble practice.
stress: Outsiders see your system better than you do, and the snack-on-skipped-lunch line proves it. Concrete and humble.
gamedesigner: Best multiplayer mechanic here: others guess your lever. The snack example makes it instantly playable.
structural: Outside eyes on your system is useful, but the lever stays a snack. The same circle could look for shared rules worth changing.
satirist: The snack-on-days-you-skip-lunch friend saves this. Outsiders spotting your lever is real advice. The three-category taxonomy is optional weight.
mythmaker: The friend asking about snacks on days you skip lunch is a real voice. Specific, warm and useful. More like this.

modeler: Best unit here: the Meadows ladder applied to a group, numbers to paradigm, with a real buffer. This is how it's done.
skeptic: Specific, and 'reaching out first is needy' matches real findings that people underestimate how welcome contact is. Strong.
clinician: 'Reaching out first is needy' is a sharp, true catch. Too dense, though. Split it into a short list.
habit: The ladder applied to a group, with a real recurring date. 'Reaching out first is needy' hits home.
contemplative: The 'reaching out first is needy' insight is precious, and it is buried under six rungs. Lead with it.
stress: 'Reaching out first is needy' is a real diagnosis. Too dense, though. Break the ladder into lines.
gamedesigner: Useful ladder applied to a group, but six rungs in one paragraph is a difficulty spike. Make it a list.
structural: The best paragraph here: a group's own rule, goal and paradigm, with a recurring date as the lever. Keep it, and copy its style elsewhere.
satirist: Finally a ladder with real rungs. 'Reaching out first is needy' is painfully specific. Bryson-grade concreteness.
mythmaker: 'Reaching out first is needy' is the real wound and it lands. The ladder jargon before it buries it. Lead with the wound.

modeler: A pleasant prayer that restates the repetition thesis. Harmless ritual glue.
skeptic: A closing prayer. It's pleasant, and I have no claim to evaluate.
clinician: Warm, small-step closing. Gentle and safe.
habit: A warm closing line that's easy to say together. It works as ritual.
contemplative: A small, warm prayer to speak together. It lives in the body.
stress: A prayer that asks nothing hard. Fine as ritual. It earns no more than that.
gamedesigner: A closing ritual gives the session an ending beat. Works.
structural: A prayer. Pleasant, and it changes nothing.
satirist: A closing prayer for a self-help club. If you keep it, label it as foma, cheerfully.
mythmaker: A plain, warm prayer, and speakable. It does its job in place.

modeler: A warm closer, and a decent statement of a reinforcing rule. Fine as a prayer.
skeptic: A ritual line; it is what it is. Nothing to believe or disbelieve, and nothing earned beyond clarity.
clinician: Gentle, small-step framing that's safe on a bad day. Its warmth is its value.
habit: A concrete closing ritual and a repeatable step. 'Worth repeating' is my whole creed.
contemplative: A prayer I could say with friends. 'Worth repeating' is gentle. Keep it.
stress: A pleasant prayer. Nothing here can fail or cost anyone. It survives only as a ritual marker.
gamedesigner: A warm, short closer people can say aloud. It works in place.
structural: A prayer about 'what we're building', yet nothing named gets built.
satirist: 'Group Closing Prayer', capitalised, for a line about habits. The words are harmless; the title is pomposity. Call it a closing line.
mythmaker: A pleasant prayer, but the sentiment comes before the group has bled together. Give it a skeptic at the table to earn it.

modeler: Pleasant prayer. A pure reinforcing wish; nothing in it checks whether the step was worth repeating.
skeptic: A prayer for groups. It does its ritual job, but the content is a truism with an em dash.
clinician: Short, warm, forward-looking. 'Small step worth repeating' is exactly the right size.
habit: Thirty seconds, aloud, together. It's specific and small, and 'worth repeating' is literally habit language.
contemplative: Thirty seconds, said aloud together. Simple and warm. Drop the second dash and the prayer breathes.
stress: A greeting-card prayer. It is defended only by the next paragraph, which admits it's corny.
gamedesigner: A ritual closer, short and sayable. It does its job but adds no insight.
structural: A group prayer about small steps. Pleasant, and it soaks up attention without pointing outward to anything.
satirist: A group closing prayer. Bokonon would charge admission. U0552 admits corniness; fold that admission in here.
mythmaker: The prayer is earnest and a bit greeting-card. It needs U0552's admission of corniness to survive.

modeler: A warm closing ritual. Corny on purpose is honest, but it asks no systems question and solves little.
skeptic: 'A little corny on purpose' disarms my objection. Ritual offered as ritual, not proof. Works, with honesty about itself.
clinician: Thirty seconds, 'corny on purpose' lowers the stakes. Wish-based, not self-attacking. Good.
habit: Thirty seconds, aloud, exact words, one wish each. Tiny closing ritual anyone can run tonight. Corny on purpose, good.
contemplative: 'A little corny on purpose' is honest and kind. Thirty seconds, one wish for each and for all. Beautiful.
stress: 'Corny on purpose' disarms the guru voice. Welcome. But a prayer asserts nothing and nothing could fail.
gamedesigner: Thirty seconds, corny on purpose: low-barrier ritual with honest framing. Playable immediately.
structural: Self-aware, short, group-owned. 'What we're building between us' is vague; build what? Name a shared project and I'm interested.
satirist: 'A little corny on purpose' is the Bokonon wink this book needs more of. Knows the costume is a costume. Thirty seconds, doable.
mythmaker: Corny on purpose is exactly the self-aware warmth I like. Ritual with a wink, and doable tonight.

modeler: Explains the prayer's double duty. It's self-commentary the reader didn't need.
skeptic: It explains its own prayer. 'Just as real' is asserted. Trim it.
clinician: Explaining the prayer deflates it. Cut, or trim to one sentence.
habit: Explaining the prayer weakens it. Cut it.
contemplative: It explains the prayer. A prayer should not need footnotes. Cut.
stress: Explaining your own prayer's double duty is the author admiring his craft. Cut.
gamedesigner: Explains the joke after telling it. Cut.
structural: Explains the prayer's double duty. It is self-commentary, not substance.
satirist: Explaining your own prayer's double meaning is a joke explained. 'Just as real' is asserted, not shown. Cut it.
mythmaker: It explains the prayer's double duty, which is explaining a joke. Trust the line and cut most of this.

modeler: Repetition building the group: plausible, but asserted. What accumulates each month? Say it.
skeptic: Repetition builds a group: asserted, not shown. Say 'the hope is' and I'd accept it.
clinician: It explains the prayer in jargon (its own Third Thing). Cut it, or say plainly why repeating it helps.
habit: 'Said every month' is the right instinct. Otherwise it's a self-referential flourish.
contemplative: The first sentence is enough. 'Its own Third Thing' explains what should simply be felt.
stress: 'The way everything in this book gets built' is the system explaining itself. Cut the grandiose tail.
gamedesigner: 'Its own Third Thing' is jargon payoff. Say it plainly: repetition is what builds the group.
structural: The group as its own Third Thing is self-referential. A group that only builds itself is a hobby, not a lever.
satirist: 'Said once, it's a nice line' almost admits it's foma, then flinches into Third Thing jargon. Finish the joke.
mythmaker: 'Said once, a nice line; said monthly, it builds itself' is a good rhyme idea. It's still told rather than shown in a group.

modeler: Repetition makes a structure you notice when it's missing. The test of a real stock. Good.
skeptic: Admits 'slightly corny', which buys credibility. 'Noticed when missing' is a usable test.
clinician: Admitting it's corny disarms the reader. 'Noticed when missing' is true. Mild.
habit: Admitting it's corny earns trust, and the repetition point is correct. Nice.
contemplative: Admitting it's corny is disarming and true. 'Something people notice when it's missing' is lovely. 'Third Thing' again is the weak part.
stress: Admitting it's corny buys credibility. Repetition building the group is a claim with a track record.
gamedesigner: Admitting the line is corny buys trust. 'Noticed when missing' is a sharp test for the Third Thing.
structural: Self-aware about corniness, and repetition building an institution is a fair point. Missed when absent is a good test.
satirist: 'Slightly corny' is the author knowing the costume is a costume. Exactly what I asked for. Keep.
mythmaker: Admitting it's corny is the Beard in the room. 'Noticed when it's missing' makes ritual earn its sentiment. Lovely.

modeler: Reciprocity epigraph. Fitting, but generic.
skeptic: A reciprocity epigraph. It's fine.
clinician: Fine epigraph, slightly transactional.
habit: Epigraph. Fine, inert.
contemplative: Simple reciprocity, warmly said. It earns its place.
stress: Reciprocity epigraph. Serviceable.
gamedesigner: Generic epigraph. Doesn't set up the Skein.
structural: A reciprocity proverb. Fine, but it isn't doing any work.
satirist: A greeting-card epigraph. Harmless, and it does no work.
mythmaker: A generic maxim. It doesn't foreshadow the Skein's real image, the thread.

modeler: A proverb about aggregation. Charming, with no structure behind it.
skeptic: Proverb epigraph. Charming, decorative, and nothing more.
clinician: Proverb works as an epigraph. Nothing for the reader to use.
habit: Vivid proverb. An epigraph, no action.
contemplative: A proverb, light and clear. It does its job as a doorway.
stress: A borrowed proverb used as ornament. It earns nothing on its own.
gamedesigner: Charming proverb, but decorative only.
structural: It promises tying up a lion, and the chapter's lion turns out to be fading attendance. Name a real lion or cut it.
satirist: A borrowed Ethiopian proverb with no attribution. Bryson would want the source. It's charming, though.
mythmaker: A vivid proverb, and the lion gives it stakes. It doesn't connect to the skein-thread images, though; the motifs compete.

modeler: A charming proverb that only gestures at aggregation. Decorative.
skeptic: A charming proverb that repeats the twelve-threads epigraph. One is enough.
clinician: A charming proverb, but decorative. It earns little.
habit: Charming proverb, but decoration. It earns nothing the section doesn't already say.
contemplative: It is a fine proverb and it repeats the twelve-thread image. Two epigraphs on one idea is one too many.
stress: A decent proverb, but decorative. It duplicates the twelve-threads epigraph.
gamedesigner: Charming but decorative. It repeats the twelve-threads epigraph, so pick one.
structural: The best epigraph in the set: collective action defeats the big thing. Now let the chapter say what the lion is.
satirist: Nice proverb, attributed. Redundant with the twelve-threads epigraph two pages back. Pick one.
mythmaker: A vivid lion, a borrowed image. It's U0542 again; one of them should go.

modeler: Many weak strands sum to a strong rope: aggregation, real structure. A fine epigraph, but it's just an image.
skeptic: Proverb: charming, unfalsifiable, and quite possibly misattributed. Decoration only; I have no reason to believe it.
clinician: Pleasant proverb about collective strength. Harmless, no step.
habit: Lovely proverb, zero instruction. Epigraph only; it doesn't tell me what to do tomorrow.
contemplative: Small things joined are strong. Gentle and simple. It does its one job and leaves.
stress: Old proverb carries the history test for free. Pleasant, but decorative; no risk taken.
gamedesigner: Nice image of many threads, but it's decoration with no move.
structural: Solidarity proverb, nearly a labor slogan. Nice, but a proverb is not a lever. Follow it with an organizing example.
satirist: Nice proverb, but a quotation wearing a hat. No number, no mechanism. Decoration unless the page proves the lion.
mythmaker: Good proverb, strong image of small things binding a lion. But it's borrowed and unreturned so far.

modeler: Redundant webs bind what a single web can't. Real network idea, compactly put, but unmeasured.
skeptic: Spider-web proverb is fluent and memorable; strength in unity is not evidence of anything specific here.
clinician: Strong image of collective strength. Reassuring for isolated readers but no step.
habit: Lion and webs: memorable, but a caption. No action, no cue.
contemplative: A single picture of the lion tied down. It is memorable, but I am left admiring it.
stress: Strength from joining is Taleb-friendly, but the lion image is unsupported. Show a case where webs failed.
gamedesigner: Pretty image, receive-only. Needs the move it illustrates.
structural: My kind of line: lone web fails, joined webs hold. Collective power in one image. Name the lion and the webs.
satirist: 'One web, and the lion walks through.' Strong proverb image, vivid and short. It teaches nothing I can do, but it sticks.
mythmaker: Lion through one web, tied down by many: striking, but who's the lion? Whose web? Great image waiting on a face.

modeler: The right question: how do you keep the stock from draining after one session? Good setup.
skeptic: It asks the question people really hit after a good first session. That's honest framing.
clinician: Names the real fade-out problem. Good bridge.
habit: Exactly the question I'd ask. Good bridge.
contemplative: A transition that asks the question. Fine, and it could be one line shorter.
stress: The fade-after-one-session question is the real one. Good framing.
gamedesigner: Great hook: the exact question I'd have after one session. Second beat earned.
structural: The right question about durability. Durability comes from structure: dues, roles, a standing date. Answer with that.
satirist: A real question, honestly posed. A one-line bridge, and fine.
mythmaker: 'One good session letting it fade.' Everyone has had that book club. Name it and you've got me.

modeler: The right sustainability question, a decay problem. Setup only.
skeptic: 'Group Practice works' is stated as fact with no evidence. The question is real; hedge the premise.
clinician: Clear question, but it doesn't answer it yet.
habit: The book-club fade problem is real and familiar. The answer has to be a system, not a sentiment.
contemplative: An honest, ordinary question. Every group meets it. Plain enough.
stress: The right question, asked plainly. 'Group Practice works' is asserted with no evidence; say 'can work'.
gamedesigner: Names the real retention problem every club hits. Good hook.
structural: Retention for a book club. A small question framed as the big one.
satirist: Every book club fading after one good session is a real, plain problem. A decent setup.
mythmaker: The book club fading after one good session is a real problem. It's stated, not felt.

modeler: Names the real decay curve: the third meeting, two dropouts. A genuine retention problem, well framed.
skeptic: Names the real failure point precisely, the third-meeting dropouts. That's the problem practitioners actually have.
clinician: The third-meeting text is painfully real. It names the fade without blaming anyone. Good setup.
habit: The third-meeting dropout text is painfully real. Great problem framing.
contemplative: The two texts at the third meeting are a real problem, plainly seen. Good.
stress: The third-meeting dropout is the real storm for any group. It's named precisely. Keep.
gamedesigner: The third-meeting dropout is the real retention problem. A great hook.
structural: The third-meeting dropout is a real organizing problem, named precisely. It's an organizer's question, so good.
satirist: Third meeting, two texts saying can't make it: the book-club death spiral, precisely observed. Funny because true.
mythmaker: Two texts saying they can't make it, third meeting: painfully true. Real stakes for any group.

modeler: A vague 'old idea from fiction', unnamed. Cite it or cut it. The distinction is fine, but the framing wanders.
skeptic: Fiction offered as precedent, and the sentences meander. Make the distinction directly and drop the vague 'old idea'.
clinician: Long throat-clearing about fiction. Cut to the distinction itself.
habit: A long throat-clear before the definitions. Cut to two sentences.
contemplative: One long sentence of throat-clearing about fiction and doctrine. Cut to the distinction itself.
stress: 'An old idea, more often in fiction' is a hand-wave. Name the source or drop the borrowing.
gamedesigner: A long throat-clear before the terms arrive. Cut to one sentence.
structural: A vague appeal to 'an old idea in fiction'. Name the source or cut it and go straight to the distinction.
satirist: 'An old idea found in fiction' is Vonnegut's karass versus granfalloon, uncredited. Name the source. Coyness reads as theft.
mythmaker: 'An old idea from fiction' is coy. Name the karass or the ka-tet outright. Hiding the source drains the borrowed magic.

modeler: Emergent pattern vs shared label is a real distinction. Vonnegut's frame is well used.
skeptic: The Vonnegut distinction is genuinely useful. 'Decides whether a community outlasts' is too strong; 'helps decide' is enough.
clinician: Literary distinction with invented terms. Interesting, and remote from anyone struggling.
habit: The Vonnegut distinction is interesting, but it's literary framing. What do I check to know which one I'm in?
contemplative: Karass, granfalloon, then new names again. Three vocabularies for one plain idea. Choose one.
stress: The Vonnegut distinction is sharp. 'Decides whether a community outlasts' overclaims; show cases of each surviving and failing.
gamedesigner: Vonnegut's distinction is a clever frame, but it gives the reader nothing to test or do.
structural: Karass versus granfalloon is a genuinely useful distinction. It's borrowed, and it's clear.
satirist: Citing karass and granfalloon is honest, and then it renames them anyway. Vonnegut's granfalloon joke is aimed squarely at that move.
mythmaker: The Vonnegut karass is a strong borrowed idea, but it's taxonomy. Show me a granfalloon falling apart.

modeler: Emergent versus labelled groups, credited properly. A good distinction. Durability claims are asserted, not modelled.
skeptic: Good borrowing, properly credited. 'Tends to outlast' rests on a novel. Say so, or find evidence.
clinician: A literary detour. A struggling reader needs the test, not Vonnegut taxonomy plus renaming. Cut to the test.
habit: Literary detour. The Hoosiers example needs footnotes. Give me the test first and Vonnegut after, if at all.
contemplative: Vonnegut, Hoosiers, a joke about renaming: the author's cleverness stands in front of the idea. Give the test without the literature.
stress: A useful borrowed distinction, credited and self-deprecating. Vonnegut's karass is cosmically designed, though, so 'nobody designed' needs care.
gamedesigner: Fun lore drop, but it's a cutscene. Hand me the test right here, not 'below.'
structural: Karass versus granfalloon is a sharp lens, and the self-aware renaming is fine. It's the setup for the test, not yet the test.
satirist: Credits Vonnegut, admits he'd find the renaming funny. Honest. But why rename karass at all? You know why. Busy, busy.
mythmaker: Karass and granfalloon are fun, and the Hoosier joke lands. Then 'Fractalism renames them' winks at itself. Story-free.

modeler: Good distinction: structure that persists versus a shared label. Vonnegut anchors it. Test is deferred, so the claim runs ahead of its evidence.
skeptic: Vonnegut's karass/granfalloon is a fair sourced distinction, 'tends to' hedges, and a promised test. Outlasting claim is untested but flagged.
clinician: Vonnegut link is engaging and clear, but it's classification talk. The test is promised, not here.
habit: Vonnegut vocabulary is fun, but it's taxonomy. The promised test is deferred. Lead with the test.
contemplative: Vonnegut's terms, then renamed again. Names stacking on names. Say what holds a group together, plainly, and skip the lineage.
stress: Borrows a tested distinction and a test you can run. Honest 'tends to'. Needs a failure case for the outlasting claim.
gamedesigner: Vonnegut anchor is a good shortcut, but it's mostly naming. Promised test is deferred. I'm holding for it.
structural: Karass versus granfalloon is a sharp distinction between real and nominal groups. Useful test for fan clubs. Needs rules and stakes.
satirist: Cites Vonnegut honestly and the Hoosiers joke. Tends to is the right hedge. Test promised. Almost the mirror I asked for.
mythmaker: Vonnegut's karass is a story-born idea, and Hoosiers is a joke. Needs a real group's face, not a taxonomy.

modeler: Skein as emergent coordination from local rules is the right shape. The thread image is apt rather than load-bearing. Fine.
skeptic: A clear definition, and 'found in hindsight' respects how we actually notice groups.
clinician: Clear image. 'You find yourself already in one' is reassuring.
habit: A clear definition with a nice thread image. No action, but it's needed.
contemplative: 'You find yourself already in one.' Gentle and true. The thread image works.
stress: Fine definition. 'Found only in hindsight' risks letting any group qualify after the fact.
gamedesigner: Clean definition with a strong metaphor. 'You find yourself already in one' resonates.
structural: A clear image of emergent community. 'Nobody assigns you' romanticizes the absence of organizers, though.
satirist: The thread-and-skein image actually works. Finding yourself already in one is a nice touch. It is still a karass.
mythmaker: Threads becoming a skein is a strong image, and 'already mid-habit' rhymes nicely. Now put two actual friends in it.

modeler: Bottom-up emergence from local rules. That's the honest plant-spiral move. The Saturday-run example grounds it.
skeptic: The Saturday-route example grounds it nicely. It's a definition, not a claim, so there's little to doubt and that's fine.
clinician: The Saturday-route friends make it warm and real. 'You find yourself already in one' is comforting, not demanding.
habit: The Saturday-route friends make it real. Still a definition. Add: look at who you've seen weekly for a year.
contemplative: Three friends, same Saturday route, six years. This I understand. Lead with them; the definition can follow.
stress: The Saturday-route example grounds the definition, and 'you find yourself already in one' resists founder ego. Good.
gamedesigner: The Saturday-run example makes 'Skein' land. 'You find yourself already in one' resonates.
structural: Emergent community without central planning, and the Saturday-run image lands. But a Skein that's never designed is never organized.
satirist: The three friends running the Saturday route for six years is lovely and real. The 'Global Form' capitals are a costume over a karass.
mythmaker: Three friends on the same Saturday route for six years: lovely, earned, human. 'Mid-habit before you notice' rhymes with the book.

modeler: Banner versus Skein: legibility versus substance. A useful distinction, and the point about under-investing in the invisible thing is sharp.
skeptic: 'Legible from outside' versus real is a useful distinction. Readers will recognise Banners they've been in.
clinician: Helps a lonely reader see why a label-group still felt empty, without blaming them.
habit: 'Legible from outside' is a crisp distinction. I recognise Banners I'm in.
contemplative: A label that feels like belonging. Honest. 'Easy to mistake for nothing' is tender.
stress: Banner versus Skein is a distinction worth having. Legible belonging versus real belonging. It holds.
gamedesigner: A good contrast term, and the 'legible from outside' trap rings true.
structural: Legible versus real belonging is a useful cut. It warns against branding substituting for substance.
satirist: A granfalloon in a new hat, but the legibility point is genuinely good. Credit Vonnegut and it improves.
mythmaker: 'Put it on a card.' The legible fake against the invisible real. I feel the temptation, so this one works.

modeler: Remove the label and see what persists. A real perturbation test. Keep.
skeptic: A falsifiable counterfactual test. Good, though people forecast their own counterfactuals poorly.
clinician: A simple, usable test. Works.
habit: A one-question test I can apply to any group tonight. Keep it.
contemplative: One question I can ask about my friendships today. Clear and kind.
stress: Remove the label: does it survive? A real stress test. Applied to Fractalism itself. Excellent.
gamedesigner: A one-question test with a clear answer. Feedback signal delivered.
structural: A clean, uncomfortable test that people can apply. It works.
satirist: A clean test that survives the bar. Keep it.
mythmaker: 'Would it survive if the label disappeared?' A clean, uncomfortable, memorable test. It earns its bold.

modeler: Separating belief from exit cost is a sharp self-test. The cost is the people. Good.
skeptic: The sharpest question in the chapter: it separates belief from what leaving would cost. Add that we're bad at answering it alone.
clinician: A powerful question, and it locates the cost in people, not foolishness. Shame-free. Keep.
habit: 'Would I believe this if leaving cost nothing?' cuts deep. It's a carry-all-day question.
contemplative: 'It is about the people.' A hard question, said without cruelty. Keep it.
stress: 'Would I believe this if leaving cost nothing?' Brutal and honest. Skin in the game, aimed at the reader.
gamedesigner: Turning the test on me is a strong personal twist. Stings in a good way.
structural: Separating belief from exit cost is a structural insight. Who sets the exit cost? Often the group's leadership. Say that.
satirist: 'Would I still believe this if leaving cost me nothing?' The most honest question in the chunk. It's aimed at the book too. Good.
mythmaker: 'Would I still believe this if leaving cost me nothing?' That's the human heart in conflict with itself. Superb.

modeler: Belonging as a monitored need, like hunger. That's a real setpoint with a balancing loop. Strong. Cite the isolation-craving study.
skeptic: One imaging finding, stretched into 'treated much as food'. That's a mechanism claimed from a correlation. Hedge it and cite it.
clinician: Belonging as hunger destigmatizes staying in bad groups. Compassionate and evidence-grounded.
habit: Interesting science, but it's backing, not a behaviour. Fine where it is.
contemplative: Belonging as hunger. It moves the reader. The heading argues; soften it.
stress: Grounded in actual neuroscience, isolation as hunger. Cite the study and it's solid.
gamedesigner: The belonging-as-hunger research grounds the claim well. A clear why.
structural: A structural, not moral, account of membership. It is exactly the frame I want. Cite the isolation study by name.
satirist: Isolation craving in the midbrain is a real finding. Name the study (MIT, 2020) and it passes Bryson.
mythmaker: Belonging as hunger gives the idea real stakes. It would be even stronger with one person who stayed in a group for its meals.

modeler: Replace the function, don't refute the content. A correct systems move: substitute the flow and the stock holds. Excellent.
skeptic: 'Replace the function, not refute the content' fits what's known about belonging and belief. Useful and well calibrated.
clinician: 'Replace the function, not refute the content' is wise, practical, and kind.
habit: 'Replace the function, not refute the content' is actionable. The standing Tuesday is a real system.
contemplative: 'Replace the function, not refute the content.' This is aikido. Blending, not clashing.
stress: Replace the function, don't refute the content. Deradicalization work bears this out. Strong.
gamedesigner: 'Replace the function, not refute the content' is actionable and memorable. A standout.
structural: 'Replace the function, not refute the content' is a real lever: build the club. Deradicalization programs run on this.
satirist: 'Replace the function, not refute the content.' Useful, true, and actionable. 'A standing Tuesday' is perfect.
mythmaker: 'Replace the function, not refute the content,' with the standing Tuesday as the image. It's wise and humane toward the other side.

modeler: Channel matters less than the repetition rate. Practical and humane. Short and right.
skeptic: Kind and practical. 'Channel matters less' is plausible but unsupported. Add 'for building repetition'.
clinician: Exactly what a socially anxious reader needs: online contact counts and isn't a failure.
habit: Kind and practical permission. Short and useful.
contemplative: Kind to the lonely and the anxious. Short and true.
stress: A humane, practical caveat. Small, true, useful.
gamedesigner: Kind and practical accessibility note. Short and earns its place.
structural: A humane, practical caveat. Short, and it earns its place.
satirist: Kind and practical. Keep it.
mythmaker: A kind, practical concession. It's short and earned.

modeler: Recruiting builds Banners. A plausible claim. The four lines that follow carry the weight.
skeptic: Sensible advice. 'Banners reliably, Skeins almost never' is too confident for something nobody has measured.
clinician: Sound redirect from recruiting to noticing what already exists.
habit: 'Notice, don't recruit' is a clear behavioural switch. Good.
contemplative: 'Notice, don't recruit' is wise. The long setup delays it; start with those three words.
stress: 'Notice, don't recruit' is good anti-ego advice. The setup to the four lines runs long.
gamedesigner: A good anti-recruiting rule, and it sets up four lenses. Fine.
structural: 'Don't recruit' quietly discourages organizing, which is the very lever groups need. Distinguish converting people from organizing them.
satirist: 'Notice, don't recruit' is good advice. It's buried under setup for the four lines. Trim the lead-in.
mythmaker: 'Notice, don't recruit' is good counsel. The proselytizer it warns against deserves one sympathetic sketch.

modeler: Practical, and it rightly favors existing repeated contact. It reads as a lead-in until the four lines follow.
skeptic: Sensible advice. 'Converting strangers builds Banners' is unsupported; compared to what? Hedge it or give a case.
clinician: Practical redirect: start with the people you already see. Low pressure, doable.
habit: 'Start with people you're already in contact with' is actionable. It lives or dies on the four lines that follow.
contemplative: 'Start with the people you already see' is gentle and right. 'Banners' needs no mention here.
stress: Anti-recruitment is a cult-proofing instinct, and history backs it. Practical and humble. Keep it.
gamedesigner: A clear directive: look at the people you already see. The four lines promise a checklist. 'Banners' is unexplained.
structural: 'Notice, don't recruit' discourages organizing outright. Who profits when groups never deliberately grow? Revise.
satirist: 'Converting strangers builds Banners' is the book catching itself recruiting. Good instinct, but 'Banners' needs a plain-word gloss.
mythmaker: 'Notice, don't recruit' is solid advice, but it has no face. Give me the neighbor you already see every week.

modeler: Grow from existing repeated contact, not recruitment. That's building from a local rule. Practical.
skeptic: Sound advice: start with people you already see. Skein/Banner jargon obscures it for a new reader.
clinician: 'Start with people you already see' is great, gentle advice. The Banner/Skein jargon clouds it.
habit: 'Start with the neighbor you talk to every week.' Concrete and redirecting. Banner/Skein jargon is a tax.
contemplative: 'Start with the neighbour you already talk to' is wise. Banner, Skein, converts and four lines make it heavy. Say less.
stress: 'Notice, don't recruit' is the anti-cult safeguard this system needs. Strong.
gamedesigner: Good practical turn toward people you already see. Banner and Skein together spike the jargon. Lead with the neighbor.
structural: Building on existing weekly contact over recruiting strangers is sound organizing advice. The Banner/Skein jargon blurs it.
satirist: 'Notice, don't recruit' is the anti-cult rule this book needs. Neighbor and lunch colleague ground it well.
mythmaker: The lunch colleague and the weekly neighbour, not converts. Wise and human. The Banner/Skein terms weigh on it.

modeler: Good advice: start from existing contact, not recruitment. Start where the loops already run. Hedged with 'tend to' appropriately.
skeptic: 'Tend to' used twice; practical advice to start from existing contacts. Good calibration. Still no evidence that these four things predict a Skein.
clinician: 'Notice, don't recruit' is gentle and starts with people already in your life. Specific, tiny first step.
habit: Real cue: people you already see weekly. Notice four things. Clear, doable, not recruiting. Name what to jot down.
contemplative: Notice, don't recruit: the neighbor, the lunch colleague. Practicable today. 'Banner' and 'Skein' are extra words I would not need.
stress: Anti-recruitment is humble: start with who you already see. 'Tends to' hedges well. Specific, falsifiable.
gamedesigner: Notice, don't recruit gives a clear starting move with people I already see. Four things to watch is a real checklist.
structural: Notice, don't recruit: start from existing ties. That's how organizing starts. Good. Missing: what the Skein does together beyond being formed.
satirist: Notice, don't recruit: sane advice, grounded in the neighbor and the lunch colleague. Banner and Skein are jargon but earn it so far.
mythmaker: The neighbor you talk to every week beats recruiting strangers. Real people, real instinct to resist.

modeler: Proximity sets contact frequency, the inflow rate. Twice a year is too slow a flow. Clear.
skeptic: Proximity has real support in research on contact and liking. A concrete, honest criterion.
clinician: Concrete and gentle. Admiration isn't failure, it's just not proximity.
habit: A concrete criterion. The twice-a-year admired person makes it real.
contemplative: The admired friend seen twice a year. I feel that one. Plain and honest.
stress: The admired-but-rarely-seen friend is a sharp, honest example. Works.
gamedesigner: A checkable question with a vivid example (seen twice a year). Plays.
structural: Concrete and checkable. Proximity is shaped by zoning, commutes and work hours. One clause would show the field.
satirist: The 'seen twice a year' example makes it real. Fine.
mythmaker: 'Admire but see twice a year' is a real person I know. Good, specific, and it costs something to admit.

modeler: Low translation cost between rules. Reasonable, though less mechanical than the others.
skeptic: Reasonable criterion. The translation image helps. Nothing here moves me.
clinician: Clear criterion. Less personal than the others.
habit: Weakest of the four. 'Without translation' needs an example.
contemplative: Clear enough. 'Without translation' is the useful phrase; the rest hedges.
stress: Reasonable. 'Doesn't require translation' is the useful phrase.
gamedesigner: Checkable, but abstract. Add a quick example of 'requires translation'.
structural: Similarity as the cost of translation is fine, but it is thin. It risks endorsing homophily without noticing.
satirist: 'A Local Rule offered doesn't require translation' is jargon for 'you get each other.' Say that.
mythmaker: It's clear but bloodless. 'Doesn't require translation' wants a scene of two people mistranslating each other.

modeler: Usable criterion with a real test (does the Local Rule translate?). No stock, but it's a filter, not a mechanism claim. Fine.
skeptic: Usable test, and the phone-rule example helps. 'Enough common ground' is undefined. Compared to what? Name a sign that it's too little.
clinician: The phone-in-kitchen example makes 'common ground' testable. Add a small check the reader can run tonight, not just a definition.
habit: The phone-in-the-kitchen example makes this something you can test tonight. Good. Turn it into one question: would they adopt my rule without asking why?
contemplative: The phone-in-the-kitchen rule makes it real. The 'not sameness' clause is fear speaking. Cut it, and trust the example.
stress: Modest, usable criterion. The kitchen-phone example tests it on the spot. No grand claim to break, so it holds.
gamedesigner: Plays well: the kitchen-phone Local Rule gives me a test signal, translation-free or not. Clear pass/fail.
structural: Clear and relatable, but it only asks whether you click with someone. It names no shared institution or project. Still a private test.
satirist: The phone-in-the-kitchen rule does the work. Skein and Local Rule are capitalized costumes on 'get along'. Keep the example, lose the badges.
mythmaker: The kitchen-phone rule helps, but it's a checklist item with nobody holding it. Show two friends who just get each other.

modeler: The Local Rule probe is a nice cheap test. Keep it.
skeptic: A behavioral test over self-report: do they try the rule? That's the right instinct.
clinician: The phone-in-the-kitchen test is concrete and low-stakes. Good.
habit: The phone-in-kitchen test is a perfect two-minute experiment. More of this.
contemplative: The phone in the kitchen after nine is a lived test, small and kind. Good.
stress: The phone-in-the-kitchen test is cheap, concrete, and can fail. Good.
gamedesigner: The phone-in-kitchen test is excellent, with a clear pass/fail signal. Model the other three on it.
structural: The phone-in-the-kitchen test is concrete and quick. Fine.
satirist: Phone-in-kitchen test is concrete and runnable. Good Bryson move.
mythmaker: The phone-in-the-kitchen test is concrete and charming. Similarity as a term is lifeless; the test saves it.

modeler: A small experiment you can run: offer a Local Rule, watch uptake. Testing and tweaking, per Sellers. Measures coupling cheaply.
skeptic: Offers a checkable probe rather than telling people how they feel. Nod-and-try test is crude but falsifiable. Nicely modest.
clinician: Quick test with a real example Local Rule. Small, low-risk, and it avoids making thin ground the reader's fault.
habit: Quick test: mention a Local Rule, watch for a nod. Specific example, observable result. Genuine rep for next time together.
contemplative: A real test: say your Local Rule, see if they nod. Small and doable. Trim 'identity, values, or context'.
stress: Concrete probe: mention a Local Rule, watch if they try it. Can fail visibly. Exactly the stress test I want.
gamedesigner: Best kind: a quick test with an observable result. They nod and try it, or need a long explanation. Clear feedback.
structural: Local Rule trial is a cheap, concrete test. But similarity alone breeds homogeneous bubbles; ask whose voices are missing.
satirist: Gives a bar-ready test: say a house rule, see if they nod. Not sameness but common ground. Concrete and usable.
mythmaker: Phone stays in the kitchen is a usable test, but it's a checklist item. Show the friend who nods, or doesn't.

modeler: Flows in both directions, or the stock drains and the thing breaks under its own weight. That's a real balancing-loop failure. Good.
skeptic: Readers will check their own lopsided ties. 'Will eventually break' is a prediction stated as a certainty.
clinician: Names extraction plainly. Useful for chronic over-givers.
habit: A one-way giving check anyone can run on a relationship today.
contemplative: One-directional giving named gently. 'Wearing a Skein's clothing' adds jargon; it can go.
stress: Calling it 'quiet extraction' names a real failure. Good.
gamedesigner: Clear test, and I can think of a one-way friendship immediately.
structural: It names extraction. Good. That is the one place this list admits power runs one way.
satirist: 'Quiet extraction' is the plain truth peeking out. Good.
mythmaker: 'Quiet extraction that will eventually break' has stakes. I can name the friend who only ever takes.

modeler: Risky disclosure deepens the connection. Fine, but name the loop: disclosure, then trust, then more disclosure, which is reinforcing.
skeptic: Fits what's known about self-disclosure and closeness. Clear and usable.
clinician: Disclosure as a test is clinically right. Add a note about pacing it safely.
habit: 'Only exchanges logistics' is diagnosable immediately. Good.
contemplative: Logistics never becomes intimacy. True, and said in one breath.
stress: Higher-risk disclosure as the depth test. Matches the research on intimacy. Holds.
gamedesigner: 'Only exchanges logistics' is a crisp failure state I can check.
structural: The logistics-only group rings true. Otherwise generic friendship advice.
satirist: 'A group that only exchanges logistics never deepens.' True, plain, and stings a little.
mythmaker: 'Only ever exchanges logistics' is the group chat I'm in. Honest and recognizable.

modeler: Use the four lines to observe, not to impose. Useful, but long. Halve it.
skeptic: 'Very likely already inside' is overconfident for an informal checklist. Otherwise good diagnostic use.
clinician: Turns the criteria into diagnosis rather than verdict, with concrete fixes. Good.
habit: Useful 'what's missing' guidance buried in a long paragraph. Halve it.
contemplative: It repeats the four, warns against misuse, and cross-references. Three sentences would hold it.
stress: Useful diagnostic, but it restates the four at length. Halve it.
gamedesigner: Useful scoring readout, but long. Turn it into 'all four = X, one missing = Y'.
structural: Useful as diagnostics, but bloated. Halve it: the gap tells you what the connection needs.
satirist: A paragraph explaining how not to misuse four bullets. Halve it. The last sentence is the useful part.
mythmaker: Useful, but it's exposition about the four questions repeating the four questions. Trim it by half.

modeler: Good diagnostic: missing criterion maps to a specific inflow (contact, disclosure, reciprocity). Name it the gap-filling flow and it's a diagram.
skeptic: Gap diagnosis is practical. 'You're probably already in a Skein' has no basis. How would you know? Drop 'probably' or justify it.
clinician: This works. Noticing instead of screening, and the gap gets named as a need, not a verdict, with three steps that are actually doable.
habit: Each missing condition maps to something you can do: more contact, more honest disclosure, check the giving. Name one first move for this week.
contemplative: Kind intent: notice, don't screen. But the Chapter 3 back-reference and the long four-part overlap tire the breath. Say the gap remedies alone.
stress: Gives each gap a diagnosis: more contact, disclosure, check the one-way giving. Specific enough to act on, specific enough to be wrong.
gamedesigner: Real feedback loop: all four true means a Skein, gaps name the next move. Score screen done right.
structural: Noticing rather than screening is honest. The fixes (more contact, disclosure) stay private. Name one thing to do together that builds the Skein.
satirist: Useful: a missing piece tells you what to do, whether that's more contact, more disclosure or checking for one-way giving. Plain and actionable. Chapter 3's 'overlap' callback is clutter.
mythmaker: Useful diagnostics, but nobody's in it. Who's the friend whose giving went one-way? Name her and I'll feel the gap.

modeler: Takes the five-people meme seriously before taking it apart. A good setup.
skeptic: Recurrence across cultures isn't evidence of truth. It shows the idea is easy to believe. Fluency, not proof.
clinician: Readable setup, but long for what it delivers.
habit: A familiar quote, a good hook. Move faster to the fix.
contemplative: A fair setup, but it sets up a fight with a quote. Begin with the old kernel and stop there.
stress: Treating cross-cultural recurrence as evidence is reasonable, but it's asserted. Give two cultures.
gamedesigner: A familiar meme makes a good hook. Fine setup.
structural: Taking the cross-cultural kernel seriously is fair. A setup that runs long.
satirist: A fair setup. Credit Jim Rohn by name, Bryson-style, before dismantling him.
mythmaker: A good setup against the five-person meme. The cross-cultural claim is asserted, not shown.

modeler: Recurrence across proverbs isn't independent evidence of mechanism. Tell me what flows between you and the five. Otherwise it's just a nice setup.
skeptic: Proverbs recurring across cultures is not evidence. It's folk wisdom repeated. 'Something real' needs the peer-influence research, not the vermilion saying.
clinician: Nice cross-cultural pattern, but it's a setup with no payoff for the reader. A lonely reader hears 'you are your bad company.'
habit: Vermilion and ink are lovely, but this is all setup and no rep. Get to what I change about who I see on Monday.
contemplative: Vermilion and ink is beautiful. It only sets up, and 'something real is being pointed at' is a promise. Point at it here.
stress: Passes the history test: independent proverbs across cultures. But 'takes seriously rather than coincidence' smuggles in an unfalsifiable stance. Say what would count against it.
gamedesigner: Good hook with the proverbs, but no second beat yet. Pure setup, no controller in my hands.
structural: The independent-recurrence point lands. But 'average of five' is about who you pick as friends. Who designs the places where you meet them?
satirist: Rohn, the Hebrew proverb, vermilion and ink: names and sources, so the Bryson test passes. 'Something real is being pointed at' just stalls. Say what it is.
mythmaker: Vermilion and ink make a lovely, old, rhyming image. Bring it back later and it will carry weight.

modeler: Habit transmission through repeated contact: the flow is named. Independent recurrence handled with the right caution.
skeptic: 'Recurrence like that isn't proof.' Thank you. Calibrated, and the plain claim it lands on is defensible.
clinician: Accessible and cross-cultural. Careful, though: it could make a lonely reader feel doomed by their company. Add agency.
habit: Interesting cross-cultural echo. Too long a runway; it says 'undersells' but the payoff comes later. Tighten it.
contemplative: 'Vermilion turns red' is beautiful. The heading and the pile of qualifiers fight Rohn. Let the old sayings speak, then stop.
stress: Cross-cultural recurrence, with 'isn't proof' attached. That's the history test done honestly. Keep.
gamedesigner: The vermilion/ink saying is lovely and resonates. All setup, though. Ask me to list my five now.
structural: Social contagion over solitary willpower is the right correction to Rohn. It names the environment, not the individual.
satirist: Rohn, Proverbs, vermilion and ink: names, sources, and 'recurrence isn't proof.' Earned wonder, honestly hedged.
mythmaker: Vermilion and ink is a gorgeous image. The ideas echo across cultures. It's still a lecture with no person catching the habit.

modeler: Influence is lumpy, not averaged: heavy-tailed impulses rather than a mean. That's the right correction to the model.
skeptic: 'Lumpy influence' rings true, and it's also a story that feels true. It's plausible, but no evidence is offered.
clinician: 'Lumpy influence' rings true. 'Loop-name flattening a Tree' jargon blurs it.
habit: 'Influence arrives lumpy' is a memorable correction. Abstract, but it lands.
contemplative: 'Influence arrives lumpy' is lovely and lived. 'Loop-name flattening a Tree' is the author performing.
stress: Influence arrives lumpy, not averaged. True to lived experience, and a fair hit on the meme.
gamedesigner: The 'Loop-name flattening a Tree' jargon hits before the point. Lead with the lumpy-influence examples.
structural: Lumpy influence beats 'average'. A nice correction. Still all interpersonal, with no feed or employer shaping the lumps.
satirist: 'Influence arrives lumpy' is a fine plain insight. 'A Loop-name flattening a Tree' is the jargon it could do without.
mythmaker: 'Influence arrives lumpy,' and the offhand comment that outweighs years. That's the real texture of a life. Lovely.

modeler: 'Half a loop called the whole shape': the meme omits your outflow back into them. Exactly my complaint. Keep.
skeptic: A fair point about direction: we underrate our own influence on others. The claim about what folds back is asserted.
clinician: Good point about agency, but no step. Say what you might seed this week.
habit: A good point, but no action. What do I seed into those five on Monday?
contemplative: You also shape them. That is the gentle half. Keep this and drop the scoring tone.
stress: Fair point about one-way influence. It lands, then 'already changed' muddies it.
gamedesigner: The one-directional critique is the sharper insight: I'm feeding them too.
structural: You shape them too. That is the spillover I want, and it's well argued.
satirist: 'Half a loop called the whole shape' is a good catch. Keep it, shorter.
mythmaker: 'Half a loop called the whole shape' is a nice line. The rest is mechanics, with no friend you've been shaping.

modeler: The point stands, but it's a third hit on the same meme. Cut to the last two sentences.
skeptic: Practical replacement for the headcount. It's repetitive, though; trim it by half.
clinician: Rehashes the four questions at length. Trim to 'use the four questions instead of the count.'
habit: 'Use the four questions instead' is the rep, but it's buried at the end. Lead with it.
contemplative: The third rebuttal of one quote. Too much. The four questions were already offered.
stress: Replaces a count with questions. Practical. A third paragraph on one meme is too many.
gamedesigner: The third critique of the same quote. Diminishing returns. Keep the last two sentences and cut the rest.
structural: Repeats the four questions at length. Cut it to the final two sentences.
satirist: The third rebuttal of one quote. The point is made. Compress it to its last two sentences.
mythmaker: It's a third flaw piled on a dead meme. The two-person comparison is good, but the paragraph sags. Cut it hard.

modeler: Yes: a headcount throws structure away, and structure is the claim. Two networks, same count, different behavior. Meadows would nod.
skeptic: A clean argument against a headcount metric: same score, different structures. Good correction of a lazy heuristic.
clinician: Dropping the headcount is a kindness. 'Dyad' versus 'Skein-thread' buries it, so say 'one close friend and four acquaintances' first.
habit: 'Ask four questions of each person' is a real instruction, but Dyad and Skein-thread jargon buries it. Give the reader a list of names to write tonight.
contemplative: Asking about each person instead of counting is good. But Dyad versus Skein-thread is the book talking to itself. Give a plain picture of two friends.
stress: Good kill of a fragile heuristic. It shows exactly where the headcount fails. Survives strain.
gamedesigner: Useful swap, count to questions, but Dyad vs Skein-thread recall is a memory check most players fail.
structural: Trading the headcount for four questions is a useful fix. It leans on Dyad and Skein-thread jargon, which hurts it for a lay reader.
satirist: The fix is good: ask questions, don't count heads. But Dyad versus Skein-thread is jargon refereeing jargon. Swap in 'one close friend, four acquaintances' and it lands.
mythmaker: Two people who score the same but differ should be a scene. Instead it's jargon arithmetic. Give me two faces.

modeler: Structure over count is the right move. 'One Dyad' and 'five Skein-threads' jargon blurs the example.
skeptic: A good contrast case, two people scoring five. Dyad/Skein-thread terms make a simple point harder.
clinician: 'On a bad week' is the right test. The Dyad/Skein-thread arithmetic makes it hard to follow. Plain words please.
habit: The two-people comparison is vivid. 'Ask the four questions of each person' is an action. Good.
contemplative: Counting Dyads and Skein-threads is intellectualising friendship. I lost the people in the arithmetic. Tell the bad week instead.
stress: 'On a bad week' is the right stress test. The Dyad and Skein-thread jargon clouds a simple contrast.
gamedesigner: Strong contrast between two people who both score five. Dyad and Skein-thread math fog it. Show the bad week concretely.
structural: The two-friends comparison is useful, but the Dyad and Skein-thread jargon and references to the four questions leave it opaque.
satirist: Two people, both score five, different bad weeks: a clean, concrete illustration. Works.
mythmaker: Two people, same count, different bad weeks. That's a scene. More of this. It earns everything.

modeler: Yes. Same count, different topology. One worn-out connection versus five parallel ones: redundancy is the stock buffer. Napkin-worthy.
skeptic: Two people with the same score but different structure: a good base-rate-versus-vignette case, and it shows why counts mislead. Vivid, but hypothetical.
clinician: Bad-week scenario shows why depth beats headcount; speaks to lonely readers and implies a concrete reframe.
habit: Two people both scoring five, then the bad week. Vivid, and makes the questions beat the count. Good case.
contemplative: One friend worn out, or five who might pick up. The bad week makes it true. A bit of counting, but warm.
stress: Bad-week stress test shows why the count misleads. Fragility versus redundancy, Taleb would nod. Best passage here.
gamedesigner: Great two-person comparison and bad-week payoff, but Dyad, Skein-threads and Chapter 13 stack jargon. Difficulty spike.
structural: Strong: redundancy in ties as resilience in the bad week. Network structure, not willpower. Best passage here. Add institutions that fray ties.
satirist: Five and five, different bad weeks. That is a Bryson-style argument with a worked example. Ending line lands. Dyad reference is the only jargon.
mythmaker: Bad week, one friend worn out versus five who might pick up. Stakes, faces, an image I'll remember.

modeler: Bond through doing, not discussing. Correct, concise and actionable.
skeptic: Doing over discussing is sound. 'The only thing' is an absolute; soften it.
clinician: Practical: do together, don't just discuss. Fine.
habit: 'Do the practice, don't discuss it' is the right instruction. Keep it.
contemplative: Practice binds and talk does not. True. The bold phrase alone nearly suffices.
stress: Practice, not discussion of practice. True of every book club that died. Good.
gamedesigner: 'Practice, not discussion' is clear design advice. Good.
structural: Doing together beats discussing. Correct, and it applies to activist groups too.
satirist: 'A group that meets to discuss Fractalism is a Banner.' Delicious self-awareness. Keep it.
mythmaker: Do it together rather than discussing it. Right, and briefly said. It needs one group doing it.

modeler: Repeated contact as the inflow to a shared stock is right. Say what drains it: skipped weeks, one-way giving.
skeptic: The doing-versus-discussing distinction is actionable. 'That is what makes a Skein' asserts a mechanism. Hedge it, or cite joint-activity bonding.
clinician: The job and moving examples are real. 'Banner' and 'Global Form' block a tired reader. Lead with 'do things together, don't just discuss.'
habit: 'Do the practice together, don't discuss it' is solid. The job decision and the move are real reps. Give a cue: the first ten minutes of every meetup.
contemplative: Do the practice, don't discuss it. True. Then Banner, Group Practice, Spiral Check and Global Form all come in one breath. Too much. Keep 'whether to take the job.'
stress: Real stakes: the job, the move. Doing beats talking about doing. Sharp, testable distinction.
gamedesigner: Love it: do the practice, don't talk about it. Concrete stakes like take the job make it playable.
structural: Finally the group does something together instead of talking. Good. But the practice names pile up, so a cold reader gets lost.
satirist: Honest point: a club that talks about the book is a fan club. Then Banner, Group Practice, Movement II, Spiral Check and Global Form all pile into one sentence. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: 'Whether to take the job' finally puts a real decision on the table. Put a friend in that chair.

modeler: Doing builds the stock; talking about it doesn't. Clear and useful.
skeptic: Doing beats discussing, which is plausible. Banner, Global Form, Spiral Check, Movement II: too many terms in one paragraph.
clinician: Do, don't discuss: sound advice. But the paragraph is stacked with jargon (Banner, Spiral Check, Global Form).
habit: Do, don't discuss. Right principle, with concrete examples (the job decision).
contemplative: 'Do the practices together' is right. Then come Banner, Movement II, Spiral Check, Global Form. Too many names. Show the friend and the job.
stress: Doing over discussing is right and guards against fan clubs. Spiral Check and Global Form make it opaque for newcomers.
gamedesigner: The doing-not-discussing rule is right. Banner, Global Form and Spiral Check in one paragraph is a vocabulary wall.
structural: Doing over discussing is right: fan clubs don't build anything. Spiral Check, Global Form and Movement II make it insider-only.
satirist: 'Fan club' is the honest line. Then Spiral Check, Global Form, Skein: three in-house terms in two sentences. Unpack.
mythmaker: The friend deciding about the job is the face. 'Global Form' jargon at the end undercuts it.

modeler: Practice repeated builds the group's form; talk about practice makes a fan club. Local rule to global form, and it holds.
skeptic: Do-versus-discuss is a sound design principle and the Spiral Check example is concrete. 'Doing that weaves Global Form' is mechanism by assertion.
clinician: Doing beats discussing, with a concrete example (job decision). Usable; slightly jargon-heavy for a newcomer.
habit: Do the practice together rather than talk about it. Real Spiral Check on a friend's job decision. Specific, startable.
contemplative: Do the practices, don't talk about them. Exactly right. The friend deciding on the job makes it live.
stress: Do the practices, don't discuss them. Skin in the doing. Fan-club warning is useful. Claim 'weaves Global Form' is soft.
gamedesigner: Do the practices, not talk about them: strong, with concrete scenarios. Fan club versus crew distinction lands.
structural: Doing together beats talking about it. That's my line. Group decides with a friend; scale it to something the group could change.
satirist: Fan club versus doing is a sharp, funny distinction, and the real Spiral Check example gives it legs. Global Form is a little much.
mythmaker: A friend deciding on the job, the group working it with her: a human scene. Fan club versus doing is sharp.

modeler: A fictional roll-call; the claim is warm but unsupported. The friend example works, the name list doesn't.
skeptic: Fictional characters count as evidence here. That makes the claim impossible to disprove. The friend example is warmer and enough on its own.
clinician: Warm and inclusive. The fiction roll-call is less useful than the friend example.
habit: Warm. The friend who already practises it resonates. No step, though.
contemplative: The friend who seeds better than anyone. Warm. The list of characters is decoration.
stress: Cartoon characters cited as practitioners isn't evidence. The friend example alone carries it.
gamedesigner: Nice idea, but it name-drops characters a newcomer may not remember. Cut the list.
structural: Warm, but a roster of cartoon characters is no evidence. The point about the unlabeled friend is enough.
satirist: A friend who'd never read this book but practices it. Nice. The cartoon-sage roll call is twee.
mythmaker: The friend who'd never read the book but seeds better than anyone. Finally a face, and a warm one.

modeler: Warm, and the vocabulary-isn't-the-thing point holds. Nothing mechanical here, and it repeats Part One.
skeptic: A humane point, and it resists vocabulary evangelism. 'Practices Seeding unknowingly' is the author reading other minds. Soften it.
clinician: Warm and freeing. It honours the friend who never reads the book. 'Keep practising alongside them' is a step anyone can take.
habit: 'Don't hand them the vocabulary' is a clear behaviour, and I can picture that friend. Works.
contemplative: This is beautiful. Don't hand them the vocabulary, keep practising beside them. It is gentle and humble, and I can live it.
stress: Ego leaves the room, which is rare and good. Telling readers not to push the vocabulary is humility with teeth.
gamedesigner: Strong. I instantly think of my friend who already Seeds. Clear move: keep practising, don't hand out vocab.
structural: Warm and easy to follow, but it gives no lever. Saying 'keep practising alongside them' points at nothing collective anyone could pull.
satirist: Bokonon would approve: the best practitioner never says the word. 'Don't hand them the vocabulary' is the most self-aware line in the chapter.
mythmaker: The friend who practices Seeding without ever having read a word: there's a face. Warm and true. Keep.

modeler: Lovely sentiment, but there's no stock here. Untracked circulation still has a balance; say what happens when it runs negative.
skeptic: 'It was a loan the whole time' is memorable and unsupported. It's a fluent aphorism with nothing holding it up.
clinician: Lovely, but it contradicts the reciprocity check and could license over-giving. Reconcile it with U0566.
habit: 'It was a loan the whole time' is a great line. The paragraph runs long.
contemplative: Kindness without a ledger is the heart of this chapter. Cut the last two sentences; they repeat.
stress: 'It will circulate back eventually' is fragile comfort. Also, untracked giving is where freeloaders hide. Address it.
gamedesigner: The ledger warning resonates, but it runs long. Cut the closing restatement.
structural: 'No ledger' is how unpaid care work stays invisible and lopsided. Who profits from untracked giving? Square this with the reciprocity check.
satirist: 'It was a loan the whole time' is a great closer. Cut the middle third of the paragraph.
mythmaker: 'It was a loan the whole time' cuts. Kindness against the ledger has real stakes. Keep it, maybe a bit shorter.

modeler: A third category to patch a binary. Taxonomy creep. It's defensible only if the next unit pays it off.
skeptic: A third category to fix the binary. It's fair, but is it needed? It mainly adds vocabulary.
clinician: A third coined term adds load for little reader gain. Fold it into the Banner discussion.
habit: A third coined term adds load. Do I need Braid to act differently?
contemplative: A third category with a new name. The book is multiplying words. Fold it into a caution about Skeins.
stress: A tenth term for a common case. Jargon creep. A named Skein doesn't need a word.
gamedesigner: A third coined term in one chapter. Difficulty spike. I lost hold of the pattern here.
structural: Another coinage. The named-but-real group is a real case. Does it need a third noun?
satirist: A third coined term for a two-term distinction. You failed your own 'pulled not pushed' test from Part Three. 'A named Skein' will do.
mythmaker: Braid is a decent coinage, but taxonomy is creeping in. Show me one band or church that became one.

modeler: Fair hybrid category. Fixing the false binary is useful, but a new term with no dynamics yet. U0577 earns it.
skeptic: Fixes a false binary, which I welcome. The examples are clear. It's a new term, though. Does it earn its keep over 'named Skein'?
clinician: A clean taxonomy addition, but it's a definition only. Nothing here helps someone figure out what their own group is.
habit: Another coined term (Braid) and no action. Running clubs and parishes help, but what do I do if I'm in one?
contemplative: Another coined word. The parish and running club are clear, but does the reader need 'Braid'? Look again at whether a plain phrase would do.
stress: A useful patch for a binary that cracked. Clear examples. Still just a taxonomy until the next unit puts it under load.
gamedesigner: Another coined term, Braid, and no move yet. Difficulty creep. Earn it by giving me a Braid check.
structural: Parish and running club are real institutions, which is good. The Braid label itself solves nothing yet.
satirist: A third coinage to patch the first two. A running club with shirts doesn't need the word 'Braid'. Cut the term and keep the observation.
mythmaker: Band, parish, running club shirts: clear images. The Braid itself is still a taxonomy box. Who's inside it?

modeler: Fixes a false binary, but coining yet another term costs more than it buys.
skeptic: A fair repair of a false binary, with a usable test. Another coined term, though. Does it earn one?
clinician: Taxonomy for taxonomy's sake. Nobody hurting needs a third category. Cut or fold it into a footnote.
habit: A third coined term stacked on two others. Taxonomy, no action. Cut it or fold it into a single sentence.
contemplative: Another category on a category. The running club with shirts is real. Do I need a word for it? Probably not.
stress: A third category patching a binary smells like the taxonomy saving itself. Fold it into the Skein test.
gamedesigner: Another new term late in the level. The self-test at the end helps. Ask whether the term earns its slot.
structural: Another coined category that adds taxonomy, not leverage. Could fold into the Skein/Banner test as one sentence.
satirist: A third coined noun to patch the first two. When your taxonomy needs a Braid, simplify the taxonomy.
mythmaker: Band and regulars, parish, running shirts: textured. But it's one more coined noun. Does Braid ever come back?

modeler: Real structure plus a visible label, coexisting. The 'would still meet without the name' test is a clean removal check.
skeptic: Neat taxonomy with a short, usable test. But more coinage; the test is lovely and I doubt anyone can run it honestly on themselves.
clinician: Braid is a clear term with a short, answerable test. Lightly useful; no emotional stake.
habit: One-line test: known by name, would still meet without it. Quick to run on any group. Term is clever.
contemplative: Another coined noun. Two strands twisted is a nice image, but the passage is classification, not living. Fewer names, please.
stress: Test is short and checkable (still meet without name?). But one more coined term; vocabulary inflation is ego dressed as system.
gamedesigner: New term with a short test, but a fourth category is feeling like more rulebook. Need a reason I'd care.
structural: Braid is a useful distinction: real ties plus a public name. Clear test. Organizing groups have exactly this shape; say so.
satirist: Band and regulars, parish, running club shirts: good examples, and a two-clause test. But Braid is the fourth coined noun; the pile grows.
mythmaker: Two strands twisted is a nice image, but the examples are a list. Give me one running club's shirt-and-all moment.

modeler: Two-condition test, survives-label-removal, is crisp and checkable. Running club is recognizable. Good taxonomy.
skeptic: Running-club example and a short, applicable test ('would you still meet without it') distinguish Braid usefully. Naming is cute; test is checkable.
clinician: Running-club example and one-line test make the Braid usable. Clear. Not especially personal.
habit: Running club test: do outsiders know you by name and would you meet without it? One crisp question I can ask tomorrow.
contemplative: Running club is good. Then Skein test, Braid, strands, a second test. Terms pile up. Let the club be the whole passage.
stress: Has a two-part test you can fail: outsiders know you, you'd meet without it. Concrete examples. Keep.
gamedesigner: Running-club example plus a two-part test gives a feedback signal. Another term to learn, though.
structural: Braid is a handy distinction between real and named groups, with a testable rule. Running club is low-stakes; try a union.
satirist: Running club with shirts is a nice example, and the test is stated. But Skein, Braid, Banner: a taxonomy of capitalized nouns. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: Running club with shirts, a parish, a band: faces you know. 'Would you meet without it?' is a sharp personal test. Braid image is clean.

modeler: Effort shifting from substance to defending the name is a real goal displacement. It's buried in a long sentence; tighten it.
skeptic: An interesting failure mode buried in a long paragraph. Cut it to the one sentence: defending the name instead of the thing.
clinician: Organizational theory, far from a struggling individual. Overlong.
habit: Dense taxonomy. The test that follows does the work, so trim this.
contemplative: 'Defending the name instead of tending the thing.' That is real. It is buried in comparisons of three states.
stress: Defending the name versus the substance is a real failure mode. Buried in a long paragraph. Cut hard.
gamedesigner: A real failure mode buried in a wall of text. One example group would carry it.
structural: The trap of defending the name is real: think nonprofits guarding their brand. The prose is overlong. Compress it.
satirist: The real point, defending the name instead of the work, drowns in parent-state taxonomy. One sentence would carry it.
mythmaker: 'Defending the name instead of the work' is a real tragedy, buried in abstract scaffolding. Tell it as a story, of a fandom or a movement.

modeler: A real drift: attention flows from tending to defending. The fan-club example nails it. Add the delay and it's a textbook goal erosion.
skeptic: The fan-club example names a recognisable drift. The risk mechanism is plausible and modestly stated. It works.
clinician: The fan-club example lands. Add one question a member can ask to catch the shift toward defending the name.
habit: The fan-club picture lands. Missing the check: count the evenings spent defending the name against the evenings spent doing the thing.
contemplative: The fan club arguing over who is real is true and sad. The sentences about the pure states are clever scaffolding. Start with the fan club.
stress: Names a real failure mode with a recognizable case. The fan club arguing over who counts is the storm, shown. Keep.
gamedesigner: Fan club arguing about real fans lands. Add a one-question tell: defending the name or tending the thing?
structural: A sharp read on how an institution drifts: the name starts defending itself. The fan-club image works. It still gives no rule to stop the drift.
satirist: The fan club arguing over who counts as a real fan is funny and true. That plain sentence carries the whole idea. It survives the bar.
mythmaker: The fan club arguing over who's a real fan is painfully recognizable. It has stakes and a fall. Good.

modeler: A good diagnostic: what does the response protect? Observable and repeatable, decision by decision.
skeptic: A usable test you can apply decision by decision. Good.
clinician: A clear diagnostic question for group leaders.
habit: Name versus thing: a usable question at the moment of criticism. Good cue.
contemplative: The test question is good. The three-way analysis afterward is too much; keep only the question.
stress: Good test: protect the name or the thing? Institutions fail it constantly. Keep it, drop 'Braid'.
gamedesigner: A good test question that redeems the Braid. Could stand without the new term.
structural: Protect the name, or the thing? A question I'd put to any institution under criticism. Keep it.
satirist: 'Protect the name, or the thing it stood for?' is a good test. It works without Braid.
mythmaker: 'Protect the name or the thing?' is a usable test. Good, and it rhymes with Tywin later.

modeler: Formalising drifts toward a Banner, and the fix is to redirect attention to practice. Sound, if expected.
skeptic: Concrete warning signs. It's sensible and unremarkable.
clinician: Good corrective: redirect to practice, don't police. Useful for organizers.
habit: Clear warning signs and a corrective: redirect to the practice. Actionable.
contemplative: 'Let the label matter less, not more.' Gentle correction without policing. Good.
stress: A sound warning against gatekeeping. Plain and actionable.
gamedesigner: Clear warning signs and a corrective. Playable checklist.
structural: Gatekeeping is a good warning. But formal structure is also how groups pull levers. Don't make formalizing itself the villain.
satirist: Practical warning signs, plainly stated. Fine.
mythmaker: Practical warning, and it's mostly a list of failure behaviors. It's fine, but it needs a gatekeeper with a reason we understand.

modeler: Has the balancing side: redirect attention, don't police harder. Policing harder feeds the loop. Good systems intuition.
skeptic: Concrete warning signs. 'Redirect attention back' is vague as a corrective. What does someone actually do on Tuesday?
clinician: Good that it says the drift 'starts from love,' so there's no shaming. The corrective is clear: go back to the practice.
habit: Drift signals are listed and the corrective is named. Make 'redirect attention' a step: open each meeting with the practice itself.
contemplative: 'It usually starts from love.' That line blends with the force instead of clashing with it. It's wise, and I could act on it this week.
stress: Admits the drift starts from love and gives a corrective. Honest about how good things go fragile.
gamedesigner: Clear warning signs and a corrective. Works as a checklist; reads like a GM note more than personal.
structural: The best institutional passage here: a schedule, a shared fund, gatekeeping. It names the structure and a corrective. Concrete governance.
satirist: Practical and self-suspicious: declaring yourself a Fractalist is the warning sign. Good. 'Starts from love' is the one human touch here. Keep.
mythmaker: 'It usually starts from love' is the humane note I wanted, a villain you understand. Show the person who books the room.

modeler: Names the drift, its loving origin, and a corrective that rebalances. A proper balancing loop. Well built.
skeptic: Sharp on institutional drift starting from love. A practical corrective, and accurate about motives.
clinician: 'Starts from love' is a shame-aware touch. 'Do the practice first' is a clear corrective. Good.
habit: Clear corrective: practice first, talk after. It names the drift signs. Useful.
contemplative: 'Do the practice first and talk about the group after' is the wise sentence. It starts from love, said kindly. Trim the rest.
stress: It names its own failure mode and says it starts from love. Rare honesty, and a concrete corrective.
gamedesigner: Practical drift warning with a clear corrective. The room-booker detail grounds it. Solid.
structural: Actual institutional analysis: how formalization drifts, gatekeeping and growth-chasing. The fix it names is a real one.
satirist: 'It usually starts from love' is sharp, true institutional sociology. Self-aware about its own cult risk. Keep.
mythmaker: 'It usually starts from love, the friend who books the room.' That's a villain drawn with sympathy. Sugar would approve.

modeler: A recap of the Third Thing. Nicely cadenced but adds nothing.
skeptic: A lovely cadence. I have no reason to believe the last line beyond its rhythm.
clinician: A graceful summary, but it repeats earlier points.
habit: A nice summary cadence, but no new step.
contemplative: 'Mostly invisible until, one day, it isn't.' A quiet ending. Drop the pillar reference.
