stress: A closing flourish that restates. 'Mostly invisible until it isn't' is unfalsifiable comfort.
gamedesigner: A summary that restates the chapter. Pleasant cutscene. Trim.
structural: A summary close. 'Mostly invisible until it isn't' is a mood, not a mechanism.
satirist: A summary sermon. 'Mostly invisible until it isn't' is pleasant foma. Trim it.
mythmaker: 'Mostly invisible until one day it isn't' is a nice cadence, but it's summary. The day it became visible is the scene you're owed.

modeler: Emergence from repeated local contact, with the payoff shown, not declared. Six people turning up is the stock finally visible.
skeptic: Lovely, and I have no reason to believe the six people. A vivid closing anecdote doing the work of evidence. Fluency, not proof.
clinician: Moving image, but 'six people turn up' could wound an isolated reader at 3 a.m. Acknowledge the reader who has no six yet.
habit: 'Six people turn up without being asked' is a great close. 'Small, local, repeated' still never names one rep.
contemplative: Six people turning up without being asked. That ending is enough. The Third Thing framing up front could fall away.
stress: Ends on a stress test: six people show up in trouble. That's the right measure. 'Everything in this book' leans grand.
gamedesigner: Six people turn up is a real payoff beat. Chapter-end reward lands, though it's a cutscene.
structural: 'Six people turn up' is good mutual aid. But 'mostly unseen' risks making invisibility a virtue when visible organizing is the lever.
satirist: 'Six people turn up without being asked' earns everything before it. 'Third Thing applied to community' is the hushed-voice part. Trim it.
mythmaker: Six people turning up without being asked is an earned payoff and an image I'll keep. This is the heart.

modeler: A cute snooze line, unrelated to closing a loop. Decorative.
skeptic: A cute epigraph. It does no work.
clinician: 'Quick to hit snooze' quietly scolds. Choose an epigraph without blame.
habit: The snooze image is relatable and cheeky. Works.
contemplative: Snooze is cute and a little glib. It performs. Choose a quieter line.
stress: Fortune-cookie epigraph. Weak opening for a closing chapter.
gamedesigner: Fun, relatable epigraph.
structural: Snooze-button scolding of the individual. And who built the alarm clock? Weak epigraph.
satirist: The snooze joke actually lands. Light, human. Keep it.
mythmaker: The snooze button is a familiar human image. It's cute and lands lightly.

modeler: Snooze epigraph decorates. No loop, no limit. Cut or swap for one that sets up the three-scale claim.
skeptic: It gives the universe intentions. Charming and unsupported, and it does nothing in this spot. Cut it or swap in an epigraph that earns its place.
clinician: The snooze framing implies the reader keeps failing to wake up. That's shame-adjacent and offers nothing to do. Cut or reframe.
habit: Snooze epigraph, but it's decoration and does no work here. Cut it, or tie it to an actual morning cue.
contemplative: A pleasant epigraph, but it ornaments and doesn't teach. The snooze joke performs a little. Let it go, or find a line that asks me to wake.
stress: Horoscope. 'The universe keeps ringing' can't fail and costs nobody anything. Cut it or swap in a line someone pays for.
gamedesigner: Snooze epigraph is cute but disconnected from the Skein beat. Filler between levels.
structural: A snooze-button epigraph. It frames waking up as a personal failing. And who profits from the alarm?
satirist: Fridge-magnet cosmology. The universe ringing a snooze alarm is foma, and it isn't even labelled as such. Cut it or make it funnier.
mythmaker: Snooze-button cuteness with no stakes. It's a fridge magnet, not an epigraph that earns its place.

modeler: A classic nested-scale chain. It fits the part's claim as an epigraph.
skeptic: An apt epigraph for scale nesting. Works in place.
clinician: A classic epigraph. 'Govern the state' is a big ask for someone barely managing a day.
habit: A fitting epigraph for the scale recap. Bigger-picture only.
contemplative: It is an old and fitting line, and a quiet frame. It asks nothing of me today.
stress: An apt classical precedent for working across scales. It does its epigraph job.
gamedesigner: Fitting epigraph for scaling up. Nothing to do.
structural: Cultivate the self first, govern the state last: inner work set up as the precondition for collective action. Who benefits from that order?
satirist: Attributed, apt, ancient. Decorative; does what an epigraph does and nothing more.
mythmaker: A classic chain, apt for scaling. Austere epigraph, it works in place, and there's no heart in it.

modeler: Growth from a small start, a nice nod to iteration. But everything that grows forever is fiction; where's the limit?
skeptic: Fluent epigraph, unfalsifiable. Ornamental; nothing holds it up beyond rhythm.
clinician: A kind epigraph about small beginnings. Reassuring, no step.
habit: Fine proverb, no step. Pairs with beginning small, but I want the sprout named, not the tree.
contemplative: A sprout becomes a tree. Quiet, patient, true. It breathes. Let it stand alone.
stress: Familiar aphorism. Nothing at stake, nothing testable. Horoscope-grade.
gamedesigner: Pleasant epigraph, zero agency.
structural: Pretty sprout line. Slogan for patience, which is also the fatalist's friend. No lever; cut or tie to a campaign.
satirist: Tao quote as wall decor. True, borrowed, and says nothing the section doesn't. Cut or pay it with a number.
mythmaker: Sprout to tree is an image, and a familiar one. Ornament unless a person plants something later.

modeler: Growth from small neglected beginnings: pretty, true, no limits named. Reinforcing loop without a balancing side.
skeptic: Pleasant aphorism with a small ache of regret. Rhymes with truth but supplies none.
clinician: Gentle growth image, easy. 'Someone walked past' stings a little; no step.
habit: Sprout someone walked past: emotional, easy. But where's the step? Pair with 'who is a sprout near you'.
contemplative: A sprout someone walked past: sweet and true. It makes me look at my feet.
stress: Sweet, cheap reassurance. Most sprouts die; the line forgets survivorship. Rework to name what kills them.
gamedesigner: Sweet end beat, but I can't do anything with it.
structural: Warm and clear: everything big started small. Also the cheerful logic of 'plant your own'. Who owns the forest?
satirist: 'A sprout someone walked past.' Short, wry, a little mournful. Funny-sad in one line; doesn't ask anything of me.
mythmaker: A sprout someone walked past: a small tragedy and a hope in nine words. Tender, but alone it needs a body and a return.

modeler: 'Same Nest at different resolutions': which part repeats the whole, and at what ratio? The scale claim rhymes and isn't shown.
skeptic: 'Same Nest, different resolutions' is asserted, not shown. Elegance is the only support.
clinician: Abstract synthesis. 'Isn't finished yet' risks feeding perfectionism.
habit: Same-Nest framing. Abstract, but brief.
contemplative: Three scales, one Nest. Clear. The last clause wags a finger; let it rest.
stress: 'The same Nest at different resolutions' is asserted, not shown. Recap with a theory-of-everything tone.
gamedesigner: A fine unifying claim, but it's all reception, no move.
structural: The claim that the scales are one Nest is fine, but culture-scale rules never appear in Part Two's practices.
satirist: 'The same Nest at different resolutions' says nothing to a skeptic. Plainly: 'It's all one practice.'
mythmaker: Same Nest at different resolutions. It's a structural recap with no person in it.

modeler: Self-similarity claimed, not shown. What repeats, and at what ratio? Habit to tone to norm rhymes. Show one rule surviving each step.
skeptic: A neat synthesis, and 'hasn't travelled yet' is gently calibrated. 'The same Nest' is still asserted, not shown.
clinician: 'Hasn't travelled yet' is gentle. Otherwise it's pure synthesis with no step attached.
habit: 'Same Nest at different resolutions' is jargon stacked on jargon. What is the one habit I watch travel from me to the group?
contemplative: The idea that habit becomes tone and tone becomes a norm is clear. 'Same Nest at different resolutions' is the head talking. It needs a scene, not a summary.
stress: 'Hasn't travelled yet' makes every failure a delay, never a refutation. Name a practice that shouldn't scale.
gamedesigner: Nice zoom idea but pure recap. Give me one habit to trace across all three scales.
structural: Habit to tone to group norm is the right figure-and-ground move. It stops before the scale where rules get written.
satirist: 'Hasn't travelled yet' is a nice plain close. 'The same Nest seen at different resolutions' is a metaphor promoted to a mechanism. Show one habit crossing scales.
mythmaker: 'Hasn't travelled yet' is a nice line. Otherwise it's architecture with no one walking through it.

modeler: Tracks one habit across three scales and admits some practices don't travel. That's the scale check I ask for.
skeptic: The pausing example makes the scale claim concrete and checkable. Better than the abstractions around it.
clinician: Pausing before you answer, traced across scales: one small habit, made visible. That's exactly how it should be done.
habit: Tracing one habit (pausing before you answer) across scales is exactly right. It's concrete and portable.
contemplative: Following one habit, the pause before you answer, is lovely and clear. 'Seen at different resolutions' is the only cold phrase.
stress: One habit traced across three scales makes the claim concrete. 'Hasn't travelled yet' is humble.
gamedesigner: Following one habit across three scales is a great demonstration. Ask me to trace one of mine.
structural: Tracking one habit across scales is a good illustration. Where it stops at group norms, it should go on to the institutions.
satirist: Pausing before you answer, followed across scales: a real example doing real work. 'Hasn't travelled yet' is gracious.
mythmaker: Following one habit, pausing before you answer, across scales: a good spine. Needs Dana here, not a hypothetical.

modeler: Suffering converted to hope 'as a loop, practised', with no stock, flow or limit. A metaphor dressed as mechanism, and crammed.
skeptic: Hope as 'trainable, not temperament' needs a citation. The paragraph crams suffering, hope and travel together. Split it or cut it.
clinician: Rushes suffering into 'usable' in one breath. That's bypassing. Acknowledge that some pain just hurts first, then offer hope.
habit: 'Hope is trainable', then no training. Give the rep or drop the claim.
contemplative: Suffering, hope, and travel crammed into one paragraph. Each deserves its own breath, or give it less.
stress: 'Hope is trainable' with no evidence, crammed in as an aside. Either support it properly or cut it.
gamedesigner: Suffering, hope and travel in one paragraph is three new ideas. Split them or cut them.
structural: Suffering, hope and travel crammed into one paragraph. Trainable hope as an inner loop is inner work standing in for change.
satirist: 'Hope is trainable' is a big claim tossed in passing. Cite hope research (Snyder) or leave it out.
mythmaker: Suffering and hope get stuffed into one paragraph as a footnote. Unearned. Either give hope a scene or cut it.

modeler: Hope as practised capacity is a nice stock. But it only reinforces. What erodes it? Name the drain or it grows forever.
skeptic: Saying hope isn't a temperament contradicts work on dispositional optimism. 'Slightly easier each time' is an empirical claim with no support given.
clinician: 'Some of it simply hurts' blocks bypassing, which is excellent. 'Watch a pain without obeying it' needs one concrete way to do that today.
habit: Hope as a practised loop is a fine reframe, but there's no cue. When does the rep happen? The next time irritation spikes, do what?
contemplative: 'Pain observed rather than pain obeyed.' Hope as a practised loop. This is tender, and it doesn't hurry past the hurt. Keep it.
stress: Doesn't rush past pain, which is good. 'Slightly easier each time' is a testable claim. Admit it sometimes isn't.
gamedesigner: Hope as a practised loop with a felt signal: next one is slightly easier. That's progress I can feel.
structural: Here suffering is friction you learn to hold, so hope becomes an inner loop. That is my alibi worry: some of that pain is a policy to change.
satirist: Calling hope a practised loop rather than a temperament is a real claim and a kind one. It grants that pain just hurts before it moralizes. Earned.
mythmaker: Hope as a practised loop, and it refuses to hurry past pain. That's earned tenderness. A named sufferer would seal it.

modeler: A summary with one good line: a Dyad amplifies what you bring. Otherwise a recap.
skeptic: Recap in a rhetorical cadence. It's readable and redundant.
clinician: 'An untended Self sends its chaos outward' makes the struggling reader the hazard. Reframe it as a need, not a threat.
habit: A clean summary of Part Two. Fine, nothing to do.
contemplative: The whole shape, simply. 'Not what you meant to bring' stings kindly.
stress: A summary of what we just read. 'Comes home to all three' is a promise no one can check.
gamedesigner: Recap number two. The player's already been through this level.
structural: Recap. 'Comes home to all three' asserts spillover without showing a channel for it.
satirist: A third recap of Part Two in one chapter. Busy, busy, busy. Cut it.
mythmaker: A summary sermon. 'Amplifies what you bring, not what you meant to' is the one keeper line.

modeler: 'Filtered, delayed and imperfect' is the honest bit: delays acknowledged. Otherwise it's recap. Fine in place.
skeptic: A tidy recap. 'A Dyad amplifies what you actually bring' sounds true because it scans. The 'filtered, delayed, imperfect' hedge helps.
clinician: A recap dense with jargon (Fold, Dyad, Skein). 'Whatever you carry untended' leans on blame. Simplify, or let it stand as a summary.
habit: Recap in jargon: tend, magnify, Fold. Nothing in it is a step. Cut it, or end on one thing to do.
contemplative: It is called one breath, but it takes four. 'A Dyad amplifies what you actually bring' is true. The Fold clause is jargon. Shorten.
stress: Clean summary, and 'filtered, delayed, imperfect' is honest hedging. It's recap, though, with nothing new at stake.
gamedesigner: Recap cutscene loaded with Fold and Dyad jargon. Idle reader. Cut or merge with U0585.
structural: A recap packed with coined terms. Self, Dyad, Skein and Fold all in one breath, with no lever at any of those scales.
satirist: 'A Dyad amplifies what you actually bring, not what you meant to' is the keeper. The rest recites the vocabulary like a catechism. Cut it to that line.
mythmaker: A recap in four jargon terms. 'Into every room' is nice, but nobody enters one. Cut it down or give it a face.

modeler: A decent recap. 'Amplifies what you bring' is a real gain claim. 'Filtered, delayed' keeps it honest.
skeptic: A summary in confident aphorisms. 'Amplifies what you actually bring' is unsupported. Hedge it or show it.
clinician: A tidy recap, but 'tend the Self' could read as pressure. It adds nothing new.
habit: A summary in one breath. Clear, but it's four imperatives with no cue. Acceptable as a recap.
contemplative: It says 'in one breath' and needs four. Remove 'filtered, delayed and imperfect' and the summary might fit an exhale.
stress: A serviceable recap. 'Filtered, delayed and imperfect' keeps it honest. Otherwise it repeats what came before.
gamedesigner: End-of-level recap made of jargon and imperatives. An idle reader's paragraph. Cut it or turn it into a self-check.
structural: A recap with no new lever. Starts at 'tend the Self', which is my exact complaint about ordering.
satirist: Summary dense with Self, Dyad, Skein, Fold. Reads like a catechism. Dana did this better next door.
mythmaker: A recap in jargon, one breath too many. A Dyad amplifies what you bring, and that line lives. The rest is a glossary.

modeler: Good compression across three scales, and the Fold closing the loop 'slowly and imperfectly' includes a delay. A recap, though.
skeptic: 'Not what you meant to bring' is the right correction for self-transparency. 'Comes back through the Fold' is hedged with 'slowly, imperfectly'. Good.
clinician: Neat recap. 'What you actually bring, not what you meant' might sting a fragile reader without a softener.
habit: Tidy recap, mostly abstract. Four claims, no action. Add one rep per claim.
contemplative: A fair summary, said in one breath as promised. 'Not what you meant to bring' is honest. It is recap, not practice.
stress: Tight recap, claims specific enough to be wrong, 'slowly and imperfectly' is honest. Fold claim still unproven.
gamedesigner: Compressed recap crammed with Dyad, Skein, Fold. Only works if you already learned them. Make it a checklist.
structural: Summary does say Skein forms around contact, not label. Still tend-the-Self first; I'd flip the order. Structure is absent.
satirist: A recap in one breath, honest about slowly and imperfectly. But five capitalized terms in a paragraph is where I start reaching for the exit.
mythmaker: A summary of nouns with nobody inside: Dyad, Skein, Fold. Lifeless recap. Return to one earlier face instead.

modeler: The practices chained into a real causal loop, each one enabling the next. That's structure as the claim. Good.
skeptic: The dependency chain is a neat claim. Each link is asserted, not checked.
clinician: Dense chain of cross-references. A reader on a bad day will get lost.
habit: The chain is clever, but it's a dependency map, not a step. Hard to hold.
contemplative: A chain of dependencies the reader must hold in the head. Draw it as a circle, or say less.
stress: An interesting dependency chain, but it references a practice not taught yet. Hard to follow. Simplify.
gamedesigner: Chains in a practice from Part Three I haven't learned yet. Onboarding skip.
structural: The dependency chain between practices is interesting, but dense. It ends at the Skein and never reaches a policy.
satirist: A chain of five cross-references, one into an unread Part Three. It's clever in a diagram and fog in prose.
mythmaker: A chain of practices recited as cause and effect. Reads like a syllabus. Show one person passing through all five links.

modeler: Actually closes the loop through the practices, which I love. Too compressed, too many proper nouns per sentence. Draw it as a ring.
skeptic: Following one person makes the circle legible. It's still an idealised path presented as typical. Admit that it often stalls.
clinician: Following one person is the right move, but the jargon chain loses her. Make it one plain scenario a reader can see.
habit: Following one person through is the right instinct, but loop, self-story, Second Pass and Skein pile up. Show her actual Tuesday.
contemplative: Following one woman is right. But the chain of self-story, Second Pass and Part Three is dense machinery. Let her be a person, not a diagram.
stress: The walkthrough idea is right, but forward references and jargon bury it. Use plain verbs and one concrete conflict.
gamedesigner: Following one player is smart, but it leans on Second Pass from a future level. Spike for newcomers.
structural: Following one person through the cycle is good: the Skein gives honest feedback back. But the jargon is dense and the loop never leaves the friend group.
satirist: Following one person is a good idea, but she walks through a glossary, not a life. Give her a name, a fight, a friend. Then it's a story.
mythmaker: 'Follow one person' and then she has no name and no life, just a run of terms. Make her real or drop the pretence.

modeler: It builds up from a local rule, closes the loop back to her, and admits stalls. Great. Jargon (Second Pass, Loop Tongue) taxes the reader.
skeptic: One anecdote doing evidence's job, but it admits it rarely runs this cleanly. Jargon (Second Pass, Loop Tongue) weighs it down.
clinician: Dana humanises it, and 'stalls for a while' is honest. Too many system names crammed in, so simplify the chain.
habit: Dana's chain is a good worked example. Too many term references (Second Pass, Part Three) slow it. Strip the cross-refs.
contemplative: Dana going cold about money is real. The chain of named practices loses me. Tell her story without the jargon.
stress: A worked case that admits stalls. That's good. The chain is too neat and jargon-heavy, so show one link failing.
gamedesigner: Dana's chain is the best payoff here. Second Pass, Loop Tongue and Part Three references trip newcomers.
structural: Dana's group handing back 'you do the cold thing with us too' is real spillover. Too many coined terms crowd it.
satirist: Dana's money fight makes the system visible, and 'rarely runs this cleanly' is the honest wink. Trim the Part Three plug.
mythmaker: Dana! A face, a cost, a turn, and the friends' 'you do the cold thing with us too' stings. Jargon tangles the middle.

modeler: A closed loop with no completion state, and the complex-versus-complicated point lands. Nice.
skeptic: Fair warning against treating the practices as a checklist. 'Badly at first' is honest.
clinician: 'Run all three, badly at first' is the shame-aware permission people need.
habit: 'Run all three, badly at first' is a good permission. No cue, though.
contemplative: 'Badly at first' is a gift. 'Complex versus complicated' is a word game; cut it.
stress: 'No completion state' is honest. But 'you'll get checklist results' is a threat with no evidence.
gamedesigner: 'No completion state' kills the sense of progress. Give me a felt milestone per lap.
structural: Not a checklist. Fine, if a little repetitive with the paragraph before it.
satirist: 'You'll get the results a checklist gets' is dry and good. The rest repeats U0585.
mythmaker: 'Badly at first, each makes the others possible' is honest. The complex/complicated callback is jargon, so drop it.

modeler: Circle versus checklist, complex versus complicated: the right distinction. Progress per lap is the stock. Works.
skeptic: 'Badly at first' and no completion state are honest expectations. This is the rare passage that lowers the reader's confidence appropriately.
clinician: 'Badly at first' and no completion state is anti-perfectionist and safe. The complex-versus-complicated tag at the end is a closing flourish that says nothing new.
habit: 'Run all three, badly at first' is the most honest permission here. Complex versus complicated is a leftover term. Still no lap cadence.
contemplative: 'Badly at first' is kind and true. The final complex-versus-complicated line is cleverness and agitates the breath. End at 'That is the progress.'
stress: 'Badly at first' is humble. But 'no completion state' leaves no way to fail. Give a sign you're regressing.
gamedesigner: No completion state, progress is easier than last month. Good felt-progress framing; checklist line lands.
structural: Circle versus checklist is fair. 'Badly at first' is honest. No collective payoff.
satirist: 'Badly at first, a little easier than last month' is honest progress talk. The complex-versus-complicated callback is fine. Survives the bar.
mythmaker: 'Badly at first' and laps that get a little easier is forgiving and true. The complex/complicated jab at the end is lecture residue.

modeler: The rising tide and the boat held down: pure image, no mechanism. Pleasant, but it doesn't earn its place.
skeptic: The rising-tide image is fluent and does no work. Compared to what? Cut it or ground it.
clinician: 'Stop holding your own boat down' implies the reader is sinking themselves. Soften it.
habit: 'Stop holding your own boat down' is lovely. Still, what's the first action?
contemplative: Stop holding your own boat down. Beautiful. The opening double negation could go.
stress: Rising-tide and boat imagery is soft. 'Let what happens happen' fails at the first storm.
gamedesigner: The boat image lands. A warm, clear payoff.
structural: 'Don't manage the water level': explicitly abandons collective building. Who profits from the reader never touching the tide? Rewrite it.
satirist: 'Stop holding your own boat down' is plain and lovely. Keep it.
mythmaker: 'Stop holding your own boat down' is a fine image. It turns the rising tide personal.

modeler: Header. Fine.
skeptic: A header. It's fine.
clinician: Signpost.
habit: Signpost. Fine.
contemplative: A drumroll. Let the next paragraph arrive unannounced.
stress: Header. Fine.
gamedesigner: Drumroll header. Fine.
structural: Heading. Fine.
satirist: 'Said plainly,' announced in bold. Just say it plainly.
mythmaker: A drumroll header. The paragraph after it can stand without the fanfare.

modeler: Transition beat. Earns nothing alone. Merge into the next paragraph.
skeptic: A transition. 'Everything has argued for it' claims more than was argued. Harmless, but it adds nothing.
clinician: A transition line that earns nothing alone. Fold it into the next paragraph.
habit: A drumroll line that delivers nothing on its own. Fold it into the next paragraph.
contemplative: A drumroll line that does no work. Cut it, and let the next sentence arrive by itself.
stress: A drumroll with no payload. Fold it into the next sentence.
gamedesigner: Pure transition line. Drumroll with no hit. Fold into the next paragraph.
structural: A transition line. It works as a hinge and earns nothing beyond that.
satirist: A drumroll with no drum. Bold throat-clearing that announces importance instead of having it. Cut it and start with the point.
mythmaker: A drumroll with nothing behind it. Fold it into the next line.

modeler: A pointed closing line. Resonant, though it carries no mechanism.
skeptic: A closing line that resonates. 'Already planting' assumes influence I can't verify, but as a prompt it's fine.
clinician: Hopeful, but 'the question is what' could prompt anxious self-audit. Offer one seed to plant today.
habit: 'The question is what.' One question worth carrying. Good closer, though I'd add 'tomorrow morning'.
contemplative: 'You're already planting. The question is what.' Simple and true. The bold preamble before it isn't needed.
stress: A strong closer that says you're already responsible. It's short and has stakes.
gamedesigner: Punchy closer with a question that sticks. It works as a final beat.
structural: A resonant close. 'Planting' stays private, though. Plant what, with whom, and against which rule?
satirist: Plain closing line, mildly grand. You're already planting is fine; the question is earned by the chapter.
mythmaker: 'You're already planting. The question is what.' A closing image with weight, if planting was seeded earlier.

modeler: Punchy, and it implies you're already in a loop. A heading with no mechanism behind it.
skeptic: Punchy and likely true of everyone, which is the problem: it's unfalsifiable and flatters the reader. Memorable, not evidential.
clinician: Reframes the reader as already acting, not failing. Warm, but 'the question is what' hints at blame.
habit: One question to carry all day. Exactly the one-question test. Short, personal, sticky.
contemplative: Short and true. It looks at me directly. But it asks nothing yet. Follow it with one small act.
stress: Punchy and personal, but a slogan. Asserts you're planting without showing what breaks.
gamedesigner: Good hook line, reframes everyday acts as planting. Needs a second beat telling me what to do about it.
structural: Punchy: you're already planting. True of everyone, but 'what' goes to personal choice only. Add 'and who owns the field?'
satirist: Neat heading with a small sting: you are planting already. Unearned until the body gives a fact, but it passes the bar.
mythmaker: Gets me: I'm already planting. A strong hook, but a heading alone has no seed in my hand.

modeler: Ends on a sensing question: what flowed in today. Gentle and personal, a good loop closer.
skeptic: A question, not an assertion; invites inspection of one's own day. Short and effective. Assumes 'planting' is happening, mildly presumptuous.
clinician: Small, immediate daily question. Safe if the answer can be 'little' on a bad day; say so.
habit: Yes. One question, tonight, about today. This is the line to carry all day. Exactly the habit hook.
contemplative: A single question I can answer tonight, with no cleverness. This is how a chapter should end.
stress: Direct question the reader can answer today. Low-risk, high-use. Good close.
gamedesigner: A direct prompt: what went in the ground today? Agency and a daily check. Strong closer.
structural: Direct, personal question that lands. But 'what did I plant' stays private; ask who you planted it with.
satirist: A closing question that makes me act: what went into the ground today? Plain, personal, no pomp.
mythmaker: 'What went into the ground today?' pins the reader to a day and a deed. Short, warm, accountable. A good last question.

modeler: You're always planting, and seeing it lets you choose. Resonant. The care-versus-fear choice lacks any mechanism.
skeptic: 'You are planting whether you mean to or not' is a reasonable point about habit. Care versus fear is a hopeful frame, not a finding.
clinician: Beautiful. But 'every repeated thought is planting' hands a ruminator new dread. Add: thoughts aren't orders, you choose what you water.
habit: 'Planting every day whether you mean to' resonates. Add a two-minute check on what you planted today.
contemplative: Plant out of care rather than fear. This is Thich Nhat Hanh's garden. Keep every word.
stress: You're planting whether or not you mean to. A strong, simple claim. Care versus fear lands.
gamedesigner: 'Already planting' lands personally. A good reframe, though there's no move.
structural: Resonant, but wholly private. Care versus fear is about motive, not mechanism.
satirist: Earnest, but it lands. 'Plant out of care rather than out of fear' is clear.
mythmaker: 'You are planting whether you mean to or not.' Care against fear is real stakes. This earns the ending.

modeler: Fast and slow stocks with compost as recycling. It almost names a flow. Keep it short.
skeptic: A compost metaphor that's consoling and unexamined. The 'better ground' claim needs a caveat.
clinician: Compost reframes failure without shame. Good. Name one fast thing to lean on.
habit: The compost image is fine, but it's sentiment without a behaviour.
contemplative: Compost as better ground. Gentle with failure. It breathes.
stress: 'Failure becomes compost' is close to antifragile. It needs a case where failure actually improved the ground.
gamedesigner: Compost is a nice failure-as-progress mechanic. Lovely.
structural: The compost metaphor lands personally. It implies no lever.
satirist: The compost line is the third 'not a consolation prize' in the chunk. Watch the tic.
mythmaker: Compost returns from the earlier image, with more weight now. That's a proper rhyme, so keep it.

modeler: Fast and slow flows, compost recycling failure back into stock. A real material loop. Good.
skeptic: Comforting gardening imagery. 'Better ground than the last' assumes failure always teaches. Often it doesn't. Say when it doesn't.
clinician: The best thing here for a bad day: a walk, a meal, one finished task. Failure becomes compost, not a verdict. Keep it as is.
habit: A walk, a meal, one task finished today: close to a system. Make it daily: pick one fast thing before nine.
contemplative: A walk, a meal, one task. Failure as compost. This is warm and lived. I can do this today.
stress: Fast wins against slow growth is practical barbell thinking. 'Better ground every time' overclaims; some failures just salt the soil.
gamedesigner: Fast wins keep you standing during slow grinds. That's reward scheduling, nicely concrete. Compost image plays.
structural: The compost image is pleasant and entirely private. A walk and a meal get no one organized.
satirist: Walk, meal, one finished task: concrete things that keep you standing. Compost as the use for failure is a metaphor that knows it's a metaphor. Good.
mythmaker: A walk and a meal keep you standing while the slow things grow underground. Compost is a fine returning image. Keep.

modeler: A benediction. The 'no promised return' honesty is good, and the forest image is warm but not structural.
skeptic: 'Anyone promising a return is selling something' is well calibrated. I appreciate the refusal to promise.
clinician: Honest and no-promise, which is moving. Light on steps.
habit: Moving. 'Shade you'll never be thanked for' sticks. No step.
contemplative: Shade you will never be thanked for. Moving and humble. The 'selling something' jab can go.
stress: 'Anyone promising a return is selling something' shows humility with skin. Planting shade for strangers is honest.
gamedesigner: The shade image moves me. Cutscene, but a good one.
structural: It finally names culture and world. 'Tend' them how? One collective act would earn the scale.
satirist: 'Anyone promising one is selling something' is the Bokonon moment. The shade-you'll-never-be-thanked-for image earns its wonder.
mythmaker: Shade you grew and will never be thanked for. The best image in the chunk. Mythic and humble.

modeler: The canopy shades out options: a real ecological mechanism, honestly flagged as a resemblance. I respect that hedge.
skeptic: Rewarded: it says outright that the canopy is a resemblance, not a demonstration. More of this, please.
clinician: The parenthetical hedging muddles the image. Keep the canopy and cut the epistemics aside.
habit: The canopy is good, but the parenthetical hedge kills momentum. Cut the aside.
contemplative: The canopy image is strong. The parenthetical hedge kills it. Trust the image or omit it.
stress: The canopy shading out options is a sharp, non-flattering point. The parenthetical hedge clutters it. Make the hedge one clause.
gamedesigner: The canopy works, then the parenthetical hedge stalls it. Move the caveat out.
structural: Commitments shading out options is interesting. The hedging parenthetical muddies it. 'That is the whole leverage' concedes too much.
satirist: The parenthetical admitting it's only a resemblance is exactly right. More of this honesty, please.
mythmaker: The canopy is great, and then the parenthetical hedge strangles it. Move the epistemics to a footnote and let the image breathe.

modeler: Canopy as shading, flagged honestly as a model, not proof. Respect. 'Considerably more than it sounds' is a claim with no number.
skeptic: I credit 'a resemblance to hold loosely, not a proof.' Then 'considerably more than it sounds' takes the calibration back. Pick one.
clinician: The canopy metaphor is lovely but abstract and hedged. A struggling reader can't take a step from it.
habit: The canopy metaphor goes on too long and hedges itself. 'Consistency buys a canopy' is a nice line, but what is the repeated act?
contemplative: The canopy is lovely, but the hedging smothers it: 'hold loosely, not a proof, more than it sounds like.' Trust the image and remove the qualifiers.
stress: It names the cost, options shaded out, and labels itself a model rather than a proof. That's skin. Respect.
gamedesigner: Canopy metaphor gets hedged into fog. Loses the player at 'considerably more than it sounds like.'
structural: The canopy metaphor is hedged until it's mush. It calls this 'the whole of the leverage available' and so quietly excuses structural action.
satirist: It credits itself as a model, not a proof, and that is Bokonon-honest. The bold 'It is a canopy' is pulpit voice. 'Commitment shades out options' is the plain sentence underneath.
mythmaker: The canopy is a strong image, then it hedges itself bloodless. Show the option a commitment shaded out, and the person who mourns it.

modeler: Canopy is a lovely stock image, and it admits it's a model, not a proof. Still no flow or delay. Name what shade accumulates.
skeptic: Rare candor: 'a model, not a proof' and the mourned novel. Shade-casting stays metaphor; say what one would actually do differently on Saturday.
clinician: Rare honesty: names the unwritten novel as real loss before reframing. No bypassing. Still missing one shade-casting step for this week.
habit: The Saturdays line lands hard. But what shade do I cast Monday? Name one repeated act to keep or drop.
contemplative: The canopy is beautiful, and the Saturdays land. Drop 'ecology... model, not proof'; end on the shade you cast.
stress: Names its own cost: the unwritten novel. Admits model, not proof. That's skin. Keep.
gamedesigner: Canopy image lands, kids-vs-novel stings. But no move or signal; 'ecology, model, proof' hedge muddies it. End on one shade to cast this week.
structural: Canopy image lands, mourning is honest. But 'the leverage you actually have' shrinks leverage to private shade. Who sets the Saturday? Name your employer.
satirist: Canopy earns its keep; the novel-vs-Saturdays line is honest grief. 'Model, not a proof' is the foma label I wanted. Keep.
mythmaker: The canopy image and the Saturdays that cost a novel give it a face and a real loss. Keep it, and bring the canopy back later.

modeler: Restates noticing a loop from inside. Repetitive. Cut.
skeptic: 'Never claimed comes standard' admits the default honestly. A good summary of the actual skill.
clinician: 'Notice while inside it' risks hypervigilance. Clarify that it means noticing lightly, not monitoring.
habit: Names the capacity being trained. Abstract summary, adequate.
contemplative: It restates the noticing for the fifth time with heavy qualifiers. One plain sentence.
stress: Restatement of the book's thesis. Nothing new under strain.
gamedesigner: Names the core skill clearly, but it's the third summary in a row. Merge.
structural: Noticing as the endpoint: inner work crowned the whole point. Noticing should feed acting with others.
satirist: A fourth summary of 'noticing.' Readers got it. Cut it.
mythmaker: It names the capacity again after the canopy already said it better. It's redundant, so cut or compress it.

modeler: The capacity under everything: observer inside the loop. Hofstadter-adjacent and honest. Light touch works.
skeptic: 'This book never claimed it comes standard' is an admitted limit. Calling noticing a loop the core capacity is fair and modest.
clinician: 'Lightly, not like a guard on watch' is exactly the anti-rumination framing I want. 'Never claimed it comes standard' removes shame.
habit: 'Notice a loop while you're inside it' is exactly the vague practice I pounce on. Notice when? Give a trigger and ten seconds.
contemplative: Noticing lightly, the way you notice breathing. Yes. But 'use it on purpose' gives no doorway. Name one moment to begin.
stress: A fair distillation, and it admits the capacity isn't standard. Still vague about what 'reaching in' actually means under pressure.
gamedesigner: Core capacity named, but 'use it on purpose' gives no feedback signal. How do I know I'm noticing?
structural: Noticing becomes the master capacity. That's inner work as the whole answer. Who rewrote the loop you're noticing?
satirist: 'The way you notice your own breathing, not like a guard on watch' is a fine distinction. Admitting the capacity doesn't come standard is refreshingly modest.
mythmaker: 'Like breathing, not a guard' is good, but it's a thesis with no one breathing. Lovely thought. Who's holding it?

modeler: Change one thing on this lap is a real intervention inside the loop. The lightness keeps it from sounding like control theory.
skeptic: Concrete cue, light attention, one small change, and an admission it isn't standard equipment. Calibrated enough to trust.
clinician: 'Notice it lightly, not like a guard on watch' is textbook defusion, and one small change per lap is a safe step. Keep.
habit: Cue (hand finds phone) plus one small change this lap. That's a rep. Keep.
contemplative: Hand on the phone, notice it like breathing. This I can live. Cut 'this book never claimed it comes standard.'
stress: Concrete trigger, one small change, and admits the capacity isn't standard. The 'all along' coda is a touch guru; trim it.
gamedesigner: Clear trigger (hand finds phone), clear move (change one thing this lap). Controller in hand. Close to a felt win signal.
structural: Noticing the phone 'lightly, like breathing' is mindfulness standing in for a product designed to be grabbed. 'Room full of people' never gets a lever.
satirist: Phone, same argument, change one thing this lap. Plain and usable. 'What this practice was asking all along' is a little church-bell; trim.
mythmaker: The hand finding the phone and the argument starting again are faces I recognise. The last line claims a payoff it hasn't set up.

modeler: A fine closing line, and short.
skeptic: A closing line. It's fine.
clinician: A neat close. Little value on its own.
habit: A nice closing beat. Earns little on its own.
contemplative: A soft ending, a circle. Good.
stress: A clean close. Ornamental, but short.
gamedesigner: Fine closing beat.
structural: A closing flourish. Harmless.
satirist: A tidy closing line, but redundant after U0586.
mythmaker: A tidy closing beat, but thin after the canopy. It could go.

modeler: A graceful close, but the loop image is ornamental here. Fine as a coda, nothing more.
skeptic: A pleasant cadence with nothing to evaluate. Fine as a closer, and it doesn't earn more.
clinician: A graceful close, but there's nothing to hold onto. Name the one smallest place to start tomorrow.
habit: 'Tomorrow morning it starts again' says when but not what. Hand me the first rep for tomorrow morning.
contemplative: A quiet, honest closing. Tomorrow morning it starts again. Small and fitting where it sits.
stress: A soft landing with no claim. Harmless, and it earns nothing.
gamedesigner: Nice loop-restart closer, tomorrow morning. Warm, but asks nothing specific of me.
structural: A graceful close. 'The room you're in' is as structural as it gets.
satirist: A cute loop-shaped sign-off, and short enough to forgive. It says nothing new, but the 'tomorrow morning' image ties the book together. Fine.
mythmaker: Tomorrow morning becomes a rhyme the next part picks up. Quiet, earned closure.

modeler: A loop closing as a book closing is a rhyme, not a mechanism. Fine as a hinge, but it carries little weight.
skeptic: Pleasant cadence, nothing to test. Remove the rhythm and it's a reminder to start tomorrow. Fine as a closer, earns little.
clinician: Gentle close, but 'begin wherever life asks' is a vague try. Name one tiny first move for tomorrow morning.
habit: 'Begin wherever life asks first' isn't a starting line. Pick one: first thought, one sentence, before feet hit floor.
contemplative: Gentle and short. A soft closing, warm, though it teaches nothing new. Let it stay small.
stress: Pleasant send-off, no stakes. Fine as a closer, but it gives no point of failure and no instruction beyond 'begin.'
gamedesigner: Nice loop-close outro and a start point. Light, but it does its job as a checkpoint screen.
structural: A graceful exit with nothing in it. 'First meeting of the day' hints at the group scale and then drops it.
satirist: Pleasant send-off, but 'close it the way a loop closes' is a bow on a bow. Fine as a coda, nothing more.
mythmaker: A graceful exit with nobody in it. Give me one person's first word tomorrow morning, not three abstract starting places.

modeler: Loop closure as daily restart, with an actionable first step: one chosen word. Small local rule, no hand-waving. Works.
skeptic: Small, doable instruction; no overclaim. 'A tone you chose' presumes more self-control than most mornings allow, but it's an invitation.
clinician: Best kind of ending: tiny, specific, doable today, and it frees the reader from 'finishing'. Safe on a bad day.
habit: Tomorrow-morning cue, first word to first person, on purpose, chosen tone. This is a rep I can do at 7:04.
contemplative: The first word you say, on purpose, in a tone you chose. This is the whole teaching. Lovely.
stress: Small, doable first step, no promise of transformation. Modest claim. I like it.
gamedesigner: Tiny, concrete first move: say the first word on purpose. Loop-close framing gives a restart, not an ending.
structural: Choosing your tone with the first person you see: pure private resolution. Soothing, and soaks attention that action needed.
satirist: Begin with the first word you say to the first person, on purpose. A tiny doable act. Loop closing is a metaphor but harmless.
mythmaker: First word to the first person, said on purpose: small, doable, a real ending beat. Earned.

modeler: A clear purpose statement: shared description so the conversation doesn't collapse into blame. Good.
skeptic: Clear statement of purpose: talking about patterns without collapsing into blame. Useful.
clinician: 'So the conversation doesn't collapse into blame' is a clear, humane purpose.
habit: A clear promise: talk about patterns without blame. That's a real problem.
contemplative: Plain purpose: talk without blame. Clear and useful.
stress: A clear purpose statement: talk patterns without blame. Good.
gamedesigner: A clear goal statement. Exactly the onboarding I want.
structural: A clear purpose: talking about patterns without blame. Useful, if modest.
satirist: A plain statement of purpose. Useful.
mythmaker: A clear purpose statement: 'doesn't collapse into blame.' Useful framing, nothing more.

modeler: Clear job statement: talk about the loop, not about blame. That's exactly what a shared diagram does.
skeptic: A clear purpose with recognisable examples. Making it about the loop rather than fault is a real, testable aim.
clinician: 'About the loop, not whose fault it is' is the shame-to-guilt move in one line. Strong.
habit: Clear purpose, real examples: the fight you keep having, the habit you slide back into. I know why to read on.
contemplative: About the loop, not whose fault it is. That is reconciliation, plainly said. A good doorway.
stress: Stakes are clear: the recurring fight, the blame. A purpose stated plainly enough to be checked.
gamedesigner: Clear goal up front: talk about the loop, not the fault. Great onboarding for a new level.
structural: Shifting the talk from fault to the loop is useful for couples. Keep it from becoming 'nobody's fault' when someone does profit.
satirist: Says plainly what it is: talk about the loop, not about whose fault it is. The best purpose statement so far. No costume.
mythmaker: 'The fight you keep having' lands for everyone. Clear promise, real stakes.

modeler: Concrete outcomes listed. Useful.
skeptic: Concrete outcomes. Good.
clinician: Clear deliverables.
habit: Outcome-focused, three concrete abilities. Good.
contemplative: Three skills named simply. Good signage.
stress: Outcome list. Functional.
gamedesigner: Concrete unlocks listed upfront. Great progress framing.
structural: A plain outcomes list. Fine, but it does no work.
satirist: Concrete outcomes. Good.
mythmaker: A promise of skills. Functional signage.

modeler: Concrete deliverables, testable. Good contract with the reader.
skeptic: Overpromises: 'stop arguing,' 'stops having a villain.' Compared to what baseline? Say 'argue less' and I'd believe it.
clinician: Clear, concrete outcomes. 'Stops having a villain' is good.
habit: Three skills, each with a payoff. This is how to promise behaviour, not insight. Keep it.
contemplative: Useful promises, but three clever 'so the X stops' clauses read like a sales pitch. Keep one and show it.
stress: Concrete promises, and good. But 'stops arguing' and 'stops having a villain' oversell. Say 'less often.'
gamedesigner: Excellent unlock list. I know what abilities I'll earn. That's a quest log.
structural: Concrete payoffs, and the group-decision one actually reaches past the individual. Good.
satirist: Promises you can check, which I respect. 'Name your scale' is undefined jargon here. 'Say a conflict twice so it stops having a villain' is the hook.
mythmaker: Practical promises, but it reads as a syllabus. 'Stops having a villain' is the one line with a pulse.

modeler: Naming the scale before the claim is a usable skill. 'Stops needing a villain' is a promise, not a stated outcome. Clear signpost.
skeptic: Useful promises, but 'argue less' and 'stops needing a villain' are stated as outcomes. Compared to what? Hedge them: 'tends to'.
clinician: Concrete promises; 'so it stops needing a villain' is lovely de-shaming. Reads as a checklist, not something felt.
habit: Clear outcomes I can test. 'Say a conflict twice' is vague until Chapter 5, but fine as a promise.
contemplative: Useful promises, but three clauses in one breath. One line per skill, and fewer parentheses.
stress: Promises are specific enough to fail: 'argue less.' Good. 'Stops needing a villain' oversells; say 'needs one less often.'
gamedesigner: Good goal-setting, but three new mechanics stacked in one line before I've learned any. Difficulty spike in the briefing.
structural: Promises group-decision skills that stop rooms reaching for failed fixes. A real collective payoff, stated plainly.
satirist: A clear promise of skills. 'Say a conflict twice' is cryptic before the chapter explains it. Workmanlike.
mythmaker: 'Stops needing a villain' is a real promise. Still a list of skills with no person in it. Show me who stops arguing.

modeler: Concrete outcomes, and 'name your scale' is a real scale check. A promise list, not an idea, but a useful one.
skeptic: Promised outcomes ('stop arguing past each other', 'less often') are specific, but stated as certain gains. Dense sentence; hedge and cut.
clinician: Concrete payoffs: name your scale, say a conflict twice. Clear promises; a little abstract about who is hurting.
habit: Outcome promises tied to behaviours: name your scale, say conflict twice, zoom levels. Concrete, though it's three, not one.
contemplative: Useful, but three promised abilities in one long italic sentence. Too much to take in at once. Offer one.
stress: Outcomes specific enough to check: fewer arguments past each other. Risky promises, which is good. Hedged with 'less often'.
gamedesigner: Tells the player what skills they unlock, like a level preview. Concrete payoffs, though some are far off.
structural: Scale naming and zoom levels for group decisions: closest thing here to seeing the system. Concrete payoffs. Add who sets the group's rules.
satirist: Names concrete payoffs: stop arguing past each other, fewer failed fixes. Specific promises, plain. A little long, but useful.
mythmaker: Real benefits, like friends who stop arguing past each other, but crammed into one dense sentence. Break it up.

modeler: Scale-tagging is my third test. But it's a promise list; show one zoom-level mismatch to earn more.
skeptic: Clear, usable skills. But 'so the room reaches for the same failed fix less' promises an effect with no evidence. Say 'may'.
clinician: Names concrete payoffs, and 'needs a villain less often' lowers blame. Good. Abilities are a bit abstract; name one first step.
habit: Three named abilities, each tied to a real moment. Good. Still no first rep: which scale do I name tomorrow, and in what conversation?
contemplative: Three promises, each stuffed with 'scale' and 'zoom level'. I cannot take it in one exhale. Say one plain thing you will be able to do.
stress: Concrete, checkable abilities. Fine promise, but nothing here says how you'd know it worked.
gamedesigner: Good goal list, but three abilities crammed in one dense sentence. Split into three short beats.
structural: Scale-naming helps groups stop talking past each other, a real lever. But it stays at conversation level; no rules or institutions named. Add one structural example.
satirist: Plain promise with three doable things. Not wondrous, but I'd say it at a bar. Useful, no costume.
mythmaker: Clear payoffs, the two friends arguing past each other is a real face. But 'zoom level' is still a lecture word; show one pair.

modeler: Navigation aid. Honest and short.
skeptic: Honest skip guidance. It respects the reader's time.
clinician: A respectful shortcut for a tired reader. Good.
habit: The best kind of respect for my time. Keep it.
contemplative: Kind to the busy reader. Honest.
stress: An honest skip guide that respects the reader's time. Good.
gamedesigner: A critical-path hint respects the player. Good.
structural: Reader-routing note. Fine.
satirist: Telling readers what they can skip is rare and honest. Keep it.
mythmaker: A helpful skip note. Practical and honest.

modeler: Useful triage. Nothing to model, but it does its job.
skeptic: Useful triage that respects the reader's limited attention. No complaints.
clinician: Triage for a reader who's short on time, with a realistic entry point. Exactly the structure Gillihan would want.
habit: Triage for busy readers is respectful and useful. 'Chapter 5 only' is the two-minute version of this part.
contemplative: Generous to a busy reader. Plain and needed. Nothing to remove.
stress: Respects the reader's time, and admits the rest is explanation. No ego. Useful.
gamedesigner: Speedrun route for busy players. Respectful of time; tutorial designers should copy this.
structural: Practical reading triage. It respects the reader's time.
satirist: A book that tells you which chapters to skip is either honest or confident. Either way, it's useful.
mythmaker: A generous shortcut for the reader. It's pure function and fine for that.

modeler: Useful triage, nothing more. It earns its place by routing the reader.
skeptic: Honest triage, respects the reader's time. Does its job as navigation.
clinician: Kind triage for a tired reader: one chapter, one argument. Useful navigation, nothing more needed.
habit: Love this. Minimum dose, plus a trigger: your next argument. Exactly how to cut reading to one rep.
contemplative: Kind to a busy reader. It does one thing plainly. Good.
stress: Honest triage. 'Where they stop' admits limits up front. Useful navigation, nothing more.
gamedesigner: Fast-path for busy players. Great onboarding courtesy: one chapter, next argument. Plays well.
structural: Useful triage. Points the reader at the one tool to try next. No politics here, and it needs none.
satirist: Honest triage for busy readers; Bryson would approve the confession that the rest is support. Useful, not interesting.
mythmaker: Useful signposting. 'Your next argument' nods at stakes, but this is a map, not a scene.

modeler: Practical reading paths. Honest about which parts carry the load. Not abstract; it helps the reader triage.
skeptic: Triage guidance respects the reader's time. Gives a try-it test in a real argument. Doesn't claim results. Pleasantly modest.
clinician: Gives a triage path and one next step. Exactly what an overwhelmed reader needs.
habit: One thing if one, three if three, try in next argument. Great triage with a clear cue. Do this.
contemplative: Kindly tells me where to begin if I have little time. Clear. A map line, not a teaching.
stress: Triage for the reader, one chapter, try it next argument. Low ego, testable.
gamedesigner: Clear fast path: one thing, then three. Good onboarding. Try it in your next argument sets the test.
structural: Practical reading triage, clear and honest. But 'your very next argument' keeps everything personal. Useful navigation, little substance.
satirist: Triage for the reader: one chapter, three chapters, rest is why. Exactly the humility a handbook needs. Practical.
mythmaker: Clear triage for a busy reader, and kind about time. Functional, no heart, and that's acceptable here.

modeler: Bridge sentence. Neutral.
skeptic: Bridge sentence. 'Quietly lose' is asserted, but fine.
clinician: Transition only.
habit: Framing. Fine, but skippable.
contemplative: Fine transition. 'Quietly lose' is a nice phrase; the rest is scaffolding.
stress: Transition. Fine.
gamedesigner: Restates U0595. Cut.
structural: Transition. Fine.
satirist: A fine bridge, with nothing in it.
mythmaker: Bridge prose. 'Sentences quietly lose the thing' needs one lost sentence to show it.

modeler: Sharp: the sentence deletes your own link in the loop. That missing arrow is the whole problem. Great example.
skeptic: Excellent example: the sentence drops the speaker's own contribution. That's exactly the asymmetry Epley documents. It works.
clinician: The example sentence hits home. But it diagnoses without a step, and could make the speaker feel accused. Point toward the fix.
habit: The 'you always shut down' example hits home. The paragraph diagnoses but doesn't yet hand over the better sentence.
contemplative: The 'you always shut down' example lands in the kitchen, where people live. It shows the problem without a lecture.
stress: The 'you always shut down' example lands. It shows the deleted half precisely.
gamedesigner: Strong hook: the shutdown sentence is instantly recognisable and shows exactly what's missing.
structural: The shut-down example is relatable and limited to two people.
satirist: The 'you always shut down' example shows exactly what an ordinary sentence drops. Concrete, sharp, and everyone has heard that line. Keep.
mythmaker: 'You always shut down when I bring it up' puts a real couple in the room. That sentence carries the whole argument.

modeler: An unfinished-by-design disclaimer. Honest, but wordy.
skeptic: It openly calls itself the least settled part. Admitted uncertainty, and I'll take it.
clinician: The honest admission of incompleteness is fine. A bit long.
habit: An honest disclaimer, but long. One sentence would do.
contemplative: Humility stretched to a paragraph becomes its own vanity. One sentence: it is unfinished.
stress: Admitting it's unfinished is humble. Two sentences of throat-clearing are too many.
gamedesigner: Honest, but a hedge before play starts. Shorten to one line.
structural: Honest that it's unfinished, and 'many hands' is good. It invites collective revision, at least of the language.
satirist: Admitting it's unfinished is good. Making a virtue of it in four sentences is less good. Trim it.
mythmaker: The humble framing is fine, but it's a disclaimer before we've seen anything. Move it to the end.

modeler: Fine humility, but it's throat-clearing. Trim to one line.
skeptic: Admits it's the least settled part and points to where it fails. That is calibration done right.
clinician: Honest about its limits, which builds trust. Nothing for a reader to use here.
habit: A disclaimer about how settled the language is. The reader can't do anything with it. Trim to one clause.
contemplative: The humility is honest. It is still a note about the book, not about my life. It could be one sentence.
stress: Admits it's unsettled and points to where it fails. Exactly the humility I want.
gamedesigner: Honest framing, but a meta beat right after the hook stalls momentum. Shorten.
structural: Honest about being unfinished. 'Many hands' gestures at collective work but never names a mechanism.
satirist: Admits it's unfinished and says where. Bokonon outlawed himself; this author at least footnotes himself. Fine.
mythmaker: An honest admission, but it's meta-commentary with no heart in it. Shorten it.

modeler: A language that grows by repetition is self-consistent. Pointing to where it fails, Chapter 8, is honest. Thin, though.
skeptic: Admits it's unsettled and points to where it fails. That's the calibration I want. The growth-by-use parallel is tidy, though it isn't evidence.
clinician: Honest about limits, which I respect. Offers the reader nothing to do or feel; it's housekeeping.
habit: Honest framing, but no action. 'Precise enough for tonight' points at a rep it never names.
contemplative: Honest humility. But it talks about the language, not to me. One sentence would hold it.
stress: Admitting it's unsettled is humility I respect. But 'grows by use' isn't a test; say what correction looks like.
gamedesigner: Honest beta label, readable. No move for me though; it's patch notes, not play.
structural: A language that grows by collective correction is the right instinct. It needs a mechanism: where do the corrections go, and who merges them?
satirist: Admits it's unfinished, which is to its credit. It's still a book praising its own humility. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: The language growing the way loops grow is a nice idea. Who corrects it? Nobody is holding it.

modeler: Self-similar claim: a language of repetition grows by repetition. Correction as feedback is stated, but it's more promise than tool.
skeptic: Rare admission: least settled, says where it breaks, and treats breakage as data. Exactly the calibration I reward. Points to Chapter 8.
clinician: Honest about limits and invites 'try tonight', and breaking is correction, not failure. Mild shame protection.
habit: Try it tonight, and breakage is the correction. Invites use with a cue. Honest. Could name which sentence to try.
contemplative: Humble: not settled, try it tonight, correct it. I trust it. A few clauses could go.
stress: Admits the unsettled state, invites correction. Humility with a pointer to Chapter 8's limits. Close to unfalsifiable only if 'correction' is vague.
gamedesigner: Invites playtesting and treats breakage as feedback. Honest, but mostly meta-talk about the language.
structural: Admits unsettledness and invites correction by use. Honest, practical, collective revision. Rare humility; I'll give it all four.
satirist: Admits it's unsettled and that breakage is the correction. Bokonon would nod. The growing-by-use logic is clever, and it says where.
mythmaker: Admitting it's unsettled and inviting correction is honest, a bit brave. No one yet shows where it broke.

modeler: Crisp epigraph that states the chapter's thesis exactly.
skeptic: A neat epigraph, and the 'lines versus loops' claim gets tested below.
clinician: A crisp epigraph that sets up the chapter's thesis.
habit: A sharp epigraph that states the chapter's thesis.
contemplative: Short and true. A little clever, but it serves.
stress: A crisp epigraph that states the chapter's real claim. Works.
gamedesigner: Crisp epigraph that sets up the chapter's rule.
structural: A neat epigraph that sets up the line-versus-loop thesis.
satirist: A crisp, original epigraph that states the chapter's thesis. Keep it.
mythmaker: A crisp epigraph that sets the chapter's whole problem in eight words.

modeler: Earns its spot: grammar has a terminal state and a loop doesn't. Compact and true.
skeptic: Memorable because of its rhythm, not its content. An epigraph that only scans, though at least it's harmless.
clinician: Elegant epigraph, and 'tomorrow morning' hints at another chance. Fine in its place.
habit: A neat line, and it nods at the morning cue, but an epigraph earns little for me. Fine to keep short.
contemplative: Simple and true. A loop has tomorrow morning. I feel it in my body. Keep.
stress: Compact and true enough. It's an epigraph doing its job, nothing more.
gamedesigner: Tight epigraph that sets the rule of the level. Works as a title card.
structural: A nice line that does nothing beyond setting a mood.
satirist: A decent epigraph: short, and it does a little work. The koan voice is creeping in, but it's only one line.
mythmaker: A crisp epigraph, and 'tomorrow morning' rhymes with the close of Part Two. Good.

modeler: Neat line: a sentence terminates and a loop recurs. It sets up the chapter's real claim efficiently.
skeptic: Lovely, and it asserts more than it shows. As an epigraph it's clear but carries no weight.
clinician: Clean epigraph, but 'wakes up with you tomorrow' could land as dread at 3 a.m. Fine in place.
habit: Neat epigraph and it sets up the morning. Does its job, nothing to do.
contemplative: A clean contrast, easy on the breath. It points somewhere but asks nothing of me.
stress: Neat line, decoration. Earns nothing on its own; the next passages do the work.
gamedesigner: Tidy hook epigraph that sets up the sentence-vs-loop contrast. Earns its spot as a title card.
structural: Neat epigraph that only decorates. It doesn't ask who wakes the loop up.
satirist: Neat epigraph, nearly a joke. It survives the bar test. It's still decoration.
mythmaker: 'Wakes up with you tomorrow morning' gives the loop a pulse and puts it in your bed. Good epigraph.

modeler: Neat: a sentence ends, a loop restarts. That's the difference between event and structure. Slogan only.
skeptic: Elegant and easy, which is the warning. A sentence-versus-loop contrast sounds profound; what would show it's true?
clinician: Evocative, though 'a loop wakes up with you' may land heavy for someone dreading mornings.
habit: Gorgeous line, but a line, not a step. Great. What do I do on Monday?
contemplative: A loop wakes up with you tomorrow. Quiet and true. Slightly clever, yet it serves the reader.
stress: Nice line, no claim to break. Pretty, not tested.
gamedesigner: Memorable line with the tomorrow-morning hook. No move, but it earns its spot as a tone-setter.
structural: Elegant line about loops versus sentences. Pure aphorism; no rule, owner or lever. Mood, not mechanism.
satirist: Decent aphorism with a hum. Loop wakes up with you is cute. But it's epigraph: pretty, no measurement, no instruction.
mythmaker: A sentence stops, a loop wakes up with you: that's a line I'll remember. Bring it back later.

modeler: A relatable prompt. Good setup.
skeptic: An immediate, relatable prompt.
clinician: A relatable everyday hook.
habit: Starts with a rep and a morning-phone cue. Perfect.
contemplative: Begins with my morning phone. Present and ordinary. Good.
stress: A relatable prompt. Fine.
gamedesigner: Opens with a move I make. A perfect tutorial start.
structural: The phone example is relatable, and it's the most engineered environment there is. Watch whether the book notices.
satirist: The phone example is universal. A good hook.
mythmaker: The morning phone check. Everyone's guilty. A great entry point, because it puts the reader in the bed.

modeler: Good hook, gets the reader to produce data. It sets up U0602, and that's all it needs to do.
skeptic: A good exercise that makes the reader produce the evidence themselves. It works.
clinician: Small, specific and doable right now. This is what a next step looks like.
habit: Yes. A rep right now, tied to a real cue: feet not yet on the floor. Exactly what I want.
contemplative: An invitation to stop and try, now, in bed. This is practice, not theory. More of this.
stress: Puts the reader on the hook immediately. Cheap, effective.
gamedesigner: Controller in my hands. Best move in the section: try it now, then get compared.
structural: A good hook. But the phone habit gets framed as yours alone, with no word yet about the app built to be checked.
satirist: A direct exercise aimed at the reader's actual morning. Cheap, but it works. Nobody gets out of bed before checking.
mythmaker: It puts the reader in their own bed with the phone. That's the right face: yours.

modeler: Good. Get a data sample from the reader before you hand them the model. That's Sellers' playtest instinct.
skeptic: Good: you commit to a sentence before seeing the argument, which guards against hindsight. Real experiment, low cost.
clinician: Small, doable, non-judgmental exercise on a habit almost everyone has. Exactly the right size of step.
habit: Perfect. Two-minute rep, an exact cue (before feet hit floor), done right now. More of this.
contemplative: Yes. A practice before the theory, in my own bed. This is how teaching should begin.
stress: A real exercise with a payoff a minute later. That's a falsifiable setup: if the sentence closes the loop, the thesis wobbles.
gamedesigner: Excellent: player acts immediately and saves the output for a payoff. Textbook tutorial beat.
structural: Good hook and personal. Notice that the question is 'why do you check', not 'who built it to be checked'.
satirist: An exercise that costs one sentence and pays off in a minute. Concrete, personal, no incense.
mythmaker: Puts the reader's own feet on the floor. The best kind of exposition: you live it before it's explained.

modeler: Well-chosen sample sentence. Familiar.
skeptic: An honest example sentence. Readers will recognise it.
clinician: Accurate, non-judgmental phrasing of anxiety relief.
habit: A sentence everyone could say. Relatable.
contemplative: I have said this sentence. It works as a mirror.
stress: A recognizable example sentence. Does its job.
gamedesigner: A model answer I recognise myself in. Works in place.
structural: A familiar sentence. It works as the specimen.
satirist: Everyone has said this sentence. It works.
mythmaker: A believable confession sentence. It does its job as the specimen.

modeler: Recognizable. But 'so I keep doing it' already half-closes the loop, so the next paragraph's 'deleted' claim is weaker.
skeptic: A plausible sample answer. It's recognisable, and it sets up the deleted feedback well.
clinician: Relatable and non-judgmental. It works as a setup.
habit: A relatable sample answer. It works only as setup for the next beat, which is fine.
contemplative: An honest little sentence, and I recognise myself. It serves the exercise well in its place.
stress: Recognizable and honest. It sets up the trap well.
gamedesigner: Model answer lets me compare my attempt. Good feedback beat, though the reveal of what's missing comes later.
structural: A believable sample sentence. It does its job as setup.
satirist: A believable sentence the reader probably wrote themselves. It sets up the reveal well. Works in its place.
mythmaker: Everyone has said this sentence. It sets up the payoff well.

modeler: The sample answer makes the trap concrete: the chain stops at relief. It does its job as an exhibit.
skeptic: A plausible sample answer. It also quietly assumes the reader's motive is anxiety. Offer two or three alternative answers.
clinician: Recognisable and compassionate sample: anxiety named, relief honest. Works as a mirror.
habit: A recognisable sample answer that lets me check mine. It works in its place.
contemplative: I recognise myself here. Plain and true. It does its job as a mirror.
stress: Recognisable sample sentence. Does its job as a specimen; scores only on recognition.
gamedesigner: Sample answer lets me check mine. Feedback signal by comparison. Small but works.
structural: A believable sample sentence, all i-frame. Fine as a setup, as long as the s-frame arrives later.
satirist: A sample answer that rings true. Readers will recognize themselves. It does its small job.
mythmaker: A real, honest voice and a small cost. It works as the setup the next passage needs.

modeler: Relatable sample: anxiety, phone, relief. A loop's first lap, with no stock and no limiter yet.
skeptic: Relatable first-person sample, honest in tone. A single anecdote, so it proves nothing, but it is only offered as an example.
clinician: Nonjudgmental anxious-morning scene; the 'it calms me' honesty avoids blame. Nothing to do yet.
habit: Real morning moment, phone for calm. Perfect cue-and-craving example, instantly recognizable. Just the right size.
contemplative: Plain, honest, human. I recognize the morning. A good seed. It needs nothing added.
stress: Relatable confession. A quote of experience, not an argument. Fine as an anchor.
gamedesigner: Instantly relatable first-person moment; the reader sees themselves. Just a seed, so the payoff must follow.
structural: Relatable phone anxiety quote. But who built the phone to be reached for? Setup is fine; blame is parked on the user.
satirist: The phone-calming line is painfully true. Plain first-person speech the reader owns. It works because there's no concept in it.
mythmaker: A real voice, anxious phone grab at wake-up. A face with a small cost. Recognisable instantly.

modeler: A reinforcing loop in one breath, relatable. But what limits it? Name the stock (anxiety) and the balancing side.
skeptic: Modest, recognizable loop, and it claims only what the reader can check. Honest, but it is one anecdote, not a base rate.
clinician: Names the anxiety loop with no blame in it. A reader at 3 a.m. recognizes themselves. Add one small interrupt step.
habit: A real cue-routine-reward loop in one breath. I can see my own 7:04 phone grab. Now give me the swap.
contemplative: Small, true, felt. I know this morning. Nothing extra. It lets the reader notice the loop without being told.
stress: Recognizable loop, and it admits the relief is real. But it's a mere anecdote; name what breaks the loop.
gamedesigner: Relatable loop, clear cause and effect. But it's a cutscene; add a 'spot your version' move.
structural: Relatable phone loop, but pure i-frame. Who designed the phone to feel like relief? Name the engagement incentives, not just the habit.
satirist: Honest, tiny, true. Everyone has done this. Names the loop without any capitalized Concept. Nothing grand, and that's why it works.
mythmaker: A person with a phone and a small cost. Lovely and plain, but nothing turns yet; the stakes stay small.

modeler: Relief now, sensitisation later: a reinforcing loop with a delayed side. A real diagnosis of what the sentence hides.
skeptic: The sensitisation mechanism is plausible and roughly matches reinforcement research. A good illustration of what the one-way sentence leaves out.
clinician: Explains reinforcement well. Add one small interruption step, like a delay before checking.
habit: Shows the loop lapping itself on my own phone habit. Insight plus mechanism.
