satirist: 'Most were never chosen, only defaulted into' is the useful sting. The examples are real. The trailing Seed cross-reference is jargon housekeeping.
mythmaker: 'Never chosen, only defaulted into' stings in the right way. The phone at every pause is your own hand.

modeler: Clear, though 'becomes' skips the interaction. A rule repeated alone doesn't make a form; coupling does.
skeptic: A plain definition.
clinician: Clear.
habit: Clear definition.
contemplative: Clear enough. A single image would help it live.
stress: Adequate definition.
gamedesigner: Fine glossary entry. No example.
structural: Plain definition.
satirist: Adequate. One example (a habit becomes a reputation) would make it stick.
mythmaker: Clear enough, but lifeless. 'Visible from a distance' wants a picture of what you'd see.

modeler: The desire path is a real stock built by local flows, and a balancing loop too: trampled grass invites more feet. Perfect example.
skeptic: The desire-path example is good. A reputation built from one person's follow-through is fine. Clean.
clinician: The path across the lawn is a clear image. Conceptual only.
habit: The path across the lawn is a great image. It's still a definition with no behaviour attached.
contemplative: The path across the lawn is a fine image. 'Meeting everything around it' is extra. The italic restatement repeats it.
stress: The desire path is a good, checkable image. A clear definition.
gamedesigner: Lawn path image is perfect. Still a definition with no prompt to spot one of mine.
structural: The desire-path image is good, and a path could be paved. The book never says who does the paving.
satirist: Shortcuts across a lawn becoming a path is the right concrete image. 'Meeting everything around it' is fog. Cut that clause.
mythmaker: The shortcut across the lawn becoming a path is a classic image. Reputation is the human half, but it's thin.

modeler: The lawn path is a genuine stigmergy mechanism: local rule, accumulating stock, visible form. Best definition so far.
skeptic: The lawn path is a good, checkable image. 'Anyone who steps back' overrates observers. Others misread us predictably, per Epley.
clinician: Path-across-lawn is vivid. 'The thing people already expect of you' could sting a struggling reader; add that paths can be rewalked.
habit: Lawn path and reputation are vivid. 'The path your evenings have worn' begs for a rep: name tonight's shortcut.
contemplative: The lawn path is perfect. 'Against whatever it meets' is ornament; let the path speak alone.
stress: Lawn path is a solid, checkable image. Reputation example lands. Clear entry.
gamedesigner: Leans on Local Rule I haven't been taught in this unit. Lawn path helps; reputation line is the real hook.
structural: Desire paths are a good structural image. The real lesson: the planners who pave them. Name who reads the Global Form and acts.
satirist: The lawn path is a good fern. 'Global Form' is a capitalized Concept, but here it does work.
mythmaker: The path worn across the lawn and 'the path your evenings have worn' make an image that comes back. Strong.

modeler: 'Same pattern' one scale up: what repeats, and at what ratio? Otherwise it's nesting, not self-similarity.
skeptic: A plain definition. 'Same pattern' at every scale is assumed, not shown.
clinician: Clear, with good examples.
habit: The examples make it graspable.
contemplative: The parenthesis gives it a body. Good.
stress: Clear. The examples help.
gamedesigner: The nested examples make it click.
structural: The nesting chain reaches culture but stops short of law and markets. Close.
satirist: The parenthetical examples carry it. Good.
mythmaker: The parenthetical ladder helps. A serviceable definition.

modeler: Nesting asserted, not a fractal. What's the ratio, and what repeats exactly? Say 'same feedback structure,' not 'same shape.'
skeptic: 'The same shape at each layer' is the book's boldest unproven claim. As a glossary entry it should say 'resembles.'
clinician: Clear, but a definition with nothing to do.
habit: A clear but abstract nesting definition. Glossary filler for my purposes.
contemplative: Clear enough, but it stays in the head. Give one homely nesting I can see, like a family dinner.
stress: 'Same shape at each layer' is where theory-of-everything creeps in. Note where the nesting breaks.
gamedesigner: Clear nesting chain, but abstract. Give me one habit and have me name its next layer up.
structural: 'Laws and markets' named as the outer layer. Good. Now give one lever at that layer.
satirist: Clear enough, but 'the same shape at each layer' is asserted, not shown. One measured example would earn the fractal claim.
mythmaker: Russian dolls with no doll-maker. Clear, but no one lives at any of the layers.

modeler: It admits only the shape repeats, not a ratio, so it isn't a strict fractal. Habit-family-market is a plausible nesting, but it rhymes more than it holds.
skeptic: Habit-to-family is fine. Habit-to-market changes the mechanism while keeping the metaphor. 'Same shape' needs more support than a doll.
clinician: Shows the habit sits inside a market built to hook you: takes shame off the individual. Good.
habit: Dolls are clear, but it's a taxonomy with no move. Which layer do I touch tomorrow?
contemplative: Phone at dinner, a table of phones. Good. The 'laws and markets' layer is one doll too many.
stress: Doll-in-doll scaling is tidy, maybe too tidy. 'Shape repeats at each layer' needs a case where it doesn't.
gamedesigner: Doll metaphor and phone-to-market ladder are clear. Still pure receiving; ask me to name my own three layers.
structural: Best of the batch: 'laws and markets', 'an app built to be checked is a market.' Now say which layer you can actually lobby.
satirist: Matryoshka plus phone-at-dinner equals a market. Clear scaling, though 'shape not size' is asserted, not shown.
mythmaker: Phone at dinner, then the family table, then the market built to be checked. The nesting dolls finally get a face.

modeler: Self-similarity with the ratio-free part honest: the shape repeats, not the size. Habit to family to market passes my scale check.
skeptic: Nest, with the phone at dinner example moving across scales. 'You stand inside all three' is asserted; correlation of scale and shape isn't shown.
clinician: Nested dolls and phone-at-dinner place the person inside the system, not as the broken part. Good framing.
habit: Doll-in-doll nesting with phone-at-dinner example. Nice scale ladder. Still no step; where's my nesting rep?
contemplative: Doll inside a doll helps. Phone at dinner is mine. But four layers of nesting is heavy; give two.
stress: Phone-at-dinner to market ladder is vivid. 'Standing inside all three' stretches; where does nesting stop holding?
gamedesigner: Doll-in-doll plus phone at dinner makes the scales click. Gives me a lens but no test of whether I nested right.
structural: Yes: habit inside family inside a market built to be checked. Names structure, finally. Add who built it and the lever.
satirist: Phone at dinner, to family, to market: nesting dolls with a rung each. Concrete ladder, plain speech. Shape not size is the useful point.
mythmaker: Phone at dinner, family, market: doll inside doll with a human thread. You stand inside all three. Good.

modeler: Correctly tied to the leverage ladder. Fine.
skeptic: A plain definition.
clinician: Clear.
habit: Fine. It points back to the ladder.
contemplative: Plain, but it leans on a ladder elsewhere. Add one example.
stress: Fine, borrowed from Meadows. Credit her.
gamedesigner: Points elsewhere for the meaning. Add one example.
structural: Defines leverage without an owner. Who holds the lever matters as much as where it is.
satirist: Fine, but it's Meadows' term. Credit her here.
mythmaker: A definition by back-reference. It's clear, inert, and fine for a glossary.

modeler: The charger beats the vow: structure over willpower, credited to Meadows. Exactly right.
skeptic: Charger versus vow is the best example here: an environment change beats a promise. That's well supported. Keep it.
clinician: The charger beats the vow. This trades willpower for a change in the environment, which is clinically sound and kind.
habit: Moving the charger out of the bedroom: environment design over willpower. A best-in-book line. Keep it exactly.
contemplative: Move the charger out of the bedroom. Small and practised. Teaching should look like this.
stress: Moving the charger beats any vow. A real, cheap, testable intervention. Best definition in the list.
gamedesigner: Charger out of the bedroom beats nightly vows. Best glossary entry: an actual move.
structural: Charger beats vow: real choice architecture. But that's a nudge at household scale. The Meadows ladder deserves a collective example.
satirist: Moving the charger beats a nightly vow: practical, funny, true. Crediting Meadows is the right citation. Keep.
mythmaker: The charger out of the bedroom beats a nightly vow. Concrete, wry and human. Keep.

modeler: A return flow with distortion and an implied delay. Decent. Naming the delay would help.
skeptic: A plain definition. 'Real' is asserted.
clinician: Interesting idea, stated simply.
habit: A clear definition with the distortion caveat.
contemplative: What you send returns, changed. That is karma said humbly. Good.
stress: 'Real but distorted' is the honest version. Fine.
gamedesigner: Clear enough, and the 'distorted on return' twist is interesting.
structural: Clear enough. Fine as glossary.
satirist: 'What goes around comes around, bent.' That's the plain version. The capital F adds pomp, not meaning.
mythmaker: 'Returning distorted' is the boomerang that comes back bent. The image is begging to be named.

modeler: A long delay and distortion, both named. The child's impatience example lands. That's a real loop with a delay.
skeptic: The child's-impatience line claims a causal path without support. 'Bent by everything it passed through' partly saves it.
clinician: 'Your child's impatience with you' is guilt fuel at 3 a.m. Add that the Fold also carries repairs back.
habit: The child's impatience coming back to you hurts in the right way. Add the behaviour: what do I bring home instead?
contemplative: The impatience coming back through your child. It is quiet and it stings, rightly. A true word.
stress: 'Bent by everything it passed through' keeps it from being karma. The child example has real skin.
gamedesigner: Your impatience returning as your child's hits hard. Memorable, though no action attached.
structural: The child's-impatience image lands hard. It is still family scale only.
satirist: Your impatience coming back as your child's is a hard, real image. 'Bent by everything it passed through' is the honest hedge. Works.
mythmaker: Your impatience coming back as your child's impatience: real stakes, a real face. The best entry here.

modeler: The unrolled record as a tree is a nice, precise image of loop history.
skeptic: A clear enough definition.
clinician: Short and readable.
habit: Still abstract. One example leaf would help.
contemplative: 'Honest, unrolled record that a Loop's name compresses' is abstraction on abstraction. A child would not follow.
stress: 'Honest, unrolled record' is opaque in isolation. Add one example.
gamedesigner: 'Root rule' and 'leaf' are abstract. I can't picture a Tree yet. Give the phone example unrolled.
structural: 'Root rule, leaf every condition': opaque without the long gloss later. Simplify.
satirist: 'Honest, unrolled record that a Loop's name compresses.' Meaningless on first read. Needs an example.
mythmaker: 'Honest, unrolled record' is abstract on abstract. Show one habit's three different Tuesdays.

modeler: A sensible case for a small vocabulary. A bit self-congratulatory.
skeptic: Says nine words, and the list above shows nine. 'Earned through direct experience' assumes the reader has done the practices.
clinician: Justifies keeping the vocabulary small. Fine, if a little self-congratulatory.
habit: Nine words is good discipline. The justification is padding.
contemplative: Restraint praised at length undoes the restraint. 'Nine words, on purpose' would do.
stress: Nine words is restraint, and good. Then U0576 adds a tenth, Braid. Practice what this preaches.
gamedesigner: A small vocabulary is good design, and capping the rulebook at nine shows it was deliberate.
structural: A small vocabulary that spreads by use is a sound design principle for any movement.
satirist: Nine capitalized nouns is a dialect only to the converted. Plus Braid, Banner and Skein. Count again.
mythmaker: Defending nine words is sensible meta. 'Spreads like a dialect' is the only spark in it.

modeler: Says nine but U0609 to U0617 shows fewer here. Check the count. The adoption argument is sound but slight.
skeptic: Justifies the term count on adoptability. It's reasonable but more bookkeeping than insight. 'How a dialect spreads' needs a source.
clinician: A reasonable justification for the vocabulary, but it's meta. Nothing for the reader.
habit: Justifies the word count. The dinner-friend test is nice, but it's meta, not action.
contemplative: It defends the word count. 'Over dinner' is nice, but the paragraph explains itself rather than serving me. It could be half as long.
stress: Capping the vocabulary is a deliberate, falsifiable design choice. Good restraint.
gamedesigner: Nine-word cap is good design thinking. Make sure all nine are actually shown before claiming the count.
structural: Nine words so it spreads over dinner is sensible design for diffusion. Plain.
satirist: Defending nine words as minimal while coining Braid elsewhere: busy, busy, busy. And Tree isn't in the list shown. Make the count match the entries.
mythmaker: 'With a friend over dinner' is a pleasant aim, but this is housekeeping. Trim it.

modeler: Adoption cost as a design constraint is sound game-design reasoning. Short and justified.
skeptic: 'And be understood' is a prediction with no evidence behind it. A friend at dinner may just stare. Fix: 'if they've read it'.
clinician: Justifying the word count. Fine for the writer, nothing for a reader in trouble.
habit: 'Say it to a friend over dinner tonight' is a real rep. Good reason for keeping the list short.
contemplative: It defends itself more than it serves me. 'Words spread by being used' is the one line to keep.
stress: Reasoned cap at nine. But 'understood by a friend tonight' is untested optimism; the friend hasn't read Parts One and Two.
gamedesigner: Design rationale for nine words. Reasonable, but tells me why, gives me nothing to do. Cutscene.
structural: A defensible restraint argument, mostly self-congratulation. Spreading by use is fine, but no lever for doing it is named.
satirist: A word-count defense nobody asked for. 'Words spread by being used' is the true sentence; cut the rest.
mythmaker: It's justifying a word count. The dinner line is the only warmth. Cut it to that.

modeler: Nine words, try one tonight. Spread by use is a sound adoption loop. Testing it on someone is a decent experiment.
skeptic: Try a word on someone, watch their reaction: a cheap field test, and 'if they stare, explain' is honest. Modest and workable.
clinician: Try one word tonight is a small, doable step, and permission for staring is kind.
habit: Try one word on someone tonight: I think we're in a Loop. Exactly the two-minute version, with a fallback if they stare.
contemplative: Try one word on someone tonight; if they stare, explain. Gentle and practicable. Good ending.
stress: Nine words, try one tonight, expect stares. Cheap experiment, modest. Good.
gamedesigner: Try one on someone tonight, and if they stare, explain: a real play prompt with built-in feedback.
structural: Try a word on someone tonight: shared vocabulary is a small group tool. Cute, modest, low-stakes. Not a lever.
satirist: Nine words on purpose, say it tonight, and 'if they stare, explain it'. Self-aware and acts as a virus you are told to read.
mythmaker: Try one on someone tonight is a nice dare, and if they stare, explain. Brief, practical, a touch dry.

modeler: Unroll a cycle in time and you get a tree. That's genuinely right, like unrolling recursion. Dense, so simplify it.
skeptic: An interesting distinction, written abstractly. Use one concrete example of unrolling a loop.
clinician: Technical philosophy of compression. Lost on most readers.
habit: Theory about theory. Nothing to do here. Move it to Part Four.
contemplative: Temporal compression, unrolled cycles, complicated chains. This lives only in the head. Cut or simplify greatly.
stress: A cycle unrolled into a tree is clever. Complicated versus complex needs plainer handling.
gamedesigner: 'Temporal compression' is heavy. The complicated-vs-complex aside adds load. Simplify.
structural: Complicated versus complex via unrolling is clever but dense. A reader needs a diagram or a cut.
satirist: The complicated-chain-has-a-diagram quip is good. The rest is temporal-compression fog. Lead with one real example.
mythmaker: Temporal compression lectured in the abstract. The diagram/Tree line is clever, but nobody's here. Trim it to that line.

modeler: Unrolling a loop into a tree of runs is good. 'A complicated chain has a diagram' is cryptic. Give one example.
skeptic: Dense. The Tree/diagram distinction asks too much at once. One example unrolled across three evenings would be enough. Cut the complicated-chain coda.
clinician: 'The night you caught it halfway' is gentle. The tail about complex versus complicated chains loses lay readers.
habit: 'I snap when I'm tired' is real, but the Tree versus diagram distinction is philosophy. Cut, or make it 'list three evenings it ran'.
contemplative: The night you caught it halfway is beautiful. The ending about complex versus complicated and a diagram is cleverness. Stop at the branches.
stress: The 'I snap when tired' unrolling helps. The complex-versus-complicated tail loses lay readers. Cut the last two sentences.
gamedesigner: 'I snap when tired' unrolled is great. Complex vs complicated tail is a second concept too many.
structural: 'I snap when I'm tired' unrolled into evenings is vivid. The complex-versus-complicated tail gets dense.
satirist: 'A merely complicated chain has a diagram' is witty. The unrolling explanation is hard going, and the fact it's needed tells me Tree is a weak word.
mythmaker: The night it was the kids, the night it was the boss: lived detail. The complicated/complex coda loses me.

modeler: Rule versus executions, the unrolled recursion. 'Only something that repeats has a Tree' is a clean, testable boundary.
skeptic: 'I snap when I'm tired' is honest and concrete. The once-run chain distinction is sharp. Keep.
clinician: 'The night you caught it halfway' credits partial success, which is shame-aware. Last sentence drifts abstract.
habit: 'I snap when I'm tired' is relatable. Add one: tonight, write down three branches of your rule.
contemplative: 'The night you caught it halfway' is tender and true. The last sentence lives only in the head.
stress: The 'only something that repeats has a Tree' boundary is a real limit. Good. 'Night you caught it halfway' resonates.
gamedesigner: 'I snap when I'm tired' unrolled into evenings is vivid and personal. Last sentence is a needless rule-lawyer edge.
structural: Rule versus instances is clear and true to life. 'I snap when tired' never asks who set the hours that make you tired.
satirist: 'I snap when I'm tired,' unrolled into nights. The tree finally means something. The last line is a nice limit.
mythmaker: 'I snap when I'm tired' and 'the night you caught it halfway' carry a real turn. The last sentence goes cold.

modeler: Names transfer and the tree must be walked: a good tacit-knowledge point. It justifies the whole practice format.
skeptic: Names travel and experience doesn't. That's a sound point, consistent with what's known about tacit knowledge.
clinician: 'Can only be walked' is a good line that justifies practice over reading.
habit: 'Names transmit, trees must be walked' justifies doing over reading. Good.
contemplative: 'A Tree cannot be handed to anyone. It can only be walked.' This is the book at its best.
stress: Names transfer, Trees don't. A true limit, and it justifies the practice format. Strong.
gamedesigner: Names can be handed over, trees must be walked. That explains why this is a practice. Great.
structural: Names travel, experience doesn't. A real point, and it justifies the practice format.
satirist: 'Names are transmissible, the thing they compress is not.' A real insight, plainly said. Keep it.
mythmaker: 'A Tree can only be walked' is a strong, mythic line. It needs the kitchen pair actually talking.

modeler: The Go proverb makes a measurable cost of the transfer problem. Concrete and memorable. Keep.
skeptic: A lovely proverb. 'Measurably worse' implies data that isn't given. A proverb isn't a measurement.
clinician: A vivid proverb. It also gently warns against misapplying tools to yourself.
habit: A great proverb with a cost framing. Memorable.
contemplative: Lose two stones. Humbling and true. A lovely proverb, well placed.
stress: The Go proverb is real history that states a cost. Exactly what I want: knowledge that makes you worse first.
gamedesigner: Love it: a real game proverb about the cost of learning names without reasons. Plays perfectly.
structural: The Go proverb is a sharp, costed example. One of the better uses of a source here.
satirist: Great Bryson move, a real proverb with a real cost. Just say 'Go.' The coy periphrasis wastes it.
mythmaker: 'Learn the openings, lose two stones' is a great proverb with a real cost. Name the game. It's Go.

modeler: A lovely history point, but L-systems (1968) predate the coining of 'fractal'. Check the chronology before leaning on it.
skeptic: Roughly accurate history. A good case of a pattern being invisible until someone named it.
clinician: An interesting history aside. No reader use.
habit: A nice history beat. No action, but interesting.
contemplative: Ferns doing it all along. A gentle surprise. Clear.
stress: A genuine historical case: ferns ignored until Mandelbrot. One case, but a good one.
gamedesigner: A nice history beat. Clear and surprising.
structural: A nice piece of history of science. A pattern stayed invisible until a tool arrived.
satirist: A lovely history with no names. Say Mandelbrot, Koch, Britain's coastline, 1967. Then it's knowledge.
mythmaker: Ferns doing it the whole time, unseen. A lovely revelation image. Mandelbrot deserves a face here.

modeler: Koch 1904, Mandelbrot 1967 and 1975: accurate, and the right kind of evidence. Pattern invisible until named. Earned.
skeptic: Checkable history. The best argument here that naming enables seeing. Evidence instead of rhythm, and I approve.
clinician: Good history, well told. Intellectually satisfying, clinically neutral.
habit: A good history story, but my question stays the same: so what do I do on Monday? Trim it.
contemplative: 'Ferns had been doing it the whole time' charms me. But the dates and the history lecture don't help me breathe. Shorter.
stress: Passes the history test with dates and names. A documented case, not an anecdote. Strong.
gamedesigner: Fun lore drop, ferns doing it all along. History cutscene; skip-friendly but enjoyable.
structural: The fern-and-Mandelbrot history is a good case of something hidden in plain sight until it got a name. Interesting and clear.
satirist: Koch 1904, Mandelbrot 1967 and 1975, and the fern was doing it all along: a pure Bryson pass. The best history in the book.
mythmaker: 'Ferns had been doing it the whole time' is a delicious line. It's history without a human cost, but it's charming.

modeler: Good history: the pattern needed a formal handle before anyone saw it. Koch to Mandelbrot is accurate. A strong anecdote.
skeptic: Good history. 'Nobody got the idea from them' is a strong universal claim. Soften it to 'the formal idea'.
clinician: Nice history, clearly told. Zero use on a bad day; it's for the curious.
habit: Nice history, zero action. It earns its place only as setup for the next paragraph.
contemplative: A sweet story, and 'ferns had been doing it the whole time' smiles. Still a history lesson.
stress: Actual dated history, and it cuts against the fern myth. That's checking the record. Respect.
gamedesigner: Nice history beat, readable. But I'm idle and the payoff waits for the next paragraph. Fine lore, not play.
structural: Good history: invisible until named. Pure intellectual history, though, with no reader stake.
satirist: Bryson test passed: Koch 1904, Mandelbrot 1967 and 1975, ferns minding their business. Best history in the batch.
mythmaker: Ferns doing it the whole time is a great rhyme. History with a punchline, though no human cost.

modeler: Nice history: the name made the pattern visible. But 'fern as fractal' has a real ratio; say what repeats and at what scale.
skeptic: Dated, specific history (Koch 1904, Mandelbrot 1967, 1975) rather than anecdote. 'It took a word to make it visible' is a tidy overclaim, but sourced.
clinician: Engaging history of naming. Easy and interesting; no practical use for someone struggling.
habit: Interesting history, a word makes the pattern visible. But it's story, not action. Cut to two sentences or add a use.
contemplative: Interesting history, but it is the author's learning and not my breath. Dates and names crowd the one point: words make seeing.
stress: Real dated history: Koch, Mandelbrot. Passes my history test. Slight tidiness, 'the whole time' is hindsight; fine.
gamedesigner: Good story, a word making a pattern visible. But it's a cutscene; I only receive.
structural: Good history: a word made a pattern visible. Interesting, but a naming story for hobbyists; nothing implies collective action.
satirist: Koch 1904, Mandelbrot 1967 and 1975: names, dates, who was wrong first. This is Bryson's road. The fern as late poster child is a delight.
mythmaker: Mandelbrot and the coast of Britain is a real story of a word making something visible. Facts, little heart; give me his doubt.

modeler: Good history: the pattern was there, the formal idea came from Koch and Mandelbrot. State the repeating part and ratio.
skeptic: Dated, checkable history, nicely told. The last line, that a word made the pattern 'catchable', is a causal claim with no evidence.
clinician: Pleasant history, no reader in it. Harmless on a bad day, but nothing to use. Cut to one line or tie to a step.
habit: Nice history, zero action. Great. So what do I do on Monday? Cut to two sentences, or end on a word to coin.
contemplative: Interesting history, told simply. But it informs the head and asks nothing of me. Name what I might notice in a fern today.
stress: Real history, dated, and humble: the pattern preceded the word. This passes my history test. Needs a case where naming failed.
gamedesigner: Nice reveal that naming enables seeing. But I'm watching history, not playing. Hand me a fern to look at.
structural: Nice history of naming making a pattern catchable. Names as tools for groups is promising, but no lever or beneficiary is shown.
satirist: Bryson would approve: Koch, 1904, Mandelbrot, 1967 and 1975. Real names, real dates. Reader learns nothing to do, though.
mythmaker: Koch and Mandelbrot give it people, and 'a word to make it catchable' lands. But nobody here has anything to lose.

modeler: Vocabulary as detector: a fair epistemic claim. Good.
skeptic: One historical case is stretched into the book's thesis. Interesting, but one example isn't a base rate.
clinician: 'Had nowhere to land' validates the unnamed experience. Kind.
habit: Explains why the words exist. Fine.
contemplative: 'Nowhere to land' is tender. The bold slogan is unnecessary.
stress: 'We build the world' is bold. The fern case supports invisibility, not world-building. Narrow it.
gamedesigner: A good payoff for the history. Ties into the vocabulary's purpose.
structural: Words make patterns catchable. Agreed. 'Carbon footprint' did the same in reverse, for BP.
satirist: A fair moral of the history. 'Make catchable' is the honest pitch. Fine.
mythmaker: 'Nowhere to land' is a good phrase, and it lands the fern history back on the reader. Solid.

modeler: Fair inference from the fern. Slightly oversells: naming makes it catchable, not caught. Keep it.
skeptic: It draws the right inference from the fern case. Going from one historical case to 'what the nine words are for' is a leap. It's modestly made, though.
clinician: 'Had nowhere to land' validates the confusion instead of blaming the reader. Nice.
habit: Argues the words are useful without showing me using one. Add one catch: the next time the week repeats, say what?
contemplative: Something already happening that had nowhere to land. That helps. The bolded thesis restatement is ornament.
stress: It uses the history well, but leaps from ferns to 'we build the world.' One case backs the visibility point, not the thesis.
gamedesigner: Ties the words to my argument that keeps repeating. Purpose is clear; payoff for the history beat.
structural: Earns the 'cannot see' claim. The examples are domestic again; there's no institutional pattern made catchable.
satirist: It ties the Mandelbrot story to why the words exist. The bold thesis is incanted rather than said. 'Nowhere to land' is the plain version.
mythmaker: 'The argument you keep having' gives the abstraction somewhere to land. The pattern hiding in plain sight earns its place.

modeler: It ties the history to the thesis honestly. 'Somewhere to land' is soft, but the recurring-meeting examples ground it.
skeptic: The fractal history shows naming helps scientists. That doesn't transfer to catching your own argument. 'Is enough to catch it' overclaims.
clinician: Ends on a tiny, light step: 'here's the Loop again' to catch it. Naming as noticing, not judging. Works.
habit: The closing cue and line are a usable habit. 'Give somewhere to land to' is clumsy; untangle it.
contemplative: The closing line is the gift. Before it, too many words explaining the words. Trim by half.
stress: One case doesn't prove words make patterns visible. Bolded thesis plus 'give somewhere to land to' is tangled; fix syntax.
gamedesigner: Lands the history into my life and hands me a catch-phrase to use next time. Hook plus move.
structural: Naming makes patterns catchable, and 'the meeting that always ends the same way' gestures outward. Catching isn't changing. Who changes the meeting?
satirist: Connects the history to the reader's recurring meeting. Bolded creed is a costume, but 'not to sound like a practitioner' shows it knows.
mythmaker: It names the reader's repeating week. 'Give somewhere to land to' is clumsy. Bring the fern back here.

modeler: Pulled versus pushed words is a useful distinction. The Tywin quote is vivid but carries more than it should.
skeptic: Pulled versus pushed is a useful distinction. A line from a fictional character isn't evidence; he's an illustration.

contemplative: Pulled versus pushed is wise. Tywin is cleverness on display; a plainer example would serve better.
stress: Pulled versus pushed is useful. A fictional villain is thin backing. Use a historical usurper.

structural: Pushed labels: finally a hook for propaganda. Ask who pushes them and why. The Tywin quote is cute but unnecessary.
satirist: Word versus Label is a useful distinction, and the Tywin quote lands. Then the paragraph explains the joke twice.
mythmaker: Tywin, at last a character carrying the idea. Pulled against pushed is clear. The king image will stick.

modeler: Pulled versus pushed, with an order-of-arrival test. A falsifiable check, which I like. The Tywin quote is apt.
skeptic: 'Did the word arrive after the thing?' is a usable test. Quoting a fictional tyrant as authority is a little ironic, though apt.
clinician: The Word versus Label test is clear and the question is usable. The Tywin quote is decoration.
habit: 'Did this word arrive after the thing, or ahead of it?' is a question worth carrying all day. The Tywin quote is a garnish.
contemplative: Did the word come after the thing or ahead of it? That is a good, honest question. The Tywin quote performs. Let the question stand alone.
stress: The test question is actionable. A fictional villain as authority is thin; a real historical case would carry more weight.
gamedesigner: Word vs Label ends with a one-question test. That's a feedback tool. Tywin quote is a good hook.
structural: Pushed labels for loyalty is the BP 'carbon footprint' move. 'Did the word arrive ahead of the thing?' is a usable test.
satirist: Word pulled versus Label pushed is a real test. 'Did it arrive after the thing?' is portable. Tywin is a fun witness. Keep.
mythmaker: Tywin's line is a memorable face, and the arrived-after-or-ahead test is sharp. It's a villain quote, though, not a heart.

modeler: A cost-per-term discipline. Fine, but it asserts the vocabulary passes its own test without showing it.
skeptic: The book grades its own vocabulary and passes itself. How would you know? Let readers run the test.
clinician: Self-justification of the vocabulary. Cut or compress.
habit: Self-justifying. Cut it.
contemplative: The vocabulary praising itself. Let the reader judge.
stress: Self-certifying: the vocabulary passes its own test because the author says so. Let readers judge.
gamedesigner: The vocabulary grading itself. Self-congratulation. Trim.
structural: Self-justifying vocabulary audit. Asserted, not shown.
satirist: 'A word must earn its learning cost.' Good standard. Braid failed it a chapter ago.
mythmaker: The vocabulary grading itself. It's defensive housekeeping with no heart. Compress it.

modeler: Every term costs the reader something, so plain phrases should win. Good, and self-applied.
skeptic: Turns the test on itself and lets plain phrases win. That's the self-check I ask for. Well done.
clinician: An honest self-test, but it's for critics, not someone struggling.
habit: The book auditing itself is fair, but the reader has nothing to do. Compress it to one sentence.
contemplative: Humble, inviting the test on itself. Still this is the book talking about its own words. Could be one sentence.
stress: Turns the knife on itself. The author puts the book's own words at risk. That's skin. Keep.
gamedesigner: Inviting me to run the test on the book is agency, but give me a specific term to try it on.
structural: Self-audit of the book's vocabulary. Honest, and inward-facing.
satirist: Run the test on this book: that's the Bokonon move, and I respect it. Now actually run it. Braid fails.
mythmaker: A principled rule with no blood in it. Turning the test on the book is fair, but it's dry.

modeler: A falsifiable test for jargon, with each term as a learning cost. I like a framework that audits itself.
skeptic: A real test for whether each term earns its place, with a failure condition stated. Exactly what I want.
clinician: Practical jargon test anyone can run at work. Intellectual, not personal, but genuinely useful.
habit: 'This test' points back at something I can't see. Spell out the test in one line, then 'Try one.'
contemplative: 'This test' arrives without context. The phrase-should-win rule is wise; state it first, plainly.
stress: Gives the reader a kill switch for its own jargon. Rare and correct. This is skin on the page.
gamedesigner: 'Try one' with a pass/fail rule: swap in a plain phrase. Real self-test. 'This test' needs its referent though.
structural: Jargon as a cost billed to everyone who must learn it is an institutional point. 'Run it at your own work' is an actual lever.
satirist: A kill switch for its own jargon. Rare honesty, Bokonon-grade. Point it at your boss's slide deck too.
mythmaker: A practical jargon test, and honest about its own words. Dry. Show one coworker's acronym failing it.

modeler: A black box judged by its predictions: an engineer's idea of a good boundary. It wanders, so cut the king rerun.
skeptic: A worthwhile nuance about closed boundaries. It's dense and needs a plainer example than kings.
clinician: Hair-splitting about closed boundaries. Too abstract for any reader in need.
habit: A nuance on top of a nuance. Losing me. Compress it.
contemplative: A defense of the king example, which needed no defense. Too much. Cut.
stress: The closed-boundary nuance is good, but it's a long patch on the king example. Compress.
gamedesigner: The closed-boundary nuance muddies the clean test. Lost the player. Cut it or give a new example.
structural: The black-box-as-valid point is good, but convoluted. Cut it to the closing sentence of U0628.
satirist: A second king paragraph explaining a nuance of the first. Over-engineered. Merge it into one sentence.
mythmaker: The closed-boundary nuance muddies the clean king image. The idea is good, but it's overexplained. One sentence would do it.

modeler: Black-box trust judged by prediction is a real modeling stance. The pilot licence makes it clear.
skeptic: A good correction: a trusted closed boundary is fine if it predicts. The pilot's licence makes it concrete.
clinician: This caveat gets tangled. The pilot's licence image doesn't rescue the 'closed boundary' abstraction.
habit: The pilot's-licence caveat is subtle hair-splitting, and it muddies a clean test. Cut it, or turn it into a recheck habit.
contemplative: Qualifying the king with the pilot's licence piles caution on caution. The mind tightens. Perhaps this belongs in a footnote.
stress: A good correction with a clear pilot example. It stops the test from becoming reflexive cynicism.
gamedesigner: Caution reverses the rule I just learned. Pilot licence helps, but the twist confuses mid-tutorial.
structural: The pilot-licence point, that trusted institutions can be good names, is a needed correction. Clear.
satirist: The pilot's licence is a good example, but the boundary talk tangles it. It's a nuance on a nuance. Shorten it to the licence and the shouting king.
mythmaker: The pilot's licence works as an image, but the argument tangles. 'Had to be shouted' is the line to keep.

modeler: Trust as predictive validity is a good point. It leans on a king setup missing here, so out of context it's opaque.
skeptic: The pilot licence point about trusting what predicts well is sound. The king is opaque without context. Restate what a Label is.
clinician: Leans on a king example the reader doesn't have here. Confusing out of context; restate the setup in one line.
habit: The king metaphor is unclear out of context, and the pilot example is half-made. What do I check when I name something?
contemplative: Kings, labels, closed boundaries. I lose the thread. The pilot alone would teach this.
stress: Pilot's licence works, but leans on a king passage I can't see. Orphaned reference; restate the Label definition here.
gamedesigner: Lost the player: king, Label, closed boundary all unexplained here. Pilot licence helps, but too much missing context.
structural: The licence point about trusting institutions that predict well is good. 'Label', 'closed boundary' and the king lean on missing context. Define them here.
satirist: References a king the reader can't see; 'closed boundary' and 'Label' are jargon on jargon. Pilot licence helps. Needs its antecedent.
mythmaker: The pilot's licence works. 'Closed boundary' and 'Label' lean on a king I never met here. Too much shorthand.

modeler: Good correction: opacity isn't the test, prediction is. Sealed names that reliably predict outcomes are fine. Sharp and fair.
skeptic: The pilot licence point is clever: trust follows predictiveness, not transparency. Test is checkable. Self-corrects its own earlier example. Good.
clinician: The licence analogy is clear and the test is crisp. Abstract, nothing for the reader to do.
habit: Pilot's licence analogy is good, but Label, Word, sealed boundary pile up. Hard to follow; state the predict test first.
contemplative: A caution layered on a caution. Pilot, king, Label, Word, test. My mind works hard here. Say it in two sentences.
stress: Self-corrects its own example and gives a predictive test, pilot's licence. Rigor I like. Dense; unpack the king story.
gamedesigner: Smart refinement, predict versus visible, but it's a footnote to a king example I haven't got here. Heavy and abstract.
structural: Label versus Word by predictive power is a sound test, but the king and pilot analogies pile up. Tighten; credentials-who-certifies is a real institutional question.
satirist: Self-correcting: the pilot's licence beats the king example. Test is predicts, not transparency. Honest, plain, a bit dense but earned.
mythmaker: Pilot's licence versus false king is a sharp test, but the argument is knotty and the king is offstage.

modeler: Good repair: the test is prediction, not opacity. Pilot's licence is a checkable mechanism. Honest fix to your own example.
skeptic: Self-correction that I like: the licence analogy swaps inspectability for predictive power, a testable criterion. Nobody has shown the test works in practice.
clinician: Pilot's licence is clear, but 'predicts' is a verdict test, not a step. Where does a struggling reader apply it?
habit: The test 'does it predict?' is usable, but buried in kings and licences. Lead with the question and one everyday name to check.
contemplative: The pilot's licence helps. But Word, Label, sealed boundary pile up. Lighten: trust what predicts well. Drop the jargon, keep the licence.
stress: Self-corrects with a predictive test. A claim that can be wrong. Pilot's licence analogy earns its keep.
gamedesigner: Pilot licence analogy plus a clear test: does it predict? That's a feedback signal. Good patch.
structural: Titles as trust predicting outcomes touches institutions: licences, kings. Good test, though it never asks who issues titles or profits from false ones.
satirist: The pilot's licence saves it, and 'predicts' is a real test. But Word, Label, king: capitalized scaffolding. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: The false king shouting his title is the good part, and the pilot's licence earns the test. No one's heart is on the line.

modeler: A word holds only while it predicts. Crisp, and it gives the Label a falsification condition.
skeptic: Good. 'Kept because keeping feels better than checking' is exactly how confidence outlives evidence.
clinician: Tidy, but abstract. Fold it into U0627 or cut.
habit: Clean two-sentence rule. Keep this, cut the paragraph above.
contemplative: 'Keeping it feels better than checking it' is the gem. The rest is technical. Keep only that.
stress: Trusted while it predicts, a Label once kept for comfort. Falsifiable. Excellent line.
gamedesigner: A crisp-ish rule, but it rests on U0627's fog.
structural: 'Kept because keeping feels better than checking' is crisp. It applies to institutional metrics too.
satirist: An abstract coda to an abstract coda. Cut it, U0627 has already said it.
mythmaker: 'Keeping it feels better than checking it' is a crisp moral hinge. Good.

modeler: A Label is a stale model nobody rechecks. Missing feedback, named. The friendship example stings.

clinician: 'The friendship still called close' stings in a useful way. Offer a gentle way to check it, not just an indictment.

contemplative: 'The friendship still called close.' That is quietly painful and true. It asks me to look again at my own life.
stress: 'Kept because keeping feels better than checking' is the fragility test, nailed. The examples hit close.
gamedesigner: Top performer rating, the friendship still called close: concrete, personal, checkable. Clear rule.
structural: The stale 'top performer' rating is a real institutional label nobody rechecks. Good. Who keeps it unchecked, and why?
satirist: The unrechecked 'top performer' rating and the friendship still called close: both sting, both are recognizable, both are plain. Excellent.
mythmaker: 'The friendship still called close' hurts the way it should. A true, earned sting.

mythmaker: Told the name of a city, still stuck at the station: good image of knowing without walking. Nobody stands there.

modeler: Short and clear.
skeptic: Clear, and it resonates.

modeler: The hometown streets land personally. Still only half a contrast. Fold it into U0645 so the cost gap reads as one claim.

structural: The hometown image lands personally. It's still purely about the individual, with nothing about who built those streets.

modeler: Situational awareness as a third skill. A real distinction, and 'not recognising it while it's happening' resonates.

mythmaker: 'Lived it thoroughly and still not recognize it while it's happening.' That's everyone's tragedy. Strong.

structural: Cross-references pile up. The point is made by U0647. Trim it.

modeler: Resolution-matching is the right skill, and the burnout question nails it. Too many tool cross-references crowd it; cut the roll call.
skeptic: The burnout question is a real calibration move: am I misattributing scale? Good. Fewer cross-references would make it easier.

stress: Burnout-or-office question has real skin. Too many cross-references to Parts One and Five clog it for a cold reader.

structural: Asking whether the burnout is the whole office's is exactly the right question. Follow it to the lever: workload rules, staffing, who sets them.

modeler: 'Nothing is running' as a valid answer is good. But a stopped loop still leaves a stock; check its level.
skeptic: Excellent: it lets 'nothing is running' be an answer, which guards against seeing patterns that aren't there.
clinician: 'Nothing is running' is a valuable anti-rumination exit. Say plainly: sometimes there's no pattern, so stop hunting.
habit: 'Is it even moving?' is a decent first question. Brief.
contemplative: 'Nothing is running' is a wise answer. 'Pole to read' assumes vocabulary not yet given.
stress: A null hypothesis, 'nothing is running.' Rare and valuable. It lets the system return no.
gamedesigner: 'No pole to read' leans on Part Five vocabulary. Interesting, but not yet playable.
structural: 'Nothing is running' is a useful null result most frameworks forget.
satirist: 'No pole to read' leans on terminology not yet taught. 'Sometimes nothing's going on' is the plain sentence.
mythmaker: 'Nothing is running' is an interesting null, but the pole jargon obscures it. Give me a marriage gone quiet rather than bad.

modeler: Finally, a zero-flow state: a stopped loop has no direction to read. That's real systems hygiene, and the marriage example earns it.
skeptic: Finally, a null hypothesis. Allowing 'nothing is running' guards against seeing patterns everywhere. The best passage in this batch.
clinician: Best anti-rumination line here: 'stop hunting.' Gives permission to put the search down. Keep exactly.
habit: 'Ask whether it's moving. If it isn't, stop hunting.' A clear stopping rule. Love a rule that tells me to quit.
contemplative: Sometimes the old fight has just stopped. Gentle and true. 'Stop hunting' is a kindness to the reader.
stress: A stopping rule. Finally the system admits it can return 'nothing.' That's what makes the rest falsifiable. Best in the batch.
gamedesigner: Best rule in the batch: it gives a fail state and a stop condition. 'Stop hunting' is real feedback.
structural: Honest null option, and a good guard against seeing patterns everywhere. It's private in scope, which is fine here.
satirist: The best thing here: a system that admits sometimes nothing is there. The marriage gone quiet does the work. Bokonon would nod.
mythmaker: A marriage gone quiet, a fight that simply stopped. Real stakes, a real image, and an honest exit. One of the best here.

modeler: A fitting proverb, if worn.
skeptic: A cliché epigraph, apt here.
clinician: Epigraph. Fine.
habit: Cliché epigraph, but on topic.
contemplative: A worn line, apt here.
stress: Cliché, but apt. Passable.
gamedesigner: Proverb epigraph. Fits, adds nothing.
structural: Cliché epigraph.
satirist: A cliché, but it at least matches the chapter. Acceptable.
mythmaker: A stock saying. It's adequate, but it adds nothing.

modeler: A closed loop where each side sees only its own input. That's mechanism compressed into an epigraph. Keep it.
skeptic: Accurate about attribution bias, and it earns its place as an epigraph. Lovely, and it happens to have support.
clinician: True, and it gently takes blame off both people. Earns its place as an epigraph.
habit: True of every fight I've had. As an epigraph it earns its spot. No action needed.
contemplative: Short, true, a little humbling. It works as a doorway. 'As far as each side can tell' could go.
stress: Sharp, true, recognizable from any fight. Earns its spot as an epigraph.
gamedesigner: Good hook. Every reader has lived this, so it does its job as an epigraph.
structural: A sharp epigraph on mutual causation. It earns its place.
satirist: Genuinely funny and true. Survives the bar test with a straight face.
mythmaker: Everyone has been on both sides of this. It's a wry, true epigraph.

modeler: A clear rule: forward, then as a loop. Good.
skeptic: 'Single most useful' is a superlative with no comparison. 'Worth making twice' is muddled phrasing.
clinician: The rule as phrased is confusing ('worth making twice'). State it simply: say it forward, then as a loop.
habit: Promises the single most useful habit. Good.
contemplative: 'Worth making twice, worth making once forward' is wordplay. Say: say it, then say your part.
stress: A clear statement of the most useful habit. Good.
gamedesigner: Promises the most useful habit, and states it cleanly. Good.
structural: A clear rule of thumb.
satirist: A clear, useful promise. 'Worth making twice' is slightly clunky.
mythmaker: A clear promise of the central habit. Fine.

modeler: Clear habit and clear trigger. It works as an instruction but gives no reason why. That's fine here, because the next unit supplies it.
skeptic: An actionable rule, but 'say it as a Loop' assumes jargon the reader may not have. Give a one-line example.
clinician: Clear, single habit. 'Say it as a Loop' is meaningless without the chapter; fine in place.
habit: Has a cue ('matters enough to say twice') and a behaviour. That's a habit, not a wish.
contemplative: The habit is good. 'Once as a Loop' means nothing to a newcomer here. Show the second sentence, plainly, in brackets.
stress: Clear one-habit instruction. Needs no grandeur and has none. Works as a hinge.
gamedesigner: Clear one-habit goal. Feedback is missing: how do I know my Loop version came out right?
structural: A plain instruction that leans on context. On its own it's just a slogan for a habit.
satirist: A clear rule, but 'as a Loop' leans on capitalized jargon. Say 'once as the circle you're both in.'
mythmaker: A clear rule, but it's a rule without a person. It's fine as a hinge. A one-line example would earn its place.

modeler: The forward pass then the loop pass is an actionable protocol. 'With your own part in it' supplies the closure.
skeptic: Making the speaker include their own part corrects for self-serving bias. Concrete and usable.
clinician: Owning 'your own part' in the circle is guilt, not shame, done right. Clear, repeatable, safe. Keep.
habit: One habit with a cue and a format. This is the book's best two-minute rule.
contemplative: Your own part in it. This is reconciliation, not scoring. I could do this tonight.
stress: Specific, includes your own part. Testable in the next fight. Where does it fail? Abuse; say so.
gamedesigner: The core move, stated as a recipe with steps. I know exactly what to do in the next fight.
structural: Forward then as a Loop, owning your part: it takes the villain out without excusing anyone. A good practical habit.
satirist: Forward, then circular, including your part. A real communication habit stated plainly. Keep.
mythmaker: 'With your own part in it' is where the cost is. That's Zuko owning his share. The heart of the part.

modeler: A familiar first-pass example. Clear.
skeptic: A familiar, honest example.
clinician: A real, recognizable example.
habit: A real sentence everyone has said.
contemplative: A sentence I have said. Plain.
stress: A real sentence people say. Good.
gamedesigner: The example is instantly recognisable.
structural: A recognizable first pass. It works as a specimen.
satirist: A perfect everyday example.
mythmaker: 'Because you raised your voice' is a real line from a real fight. Good.

modeler: Closes the loop out loud: two local rules feeding each other. That's exactly the machinery.
skeptic: A good concrete second pass. The reader can imagine saying it.
clinician: A good model. But a reader who is being yelled at may over-own it. Add a safety caveat about abusive dynamics.
habit: A concrete second-pass script. Copyable tonight.
contemplative: Owning your part, out loud. This is how to fight, gently.
stress: Concrete second pass. You can actually say it out loud.
gamedesigner: The second pass shown concretely. That's the tutorial demo.
structural: A concrete, sayable second pass. Good.
satirist: The second pass, demonstrated. Readers can do this tonight. Excellent.
mythmaker: The second pass costs the speaker something to say aloud. That's stakes, so this is the turn.

modeler: A one-pass story always starts the loop with the other person. A precise, predictable bias. Excellent.
skeptic: Correctly names the self-serving direction of bias. 'Always' overclaims; 'usually' is enough.
clinician: 'Both are true; it sits next to it' avoids self-blame. Strong. Needs a line excluding abuse.
habit: The villain becomes a shared loop. Insight and tool together.
contemplative: A villain becomes a shared loop. Understanding is love's other name. Keep.
stress: The first pass always starts with the other person. A sharp, falsifiable observation. Strong.
gamedesigner: 'It always makes the loop look like it started with them.' A great insight.
structural: It works between equals. Caveat: a 'shared loop' can launder power gaps, boss and worker. Flag asymmetric cases.
satirist: 'The first pass always makes the loop start with the other person.' A sharp, true, useful observation.
mythmaker: Villain and victim become two Local Rules, and it doesn't straw-man the first pass. Exactly the courtesy I want.

modeler: The line-loop-tree mantra again. It adds length, not mechanism. Cut most of it.
skeptic: Repeats the line-loop-tree mantra and blurs the clean practice. Cut most of it.
clinician: Re-explains the line/loop/tree idea. Redundant and dense. Cut most of it.

modeler: Two passes for two views is sound. The em-dash aside about the tree overloads the sentence; give it a line of its own.

clinician: It validates how the moment felt first, which is good. The tree clause gets murky; say it's for a calm day.
habit: Justifies the two passes, then wanders into trees. Cut the last clause or give 'outside the argument' a when.

satirist: Loop, tree, passes: busy, busy, busy. The plain sentence underneath: you named the fight, not its history. Say that.
mythmaker: 'Every time this fight played out slightly differently' is lovely, but buried in abstraction. Show two of those fights side by side.

modeler: It justifies two passes structurally, and admits the loop isn't the tree. Nice humility about the limits of the summary.

contemplative: Gentle, and honest about the slower work. The tree aside feels added. One breath shorter.

structural: Honest that the tree needs slower work. Still all within the couple. Nothing reaches the conditions that keep producing the fight.
satirist: Admits the loop isn't the whole tree and sends that work to a calm day. Honest and practical.
mythmaker: Last month's version of the fight gives the tree a history. It's honest about the slow work.

modeler: Rehearse on paper when the stakes are low. A sound training protocol.

structural: Rehearsing on paper is a concrete, doable practice.

mythmaker: Rehearse on paper when nothing's at stake. Practical and kind. It works.

modeler: Attributed epigraph, on topic. Fine.

modeler: Pleasant, but it says nothing about what makes agreement fast. Name the missing balancing input, the dissenting window, or cut it.

modeler: Agreement from one viewpoint is not coverage. Fair point about scale and perspective, as a one-liner.

clinician: Clear image of partial views. No next step.
habit: Nice aphorism about one window and the back of the house. No step. Epigraph only.
contemplative: Five at one window and nobody saw the back. Clear and humbling. A pretty line that asks nothing.

gamedesigner: Nice aphorism, but nothing to do.
structural: Good epigraph about shared blind spots, close to groupthink. Decorative as placed; fix by applying it to a real institution.
satirist: Five at one window agree, none saw the back. Nice, but a lone aphorism; the claim needs an example of what was missed.
mythmaker: Five at a window never seen the back of the house: a cool image. Epigraph, but it will hold.

modeler: Agreement is not coverage. Good perspective image, but no mechanism for how views get combined.
skeptic: Agreement is not coverage. A modest, accurate line about perspective, and it doesn't claim to know what the five feel.
clinician: Makes disagreement non-shaming: nobody is wrong, nobody sees it all. Safe on a bad day. Add what to ask next.
habit: Sticks and stings a bit. But it diagnoses without prescribing. Add the one question: who is standing at the back door?
contemplative: One image, no extra words. I recognise my own certainty in it. Humble and true.
stress: Agreement is not coverage. Modest and true. Good guard against false consensus.
gamedesigner: Vivid and personal. Works as an epigraph, but I want a predict-or-test hook.
structural: Good figure/ground image: agreement without the whole picture. Gestures at s-frame blindness but names no mechanism or lever.
satirist: Five people at a window: lovely, plain, true. Shows perspective without the capital P. Pass it to the bar.
mythmaker: Five people at one window: I can see them. The unseen back of the house is the image. Return to it later.

modeler: Names a specific failure the ritual corrects. Good.

modeler: The no-repeat rule forces boundary variation. A clever, simple constraint.

clinician: A concrete, enforceable rule. Usable.

modeler: The no-repeat rule is a real constraint that forces a lens change. A local rule producing group behavior. Good design.

mythmaker: The parent's overspending line and 'I buy when stressed' give it faces. The no-repeat rule is the plot twist. Works.

clinician: Good diagnosis of a group stuck at one scale.

satirist: Charming, true, and it gives permission to fail. Good epigraph.
mythmaker: The child saying 'I goed' is warm and forgiving. Exactly the courage the exercises ask for.

modeler: Cute, and iterative learning is right, but it's a quip. Speaking badly is the feedback loop; say so.
skeptic: Overregularization joke, charming; 'speaking badly counts' is plausible learning theory. Epigraph, though, so just decoration.
clinician: Permission to be bad at it is shame-reducing, but it's only an epigraph.
habit: Say I goed and you're speaking: permission to be bad at it. Encouraging, but give me the first sentence to say.
contemplative: Say 'I goed' and you are already speaking. Warm and permission-giving. It breathes.
stress: Cute, grammar-error image of learning by speaking badly. No claim to stress.
gamedesigner: Permission to be bad on day one is great learning-curve design. Short, friendly.
structural: Speak badly, you're already fluent. Encouraging, cute. Low stakes, no mechanism.
satirist: 'I goed' is funny and right: speak it badly first. Cute, short, a bit cryptic as an epigraph without the body.
mythmaker: Speaking badly counts as speaking: encouraging and funny. Slight; the toddler's face would help.

modeler: A real loop: output feeds correction. Lovely. Name the stock, the learner's grammar, and what drains it.
skeptic: Overregularization is real, but one cute anecdote is carrying a general claim about how correction works. Lovely; how would you know?
clinician: Shame-reducing: mistakes are part of speaking. Warm and clear. A reader afraid of failing could lean on this.
habit: Charming and clear, but I finish it with nothing to start. Say what 'talk first, correct later' looks like at a desk.
contemplative: Gentle and true. Practice comes before correction. I can hold this with my children. Nothing to cut.
stress: Pretty, but a toddler isn't evidence. Where does 'act before correcting' fail? Surgeons, pilots.
gamedesigner: Sticky image that lowers the stakes of starting. No action attached.
structural: Cute, individual-scale aphorism. Acting before perfecting is fine, but nothing about collective action or who sets the rules.
satirist: 'I goed' is a genuine small marvel and says it plainly. Slightly cute, claim is stronger than the evidence.
mythmaker: A toddler saying 'I goed' is a real face and a sweet turn. Correcting grows out of talking. Lovely thought, and I know who's holding it.

modeler: Short framing. Fine.
skeptic: Lead-in.
clinician: Lead-in.
habit: Setup line.
contemplative: Plain and short. Fine.
stress: Setup. Fine.
gamedesigner: A difficulty curve announced. Fine.
structural: Setup. Fine.
satirist: A fine lead-in.
mythmaker: A setup line. Fine.

modeler: Clean signposting, nothing more. It's fine as a bridge, and it doesn't need to score.
skeptic: Serviceable signpost with a sensible ladder of difficulty. Nothing to object to, nothing to admire.
clinician: 'Speaking it badly until you don't' is kind permission to be clumsy. Otherwise it's just a menu.
habit: Just a signpost. 'Speak it badly until you don't' is right, but the reps come later.
contemplative: 'Speaking it badly until you don't' is honest and kind. A short line of passage between epigraph and exercises, and it does that.
stress: Signpost only. Fine as connective tissue, earns nothing alone.
gamedesigner: A difficulty curve stated up front: solo, duo, group. That's good onboarding architecture.
structural: Pure signposting. Fine, but it earns nothing.
satirist: A transition sentence. Fine, and nothing more. 'Speaking it badly until you don't' is the one good phrase.
mythmaker: Pure scaffolding with no blood in it. Keep it short or fold it into the exercises.

modeler: Graduated exposure, solo to dyad to group, is a sensible difficulty ramp. Plain setup.
skeptic: Structural setup, clear. The language analogy is asserted, not shown.
clinician: 'Speaking it badly until you don't' normalises failure; graded exposure is sound. Framing only.
habit: Good ladder structure, but it's just an announcement. Fold it into the first exercise.
contemplative: Kind framing, speaking badly until you don't. Just a doorway.
stress: Graduated exposure is a sound structure. Setup line; the exercises must carry it.
gamedesigner: Escalating difficulty ladder: solo, pair, room. That's proper level design. Clear.
structural: Escalating from paper to partner to room is the right spillover order. It's only a framing line.
satirist: Plain setup with escalating exposure. Nothing to mock, nothing to love.
mythmaker: The three steps of growing exposure are good stakes on paper. Name who's in that room.

modeler: Three exercises with rising exposure: a staged trial. Test and tweak, as Sellers says. Clear and usable.
skeptic: Graduated exposure, alone to a room, is sensible. 'Speaking badly until you don't' is gentle on error. No overclaim.
clinician: 'Speaking badly until you don't' normalizes failure; graded exposure from paper to a room is Gillihan-like.
habit: Three exercises, each a step more exposed: paper, one person, a room. A graduated ladder. Speak it badly: great.
contemplative: Speak badly until you don't. Alone, then one, then a room. Gentle and practicable. A good order.
stress: Escalating exposure: paper, one person, room. Calls bad speaking the way. Staged risk, modest.
gamedesigner: Exposure ladder: paper, one person, a room. Textbook difficulty ramp. I'm in.
structural: Alone, then pair, then room: graduated exposure, expands to teams and families. Practical practice ladder, still no structural target.
satirist: Learn a language by speaking it badly. Three exercises, each more exposed, ending with a room. Gentle ladder, honest framing.
mythmaker: Badly until you don't, each step more exposed: a good ramp. Reads as a plan, not a scene.

modeler: Sentence, then diagram, reveals where the leverage sits. Concrete. Good.
skeptic: Concrete, and the 'sometimes' is properly hedged.
clinician: A specific solo exercise with a payoff. Good.
habit: A real solo rep with clear steps and payoff. Keep it.
contemplative: Write it, draw it, say it aloud. Three gentle steps. Good.
stress: An actionable solo drill with a concrete payoff, beginning versus end lever.
gamedesigner: A solo drill with a payoff (seeing where the leverage sits). Playable.
structural: Concrete. The insight that the lever sits early in the loop is good. Still a solo exercise.
satirist: Seeing that you're pushing the end of the loop instead of the start is a concrete payoff. Good.
mythmaker: Your own loop on paper, with the lever near the beginning. Practical and personal.

modeler: Reflecting someone's story back as a loop exposes the hidden villain. A good paired drill.
skeptic: Good. An outside reflection corrects the villain built into the speaker's story.
clinician: Reflective listening, structured. Clinically sound and concrete.
habit: Two minutes, reflect it back, correct it. Bungay Stanier would approve.
contemplative: Two minutes uninterrupted, then reflect. Deep listening made into practice. Beautiful.
stress: The mirror exercise exposes the smuggled villain. Good, testable.
gamedesigner: A correction loop built in: the speaker fixes the sketch. A real feedback system.
structural: A doable pair exercise. 'Linear storytelling smuggles a villain' earns it.
satirist: 'Linear storytelling smuggles in a villain' is a good line, and the exercise is doable. Keep it.
mythmaker: 'Smuggles in a villain by default.' A great exercise with a sharp payoff. Keep it.

modeler: A live decision with a debrief. Fine.
skeptic: 'Both outcomes count as working' makes the exercise impossible to fail. Name an outcome that means it didn't help.
clinician: 'Both outcomes count' is nicely non-failing. Fine.
habit: Real decision, with a debrief question. Good.
contemplative: A real decision, not a hypothetical. Both outcomes count. Kind.
stress: 'Both outcomes count as working' is unfalsifiable. Add an outcome that counts as failure.
gamedesigner: The debrief question is a good feedback signal.
structural: Applied to a real group decision. The right direction.
satirist: 'Both outcomes count as working' is a little unfalsifiable, but it's practical. Fine.
mythmaker: Real decision, real debrief. It's functional and fine.

modeler: Has an actual test with a failure condition: nobody heard anything new. That's how you tune a design. Good.
skeptic: It states a failure condition: if no one heard anything new, it didn't work. More of this, please.
clinician: Real decision, clear debrief, honest fail condition. Solid structure in Gillihan's sense.
habit: A real decision plus a debrief with a pass/fail test. Concrete. It needs a time box: ten minutes, max.
contemplative: A real decision, not a hypothetical: good. The last line is a fine honest test. 'Spiral Check' still needs one plain word beside it.
stress: Real decision, real debrief, and a stated failure condition. That's how you test a practice.
gamedesigner: Finally an explicit win/lose condition: no new thought heard means it failed. More of this everywhere.
structural: Applied to a live group decision, with a test for whether it failed. That's practice that can actually spill over into collective choices.
satirist: The fail condition is honest: 'no one heard anything new' means it didn't work. Good. The rest is procedure.
mythmaker: A real decision and an honest test of failure. Good. Still nobody in the room, though, so give one example debrief.

modeler: It has a real success and failure criterion, a rare thing. A testable debrief. Good.
skeptic: It states a failure condition: 'if no one heard anything new, it didn't.' That makes it a falsifiable exercise. Good.
clinician: Real group exercise with an honest success test, but leans on an undefined Spiral Check ritual. Restate the rule here.
habit: A real decision and a clear success test, good. But it leans on Chapter 6's ritual; restate the steps in one line.
contemplative: Too many cross-references and rules. 'I hadn't seen it from there' is the heart; build around it.
stress: Real decision, explicit failure condition: nobody heard anything new. That's a falsifiable exercise. Good.
gamedesigner: Real task with a real debrief signal, nice. Assumes I remember Chapter 6 ritual and scale rules; recap them.
structural: A real decision, a real group, a falsifiable debrief. This is the collective lever I want. Keep it.
satirist: 'Spiral Check', 'ritual', 'exactly as written': here comes the vestry. The debrief test is good, but it leans on Chapter 6 jargon.
mythmaker: 'I hadn't seen it from there' is the human beat. Otherwise it's procedure resting on Chapter 6.

modeler: A real group experiment with a falsifiable debrief: did anyone hear something new? Rule of no repeated scale forces perspective. Good.
skeptic: Debrief with a failure criterion: 'if no one heard anything new, it didn't work'. That is a falsifiable test. Excellent calibration.
clinician: Specific ritual with a debrief and criteria. Real decisions raise stakes; fine with a safe group.
habit: Real decision, round once, no repeated scale, debrief with a test for whether it worked. Specific and runnable. Best kind.
contemplative: A real exercise, but dense: rules, ritual, debrief, three outcomes. Too much to hold. Cut to go round once, then ask.
stress: Success criteria stated, including failure: nothing new heard means it didn't work. Falsifiable and honest. Excellent.
gamedesigner: Real decision, a defined round rule, and an explicit pass/fail debrief. Best feedback signal in this set.
structural: Live Spiral Check on a real group decision, with honest test of whether anything changed. That's group deliberation with teeth. Strong.
satirist: Debrief criterion is brave: if no one heard anything new, it failed. A ritual that admits it can fail passes the Bokonon test.
mythmaker: I hadn't seen it from there: a real human beat. Debrief test is honest about failure.

U0666.chapter: 8. On the Limits of This Language (So Far)

modeler: Tautological epigraph. Weak.
skeptic: An apt epigraph for a chapter about limits.
clinician: Epigraph.
habit: Epigraph, inert.
contemplative: A tautology as epigraph. It adds nothing.
stress: Generic epigraph.
gamedesigner: Filler epigraph.
structural: Cliché epigraph.
satirist: Rumsfeld-adjacent filler. Cut it.
mythmaker: A platitude epigraph.

modeler: Honest about error, which I like. As an epigraph it promises limits, and the next units deliver them.
skeptic: The right sentiment for a limitations chapter. It works as an epigraph only because the chapter actually does it.
clinician: Honest framing; it models admitting limits without shame. Light, fine.
habit: A fine epigraph for a limits section. It earns its place quietly.
contemplative: Humble and true. A good bow before the limits. It asks nothing of me, and that is fine here.
stress: Says exactly what I want from a map. Earns its place by heading the limits section.
gamedesigner: Honest framing line that works as a transition. Low stakes.
structural: An honest-map epigraph. It works as framing for the limits section.
satirist: A decent epigraph for a limitations section, and it's self-aware. Keep it.
mythmaker: An honest-map line, quietly good. It earns trust before the limits section.

modeler: A well-phrased line about honest models. Earns it as a lead-in to the failure modes.
skeptic: A principle of disclosed uncertainty. I like it, provided the following pages honour it.
clinician: Good honesty epigraph. Fine in place.
habit: Honest epigraph. Fine.
contemplative: Honest and gentle. A map that confesses. Good.
stress: Right sentiment for the limits chapter. Epigraph only.
gamedesigner: Good honesty hook before the limits section. Does its job as a card.
structural: A good honesty epigraph that sets up the limits chapter.
satirist: A good maxim, and the next passage practices it. It earns its place.
mythmaker: A handsome epigraph with a good itch. It does its job.

modeler: Honest maps flag their edges. Fine epigraph and the right stance; no mechanism.
skeptic: The map-honesty epigraph sets up the limits section well. Aphorism, unproven, but it does its job as a promise.
clinician: Humble line about honest maps. Pleasant, no step.
habit: Honest-map line is lovely, but it's an epigraph. The next paragraph does the real work.
contemplative: Honest maps tell you where they are wrong. True and calm. Still an ornament more than an instruction.
stress: Good attitude: maps tell where they're wrong. But a quote, so no test.
gamedesigner: Honest-map line sets up the limits section nicely. No play.
structural: Honest-map epigraph. Pleasant; says nothing a reader can pull.
satirist: Honest maps tell you where they are wrong: true and cute. A section epigraph; the next paragraph does the real work.
mythmaker: Honest maps tell you where they're wrong: sets a tone of humility. Ornamental, but fits.

modeler: Models as maps with failure marks, sound. Metaphor only; show who marks the bog and who updates the map.
skeptic: Admits fallibility and tells me where to check. Fluent, but the content is sound: models fail at known places.
clinician: Honest, non-blaming line about imperfect models. Lovely, but no action. What does the reader mark on their own map?
habit: Good line, no behaviour. Where do I mark the bog? Turn it into a step: write one 'wrong here' note on your map.
contemplative: The bog is a plain, lived image. Honesty as marking danger. Short enough for one breath.
stress: Marking the bog is the right instinct: admit where you're wrong. Short, humble, usable.
gamedesigner: Lovely line, easy to get. Nothing asks me to do anything.
structural: Sound line about honest maps flagging hazards. Closest to a lever: mark the bog for others. Still a sentence, not an action.
satirist: Bog before you walk into it: good line, survives a bar. But it's an aphorism hiding any actual advice.
mythmaker: The marked bog is a vivid, usable image, a map-maker with a conscience. Short enough to carry and bring back later.

U0667.chapter: 8. On the Limits of This Language (So Far)

modeler: Framing line. Fine.
skeptic: An honest lead-in.
clinician: Lead-in.
habit: Setup.
contemplative: Plain honesty. Fine.
stress: Setup. Honest tone.
gamedesigner: Setup line.
structural: Setup. Fine.
satirist: A plain setup for honest gaps. Fine.
