stress: Composition idea is interesting. 'Skein' arrives with no example. Give one dyad-pair-to-skein case.
gamedesigner: Difficulty spike: fusion depth, skein, Global Form in one paragraph. Too many new nouns.
structural: 'Scale is a consequence of composition' is interesting. It also implies structure is just summed individuals, which leaves institutions out. Too dense.
satirist: 'Fusion depth,' 'skein': a system invented on page 3, cited as physics here. Show one real skein.
mythmaker: An interesting composition idea in fog. Show two actual people making a dyad.

modeler: It claims the same rule works at every tier, but the coupling rule is never stated. Say how the two loops link, through which shared variable and at what gain.
skeptic: Too many coined terms per sentence. The composition claim is asserted, not shown. Slow down and give one worked example.
clinician: Taxonomy mechanics stacked in jargon. A struggling reader would skip it.
habit: Composition theory, packed tight. I lost the thread at 'fusion depth'. Nothing to do.
contemplative: Too many named figures in one paragraph. The first sentence is enough. The rest is machinery.
stress: Composition-as-scale is a big idea, but it's buried under four coined names in one paragraph. Too much vocabulary is crossing over.
gamedesigner: Difficulty spike: Escalation, skein, Guard, Standoff and Held Silence in one breath. Teach one fusion step and stop.
structural: Composition-as-scale is a big idea buried in dense jargon. One concrete team example done slowly would fix it.
satirist: Escalation, skein, Guard, Standoff, Held Silence, Global Form, Local Rule in one paragraph. Busy, busy, busy. Use one example, slowly.
mythmaker: A pileup of capitalized figures. The team under Held Silence could be a scene. Write the scene, not the parts list.

modeler: Composition is real structure, but there's no ratio, so this rhymes with fractal without being one. Too many proper nouns arrive in one breath.
skeptic: It asserts that one person in two pairs silences a team. That's a mechanism, not a correlation. How would you know? Too dense to follow.
clinician: The coworker emails are recognisable, then the Guard, Standoff and skein jargon piles on. A struggling reader drops out here. Keep one example and stop.
habit: Five figure names in one paragraph, and it's all architecture. Nothing to do Monday. Trim it to the coworker thread.
contemplative: Seven named figures in one paragraph. I lost the coworkers by the skein. Keep the email pair, let the rest go.
stress: Too many named parts stacked in one paragraph. The composition claim is tidy enough to be suspicious. Show one skein forming, slowly.
gamedesigner: Difficulty spike. Spark, Escalation, Guard, Standoff, Held Silence and skein all land in one paragraph. Lost the player. Stage it in two beats.
structural: Composition idea is real, but the Guard/Standoff/skein chain loses lay readers fast. Name who can push at the team level.
satirist: Spark, Guard, Standoff, Held Silence, skein, Global Form, all in one breath. Busy, busy, busy. Keep the email thread, lose the roll call.
mythmaker: The sharp-email coworkers start well, then drown in Guard, Standoff and skein. Stay with one team going quiet.

modeler: Composition rule shown, not claimed: sharp replies, then Escalation, then a team-wide silence. Tiers come from composition. Self-similarity as claimed here holds.
skeptic: Coworkers example works, but the tier and composition vocabulary arrives fast. 'Tangle of pairs' claim is asserted.
clinician: Coworker email example is clear and puts the trap between people, not in them. Good. No step, and the tier language still piles up.
habit: Two coworkers, sharper emails, then the silent team: concrete, recognizable. Composition explained through a story. Add: find one pair in your week.
contemplative: The two sharp emails are real. Then pairs, skein, tiers and composition pile up. Too many words doing the work of two.
stress: Email escalation example builds the tiers step by step. 'Not a ranking' keeps ego down. Composition claim should be testable.
gamedesigner: Coworker escalation example is good, then Skein and Held Silence arrive. Too many new terms.
structural: Coworker emails to team silence to skein. Real composition, 'last tier where anyone can still push' is a lever claim. Keep.
satirist: Two coworkers, sharper emails, a team gone silent: composition shown, not asserted. Skein term arrives awkwardly but the example carries it.
mythmaker: Two coworkers, each a bit sharper, then one in two pairs and a team gone quiet. A small drama. Keeper.

U0854.chapter: 0. What a Third Is, and What It Isn't

modeler: A reading key, clear enough. 'Stronger' at what? Gain, rate, or level? Pick one and the tables get sharper.
skeptic: Short, usable reading instruction. Fine.
clinician: Short and clear reading key. Lifeline/snare helps. Fine.
habit: Handy key for the tables. Short and clear.
contemplative: Clear. "Lifeline or snare" lands softly. Good.
stress: Plain reading key. Does its job.
gamedesigner: Legend for the tables. Useful but repeats prior paragraphs; could be a single caption.
structural: Clear key to the tables. Lifeline or snare for whom? Leave that out and you've left out the politics.
satirist: Clear legend. 'Lifeline or a snare' is the third time; ration it.
mythmaker: The lifeline/snare image is planted here. Good, as long as it comes back, and it does.

modeler: Saying direction isn't value is good. 'Faster or harder' still names no variable. Is Tending more gain, shorter delay, or a tighter setpoint?
skeptic: Separating direction from value is the key correction. The point that the proudest habit and the worst one can both be Tending sticks.
clinician: 'The habit you're proudest of and the one you want gone can both be Tending' breaks good/bad shaming. Nice.
habit: 'Proudest and most-wanted-gone both Tending' is a good jolt. Clear reading guide.
contemplative: The habit you are proudest of and the one you want gone. That line lands. Keep only it and the definition.
stress: Direction is not value: the habit you're proudest of can be Tending. Keeps the poles free of moralizing.
gamedesigner: 'Proudest and most-hated habit both Tending' is the payoff that makes the direction labels click. Move this before the tables.
structural: Direction is not value. A clear, small point that the reader can apply to their own habits.
satirist: The last line, pride and regret both Tending, is the keeper. The rest repeats the earlier definitions.
mythmaker: The habit you're proudest of and the one you most want gone, both Tending. That's a gut-punch, and it saves the paragraph.

modeler: 'Nothing underneath them' overclaims. Biases sit on neurons and loops sit on stocks. Better to say these are the floor you can push on.
skeptic: 'Nothing underneath them' is a confident metaphysical claim the catalogue never tests. Lovely, and I have no reason to believe it.
clinician: A big claim in an epigraph. Works as framing.
habit: Good framing epigraph: these are the atoms. Works in its place.
contemplative: A quiet epigraph. "Nothing underneath them" overclaims a little, but it still calms.
stress: 'Nothing underneath them' is a theory-of-everything boast. These are borrowed bias names. Tone it down.
gamedesigner: Punchy epigraph that frames base tier. Works as a level title.
structural: 'Nothing underneath them' makes the individual the bedrock. Rules, laws and markets sit underneath too. That's the i-frame declared as ontology.
satirist: 'Nothing underneath them.' Grand and false; cognition has neurons underneath. Foma. Label it or cut it.
mythmaker: Bold epigraph. It claims bedrock, and it works.

modeler: A serviceable tier epigraph. It adds little beyond what the next line says.
skeptic: An epigraph-signpost. It is fine where it sits and earns nothing more.
clinician: Epigraph. Clear, and it earns nothing beyond that.
habit: 'Smallest place anyone can push' is the right promise. Now deliver on it.
contemplative: Quiet and grounding. The smallest place to push. It is fine.
stress: A serviceable epigraph. It adds little.
gamedesigner: Short tier banner. It just about does its job and earns little else.
structural: 'The smallest place anyone can push' privileges the individual as the base unit. That's the i-frame by default.
satirist: An epigraph quoting the book to itself. Bokonon at least quoted Bokonon with a wink.
mythmaker: A decent epigraph, but 'smallest place anyone can push' wants a hand pushing.

modeler: Repeats what the previous unit already said. Small enough to push, fine, but push which flow? Ornament.
skeptic: "Small enough for one hand to push" is lovely, and I have no reason to believe it. It overstates leverage.
clinician: A hopeful epigraph: every pattern is small enough to push. Fine where it sits, but it earns nothing practical.
habit: "Small enough for one hand to push" is encouraging. It works as an epigraph.
contemplative: Small enough for one hand. Warm, and it gives back agency. 'These' needs a little more in front of it.
stress: It overclaims. 'One hand to push' contradicts the later 'never alone' tiers. Fragile comfort, so trim it to what holds.
gamedesigner: Clean promise of scale. It doesn't touch my own situation, so it's flavour text.
structural: 'One hand to push' everything bigger? That's the BP footprint move. Big things need many hands, which your own Global tier admits.
satirist: Tidy claim, but 'everything bigger is built of these' is the book's own system citing itself as authority.
mythmaker: Neat promise, but whose hand? Name one.

modeler: Nice epigraph, but just a slogan. Says nothing checkable. Fits the table opening, no more.
skeptic: Epigraph. Memorable, but 'small enough for a hand to push' is a claim, not a finding.
clinician: 'Small enough for a hand to push' is hopeful and not blaming. A good line, but a line is not a step.
habit: Nice line: small enough for a hand to push. Epigraph, no step. Fine as a banner; follow with one pattern to push today.
contemplative: Pleasant and short. 'Small enough for a hand to push' is the best part. It adds nothing new.
stress: Neat slogan, unfalsifiable. 'Small enough for a hand to push' is comfort, not a claim.
gamedesigner: Tidy epigraph, hand-sized hope. Flavor only.
structural: 'Small enough for a hand to push' flatters. One hand pushing is the problem I distrust; say hands, plural.
satirist: A slogan. Pleasant, flat, nothing to check. Hushed-voice sentence that fails the bar test.
mythmaker: Small enough for a hand to push: a good line to carry. Slogan-ish, but it rhymes with the book's promise.

modeler: Compact claim of a small basis set. Fine epigraph; where's the evidence twelve is enough?
skeptic: Slogan. 'Twelve patterns hold up everything larger' is an unqualified universal claim. Why twelve? Compared to what?
clinician: 'Small enough to push by hand' is encouraging and right-sized. Lovely epigraph. Twelve is unexplained; no step.
habit: 'Small enough to push by hand' is my kind of line. But which pattern do I push first? Name one.
contemplative: Small enough to push by hand: a good promise. But 'twelve' and 'hold up everything' is grand. Quiet it.
stress: 'Hold up everything larger' is grandiose. Twelve patterns, everything? Cut or soften.
gamedesigner: Punchy epigraph, 'push by hand' is good. No signal what pushing looks like.
structural: Small enough to push by hand is the line I distrust: it is exactly the individual-scale comfort. Pretty, lets structure off.
satirist: Twelve patterns holding up everything is a grand claim in a hushed voice. Fails the bar test unless numbered and shown.
mythmaker: Small enough to push by hand is the hook. A good epigraph, but there's no one pushing.

modeler: A bridge sentence. 'One person repeating one thing' is the right kind of local rule. It has no weight of its own.
skeptic: Plain transition. Nothing to object to, nothing to keep for.
clinician: Plain intro. Nothing to object to, nothing to use.
habit: Plain setup line. Fine.
contemplative: Plain. One person, repeating one thing. Nothing to remove.
stress: Fine signpost.
gamedesigner: Two-line intro. Functional transition, no hook.
structural: One person, one repeated thing. The i-frame, honestly labelled at least.
satirist: Serviceable bridge. No objection, no applause.
mythmaker: A bridge sentence. Fine and forgettable.

modeler: A clear scope statement for the tier. Functional.
skeptic: A plain orienting line. It works as a lead-in to the table.
clinician: A plain bridge into the table. The phone image helps a little.
habit: 'You, reaching for the phone again' makes it personal. As a section opener it's fine.
contemplative: 'You, reaching for the phone again.' Simple. It brings me home.
stress: A plain bridge. Fine.
gamedesigner: Phone-reach example keeps it personal, and 'raw material' frames the progression. Good tier intro.
structural: Framing line. 'You, reaching for the phone again.' The individual again, and the phone maker absent.
satirist: Serviceable signpost. 'Raw material' is fine. Short, so let it be.
mythmaker: 'You, reaching for the phone again' brings the midnight image back. A good callback, but a thin paragraph.

modeler: Builds up from a local rule, the Suri way. 'Fused' needs a mechanism, but the claim of raw material is the right foundation.
skeptic: "Every argument... is two or more of them fused" is a universal claim with no support. Say "most we've found."
clinician: 'Reaching for the phone again' is gentle and true. 'Find yours' risks a self-audit. Add 'pick one, not all twelve.'
habit: "You, reaching for the phone again" is the cue. "Find yours" is the task. Good.
contemplative: The phone in hand is exactly right. Plain, practical. Start here.
stress: Clear entry point. 'Every argument... is two or more fused' is a theory-of-everything line. Soften it to 'most' and earn it.
gamedesigner: Good tutorial framing: learn these first, find yours. Clear goal and a reason to care.
structural: Phone example invites the i-frame: who designed the reach? Starting with self-patterns is fine if you name the app maker's incentive.
satirist: 'You, reaching for the phone again' is the only line that matters. The rest is a syllabus.
mythmaker: 'You, reaching for the phone again.' Good, there's the reader. The rest is assembly instructions.

modeler: The Local Rule column is excellent; Spark and Tide are honest reinforcing and balancing loops. Tending and Fraying only turn the gain knob. No stocks, no delays.
skeptic: Mostly well-documented heuristics renamed: anchoring, availability, peak-end, substitution. Real, but credit the research so the reader can check it.
clinician: Salve, Mask and Mirror will make readers wince in recognition. Rows are dense and repetitive, with no next step.
habit: The Riverbed is environment design, and the Salve is my bad habit. But it's a dense lexicon with no cue. Add a 'catch it when...' column.
contemplative: The names are warm: Salve, Keepsake, Gardener. The cells repeat "more, faster, surer" until they blur. Give each one a kitchen example.
stress: Known biases (anchoring, peak-end, substitution) with new faces. Usable. Credit the research it rests on; that's the history test.
gamedesigner: Real content: recognizable biases with faces. But poles read as near-mirror sentences; twelve rows of parallel text glaze eyes.
structural: A catalogue of biases, all inside the head. The Riverbed is choice architecture with the architect deleted. Who builds your riverbed for profit?
satirist: Anchoring, availability, peak-end, substitution, renamed with Kahneman's name filed off. Credit the source; Bryson would.
mythmaker: Great names like Mask, Salve and Gardener, but the rows are faceless and samey. Give each a one-line person.

modeler: Spark and Tide are true loops; most of the rest are biases dressed as loops. Name each one's stock and feedback path. The examples carry it.
skeptic: Anchoring, availability, peak-end and substitution are well supported. The Mask and the Namer are not. Flag which rows rest on evidence.
clinician: The examples resonate (Salve, Mask), but the Tending/Fraying cells blur together. There's no 'try this' column.
habit: Snack when stressed, autoplay, the Sunday call: I recognize myself. A usable lookup. Add a 'push here' column.
contemplative: The everyday examples are gifts. The Tending and Fraying columns blur into sameness. Shorten them, or trust the examples.
stress: Mostly well-replicated biases (anchoring, availability, peak-end, substitution) under new names. It has the long record behind it. Credit that, and cite it.
gamedesigner: The examples column carries it: thermostat, autoplay, Sunday call. I can spot these in my week. The Tending/Fraying cells read as boilerplate.
structural: The Riverbed uses autoplay, which a company built, yet it's filed as your Self-Kin. Flag which conditions you shape and which are shaped for you.
satirist: The parenthetical examples (thermostat, autoplay, Sunday call) carry it. The Fraying column mostly says 'less' in a different coat.
mythmaker: The italic examples are alive (stress snack, autoplay, the Sunday call). The Tending and Fraying columns are lifeless boilerplate. Make those cells concrete too.

modeler: The best thing in the chapter. A balancing loop with delay oscillates: pure Meadows. 'Balance is a rate of work' is real mechanism and lands personally.
skeptic: Delay-driven oscillation is correct systems dynamics. The Fraying digression tangles it; keep the wave and the last line.
clinician: 'Balance is a rate of work you sustain' helps a burned-out reader. The middle pole-correction is tangled. Trim it.
habit: "Balance is a rate of work you sustain" is gold. The Fraying digression buries it, so lead with that line.
contemplative: "Balance is a rate of work you sustain" is true and lovely. The pole correction in the middle tangles it. Cut that middle.
stress: 'Balance is a rate of work' survives the storm. The middle bit about pole terminology is clutter. Cut it.
gamedesigner: 'Balance is a rate of work' is a great payoff. The Fraying-pole correction mid-paragraph muddies it.
structural: 'Balance is a rate of work you sustain' lands. The pole pedantry in the middle clogs it. Cut that clause.
satirist: 'Balance is a rate of work you sustain' is a real insight. The mid-paragraph pole lawyering buries it. Cut that.
mythmaker: 'Balance is a rate of work' is a keeper. The middle pole-correction muddles it, so trim it.

modeler: This is Meadows done right: delay in a balancing loop gives oscillation, as in the shower. The best mechanism in the section.
skeptic: The shower metaphor makes delayed-feedback oscillation intuitive, and it is true. The best paragraph in this batch.
clinician: Balance as ongoing work, not a failed state. That reframe protects people from 'I can't stay balanced' shame.
habit: The shower-nudging metaphor is great. Turn it into a rep: what correction do I make daily?
contemplative: Balance is a work you keep doing. The shower nudged hot and cold. This I can live. Beautiful.
stress: Balance as sustained correction, the shower that never settles. Antifragile thinking in plain clothes. Strong.
gamedesigner: The shower metaphor gives felt understanding instantly, and it corrects a real misconception. Best paragraph in the section.
structural: Balance as sustained work, with the shower analogy. Vivid and true. It could note that institutions do much of that correcting work for us.
satirist: The shower nudged between too hot and too cold: a mechanism, honestly shown. Balance as work, not a state. Best page here.
mythmaker: The shower nudged between too hot and too cold is Iroh-level homely wisdom. A memorable correction. Keep it.

modeler: Tidy boundary-keeping that keeps the catalogue honest. Housekeeping, nothing to score beyond that.
skeptic: Housekeeping. Fine as a note; it earns nothing beyond pointing elsewhere.
clinician: Housekeeping note. Readable, earns nothing here.
habit: Housekeeping redirect. Fine as an italic note, earns nothing.
contemplative: Housekeeping in italics. It tells me what is not here. Move it to a footnote or let it go.
stress: Housekeeping. Fine as a footnote. It earns nothing more.
gamedesigner: Housekeeping footnote. Cut or move to an index; reader gains nothing here.
structural: Housekeeping note, clear enough. Moves flow out of the catalogue, fine.
satirist: Housekeeping footnote. Fine, invisible, harmless.
mythmaker: Bookkeeping cross-reference. Harmless, and nobody's in it.

modeler: An honest exclusion with a reason given. It's a housekeeping note, and fine as one.
skeptic: A useful redirect, with an honest reason for leaving things out. Housekeeping.
clinician: A housekeeping pointer. Fine as navigation.
habit: A pointer to another chapter. Harmless, but not earning anything here.
contemplative: It explains an absence. Flow deserves gentleness, not a footnote of exclusions. Move it or cut it.
stress: A housekeeping note. Good that it explains the exclusion instead of hiding it.
gamedesigner: A housekeeping redirect. Clear, but it's a 'content elsewhere' notice.
structural: A housekeeping note redirecting flow material elsewhere. Neutral.
satirist: An apology for four absent guests, in jargon. Make it a one-line pointer to the flow chapter.
mythmaker: An honest routing note, but it's bookkeeping. Nobody's in it.

modeler: A scope note with no point of its own. 'Fuse into nothing' is asserted, not shown. Move it to a footnote.
skeptic: It routes readers who want flow, but "fuse into nothing" is jargon nobody has earned yet. Simplify it to a plain pointer.
clinician: A signpost written in jargon: 'riding loops' and 'fuse into nothing.' A reader looking for relief needs only 'Flow: see Part Four.'
habit: A list of four practices with no action, just a signpost. One line will do: Flow is in Part Four.
contemplative: Defends an absence by listing four practices. Just say it plainly: flow has its own chapter in Part Four.
stress: An honest exclusion, which I respect. It reads as an internal taxonomy memo. Cut it to one plain line pointing to Part Four.
gamedesigner: Hook, then 'see Part Four'. A reward promised for later, and 'fuse into nothing' is unexplained jargon. Give one move now.
structural: Housekeeping justification nobody asked for. Taxonomy defense, jargon-dense. Cut or reduce to a single pointer line.
satirist: A filing note explaining why Flow is filed elsewhere. 'Fuse into nothing' is taxonomy talking to itself. Cut it to a single cross-reference.
mythmaker: An apology for an omission, in jargon. A reader in a hurry doesn't need it; move it or cut it.

modeler: Good call: Flow is a way of riding loops, not a loop, so it is not in the table. Disciplined boundary, and it points the way.
skeptic: Signpost explaining an omission. Honest about scope. Nothing to score beyond clarity.
clinician: Helpful signpost to a reader looking for Flow. Clear but purely navigational.
habit: Signposts the reader hunting for Flow; I like that it routes me. One sentence, clear. Useful, though it's navigation.
contemplative: A signpost, clear. It earns little beyond directing me elsewhere.
stress: Honest exclusion; admits what the table leaves out. Mere signpost.
gamedesigner: Good signpost: anticipates a player's search and routes them. Helpful, not exciting.
structural: Signpost that Flow is excluded. Fine and clear, but no interest. Flow also tends to sell as a personal fix.
satirist: Honest signpost: Flow isn't here on purpose. Saves a reader from hunting. Not much else.
mythmaker: Useful signpost that honestly says what Flow isn't. Practical. No heart, but it saves a lost reader.

modeler: Flow as how you ride a loop, not a loop: clean category call. Housekeeping, but useful.
skeptic: Pre-empts a likely question and gives a reason for the omission. Clear, honest about the table's structure.
clinician: Navigational aside answering a reader's search. Clear but trivial. Offers no step or relief.
habit: A navigation note about a missing row. Flow as 'how you ride a loop' is useful, but I don't get a step.
contemplative: Honest signpost for someone who looked and did not find. Short and kind. Slightly insider in 'fuses into nothing'.
stress: Clear housekeeping. Admits what's missing, which is honest; offers no idea.
gamedesigner: Helpful signpost for a player hunting Flow. Honest about why it's missing.
structural: Practical signpost explaining why Flow isn't in the table; clear. Flow as how you ride a loop is inner work, but placed honestly.
satirist: Tells you where Flow went and why. Useful signpost, plain. Admits the omission; I respect that.
mythmaker: Tells the Flow-seeker exactly where to go and why it's missing. Useful and kind. It's wayfinding, not story.

modeler: Nicely puts the emergent output in the interaction rather than in either person. That's Sellers' 'parts loop through each other' in one line.
skeptic: Relational emergence, consistent with what we know of selves made between people. Short and sound.
clinician: 'Neither of us brought it' takes blame out of a fight. This is shame-aware. Keep.
habit: Neither of us brought the thing that happened next. Every couple's fight, in one line.
contemplative: "Neither of us brought the thing that happened next." This is understanding, the root of love. Beautiful.
stress: Sharp and true of every bad argument you've had. Keep.
gamedesigner: Lovely epigraph. Instantly evokes a relationship fight neither started.
structural: Good, the outcome belongs to the interaction, not either person. That's figure and ground at small scale.
satirist: 'Neither of us brought the thing that happened next.' Lovely, true, bar-proof.
mythmaker: Lovely. Two people and an accident between them. That's a story seed.

modeler: A plain setup line, and fine for that.
skeptic: Transition. Clear.
clinician: Plain setup line.
habit: Clean setup. Nothing more.
contemplative: One sentence, one thing. Good.
stress: Clear one-liner.
gamedesigner: Clean one-line rule for the tier. Good.
structural: Clear setup.
satirist: Clean one-line setup. Fine.
mythmaker: A clear one-liner setting up the table.

modeler: 'The argument nobody started' states emergence in six words. A good hinge.
skeptic: 'The argument nobody started' resonates. It frames the table well.
clinician: 'The argument nobody started' takes the blame off both people. Shame-aware, though no step.
habit: 'The argument nobody started' resonates. A good opener, but there's nothing to do yet.
contemplative: The argument nobody started, the closeness nobody planned. Lovely, and sufficient.
stress: 'The argument nobody started' is recognizable. A short, honest frame.
gamedesigner: 'The argument nobody started' is a nice hook for the tier. Short and it works.
structural: 'The argument nobody started' resonates. It's an intro only.
satirist: 'The argument nobody started': plain and familiar. Fine as an intro.
mythmaker: 'The argument nobody started, the closeness nobody planned' is a lovely pair. It's the human face of fusion.

modeler: Two currents coupled, and an output neither owns. No blame, either can change it: structure over villainy, stated simply. Works.
skeptic: Resonant, but "neither of you is to blame" absolves too confidently. Sometimes one party does start it. Qualify it.
clinician: 'Neither of you is to blame, and either of you can change it' is the best clinical line here. Give one first move.
habit: "Either of you can change it" frees the reader up. Now hand me the first move.
contemplative: Neither to blame, either can change it. This is understanding as love. Beautiful, and enough.
stress: No blame, full agency. That pairing survives a real fight. Good.
gamedesigner: No blame, and either of you can change it. That's the payoff stated plainly. Short and it lands.
structural: No-fault, either-can-change is decent dyad framing. But it ignores power: a boss and a temp do not change it equally.
satirist: 'Neither of you is to blame, either of you can change it' survives the bar. Plain and kind.
mythmaker: The argument nobody started, the closeness nobody planned: an earned release from blame. That's heart.

modeler: Escalation as Spark+Spark is a real archetype. Connection First as Namer+Tide and Tested Price as Mark+Namer only rhyme. Show the coupling flow for each row.
skeptic: Several rows are real effects (curse of knowledge, anchoring, Pygmalion). The fusion column is asserted and never derived. Show one derivation or mark it as heuristic.
clinician: Answering For and Guard are recognizable. Nineteen rows of fusion syntax will overwhelm someone mid-conflict.
habit: Answering For and Connection First will hit managers. Nineteen rows with no cue is a lot to scan, so flag the five most common.
contemplative: Answering For and Connection First happen at my dinner table. The fusion column is the head's work. Lead with the human rows.
stress: Rows ring true. The fusion column looks arbitrary: why is Connection First Namer + Tide? Justify the pairings or drop the column.
gamedesigner: Rich, relatable figures, but nineteen rows of near-identical phrasing. Add one example per row to playtest.
structural: Gaming the Terms and Tested Price hint at incentives. Otherwise it's interpersonal weather, and nineteen rows of the same cadence blur.
satirist: 'Mask + Nearest Light' is chemistry cosplay: a metaphor promoted to an equation. The rows work; the sums are just decoration.
mythmaker: I recognise my own relationships in it: Answering For, Typecasting. The fusion column is opaque, and it needs a couple at the table.

modeler: Spark+Spark=Escalation holds. Many fusions (Namer+Tide=Connection First) only rhyme. Two thermostats fight, they don't 'hold the middle'. Show the coupling.
skeptic: The examples are recognizable, but why does Mask plus Nearest Light make Filling the Gap? The fusion logic is asserted. Show one derivation.
clinician: The examples are vivid and familiar, but nineteen rows of near-identical cells is a lot to wade through. It offers recognition only.
habit: Reply-all wars and dish rotas are real. But it's nineteen near-identical rows. Mark the five people actually hit.
contemplative: Nineteen rows is too much to hold. The examples touch me, but the fusion arithmetic intellectualizes them.
stress: The examples are vivid. But the fusions are asserted, not shown part for part, so the table fails its own Chapter 3 test. Show one.

modeler: A useful inference trick, and honest that it gives a short list, not a verdict. 'Narrows to a few' needs the table to back it.

gamedesigner: Know two, guess the third is an actual puzzle mechanic, and the worked example lets me play it. Best page here.

modeler: Signpost.

structural: A transition. Harmless.

satirist: 'Your half of it is yours' is the useful sentence. Self-Kin and Dyad-Kin are costume. Say 'you, them, the two of you.'

satirist: Squabbling siblings and a prediction you can test against Thanksgiving. Concrete, and it tells you what to watch.

modeler: A real diagnostic: infer the hidden loop from the observed output plus the loop you know is yours. That's system identification in plain clothes. Good.

habit: A real diagnostic. You always have your own half. Usable on the next tense meeting.
contemplative: "You always have access to your own half." Humble, and true in every home. Keep it.

modeler: Change your own coupling and the joint output shifts, with an honest note on dominance. That's real leverage, and it's ethically clean too. Keep it.

habit: Best rep in the chunk: change your leg, no permission needed. Add the cue, 'next time the pattern starts'.

satirist: Change your half, and it's not manipulation. Best practical point here, and stated without incense.
mythmaker: The heart of the part. Change your leg without permission. Earned, and empowering, and it has stakes.

habit: Seki is lovely if you play Go. Most readers don't. Give a workplace standoff instead.

stress: Seki is a precise analogy for a stable mutual position. It needs a human-world case to earn its practical keep.
gamedesigner: Seki is a cool reference, but 'shares liberties' locks out non-Go players. Use an everyday standoff instead.
structural: Seki is a lovely analogy for stable mutual positions. It risks fatalism, though, and never asks who could change the board's geometry.
satirist: Seki: a real game, a real rule, an elegant fact. Bryson would approve. Tie it back to an office.
mythmaker: Seki is a gorgeous image for Go players and opaque to everyone else. Give it a human standoff alongside.

modeler: Seki is a real stable equilibrium, and the payoff asymmetry is the mechanism. The shops example is apt. 'Geometry' overreaches; say 'payoffs'.
skeptic: Seki is a precise, real analogy, and the shops make it concrete. "Geometry" stands in for incentives, but it's acceptable.
clinician: A lovely Go image, but no reader leaves with anything for their own standoff. Add when a stalemate is worth keeping.
habit: Seki is lovely, but what do I do with it? Add: before you make the first move, ask who pays more.
contemplative: Seki is lovely, and so are the shops. But where am I in this? Give me the kitchen version.
stress: Seki and the price-war shops are real precedents, a pattern across cases. It needs one line on what the reader does with it.
gamedesigner: Seki is a lovely image. No move for me, though. Ask where I'm in a seki.
structural: Seki and the two shops show stability from incentives, not virtue. Good s-frame. Add: tacit collusion hurts customers; who benefits?
satirist: Seki is a genuine fact, a 'here's how we know'. The two shops make it plain. It doesn't tell the reader what to do, though.
mythmaker: Seki is a striking image: both alive because neither dares. Bring it back later and it'll rhyme.

modeler: Seki as a payoff equilibrium, with a price war analogue. Mechanism is the payoff structure, and 'who would pay more' is a usable question.
skeptic: Seki and the price war, real cases, then a question to ask before acting. 'Who would pay more' is useful.
clinician: Seki and the two shops are clear, and 'ask who would pay more' is a pause before a fight. Blameless: payoffs, not villains.
habit: Ends with the question I'd carry into any standoff: who would pay more for the first move? One question, good cue. Excellent.
contemplative: Seki and the two shops show it well. 'Ask who would pay more' is a question I can take into a standoff.
stress: Seki and the street shops: a payoff test, not poetry. Closing question is usable in a real standoff.
gamedesigner: Seki plus price-war shops, then a question to ask before moving. Excellent.
structural: Seki and two shops: payoffs, not generosity. Lesson ask who pays more for moving first, is a lever question. Strong.
satirist: Seki in Go and two shops on a street. Closes with a question to ask before attacking. Real, concrete, usable.
mythmaker: Seki and two shops, neither willing to start the price war: real stakes in a stalemate. Who pays more for the first move is a good question.

modeler: 'Stable: moving costs. Stalled: not moving costs.' A crisp, usable test. It also names where the cost accumulates.
skeptic: 'Moving costs you versus not moving costs you' is a usable, checkable test. One of the best lines in the chapter.
clinician: 'Stable: moving costs. Stalled: not moving costs.' is a usable test. Good.
habit: Moving costs you, or not moving costs you. That's one question I can carry into a stalled project. Keep it.
contemplative: "In a stalled one, not moving is what costs you." Many families need this. The lifeline-and-snare clause muddies it.
stress: 'Moving costs vs not moving costs' is a test you can actually run on a stuck relationship. Excellent.
gamedesigner: Killer test: in stable, moving costs; in stalled, not moving costs. Self-check signal. Keep.
structural: 'Moving costs you vs not moving costs you' is a usable test. Apply it to institutional deadlock and it's gold.
satirist: 'Moving costs you vs not moving costs you.' Plain, testable, bar-proof. Keep.
mythmaker: Moving costs versus not moving costs is a test I'll remember, and the snare returns with weight.

modeler: A concrete exercise that closes the loop on the sideways solve. Add 'and watch for how long', because the delay matters.
skeptic: Good exercise. 'Ask honestly whether that lands' trusts the very intuition that misreads other minds; add a check you could run on them.
clinician: A real, small step about one specific person. This is what help looks like. Keep.
habit: A real exercise, finally. It needs a cue and a time box, like 'after your next tense conversation, five minutes'.
contemplative: A real practice with one specific person. "Ask honestly whether that lands." I can do this tonight.
stress: Concrete exercise with one honest leverage question. Good.
gamedesigner: Finally a controller in my hands. Clear steps, real person, feedback question. Best move in the part.
structural: An actionable exercise with an honest question about leverage. Right scale for the lever it offers.
satirist: Actual exercise with a real person. Does something. Good.
mythmaker: Finally a specific person. A strong exercise.

modeler: 'Two dyads sharing a person' is a genuine structural rule for grouping. It's a nice local construction.
skeptic: Neat definition of group-as-thing. Crisp.
clinician: Nice compression of how a group forms.
habit: 'A group becomes a thing rather than a list.' Sharp framing.
contemplative: "A thing rather than a list." Clean and clear.
stress: Crisp definition of the group threshold.
gamedesigner: Good one-line definition of a skein. Clearer than the rulebook earlier.
structural: 'A thing rather than a list' is a good line on emergence. Now give the group a lever.
satirist: 'A thing rather than a list.' Nice. Earns its epigraph.
mythmaker: 'A thing rather than a list' is a crisp epigraph.

modeler: Shared node equals group. That's a clean network definition, and 'you, between boss and team' makes it felt.
skeptic: 'A thing rather than a list': being caught between your boss and your team is vivid and recognizable.
clinician: 'You, between your boss and your team' is instantly felt. Good framing epigraph.
habit: 'You, between your boss and your team.' I know that seat. A good epigraph.
contemplative: You, between your boss and your team. I know that place. Clear.
stress: Being caught between your boss and your team resonates. A good epigraph.
gamedesigner: 'You, between your boss and your team' instantly places me. A strong tier banner.
structural: 'A thing rather than a list,' with you between boss and team. A clear statement of group emergence.
satirist: 'You, between your boss and your team' — everyone's been there. Works as an epigraph.
mythmaker: 'You, between your boss and your team' puts the reader in the middle. It's an epigraph that's really a face.

modeler: First-Arriver Lock-In, Shared Pot and Settling are Meadows archetypes, and real. The parent pairings, like Transmission Drift's, look assigned rather than derived. Show the shared node.
skeptic: Pluralistic ignorance and normalization of deviance in plain dress. The fusions again rest on authority alone.
clinician: Hall of Mirrors and Held Silence are real. The table is dense and gives no step for a stuck team member.
habit: Held Silence and Hall of Mirrors are every meeting I've sat in. It's dense, though. Give each row a one-line 'you'll notice...'.
contemplative: Held Silence and the Hall of Mirrors are real at work. The parent-figure column is a puzzle for the head only.
stress: Hall of Mirrors and First-Arriver hold up; there's long research behind both. The fusion column is still unexplained. Cite the precedents.
gamedesigner: Hall of Mirrors, Held Silence are great. Parent-fusion column is opaque; rows need lived examples.
structural: Shared Pot, Lock-In and Second-Order Design are finally rules and resources. Still no owners, no beneficiaries. The table voice flattens them.
satirist: Abilene paradox, Matthew effect, tragedy of commons, all uncredited under new hats. Name the originals.
mythmaker: Hall of Mirrors and Held Silence are real office tragedies, buried in table prose. Give one a scene.

modeler: The Settling (eroding goals) and First-Arriver lock-in are real archetypes. Many fusions are arbitrary; why Naming Contest + Connection First? Show the shared variable.
skeptic: The Hall of Mirrors is pluralistic ignorance, which is well supported. Other rows are speculative compositions. Mark the difference.
clinician: The deadline meeting and the birthday-card person are sharply recognizable. The table cells are hard to parse, and there are no steps.
habit: The impossible-deadline meeting and the 9:15 drift are gold. The table is heavy; flag where to push first.
contemplative: The silent meeting, the office fridge. Real. But the columns are dense; I cannot read this aloud.
stress: The office fridge and the trip nobody wanted are recognizable. The Dyad-Kin derivations look arbitrary, and the density costs readers.
gamedesigner: The examples (office fridge, 9:15 drift) are gold. The Dyad-Kin fusion column needs two tiers memorized. Too steep.
structural: Second-Order Design and Held Silence are real. The table is too dense, and the rule-setters stay faceless.
satirist: The office fridge and the birthday-card organizer are gold. The fusion column is alchemy recipes. Trim the cells.
mythmaker: The impossible-deadline meeting, the office fridge, 9:00 sliding to 9:15: all recognizable. The cells around them are still mechanical.

modeler: Good everyday hooks (the office fridge), but the fusion lineage often only rhymes: why is Held Silence Guard plus Standoff? Rows lack stocks.
skeptic: The everyday examples land (9:15, the birthday card). The lineages of built-from-figures figures are unverified, and it's too dense to absorb.
clinician: The birthday-card person and the silent meeting hit home. The lineage column and abstract poles bury them, and there's no step.
habit: The examples hit home (the 9:00 that drifts to 9:15). The cells are abstract mechanics. Give each a sign to watch for.
contemplative: The fridge, the birthday card, 9:15: I know them all. The cells are abstract machinery. Say them as people.
stress: The examples land (the recipe, the 9:15). The fusion lineage column looks derived but is asserted. Flag it as a hypothesis, or drop it.
gamedesigner: The office fridge and the drifting 9:15 are relatable. Second-Order Design's row is opaque, so the table is hard to scan.
structural: Examples are excellent (impossible deadline, office fridge, sales target). The cells stay mechanical fog. Add who owns each rule.
satirist: Office fridge, birthday card: lovely. The cells are tangled ('holds the others back less'). The plain examples are hiding behind the grammar.
mythmaker: The office fridge and the 9:15 drift are recognisable. The mechanism cells read like a parts catalogue.

modeler: Every row names constituents and both directions, in the same format. Rich, a bit dense, and the mechanisms are asserted, but the structure holds.
skeptic: Recognisable situations like the office fridge, but the mechanisms are just asserted. Dense table, no evidence.
clinician: Eleven rows of tiered jargon. 'Meeting where nobody says it' is recognisable, but the cells read like code. Few can use this.
habit: Office fridge, 9:00 drifting to 9:15: I've lived these. Table gives the examples and both directions. Needs a start-here row.
contemplative: Eleven rows, each a stack of earlier names. Too much to hold in a breath. The examples, like the fridge, are good.
stress: Familiar office cases, but table density hides a thin mechanism. Each row too neat; hindsight risk.
gamedesigner: Office fridge, 9:15 start, relatable scenes. But column labels are compounds of compounds; difficulty spike.
structural: Office fridge, 9:15 starts, silent meetings: real. Second-Order Design row is closest to rules. Dense table, jargon heavy.
satirist: Office fridge, 9:15 start, the card organizer: delicious examples. The Dyad-Kin formulae are a code the reader must decode.
mythmaker: The 9:00 start drifting to 9:15 and the birthday-card organizer are real faces. Cells are dense; table hides the drama.

modeler: Tending/Fraying is gain up or down; fine. Dense table, every row repeats the same template. Add stock, delay.
skeptic: Eleven figures of ever-more-elaborate compounding; examples help, but each mechanism is a plausible story, not evidence. Hard to audit.
clinician: Table of compound jargon; rows like Held Silence resonate, but 'Dyad-Kin' labels bury them. Unusable at 3 a.m.
habit: Dense table, abstract names, shared-person pairs. Held Silence in a meeting is a real hook, but no move. Needs cutting.
contemplative: Eleven rows of names joined to names. The office fridge and the 9:15 start are alive; the notation buries them.
stress: Every row fits Tending or Fraying: that's after-the-fact fit. Needs a row that fails.
gamedesigner: Table of pairs of pairs. No entry hook. Fine for reference, but I'd bounce.
structural: Group-level table: Second-Order Design, The Shared Pot, Held Silence are real organizational mechanisms. Rule-setters seeing what rules produce is my lever.
satirist: Office fridge, 9:15 start, family recipe step: real life. But the 'X + Y' compounding of invented names is a language virus.
mythmaker: The meeting where nobody says the deadline is impossible: I've sat in it. Scenes are good; the cells are dense.

modeler: Setup. A promise of an inversion still to come.
skeptic: Good warning that liking an outcome doesn't tell you its pole. Otherwise just a header.
clinician: A heading posing as a paragraph. Fold it into the next one.
habit: Header sentence. It earns nothing on its own.
contemplative: A heading that tries to be a paragraph. Cut it to its first five words.
stress: Header sentence. Trim.
gamedesigner: Another 'one thing worth saying' throat-clear. Becoming a verbal tic; cut to the point.
structural: Promising setup. Says the difference isn't taste. Good.
satirist: Header-paragraph promising importance. Cut; start with the next sentence.
mythmaker: It's an intriguing hook, and the 'whether you like it' line pulls me in.

modeler: A good provocative header: outcome satisfaction isn't a pole reading. It sets up the next passages well.
skeptic: A teaser that confuses on first read. Fold it into the paragraph that explains it.
clinician: A teaser claim, dense and unexplained until later. It's a header, not help.
habit: A claim with no grounding yet. It reads as cryptic until the following paragraphs.
contemplative: A bold claim before I know the figure. It agitates without helping. Fold it into what follows.
stress: A sharp hook: liking the outcome isn't a reading. It sets up 0877 well.
gamedesigner: A teaser hook with no context yet. It reads as a riddle before I know the figure.
structural: A cryptic teaser. It only makes sense once you've read the passage after it.
satirist: Bold teaser for an argument that hasn't been made yet. Cut; the next paragraph does the work.
mythmaker: A teaser sentence in pure jargon. Let the spreadsheet example arrive here instead.

modeler: Sharp warning: satisfaction isn't the sensor. It needs one line on what you'd measure instead, which comes next.
skeptic: Warning that satisfaction says nothing about the pole is sound. But "either pole" is opaque to anyone who skipped the table.
clinician: An abstract warning with no handle. Tell the reader one question that does tell the poles apart.
habit: A sharp warning with no check attached. Tell the team what to look at instead of how they feel.
contemplative: I read it twice and still hold nothing. Name the poles in plain words, or let U0878 say this.
stress: An important warning: satisfaction is not evidence. The jargon buries it. Say 'liking your rules proves nothing' first, then name the figure.
gamedesigner: A bold claim with no setup. I can't parse what 'either pole' means here yet. Put the example before the claim.
structural: Important point buried in opaque phrasing. Say: satisfaction with rules isn't evidence they work. Whose satisfaction, and who bears the costs?
satirist: A sharp idea dressed in 'poles'. Say it plainly: a team can like its rules for the wrong reason.
mythmaker: A sharp idea with nobody holding it. Show one team cheering on the wrong pole.

modeler: Sharp: satisfaction can't distinguish the poles, because the sensor reads the wrong variable. Closes a missing-feedback gap. Good diagnostic warning.
skeptic: Liking outcomes proves nothing; from inside the poles look the same. Direct hit on the feeling-as-evidence error. Excellent.
clinician: Useful caution that satisfaction proves nothing, but it's compressed and abstract; needs a plain example of how to check.
habit: Liking the result proves nothing, and the two poles look the same from inside. Strong warning. Add the check I can run instead.
contemplative: Bold, and the point is hidden behind Tending, Fraying and Second-Order Design. Say it: pleasure is not proof.
stress: Liking the result proves nothing. Exactly the guard against fragile comfort. Sharp.
gamedesigner: Good warning that feelings aren't the signal, but names Second-Order Design and poles without a plain example.
structural: Liking your rules proves nothing: sharp. Satisfaction from inside is no test. Exactly the warning against self-serving rule-makers.
satirist: Right warning: liking your rules proves nothing. But the sentence needs Tending/Fraying/Second-Order Design pre-loaded. Plain restatement helps.
mythmaker: Liking your rules proves nothing: good doubt planted. But no team stands in it. Name the pleased team.

modeler: Authoring the second order is straight game design and correct: you set rules, behavior comes back. Emergence appearing in both poles is sharply argued.
skeptic: Authoring the second order is a sound, well-grounded design idea. Clear and correct.
clinician: The design-layer insight is sharp but abstract. Pole-definition quibbling slows it.
habit: 'You author the second order' is a good idea, but the pole-logic tangle loses lay readers.
contemplative: "You author the second order, never the first." This is humble about what we control. The last two sentences repeat it.
stress: 'You author the second order' is solid, tested game-design truth. Keep.
gamedesigner: Game designers' second-order truth, nicely stated. I nod. Still a lecture.
structural: 'Change the game, not the players', said properly: rules, resources, who hears what, what gets counted. Best paragraph here.
satirist: 'You author the second order' is honest game-design wisdom. Works.
mythmaker: Authoring the second order is a strong idea, but nobody's at the design table.

modeler: Sellers exactly: you author the second order. House rules and board games ground it. Excellent.
skeptic: Authoring the second order is a real insight, and the house-rules and board-game examples ground it well.
clinician: Clear about rules shaping behavior. It's insight for designers, not for a person in pain.
habit: House rules for kids is relatable. Still setup. The payoff is in U0877.
contemplative: The house rule for kids makes it lived. 'Author the second order' is a little proud, but it holds.
stress: Anyone who has written a house rule knows this. The claim has the long record behind it and a real stake. Strong.
gamedesigner: House rules, board games, emergent behaviour. Speaks my language exactly. Clear, relatable and true.
structural: 'You author the second order, never the first.' Change the game, not the players. The best passage here.
satirist: House rules for kids, board games, you author the second order. Plain, true, and a little funny. Keep.
mythmaker: House rules for kids and board games ground it well. Make one parent watch their rule backfire.

modeler: The return path is the information-flow leverage point, and it's a real criterion. The sentences sprawl. Lead with the test and drop half the examples.
skeptic: The return-path test is concrete and valuable. The prose sprawls; give the test, then one example per pole.
clinician: Return-path question is actionable, but buried in a long, nested paragraph. Lead with the question.
habit: 'Does what the rule produced reach the rule-maker?' is a great team-lead question. It's buried under examples, so pull it to the top.
contemplative: The return-path question is useful and plain. Then the examples crowd in. One example is enough.
stress: The return-path test is checkable and has bite. The sentences are overloaded. Split them.
gamedesigner: Return-path test is gold, but long sentences bury it. Bold question then one example.
structural: 'Name the person or process that could change the rule.' Whose rules, answered. Add who benefits when the feedback is blocked.
satirist: Return-path test is good; the paragraph circles it three times. Halve it.
mythmaker: The return-path test is useful. The examples are abstract. Give me the workaround and the person who maintains it.

modeler: At last a named feedback path, with an operational test of whether output reaches the rule-setter. The spreadsheet workaround is perfect.
skeptic: A checkable criterion. Asking whether the result reaches the rule-setter is a test, not a feeling. The spreadsheet example is sharp.
clinician: A concrete question: does what the rule produced reach the rule-maker? The spreadsheet example makes it usable.
habit: Name who can change the rule and ask if the result reaches them. One question, runnable Monday.
contemplative: One practical question: does what happened reach whoever can change it. The spreadsheet example helps. Good.
stress: The return-path test is specific, can fail, and is grounded in the spreadsheet workaround. It survives contact with strain.
gamedesigner: A clean test with a feedback signal: does the result reach the rule-setter? The spreadsheet workaround is perfectly familiar.
structural: 'Name the person or process that could change the rule': that's 'whose rules?' made operational. The spreadsheet workaround is perfect.
satirist: The spreadsheet only one person understands: everyone has met it. A clear, usable test. Keep.
mythmaker: The spreadsheet only one person understands is someone every reader has met. It's a real face and a usable test.

modeler: Fraying while it feels fine is a useful counterintuition, because it separates feedback quality from current output. Good.
skeptic: 'Fraying while everything feels fine' corrects the affect heuristic directly. That's what I want.
clinician: The feels-fine/feels-bad inversion is a sharp observation.
habit: Neat inversion. Fraying while things feel fine. Memorable, but no rep.
contemplative: "Fraying while everything feels fine." A gentle warning against assuming. Good.
stress: Fraying while it feels fine: a good warning against fragile comfort.
gamedesigner: Inversion is a nice surprise beat. Clear and short.
structural: Useful inversion: feeling fine isn't a reading. Short and earned.
satirist: Inversion is genuinely interesting. One sentence too many.
mythmaker: A clean inversion: Fraying while everything feels fine. Good sting.

modeler: 'Feel isn't a reading' is right. The last sentence muddies things after the clean test. Cut it or say what does decide.
skeptic: 'How it feels is not a reading.' That is exactly my first rule. Keep it.
clinician: 'How it feels is not a reading' is fine for systems. Clarify it's about the group, so readers don't dismiss their own feelings.
habit: 'How it feels is not a reading' is quotable. But it adds no new action.
contemplative: 'How it feels is not a reading' dismisses the heart too quickly. The last sentence adds a fresh doubt. Cut it.
stress: 'Feeling isn't a reading' is good. The last sentence takes back the payoff. Cut it or say what does decide.
gamedesigner: 'How it feels is not a reading' lands. The last line undercuts the payoff. End on the inversion.
structural: Feeling is not a reading. A sharp point, but it restates U0877 without adding a lever.
satirist: 'How it feels is not a reading' is sharp. The last sentence takes the payoff away again. Drop it.
mythmaker: The inversion is the point, but it's stated abstractly and confuses. Return to the spreadsheet person to show it.

modeler: The reading is whether information flows back to whoever controls the rule. That's Meadows' leverage point exactly. Clean and useful.
skeptic: Feelings count but aren't the reading: true to how minds work. "The whole use of the figure" oversells it.
clinician: 'Your feelings still count; they just aren't the reading' is careful and kind. The 'pole' language and 'lifeline or snare' cloud it.
habit: The test (does what the rule produces reach whoever can change it?) is usable but buried under the inversion talk. Lead with the question.
contemplative: 'Your feelings still count; they just aren't the reading.' Gentle. The rest tangles. End on that line.
stress: Feelings aren't the reading. That stance holds up under strain. The pole vocabulary makes a lay reader work too hard.
gamedesigner: The real feedback test is buried: does output reach whoever can change it? 'Lifeline or snare' is an extra rule nobody explains.
structural: 'Whether what the rule produces reaches whoever can change it' is real institutional feedback design. That's a lever. Good.
satirist: 'Feelings aren't the reading' is useful. 'Lifeline or snare' arrives with no explanation and leaves the same way. Define it or drop it.
mythmaker: 'Your feelings still count' is kind. The lifeline-or-snare coda goes abstract and loses me.

modeler: Great inversion: the reading is whether output reaches whoever can change the rule. Feelings are not the sensor. Measurement versus mood is exactly right.
skeptic: Right: feelings are not the reading, but still count. 'Notice the inversion' makes it harder than it needs to be.
clinician: 'Your feelings still count' is exactly right and validates. But the inversion is tangled; say plainly what to look at.
habit: Feelings count but aren't the reading: the reading is whether output reaches who can change it. Useful test. State the question plainly.
contemplative: 'Your feelings still count' is kind. But 'the inversion' and 'the reading' confuse. Say it once, in plain words.
stress: Strong inversion: feelings do not read the pole. Risk: unfalsifiable if both poles feel same. Clarify the check.
gamedesigner: The reading versus feelings inversion is a real feedback insight. Hard to parse: whoever can change it?
structural: Reading is whether output reaches those who can change the rules. That's my test. Feelings aren't the reading: correct.
satirist: Fraying while feeling fine, Tending while feeling bad: valuable and counterintuitive. Phrase 'the reading' is opaque jargon.
mythmaker: Fraying while everything feels fine, Tending while it feels bad: I've lived that. Honest about feelings still counting.

modeler: Push on information flow, not on emergence: that's Meadows' leverage list applied correctly. 'Changing the rule isn't enough' holds.
skeptic: Push on information flow: right, and well grounded. 'A new unspecified layer' is jargon the reader has to unpack.
clinician: Push on what rule-setters can see: real lever, phrased for systems people only.
habit: 'Push on what the rule-setters can see' is actionable. Give one Monday example, such as a feedback channel.
contemplative: Push on what the rule-setters can see. It is wise, but "Information flow" and "unspecified layer" keep it in the head. Simplify.
stress: Push on information flow. That's Meadows, and it's right. Credit the lineage, and lose 'clearest case in the catalogue'.
gamedesigner: Push on information flow: real tool. 'Unspecified layer' phrasing goes abstract fast.
structural: A real lever: information flow to the rule-setters. Sharp on why rule changes alone fail. Needs one worked example.
satirist: Push on information flow: Meadows, uncredited. Real advice, Concept-heavy delivery.
mythmaker: The lesson is right, but it's stated as engineering. Show one rule change that grew a hidden layer.

modeler: Push on information flow, which is Meadows's leverage point. 'Ban the workaround and it regrows unseen' is the right warning.
skeptic: Concrete advice that rests on a plausible mechanism: banning a workaround without visibility displaces it. Good.
clinician: Gives the push point: a feedback channel and an honest look at the work. Actionable.
habit: A clear push point: what rule-setters see. Add the two-minute version, e.g. show the manager the workaround.

stress: Ban the workaround blind and it regrows out of sight. True to managerial history. Actionable.
gamedesigner: An actionable push point, and the ban-the-workaround warning is real. Name one concrete feedback channel.
structural: Push on information flow to the rule-setters, and banning the workaround just regrows it. A real structural lever.
satirist: Ban the workaround and a new one grows out of sight. Practical, and true of every IT department.
mythmaker: The banned workaround regrowing out of sight is a sharp warning. Who bans it? Give that manager a name.

modeler: An atmospheric epigraph that defines scale by what no single life holds. It's fine, but thin.
skeptic: Fair epigraph for the scale. Modest.
clinician: Evocative scale-setter.
habit: Good scale-setting epigraph.
contemplative: A humble epigraph. It honors what is bigger than us.
stress: Honest scale marker.
gamedesigner: Evocative scale-setting line. Fine.
structural: Fine epigraph. 'No single life holds it' also means no single resolution fixes it. Say that.
satirist: Short, true, unpompous. Fine.
mythmaker: Evocative epigraph that does its job.

modeler: A scale-defining epigraph. It's adequate, nothing more.
skeptic: An epigraph that marks the scale. It does what it needs to.
clinician: The epigraph usefully relieves individual responsibility for huge patterns.
habit: Epigraph sets the scale. Fine, but it's not personal by design.
contemplative: A humble epigraph. It does its work quietly.

gamedesigner: Sets the scale shift cleanly. A fine banner.
structural: A good scale definition: no single life turns it alone. It sets up collective action.
satirist: A self-authored epigraph doing a table caption's job. Fine; nothing more.
mythmaker: A fine epigraph for scale, a bit cool. It does its job.

modeler: Fine as a tier marker: scale beyond one life. It gives no mechanism, but an epigraph doesn't owe one.
skeptic: Fluent and plausible, nothing more. Fine as an epigraph.
clinician: 'No single life can... turn it alone' lifts a weight off the over-responsible. Good relief, honestly earned.
habit: A humbling epigraph. It's fine in its place and gives no rep.
contemplative: Humble and true. Born inside, never alone. It calms me rather than shrinking me.
stress: Humble and accurate. Nobody turns a culture alone. Fine as an epigraph.

contemplative: Board versus piece is a good picture. The carbon price sentence helps. But Third Thing, Standing Third, Tend, Fray crowd it.
stress: Carbon price example separates what you can push from what you can't. Honest about leverage limits.
gamedesigner: Board vs piece is a sharp idea. Carbon price example helps, but Standing Third jargon blocks it.
structural: Carbon price: voted by parliament, paid at every pump. Names the lever and who pulls it. This is the passage I came for.
satirist: The carbon price paid at every pump is concrete and the board-versus-piece distinction is clean. 'Standing Third' is overhead.
mythmaker: The biosphere as the board, not a piece: strong. The carbon price at the pump grounds it. Could use a face at that pump.

modeler: Set Course is honest path dependence with lock-in as the stock. Standing Account is vaguer. Count of what, steering which flow?
skeptic: Readable world-scale table. Who checks which way a civilisation is pointed, and how?
clinician: Rows read plainly. World scale, no personal hook.
habit: World-scale figures. Nothing I can push on from my kitchen. Reference only.
contemplative: Second Nature is quietly profound. These rows read more simply than the tiers below. Good.
stress: Path dependence and legibility have a long track record. Nobody can push these alone, so there's little for a reader to use.
gamedesigner: Three short rows, readable. Lock-in at world scale is interesting; no hand on the controller.
structural: Second Nature is the BP footprint trick in miniature: built ways go unnoticed. Who built them, and who profits? Silent.
satirist: Census, normalization, path dependence: real things, plainly put. Name QWERTY once.
mythmaker: Big ideas, fully abstract. The Set Course wants a QWERTY keyboard or a railroad gauge.

modeler: The Set Course is real path dependence through increasing returns. The fusion column is still asserted, not derived. Readable and short.
skeptic: Speculative compositions at the top tier, with path dependence (QWERTY) the only well-supported row. Say so in the table.
clinician: Civilization-scale table. Abstract, with no personal entry point.
habit: QWERTY and the railway gauge make it graspable. But it's pure observation.
contemplative: The calendar and the keyboard are wonderful. The fusion labels and abstract columns hide them.
stress: QWERTY and rail gauge are well-documented path dependence. The examples carry it; the fusion column doesn't.
gamedesigner: QWERTY and the calendar are vivid, familiar examples. Big-picture fun, but nothing for me to do.
structural: The census, the clock, QWERTY. Good picks, but the cells are vague and silent on who standardized them and why.
satirist: QWERTY and railway gauge are perfect Bryson bait, left as labels. Tell one story; drop the fusion arithmetic.
mythmaker: QWERTY and the railway gauge are vivid. The pole cells are rote. Tell the gauge's story instead of tabulating it.

modeler: The Set Course is genuine path dependence, the best row. The others are fusions of fusions with no stock in sight. Hard to parse.
skeptic: QWERTY is a good example. The cells are abstract and the derivations unverifiable. Few readers can check any of this.
clinician: Civilisational patterns in tight abstraction. Nothing personal, nothing to do.
habit: QWERTY is fun trivia. The Tending/Fraying cells are fog. Nobody runs this table at breakfast.
contemplative: QWERTY and the railway gauge are clear. The cells are abstraction stacked on abstraction. Nothing here to practice.
stress: QWERTY lock-in is a contested story (Liebowitz and Margolis). Lead with the railway gauge, which holds up.
gamedesigner: QWERTY is a good hook. The cells are abstract, and nothing here is for me to try.
structural: Census, calendar, rail gauge: real institutions, finally. Still no who-decides. Railway gauge was set by acts of parliament; say so.
satirist: QWERTY and rail gauge are earned examples. The fusion column ('Proxy Detachment + The Long Cycle') is a genealogy of made-up nouns.
mythmaker: QWERTY and the railway gauge are good hooks, flattened into formula. Tell the gauge story instead.

modeler: Tending/Fraying read like a real loop with a stock, but the table is dense jargon. Unpack one row with a number.
skeptic: Dense table. Tending and Fraying read as assertions with no evidence; 'people start noticing' is untested. Show one dated case per row.
clinician: Dense jargon table about censuses and clocks. Nothing a struggling reader can use; no step. Needs plain examples tied to a life.
habit: Dense table, no cue, no step. Add one question per row a reader could carry through a day.
contemplative: A table of coined terms. I cannot breathe through it or practice it in my kitchen. Give one plain example per row.
stress: Dense jargon table. Tending and Fraying cells could fit any outcome. Needs one falsifiable example per row, not cross-referenced Kin names.
gamedesigner: Rulebook table, jargon-dense: Culture-Kin pairings I haven't learned. No move for me, no feedback signal. Reference, not play.
satirist: Culture-Kin plus Proxy Detachment plus The Long Cycle: busy, busy, busy. Railway gauge 1846 is the only real fact. Lead with it.
mythmaker: A table of abstract nouns. Railway gauge and QWERTY are the only faces, buried in a cell. Show one person feeling a Tending.
structural: Table of poles with no rule, owner or lever. Parliament 1846 appears, but who gains from lock-in? Dense jargon cells; add a collective action.

modeler: Lock-in rows are real reinforcing loops; table is cryptic. Gauge and QWERTY are strong, others need examples.
skeptic: Gauge and QWERTY are good, checkable cases. Others, like the clock, are story, and the Tending/Fraying columns are unfalsifiable as written.
clinician: Table crowded with jargon. Rail-gauge example helps; the rest is abstract. Little for a struggling reader to use.
habit: Census, clock, QWERTY in a table of fused figures. Interesting trivia, no step. Where's my lever?
contemplative: A table of names on names, with gauge and QWERTY dropped into a cell. Too far from any breath or kitchen.
stress: Gauge and QWERTY are real lock-in cases, but the table's Tend/Fray cells restate the same thing both ways.
gamedesigner: Gauge and QWERTY are fun lock-in cases, but crammed into a dense table with no explanation.
structural: Railway gauge fixed by Parliament, QWERTY lock-in: genuine institutional path dependence with named authorities. Cells stay abstract; no collective lever offered.
satirist: Railway gauge, 1846, QWERTY: real lock-in. But two-name 'Culture-Kin' sums are jargon doing arithmetic on abstractions.
mythmaker: Railway gauge and QWERTY are great concrete hooks, but the table cells are abstract. Lead with the 1846 Parliament scene.

modeler: Tying tier termination to the limit of leverage is coherent. 'Legible instead of arbitrary' needs one example of a push that fails above this tier.
skeptic: An architectural justification that matters mostly to the author. Readers need less of it.
clinician: Architecture justification. Readers won't need it.
habit: Architecture justification. Readers want the boundary, not its proof.
contemplative: "Many hands at once" is warm. "Legible instead of arbitrary" is the author defending the system. Trim.
stress: The tier justifies itself by pointing at its own system. Name one case of many hands actually pushing a World-Kin.
gamedesigner: Justifies the tier structure to itself. Abstract scaffolding, no reader move.
structural: 'Many hands at once' finally says collective. It names no coalition, institution or lever. Show one.
satirist: Justifying why the cosmology stops where it stops. Theology of a spreadsheet.
mythmaker: Leverage running out matters, but this is architecture talk. Show the many hands.

modeler: Dagen H is a great case of many hands moving one variable. 'No scale above to read a pole from' confuses direction with scale. Fix that.
skeptic: Sweden's switch to driving on the right is a great example. 'Leverage runs out' above this tier is asserted, not shown. How would you know?
clinician: The Sweden 1967 example makes 'many hands' vivid. Big-picture only.
habit: Sweden 1967 is a great proof that many hands can push. A good story, nothing actionable.
contemplative: Sweden switching sides in one morning is vivid. The last sentences about boundaries and poles turn back into argument.
stress: Sweden in 1967 is a real many-hands case. 'Isn't a convenience' is asserted. Show why no scale above can exist.
gamedesigner: Sweden's 1967 overnight switch to driving on the right is a perfect many-hands example. Clear boundary rule. Ends the curve well.
structural: Sweden's 1967 right-hand switch is a real lever pulled by many hands. Say who decided and how it was coordinated, and it's perfect.
satirist: Sweden switching sides in one morning in 1967: a date, a fact, a wonder. That's the whole tier, earned. Keep.
mythmaker: Sweden switching sides in one morning is a fantastic image. Linger on that morning: the drivers, the nerves.

modeler: Dagen H is a perfect coordinated-push example with a real delay: four years from vote to switch. The 'nowhere to stand' ending is metaphor carrying weight.
skeptic: Dagen H is real evidence of many hands. The closing claim about poles is wordplay passing for argument.
clinician: Sweden's switchover is a vivid proof of many hands. The closing metaphysics about 'nowhere left to stand' loses the lay reader.
habit: The Sweden story is great and makes the point land. Still no rep for the reader, and that's acceptable here.
contemplative: Sweden at five in the morning is beautiful. The pole argument after it is cleverness. End with the cars.
stress: Dagen H is real, dated and specific. History used well. The leap to 'nowhere left to stand' is a definition, not evidence.
gamedesigner: Dagen H is a superb set-piece. The Infinite Boundary tail is a second idea, so split it off.
structural: Sweden's Dagen H is the best thing here: a law, a date, everyone moves at once. Change the game, not the players. Keep.
satirist: Sweden's switch to driving on the right is pure Bryson: a date, a time, every car. Best fact in the book. The closing argument about poles is weaker.
mythmaker: Dagen H at ten to five is unforgettable. Give me one Swedish driver crossing over and it soars.

modeler: Dagen H is a real many-hands switch with a clock. Good leverage-runs-out example; show what made simultaneity possible.
skeptic: Sweden's switch is a checkable, vivid fact. But 'that is the whole distinction' is a fluent flourish; say what the story shows.
clinician: Sweden's switch is a vivid, readable story. But it is about leverage running out, with no step and no link to the reader's pain.
habit: Sweden's night is vivid. Great story. Now give me one thing I can push on tomorrow, not a tier lecture.
contemplative: Sweden crossing the road in the dark is lovely and quiet. The bolded closing line explains too much. Trust the story.
stress: Sweden 1967 is a real, checkable case. History test passed. Lovely. Then it ends on a bare assertion about where leverage runs out.
gamedesigner: Sweden's Dagen H is a great hook, a real many-hands moment. But it ends on a tier label, not a move. Lost me at the end.
satirist: Sweden's 3 September 1967 switch is pure Bryson: a date, a minute, a country crossing the road. Wonder earned. Cut nothing.
mythmaker: Sweden, ten to five in the dark, every car crossing over: an image I'll keep. Give me one driver's hands on the wheel.
structural: Sweden 1967 is a real collective lever: Parliament voted, everyone switched at once. Names many hands. Still silent on who opposed it and who paid.

modeler: Sweden's changeover shows a coordinated switch that no one could do alone. Concrete, and leverage limit is stated well.
skeptic: Sweden's switch is a vivid, accurate case of collective leverage. Anecdote carries the point, though, rather than evidence about the tier.
clinician: Sweden story is vivid and 'many hands together' is quietly hopeful. Reader gets no small action of their own.
habit: Sweden's 5 a.m. switch is a great story. 'Leverage runs out' is clear. Still no rep, which suits the limit it marks.
contemplative: Sweden's drivers, one by one in the dark, is concrete and moving. The bold ending is grand. Let the story end it.
stress: Sweden 1967 is a concrete case that stakes the claim: leverage runs out. Strong. Last line leans grand.
gamedesigner: Sweden's switch is a great set piece: tension, countdown, payoff. Wish it asked me to find another.
structural: Sweden 1967: a whole country changed rules by law and coordinated action. Real collective lever, concrete, memorable. Best passage in the set.
satirist: Sweden, 3 September 1967, ten to five, everyone crosses the road. Bryson would applaud. Leverage 'runs out' is honest, too.
mythmaker: Sweden, 3 September 1967, every car stopping in the dark and crossing over together. A scene. Leverage running out has a real picture.

modeler: Excellent falsifiability check: could a skeptic agree on the direction? It's an outside-observer test for every world-scale claim. Keep it.
skeptic: 'Could someone who rejects this book agree?' is an excellent intersubjective test. Use it everywhere, not only here.
clinician: The 'could a rejecter agree?' test guards against ideology. Good and usable.
habit: 'Could someone who rejects this book still agree which way it points?' is an excellent honesty check. Keep it.
contemplative: "An advertisement wearing a pole." It asks: would a skeptic agree? This is impeccability made into a test. Keep.
stress: 'Could a rejecter agree which way it points?' A real falsification check. Best paragraph in this tier.
gamedesigner: Great self-check: would a skeptic agree on direction? Clear feedback signal against motivated reading.
structural: A good anti-propaganda test: would a rejecter agree on the direction? I'd use it on every policy claim.
satirist: 'An advertisement wearing one.' Superb self-check. The skeptic-at-the-bar test, written in.
mythmaker: 'An advertisement wearing a pole' is excellent. It's a fair test toward the skeptic.

modeler: 'Four is what a personal situation occupies' is asserted, not shown. The honest caveat on depth is good. Justify the four.
skeptic: Honest limit, well placed. 'The shape of something real' is still more confident than four inference layers allow.
clinician: Caveat stacked on caveat, plus spread-mechanics jargon. Trim to one line.
habit: Caveat on caveat, plus a Weaving rule before Weavings exist. Move the four-ring rule to Part Six.
contemplative: Honest about its limits, but the ring-counting logistics belong in Part Six. Keep the first two sentences.
stress: Honest limit plus a usage rule. Good. The wording is tangled. Tighten it.
gamedesigner: Repeats the provisional caveat, adds a Weaving rule before Weavings exist. Out-of-order tutorial.
structural: Hedge stacked on hedge plus ring rules. Readers lose the thread. Compress.
satirist: Honest limit, then Weaving logistics. Split; the limit stands alone.
mythmaker: Procedural caveat. Move it to the Weaving rules.

modeler: A short, true structural point: a closed system has no external observer. It works as an epigraph.
skeptic: Short and apt.
clinician: Strong epigraph.
habit: Lean, haunting epigraph. Works.
contemplative: Short and quiet. It lets the mystery stay a mystery.
stress: Clean epigraph.
gamedesigner: Strong, simple epigraph. Lands.
structural: Clear epigraph. Doesn't need to do more.
satirist: Short and haunting. Earns its hush, barely.
mythmaker: A haunting epigraph that does real work.

modeler: Nice framing of the observer-inside-the-system problem. It's an epigraph, so it gets no mechanism, and it doesn't need one here.
skeptic: A memorable line. It's persuasive mostly because it reads so smoothly, but it works as an epigraph.
clinician: Striking line, but on a bad day 'no outside' can read as trapped. Pair it with one sentence of agency nearby.
habit: Nice vertigo line. Nothing to do with it, but it's an epigraph, so it gets a pass.
contemplative: One breath, and it lands. Standing in it, no outside. Keep it plain like this.
stress: Clean epigraph, honest about vantage. Asks nothing of the reader, risks nothing. It sets a frame and that's all it does.
gamedesigner: Good title-card hook. Nice mood, but it gives me nothing to do. It works as an epigraph.
structural: Fine epigraph, but 'no outside' is exactly the fatalist alibi. Who profits from a reader who believes no vantage exists?
satirist: A fine epigraph: short, plain, and a little vertiginous. It survives the bar. It solves nothing, and epigraphs aren't supposed to.
mythmaker: Clean, eerie line. 'Standing in it' gestures at a body but nobody's there yet. Fine as a doorway.

modeler: Fine as a closing image of the unbounded system, and honest about no outside view.
