skeptic: Elegant and unfalsifiable. Harmless as an epigraph.
clinician: A graceful epigraph, and harmless. It earns its place as a pause, not as help.
habit: An atmospheric epigraph. It does its job and gives no action.
contemplative: Standing in it, never seeing it finished. Quiet, humbling, kind. Keep it.
stress: A decent epigraph. Humble about the whole. Nothing to stress-test, nothing to use.
gamedesigner: Evocative, and it puts me inside the frame. Works as a chapter opener.
structural: Pretty, and harmless. Lets everyone off the hook by being about everything. Fine as epigraph, no lever.
satirist: Earns its awe by being modest. It survives at a bar, just.
mythmaker: 'You are standing in it.' Simple and haunting. Works.

modeler: Lovely image of being inside the loop. No stock or flow, but an epigraph can carry that.
skeptic: Lovely, and I have no reason to believe it. Fluent epigraph, no content to test.
clinician: Gently relieves the pressure of needing the finished picture. No guilt in it, but no next step either.
habit: Lovely line, zero action. Fine as an epigraph; it asks nothing of me at 7:04.
contemplative: Short, humble, one breath. It places me inside the pattern without arguing. Nothing to remove.
stress: Humble about the author's vantage, and it lands. But as an epigraph it is unfalsifiable; nothing could count against it.
gamedesigner: Nice epigraph, evocative, one beat. Pure cutscene though: no goal, no action.
satirist: Pretty and true. Passes the bar test only barely; it is a mood, not a tool. Keep as epigraph.
mythmaker: Lovely. Nobody ever stood outside to see it finished. It puts me inside the story.
structural: Pretty, but pure mood. 'Standing in it' risks fatalism: no one outside, so no one acts. Who does this excuse?

modeler: The no-vantage, no-pole logic follows from the book's own rules. The terminal-object borrowing is flagged honestly, but it adds jargon without adding mechanism.
skeptic: Credit for saying the terminal object is a borrowed word, not a proof. Still dense for a lay reader.
clinician: Terminal-object math loses lay readers. Keep 'no outside, so no pole'.
habit: The terminal-object borrowing will lose most readers. 'No outside, so no pole' carries it alone.
contemplative: The borrowed math term decorates. "What terminates has no outside" is enough on its own.
stress: Borrowing 'terminal object' dresses a metaphor up as rigor. It admits it's not a proof. Better still to drop the math.
gamedesigner: Terminal object aside spikes difficulty. Core claim, no vantage so no pole, is enough.
structural: The terminal-object borrowing is clever but opaque to lay readers. Interesting, and inert.
satirist: Terminal object borrowed 'not as proof': then why borrow it? Pomp in a lab coat.
mythmaker: The terminal-object jargon chills it. 'What terminates has no outside' alone would do.

modeler: Clean termination argument: no scale above means no vantage, which means no pole. The riverbank image earns its keep. A recursion base case done properly.
skeptic: The derivation only follows from rules the book wrote for itself. The river image helps, but 'vantage', 'pole' and 'recursion chain' pile up.
clinician: The river image helps, but the chain of poles, vantages and scales is a logic puzzle. Nobody struggling gets anything to hold here.
habit: The river-bank image works, but 'vantage, scale, recursion chain' reads like a proof. No rep here. Keep the bank, cut the logic chain.
contemplative: A chain of rules, then a river. Keep the river and the last line. Let the logic go.
stress: The logic chain is tidy and the river line lands. But 'aggregated never averaged' and the jargon pile-up lose the lay reader.
gamedesigner: The river-bank image is good, but pole, vantage, scale and recursion chain land at once. Difficulty spike. Lead with the bank.
structural: Tidy derivation from internal rules, river image helps. But pure cosmology: no rule, no owner, no lever. Dense for lay readers.
satirist: The river bank line is the whole argument. 'Pole read from a vantage, recursion chain ends here' is jargon on top of it. Lead with the bank.
mythmaker: The river bank is a lovely image, buried under the vantage-scale-pole syllogism. Lead with the bank, cut the logic chain.

modeler: The riverbank analogy explains why there are no poles. 'Added up, never averaged' is a nice precision. The pole claim is still more image than mechanism.
skeptic: The river bank works. "Added up and never averaged" sounds precise and means little. Compared to what?
clinician: The river bank makes the logic clear. It's pure cosmology, with no human handhold.
habit: "Added up and never averaged" is opaque. It's pure abstraction, so cut it to the riverbank line.
contemplative: The riverbank is good. 'What has no outside has no pole' is the author admiring a phrase. Let the river do it.
stress: Unfalsifiable by construction, but it says so plainly and claims nothing from it. Acceptable, barely.
gamedesigner: The river bank makes 'no pole' intuitive. A clear rule, but a cutscene beat.
structural: River bank metaphor is clear. But 'no pole, nowhere to stand' risks fatalism at exactly the scale where policy matters most.
satirist: The riverbank image is plain and works. 'Added up and never averaged' is decoration. The point is clear and abstract only.
mythmaker: The riverbank is a clean image, then logic takes over. Put someone on that bank.

modeler: Good: a pole needs a vantage, so the whole has no gauge. That's a system boundary argument, fairly stated.
skeptic: The riverbank image is clear and honestly admits no vantage point. Why no poles follows from the metaphor, not from evidence.
clinician: Riverbank image is clear and honest about limits. Still no action for a reader, and it never touches their pain.
habit: Riverbank works. But the payoff is 'what you can push are the figures below': which one, when? Name a cue.
contemplative: The riverbank helps me see. Then the catalogue talk and the 'pole' logic crowd it. Let the river carry it.
stress: Riverbank image is clean, and it admits the limit: no pole, no verdict. Honest restraint. Still pure framing, no use.
gamedesigner: Riverbank image makes the no-pole rule clear. But it's a rule I can't play; it only tells me what's off the board.
satirist: Riverbank gives the abstraction a post to hang on. Admitting there is no vantage point is admirably unpompous.
mythmaker: Water climbing the post earns the point that no bank sees everything. Short on stakes, but the image works.
structural: Riverbank image is clear, and 'what you can push are the figures below' points to levers. Yet the limit risks excusing inaction.

modeler: Nice: a pole needs a vantage, and the whole has none. Stock-reading from outside is real systems thinking. Still no mechanism for what 'pushing figures' does to the sum.
skeptic: The bank metaphor is clear and honestly limits the claim. But no practical use; 'push the figures nearest your hands' is advice with no support.
clinician: Riverbank image is clear; 'no reason to wait' plus pushing nearby figures gives a small next step. Slightly abstract, but safe and non-blaming.
habit: Nice river image, and 'push what's nearest your hands' nearly gives an action. But which figure, what push, when? Name one nearby figure and one two-minute move.
contemplative: The riverbank is plain and true, and the ending is kind: push what is near your hands. Too much catalogue talk before it.
stress: Honest about where the metaphor stops, and the river image is clear. But 'start near your hands' is thin. Name one figure to push, and how.
gamedesigner: Riverbank image lands the no-vantage-point idea nicely. But it's a cutscene: no move for me. Close with one figure to push today.
structural: Good that it points at pushable figures, but no rule, owner or lever is named. Say which figures a group could push.
satirist: The riverbank post is a real picture. But 'every figure added together' is a capitalized Concept doing little. Name one figure you can actually push.
mythmaker: The riverbank post is a real image, but nobody's on the bank. Give me a name and what they lose by waiting.

modeler: Cute acronym. The denominator metaphor is decorative, a rhyme with fractions rather than a mechanism. Cut it or keep it as a wink.
skeptic: The G.O.D. joke persuades by charm, not content. Fluency doing the work. Trim it.
clinician: The playful GOD acronym works. The denominator explanation is clear enough.
habit: The G.O.D. joke lands, and the denominator gloss is clear. A charming beat, no action.
contemplative: The initials joke is cleverness performing, and it may wound a believer. The denominator image is fine without it.
stress: The GOD acronym wink undercuts the restraint around it. Cute and fragile. Cut.
gamedesigner: GOD joke is charming; the denominator explanation is muddy. Trim to the gag plus one line.
structural: The acronym joke plus fractions talk. Cute, and it does no work. Cut.
satirist: G.O.D. acronym: finally Bokonon walks in. Keep the wink; trim the denominator lecture.
mythmaker: The G.O.D. joke has charm and a wink of heart. The fraction gloss is a nice touch.

modeler: The denominator gloss is precise: one base everything is written over. The pun is honest. It does nothing in practice.
skeptic: The denominator gloss is clear. The joke on the initials gets ahead of any argument for it.
clinician: Clever, and the denominator gloss is clear. It's wordplay, not help. Fine as color, earns nothing practical.
habit: Clever denominator gloss and an honest wink. Still pure framing. Fine as a short aside, nothing to do Monday.
contemplative: The initials joke shows off. The denominator image teaches. Keep the teaching and let the wink go.
stress: Winking at G.O.D. is ego dressed as wit. The denominator gloss is clear but buys nothing. Cut the joke or justify it.
gamedesigner: The wink plays well and the denominator gloss is clear. Still a cutscene though, since the reader has no move.
structural: A GOD acronym gag plus a fractions lesson. Clear enough, does no work. Cut or fold into U0894.
satirist: G.O.D., and they know it. That's Bokonon-grade self-awareness. The fraction explanation actually lands. Keep it.
mythmaker: The joke has a wink and a person behind it. Denominator gloss lands. Still no face, only 'practitioners.'

modeler: The common-denominator arithmetic is a correct, cute picture of a shared base. The pun is self-aware. It holds as a definition, not a mechanism.
skeptic: The fraction analogy doesn't carry "written over." The joke undercuts the seriousness that follows. Cut it, or make the math do work.
clinician: The fractions help, but 'written over' stays murky, and the in-joke distracts. Cut the joke and keep the denominator.
habit: The acronym wink and the fraction lesson pull against each other. It's clever and gives nothing to do.
contemplative: The initials joke stands in front of the idea. Ego, gently said. The fractions are clear; the last line dissolves.
stress: The GOD wink is clever-cute, the author grinning in front of the idea. The fraction analogy is fine. Cut the joke or own it shorter.
gamedesigner: The fractions example is neat and the pun is winking. 'Written over' stays foggy. No action.
structural: GOD acronym wink plus fractions lesson. Clever, inert. Nothing for anyone to do, organize or vote on.
satirist: It knows what the initials spell and says so. Bokonon would approve. The fractions illustration is correct and plain.
mythmaker: The wink at the initials is charming and the fractions are clear. A lecture with a grin, but still a lecture.

modeler: Common denominator is real arithmetic, not decoration. The mapping to patterns is still a rhyme, but a clean one.
skeptic: The fractions arithmetic is correct and clarifying. The leap to 'the whole is the bottom' is analogy, not argument.
clinician: Common-denominator metaphor is neat and clear. It is pure abstraction; nothing the reader can try today.
habit: Clear fractions metaphor, pure abstraction. Great. So what do I do Monday with 'a different top'?
contemplative: Common denominators are a gentle picture. A little clever, yet it clarifies. Does it ask me to do anything?
stress: Common-denominator fractions make the point plainly. Clever, but it's a gloss. Nothing here could be wrong, so nothing is tested.
gamedesigner: Sixths example is a clean tutorial, I can check the arithmetic myself. But it's a naming gloss; no action for the reader.
satirist: Sixths, thirds, halves: actual arithmetic doing actual work. Rare. The silly capitalized name is quietly cut down by a sum.
mythmaker: Halves, thirds and sixths over a shared bottom is clever and clear. Tops and bottom could be people, but the trick lands.
structural: Common-denominator analogy is tidy and clear. Zero levers, zero rules. Pure bigger-picture ornament; who profits from believing it?

modeler: Common denominator is a clean, checkable analogy, and it builds from arithmetic. But it names no stock or flow; 'written over' is still a rhyme.
skeptic: Common-denominator analogy is tidy and easy, but it's a metaphor doing the work of an argument. Why should routines and calendars share a bottom?
clinician: Fractions analogy is clear and neat, but it's pure explanation. No step, nothing a struggling reader can use. Add one thing to do.
habit: The fractions analogy is clear and tidy. Great. So what do I do Monday? Nothing here to act on; add one question: which 'top' is yours?
contemplative: Fractions to explain a name. Clever, and it pulls me into my head. Say simply: one whole under every routine.
stress: Fractions are a clean, checkable image of a shared base. Nothing here could fail or be tested. Show a case where the common bottom changes a choice.
gamedesigner: Fractions analogy teaches the rule fast, and the tops/bottom image sticks. Still no controller in hand: have me write my routine over the whole.
structural: Neat fraction image, but it is vocabulary, not mechanism. Nothing here says whose rules or which lever.
satirist: Sixths earn their keep: concrete, checkable, a wink at the pun. But then it waves at 'morning routine' and stops. Show one real denominator.
mythmaker: Tidy sixths, zero blood. Fractions need a person who has to square a morning with a country's calendar.

modeler: 'Drift without will' is the right systems framing: an aggregate trajectory nobody authored. Honest and well-judged.
skeptic: 'The largest real thing there is' is an unsupported superlative. Drop it and say only that the aggregate has a drift.
clinician: The 'drift' idea is respectful and clear.
habit: 'The largest real thing there is', and not reachable by petition. Honest and moving.
contemplative: "A drift, not authored, not reachable by petition, the largest real thing." Moving, but the sentences are heavy. Breathe between them.
stress: 'Largest real thing there is' can't be checked. Calling it a drift with no will is honest; the superlative isn't.
gamedesigner: 'Drift, not will' is a memorable, honest move. Plays for believers and skeptics alike.
structural: 'Not reachable by petition' flirts with fatalism. Make clear that petition still reaches every tier below.
satirist: 'Largest real thing there is' is unearned wonder. Give drift one example or demote it.
mythmaker: Drift with no author, the largest real thing. It treats the believer with courtesy, and that moves me.

modeler: The stadium-crowd drift is real emergence: an aggregate with no controller. It's good that petition is moved to the tiers where it works.
skeptic: The crowd image earns its keep: a drift that nobody chose. 'Nothing you are part of is larger' is asserted, not shown.
clinician: Honest, and the stadium crowd works. 'No petition reaches it' may sting a praying reader. Acknowledge that loss before moving on.
habit: Stadium crowd drift lands for a believer. 'Petition reaches every tier below' points toward action but never names one push.
contemplative: The crowd leaving the stadium is beautiful, and it is buried. Tiers and petitions agitate. Say less.
stress: Good. It says plainly that petition doesn't reach the top and points to where pushing works. The stadium crowd survives strain.
gamedesigner: The stadium-crowd drift is a great image, and 'petition reaches every tier below' gives the player a lever back.
structural: Earns it: the drift answers no petition, so push on the tiers that do. That redirects attention to levers. Stadium crowd image lands.
satirist: The stadium crowd turns a theology into a fact you've lived. It's honest with believers without sneering. 'No petition reaches it' is plain and brave.
mythmaker: The stadium crowd is the image, and it treats the believer with respect, not as a straw man. 'No petition reaches it' stings honestly.

modeler: A respectful seam with faith that stops on purpose. Not my department, but the boundary is drawn cleanly.
skeptic: Respectful about faith and clear about where it stops. Good boundary-setting.
clinician: Respectful seam with faith. A believer won't feel attacked. Keep.
habit: A respectful seam with faith, and it stops on purpose. Good restraint.
contemplative: It blends with faith instead of clashing. "It stops on purpose." This is gentle and respectful.
stress: Stops on purpose and doesn't compete with faith. That's humble and hard to break.
gamedesigner: Respectful seam with faith. Clear stopping point. Good level boundary.
structural: A graceful seam with faith. Irrelevant to who pulls which lever, but clear and honest.
satirist: Gracious seam with faith. 'Stops on purpose' is honest. Keep.
mythmaker: A generous seam with faith, no straw man. It stops on purpose, and that's earned.

modeler: 'Fatalism is uncheckable from any held vantage' is a neat move. Unverifiable isn't the same as false, though, so say 'idle', not 'unavailable'.
skeptic: Making fatalism uncheckable is a clever, practically freeing move. The paragraph sprawls; cut the leverage-ladder detour.
clinician: Defuses 'it was always going to happen', a hopelessness thought. Valuable, but the prose is thick. Lead with the plain line.
habit: Killing 'it was always going to happen' is truly useful, but it's wordy. Give the rep: catch yourself saying it, and ask what you'd do differently.
contemplative: Freedom from "it was always going to happen" is a real gift. The framing heading and the cross-references bury it.
stress: The fatalism argument is clever, but unverifiable cuts both ways. Is free action checkable either? Concede that, then keep.
gamedesigner: Fatalism made unavailable: real payoff. Too many qualifiers and cross-references; tighten to three sentences.
structural: It disarms fatalism, which I want. It stops short: say what fatalism excuses, and the lever it was hiding.
satirist: Fatalism made uncheckable: genuinely useful. Lead with that sentence; cut the cross-references.
mythmaker: Fatalism made unavailable gives real relief. The cross-references at the end dilute it, so trim them.

modeler: A repetition of the preceding chapter. Cut it, since it's already said.
skeptic: A plain closing line. It repeats U0894.
clinician: 'It is not addressing you' protects against magical thinking. Good close.
habit: A firm three-line close. Works.
contemplative: Three short sentences, plain and calm. This is how the whole chapter should sound.
stress: Fine coda.
gamedesigner: Clean closer. Short, repeats but lands.
structural: A clean closing denial. Fine.
satirist: Plain. Good. Third repetition of 'no will' though.
mythmaker: A cool, clean closing beat.

modeler: Reassuring, but it only restates U0896. Fold it in, or give it a test for telling 'message' from noise.
skeptic: A useful guard against seeing meaning in noise. But 'it is not' claims a certainty nobody inside the whole could have.
clinician: Good grounding for an anxious reader reading omens: it isn't a message. 'Yours to push on' returns agency without blame.
habit: Good reframe for a spooky-sign moment. Give it a cue: when it feels like a message, name one thing below it to push on.
contemplative: A gentle release from reading omens. One clear sentence would do. Drop 'and nothing more'.
stress: A falsifiable disavowal that sends the reader back to tractable tiers. A modest claim that holds.
gamedesigner: Clean payoff that hands the controller back with 'yours to push on.' Short, which suits it.
structural: Good that it refuses cosmic messaging and hands agency back. 'Yours to push on' is still private. Name one collective tier.
satirist: A plain, consoling coda. It mostly restates U0896. The tier-pushing line is the only new thing, so fold it in or cut.
mythmaker: Speaks to someone who has felt the universe nudging them. Kind, firm. Bring back the stadium crowd here to give it rhyme.

modeler: A true line, but it's a slogan. Its value depends on the stopping rule that follows.
skeptic: Correct, and a needed caution.
clinician: Wise epigraph. It does its job.
habit: Right epigraph for the right chapter.
contemplative: A true and simple epigraph.
stress: Good corrective epigraph.
gamedesigner: Good epigraph, sets the right expectation.
structural: A good epigraph against taxonomy for its own sake.
satirist: Self-deflating epigraph. Fine.
mythmaker: Sharp, a little rueful. It works.

modeler: A filter rule stated well. Model the decision, not the inventory. That's usable.
skeptic: Practical and modest. A rule of thumb I can actually use.
clinician: Practical and kind: keep only what changes behavior. Cuts the tendency to over-catalogue yourself. Works in its place.
habit: 'Keep the few names that change what you do.' Finally, a filter I can use. Great epigraph.
contemplative: Plain and useful. Keep the few names. It practices what it says.
stress: Sound working rule. Generic, though. Any productivity book says it.
gamedesigner: Practical rule in one line: keep the names that change what you do. Clear success condition.
structural: Useful rule: keep the names that change what you do. Practical, plain. A small epigraph, but it pulls its weight.
satirist: Useful advice with no incense. A rare epigraph that tells you what to do.
mythmaker: Practical maxim, no heartbeat. Works as a signpost, not as a line anyone carries home.

modeler: Every model is a compression; keep the variables that change decisions. Good modeling advice in a single line.
skeptic: Parsimony advice I endorse: keep only the names that change behaviour.
clinician: Good anti-overwhelm advice: keep only the names that change what you do. That's permission to stop collecting.
habit: "Keep the few names that change what you do" is my creed. Now tell me how many: three?
contemplative: Keep the few names that change what you do. That is this whole teaching in one breath.
stress: The best epigraph here. It is anti-grandiose about the book's own catalogue. Keep.
gamedesigner: A practical design rule: keep the names that change what you do. Good guidance on scope.
structural: Good discipline: keep only names that change behavior. Applies to taxonomies like this one. Short, earns its place.
satirist: Borges in a sentence, plus actual advice: keep the names that change what you do. Good.
mythmaker: A practical, memorable line. 'Get you home' almost gives it a traveller.

modeler: 'Four or five run your life' is a useful sizing claim and it lowers the burden. Taxonomy, not pantheon: good.
skeptic: 'The rest describe other people's' is the bias blind spot, endorsed instead of flagged. We see biases in others first; warn the reader.
clinician: 'Four or five run your life, don't memorize' relieves pressure. Kind.
habit: Four or five run your life, so don't memorise. That's a permission slip I needed. Ask which four.
contemplative: "Four or five run your lives." This frees me from memorizing. Warm and practical.
stress: 'Taxonomy, not a pantheon', four or five that matter. Modest and true. Keep.
gamedesigner: Relief for players: you'll use four or five. Lowers the learning curve. Great.
structural: Honest: four or five run your life. Note: they're all your inner ones, unless the book shows the outer.
satirist: 'Taxonomy, not a pantheon.' Four or five run your life. Honest and human.
mythmaker: 'Four or five run your lives' gives me a personal hook. Good.

modeler: Predicts, compresses, enables is a real acceptance test. 'Climate, not Tuesday' is Meadows' behavior over time exactly. Strong.
skeptic: 'It feels true is not among them': thank you. Predict, compress, enable are real criteria. Climate, not Tuesday, lands.
clinician: Climate-not-Tuesday is great. The paragraph overruns; split the three criteria into a list.
habit: 'Climate, not Tuesday' is great, but it's buried in an overlong paragraph about adding figures, which most readers never will.
contemplative: "Climate, not Tuesday" is lovely. The paragraph is three paragraphs. Give each test one line.
stress: Predict/compress/enable is a real bar. 'Climate, not Tuesday' is fair, but say what climate result would disconfirm a figure.
gamedesigner: 'Climate, not Tuesday' is excellent. Paragraph overloaded; split predict/compress/enable into a list.
structural: 'Enables: where to push' is the right admission test. 'Climate, not Tuesday' is good. Too long. Make enabling mandatory.
satirist: 'Climate, not Tuesday.' Great line inside a crowded paragraph. Cut the Part Four detour.
mythmaker: 'Climate, not Tuesday' is memorable, but it's buried in a long rubric. Break it up.

modeler: Predict, compress, enable is a real admission test, and climate-not-Tuesday sets a falsification condition. Proper modeling hygiene.
skeptic: Excellent. It rules out 'feels true', names what would prove a figure wrong, and separates climate from Tuesday. That's calibration done right.
clinician: Useful test, and 'Climate, not Tuesday' is great. But the Part Four aside and the stacked clauses bury it. Simplify the first bullet.
habit: Predicts, compresses, enables: a real three-part test. 'Climate, not Tuesday' sticks. Ditch the 'Density, not length' fragment.
contemplative: 'Climate, not Tuesday' is lovely. The qualifiers pile up around it. Three verbs and three lines would do.
stress: Best kind of passage: it names its own failure condition. 'Climate, not Tuesday' gives the figures a test they can fail.
gamedesigner: Real win conditions here: predicts, compresses, enables. 'Climate, not Tuesday' sets player expectations. Good feedback design.
structural: 'Enables: where to push' is the right test, and 'climate, not Tuesday' is sharp. It should ask who the push is aimed at.
satirist: 'Climate, not Tuesday' is the best line in the batch. It's an actual falsifiability test. 'Density, not length' is dangling, so place it.
mythmaker: 'Climate, not Tuesday' is a keeper. The rest is a rubric. Show one figure earning its place in an actual week.

modeler: A parsimony stopping rule for a tool that always answers. That's the missing balancing loop on interpretation itself. Good.
skeptic: A tool that always answers is a hazard: true, and rarely admitted. Parsimony as a stopping rule is right.
clinician: 'Stop at the simplest reading' is an anti-rumination rule. Exactly right. Keep.
habit: Stop at the simplest reading. A clear rule that prevents the over-analysis spiral.
contemplative: "The simplest reading is correct, and you stop at it." Simplicity as discipline. Yes.
stress: 'A tool that always has an answer' names this system's own hazard. Rare honesty.
gamedesigner: Stop at the simplest reading. Clear rule, honest about the tool's hazard.
structural: A sharp self-limit: a tool that always answers. Parsimony rule earned.
satirist: A tool that always has an answer. Self-aware and practical. Occam, credited would be nicer.
mythmaker: 'A tool that always has an answer' is a vital warning, plainly put.

modeler: 'Does the extra figure change the action?' is a decision-relevant test of whether a model is worth its complexity. Excellent.
skeptic: 'Does the extra figure change what you'd do?' is the best decision test in this chunk. Keep.
clinician: 'Does the extra figure change what you'd do?' is a clean stopping test.
habit: 'Does the extra figure change what you would do?' That's the one question. Carry it all day.
contemplative: "Does the extra figure change what you would do?" A practice test I can carry. The patch remark can go.
stress: 'Does the extra figure change what you'd do?' A decision test, not a vibe test. Excellent.
gamedesigner: 'Does the extra figure change what you'd do?' Perfect feedback test. Keep.
structural: 'Does it change what you'd do?' is the action test, the one I keep demanding. Good.
satirist: 'Does the extra figure change what you would do?' The Stephenson test, built in. Keep.
mythmaker: The practical stopping test is useful, if bloodless.

modeler: Names both failure modes with the floor between them. The missed-phone-call line is vivid. It's the bounded model done right.
skeptic: 'Feels like insight the entire way down' names the fluency trap precisely. Both failure modes are covered.
clinician: Names over-reading as rumination that feels like insight, and under-reading as essentialism. Excellent.
habit: A missed phone call as a Skein-Kin. Funny and true, but long. The traffic line does this work better.
contemplative: "A missed phone call is a Skein-Kin." This made me smile and look at myself. The last sentence runs long.
stress: Both failure modes named, plus a floor. Over-reading 'feels like insight the whole way down' is exactly right.
gamedesigner: Both failure modes named with a great 'missed call is a Skein-Kin' jab. A bit long.
structural: Both failure modes are real. The run-on dilutes it. Tighten.
satirist: 'A missed phone call is a Skein-Kin.' Funny at its own expense. Exactly right.
mythmaker: 'A missed phone call is a Skein-Kin' made me laugh and wince. Both failures get faces.

modeler: Traffic is a complete reading. Sometimes the null model wins, and the book is wise to say so.
skeptic: Sometimes it's traffic. Perfect base-rate reminder, plainly put.
clinician: 'Sometimes he was late because of traffic.' Perfect. Readers will remember this one.
habit: 'Sometimes he was late because of traffic.' Perfect. Plain, usable, humane.
contemplative: Sometimes he was late because of traffic. Here is the whole teaching. I would cross out nothing.
stress: 'Late because of traffic.' The book deflates itself. Best line in the chunk.
gamedesigner: Traffic line is perfect. Shows the plain version. Funny, grounding, playable.
structural: 'Late because of traffic' is a complete reading. Lovely. Sometimes structure really is just the road.
satirist: 'Sometimes he was late because of traffic.' The best sentence in the chunk. Bokonon would sign it.
mythmaker: He was late because of traffic. Finally a human, and a great deflating beat.

modeler: Honest that a name is a compression over a varied tree. 'Use the name, then look' is the right modeler's humility.
skeptic: 'Use the name to find the thing, then look at the thing.' Admirable epistemic humility.
clinician: 'Use the name, then look at the thing.' Good, brief humility.
habit: 'Use the name to find the thing. Then look at the actual thing.' A good closing instruction.
contemplative: "Use the name to find the thing. Then look at the actual thing." This is presence, plainly taught.
stress: Use the name to find the thing, then look at the thing. A solid limit.
gamedesigner: 'Use the name to find the thing, then look' is a good closing instruction.
structural: Map, not territory, said well. 'Then look at the actual thing.'
satirist: 'Ten thousand particular fires.' Honest about its own compression. Good closer.
mythmaker: Ten thousand particular fires is a good image, and it pays off later with the grandmother.

modeler: Map versus territory, stated honestly. 'Use the name to find the thing, then look' is the right protocol for any model.
skeptic: It admits the names are compressions and sends you back to the actual thing. This is what I came for.
clinician: Exactly right: the label isn't you, go look at the actual thing. It's an anti-shame move with a clear next step.
habit: 'Use the name to find the thing... Then look at the actual thing.' Two steps I can actually run. Kitchen, team, self. Love it.
contemplative: Kitchen, team, yourself. Then look at the actual thing. This is honest and lived.
stress: Humility with teeth. It admits the map flattens the territory and orders you to look at the actual thing.
gamedesigner: Plays well. Find it in your kitchen, then look at the real thing. That's an explicit move with a check built in.
structural: Honest about compression. But 'kitchen, team, yourself' never gets as far as the institution. Add the rulebook to the places to look.
satirist: The book admits its names are flattened fires and sends you back to your kitchen. Bokonon would sign it. Loop/Tree jargon is the only smudge.
mythmaker: Ten thousand fires, and yours is one of them: here's the turn to the reader's own kitchen. Earned humility.

modeler: A lovely line, and the decomposition flow is implied. It does its job as tone.
skeptic: Lovely, and it makes no claim to test. Fine as an epigraph.
clinician: Beautiful, but cold at 3 a.m. for a grieving reader. Pair it with an acknowledgment of loss.
habit: A quiet, strong epigraph.
contemplative: Simple and calm. It sits well with grief.
stress: Stark and unconsoling, which is right for this chapter.
gamedesigner: Quiet, resonant epigraph. Works.
structural: Quiet epigraph. Fine in place.
satirist: Quiet, plain, earns it.
mythmaker: Stark and beautiful. It returns at the chapter's close with full weight.

modeler: A gentle image, but it's metaphor only. It works as an epigraph and shouldn't be asked to carry more.
skeptic: Lovely, and I have no reason to believe the field 'grows something'. It's mood, not a claim.
clinician: Lovely, but 'does not mourn' could feel cold to someone grieving. It leans toward bypassing unless the chapter names the hurt first.
habit: Gentle and clear. Sets up the death chapter fine. It's an epigraph, so no rep expected.
contemplative: Soft and true. It calms on the exhale.
stress: Pretty, and it costs nothing. Fine as an epigraph, but it softens a death chapter before the chapter earns that.
gamedesigner: Evocative and clear, but the reader just watches. Fine as a chapter epigraph.
structural: Pretty consolation and no stakes. It lets everyone off the hook with gentleness.
satirist: Gentle and plain about death. It works out loud. It's slightly hushed, but it's earned by the chapter.
mythmaker: The field image is warm and grave. It comes back in U0919 and closes the loop, which is good craft.

modeler: Tender, and it gives the decomposition flow its due. No machinery, but it's an epigraph.
skeptic: Gentle, and it permits mourning. Pure consolation, but it doesn't pretend to be more.
clinician: 'You may mourn' comes before the consolation. That order avoids bypassing, and it matters.
habit: A gentle epigraph that earns its place on tone, not action.
contemplative: Permission to grieve, and a field that grows. Tender. It does one thing well.
stress: Consolation without a promise. It survives grief because it doesn't deny the loss.
gamedesigner: Gentle and resonant. It does its epigraph job.
structural: Consolation, not action. Fine for a mortality chapter; I have no quarrel and little interest.
satirist: Gentle, unsentimental, and it lets you grieve. Works without the hushed voice.
mythmaker: Grief allowed and then quietly answered. Earned, and it sets up the field image well.

modeler: Thirds as survivors is honest about selection. Persistence is the exception, not the norm. Good framing.
skeptic: Framing persistence as the exception is honest about base rates. Good.
clinician: Opens death by calling most of us the unexceptional rest. It risks a 'my life doesn't matter' reading.
habit: An honest pivot to 'nearly everyone'. It lands personally, no action yet.
contemplative: "What happens to the rest of us." Humble, and honest about most lives.
stress: Starts with the base rate: most people don't persist. Honest framing.
gamedesigner: Good honest framing, but the first sentence is a knot. Lead with 'most of us don't become one.'
structural: A tangled framing sentence. The point, that most patterns fade, could take one line.
satirist: Setup tangled; 'exception' and 'aspiration' fight. Say: most of us don't become patterns. That's this chapter.
mythmaker: Real stakes at last: 'what happens to the rest of us.'

modeler: Plain and unhedged. There's no mechanism to check, but it's consistent with the no-fixed-self model. It earns trust.
skeptic: Plainly stated and scoped to 'nothing in this framework supports it'. That's appropriately calibrated.
clinician: Honest, but no acknowledgment that this is frightening or grievous. Name the fear before the facts.
habit: Plain and brave. No habit here, and none needed. It earns its weight.
contemplative: Said plainly, without false comfort. Ruiz's impeccability, applied to death.
stress: A claim that takes a risk: the experiencer does not continue. Most comfort books won't say it. Respect.
gamedesigner: Plain, brave statement. Clear. Hits personally. No move, but earns its place.
structural: Plain and unflinching about death. Outside my beat, but it earns its place.
satirist: 'The experiencer does not continue.' Brave plain speech. Survives the bar.
mythmaker: Brave and plain about death. No pep talk, and that's earned.

modeler: Signpost.
skeptic: Transition. 'None require anything beyond what's true' is pre-emptive confidence; let the three items earn it.
clinician: Clean transition.
habit: Setup line. Fine.
contemplative: A plain hinge. Good.
stress: Transition.
gamedesigner: Setup line; good beat structure for three items.
structural: Transition. Clear.
satirist: Simple pivot. Fine.
mythmaker: A hinge sentence. Fine.

modeler: A bare signpost with no content. Could merge into U0912's opening.
skeptic: A clean transition. 'None of them is you' sets up an honest framing.
clinician: Plain, and it speaks to death anxiety directly. 'None of them is you' is blunt. Honest, but a fearful reader needs gentleness nearby.
habit: A clean hinge sentence. It does its one job and nothing more.
contemplative: Quiet and kind. It does its one job.
stress: Pure transition. 'None of them is you' is honest, but on its own it carries no weight.
gamedesigner: Good tension beat. 'Three things' promises a countdown, so the reader leans in.
structural: A clean signpost that does what it says. Nothing structural, and nothing structural needed here.
satirist: A clean hinge sentence. 'None of them is you' is honest, and good. It does no other work.
mythmaker: Short hinge that faces death honestly: none of it is you. The stakes are plain.

modeler: Matter, transmission and process: three real flows that outlast the stock. Clean decomposition of continuity.
skeptic: "None of them is you" fits a relational self. A modest, defensible claim.
clinician: 'None of them is you' lands cold on a grieving reader. Acknowledge the loss first, then offer what continues.
habit: A clean three-part list that's consoling and plain. Fine.
contemplative: Three things, plainly named, without false comfort. Simple and true.
stress: 'None of them is you' is the honest part. It refuses the cheap afterlife. That holds.
gamedesigner: A clean three-item list that's easy to hold. It sets up the next beats well.
structural: Clear three-part legacy claim. 'What you passed on' could point to institutions you built. Doesn't, but it's tidy.
satirist: Three plain continuations, with 'none of them is you' said straight. Honest consolation.
mythmaker: A tender triad, honestly withheld from consolation. It needs a person you'd mourn to carry it.

modeler: A real conserved stock with closed accounting, the bathtub with no drain out of the universe. Mechanism, finally, and humane.
skeptic: Conservation of matter: true and clearly labelled as the least controversial claim. Fair.
clinician: Conservation framing is clear and modest.
habit: Clear physics comfort. Accurate, if a little padded.
contemplative: The riverbed image is gentle. "Conveniently" and "least controversial claim" are defensive. Let the image stand alone.
stress: Conservation is real physics, and the claim is modest. Holds.
gamedesigner: Riverbed image plus conservation is easy and grounding. Slightly over-qualified.
structural: Conservation as comfort. Clear, minor. The riverbed image is decent.
satirist: Conservation, named as a law. Bryson-grade. Drop 'conveniently'.
mythmaker: The riverbed returns, and that's good rhyme. The physics aside is a touch lecture-y.

modeler: Finally a real conservation law instead of a metaphor. The material stock cycles, and the riverbed image fits the flow.
skeptic: It cites a real law, labels it as one, and stays within what the law says. Good.
clinician: Clear physics, but it risks consolation-by-carbon. That doesn't touch the actual fear. The next unit rescues it.
habit: Riverbed plus conservation law: plain and grounded. Consoling but not actionable, which is fine for this chapter.
contemplative: The riverbed and the carbon are tender and true. 'Not just a comforting way of speaking' is defensive. Cut it.
stress: Rests on an actual law, not a mood. The riverbed image works. It still slides toward comfort before the next paragraph corrects it.
gamedesigner: The riverbed plus conservation is plain and grounded. Personal through the carbon in you. No move, but it earns its spot.
structural: Accurate physics and plain language. It's grief comfort, outside my brief. Fine in its place.
satirist: Conservation of mass, carbon that was something else first: Bryson-approved wonder with the physics showing. Solid.
mythmaker: Riverbed and carbon give it weight. This is comfort you can touch, though a named body (a parent, a pet) would deepen it.

modeler: A real second law: the arrangement is held by continuous throughput, a dissipative structure. Pairing it with conservation is honest physics. Excellent.
skeptic: Pairing the second law with conservation is honest. The last clause tells the reader how to feel; cut it.
clinician: Honest second law. 'Let yourself find it reassuring anyway' edges toward bypass. Shorten and allow it not to reassure.
habit: 'The arrangement was the part that was you' hits hard. The paragraph runs long; trim the last sentence.
contemplative: "You are not going anywhere, and you are not staying as you are." Exquisite. The thermodynamics around it is too much.
stress: Pairs the second law with the comfort. Good. The last clause slides back into self-soothing. Cut it.
gamedesigner: 'Nothing lost, nothing stays' is strong; paragraph rambles after it. Cut the back half.
structural: Pairing both laws is honest and striking. Overlong, the final clause especially. Trim.
satirist: Second law beside the first: honest consolation. Name entropy outright; you've earned it.
mythmaker: Nothing is lost, nothing stays. Honest consolation with its cost shown. It's long, though.

modeler: Best systems passage here: the arrangement is a stock held by a continuous maintenance flow, and death is that inflow stopping. Clear and correct.
skeptic: Putting the second law beside conservation refuses the half-truth. Rare honesty about what consolation can and can't claim.
clinician: Refuses to bypass: it names what stops and doesn't pretend. That earns trust. No step, but none is owed here.
habit: 'Conservation is why nothing is lost. The second law is why nothing stays.' Strong pair. Pure insight, though, and no behaviour.
contemplative: 'Not going anywhere, not staying as you are.' Beautiful. The middle explains too much, so trim the work-of-living sentence.
stress: This is the storm-tested version. Putting the second law beside conservation refuses fragile comfort. Accurate, and it stings.
gamedesigner: Best beat in the chapter. The two laws work as two rules, and the twist is honest. A real second beat after the hook.
structural: Pairing conservation with the second law is honest and elegant. 'Holding any arrangement takes continuous work' could apply to institutions too. Say so.
satirist: The second law gets its turn, so nobody is cheated with half the physics. 'You are not going anywhere, and not staying' is genuinely good.
mythmaker: 'The arrangement was the part that was you.' That's the cost stated without flinching. Best paragraph in the chapter.

modeler: Habits as flows that already left: true. It needs the balancing side, decay with each hop. Chapter 9 supplies it later; nod to it here.
skeptic: Plausible social transmission, but the kindness-becomes-habit story is a vivid anecdote, not evidence. One hedge would do.
clinician: Small kindnesses already transferred: warm and true. One of the safer comforts here.
habit: The small kindness that became someone's habit. That's habit transfer, and it's personal. Lovely.
contemplative: "The small kindness that became someone else's habit." This is interbeing. Beautiful. "Fold" and "Nest" could be plain words.
stress: Only the kindnesses travel here. Your cruelties fold outward too. Admit that or it's fragile comfort.
gamedesigner: Concrete examples of transmission, emotionally live. Best of the three.
structural: The best spillover idea in the death chapter: habits leave you and enter other people. Extend it to organizing.
satirist: The kindness that became someone's habit: concrete, moving, true. 'Fold' jargon unnecessary.
mythmaker: The small kindness that became someone's habit has a face and real tenderness.

modeler: 'Capacity borrowed, unowned' is metaphor dressed as fact. No stock, no flow. Either say it's a shared biological capacity or call it consolation.
skeptic: An overconfident claim about the self: an unowned observing capacity 'borrowed' by everyone is metaphysics stated as fact. Mark it as speculative.
clinician: The unowned observing self is abstract and long. A grieving reader gets lost.
habit: A beautiful idea, but the clauses pile up. Split it into three short sentences.
contemplative: The borrowed noticing is a true and tender thought. The last sentence runs on. End at "never scarce or personal."
stress: 'Noticing carries on, unowned' sneaks metaphysics in. Nothing could disconfirm it. Mark it as a stance, not a fact.
gamedesigner: Observer-as-borrowed idea is lovely but the long final sentence loses me.
structural: An unowned observer is a big claim in tangled syntax. Shorter, or it stays opaque.
satirist: Hushed-voice paragraph. 'Unowned noticing' is foma; label it as such or trim.
mythmaker: Moving idea, but the sentences sprawl. Tighten the last one.

modeler: Asserts an unowned capacity with no mechanism. The 'stranger borrowing' line muddies it. Say what persists, and where.
skeptic: 'The same capacity in everyone' treats other minds as transparent. How would you know? It reifies the 'observing self' it is supposed to dissolve.
clinician: Observing self explained cleanly, Harris would nod. But 'you don't get to keep it' lands cold. Soften it or tie it to present use.
habit: The 'stranger catching their own mind mid-thought' line is relatable. Could hand me a two-second noticing rep, but doesn't.
contemplative: Borrowed noticing is a gift. The last sentence tangles. Say it simply: it was never yours to keep.
stress: Observing self as unowned is unfalsifiable, and nothing could break it. The abstraction also blurs. Name what would count against it.
gamedesigner: The 'stranger catching their own mind' image works. You could add a prompt like 'notice it now' to make it a move.
structural: An unowned observing self is abstract and a little slippery. Pure inner metaphysics with no spillover into anything shared.
satirist: 'Borrowing the observing self' is foma without the label. It's lovely in a hushed voice and wobbly at the bar. Say it's a way of seeing, not a fact.
mythmaker: The stranger catching their own mind is the face, and it's a quiet one. The consolation feels paid for, if a little thin.

modeler: Moving. But 'same kind' of watching isn't the same watching; the slide from kind to the thing itself does the work.
skeptic: Says observing selves are the "same kind" across strangers with no support. It's the true-self claim, inverted. Hedge it as a way of seeing.
clinician: It borrows ACT's observing self for metaphysics. 'Never yours to keep' could unsettle a dissociating reader at 3 a.m. Keep the exercise and drop the claim.
habit: "Catch your own mind mid-thought, right now" is a real two-second rep. Nice. The rest is philosophy.
contemplative: 'Catch your own mind mid-thought, right now.' At last, an invitation to look. The book should ask this more often.
stress: Sleight of hand: the same kind of watching isn't the same watcher. Name that gap or this becomes a horoscope.
gamedesigner: 'Catch your mind mid-thought, right now' puts a controller in hand. Rare agency in this part.
structural: Inner-work metaphysics. Not harmful here, but observing-self talk is exactly where action quietly goes to die. Keep it brief.
satirist: 'Same kind of watching' quietly becomes 'never yours'. Sleight of hand. Label it as consolation, not deduction.
mythmaker: 'Catch your own mind mid-thought' puts me inside it. 'The shape it took for a while' stays with me.

modeler: Independent convergence leans on contact being absent, and Buddhist and Stoic lines touched. Count the contacts honestly, or the evidence weakens.
skeptic: Traditions converging may reflect shared human cognition, not a shared truth. Same minds, same illusion. Address that rival explanation.
clinician: Leans heavily on convergence as evidence. Repetitive hedges; trim.
habit: An evidential argument where the reader wants comfort. Halve it.
contemplative: It argues for the evidence instead of resting in it. The hedges come again and again. Halve it.
stress: The appeal to history is good, but shared human wiring explains the convergence too, so it isn't independent. Concede the confound.
gamedesigner: Leaning on convergence as evidence feels like a lecture defending itself. Shorten, hedge less.
structural: Leans on convergence as evidence and hedges 'little or no' thrice. The hedges eat the point.
satirist: 'Traditions separated by oceans,' unnamed. Name anatta, the Upanishads, whoever. No fern, no ratio.
mythmaker: A fair use of the earlier figure. Name one tradition to give it a face.

modeler: Good: it names the confound of shared cognitive architecture. Convergence counted honestly beats convergence asserted.
skeptic: It counts the evidence and admits a shared cognitive cause. Then it overreaches: agreement that comes from how minds are built isn't independent evidence of truth.
clinician: Good epistemic honesty about the evidence. It's comparative religion though, not care. Nothing a struggling reader can use.
habit: Honest evidence-counting, and the hedges are fair. It's a lit review, not a practice. Trim it to the three names plus the caveat.
contemplative: An argument counting its evidence. Zhuangzi singing is enough. Let the traditions speak and the hedging rest.
stress: Counts its evidence and concedes the shared-wiring confound. Three cases is thin history, but the hedge is honest.
gamedesigner: Honest about its evidence, but it's a lecture. The reader weighs nothing. Ask them which tradition they'd test.
structural: Credit for honest evidence-counting and the cognitive-architecture caveat. It's still a survey of traditions, with no lever.
satirist: Names, centuries, and an honest 'not proof' hedge. Good. 'Same real pressure' still overclaims a little. Shared brain wiring is a confound, not a confirmation.
mythmaker: Zhuangzi singing at his wife's death is a blazing image, then it gets filed under evidence. Stay in that scene one more beat.

modeler: Counts the evidence honestly and names the shared-architecture confound. 'Rules out the cheaper explanation' overclaims; say it weakens that explanation.
skeptic: It counts the evidence and names the shared-cognition confound. Good. "Rules out" still overstates. Say "makes less likely."
clinician: Zhuangzi wept first, so grief comes before acceptance. Honest about weak evidence. I trust it more for that.
habit: Zhuangzi drumming is memorable. The hedged evidence-weighing runs long. Trim the caveats to one sentence.
contemplative: Zhuangzi drumming is a gift. The hedges pile up after it. Tell the story, say honestly that it's not proof, and stop.
stress: It counts the evidence honestly and names a weakness. Then it overreaches: shared minds don't rule out borrowing. Drop 'rules out' and say 'weakens'.
gamedesigner: The drumming-on-a-bowl story hooks, and the honesty about weak evidence earns trust. Long, but it reads.
structural: Honest about evidential limits, which I respect. Off my beat entirely; no rules, no lever, nothing collective.
satirist: Zhuangzi drumming on a bowl, and the author weighs his own evidence. It even concedes that the shared wiring weakens the case. That's earned.
mythmaker: Zhuangzi drumming on a bowl is exactly the face this needs. Honest hedging too. Strong.

modeler: A leaky nested pattern, open-system thinking turned toward grief. It's well done, though 'mostly good' is asserted rather than shown.
skeptic: It tells the reader what their fear 'runs on' without knowing. Relational self is defensible; the diagnosis of the reader is not.
clinician: Jumps to 'never separate' and 'mostly good' before honoring grief. That is classic bypass. Add one line saying loss hurts.
habit: 'You were never as separate as the fear assumes.' Real resonance.
contemplative: "Never as separate as the fear assumes." Here is real comfort, and it is honest.
stress: Strong reframe of the fear. 'Mostly good' is unearned. Drop it and the paragraph survives.
gamedesigner: 'Never as separate as the fear assumes' lands. Real comfort, clearly argued.
structural: 'Never as separate as the fear assumes' is the anti-i-frame at its most humane. Works.
satirist: 'Never as separate as the fear assumes.' Earned, and plain enough.
mythmaker: 'Never as separate as the fear assumes.' This comfort is paid for, not handed out.

modeler: 'No warehouse for deferred living' is a sharp stock image, and 'what am I seeding' is actionable. Strong landing.
skeptic: A practical upshot: judge today's rule on its own merits, not on legacy. Actionable and appropriately modest.
clinician: A real question to carry today. Soften 'defend as good' so it doesn't turn into self-indictment.
habit: 'What am I seeding into the Nests I'm part of, right now?' One question, tied to today. This is the rep.
contemplative: "What am I seeding, right now?" I can live that question. The Trap jargon in front of it should go.
stress: 'No warehouse where deferred living gets cashed in.' A claim with stakes, and a working test for today. Keep.
gamedesigner: Turns death into today's move: what am I seeding now. Real agency. Keep.
structural: 'What am I seeding into the Nests' is good. It stays private. Add the Nests you could join, not just the ones you're in.
satirist: 'No warehouse where deferred living gets cashed in.' Does something today. Keep.
mythmaker: 'What am I seeding' turns the death chapter into today's choice. Strong stakes.

modeler: A quiet close that does tone work. It earns its place by restraint.
skeptic: A graceful close. Rhythm doing most of the work, but it claims little.
clinician: 'Nothing small about that' is a kind landing. Keep.
habit: A graceful close. Leave it alone.
contemplative: "There is nothing small about that." A gentle ending. Perfect as it is.
stress: Plain ending without inflation. Works.
gamedesigner: Beautiful closer. Short, earned.
structural: A plain, dignified close. Earned.
satirist: Gentle close. Slightly hymnal, but it holds.
mythmaker: The epigraph returns with weight. A perfect closing image.

modeler: A humane close, but it repeats the epigraph almost word for word. Trim one of the two.
skeptic: Plain and humane. 'Nothing small about that' is reassurance that asserts its own warrant.
clinician: Shame-aware: an ordinary life isn't a failure. 'Nothing small about that' is the empathy line this chapter needed.
habit: Warm close, and 'you and I included' earns it. Nothing to do, but nothing should be here.
contemplative: Gentle and unafraid. 'Nothing small about that' heals. Keep it.
stress: Plain and unflattering, with 'you and I included'. Moving, but it restates the epigraph.
gamedesigner: A quiet landing that works emotionally. Repeats the epigraph, so not much new.
structural: Gentle and humane. 'Nothing small about that' consoles, but it also quietly normalizes having no effect.
satirist: It repeats the epigraph almost word for word. 'Nothing small about that' is a kind sentence. The rest is an echo.
mythmaker: Callback to the field and 'you and I included.' The rhyme lands, and the dignity it offers is earned.

modeler: Plain and kind. It restates the epigraph, though; one of the two could go.
skeptic: Plain and kind. It flatters no one with a special fate. Fine.
clinician: 'Nothing small about that' gives dignity to an ordinary life. It's close to bypassing, but rescued by plainness.
habit: "Nothing small about that" is warm, plain and fitting. Keep it.
contemplative: 'Nothing small about that.' Plain, and dignified. Drop 'simply, eventually' and it breathes better.
stress: Plain and unflinching about ordinary death. It mostly repeats U0908. Merge them.
gamedesigner: Quiet payoff beat. It lands emotionally without lecturing.
structural: Gentle, plain. Repeats U0908. Merge them; one is enough.
satirist: 'Nothing small about that' finishes the death chapter with dignity, not incense.
mythmaker: The field image returns with weight, and 'nothing small about that' is earned. A rhyme paid off.

modeler: The book's thesis line. Local rules build global form unseen. Fair.
skeptic: The book's thesis line. Fluent; its truth rests on everything before it.
clinician: The core mantra. Fine.
habit: The book's thesis as an epigraph. Earns its spot.
contemplative: The book's breath in one line. Beautiful.
stress: Motto. Fine.
gamedesigner: Thesis epigraph. Works.
structural: The thesis line, memorable. Also exactly the sentence a system's beneficiaries would like you to believe.
satirist: The mantra again. Fine as epigraph; less fine as the third reprise.
mythmaker: The book's mantra, and it rhymes with the close. It works.

modeler: The thesis line. It's fair as an epigraph, and the following pages have to supply the local rule.
skeptic: A fine statement of the thesis. Elegance is not evidence, but as an epigraph it's fair.
clinician: Memorable thesis line. Abstract only, which is fine for an epigraph. Nothing to act on.
habit: It's the book's thesis in one line. Memorable. Not a cue, not a rep.
contemplative: Clear, though a little grand. It earns its place as the chapter's door.
stress: The thesis in seven words. Nice, and it can't be broken. Treat it as a motto, not a claim.
gamedesigner: The thesis line as an epigraph. Clear, nothing to do.
structural: The thesis in seven words. It skips who decides which repetitions get amplified, and amplification is where power sits.
satirist: The book's thesis as a motto. It's short enough to carry and grand enough to be suspicious of. It passes.
mythmaker: Thesis line that's memorable, with no face. It gets earned later, by the grandmother.

modeler: The local act builds the global form, with 'this morning' grounding it. That's the whole thesis in a line. Keep.
skeptic: "You did some of it this morning" grounds the abstraction in a checkable act. It works.
clinician: 'You did some of it this morning' says the reader matters without inflating them. A good epigraph.
habit: "You did some of it this morning" ties to my morning. Great epigraph.
contemplative: 'You did some of it this morning' brings it home. Lovely.
stress: It grounds the grand claim in this morning's habits. That modest anchor works.
gamedesigner: 'You did some of it this morning' makes it immediate and personal. Good hook.
structural: Nice inversion: you built the world this morning. Spillover is implied but not named. Which repetitions feed institutions?
satirist: 'You did some of it this morning' takes the grandeur down to breakfast. Nicely done.
mythmaker: 'This morning' drops the cosmic down to the reader. Lovely.

modeler: Setup framing it as a mechanical exception. Fine, but thin.
skeptic: Framing transition. Clear and honest about rarity.
clinician: 'Not for the especially deserving' heads off shame. Good.
habit: A transition that re-explains the last chapter. Shrink it to one sentence.
contemplative: A preface defending the chapter before it. Begin with the next paragraph instead.
stress: Says up front that this is the exception. Good, though wordy.
gamedesigner: Transition that over-explains ordering. Trim to one sentence.
structural: Throat-clearing before the chapter. Cut to the mechanism.
satirist: Framing paragraph. Could be one sentence.
mythmaker: Careful framing. It's needed but it carries no heart.

modeler: Says 'mechanically' without giving the mechanism. That job is left to U0922, so this is only a transition.
skeptic: A useful frame against reading survival as merit. 'Mechanically' promises a mechanism the chapter only half supplies.
clinician: 'Not a reward for the especially deserving' heads off a worth-ranking. Good guardrail, though it's mostly transition.
habit: A clear signpost: the exception versus the general case. It's throat-clearing, though. Could go down to one sentence.
contemplative: A signpost looking backward. 'Mechanically' is cold. The chapter could simply begin.
stress: Good guardrail against a meritocracy myth ('not a reward for the deserving'). Still just signposting.
gamedesigner: Recap transition, readable but idle. Fold it into the next paragraph.
structural: Transition text. 'Mechanically, not a reward' is good anti-meritocracy, but the mechanism goes unnamed. Who amplifies?
satirist: Signposting. 'Mechanically' does honest work against the reward reading. Otherwise it's a hallway.
mythmaker: Throat-clearing transition. Nothing at stake. Fold it into the next paragraph or cut it.

modeler: Transition only. 'Kept repeating' is the right mechanism but gets no development here.
skeptic: "Not a reward for the deserving" resists the just-world story. Honest framing.
clinician: 'Not a reward for the deserving' heads off the shame of an unremembered life. Important framing, cleanly done.
habit: A framing bridge with nothing to do. Acceptable, but it could be shorter.
contemplative: Honest that it isn't a reward. It's a bridge more than a teaching, and that is fine.
stress: 'Not a reward for the deserving' admits luck. That's the anti-hindsight move I want. Good.
gamedesigner: A transition that sets the stakes clearly. It's a level-select screen with no input.
structural: 'Not a reward for the deserving' is a welcome anti-meritocracy line. Survival depends on others repeating. That's a structural truth.
satirist: Refuses to make transcendence a merit badge. Plain, slightly dry, fine.
mythmaker: A clear hinge that refuses false reward, which I respect. Still no one in it.

modeler: Survival by others' repetition is a genuine transmission mechanism. Honest, but give a replication rate or decay.
skeptic: 'Not a reward for the deserving' is the right calibration: survival by repetition, not merit. Refreshingly unflattering.
clinician: Says plainly that survival isn't a reward for the deserving. That is shame-aware and takes the sting out of failure. Still no step.
habit: Honest framing, but a bridge paragraph. No behaviour, no cue, no question to carry.
contemplative: Honest and plain, and it does not flatter the reader. But it is only a bridge. It asks nothing of me.
stress: Survival is luck, not merit. Good: skin shown, no flattery. Says some patterns last whether or not the originator knew.
gamedesigner: Honest transition, lowers the stakes. But it recaps and promises; nothing to do or predict here. Cutscene.
satirist: Plain and honest: survival by repetition, not merit. But it's a hinge sentence; it asks nothing and shows nothing.
mythmaker: 'Not a reward for the deserving' is honest and humbling. Still all abstraction. Name one person whose pattern outlived them.
structural: Honest that survival owes to others repeating, not merit. Good. But no rule or institution named; what makes repetition happen?

modeler: Recipe survival through repetition is a real copying loop, but no rate, no decay, no limit named. Tell me what drains the pattern, then it earns more.
skeptic: Admits survival is rare and undeserved, which I like. The recipe image is easy; 'goes to ground' is asserted with no base rate.
clinician: 'Not a reward for the deserving' defuses shame well; recipe image is warm. No action, and the final clause muddles.
habit: Family-recipe image works, but it's pure framing. No cue, no step, no question. Say what the reader does with a surviving pattern tomorrow.
contemplative: The recipe is warm. The last clause tangles. Say less: a few patterns last because people kept cooking them.
stress: Good: survival is luck of repetition, not merit. The family recipe lands. The last clause is muddled. Say how often patterns survive, with a count.
gamedesigner: Family-recipe image gives a felt hook and honest framing. No action for the player; it's a chapter-opening cutscene.
structural: Survival by repetition is true but unowned. Who repeated it, and who benefited? Recipe metaphor is a mood, not a mechanism.
satirist: Nice recipe image, strangled by the last clause, which says nothing. Busy, busy, busy. Cut 'whether or not' and say the plain thing.
mythmaker: The family recipe is warm and I'll remember it. The ending clause tangles; name one cook and let the image return later.

modeler: Transcendence redefined as replication past the author is a clean operational definition. It's a transmission threshold, so name the threshold.
skeptic: Redefining transcendence as wide repetition wins by definition. Admit it's a stipulation, not a discovery.
clinician: Redefines transcendence in dense terms. Say it in one plain sentence.
habit: Defining transcendence as repetition past the author is a big idea in a tangled sentence. Shorten it.
contemplative: "An ordinary act, repeated past its author" is lovely. The list of mechanisms before it weighs it down.
stress: Relabeling cultural survival as 'transcendence' is grandiosity by definition. Say 'persistence' and lose nothing.
gamedesigner: Transcendence redefined is a big idea, but jargon pileup: Nests, Transmission Drift, Received World.
structural: Transcendence as repetition past its author is a bold, clean idea. Bogged down in callbacks.
satirist: 'That is transcendence.' Said straight-faced at a bar? No. Say 'outliving its author'.
mythmaker: Transcendence as repetition past its author is a big, clean idea.

modeler: Transcendence as replication past the author's maintenance is a real threshold in a transmission loop. It's deflationary in the right way.
skeptic: The deflationary definition of 'transcendence' is welcome. Four coined terms in one sentence bury it.
clinician: Four coined terms in one sentence. The plain definition at the end is good, so lead with it.
habit: Local Rule, Nests, Transmission Drift and Received World stacked in one sentence. Too much jargon. Lead with 'an ordinary act repeated past its author'.
contemplative: Five coined terms in one sentence. Keep the last line, 'an ordinary act, repeated past its author'. It is enough.
stress: Deflating 'transcendence' is the right move. But stacked jargon (Nests, Transmission Drift, Received World) buries it.
gamedesigner: Standing Third, Local Rule, Nests, Transmission Drift, Received World all in one sentence. I lost the player. Unpack one at a time.
structural: Demystifying transcendence as repetition is good. But the institutions that do the repeating (schools, firms, law) go unmentioned. That's the mechanism.
satirist: Local Rule, Nests, Transmission Drift, Received World: four invented proper nouns propping up one plain sentence. Busy, busy, busy. Keep only the last clause.
mythmaker: Jargon pileup (Local Rule, Nests, Transmission Drift, Received World). Lovely thought, who's holding it? Give me the first person who repeated it.

modeler: It strips 'transcendence' down to a repetition rate that outruns its author. That's deflation done right: a mechanism, not mysticism.
skeptic: A deflationary definition, explicitly not grander. That's how to borrow a loaded word.
clinician: It defines the word plainly, then buries it under Nest, Local Rule and Transmission Drift. Strip the jargon.
habit: The definition is plain, but the Nest jargon creeps in. Ask me: which of your daily acts would outlive you?
contemplative: Good that it brings a big word down to size. Then Nest, Transmission Drift, Received World. Say 'families, crews, towns' and stop.
stress: A deflated definition, and it's welcome. 'Every Standing Third began as someone's Local Rule' is unprovable origin myth. Say 'most, plausibly'.
gamedesigner: Nest, Local Rule, Transmission Drift and Received World all pile up. Too many callbacks for one definition.
structural: Deflationary transcendence via transmission is good. Missing: institutions are how local rules outlive authors. Say laws, unions, charters.
satirist: Takes a Capitalized Word and shrinks it to a plain definition. Exactly the move I want. The Nest jargon could go.
mythmaker: Plain definition, good restraint. It needs one founder whose small habit outlived her.

modeler: Nice local-rule-to-persistence build: act, copy, drift, outlive author. Deflates the grand word. Needs a decay term.
skeptic: Plain definition that deflates its own grand word. Good. 'Nothing grander' earns trust.
clinician: Demystifies 'transcendence' in plain terms, avoiding grandiosity. Nothing for the reader to do; mostly definitional.
habit: Plain definition, readable. Still all theory; show one ordinary act I could repeat starting tomorrow.
contemplative: 'Nothing grander' is good impeccability. The long list of families, crews, towns and unions is more than needed.
stress: Deflates its own grand word: 'nothing grander.' That is ego kept in check. Plain definition, though it solves nothing yet.
gamedesigner: Clear definition of transcendence, plainly stated. Good rule. Still lecture; I'm not asked to find one in my own life.
satirist: 'Nothing grander' is Bokonon's wink: deflating its own sacred word. Families, unions, charters supply concrete hosts. Nicely done.
mythmaker: Families, crews, unions, charters: a pattern outgrowing its author is the heart of it. Needs one actual author with something to lose.
structural: Names unions, charters, towns, families as carriers. Institutions as the means of persistence: my kind of paragraph. Name who funds and defends them.

modeler: Good: local rule, copied, drifts, outlives author. That's a self-sustaining loop built from a small rule. Missing: the balancing side, what stops copies.
skeptic: Deflates 'transcendence' to repeated copying, a modest, checkable claim. Honest. Still no evidence that Standing Thirds began as individual rules.
clinician: 'Small enough to be yours' is safe and dignifying; ordinary acts matter without grandiosity. Implies a step: start a small rule.
habit: Plain definition, and 'small enough to be yours' is warm. Still no step. Add: name one ordinary act you repeat that others could copy.
contemplative: Humble and plain; 'nothing grander' is honest. 'Small enough to be yours' touches me. Still no act to do today.
stress: Deflates its own grand word to 'nothing grander'. That is ego under control. Still no history: cite one real practice that made this journey.
gamedesigner: Nice promise that my small rule could outlive me. But three coined terms in one paragraph: difficulty spike. Name one and drop the rest.
structural: Unions and crews are the right carriers; I'm half-pleased. But name which Local Rule, whose institution. Spillover is gestured at, not shown.
satirist: Defines the grand word down to 'nothing grander.' Bokonon would nod. Still leans on Transmission Drift and Received World as authorities.
mythmaker: Plain and honest, but abstract nouns carry it. Show one Local Rule becoming a union custom, with a face at the start.

modeler: Finally the balancing side: most patterns fade within a generation. The honest gradient beats a binary. Good.
skeptic: The honest gradient with ordinary examples. Good calibration about the common case.
clinician: 'This is not failure' about fading patterns is shame-aware and concrete. Keep.
habit: A habit your kids picked up from watching you. Concrete images and an honest gradient.
contemplative: A habit your children picked up from watching you. True in every home. "This is not failure" is kind.
stress: An honest gradient with a realistic base rate. Good.
gamedesigner: Gradient with relatable examples: kids' habits, friends' phrases. Plays well.
structural: A concrete gradient: a phrase your friends still use. Relatable and plain.
satirist: The friend's phrase you can't source. Concrete, warm, true.
mythmaker: A habit your children picked up, a phrase friends still use. Faces, gently.

modeler: Skein-scale persistence is plausible and humane. It adds a rung but no new mechanism.
skeptic: Recognisable and modest. Fine.
clinician: Humane, resonant middle case.
habit: Relatable middle rung. Fine.
contemplative: Warm and simple. "Not a small thing to have happened." Good.
stress: Modest and checkable: people really are imitated by name after they die. Fine.
gamedesigner: Concrete middle rung. Readers think of someone they know. Good.
structural: Secondhand influence at Skein scale. Humane and clear.
satirist: Plain and fair. Modest claim, modestly said.
mythmaker: The person invoked by name years later is an image that's real and moving.

modeler: The block-party neighbor lands emotionally. The missing piece is what sets the threshold for secondhand persistence: repetition rate, or drift tolerance?
skeptic: A recognizable, checkable example that needs no metaphysics. Modest and true to how reputations actually spread.
clinician: Coach, teacher, block-party neighbor: warm and recognizable. 'However far short of legend' protects readers from feeling insufficient.
habit: The block-party neighbor is perfect, and I know that person. Ask me which of my repeats someone might copy, and you've got a question.
contemplative: The neighbor who ran the block party. I know her. Warm and plain.
stress: A real, checkable pattern: the coach remembered by name. Modest, and it holds. It doesn't solve anything, though.
gamedesigner: The coach and block-party neighbor are instantly recognizable, and the reader can name their own. Plays well.
structural: The block-party neighbor is a real lever: organizing that outlives its organizer. More of this, and say outright that it's collective work.
satirist: The coach and the block-party neighbor are real people I know. 'No metaphysics needed' is the right straight face.
mythmaker: The coach, the teacher, the block-party neighbor: finally faces. Every reader knows one, and that's what hits.

modeler: The Spark is a reinforcing-loop structure, not someone's habit, so the grandmother origin conflates structure with an instance. Charming, but category error.
skeptic: The grandmother origin is a just-so story, at least flagged with 'possibly'. Charming, and evidentially empty.
clinician: The grandmother image charms. Mythic, not practical.
habit: The grandmother who couldn't stop starting things. Best image in the part.
contemplative: Someone's grandmother who could not stop starting things. Tender, and real. This is the face the catalogue needed.
stress: The grandmother origin is a myth propped up by 'possibly' twice. Charming, but it's a neat story with no evidence.
gamedesigner: Grandmother Spark is a terrific image. Origin myth that feels earned.
structural: The Spark's face as someone's grandmother is a charming origin myth. Abstractly satisfying, practically nothing.
satirist: The Spark as someone's grandmother. Charming, self-aware myth-making. Bokonon-approved.
mythmaker: The grandmother who couldn't stop starting things is the best face in the chunk. It's the origin myth done right.

modeler: Personhood wearing off through repetition is a lovely, plausible decay mechanism. It's honest that this is a story, not a record.
skeptic: It's labeled a story, not a record, and says 'nobody can check'. Exactly the calibration I ask for.
clinician: The grandmother who couldn't stop starting things is lovely and humanizing. It's offered as a story, honestly. Resonates.
habit: The grandmother who couldn't stop starting things is a lovely, concrete image. It's still an origin story, not a practice.
contemplative: The grandmother who could not stop starting things is the heart here. It is long getting to her. Begin closer.
stress: Labelling the origin myth 'a story, not a record' is the right humility. The grandmother is charming. 'Nobody can check' is the honest tell.
gamedesigner: The grandmother who couldn't stop starting things is a great hook, and 'you may know someone like her' invites a guess.
structural: A charming grandmother origin, honestly flagged as a story. It romanticizes anonymous persistence and ignores who funded the spread.
satirist: Offered 'as a story, not a record.' Bokonon's own move. The grandmother who couldn't stop starting things is the earned wonder.
mythmaker: The grandmother who couldn't stop starting things is a myth's origin in miniature, and an image I'll remember tomorrow.

modeler: You can't aim at an emergent outcome directly. That's correct and consistent. It repeats earlier chapters, though.
skeptic: 'Can't aim at it directly' is consistent and humble. Good.
clinician: Right stance: don't aim at legacy. But 'tend a Local Rule honestly' is vague. Give one example.
habit: 'Tend a Local Rule honestly' is right, but which one, starting when? Add a two-minute version.
contemplative: "You can only tend a Local Rule honestly." This is purpose without grasping, very like ikigai. A little long, but it earns it.
stress: You can't aim at legacy, only tend the rule. Anti-ego, Holiday-grade. Keep.
gamedesigner: Can't aim at it, only tend honestly. Clear guidance, removes a bad goal.
structural: Can't aim at becoming a Third, so tend honestly. Fine for a person. Movements do aim, though. Note the difference.
satirist: Can't aim at it, like flow. Honest and humane.
mythmaker: An honest refusal to make it a goal. It's earned and humane.

modeler: The closing recap overruns. Three restatements of points already made. Cut it to the first two sentences.
skeptic: An overlong coda that restates the last two chapters. Cut it to the thesis line and the final sentence.
clinician: Lovely, but it recaps three chapters in one breath. Cut by half.
habit: A strong finale, but it runs one sentence too long. End on 'which of your own small acts'.
contemplative: The fire image is lovely. The paragraph keeps ending, then begins again. Stop after "around the next fire."
stress: 'The whole shape of this book' is the author admiring the work. A long recap. Cut to two sentences.
gamedesigner: Good finale but overstuffed; the third sentence re-explains Going to Ground. End on 'which of your acts.'
structural: A big reprise that sprawls. Cut the material-circulation callback and keep the fire.
satirist: Third summary of the same thought. Busy, busy, busy. End at 'next fire'.
mythmaker: The story told around the next fire is a lovely rhyme. The last lines over-explain slightly.

modeler: A strong summation that keeps the balancing side: most patterns go to ground. Growth isn't promised.
