habit: A scripted opening line said aloud: a tiny, startable ritual. 'Real, and partial' is worth repeating.
contemplative: 'Real, and partial,' said aloud. A good breath before the cards. The last sentence can soften.
stress: 'Real and partial' is the right humility ritual. It repeats U0955, so consolidate the two.
gamedesigner: A spoken ritual is a small move, which is nice. It's still mostly framing, with no feedback attached.
structural: 'Real and partial' is honest, but it repeats U0955. Merge them.
satirist: A spoken incantation before reading. That's the sacred costume again; label it a reminder, or cut. 'Real and partial' is the keeper.
mythmaker: 'Real, and partial' is a good vow, and the Boundary returns here with some weight. The rhyme is working.

modeler: 'Real and partial' is the bounded-observer stance. It sets the right epistemics without overclaiming.
skeptic: 'Real, and partial' is good calibration language. It says loosely how loose to hold the reading, though not what would make it wrong.
clinician: 'Real, and partial' is defusion done right: take it seriously, hold it loosely. A great line to say before reading.
habit: The italic line is sayable. The last sentence drifts back into abstraction; cut it.
contemplative: "Real, and partial" is a good breath before reading. The last sentence decorates. Stop after "hold loosely."
stress: 'Real, and it is partial' is the right humility. It repeats U0955 almost verbatim. Pick one place to say it.
gamedesigner: Nice calibration line, real but partial. Pure reminder though, no move or signal. Could be folded into U0955.
structural: 'Real and partial' is good epistemic hygiene. It doesn't touch who benefits from anything.
satirist: 'Real, and it is partial' is fine. Reciting it aloud is the costume showing. Make it a reading note, not an incantation.
mythmaker: 'Real, and partial' is a decent mantra, but it's said to nobody. Show the moment someone needs it, mid-reading, tempted to believe too hard.

modeler: Real but partial is honest model humility. Come back when a card feels too right is a good guard.
skeptic: 'Come back whenever a card starts to feel too right.' This is my fluency check, built into the practice. Excellent.
clinician: 'Real and partial' is a very good guard against a card feeling too right. Tells the reader what to do when it happens.
habit: Real cue: 'whenever a card starts to feel too right.' Trigger plus a phrase to say. This is a habit.
contemplative: 'Real, and partial' is kind and honest. 'Whenever a card feels too right' is a practice I can keep.
stress: Guard against over-trusting a card: 'when it feels too right.' Nice, a built-in warning on confirmation bias.
gamedesigner: Real-but-partial is a good check on overconfidence, with a trigger: when a card feels too right. Clear mid-game cue.
satirist: 'Real and partial' is honest, and 'when a card feels too right' is the best warning in the book.
mythmaker: 'Real and partial' is a good, earned caution. 'Whenever a card starts to feel too right' is exactly the moment to need it.
structural: Holding readings loosely is good epistemics, but it also licenses inaction. 'Real and partial' fits any outcome.

modeler: Plain operating instructions, with each ring's scale defined. Does the work.
skeptic: Clear procedure. The definitions of the four rings are useful. The last sentence is redundant.
clinician: Clear procedural steps and plain gloss for each ring. It works as instructions.
habit: A clear procedure: what each ring reads for. Runnable. The last sentence about priority can go.
contemplative: Clear instructions, a little long. The last sentence about priority is a worry the reader never had. Remove it.
stress: Clear procedure. Repeats U0962; trim the duplicated ring descriptions.
gamedesigner: Clear rules for each ring. Repeats the layout chapter a bit. Lose the restated nesting.
structural: The Culture ring is 'beyond any group you could name', so structure is a mood here, not a mechanism. Name institutions.
satirist: Workable instructions that repeat Chapter 3. Trim the restatement.
mythmaker: Procedure written as a Kin litany. Who is asking? Name one conundrum and walk it through.

modeler: Same question asked at four scales is a decent scale check. But nothing says what actually links one ring to the next.
skeptic: Clear procedure, and 'no extra weight' to the first card is a real anchoring guard. I approve of it.
clinician: Clear procedure and good no-extra-weight rule. 'What is happening in me' needs a time limit, or it turns into rumination.
habit: One question at four scales: a real rep. But four ring names before breakfast? Give me the plain-language version of each ring inline.
contemplative: The one question asked at four scales is lovely. The four Kin names fog it. Use plain words first: me, us two, the group, the culture.
stress: Clean procedure. 'No extra weight to the first card' is a real check against primacy bias. Still tarot until it says what would count as a miss.
gamedesigner: Controller in hand: one question, four scales, clear layout. Ring names lean on Chapter 3, but the question teaches them.
structural: Clear procedure, but 'culture beyond any group' is asked as a mood. No rule, no owner, no lever. Name who sets the culture-level terms.
satirist: Four Kin cards in Chapter 3 order: the costume shows. The four plain questions underneath carry it. Lead with them.
mythmaker: Four scales, one question: a solid frame. But the cards have no hands on them. Walk one real worry through all four rings.

modeler: The Mondays example walks all four scales. Giving the first card no extra weight blocks false first-cause reasoning.
skeptic: The Mondays example is concrete. 'Give the first card no extra weight' is a real anchoring correction. Good.
clinician: Dreading Mondays is concrete and relatable, and the rings spread responsibility across the system. Giving the first card no extra weight is wise.
habit: The Monday-dread example makes this runnable tomorrow. Exactly the kind of worked case I want.
contemplative: Dreading Mondays makes the rings real. The kin labels in parentheses clutter it. Trust the plain words: me, us two, the group.
stress: The Monday example is concrete and familiar. 'No extra weight' to the first card blocks anchoring. Good.
gamedesigner: The dreading-Mondays example is the level I wanted. Instructions plus a worked run. Strong.
structural: The Monday dread runs up to work culture, which is good. Then it stops at noticing. Add: who sets the workload, and who could you raise it with?
satirist: Dreading Mondays carries the whole method, and 'no extra weight' to the first card is sensible. Strong.
mythmaker: Dreading Mondays, the manager, the team: finally a protagonist. Walk me through what each card says to that person.

modeler: Strong. Different scales can run opposite trends at once, and that's the payoff of multi-scale sensing. Keep the example.
skeptic: Good: it resists forcing coherence, which is the mind's favourite trick. The run-on wants trimming.
clinician: Mixed states aren't contradictions, which helps an anxious mind. The Tending/Fraying jargon blurs it; give a human example.
habit: Useful permission: disagreement between rings is the data. Saves readers from forcing a single story.
contemplative: 'Not a contradiction to resolve' is a gentle teaching. The second half restates it with Tending/Fraying jargon. Halve it.
stress: Disagreement between scales as information. A real idea that survives contradiction instead of hiding it.
gamedesigner: Good rule: disagreement between rings is the data. Show it as a quick example readout.
structural: Letting scales disagree is the figure-and-ground insight. It works abstractly, but no example points to a lever.
satirist: A real idea: disagreement between scales is data, not error. One concrete scenario would land it.
mythmaker: A good idea, that disagreement is information, but Tending and Fraying stay abstract. Show the person thriving while their team frays.

modeler: Intriguing, but it reads as a riddle until the next section explains it. A header shouldn't need decoding.
skeptic: A clear enough teaser.
clinician: An opaque epigraph. Nothing lands for a reader yet.
habit: Means nothing until you've read the chapter. Make the epigraph say what the spread is for.
contemplative: Intriguing, but a little clever. I don't yet know what 'made of' means. It's fine as a hook, nothing more.
stress: Cryptic until the chapter explains it. Earns nothing on its own.
gamedesigner: Strong hook: only two cards, then derive the rest. I want to play this.
structural: A cryptic epigraph. It means nothing until you've read the catalogue.
satirist: A teaser, not a thought.
mythmaker: Cryptic in a way that doesn't invite you in. 'Everything they're made of' needs a human hook.

modeler: Building up from the bottom, my favourite move. As an epigraph it promises a mechanism without showing one.
skeptic: Readable, but 'followed all the way up' promises a chain of causes it hasn't shown yet.
clinician: Tidy summary of the spread, but it gives the reader nothing to do or feel.
habit: Pretty, but 'the large thing you took as given' means nothing until I've done the spread. Name one example.
contemplative: Cryptic before the reader has the spread. 'Followed all the way up' means nothing yet. Give the reader an image, not a riddle.
stress: Readable, but it promises a climb with no risk attached. Just a teaser. Tell me what the climb costs.
gamedesigner: Good hook line, small to large. It promises a climb but gives no move yet.
structural: Tracing personal habit up to the 'given' is the right instinct. An epigraph offers no lever, but it frames the spread honestly.
satirist: Nice upward reach, but 'the large thing you took as given' is a riddle until you name one.
mythmaker: Nice upward pull. 'The large thing you took as given' stays vague; name one, like the rent or the divorce rate.

modeler: Emergence from the local rule upward, and it implicates the reader. Exactly the direction I want.
skeptic: A memorable reversal: the 'given' has your hands in it. Fluent, and it promises a discovery before any evidence is checked.
clinician: 'Your hands in it' could land as blame at 3 a.m. Add 'alongside others' hands' to keep it shared.
habit: 'Your hands in it' stings in a good way. A strong epigraph.
contemplative: "Your hands in it" lands. "Climb" and "two cards about you" need the chapter first. Too much is packed into one line.
stress: 'Your hands in it' is a strong idea about owning your part. 'Climb' is opaque before the reader knows the spread.
gamedesigner: Great hook: your hands in 'just how things are'. It promises a reveal I want to earn.
structural: 'Your hands in it' is a fair correction to fatalism. It risks pinning structure on the reader, though. Name the other hands too.
satirist: 'Your hands in it' has a little sting. That's a good one, and it promises a real payoff.
mythmaker: 'Your hands in it' is a real image with a sting of complicity. Zuko-grade self-recognition in one line.

modeler: Now we're talking: figures composed of each other, walkable. This is the build-up-from-local-rule idea. Earned.
skeptic: Self-congratulatory ('unlike any other deck'). 'Composition can be walked' means nothing yet. Cut the throat-clearing.
clinician: Insider excitement about deck mechanics. The reader needs to know why this helps them, not what makes the deck unique.
habit: Hype for the deck's uniqueness. Tell me when to use this, not why it's special. 'Large, rare questions' is the only usable bit.
contemplative: The author admires his own deck here. Say what it does, not how unlike other decks it is.
stress: 'Unlike any other deck': the author admiring his own invention. Show the difference, don't announce it.
gamedesigner: Hype with jargon ('composition can be walked'). Show the walk instead of announcing it.
structural: Insider excitement about deck mechanics. It's a selling point for the deck, not for the reader.
satirist: 'The composition can be walked' sounds like a hushed-voice claim. Say how in one plain line.
mythmaker: It promises the deck's special trick, but it sells instead of showing.

modeler: 'Built from something you do' is the right claim: a local rule makes the global form. It says when to use the spread, but not how.
skeptic: Givens built from what you do is a real idea. 'Made of each other' is asserted rather than shown.
clinician: 'Built from something you do' risks self-blame on a bad day. Add 'built partly, and not your fault.'
habit: 'Built from something you do' lands. Still no cue for when to reach for it. What does a large, rare question sound like?
contemplative: 'Something you treat as just how things are' could be built from what you do. That stays with me. Short, and true.
stress: The idea that what you take as given may be something you're doing is a real itch. 'Figures made of each other' is jargon that hides it.
gamedesigner: Sets the stakes for a rare boss fight. Still a cutscene. Hand me one sample question right here.
structural: Built-from-what-you-do is a decent s-frame hook. 'Made of each other' is jargon, and it never asks who else is doing the building.
satirist: 'Figures made of each other.' Busy, busy, busy. Give one example of a given thing built from a habit.
mythmaker: Big promise, but 'figures made of each other' is fog. Show one thing you'd call fate turning out to be your habit.

modeler: Bigger figures built from smaller ones is Do-Plants-Know-Math logic. 'Every team I join' hooks well.
skeptic: 'Every team I join' is a sharp, personal hook. 'Might turn out' is properly hedged.
clinician: 'Alongside everyone doing it with you' properly softens self-blame. 'Bigger figures made of smaller ones' needs a plainer gloss.
habit: The team question is gold. The second sentence is fog. Keep the question and cut the deck theory.
contemplative: The team question is a real one. The last sentence turns abstract and loses me. Say "small patterns build big ones" and stop.
stress: 'Every team I join ends up the same' is a real, uncomfortable question. Reserving the spread for rare questions shows restraint.
gamedesigner: 'Every team I join' is a sharp, relatable entry question. The last sentence goes abstract. Fine.
structural: 'Alongside everyone doing it with you' is figure and ground done right. It still needs one collective lever.
satirist: 'Why does every team I join end up the same?' hooks anyone. The last sentence drifts into deck mysticism; trim it.
mythmaker: 'Why does every team I join end up the same?' is a haunting question with a face behind it. The deck-mechanics sentence goes limp afterward.

modeler: Crisp contrast: draw twice, derive the rest. Good.
skeptic: A crisp contrast. Fine.
clinician: A clear contrast sentence, nothing more.
habit: A clear contrast, and it's redundant. Fold into U0985.
contemplative: Clear, and a useful bridge. Two short sentences do the job.
stress: Clean contrast line. Fine as setup.
gamedesigner: Crisp contrast, quick to read. Fine as a transition.
structural: Clear contrast, but procedural only.
satirist: A clean contrast. It's a transition, nothing more.
mythmaker: A clear contrast in one breath. Serviceable.

modeler: Clear contrast: two draws, then derive the rest. Works as a quick instruction.
skeptic: A plain transition. It does its job and adds nothing beyond that.
clinician: Plain contrast, but it's only a transition.
habit: Clear contrast, clear count: two cards. Fine as a signpost.
contemplative: A clear contrast, plainly said. It does its one job. Nothing to live here, only a direction.
stress: Clear contrast, does its job as a pointer. No stakes, no claim.
gamedesigner: Clean contrast with the earlier spread, but it's pure rules text. Could fold into U0986.
structural: Pure mechanics, contrasting it with another spread. Clear, but it does nothing for anyone outside the card table.
satirist: Clear procedural bridge, nothing more. Fine as connective tissue. Could fold into the next line.
mythmaker: A clean bridge with no heartbeat. That's fine for a hinge line, but it earns nothing more.

modeler: Transitional contrast. Clear, but does no work on its own.
skeptic: Transitional and clear. It earns nothing more.
clinician: A plain procedural contrast. Fine in place and nothing more.
habit: A transitional sentence that's clear and earns nothing. Merge it into the next passage.
contemplative: Mechanics only. It is clear, but it gives me nothing to live. Fold it into the next passage.
stress: Clear contrast with the Four-Point. Procedural, nothing to break.
gamedesigner: A transitional rule statement, clear but inert. Merge into U0983 or U0986.
structural: Plain mechanics. It's clear and earns nothing else.
satirist: Pure plumbing. Clear enough, but it could be one clause inside the next paragraph.
mythmaker: Pure stage directions. 'Rung by rung' wants a ladder you actually see someone climb.

modeler: Contrast with Four-Point is clear but it's a transition line. Little earned beyond orientation.
skeptic: Transitional contrast. Clear, but nothing to act on or believe yet.
clinician: Orientation line that only makes sense with the surrounding chapter. Jargon-dependent, and it tells me nothing a reader can do.
habit: Transition line only. Tells me the count, not what I do. Fold into the next step.
contemplative: Counting cards against other spreads. Procedure, not presence. Say what this reading is for.
stress: Bridging sentence only. Clear but carries no content of its own.
gamedesigner: Variant rules in one sentence: two cards, climb the rest. Reader hasn't learned Four-Point yet here. Sets up but gives no play.
satirist: Four-Point, two cards, rung by rung: a sentence made of the book's own vocabulary. Say what the reader actually does.
mythmaker: Procedural signpost. Understandable, but nothing to feel. It needs a sentence of why this version exists.
structural: Bookkeeping line about card counts. No claim about rules or levers. Cut or fold into the example.

modeler: Sampling with replacement, justified. 'Running at you' frames the second input properly. Clear and concrete.
skeptic: Concrete. But 'the pattern running at you' invites mind-reading the other person. Flag that this is a guess.
clinician: 'The pattern you run, the pattern running at you' is blame-neutral and two-sided. A healthy frame.
habit: Concrete step with a sharp frame: the pattern you run versus the one running at you. Good.
contemplative: 'The pattern you are running, and the pattern running at you.' Simple and true. I feel it.
stress: 'The pattern you run, and the one running at you.' Concrete and personal. Holds.
gamedesigner: 'The pattern you run vs. the one running at you' is a great personal frame. Clear draw rule.
structural: 'The pattern running at you' at least admits outside forces. It shrinks them to a single person or 'the situation'.
satirist: 'The pattern you run, and the one running at you' is a genuinely good frame. Plain and personal.
mythmaker: 'The pattern running at you' is a real antagonist at last. The mechanics around it still clog it up.

modeler: A stage direction. It's fine where it sits.
skeptic: Stage direction. Harmless.
clinician: A stage direction. Fine in place.
habit: A stage direction posing as a paragraph. Fine as a bold step label, doesn't need to stand alone.
contemplative: A breath between steps. Good.
stress: Stage direction. Fine.
gamedesigner: A good pacing beat. A pause button.
structural: A stage direction.
satirist: Stage direction. Fine as a bold line.
mythmaker: A dramatic pause that works as a beat. Fine.

modeler: 'Worked out, not dealt' is the plant-spiral lesson in five words. Keep it.
skeptic: Clear instruction. 'Worked out' implies more rigour than choosing from a catalogue gives.
clinician: Crisp instruction. It works as a hinge and earns little on its own.
habit: Bold, short, actionable. Stop drawing. I know exactly what to do with my hands.
contemplative: 'Worked out, not dealt.' Five words carry the whole method. This is beautiful, and it is enough.
stress: 'Worked out, not dealt' is crisp. It's an instruction, not an idea, and it gets the job done.
gamedesigner: Crisp rule callout. Duplicates U0984, so keep one of them.
structural: A procedural bold line. Readable, and empty of any stake.
satirist: 'Worked out, not dealt' is crisp. A rule doing its job, nothing else.
mythmaker: A firm rule that reads clearly. It's only procedure; nobody's standing at the table.

modeler: Clean split between chance and derivation. Useful rule, but slight as a standalone.
skeptic: Separating chance from work is sensible discipline. It stops randomness doing the reasoning.
clinician: A clear stopping rule. 'The rest is yours to find' is empowering, not heavy. Works.
habit: A firm rule, but 'the rest is yours to find' doesn't tell me how. Point straight to the first check.
contemplative: "Chance has had its say, the rest is yours." This is quietly good. The bold shouts it, though, and it doesn't need to.
stress: It confines chance to two draws and puts the rest on you. A good design choice that cuts down the horoscope surface.
gamedesigner: Clear phase change from dealt to derived, a good rule. Bolded but it gives no move of its own. Merge with U0987.
structural: A procedural line with a nice turn of phrase. There's no substance beyond the rule.
satirist: 'Chance has had its say' is bold type for a procedural note. Unbold it; it isn't scripture.
mythmaker: 'Chance has had its say' has some rhythm to it. It's a clear rule, and that's about all it is.

modeler: Stop drawing; derive the rest by checking it's happening. Good discipline against fiction.
skeptic: Stopping the dealing and asking 'is it actually happening?' separates the dealt from the derived. Good discipline.
clinician: 'Then stop drawing' is a clear stopping rule that limits spirals. Good boundary and one question. Short and usable.
habit: Good stopping rule and one repeated question: is it actually happening? Single question, repeatable. Nice.
contemplative: 'Then stop drawing' is good. Then 'worked out, not dealt' and the rung question arrive too fast.
stress: Stops chance at two and demands 'is it actually happening?' at every rung. Reality check built into the procedure.
gamedesigner: Clean stop rule and a repeated question as the loop mechanic. Crisp. But it's short and relies on rules elsewhere.
satirist: Stop drawing, ask is it happening. Clear instruction that keeps chance from becoming oracle.
mythmaker: Chance has had its say: a crisp stop. Gives a clear rule. Why does stopping matter to the person drawing?
structural: 'Is it actually happening?' is a good evidentiary discipline, clearly stated. Narrow; it demands no rule or lever.

modeler: Stopping rule is sound: cards limit generation, rest is reasoned. 'Is this actually happening?' is a real reality check against runaway story-making.
skeptic: 'Is this actually happening?' is the right skeptical check, and stopping draws limits invention. Best line so far; wants a how-would-you-know method.
clinician: 'Is this actually happening?' is a grounding step, and 'cards cannot invent your life' curbs over-reading. Good, safe.
habit: 'At each rung, ask one thing first: is this actually happening?' One question, tightly cued. Exactly what I want. Keep it.
contemplative: 'Is this actually happening?' is the whole practice. Honest limit on the cards. Good; trim 'invent your life'.
stress: Strong: 'is this actually happening?' is the break-it test built in. Admits cards can't invent your life. Add what to do if the answer is no.
gamedesigner: Clear stop condition and a checkpoint question per rung. Good feedback hook: is this actually happening? Tight and playable.
structural: A reality check is practical and keeps the reader honest. Not a structural point, but it blocks invented stories.
satirist: Stop, then ask 'is this actually happening?' Best sentence in the set: a brake on the system's own pretensions. Plain and useful.
mythmaker: 'Is this actually happening?' is a good honest brake. Direct, but there's no face and no cost named.

modeler: A real composition rule, and it says 'no fusion' out loud, which I like. Heavy catalogue dependence makes it hard cold. Add one worked pair.
skeptic: Admitting most pairs don't fuse is good calibration. The catalogue mechanics are opaque without the catalogue at hand.
clinician: Catalogue lookup logic, dense. 'Making nothing together' is a kind reading; surface it more plainly.
habit: The lookup procedure is real, but the catalogue jargon buries it. Number the steps: look up, check present, record.
contemplative: 'Making nothing together, and that is the reading' is gentle wisdom. The catalogue mechanics around it are dense. Simplify the steps.
stress: Allowing a null result ('making nothing together') is honest. Prose is tangled; split it into steps.
gamedesigner: The lookup mechanic is buried in hedges. Lost the player. Use a worked example: these two cards fuse into this.
structural: Catalogue lookups that only make sense with the appendix open. Opaque to anyone outside the book.
satirist: Lookup-table liturgy. 'Making nothing together, and that is the reading' is the one keeper.
mythmaker: Catalogue lookups. 'Making nothing together' could hurt, if two named people stood in it.

modeler: Good that most pairs fuse into nothing. That's honest. Escalation is a reinforcing loop, so name what caps it.
skeptic: Letting 'fuse into nothing' count as a reading is honest, and so is checking it's happening. Catalogue jargon hides both.
clinician: 'Check it's actually happening' is a real reality test. Catalogue jargon buries it.
habit: 'Check it's actually happening' is the best rep here. The catalogue jargon buries it. Lead with the check.
contemplative: 'Most pairs fuse into nothing, and that is the reading' is wise. Catalogue jargon crowds it. The Sparks example helps, so lead with it.
stress: 'Most pairs fuse into nothing' is honest, and so is checking it's actually happening. Buried under catalogue jargon a newcomer can't parse.
gamedesigner: The 'check it is actually happening' step is real feedback. But catalogue fusing plus two new terms is a difficulty spike. Lost newcomers.
structural: The 'check it is actually happening' discipline is good. Catalogue-fusion jargon hides it; Escalation lands only for readers who already know the deck.
satirist: Two Sparks make Escalation: a concrete, checkable example. 'Most pairs fuse into nothing' is honest. Good.
mythmaker: 'You raising the stakes, them raising back.' Finally two faces. The catalogue jargon smothers them, so give them names and a fight.

modeler: Good evidence check. But Escalation is pure reinforcement. What caps it? Name the balancing side: exhaustion, an exit, a referee.
skeptic: 'Can you point to the last time' is exactly the evidence check I want. 'Most pairs list nothing' respects the base rates.
clinician: 'Can you point to the last time?' is a superb reality-check against rumination. Catalogue jargon buries it. Lead with the question.
habit: 'When did they last raise back?' is a perfect check. The catalogue and Kin jargon buries it. Lead with the question.
contemplative: "Can you point to the last time?" is the heart of it. The catalogue talk buries that heart. Lead with the checking.
stress: 'Can you point to the last time' is a real falsification check at every step. Letting 'nothing' count as an answer is honest. Strong.
gamedesigner: The 'point to the last time' check is an excellent feedback signal. But Spark, Escalation, catalogue and Dyad-Kin all at once is a difficulty spike.
structural: The evidence check ('the last time they raised back') is good. The catalogue jargon buries it.
satirist: The 'when did they last raise back?' check is excellent. It's buried under Spark, Escalation, Dyad-Kin and catalogue; the jargon fog loses lay readers.
mythmaker: 'You raise, they raise back' has blood in it, but the catalogue jargon smothers it. Keep the two people and lose the bookkeeping.

modeler: Is this actually happening? Escalation is a true reinforcing loop built from two local rules, and most pairs make nothing. Excellent.
skeptic: 'Can you point to the last time?' is the test I'd ask. 'Most pairs list nothing' admits null results. Good.
clinician: 'Can you point to the last time?' keeps readings evidence-based, and 'most pairs list nothing' is honest. Escalation example is concrete. Strong.
habit: One question, tested against a real moment: 'point to the last time.' Evidence check is the rep. Slightly long.
contemplative: The question is good: is this actually happening? But Spark, Escalation, catalogue and Dyad-Kin in one paragraph is too much.
stress: Strong: 'Most pairs list nothing... that is the reading.' The method can come back empty. That is falsifiability.
gamedesigner: Concrete walk-through with a test: can you point to the last time? That's a feedback signal. Names stack up (Spark, Escalation), spiking difficulty.
satirist: 'Can you point to the last time?' is the good test. Then Spark, Escalation, Dyad-Kin pile up. Cut a term.
mythmaker: You raise, they raise back, and 'can you point to the last time?' is a real test. Most pairs list nothing: honest. Good.
structural: Escalation test: point to the last time. Evidence-demanding and clear. Honest that most pairs make nothing. Still interpersonal; add an institution.

modeler: 'The choosing is the reading' puts a human judgment step into the derivation. That's honest. It needs an example to be followable.
skeptic: 'You know which pairing is present' is overconfident self-knowledge. Choosing introduces exactly the bias the draw was meant to bypass.
clinician: 'The choosing is the reading' is a good line buried in combinatorics. Simplify the mechanics.
habit: 'The choosing is the reading' is strong. The pairing mechanics are opaque. A worked example would rescue it.
contemplative: 'The choosing is the reading' is right. 'Paired with another that shares a Self-Kin' loses me. Show one worked example.
stress: 'The choosing is the reading' lets the reader pick the confirming answer. Add a check against motivated choice.
gamedesigner: 'The choosing is the reading' is real agency, but the combinatorics are opaque. Needs a diagram and an example.
structural: The derivation steps are hard to follow. Choosing the Culture link is where you'd name who writes the rules, and nobody gets named.
satirist: 'Most don't' is the only laugh in Part Six's machinery. The rest needs the catalogue open just to parse.
mythmaker: 'The choosing is the reading' is a strong turn. The ladder of Kin around it is lifeless. Lead with the choice.

modeler: Choosing a pairing you can point to is a real test. But the jargon (Rising Bar, Shared Pot, World-Kin) is too thick for a newcomer to follow.
skeptic: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story' is excellent. The rest drowns in figure names.
clinician: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story' is excellent. Its surroundings are dense.
habit: 'Pick the one you can point to' is gold. Too many named figures around it. Cut the examples to one.
contemplative: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story' is impeccable. Bury fewer names around it and cut the World-Kin aside.
stress: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story' is a good guard against the narrative fallacy. 'Most don't' is earned humility. Too much jargon.
gamedesigner: 'Pick the one you can point to' is great agency. Then five new figure names in one paragraph. Cut the examples to one.
structural: First-Arriver Lock-In and the Shared Pot are real structural shapes, buried in derivation rules. Name whose rules lock the first arriver in.
satirist: 'Pick the one you can point to' and 'Most don't' earn their keep. The Lock-In and Pot jargon pile-up buries them.
