modeler: Composition rule plus 'pick what you can point to' is solid. Catalogue jargon stacks up fast; one diagram would rescue it.
skeptic: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story' is excellent. It's buried under heavy jargon; simplify the derivation.
clinician: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story' is gold. The term stack (Dyad, Skein, First-Arriver) overwhelms lay readers.
habit: 'Pick the one you can point to' is the only rep in a wall of taxonomy. Cut the names and keep that rule.
contemplative: Too many names at once: Rising Bar, Lock-In, Culture-Kin. Yet "the choosing is the reading" shines. Keep that line, thin the rest.
stress: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story' is excellent. The catalogue jargon buries it. Simplify the names.
gamedesigner: 'The choosing is the reading' is great agency. But it piles on three new named figures in one paragraph. Lost the player. Slow it down.
structural: First-Arriver Lock-In is a real structural mechanism. 'The choosing is the reading' turns it back into introspection. And the jargon is thick.
satirist: First-Arriver Lock-In plus the Rising Bar: a system invented on page 3 now cited as authority. 'The choosing is the reading' is foma.
mythmaker: A thicket of capitalised figures. 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story' is the heart. Build the paragraph around it.

modeler: Composing figures upward is the right build-from-local-rules move, but the pairing jargon is thick. Walk one chain slowly.
skeptic: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story' is sound. But the pairing machinery is hard to follow.
clinician: Rule 'pick the one you can point to' is sound, but this is a dense jargon chain. Hard to follow on a bad day.
habit: Derivation steps are runnable, but jargon-heavy: Skein-Kin, Rising Bar, Lock-In. Too many names; give a plainer worked example.
contemplative: Pair, derive, name, choose, repeat. This is mechanism, not breath. 'Pick the one you can point to' is the only gem.
stress: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story.' Excellent. But the pairing chain is dense; trim.
gamedesigner: Choosing the pairing you can point to is real agency and a check. But three new terms in one paragraph; I lost the pattern.
satirist: Rising Bar, First-Arriver Lock-In, Skein-Kin: invented systems citing each other. 'Pick the one you can point to' is the only plain sentence.
mythmaker: Pick the one you can point to, not the one that suits the story: good rule. Too much pairing machinery; I'm lost in the kin.
structural: Climbs dyad to group to culture with First-Arriver Lock-In: a mechanism with winners. Insists on checking against life. Name who benefits.

modeler: Escalation joining Rising Bar into Lock-In is a real reinforcing structure, scale-climbing with choice. Kin-naming pile-up buries it; define fewer terms.
skeptic: Tells the reader to pick what they can point to, not the better story. That is my rule exactly. 'Only you know' overtrusts introspection, though.
clinician: 'Pick what you can point to, not the better story' guards against self-narrative. But dense naming overwhelms a tired reader.
habit: Real procedure: pair, choose what you can point to in your life. Good rule. But the kin jargon stacks up; trim to one example.
contemplative: Kin upon kin: the head is full before the heart is asked. 'Not the better story' is true. Lose the nesting.
stress: 'Not the one that makes the better story' guards against hindsight. Good. But the Kin vocabulary is a pile-up; trim terms.
gamedesigner: Real choice with a rule: pick what you can point to. But Dyad, Skein, Culture, World, Self all at once. Difficulty spike; stage it.
structural: Group-level patterns are the right scale. Prose is thick with kin-jargon. Show one real workplace lock-in and who set it.
satirist: Dyad-Kin, Skein-Kin, Culture-Kin: hyphenated virus. The 'pick what you can point to' rule saves it. Lead with that, drop two kins.
mythmaker: 'Pick the one you can point to, not the better story' is a real moral choice. Buried under kin-terms; unpack it.

modeler: Each depth accounts for the one below, so the big thing is assembled from small steps. That's the plant-spiral lesson exactly. Keep.
skeptic: 'Accounting for' claims a mechanism the lookup table can't establish. 'Seeing the steps' is how a story feels, not how evidence looks.
clinician: Watching something small become something 'given' can reduce shame about inherited patterns. Say that outright; it's currently abstract.
habit: Watching a small self pattern build into the 'given' world is compelling. The comparison prose is dense. Lead with that image.
contemplative: The last sentence is the heart: a small self-scale thing becoming the given world. The comparison before it is excess.
stress: Claims depth that 'accounts for' the level below. That's asserted, not shown. One worked example would test it.
gamedesigner: Payoff stated well: watching small become large, with the steps visible. Lead with this to motivate the hard rules.
structural: Watching a self-scale habit become something 'simply given' is the structural reveal I want. It stops before naming any lever.
satirist: The last sentence earns real wonder: the small thing becoming the 'given'. Cut the comparison preamble.
mythmaker: 'A small thing turns into a large thing you treated as given' is the heart of the book. It deserves a story, not a comparison table.

modeler: Each level made of the one below, and the Long Cycle supplies the balancing fall. That's real structure and you can follow every step.
skeptic: 'You see every step.' You see steps you chose. A derived chain is a story, not something you observed. Say so.
clinician: Vivid chain. Say plainly that seeing your step in it isn't blame, or the depressed reader will make it blame.
habit: The example ladder helps me see it. Still a revelation, not a rep. What do I write down at each rung?
contemplative: Watching a small push grow into what you took as given touches me. 'Long Cycle' arrives unexplained. Say rise and fall alone.
stress: Small moves building into a large given is a strong frame. But 'you see every step' smells like hindsight dressed up as derivation. Show me one that broke.
gamedesigner: The payoff beat finally lands: watching a small push grow into a given. The Long Cycle arrives unexplained, though.
structural: Small push to compounding lead to 'given' cycle is real s-frame insight. It stops at watching; 'who rewrote the rules' never comes up.
satirist: The chain from pushing a bit higher to the Long Cycle is followable. Name one real Long Cycle and it gets wonder.
mythmaker: Small to large, step by step: that's a real rhyme. 'Two people' still need faces, and so does the Long Cycle.

modeler: Local push grows into lock-in and then the Long Cycle, which rises and falls, so it has a balancing side. Each level made of the one below. Earned.
skeptic: 'Each made of the one below' claims a mechanism where correlation is likelier. The not-blame turn is humane. Add the uncertainty at each step.
clinician: 'Finding your own push is not blame' is exactly the right sentence. The jump to the Long Cycle is too abrupt to follow.
habit: 'Not blame, just where the chain begins' is kind and true. The Long Cycle leap loses me. Show one concrete step.
contemplative: "Not blame... where the chain begins" is gentle and wise. The Long Cycle arrives unexplained. Slow down and show one step plainly.
stress: 'Not blame, where the chain begins' is well judged. The jump from Lock-In to Long Cycle skips the check it just praised.
gamedesigner: The payoff beat is welcome, but the Long Cycle arrives unearned. Walk me through each step of the climb before the reveal.
structural: It describes cumulative advantage, then credits your push alone. Who wrote the field's rules that let the leader keep leading? Ask that.
satirist: 'Not blame, where the chain begins' is humane. The Long Cycle arrives unannounced, and the example skips a rung. Show the step.
mythmaker: You and a rival pushing higher, and 'not blame, where the chain begins': that's earned grace. 'Long Cycle' needs a face too.

modeler: Each depth made of the one below: real self-similar nesting with the rival loop. Your push at the bottom is honest.
skeptic: 'Every step is one you checked' is overconfident for a chain from rival to Long Cycle. Mechanism is asserted; the not-blame line helps.
clinician: 'Finding your own push is not blame. It is where the chain begins.' directly heads off self-blame. Careful and humane.
habit: Worked example lands, and 'finding your push at the bottom is not blame' resonates. But it's summary, not instruction.
contemplative: 'Not blame. It is simply where the chain begins' is kind. The climb of terms around it is not.
stress: Follow-the-example walk is concrete. 'Not blame' lands. Risk: tidy chain looks like hindsight, but each step is checked.
gamedesigner: Payoff beat: the chain rises from my own push to the Long Cycle. Felt progress, a rewarding reveal. Blame-free line lands.
satirist: Rival, push, lead, field-wide cycle: a chain a reader can follow. 'Not blame, just where the chain begins' is kind and true.
mythmaker: Finding your own push at the bottom is not blame, just where the chain begins. Earned and kind. The best line here.
structural: Rival escalation scaling to a field is a real structural story. 'Finding your push at bottom' risks i-frame, but 'not blame' helps.

modeler: It names where the work happens, the derivation steps. That's useful process guidance, not ceremony.
skeptic: Slowness as the point is defensible. But 'deciding honestly' assumes honesty is available on request. How would you check?
clinician: Honest pacing guidance. Slowness here guards against magical shortcuts.
habit: Tells me where the time goes and what a rushed reading skips. Useful pacing guidance.
contemplative: Slow on purpose. Honest pairing is the work. This teaches patience plainly.
stress: Says where the work actually is. Rushing kills it. A modest, useful claim.
gamedesigner: Tells me where the effort goes, which is useful. Add a check for telling a pairing is honestly real.
structural: A fair warning against rushing, but it's housekeeping.
satirist: An honest claim about where the work is. 'Ten minutes' is a nice concrete jab.
mythmaker: Honest instruction about slowness. It works.

modeler: 'Name where you've seen it running' is a proper check against what actually happens. Slow on purpose, and it says why.
skeptic: 'Name where you've actually seen it running' is a real evidence test. Good.
clinician: Good honest test: name where you've seen it running. It's concrete and checkable.
habit: 'Name where you've actually seen it running.' That's a test I can run. Give a time budget per step.
contemplative: Slowness as honesty, not ceremony. 'Name where you have actually seen it' is a test I can keep. Good.
stress: 'Name where you've actually seen it running' is a real falsification test. The slowness is justified, not ceremonial. Good.
gamedesigner: Best feedback signal in the spread: can you name where you've seen it running? Clear pass/fail.
structural: 'Name where you've seen it running' is a solid evidence test. Still private contemplation; the time spent goes nowhere collective.
satirist: 'Name where you have actually seen it running.' An honest test, said plainly. Keep.
mythmaker: 'Name where you've seen it running' is an honest test. A useful scold, though it has no image to carry it.

modeler: The observation test ('which table, which week?') is the right falsifier. Slowness justified by the work it does.
skeptic: 'If you can't, it's a story.' The best falsification test in the set. Keep it as written.
clinician: 'Which table, which week' is an evidence test that grounds the reader instead of feeding rumination. Strong.
habit: 'Which table, which week?' is a real test, and it's stated as one. Excellent.
contemplative: "At which table, in which week?" If you can't say, it's a story. Ruiz would nod. This is impeccable.
stress: 'Which table, which week? If you can't, it's a story.' This is the best stress test in the section. Keep it as written.
gamedesigner: Gives the test: which table, which week. That's a real feedback signal. Keep.
structural: 'Name the table, name the week' is solid falsification. It's an honest method, but it points at nothing to change.
satirist: 'At which table, in which week? If you can't, it's a story.' That's the Bryson test inside the book. Best paragraph here.
mythmaker: 'Which table, which week? If you can't, it's a story.' A sharp test. Give us one reader failing it.

modeler: Where did you see it running, which table, which week: good testability. Rushing skips the working part.
skeptic: 'Can you name where you've seen it, which table, which week? If not, it's a story.' Exactly the evidence standard. Keep.
clinician: Test of 'which table, which week' keeps reading grounded and warns against story-making. Practical. Slightly prescriptive about time.
habit: Strong test: which table, which week? Specific cue for honesty. Slowness warning is useful. Give a minimum time.
contemplative: Honest: if you cannot say where you saw it, it is a story. Practiced, plain. Slightly long.
stress: Best test yet: name the table and the week or it's a story. Failure is named. Rushing skips the work.
gamedesigner: Gives the pacing rule and a feedback test: where, which table, which week. Calls out skipping. Playtester-approved.
satirist: 'Which table, which week?' is a Bokonon test built into the method. If you can't, it's a story. Admirable.
mythmaker: 'Which table, which week?' makes the check concrete. Ten minutes skips the only part doing work. Honest, bracing.
structural: Demands naming where, which table, which week: anti-vibe discipline. Useful warning against stories. Personal and procedural; no lever.

modeler: A named limit on the recursion, with a stated stop condition. Rare and welcome. The last line is a good guardrail.
skeptic: A limit stated plainly, with a failure test. More of this, please.
clinician: A firm stop against cosmic storytelling, which guards against grandiosity. Good guardrail.
habit: A clean stopping rule. Clear, but it guards against cosmic storytelling, not a daily need.
contemplative: A clean limit, and 'telling a story about the universe' is a gentle, honest warning.
stress: A stated stopping rule against cosmic storytelling. Exactly the limit I want. Keep.
gamedesigner: Clear failure state: past World-Kin, you're storytelling. A good boundary marker.
structural: A plain limit on cosmic storytelling. Fine, and minor.
satirist: 'Started telling a story about the universe' is the costume admitting it's a costume. Good.
mythmaker: 'Started telling a story about the universe' is a sharp, funny limit. Good.

modeler: A limit that's named and enforced. Exactly what a loop should have. 'Come back down to the two cards' is a good reset.
skeptic: A stated limit against the grandiose story. Rare and welcome.
clinician: Strong guard against cosmic bypassing. 'Come back down to the two cards' is a grounding step.
habit: 'Come back down to the two cards you drew.' A clean reset move. Good limit with an action attached.
contemplative: 'Come back down to the two cards you drew.' A gentle return, plainly stated. The Boundary sentence repeats itself, so trim it.
stress: Best guardrail here: a stated stop against cosmic grandiosity. 'Come back down to the two cards' is humility with teeth.
gamedesigner: Clear boundary wall and a clear 'return to start'. It's a rule I accept, not one I play.
structural: A sensible guard against cosmic storytelling. A metaphysical limit, not a structural one; no reader acts differently because of it.
satirist: Bokonon would approve: it admits where the story about the universe starts. 'Come back down' is good.
mythmaker: A good boundary, and 'Come back down to the two cards' lands. Still a lecture; show someone overreaching.

modeler: A named limit on the recursion. A chain that knows where it stops is rarer than it should be.
skeptic: A plain limit on overreach. Calling a cosmic explanation a story is exactly right.
clinician: Good brake on grandiose spiralling: come back down to your two cards. A safe ceiling.
habit: A clear guardrail with a clear return move. Fine. It doesn't need the second sentence.
contemplative: "Come back down to the two cards" is good blending. Its middle repeats what the Boundary passage already said.
stress: A system that names its own ceiling and says to come back down. That is the opposite of a theory of everything. Respect.
gamedesigner: A good boundary, and 'come back down' is a clear fail-state reset. Short and playable.
structural: Good: it blocks cosmic overreach and sends the reader back down. It's a sound limit with no lever.
satirist: A system that tells you when you're bullshitting about the universe. Bokonon would approve. Plain and needed.
mythmaker: An honest limit, plainly said. 'Come back down to the two cards' is a good homecoming beat.

modeler: A stop rule at the boundary prevents explaining the universe. Good limit, stated plainly.
skeptic: Names the failure mode, explaining why the universe is as it is, and sends you back. Calibrated limit.
clinician: Clear stop rule: if you start explaining the universe, come back to the two cards. Prevents rumination spirals. Safe.
habit: Clear boundary and a redirect: come back to the two cards. Good, though it's mostly a warning.
contemplative: A good plain limit. 'Come back down to the two cards' is warm. Little else for me to do.
stress: Hard stop at the World-Kin; grandiose drift gets named as leaving the practice. Good fence.
gamedesigner: Clear boundary rule with a recovery move: come back down to your two cards. Good guardrail, brief.
satirist: Fences off cosmic storytelling by name. A system that polices its own pomposity. Rare and good.
mythmaker: A clear stop with a clear tell: you've started telling a story. Come back to the two cards. Disciplined.
structural: A limit that stops cosmic storytelling and sends you down to two cards. Sensible, though 'come back down' redirects to the personal.

modeler: A real question the reader will feel. It earns its place.
skeptic: The right question to ask before claiming another's mind. Epley would approve of the doubt in it.
clinician: A humble question to open with. Warm and consent-shaped.
habit: One good question, worth asking before any advice. Bungay Stanier would nod.
contemplative: A humble question to ask before helping anyone. It moves me.
stress: A good humble question to open on.
gamedesigner: A question aimed straight at the reader. Good hook.
structural: A humane question, and it lands. It's interpersonal only.
satirist: A real question that a person might actually ask. Works as an epigraph.
mythmaker: A question asked to someone's face. Tender and true.

modeler: Short, humane check on the reader before the reading. Does its job as an epigraph.
skeptic: Asking the question Epley would ask before presuming another mind. Short and earned.
clinician: Lovely. It's empathy before interpretation, exactly what dissolves shame.
habit: One question, carried before every reading. Exactly what I want. Keep it.
contemplative: Understanding before speaking. This is love's other name, asked as a question. Keep it exactly as it is.
stress: Humble question asked before you act. Small and true. I'll take it.
gamedesigner: Nice self-check question for the reader. It works as a gate before drawing.
structural: Humility before reading someone else. Interpersonal decency only, and easy to grasp.
satirist: A humble question that survives the bar. Works.
mythmaker: The reader asks it of a friend, and the doubt is warm. One line that earns its place.

modeler: Humane check before reading for someone. Personal, not mechanical.
skeptic: Epley would approve: it questions how well you know another mind before acting. It needs a follow-up on how to check.
clinician: An empathy check before helping someone else. Brown would approve. A short, usable question.
habit: One question, asked before acting. Bungay Stanier would frame it.
contemplative: Understanding is love's other name. This line lives it. Keep it exactly as it is.
stress: A humble question to ask before reading for someone else. Small, and it earns its place.
gamedesigner: Fine as a section epigraph, but I get no hint what to check to know I understand them. Pair it with a signal.
structural: A decent humility check for whoever reads for someone else. It's interpersonal and small.
satirist: A humble question to ask before reading someone else's cards. Plain, decent, and it survives the bar.
mythmaker: A reader caring for someone else before acting: Iroh pouring tea. Lovely.

modeler: Checks understanding before reading: nice human gesture. No mechanism and no concrete payload.
skeptic: Checking whether you understand the other person first respects Epley's point about misjudging minds. Short and usable.
clinician: Caring check before giving a reading is good practice. A single line with no step of its own.
habit: One question, said before acting. Perfect size. Tells me what to say before helping a friend.
contemplative: Do I understand you well enough? Understanding is love's other name. It asks me to listen. Small and true.
stress: Nice check on the helper's own ego. But it's an epigraph; it asserts no test.
gamedesigner: Good ritual question before reading someone else's cards. Short, usable consent check. Epigraph only.
satirist: A real sentence a friend could say. Human, short, a pause before advice. Nice.
mythmaker: Asking whether you understand someone before drawing for them is a good human moment, but it's only one line.
structural: Warm epigraph, one line. Interpersonal courtesy; no rules, no levers. Pleasant, not earned for structural work.

modeler: Reader-check before reading is a feedback step, nice. But a single line; what does the answer change? No loop shown.
skeptic: Self-doubt in the reader's voice is rare and welcome. As a line it's tiny and doesn't say how anyone would check understanding.
clinician: Check for understanding before advice: empathy first, as Brown would. Short and safe. Fine as a facilitator line.
habit: One question, asked before advice. That's the anti-Advice-Monster move. Add when the reader asks it, and of whom.
contemplative: Understanding is love's other name. Asking first is exactly right. Beautiful and small.
stress: Humble: the reader asks whether they understand before acting. That's skin. Short and clear. Needs a way to find out the answer is no.
gamedesigner: Nice check-in line, creates consent and a feedback beat. But it's a bare epigraph; show what 'understand' looks like.
structural: Humble framing, personal. But understanding the person is the individual frame again. Understand the room too.
satirist: The reader asks permission before pronouncing. Humble, human, actionable. Rare moment of the book doubting itself.
mythmaker: A reader with a voice at last, asking permission to read someone. Intimate, but I want the answer back.

modeler: A cross-reference sentence. Fold it into the next paragraph.
skeptic: A cross-reference, clear and inert.
clinician: Bookkeeping cross-reference. Merge it into the next paragraph.
habit: Pure cross-reference. Cut it or make it a parenthetical.
contemplative: Only a cross-reference. It does no work alone. Fold it into the next paragraph or cut it.
stress: Pure cross-reference. Cut or merge into U0994.
gamedesigner: Pure cross-reference, no move. Cut it, or merge it into the next paragraph.
structural: A cross-reference sentence with no content. Fold it into the next paragraph.
satirist: A cross-reference posing as insight. Cut it, or merge it into the next paragraph.
mythmaker: Pure cross-reference. Cut it, or fold it into the next paragraph.

modeler: An actual feedback loop: output, response, adjusted next output. The response folds into the next card. Mechanism, not metaphor. Trim the preamble.
skeptic: Practical, but folding answers back until it 'sounds like theirs' is the cold-reading method. Name the Barnum risk outright.
clinician: Check whether it lands, actually wait, and use their words. That's real empathic technique. Trim the length.
habit: Best instruction in the Weaving section: one card, ask, wait, fold their words in. It's twice as long as it needs to be.
contemplative: Deep listening made into a method, beautifully. But 'the one thing this chapter most needs you to actually do rather than skim past' is fear. Cut it.
stress: Solid listening technique. Admit it is also how cold reading works: specificity comes from them, not the cards.
gamedesigner: A real feedback loop: reveal, ask, wait, fold the answer in. The best mechanic here. Trim the self-importance at the start.
structural: Real listening technique, clearly told. It's long, and dyadic intimacy is all it offers.
satirist: The best technique in Part Six, buried under 'the one thing this chapter most needs.' Lead with the instruction.
mythmaker: Real craft: wait for the answer and fold their words in. It's long, though. Trim the 'this chapter most needs' throat-clearing.

modeler: A miss counts as signal, the error term feeds the next pass. Good. Drop the Gardener tag at the end.
skeptic: Valuing misses is good. But 'feels more specific' is the very sensation cold readers produce. Feeling it isn't validating it.
clinician: 'Let a miss be as useful as a hit' takes pressure off reader and listener alike. Shame-free.
habit: A miss counts as much as a hit. The cure for the Advice Monster, applied. Keep, and trim the Gardener tag.
contemplative: A miss is as useful as a hit. This is understanding as love. It's a little long, but it earns its place.
stress: 'A miss is as useful as a hit' means nothing can fail. Name what a bad reading looks like.
gamedesigner: Explicit success signal: by the last card the reading sounds more like them. Misses count as data. Great design.
structural: Treating misses as information is good practice. It solves a reading's problem, not a real one.
satirist: A miss is as useful as a hit: true and practical. The 'Gardener's pattern' tag at the end adds nothing.
mythmaker: A miss is as useful as a hit. A reading that grows into the other person's language. That's a relationship. Keep.

modeler: Cliché. Replace it with the real mechanism: an unauthored object lowers the social cost of disagreeing.
skeptic: A cliché epigraph, and groups also err together. Compared to what?
clinician: A cliche epigraph. Harmless, earns little.
habit: A cliché epigraph. Replace it with the real insight: nobody authored the card, so disagreeing costs nothing.
contemplative: Plain, near cliché. It serves, barely.
stress: Cliché. Replace it with the U0997 insight.
gamedesigner: A cliché epigraph that adds nothing. Replace it with the 'nobody authored the card' idea.
structural: A cliché epigraph. Replace it with the external-object point below.
satirist: A cliché, and arithmetically underwhelming. Find a better line.
mythmaker: A cute line that says nothing a reader didn't already know.

modeler: No author means anyone can argue with it, so it gets corrected. Neat.
skeptic: Neat point: no author means no authority. Fluent, and for once that fluency has something under it.
clinician: Healthy anti-authority line. Fine as an epigraph.
habit: Nice permission line. No behaviour attached on its own. Works only as a doorway.
contemplative: Simple and freeing. It gives the room permission to disagree. A little clever, but it serves.
stress: Sharp: having no author turns into permission to argue. It holds up as long as the group really does argue.
gamedesigner: Neat inversion: authorlessness invites argument. Sets up the disagreement mechanic well.
structural: Authorless means contestable: a nice line about legitimacy. I'd like it applied to rules people actually live under, not just cards.
satirist: Dry and true. Authorless cards make arguable cards. A good line.
mythmaker: Neat democratic idea. Clever more than moving, and nobody's arguing on the page.

modeler: Real social mechanism: a neutral third object lowers the cost of face, so more dissent flows. Nice.
skeptic: A plausible social mechanism: an external object lowers the cost of disagreeing. Worth testing. Crisp.
clinician: Externalizing the problem lowers shame in a room. A smart, compact insight.
habit: A sharp insight into group dynamics. Pair it with one line on how to use that safety tonight.
contemplative: A true and kind insight about saving face. A little clever in its turn, but it serves the group.
stress: A sharp read on group dynamics: an author-less card lowers the cost of disagreeing. Real insight.
gamedesigner: Smart insight: the card as a neutral third player takes the face cost out of disagreeing. Plays well in groups.
structural: A real mechanism: a third object lets a group dispute safely. That's institutional design in miniature, and I respect it.
satirist: Genuinely witty and genuinely true: the card as a face-saving third party. This explains why the thing works at all.
mythmaker: Sharp social insight, and it solves a real room problem. I'd love one scene of the face that was saved.

modeler: Excellent. It names the flow it changes: disagreement cost drops because nobody authored the card. Specific, testable.
skeptic: Plausible mechanism: an object no one wrote lowers the social cost of dissent. It's unsupported, so say 'probably' and it's good.
clinician: Sharp point: an object nobody authored makes disagreement socially cheap. Real group-dynamics insight.
habit: Sharp mechanism: an external object lowers the social cost of disagreeing. That's real group design. Keep.
contemplative: Insightful: a card nobody authored makes disagreement cost nothing. That is gentle social design. Keep it.
stress: An object nobody authored makes disagreement cheap. A specific, testable mechanism. Strong.
gamedesigner: A sharp insight: an external object makes disagreement socially free. This is the real reason for the mechanic. Keep.
structural: Finally a mechanism: an object nobody authored lowers the social cost of disagreement. That's a design lever any group can pull.
satirist: Real mechanism: nobody authored the card, so disagreeing with it is cheap. This is a Bryson-grade insight.
mythmaker: An object nobody authored makes disagreeing free. A genuinely smart social insight. Keep.

modeler: Clear placement in the session. Functional.
skeptic: Procedure dense with in-house names. A newcomer can't follow the sequence.
clinician: A usable structure, but it assumes you know the Group Practice rounds. Name them briefly.
habit: Places the step in a sequence, but assumes I remember three named rounds. Recap them inline in a few words.
contemplative: Usable only if you remember Part Two's rounds. Name the steps simply, or point to them in one word.
stress: Procedure leaning on jargon from elsewhere. Spell out the steps or point to them cleanly.
gamedesigner: Assumes I remember three Group Practice rounds. Onboarding gap. Restate them in one line.
structural: It names rituals from elsewhere in the book and gives no reason for them. It reads as filler between better passages.
satirist: Four proper nouns in one sentence. Usable only by someone holding Part Two open.
mythmaker: A procedural splice that leans on Part Two vocabulary. Necessary, and dry.

modeler: Drawing last, onto the room's own words, is a sensible order. Plain procedure.
skeptic: Drawing last, after people have spoken, cuts down on cards steering talk. Sensible order.
clinician: Clear structure, and drawing last protects people's own words. It's usable.
habit: Sequenced, timed, placed: draw last. That's a real protocol a group can run Thursday.
contemplative: Usable, but Seven Iterations and leverage points assume too much. The last line is warm: the room's own words to land on.
stress: Sensible sequencing: the draw comes last so it lands on real words. Plain and usable.
gamedesigner: Sensible structure, but 'as usual' and 'Seven Iterations' assume a tutorial I may have skipped. Add a one-line recap.
structural: Drawing for the shared situation instead of one person is the right frame shift. The group gets a concrete structure, though leverage stays vague.
satirist: Seven Iterations, leverage points, Four-Point: three systems invented earlier, cited like scripture. The idea of drawing last is good.
mythmaker: A practical structure, and 'the room's own words' is lovely. The room has no people in it yet.

modeler: A clear procedure, with loop and leverage point named per person. Drawing last so the cards land on the room's words is smart.
skeptic: The structure is usable, but 'Seven Iterations' and 'leverage point' assume earlier chapters. 'Drawn last' is a smart ordering choice.
clinician: A workable structure, but 'Seven Iterations' and 'leverage point' assume prior chapters. One plain sentence of recap would fix it.
habit: A real sequence: what to do and when ('before the close'). Usable.
contemplative: Seven Iterations and leverage points come in a rush. "The room's own words to land on" is lovely. Lead with the room.
stress: Drawing last, so the cards land on the room's own words, is smart sequencing. 'Seven Iterations' needs a gloss.
gamedesigner: Clear session structure with good sequencing, cards drawn last. The Seven Iterations goes unexplained here; a one-clause gloss would help.
structural: Drawing for the shared situation, with each person naming a leverage point. That's collective by design. Good.
satirist: The Seven Iterations show up undefined, plus leverage points. The 'drawn last' logic is smart, but a newcomer needs a gloss.
mythmaker: Procedure piled on jargon: Seven Iterations, leverage point. 'The room's own words' is the only warm bit. Lead with it.

modeler: Sequencing: room's words first, cards last. Sensible, and the group becomes the stock the card lands on.
skeptic: Sensible order: the room speaks first, cards land on their words. Reduces anchoring on the card.
clinician: Clear sequence: room speaks first, cards come last, on a shared situation not a person. Protects individuals from being singled out.
habit: Clear sequence: round, then one Weaving before close. Concrete timing. Leans on jargon like Seven Iterations.
contemplative: 'Let the room speak first' is wise. Seven Iterations, loops and leverage points bury it. Say it simply.
stress: Sensible sequence: room speaks first, cards after. But 'Seven Iterations' and 'leverage point' assume earlier chapters.
gamedesigner: Clear turn order: room speaks first, cards land last. Good session structure. Seven Iterations assumes prior onboarding.
satirist: Room speaks first, cards land last. Sensible sequencing. Seven Iterations name is a mouthful but it's explained inline.
mythmaker: Cards land on the room's own words. Good logic, clear order. Needs a room: whose team, what shared problem?
structural: Group names loops and small leverage points, then a shared card. Real collective step. Good. Add that shared situations carry rules and owners.

modeler: Good sequencing: group's own words as input, cards drawn last, about the shared situation. A small feedback structure that works. Concrete and runnable.
skeptic: Drawing for the shared situation, not a person, avoids reading minds. Concrete and sensible; 'cards land on the room's words' is asserted.
clinician: Drawing for the shared situation, not for any person, avoids targeting someone. Clear, concrete structure. Jargon a bit heavy.
habit: Real structure with sequence and a timing cue: before the close. Great. But many named terms; shrink to the three-step version.
contemplative: Letting the room speak first is wise. Seven Iterations and Four-Point Weaving crowd it. Say it as a family would.
stress: Real sequence: room speaks first, cards come after, about the shared situation. Sound design. Too many capitalised terms for a stranger.
gamedesigner: Clear turn order, and drawing last is smart pacing. Group has goals, steps and a target. Needs a signal for done.
structural: Best here: a shared situation, the room speaking first, a leverage point per person. Group practice, not solo reflection.
satirist: Real steps, real situations: deadlines, chores. Drawing last so cards land on the room's words is smart. Seven Iterations is costume but explained.
mythmaker: Useful facilitation, procedural. 'Cards land on the room's own words' is the live bit; give me one group's moment.

modeler: Distributing the reading prevents one voice capturing it. Practical rules for odd group sizes too. Solid.
skeptic: Distributing the voices prevents one interpreter capturing the room. A sensible, concrete safeguard.
clinician: Distributed voice keeps one person from owning the reading. Clear, practical rules for odd group sizes.
habit: Clear rules for every group size, and the reason fits in one line. Runnable tonight.
contemplative: Practical and fair. 'One person's interpretation with the group in attendance' is a fine, true warning.
stress: Practical guard against one voice capturing the reading. Good design.
gamedesigner: Good turn-taking rules with edge cases for group size handled. The 'one voice' failure is well caught.
structural: Spreading interpretation so no one voice owns it is a real anti-capture rule for groups. It's concrete and usable.
satirist: Practical logistics with a good reason: one voice turns a reading into a lecture.
mythmaker: 'One person's interpretation with the group in attendance' is a knife of a line. Practical too.

modeler: Spreading the reading out so one voice doesn't take over is real design. The closing jab at the usual talker lands.
skeptic: Spreading the reading voices guards against one interpretation taking over. 'That voice is yours' lands.
clinician: 'If you usually talk, that voice is yours' names a behavior without shaming. Good.
habit: Role assignment with edge cases, and 'if you usually talk, that voice is yours.' Ouch. Good.
contemplative: 'If you are the one who usually talks, that voice is yours.' It names the ego gently. Practical and kind.
stress: Built against ego. 'If you usually talk, that voice is yours' names who pays. Excellent.
gamedesigner: Real turn-taking rules with edge cases handled. 'If you usually talk, that voice is yours' hits hard.
structural: Real anti-capture mechanism: no single voice narrates. It names who usually dominates. A governance rule a group can actually adopt.
satirist: 'If you are the one who usually talks, that voice is yours.' A sharp aim at the room's real problem. Keep.
mythmaker: 'If you are the one who usually talks, that voice is yours.' That's a Beard moment, a gentle accusation. Works.

modeler: Attribution to structure rather than an individual, which is Meadows' core point. 'Practice versus tribunal' lands.
skeptic: A strong rule against scapegoating. 'The entire difference between a practice and a tribunal' is earned here.
clinician: Protects the person a card 'obviously fits' from being made the scapegoat. Practice, not tribunal. Exactly right.
habit: A crucial guardrail: the group's pattern, never a member's. 'Practice versus tribunal' sticks. Keep.
contemplative: This protects the vulnerable. Practice, not tribunal. 'Second Pass' jargon dims it. Say plainly: look at what we all do.
stress: 'A practice or a tribunal.' A real failure mode, named with a real guard. Keep.
gamedesigner: A strong safety rule: a card fits one person, so it's at risk. 'Practice vs tribunal' sticks. Gloss 'Second Pass'.
structural: Excellent figure and ground: ask what the group does that keeps one person's pattern easy. That's anti-scapegoating with teeth.
satirist: 'Practice versus tribunal' is a strong, plain distinction. It solves a real group-harm problem.
mythmaker: Practice versus tribunal. Everyone has watched a room turn on one person. Real stakes, and fair to the accused.

modeler: Several independent checkers make the error signal stronger. Good, but it largely repeats U0995.
skeptic: Several people checking at once can also be conformity at once. Add a guard against groupthink, such as dissent stated first.
clinician: Welcomes disagreement and gives a step: say what it isn't. Good.
habit: 'Say what it isn't, out loud' is a concrete move. Good.
contemplative: 'Good.' I like the blending here. It repeats U0995's idea, though. Keep it short.
stress: Opening with 'Good.' immunises the card again. Useful step, but say when the deck itself is the problem.
gamedesigner: 'Good.' Disagreement becomes input for the next ring. Clean feedback rule.
structural: It says the same as U0995. Trim it.
satirist: 'Good.' is a nice beat. It largely repeats U0995 at group scale. Fine.
mythmaker: 'Good.' is a nice beat, but it repeats U0995 nearly word for word. Trim the echo.

modeler: A miss is an error signal that reshapes the next ring. That's a balancing loop with several checkers. Good.
skeptic: Treating a miss as data and saying it before the explaining-away starts is exactly right.
clinician: Disagreement is welcomed and given a concrete move. That's safe for the dissenter.
habit: Say what it isn't, out loud, before anyone explains it away. Concrete conversational rule. Works.
contemplative: 'Good.' It blends with the force instead of clashing with it. Saying what it isn't before explaining it away is real practice.
stress: Saying the miss out loud before it's explained away is good. 'Misses tell as much as hits' is close to unfalsifiable. Watch it.
gamedesigner: Turns a miss into a scoring event. Say what it isn't before explaining it away. Plays beautifully.
structural: Dissent spoken before the explaining-away is a usable group norm. Small, but it is a lever.
satirist: 'Good.' is the right first word. Saying what it isn't before anyone explains it away is a usable rule.
mythmaker: It welcomes dissent, which is good. Let us hear one person say 'that's not me' and watch the next ring change.

modeler: A miss treated as signal that reshapes the next ring is feedback done right. Good concrete script.
skeptic: Disconfirmation said aloud before anyone explains it away. That is calibration in practice, and good.
clinician: Welcomes the miss and has people say it out loud. Healthy group process, clearly given.
habit: Say what it isn't, out loud, before anyone explains it away. Great move with a concrete script.
contemplative: "Good." This meets force by blending. Saying aloud what it isn't is a practice I can use with family.
stress: It welcomes the miss and makes people say it before anyone explains it away. Disconfirmation built into the method. Good.
gamedesigner: Treating a miss as feedback is good design. Saying out loud what it isn't is a concrete move. Keep.
structural: Several people checking the card at once beats solo reading. It's a concrete rule for stopping people from explaining a miss away.
satirist: 'That's not us; we go quiet' is a real-sounding line, and it treats misses as data. Good group practice.
mythmaker: 'We don't compete, we go quiet.' A voice in the room! Disagreement treated as data is generous to the doubter. Works.

modeler: A miss is data: say what it isn't, aloud. That's testing and tweaking, Sellers-style. Good.
skeptic: Treats a miss as data and asks people to say what it isn't before explaining away. Good.
clinician: 'Good' on disagreement, plus a concrete script ('that's not us'). Gives permission to reject the card. Safe and actionable.
habit: Gives the exact script: say what it isn't, aloud, before explaining away. Real behaviour with an example line.
contemplative: 'Good. A miss tells the group something' is gentle. The example line is practiced. Lovely.
stress: A miss counts as data, and the example line is specific. Group names what it isn't. Good stress-test habit.
gamedesigner: A miss is data, and the move is to say what it isn't. Excellent feedback design with a sample line.
satirist: A miss is data, and the sample line 'we don't compete, we go quiet' shows how. Excellent.
mythmaker: 'That's not us; we don't compete, we go quiet.' Real voice in the room, and a miss that teaches. Good.
structural: Disagreement said aloud, checked by several people, reshapes the reading. Good group-level habit. 'We go quiet' still leaves rules unasked.

modeler: It closes the loop with a repeated action, so insight turns into a flow. 'A pleasant evening and nothing else' is right.
skeptic: Insisting on a repeated behaviour over insight is right. The last line is sharp.
clinician: One small thing each person will repeat, so insight gets a next step. Exactly what I want.
habit: 'Insight and no Local Rule has produced a pleasant evening.' That's my whole religion. One small repeatable seed each. Perfect.
contemplative: One small thing each person will repeat. Insight becomes practice. 'A pleasant evening and nothing else' is honest.
stress: 'A pleasant evening and nothing else.' Demands output. I like it.
gamedesigner: Ends with a commitment move. 'Pleasant evening and nothing else' is a great line about failure.
structural: 'A pleasant evening and nothing else' is the right jab. The seed is still a private habit; make it a shared commitment.
satirist: 'A pleasant evening and nothing else' is the right kind of cruelty. Keep it.
mythmaker: 'A pleasant evening and nothing else.' Wry and earned. A concrete seed. Works.

modeler: Insight with no Local Rule changes no flow, so it's right to ask for a seed. 'Pleasant evening and nothing else' stings.
skeptic: Demanding a behaviour rather than an insight is the right call. 'Nothing else' slightly overstates it.
clinician: Exactly right: one small repeatable thing. Insight without a step gets called out.
habit: One small thing you'll repeat before next time. This is the whole book in a habit. Best close.
contemplative: One small thing you will actually repeat. This is the practice test passed. 'Pleasant evening and nothing else' is honest.
stress: 'Pleasant evening and nothing else' puts skin in it. Demanding one repeated action is the right test.
gamedesigner: The seed is a concrete exit quest. 'Pleasant evening and nothing else' is an honest fail state.
structural: Rightly damns insight with no action. But 'seed' is a private repeat; make it a shared commitment the group checks next time.
satirist: 'A pleasant evening and nothing else.' Finally a laugh, and it's aimed at the right target.
mythmaker: 'A pleasant evening and nothing else' stings nicely. Show us the seed. What did someone actually promise?

modeler: Sensor, not controller, said cleanly. Fine header.
skeptic: A correct slogan. It works only if the section beneath it delivers, and it does.
clinician: A crisp principle line that sets up the cautions.
habit: Clean and memorable epigraph.
contemplative: Five words that guard against misuse. Impeccable.
stress: Right stance, compressed. Fine epigraph.
gamedesigner: A clean, memorable rule. Works.
structural: Clean, but a standard disclaimer.
satirist: A clear motto with zero surprise. Acceptable as a header.
mythmaker: Crisp. It carries the chapter's thesis.

modeler: Fine slogan, but it says nothing new. The thermometer passage later does this job better.
skeptic: Tidy slogan. The next section has to back it up, and it does.
clinician: Hands agency back cleanly. It works as a refrain.
habit: Tidy slogan. Fine as an epigraph; doesn't hand me a rep.
contemplative: Four words, two sentences, complete. It returns judgment to the person. Nothing to remove.
stress: Short, puts agency back where it belongs. Does its job as an epigraph.
gamedesigner: Clear motto, but it restates what's elsewhere. It's filler between sections.
structural: Puts agency with you. That's fine, but it's i-frame: 'you decide' alone, never together.
satirist: Fortune-cookie tidy. True, but the next paragraphs say it better. Cut or sharpen.
mythmaker: A tidy maxim with no blood in it. It works as a hinge but won't haunt anyone.

modeler: Clear rule, but it repeats the thermometer passage. One of the two could go.
skeptic: A slogan. It's correct, and the next units do the real work. Fine as an epigraph, and it earns little.
clinician: Puts agency back in the reader's hands. A clean, protective line.
habit: Crisp, but it's a slogan. It works only if a later line tells me what to do when I catch myself deferring.
contemplative: Short, firm, and kind. Nothing to remove.
stress: Sets the authority line plainly. Short and useful.
gamedesigner: Clean slogan, but it repeats U1013. One of them can go.
structural: Keeps the agency with the reader. Clear, but it's just a slogan.
satirist: Blunt and correct. It's the sentence every horoscope should be legally required to print.
mythmaker: Clear and firm. It's a slogan, though, and it'll need a scene later to earn its weight.

modeler: Describe, don't command. Short guard against obeying the model. Practical.
skeptic: Right guardrail: cards describe, you decide. Concise. Slightly slogan-like, but it constrains.
clinician: Reader keeps authority over the card. 'Set it down' is a clear, small action. Strong safety line.
habit: A usable rule: if you catch yourself obeying a card, set it down. Cue is the catch. Good.
contemplative: Three short sentences I could live by. 'Set it down' is lovely. Nothing extra.
stress: Short, blunt guard: if you obey the card, put it down. Sound, though thin on how to tell.
gamedesigner: Strong guardrail, short, memorable: if obeying, set it down. A rule, no feedback loop but a clear signal.
satirist: Cards describe, you decide, set one down if obeying it. Perfect anti-virus clause.
mythmaker: Cards describe, you decide: set it down if you catch yourself obeying. A good guard against the oracle.
structural: Healthy anti-obedience line. Clear. But decision stays with the individual; no collective lever.

modeler: Throat-clearing. Cut it, or fold it into the first caution.
skeptic: A preamble. Could be cut without loss.
clinician: A throat-clearing transition. Could go.
habit: Throat-clearing. Go straight to the cautions.
contemplative: A throat-clearing sentence. Begin with the cautions themselves.
stress: Honest preamble. Short enough.
gamedesigner: Throat-clearing. Cut it and go straight to the cautions.
structural: Throat-clearing before the cautions.
satirist: Throat-clearing. Cut it and start with the cautions.
mythmaker: The idea that insight tools double as avoidance tools is good, but it's stated flatly. Show someone hiding behind a card.

modeler: Hiding behind a card is a recognisable failure. A clean lead-in to the cautions.
skeptic: 'Draw, nod, and never face it' names a real avoidance move. Good set-up.
clinician: Honest about avoidance via cards. It needs the one step that follows.
habit: 'Draw, nod, and never face it' stings because I'd do it. No counter-move given here, though.
contemplative: 'Draw, nod, and never face the thing.' I recognize myself in that. The opening clause about cautions is extra.
stress: 'Draw, nod, and never face it' is the honest failure named up front. Good self-suspicion.
gamedesigner: 'Draw, nod, and never face it' names a real exploit players will use. Good warning hook.
structural: It admits the cards can be an alibi for avoiding things. Honest, and only a preamble.
satirist: 'Hidden behind as easily as looked through' is plain and sharp. Draw, nod, never face it: recognisable.
mythmaker: 'Draw, nod, and never face the thing' is a real flinch I recognise. Good.

modeler: Honest about the avoidance failure mode. Short setup line.
skeptic: Honest about avoidance: 'draw, nod, and never face it.' It names the reader's likely self-deception.
clinician: Names avoidance honestly but stops there. Give one sign that you're hiding behind the card.
habit: 'Draw, nod, never face it' names the failure honestly. Give me one tripwire for catching it.
contemplative: "Hidden behind as easily as looked through" is honest self-knowledge. The second sentence is only a bridge. It could go.
stress: Honest about how the tool fails, which I value. As a setup line it does no work of its own.
gamedesigner: 'Draw, nod, never face it' is recognisable. Give me a tell that I'm hiding, so I can catch it.
structural: It admits the practice can become an alibi, and that admission is exactly the right worry. Now say what to do instead.
satirist: 'Draw, nod, and never face it' catches the reader's own dodge. Honest. Keep.
mythmaker: 'Draw, nod, and never face the thing' is a real flinch I recognise. A good setup for the cautions.

modeler: A nod that costs nothing is a sharp tell for a loop with no feedback. Hidden behind versus looked through works.
skeptic: 'A nod that costs you nothing' names the exact failure of confirmation. Honest about the tool's misuse.
clinician: Names a real risk, the nod that costs nothing, and offers a tell. Honest. Slightly points inward at the reader but not shaming.
habit: 'A nod that costs you nothing' is a precise tell. Self-check cue. Name the follow-up question to ask.
contemplative: 'A nod that costs you nothing' is a precise warning. I would keep it as it is.
stress: 'A nod that costs you nothing' is the tell. Names fragile comfort, precisely. Wish it said how to check.
gamedesigner: Names the failure mode: nodding that costs nothing. A tell I can self-check. Sharp playtest note.
satirist: A nod that costs nothing: the tell. Sharp and sly, a little rueful. Wish more of the book sounded like this.
mythmaker: 'A nod that costs you nothing' is the tell I'd pay for. Sharp and self-aware.
structural: Warns the nod that costs nothing: exactly the alibi I hunt. Names how the device can excuse inaction. Strong, clear.

modeler: Present tense, not future. Clear, though it's said elsewhere already. Keep it short.
skeptic: Description over prediction is well drawn. The Spark example makes it concrete.
clinician: Describes, never predicts. That guards an anxious reader against dread-by-card. Solid.
habit: Clear 'describe, not predict' rule. Turn it into a habit: ask 'where is this running right now?'
contemplative: Present tense, not future tense. Clear. The 'category error' line scolds. Let it go.
stress: Good anti-prophecy line, but 'describes' can't be wrong either. Say how a description could fail.
gamedesigner: Present tense, not future, with the Spark as an example. Clear. Drop the 'book already warned' callback.
structural: Present tense, not prophecy. Necessary, but obvious.
satirist: Present tense, not future: the honest line every divination book skips. Good.
mythmaker: 'The Spark doesn't mean a fire is coming' is clear and useful. A little preachy at the end.

modeler: Confirmation is not accuracy. A real failure mode, plainly named. Good.
skeptic: A flicker of recognition isn't accuracy: Kahneman's point, well applied. The best caution in the section.
clinician: Fair point, but 'the useful one is uncomfortable' can lure a depressed reader toward self-punishing readings. Add a brake.
habit: True and stings. Give the check: before drawing, write what you already believe, then compare.
contemplative: A flicker of recognition is not truth. This is Ruiz's warning about assumptions. Well said.
stress: Recognition is not accuracy. The book confronting its own main weakness. Keep.
gamedesigner: Names the flicker-of-recognition trap and gives a signal: useful readings feel uncomfortable. Strong.
structural: Confirmation bias, honestly applied to its own tool. Useful for the reader, and private.
satirist: The flicker of recognition is not evidence. Plain, true, bar-proof.
mythmaker: The flicker of recognition versus the uncomfortable card. Everyone has felt that satisfying nod. Keep.

modeler: A sound guard against excusing harm, but the Fold, Held Silence and Slow Hand references assume a lot. Say the rule first.
skeptic: An important ethical guard buried under Held Silence, the Slow Hand and the Fold. Say it in plain words first.
clinician: Rightly forbids using cards to accuse others or excuse harm. Named figures obscure it; spell out the behaviors.
habit: Important ethics, but leans on Fold and figure names I may not remember. State the stop rule plainly up front.
contemplative: An important guard against excusing harm, but you need to know four named figures and the Fold first. Say the principle plainly first.
stress: A necessary ethical brake. Pin it to one concrete misuse scenario.
gamedesigner: Important ethics, but it leans on Fold, Held Silence and Slow Hand together. Needs a plain-language stop rule up front.
structural: It refuses 'how things are done here' as an excuse for harm. Good, but say who benefits from that excuse.
satirist: Right ethics, but it's a jungle of names (Fold, Held Silence, Slow Hand). Say 'cards don't excuse harm' first.
mythmaker: An important guardrail, but Held Silence and the Slow Hand are names without faces here. Ground it in one harm excused.

modeler: A needed guardrail against using cards to excuse harm. Clear and specific.
skeptic: Refuses to treat a card as evidence of guilt or as an excuse. Exactly what a skeptic wants.
clinician: Crucial safety. Cards never excuse harm. Setting them down is a clear action.
habit: Clear stop rule: set the cards down when they explain away harm. Concrete enough.
contemplative: The ethic is right and needed. The card names are opaque to a newcomer. Say the harm plainly and let the names follow.
stress: Bars the cards from excusing harm and names who benefits from the excuse. Concrete and necessary.
gamedesigner: Important safety rule, but Held Silence, Slow Hand and the Fold stack jargon. Lead with the plain rule.
structural: Finally asks who profits: 'just how things are done here' serves the harmer. Add a lever: report it, organize, refuse.
satirist: A necessary guardrail, plainly put. Held Silence, Slow Hand and the Fold are three proper nouns for one warning.
mythmaker: A colleague's cruelty and the excuse that serves the cruel. Finally real stakes, handled with moral courage.

modeler: Needed guardrail: a card is neither evidence nor pardon. Concrete examples make it stick.
skeptic: 'A card is not evidence' says it outright. It is a strong guard against using the reading to excuse harm.
clinician: The most important safety passage here: cards never excuse harm. Clear, protective, and it gives a step: set them down.
habit: The 'set them down' trigger is right. The card names and the Fold reference make it hard to parse quickly.
contemplative: This protects people from harm and refuses the excuse. "Set them down" is right. Weighty, and needed.
stress: 'Not evidence, not a pardon': it names who benefits from the excuse. This is where a system takes real responsibility for its misuse. Keep.
gamedesigner: Important guardrail, but Held Silence, Slow Hand and the Fold all land at once. Make the point with plain examples.
structural: It catches the 'how things are done here' excuse and names who it serves. Then it prescribes examining yourself. Add: report it, organize, act.
satirist: 'Not evidence, not a pardon.' A serious guardrail, stated plainly. 'The Fold' is jargon, but the point survives it.
mythmaker: The colleague's cruelty gives this real stakes, and it refuses the cheap pardon. Strong moral spine.

modeler: Best paragraph here: complicated versus complex, defined by whether anything feeds back. And it admits the tool manufactures depth. Keep.
skeptic: 'The mind is very good at finding pattern in whatever it's handed.' Honest about the tool's own failure mode. Keep.
clinician: Complicated versus complex, with plain examples. It warns honestly against manufactured depth.
habit: Complicated versus complex, with plain examples like a broken appliance. Prevents wasted readings. Strong.
contemplative: A tax problem, a broken appliance. Concrete and humbling. 'Manufacture depth' is the truest caution in the chapter.
stress: 'Can manufacture depth that was never there.' The author naming his tool's failure. Best in chapter.
gamedesigner: Tax problem, broken appliance: concrete examples of what not to bring. Honest about manufactured depth. Good.
structural: Complicated versus complex: it tells the reader when to put the tool down. A rare, honest, practical limit.
satirist: A tax problem, a broken appliance: finally, objects. 'Manufacture depth' is the book's most honest self-diagnosis.
mythmaker: Tax problem, broken appliance. Finally the mundane. 'Manufacture depth that was never there' is honest. Keep.

modeler: A gate test: does anything feed back into itself? 'Go fix the part' is exactly right. Keep.
skeptic: A real gate test before use. The final clause about acceleration is clutter; end at 'pile.'
clinician: 'Put the cards away and go fix the part.' A concrete gate, and it stops pattern-hunting rumination.
habit: A real cue and a single gate question: does anything feed back? If not, go fix the part. Excellent.
contemplative: 'Put the cards away and go fix the part.' Lovely. The final clause about acceleration is clutter. Cut it.
stress: A real gate: no feedback, no cards. Drop the final clause about acceleration.
gamedesigner: A real gate question before play: does anything feed back? Tutorial-perfect. Cut the last clause.

modeler: A neat self-reference line, close to Hofstadter's. It earns its place as a header.

modeler: The observer is left off the map. A nice nod toward Hofstadter, but light on mechanism.

modeler: A real self-reference point: the observer inside the system is missing from their own model. Tight.

satirist: Short, true, and lightly funny. An epigraph that earns its place.
mythmaker: A strong image. Bring the map-holder back later so it rhymes.

modeler: A model can't include its holder: Hofstadter-adjacent and true. Epigraph earns it.

clinician: Short and humble; reminds that no view includes the viewer. Nice, but gives no step.

gamedesigner: Tidy aphorism, the map can't show its holder. Cutscene line; no move.

mythmaker: No map shows the person holding it. Small and true. Hangs there with nothing to return to, but it sticks.

modeler: Self-reference done right: the map-holder is part of the system. Hofstadter would nod if the holder changed the reading. Show how.

clinician: Points the question to the self gently, no blame. Slightly risks self-focus, but the question is bounded and usable.

contemplative: The map never shows its holder. Quiet and true, and it asks me to look at myself. Nothing extra.

gamedesigner: Strong hook line, and it asks me to turn the lens on myself. One beat, no follow-up move or check.
structural: Whose rules, in one line. I'd frame it. Who drew your map, and who benefits? Add that and it has teeth.
satirist: Short, true, a little sly. Maps don't show their holder. Survives a bar. Nothing to do yet, but it points inward.
mythmaker: Lovely thought, and it asks who's holding it. A map-reader with something to lose; now give the reader a face.

modeler: Filler. Cut it.

modeler: Diagnostic, not prescriptive. It separates sensor from actuator. The last clause runs long, so trim it.

modeler: The thermometer analogy is apt: a sensor, not an actuator. It keeps the decision loop with the human.

modeler: Loop versus branching is the right structural distinction, and the open gap is named honestly. I respect that.

contemplative: An honest admission, but it is long and stays in the head. Two sentences would do: forks aren't loops, and no layout exists yet.

mythmaker: 'Take the job or stay' gives it a face. Admitting the gap is honest. 'Compare notes' is a charming image.

satirist: Bricks in a shape nobody will see finished. Lovely, close to Cathedral-builder talk. Works aloud.

modeler: Keeping time together has a real function, but which stock does it fill? Name what the shared rhythm builds up.

structural: Correctly treats synchronized occasions as coordination infrastructure. This is the collective mechanism I want named.
satirist: Real holidays, a real function claimed. Fine. 'No honest reason to leave that work undone' is a little self-serious.
mythmaker: A sweeping roll call of holidays, but no one sits at a single seder. Give me one table.

modeler: Synchronization as coordination work no daily practice can do is a real mechanism. Solid motivation.
skeptic: 'Widespread deserves to be taken seriously' is reasonable, but widespread is not proof that it works. State the function claimed and its evidence.
clinician: A respectful survey of traditions and a clear argument. Intellectual more than personal.
habit: The seder image is vivid. It argues the case but gives me nothing to do yet.
contemplative: The seder image is strong and respectful. The final sentence is a list of the book's own terms. End on "no daily practice can do alone."
stress: It checks the idea against the long record across traditions. That's the history test passed: a pattern, not an anecdote.
gamedesigner: The seder opens strong. Then the list of holidays and the jargon in the last line idle me. Ask the reader which occasion they return to.
structural: It argues that coordination does what private practice can't. That's the s-frame I want. Next, name what the gathered people should change.
satirist: The seder grounds it with real traditions named. The last line turns the book's own jargon into a duty. Busy, busy, busy.
mythmaker: The seder opening is vivid, then it drifts into a list and jargon. Stay at the one table, with one child asking.

modeler: Seder is a vivid synchronised-repetition case. The jump to the book's work is asserted, not shown.

clinician: Seder and other traditions make shared occasions feel familiar, and 'think of the one you return to' invites a small reflection. Warm and clear.
habit: Seder image and 'think of the one you return to' is a decent prompt. Rest argues; make that prompt the action.
contemplative: The seder child asking at a thousand tables is moving. The list of holidays and the last sentence are heavy.
stress: Real traditions, vivid seder. But 'widespread, so serious' is popularity, not proof. Also, the 'work no daily practice can do' claim is unsupported.
gamedesigner: Seder child asking the same questions is a great hook, and 'think of the one you return to' is a prompt. Good agency.
satirist: Seder, Vesak, Diwali: real occasions, not invented. Wonder is earned by a child asking at thousands of tables.
mythmaker: The child asking the same questions at thousands of tables: a face and a return. List of holidays is a bit flat.
structural: Many tables, same night: shared occasions as coordination, a collective mechanism. Seder is vivid. Don't forget who sets the calendars.

modeler: An honest refusal to fake an origin. Consistent and clear.

mythmaker: The grandmother's roast pan is perfect: a face, a habit and a lost reason. The jargon sentence after it dilutes it.

modeler: The roast pan nails a rule that outlives its reason, a delay with a stale goal. It admits hardening and points to checks.

gamedesigner: The roast pan is gold. 'Received World's Tending as a snare' is a difficulty spike right after it. Cut that line.

mythmaker: The grandmother's roast pan is a perfect image. 'Received World's Tending as a snare' clunks right after it. Trust the pan.

modeler: Backward versus forward is a real distinction: the pan example shows a loop outliving its purpose. Aimed, hardenable, honest.

clinician: Turning versus commemoration is clear, and the roast example is memorable. Forward-pointing, so not stuck in the past.
habit: Sharp definition and the grandmother's pan example is memorable. Still no action; where's my first Turning?
contemplative: The grandmother's pan is a tender, true image. The definition in bold is a mouthful. Let the roast speak.
stress: Sharp definition with the roast-end failure case. Admits a Turning can harden. A claim that can be wrong.
gamedesigner: Crisp definition, backward versus forward, with the grandmother's pan. Clear rule, good example. No action for me yet.
satirist: The roast-pan grandmother is a perfect little fact. Backward versus forward is a distinction you can use.
mythmaker: The grandmother's too-small pan and the cut roast: that's the human cost of a dead ritual. Backward versus forward, vividly.
structural: Forward-aimed shared occasion versus hardened commemoration. Grandmother's pan is sharp. Aimed at what, though, and who benefits?

modeler: A header. Fine.

mythmaker: The holiday you'd miss most is the right door in: a real loss, tested on your own life.

modeler: The real goods: synchrony opens the loop, and content decides what compounds. 'Content is load-bearing.' Too long, and the Tending jargon gets in the way.

clinician: 'Content is load-bearing' is a real insight, but the paragraph sprawls. Split it and cut the cross-references.
